5.document_title: Women's Health in New Zealand: Historical Perspectives, Disparities, and Community Activism from Colonial Times to the 21st Century
5.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines women's health in New Zealand from the 1800s to 2000s, analyzing health disparities across ethnic groups. It traces how European colonization introduced infectious diseases that devastated Māori populations while Pākehā women experienced improved health. Key findings reveal significant inequities: non-Māori women born in 2007 could expect to live 83 years versus 75.1 for Māori women. Maternal mortality for Māori women reached 23 per 1,000 live births in 1920, compared to 6.5 for Pākehā women. By the 2000s, major causes of death were cancer, cardiovascular disease, and respiratory disease, with Māori women experiencing cardiovascular disease at 4.2 times higher rates and diabetes mortality 10 times higher. Pacific Island women faced elevated mortality from heart disease, stroke, and diabetes, with 48% obesity rates. The document extensively covers health activism including the Young Māori Party (1889), Women's Christian Temperance Union, Te Puea Hērangi's medical clinics, the Family Planning Association (1936), the Māori Women's Welfare League (1951), and feminist health activism of the 1970s-1980s including the cervical cancer scandal. It highlights Māori-centered health models incorporating emotional, physical, whānau, and spiritual wellbeing that challenged mainstream healthcare approaches.

9.document_title: Child and Youth Health in New Zealand: Comprehensive Analysis of Health Disparities, Infectious Diseases, and Healthcare Services
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines child and youth health in New Zealand, documenting a significant decline from being a global leader to ranking in the bottom third of OECD countries by the early 21st century. Key health challenges include exceptionally high youth suicide rates (15.6 per 100,000, highest among OECD nations), elevated infant and child mortality, and substantial health disparities among Māori and Pacific children. Major health concerns encompass sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI), childhood obesity (12% overall, 30% for Pacific children), asthma (25% of children), and infectious diseases including meningococcal disease and rheumatic fever. The document traces infectious disease evolution from the 19th century through contemporary challenges, noting that while immunisation programmes have controlled many diseases, poverty-related conditions persist at higher rates than other OECD countries. Youth health issues include accidents (car crashes leading cause of unintentional injury deaths among 15-24 year-olds), sexual health concerns, substance use (57% of 15-17-year-olds and 86% of 18-24-year-olds consumed alcohol in 2014/15), and declining smoking rates (from 28% in 2000 to 6% in 2014). Health disparities are linked to socioeconomic factors including deprivation, inadequate housing, and income inequality. Primary health initiatives include Plunket (founded 1907), School Medical Service (established 1912), and modern integrated youth health centers. Major pediatric facilities include Starship Hospital (opened 1991) and Kidz First Children's Hospital (established 2000). New Zealand ranked 29 out of 30 OECD countries for child health and safety in 2009.

[Page 11] Improved indicators In the 21st century Māori wellbeing outcomes have improved across a number of social and economic indicators. 10.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the demographic history of Māori in New Zealand from pre-1840 through the early 21st century. [Page 12] The rapid reduction in Māori tuberculosis mortality between 1945 and 1961, in a period when medical treatments were not yet fully developed, was a triumph for public health in New Zealand. In the 1930s Dr Harold Turbott carried out a health survey among Māori on the East Coast, which showed high levels of conditions that usually accompanied tuberculosis poverty, malnutrition and overcrowded housing. The survey stimulated an attempt to reduce health inequalities between Māori and non Māori, focusing especially on tuberculosis. Health policy was synchronised with social policy following the passage of the Social Security Act 1938. Measures included taking chest X rays of 10% of Māori each year, sending people with tuberculosis to sanatoriums, and giving families of tuberculosis patients nutritional supplements, income support and top priority for state housing assistance. Men, women and life expectancy As well as a continuing increase in life expectancy there was a gender shift. Until 1945 Māori men had a greater life expectancy than women, although for some cohorts of men bursts of improvement in life expectancy were followed by periods when life expectancy decreased slightly. From 1951 this changed, reflecting the Pākehā pattern of women tending to live longer than men. In 1951 Māori life expectancy was 54 for men and 56 for women, and by 1961 it was 59 for men and 61 for women. In 1976 it was 63 for men and 68 for women, rising to 67 for men and 71 for women in 1996. Analysis of the life expectancy of particular birth cohorts suggests that Māori born in the early 1940s, especially men, were more likely to die by the time they reached their sixties than non Māori. The life expectancy gap between Māori and Pākehā narrowed considerably from the 1970s. However, in the 21st century Māori life expectancy was still below non Māori levels. In 2013 Māori men could expect to live to 73, compared with 80 for non Māori men. Māori women had a life expectancy of 77, compared with 84 for non Māori women. Disease trends and health policy Changing causes of death In the 21st century Māori and Pākehā faced similar health issues. There had been a shift in causes of death, from communicable to non communicable diseases. For both Pākehā and Māori, acute infectious, respiratory and diarrhoeal diseases and tuberculosis had given way to causes of death such as heart conditions, strokes and cancers. These chronic disorders, generally associated with old age, did occur in the past, but were more prominent in the 21st century because most people survived longer.

14.document_title: Death Rates and Life Expectancy in New Zealand: Pākehā and Māori Populations - Historical Trends and Policy Implications
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines death rates and life expectancy trends in New Zealand from the 18th century to the early 21st century, comparing Pākehā (European) and Māori populations. It traces the epidemiological transition from infectious diseases to lifestyle-related conditions. Pākehā settlers in the 19th century enjoyed higher life expectancy than Britain due to better living conditions, superior diet, high per-capita GDP, and dispersed settlements. Pākehā women became the first population worldwide to reach 55 years life expectancy in the late 1870s. Colonization devastated Māori populations through introduced European diseases (measles, tuberculosis, whooping cough) and poverty, reducing life expectancy to 23-25 years by 1891-1896. From the 1890s onward, Māori life expectancy gradually improved through better hygiene, state health interventions, and post-WWII urbanization. Key milestones include the 1913 smallpox containment, the 1921 establishment of the Division of Māori Hygiene, and major tuberculosis reduction efforts between 1945-1961. By 2013, non-Māori life expectancy reached 84 for women and 80 for men, while Māori achieved 77 and 73 respectively. An Oxfam report on inequality published in January this year drew media attention to the issue by pointing out that the world’s 85 richest people have as much wealth as its poorest 3.5 billion. That report followed on from work by the World Economic Forum that reported widening income disparities as the second greatest worldwide risk in the next 12 to 18 months. Since the 1987 Immigration Act, New Zealand has become one of the most ethnically diverse nations with 213 ethnic groups. Auckland, hosting 40% of ethnic migrants, is now more diverse than Sydney, London, or Los Angeles, with Asian populations at 23% expected to overtake Maori as the largest ethnic minority by the 2020s. The document explores how diversity has manifested geographically through 'ethnoburbs' and ethnic precincts, exemplified by Northcote's transformation into an 80% Asian business district. New Zealand faces significant demographic challenges: single-person households have risen from one in ten to one in four, family structures have fundamentally shifted, and urban growth is heavily concentrated in major cities while many regional areas face permanent decline. Examples include Waiouru declining from 1,647 to 738 residents between 2001-2013, and Ruapehu District declining 12% since 2006. Rising income inequality grew faster than most OECD countries between 1985-2008, with the top 10% earning nine times more than the bottom 10%. Urban spatial segregation is increasing, with wealthy residents moving to city centers while lower-income populations are pushed to peripheries, creating housing affordability crises. The analysis contrasts compact urban intensification versus greenfield sprawl approaches. New Zealand's attitudes toward Asian immigration have warmed significantly since the 1990s, though challenges including stereotyping and workplace discrimination persist. Resilience across New Zealand's diverse communities will be essential for navigating the future.

23.document_title: How the 1918 flu spread
23.document_summary: This article examines the 1918 influenza pandemic that infected 500 million people and killed 50-100 million globally. The mortality rates varied significantly by location—Tasmania experienced less than 0.1% mortality while Western Samoa saw 22%. Research by New Zealand and Australian scientists identifies key factors explaining these disparities: prior exposure to non-lethal flu viruses, social isolation, and ethnic immune system differences. Māori populations were 10 times more likely to die than Pākehā, attributed to higher poverty rates and crowded living conditions. Interestingly, Māori experienced equal mortality between genders, unlike other populations. In Samoa, the virus spread fastest among the highest social classes due to cultural practices where people gathered around sick chiefs. The article notes that bacterial pneumonia, not influenza itself, was the primary cause of death—a condition now treatable with antibiotics. Modern global interconnectedness makes such widespread mortality unlikely to recur.

24.document_title: The Pursuit of Happiness: Science, Neuroscience, and the Path to Wellbeing
24.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores happiness through scientific research, neuroscience, and personal narratives. Key findings reveal that genetics account for 60-80% of happiness differences, while the happiness formula (H=S+C+V) incorporates set points, circumstances, and voluntary activities. Margaret Heaney's story as a lottery winner demonstrates that money provides security only up to approximately $10,000 annually, with diminishing returns beyond that. The "hedonic treadmill" concept explains how people quickly adapt to improvements without lasting satisfaction. Neuroscience research shows the left prefrontal cortex processes positive emotions while the right processes depression. True happiness emerges from relationships, meaningful work, helping others, gratitude, mindfulness, and present-moment awareness rather than material accumulation. Key concepts include flow states, the importance of pursuing goals over achieving them, and how accepting life's randomness can be liberating. The collection challenges the "positive thinking" movement, demonstrating that happiness is relative—lottery winners and individuals with disabilities often reach similar happiness levels through different paths. Ultimately, happiness is not a commodity but a state cultivated through meaningful relationships, autonomy, fulfilling work, and personal growth.

25.document_title: State of Mind: Mental Health in New Zealand - Treatment, Recovery, and Brain Research
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores mental health in New Zealand through multiple perspectives. It examines the rising prevalence of mental illness, now the third-highest cause of ill health, and follows personal accounts including Gemma's journey through suicidal ideation, anxiety, eating disorders, depression, PTSD, and OCD. Key statistics reveal that one in five New Zealanders sought help for mood or anxiety disorders in 2017, with diagnoses increasing from 10.4% to 16.7%. Treatment challenges are addressed, noting that antidepressants don't work for everyone—the STAR*D trial showed only one-third achieve remission with their first medication. The piece contrasts traditional hospital-based care with modern community-based alternatives like Kotuku House and Te Whare Mahana, which provide peer-support environments and therapeutic interventions such as dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). It emphasizes that psychotherapy is as effective as antidepressants for mild to moderate depression, yet medication remains more accessible due to cost barriers. The document advocates for better public awareness, person-centric services, integrated treatment approaches, and reducing stigma surrounding mental illness.

34.document_title: Health Minister Shane Reti Scraps Hawke's Bay Ethnicity-Based Healthcare Policy
34.document_summary: Health Minister Dr Shane Reti intervened to remove ethnicity-based eligibility criteria from a Hawke's Bay healthcare policy targeting young Māori and Pasifika people aged 14-24 for free GP and nurse services. The decision reflects the broader debate over addressing health inequities versus race-based service allocation, highlighting tensions between equity-focused healthcare approaches and the current government's policy direction on service eligibility criteria.

35.document_title: Māori Students in Medical Admissions Scheme Show Higher Graduation Rates
35.document_summary: Research published in The New Zealand Medical Journal demonstrates that Māori and Pacific students participating in the Māori and Pacific Admissions Scheme (MAPAS) at the University of Auckland graduate at significantly higher rates than other Māori and Pacific students. Established in 1972, MAPAS provides comprehensive support including a foundation programme (Hikitia te Ora), academic assistance, pastoral care, and cultural support throughout students' degrees. Dr Rhys Jones reports that MAPAS students achieve pass and graduation rates 15-23 percentage points higher than average. The programme addresses critical health workforce inequities, as only 5.1% of medical practitioners are Māori and 2.4% are Pacific people—far below population representation. Pro-equity programmes like MAPAS are essential for producing a culturally competent health workforce that can better serve underserved communities and address persistent health inequities in Aotearoa New Zealand.

36.text:
[Page 2] approached for comment. The health inequities between Māori and Pasifika communities and Pākehā were well known. Non Māori had a life expectancy seven years greater than Māori. Under the previous Labour government, Te Whatu Ora Health New Zealand introduced an Equity Adjustor Score, which aimed to reduce inequity in the system by using an algorithm to prioritise patients according to clinical priority, time spent on the waitlist, geographic location (isolated areas), ethnicity and deprivation level. Some health officials argued ethnicity was just one of five factors considered in deciding when a person gets surgery, and that it was an important step in addressing poor health outcomes within Māori and Pacific populations. Reti, then National's health spokesman in opposition, was highly critical of the tool even as he acknowledged long standing inequities. "While there has been historical inequity that has disadvantaged Māori and Pasifika people, the idea that any government would deliberately rank ethnicities for priority for surgery is offensive, wrong and should halt immediately," he said in June last year. "The way to improve Māori and Pasifika health is through better housing, education and addressing the cost of living, not by disadvantaging others." 39.document_summary: A Health and Disability Commissioner report analyzing 1,800 complaints from disabled people between 2023-2025 reveals systemic barriers in New Zealand's health system. 40.document_summary: Rural New Zealand faces a critical healthcare crisis with patients dying from preventable causes due to inadequate medical services and severe resource constraints. Despite rural communities producing 80% of New Zealand's export earnings, they experience significantly higher mortality rates, limited access to healthcare facilities, and acute doctor shortages. Surgeon Vanessa Blair highlights systemic failures within the healthcare system, including cases of misdiagnosis and preventable deaths at rural hospitals lacking adequate staffing levels. Research demonstrates that rural residents experience twice the preventable disease mortality compared to urban counterparts, elevated suicide rates, and poor access to specialist services. Rural hospitals such as Taupō operate at approximately half their required staffing levels, exacerbating the healthcare equity gap. While the government has introduced workforce initiatives including accommodation allowances, locum funding, and relocation programs to attract healthcare professionals to rural areas, healthcare experts argue these measures are insufficient without substantial increases in central government funding and systemic healthcare reforms.

41.document_title: Pharmac and Te Tiriti: Changes Labelled 'Performative', Some Question Relevance
41.document_summary: Health Minister David Seymour has directed Pharmac to remove Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations from its decision-making, instead focusing on data-driven health outcomes. The directive is supported by Pharmac board chair Paula Bennett and patient advocate Malcolm Mulholland, who argue this approach will better serve all New Zealanders including Māori. However, former Māori Health Authority clinical lead Dr Rawiri McKree Jansen criticizes the move as "performative," noting that Māori miss out on approximately one million prescriptions annually due to inequitable healthcare access. Jansen contends Pharmac should focus on optimizing medicine utilization rather than removing equity considerations. Seymour's letter also directs Pharmac to consider broader fiscal impacts of funding decisions, such as preventing costly interventions. Bennett emphasizes the change won't disadvantage Māori and maintains focus on delivering medicines for all New Zealanders. The directive also requires improved transparency and timeliness reporting from Pharmac.

42.text:
[Page 1] Cure Kids says a new study shows Pasifika children in Aotearoa are 115 times more likely to be hospitalised with acute rheumatic fever than European children. The fourth State of Child Health Report showed Pasifika, Māori and children in low socio economic areas were disproportionately affected by respiratory conditions, rheumatic fever and heart disease, skin infections, dental disease and mental health problems. Cure Kids head Frances Soutter said urgent national action was needed to ensure all tamariki and rangatahi had access to proper healthcare, housing and nutrition to reverse the trend. "Too many of our children are experiencing preventable illnesses, with the burden falling disproportionately on Māori, Pasifika, and those living in areas of high deprivation. By targeting these risk factors, we can reverse these trends and generate long term benefits for New Zealand's population that far exceed the initial costs," Soutter said. The report developed in collaboration with the NZ Child and Youth Epidemiology Service at the University of Otago showed a 44 percent increase in the number of children under a year old being hospitalised with respiratory problems over the last 20 years. It said respiratory conditions were the leading cause of acute hospitalisations for children, with infants under one year being particularly vulnerable. The University of Auckland's Dr Anneka Anderson said the study was a "huge wake up call" that more needed to be done to address poverty and poor living conditions and break down barriers to healthcare. She said a one size fits all approach to health would only make matters worse. "Saying that we should treat everyone the same actually promotes inequity. It's a bit like saying we shouldn't have special carparks for non able bodied people. "We have different services to try and level up the playing field, and taking that away always leads to a disaster." She said the Covid 19 pandemic had provided an ideal case study to show the power of tailoring a health response towards ethnic and cultural groups. "The government responded with a one size fits all approach and we saw huge differences in vaccine uptake for Māori than for non Māori. As soon as the control and resources were handed back to Māori providers to provide a 'for Māori, by Māori' service we saw the uptake increase. "So we see that this rhetoric that ethnicity doesn't count and shouldn't be taken into account for different health services hasn't worked in the past, and there's no way it's going to work in the future." Anderson said in addition to working to address poverty and basic living wages health services needed to be designed with a "rights based lens" to cut the inequities across the population. "We live in such a resource rich country. [Typically] in low economic countries we see these high rates of rheumatic heart disease. In Aotearoa we shouldn't be seeing those. This is a completely preventable disease. So it shouldn't be there and I think the fact that it is there is a huge wake up call that we're not doing things right." 43.document_title: Pasifika and Māori Dying a Decade Earlier from Heart Disease, New Report Finds
43.document_summary: A new Cardio Impact Report commissioned by Kia Manawanui Trust and prepared by Otago University reveals alarming health disparities in Aotearoa New Zealand. Māori and Pasifika populations die from heart disease approximately ten years younger than Pākeha (European New Zealanders). The report highlights that Pasifika have the highest hospitalization rates for heart issues, with nearly 1,000 per 100,000 hospitalized in 2022. Key findings include: half of heart attack patients are not treated within accepted timeframes; Ischemic Heart Disease prevalence soared among Pasifika between 2022-2024; heart failure rates have risen sharply since 2020; and Pasifika lose significant years of life to cardiomyopathy (31.5 years) and chronic ischemic heart disease (20 years). Sir Collin Tukuitonga emphasizes the need for targeted interventions addressing smoking cessation, improved primary care access, and subsidies for Māori and Pacific peoples, warning that a one-size-fits-all approach will perpetuate existing inequities.

44.text:
[Page 1] Aotearoa's role in Pacific mental health statistics ByChristina Persico 2025 01 03 07:14:03+13:00 A new study shows Pasifika living in Aotearoa may have higher psychological distress rates A new study has shown Pasifika living in Aotearoa may have higher psychological distress rates compared to those living in their homelands. Lead author Joanna Ataera Minster, who is completing her PhD in the University of Otago Department of Psychological Medicine, said mental health varies within the Pacific population. "When we compared different groups of Pacific adults, the rates of diagnosed mood and anxiety disorders were higher among those born in Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ born) than overseas born Pacific, with rates appearing to increase as time spent in Aotearoa New Zealand increased," she said. The research team examined five consecutive years of data from the annual New Zealand Health Survey (NZHS), spanning 2014/15 2018/19. "In this circumstance, a lot of Pacific researchers talk about the impact of acculturation, which is how our culture changes as Pacific people when we've migrated from our Pacific ancestral homeland to Aotearoa, New Zealand. "The things that come along with that ...when population groups migrate to another country is the weakening or the loss of our social structures and also it disrupts the way we transmit our cultures. "And we have to take on a new language, and so our language declines as well." Ataera Minster referred to a phenomonen known as the "healthy immigrant effect". "So we come and our health outcomes are slightly better than people that are already living here. And then over time, you see this decline, and again to do with the stresses associated with that acculturation process. "But also, we have to remember that before we migrated here, we were also colonized populations. So there's also the trauma of that." Data from 4335 Pacific adults and more than 50,000 non Māori, non Pacific (nMnP) adults was compared. The study found Pacific adults experience disproportionately higher rates of psychological distress than non Māori, non Pacific adults in Aotearoa New Zealand. It found high rates of psychological distress but lower rates of diagnosed mood and anxiety disorders in Pacific adults. The researchrs said this is consistent with literature on mental health service use in Pacific adults, and suggests ongoing barriers to mental health care need to be addressed for Pacific peoples. It also found the mental health inequities and within Pacific differences persisted, even after the researchers accounted for various different factors such as socioeconomic and demographic. "It isn't clear from our research why these differences exist, but we can surmise from related studies that the social and cultural determinants of mental health are likely contributing factors," Ataera Minster said. "These socio cultural determinants include things such as exposure to racism, challenges surrounding one's cultural and ethnic identity, stressors associated with migration and acculturation, and the ongoing impacts of colonisation." 44.document_title: Aotearoa's Role in Pacific Mental Health Statistics
44.document_summary: A comprehensive study led by Joanna Ataera-Minster from the University of Otago examines mental health disparities among Pasifika populations in Aotearoa New Zealand. Analyzing five years of New Zealand Health Survey data (2014/15-2018/19) from 4,335 Pacific adults and over 50,000 non-Māori, non-Pacific adults, the research reveals that Pasifika living in Aotearoa experience significantly higher rates of psychological distress and diagnosed mood and anxiety disorders compared to overseas-born Pacific populations. Key findings demonstrate persistent mental health inequities within Pacific communities, with NZ-born Pacific adults experiencing substantially higher disorder rates than their overseas-born counterparts. The study attributes these disparities to multiple interconnected factors including acculturation processes, weakening social structures, disruption of cultural transmission, and ongoing impacts of colonization. Notably, despite elevated psychological distress rates, Pacific adults show lower diagnosed disorder rates, suggesting significant barriers to mental health care access. The research underscores the critical role of socio-cultural determinants—including exposure to racism, cultural identity challenges, migration stressors, and colonization trauma—in contributing to these mental health inequities. This study provides essential evidence for understanding and addressing health disparities in Pacific communities.

[Page 1] Māori life expectancy increases more than other ethnic group Stats NZ ByEmma Andrews Reporter 2025 08 01 14:46:51+12:00 Life expectancy for Māori has increased more than any other ethnic group in New Zealand, Stats NZ has revealed this week. Despite Māori having the lowest life expectancy at birth, there has been a 3.1 year increase from the 2005 2007 to 2022 2024 periods, taking it to 75.8 years. Over the same time frame, life expectancy at birth for people who are Pākehā or other ethnicities each increased by 1.5 and 1.6 years. "Although life expectancy has increased since 2005 2007, the size of this increase has reduced over the past five years across all ethnicities while Māori have continued to show some of the largest increases," Stats NZ population estimates and projections spokesperson Victoria Treliving said. "Across all ethnic groups, male life expectancy has increased faster than for females." In 2022 2024, life expectancy at birth was: 81.8 years for the entire population of Aotearoa New Zealand. 82.8 years for people who identify with European or Other (including New Zealander) ethnicities. 76.9 years for people who identify with a Pacific ethnicity. 86.3 years for people who identify with an Asian ethnicity. Regional trends The 2022 2024 data suggested that regional trends have remained consistent since data was first obtained for the 1990 1992 period. The Tasman region was estimated to have the highest life expectancy at birth for both males and females, 82.8 and 85.7 years, respectively. Auckland currently sits as the second highest region at 81.1 years for males and 84.3 years for females. Life expectancy at birth in Gisborne was and has consistently been the country's lowest with 77.9 years for males and 81.5 years for females. Of the 53,000 living in the Gisborne region according to the 2023 Census, 52.9 percent identify as Māori, compared to the 9.7 percent of the Tasman region who identify as Māori. "Subnational differences in life expectancy at birth reflect several interrelated factors, including health and socioeconomic factors," Treliving said. What about the rest of the country? Life expectancy for the total population barely increased between 2017 2019 and 2022 2024. While male life expectancy grew from 80.0 to 80.1 years, it stalled at 83.5 years for females. "The increase in life expectancy over the last five years is the smallest since the early 1960s, when it dropped for males. It also follows a relatively small increase of 0.5 years for males and 0.3 years for females between 2012 2014 and 2017 2019," Treliving said the latest population projections assume that life expectancy could continue to increase in the future. Based on national population projections: 2024 (base) 2078 life expectancy at birth could climb to: 82.3 years in 2033 and 84.6 years in 2048 for males, and 85.4 years in 2033 and 87.4 years in 2048 for females. 46.document_title: Half of Heart Attack Patients Not Treated Within Accepted Timeframes in New Zealand
46.document_summary: A new Otago University report commissioned by cardiac advocacy charity Kia Manawanui Trust reveals critical failures in New Zealand's cardiac care system. Key findings show that half of all heart attack patients are not treated within internationally accepted timeframes, and New Zealand has only one-third of the cardiologists it needs. The report calculates the total cost of heart disease to the economy at $13.8 billion annually. Significant disparities exist, with Māori and Pacific people hospitalized or dying from heart disease over a decade earlier than other New Zealanders. Regional variations are stark, with areas having the highest death rates (Tairāwhiti, Lakes, Whanganui, Taranaki) having the fewest cardiac specialists. The workforce shortage is severe, with cardiology sonographers declining from 70.4 in 2013 to 43.5 in 2024 despite population growth. The trust calls for immediate government investment in cardiac infrastructure and a national strategy to recruit and retain cardiology staff.

[Page 1] Mental health patients find it harder to access GPs, study finds ByRayssa Almeida Reporter 2024 11 29 06:28:35+13:00 Mental health patients in New Zealand face significantly worse experiences in primary healthcare compared to those without mental health conditions, according to a national study conducted by the University of Otago. The study, published in the New Zealand Medical Journal, analysed responses from a Health Quality and Safety Commission survey that asked about people's experiences with general practice services. The findings revealed critical barriers to accessing care, with 26.8 percent of mental health patients unable to secure a GP appointment in the past year, compared to 19.6 percent of the general population. Deep rooted systemic issues Ruth Cunningham Lead researcher Ruth Cunningham said the disparities reflected deep rooted systemic issues, including stigma and the pressures on the healthcare system itself. "When the system is under stress... our cognitive biases come through, and we're even more likely to treat people differently because of those biases," she said. "In those cases... providers [need to] think about the experience that people with mental health conditions are having [at the doctor.. but [it] can become harder when the system is under stress." Cunningham emphasised the importance of medical professionals being aware of their biases and how these affect patient care. "The way in which a diagnosis of mental health conditions, problematic substance or addiction, can get in the way of providing high quality care is not something that is often talked about, but is a very important issue." Stigma also discourages patients from seeking care, Cunningham noted. "Experiences of stigma and discrimination... understandably [lead people to] disconnect from the provider or they simply don't go back." Connection and representation The study highlighted that disparities were even more significant for Māori with mental health conditions, who consistently reported greater challenges in accessing care, feeling respected, and having their concerns heard by healthcare providers. For instance, Māori with mental health conditions were 7.7 percent more likely than non Māori to report difficulties in securing a GP appointment within the past year. Cunningham pointed to the need for a more diverse healthcare workforce to improve patient provider relationships. "For Māori, the difference in care was exacerbated... even more adverse experiences of care," she said. "This is all about connection and relationships... and increasing Māori and Pasifika healthcare workforce representation. The patient needs to connect to their providers and, if that doesn't happen, they might not come back to seek treatment." Despite the disparities, Cunningham said there were positive developments within the healthcare system. "But we must continue to listen, address biases, and ensure care meets everyone's needs. Even in a stressed system, treating people with kindness and respect remains essential." Related

51.text:
[Page 1] Hine Moeke Murray says services have been jumping through hoops to meet the political outcomes of the government of the day. Māori, Pacific people and young people are not being prioritised when it comes to accessing mental health support, a new report has found, despite evidence clearly demonstrating these groups need a higher level of support. The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission has reported that fewer people are able to access kaupapa Māori primary mental health services, and that funding for these services has not kept pace with other mental health investment. Only 29 percent of Māori who access specialist service use kaupapa Māori services, and young people are increasingly being declined for specialist help after being referred. The report notes the age standardised rate of suicide deaths is highest among Māori men aged 25 to 44 years, Maori and Pasifika being more likely to be kept in solitary confinement, and young people increasingly being placed in adult in patient services, that are potentially unsafe. htt ps://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/ninetonoon/audio/2019039437 /proportion of kaupapa maori mental health services funded drops Carole Koha has worked in Mental Health and Addictions for the past 35 years. She is currently the chief executive of Te Waka Whaiora, a kaupapa Maori mental health and addictions support service based in Porirua. "We talk about choice, you talk about who access's what services, Māori don't have a choice. When you come against 20 non Māori organisations and maybe one Māori organisation within a community they will definitely referred to the non Māori organisation, because either A) there's no trust or B) we're not funded to deliver clinical services," she said. There were a whole range of reasons Māori continued to go to non Māori services and she said it was not that Māori services were not in a position to deliver, they just did not have the funds. "So by the time they do access services they're in a crisis, but there aren't enough services to meet that particular crisis so the burden becomes a whānau burden, and sometimes within all cultures not just Māori whānau are actually the reason why our tangata are where they are." Hine Moeke Murray is chief executive of Te Kupenga Net Trust, based in Gisborne, a kaupapa Maori organisation providing peer support and advocacy in mental health and addictions. She said a huge part of the issue was that many Māori did not meet the criteria for intervention. "It's no longer intervention, it's no longer prevention we are doing critical response to our whānau because they couldn't get through the doors in the first place." Without stable funding and strong relationships with clinical services it's very difficult to achieve better outcomes for whānau Māori, she said. "When we talk about intervention our whānau can come to a community organisation absolutely, if they need further clinical intervention because they may need some specialist care and they don't meet the criteria of that service where to from there? Where to from there? They get bounced back into the community and when something goes wrong it's the community organisation that's blamed." Services were jumping through hoops to meet the political outcomes the government of the day required, which created huge pressures on services as well, she said. "If there's no services out there that can meet the needs of our babies, all of our people, then how do we change the system because it is system driven." Koha said there were pockets of funding going out to Māori services, but not enough to make positive long term outcomes. The system was still not meeting the needs of rangatahi, she said. "We have a rangatahi portion within our contract but we don't have a clinical [portion], so what I've had to do is employ clinicians out of some of our little bit of surplus that we have. We're not contracted to do it but we need to do it because I'm finding that that's a gap." Minister acknowledges inequitable mental health outcomes In a statement to RNZ, Minister for Mental Health Matt Doocey acknowledged Māori had inequitable mental health outcomes, particularly in suicide rates. "That is why when I launched the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, this had multiple specific actions that were for Māori, to acknowledge those inequities. "I am committed to working with community groups and Health NZ to ensure we are improving outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori. That is where the mental health and addiction targets come in. I have been very clear that we are not just celebrating when we reach the targets at a national level. What is most important is getting into the data and ensuring that all groups are reaching the targets. This includes Māori. If there's a region and group not meeting the target, I expect additional focus to be put into that area." "We have invested additional funding, whether it be through the Innovation Fund or the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, for Māori, and I committed to continuing to work with our community organisations to get more funding out the door where needed. The commission's report noted seclusion otherwise known as solitary confinement was often a traumatising experience and the Ministry of Health reported that Māori in adult in patient services were 6.6 times more likely to be secluded than non Māori. Doocey said seclusion was an issue he had been closely looking at and one he cared strongly about addressing, including for Māori. "Each individual case is a clinical decision, and I expect that the appropriate processes and assessments are followed. "The Mental Health Bill currently before Parliament seeks to further reduce the use of seclusion. This includes requiring the person in charge of a service to report annually to the Director General on the steps taken to eliminate the placement of people under compulsory care in seclusion. "The Bill as it currently stands will limit the use of seclusion and strengthen safeguards. It also prohibits the use of seclusion for people under the age of 18. I am committed to the goal of getting to zero seclusion overtime." Sign up for Ngā Pitopito Kōrero, a daily newsletter curated by our editors and delivered straight to your inbox every weekday. 2.fileDescription: Health Minister Dr Shane Reti intervened to remove ethnicity-based eligibility criteria from a Hawke's Bay healthcare policy targeting young Māori and Pasifika people aged 14-24 for free GP and nurse services. OurHealth Hawke's Bay had initially included ethnicity alongside other factors like deprivation and health conditions. Following criticism from the ACT party and Reti's directive, the policy was changed to remove Māori and Pasifika as eligible groups, aligning with the Government's prioritization of need over population targeting. The decision reflects the broader debate over addressing health inequities versus race-based service allocation, highlighting tensions between equity-focused healthcare approaches and the current government's policy direction on service eligibility criteria.

chunkHighlights.text:
approached for comment. The health inequities between Māori and Pasifika communities and Pākehā were well-known. Non-Māori had a life expectancy seven years greater than Māori. Under the previous Labour government, Te Whatu Ora - Health New Zealand introduced an Equity Adjustor Score, which aimed to reduce inequity in the system by using an algorithm to prioritise patients according to clinical priority, time spent on the waitlist, geographic location (isolated areas), ethnicity and deprivation level. Some health officials argued ethnicity was just one of five factors considered in deciding when a person gets surgery, and that it was an important step in addressing poor health outcomes within Māori and Pacific populations. Reti, then National's health spokesman in opposition, was highly critical of the tool even as he acknowledged long-standing inequities. "While there has been historical inequity that has disadvantaged Māori and Pasifika people, the idea that any government would deliberately rank ethnicities for priority for surgery is offensive, wrong and should halt immediately," he said in June last year. "The way to improve Māori and Pasifika health is through better housing, education and addressing the cost of living, not by disadvantaging others." - This story was originally published by the New Zealand

While Asian populations showed better health outcomes, they faced language barriers. Government policy and district health boards made reducing inequalities a statutory obligation, though targeted public health initiatives have not reached all eligible populations.

chunkHighlights.text: Life expectancy, mortality and ethnicity

Life expectancy for Māori improved dramatically over the 20th century, and the considerable gap between Māori and Pākehā life expectancy narrowed rapidly after the Second World War. Non-Māori life expectancy

increased rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s, but the increases for Māori were small. However, the gap narrowed in the early 21st century. In 2012-14 life expectancy at birth was 83.9 years for non-Māori women, 80.3 for non-Māori men, 77.1 for Māori women and 73 for Māori men. Life expectancy at birth was 78.7 years for Pasifika females and 74.5 years for Pasifika males.

In the early 21st century Māori had the highest all-age mortality rates, followed by Pacific people. The gap in mortality rates between these two groups and Europeans and others (mainly Asians) widened in the 1980s and 1990s. This was probably related to the economic restructuring of the time, which had a big impact on Māori and Pasifika employment and income. The gap narrowed from the late 1990s to the early 2000s, a time when the economy recovered and health policies began to address health inequalities.
The Asian population (which included a large proportion of recent migrants) had the lowest mortality rate over this period. This reflected the good health of most migrants.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores death and dying practices in New Zealand, covering cultural, religious, and legal dimensions. It traces the evolution of dying locations from home-based care in the 1800s to modern hospital and hospice settings, detailing post-death practices including embalming, Māori tangihanga rituals, funerals, burials, and cremation. The document compares Māori and Pākehā traditions, covering bereavement leave provisions and grief support services. It documents the professionalization of funeral services, with approximately 80 funerals held daily across New Zealand, averaging $8,000-$10,000 in costs. Cremation history is traced from the first society established in Lawrence, Otago in 1875 through modern crematoria, noting the increase in cremation rates from a minority practice in the 1960s to approximately 70% by the 2010s. The document addresses cultural and religious considerations for various faiths and discusses euthanasia, detailing New Zealand's legal journey from prohibition to legalization in 2021 through the End of Life Choice Act. Key statistics indicate that in 2017, 33,339 people died in New Zealand, with median death ages of 78 for men and 83 for women. It emphasizes the importance of rituals and rites across religious and non-religious traditions and the development of hospice care beginning with the Little Company of Mary in 1913.

chunkHighlights.text: Dying and bereavement

The number of deaths in New Zealand climbs each year as the population increases and ages. In 2017, 33,339 people died in New Zealand. Only 4% of those who died were under 40 years old, compared to 9% in 1990. The median age at death in 2017 was 78 years for men and 83 years for women. Age at death still differs significantly for Māori and non-Māori – on average Māori die younger.

7.fileDescription: A new Otago University report commissioned by cardiac advocacy charity Kia Manawanui Trust reveals critical failures in New Zealand's cardiac care system. Key findings show that half of all heart attack patients are not treated within internationally accepted timeframes, and New Zealand has only one-third of the cardiologists it needs. The report calculates the total cost of heart disease to the economy at $13.8 billion annually. Significant disparities exist, with Māori and Pacific people hospitalized or dying from heart disease over a decade earlier than other New Zealanders. Regional variations are stark, with areas having the highest death rates (Tairāwhiti, Lakes, Whanganui, Taranaki) having the fewest cardiac specialists. The workforce shortage is severe, with cardiology sonographers declining from 70.4 in 2013 to 43.5 in 2024 despite population growth. The trust calls for immediate government investment in cardiac infrastructure and a national strategy to recruit and retain cardiology staff.

9.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

chunkHighlights.text: Though the gap was closing in the 21st century, clear heath disparities remained. In 2012–14 Māori life expectancy at birth was 6.8 years lower than non-Māori for women and 7.3 years for men. In the 2010s Māori men were almost three times as likely as non-Māori men to die of lung cancer; Māori women were over four times as likely as non-Māori women. Māori died from heart disease at more than twice the rate of non-Māori. Māori were twice as likely to have diabetes as non-Māori, and diabetes complication rates were also higher. Despite great improvements, and a significant rise in life expectancy, Māori were still worse affected than non-Māori by almost every known health condition.

10.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines women's health in New Zealand from the 1800s to 2000s, analyzing health disparities across ethnic groups. It traces how European colonization introduced infectious diseases that devastated Māori populations while Pākehā women experienced improved health. Key findings reveal significant inequities: non-Māori women born in 2007 could expect to live 83 years versus 75.1 for Māori women. Maternal mortality for Māori women reached 23 per 1,000 live births in 1920, compared to 6.5 for Pākehā women. By the 2000s, major causes of death were cancer, cardiovascular disease, and respiratory disease, with Māori women experiencing cardiovascular disease at 4.2 times higher rates and diabetes mortality 10 times higher. Pacific Island women faced elevated mortality from heart disease, stroke, and diabetes, with 48% obesity rates. The document extensively covers health activism including the Young Māori Party (1889), Women's Christian Temperance Union, Te Puea Hērangi's medical clinics, the Family Planning Association (1936), the Māori Women's Welfare League (1951), and feminist health activism of the 1970s-1980s including the cervical cancer scandal. It highlights Māori-centered health models incorporating emotional, physical, whānau, and spiritual wellbeing that challenged mainstream healthcare approaches.

chunkHighlights.text: Below the radar

Diabetes was unknown in the Pacific before the Second World War, and in the 2000s the rate among Māori could only be estimated. Professor Chris Cunningham of Massey University’s Research Centre for Māori
Health suspected that ‘well over’ half of those with the disease didn’t know it.
Diabetes

Diabetes reached epidemic level in some Māori communities in the 2000s. In 2005 Māori women were 10 times more likely to die from diabetes than the general population (at 6.5 times that of the general population, the rate for Māori men was also very high).
Risks

Smoking, hazardous drinking, obesity, limited physical activity and low fruit and vegetable intake all increase the likelihood of health problems. Unemployment increases risky behaviour, and Māori were hit particularly hard during recessions and state restructuring from the 1970s on.
Medical care

Access to health care is limited by cost, availability of doctors, and attitudes of medical personnel. Health problems are strongly concentrated among poorer women – for example, 50% of Māori women with cancer come from the bottom two deprivation deciles. Medical personnel have sometimes provided a lesser quality of care to Māori. Evidence that the care of women during childbirth has been affected by the mother being Māori is particularly strong.

11.fileDescription: A comprehensive State of Child Health Report developed with the NZ Child and Youth Epidemiology Service reveals critical health disparities in Aotearoa New Zealand. The report documents alarming statistics including Pasifika children being 115 times more likely to be hospitalised with acute rheumatic fever compared to European children, and a 44% increase in respiratory hospitalisations for children under one over the past two decades. Pasifika, Māori, and children in low socio-economic areas face disproportionate health burdens from respiratory conditions, rheumatic fever, heart disease, skin infections, dental disease, and mental health problems. Dr Anneka Anderson criticises the government's "one-size-fits-all" health approach, arguing it ignores evidence and perpetuates inequity. The report advocates for tailored, culturally-responsive health services delivered through a "rights-based lens," highlighting the success of COVID-19 vaccine uptake when Māori providers delivered "for Māori, by Māori" services. Cure Kids emphasises that urgent national action is required to address underlying social determinants including poverty, housing, and nutrition to reverse preventable illness trends and achieve equitable health outcomes for all children.

chunkHighlights.text: Cure Kids says a new study shows Pasifika children in Aotearoa are 115 times more likely to be hospitalised with acute rheumatic fever than European children. The fourth State of Child Health Report showed Pasifika, Māori and children in low socio-economic areas were disproportionately affected by respiratory conditions, rheumatic fever and heart disease, skin infections, dental disease and mental health problems. Cure Kids head Frances Soutter said urgent national action was needed to ensure all tamariki and rangatahi had access to proper healthcare, housing and nutrition to reverse the trend. "Too many of our children are experiencing preventable illnesses, with the burden falling disproportionately on Māori, Pasifika, and those living in areas of high deprivation. By targeting these risk factors, we can reverse these trends and generate long-term benefits for New Zealand's population that far exceed the initial costs," Soutter said. The report - developed in collaboration with the NZ Child and Youth Epidemiology Service at the University of Otago - showed a 44 percent increase in the number of children under a year old being hospitalised with respiratory problems

over the last 20 years. It said respiratory conditions were the leading
cause of acute hospitalisations for children, with infants under one year being particularly vulnerable. The University of Auckland's Dr Anneka Anderson said the study was a "huge wake-up call" that more needed to be done to address poverty and poor living conditions and break down barriers to healthcare. She said a one-size-fits-all approach to health would only make matters worse. "Saying that we should treat everyone the same actually promotes inequity. It's a bit like saying we shouldn't have special carparks for non able-bodied people. "We have different services to try and level up the playing field, and taking that away always leads to a disaster." She said the Covid-19 pandemic had provided an ideal case study to show the power of tailoring a health response towards ethnic and cultural groups. "The government responded with a one-size-fits-all approach and we saw huge differences in vaccine uptake for Māori than for non-Māori. As soon as the control and resources were handed back to Māori providers - to provide a 'for Māori, by Māori' service - we saw the uptake increase. "So we see that this rhetoric that ethnicity doesn't count and shouldn't be taken into account for different health services hasn't worked in the past, and there's no way it's going to work in the future." Anderson said - in addition to working to address poverty and basic living wages - health services needed to be designed with a "rights based lens" to cut the inequities across the population. "We live in such a resource rich country. [Typically] in low economic countries we see these high rates of rheumatic heart disease. In Aotearoa we shouldn't be seeing those. This is a completely preventable disease. So it shouldn't be there and I think the fact that it is there is a huge wake-up call that we're not doing things
right." Related

12.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines child and youth health in New Zealand, documenting a significant decline from being a global leader to ranking in the bottom third of OECD countries by the early 21st century. Key health challenges include exceptionally high youth suicide rates (15.6 per 100,000, highest among OECD nations), elevated infant and child mortality, and substantial health disparities among Māori and Pacific children. Major health concerns encompass sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI), childhood obesity (12% overall, 30% for Pacific children), asthma (25% of children), and infectious diseases including meningococcal disease and rheumatic fever. The document traces infectious disease evolution from the 19th century through contemporary challenges, noting that while immunisation programmes have controlled many diseases, poverty-related conditions persist at higher rates than other OECD countries. Youth health issues include accidents (car crashes leading cause of unintentional injury deaths among 15-24 year-olds), sexual health concerns, substance use (57% of 15-17-year-olds and 86% of 18-24-year-olds consumed alcohol in 2014/15), and declining smoking rates (from 28% in 2000 to 6% in 2014). Health disparities are linked to socioeconomic factors including deprivation, inadequate housing, and income inequality. Primary health initiatives include Plunket (founded 1907), School Medical Service (established 1912), and modern integrated youth health centers. Major pediatric facilities include Starship Hospital (opened 1991) and Kidz First Children's Hospital (established 2000). New Zealand ranked 29 out of 30 OECD countries for child health and safety in 2009.

Despite these bleak statistics there were some improvements. 13.fileDescription: The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission's latest report reveals that nearly a quarter of young people reported high levels of psychological distress in the month before the survey. Key findings include: 14% of people aged 15+ experienced high or very high psychological distress in 2024-25 (609,000 people), with significantly higher rates among Māori (22.5%), Pacific peoples (24%), young people (23%), and disabled people (35.5%). Young people experienced nearly three times the overall average rate of intentional self-harm requiring hospitalization. Access to specialist services has decreased, though primary and community services improved. The report highlights that seclusion rates remain too high, with Māori in adult inpatient services 6.6 times more likely to be secluded than non-Māori. Three key recommendations include publishing a national seclusion plan by 2027, collecting outcomes data from service users, and developing an action plan to meet Māori and whānau needs. Positive developments include improved workforce vacancy rates and increased mental health training enrollment.

nearly a quarter of young people reported high levels of psychological distress in the month before the survey. In 2024-25, 14 percent of people aged 15 years and over had experienced "high" or "very high" psychological distress in the four weeks prior to the survey, equivalent to 609,000 people - more than double the rate seen a decade ago. Some groups experienced much higher rates of psychological distress, including Māori (22.5 percent), Pacific peoples (24 percent), young people (23 percent) and disabled people (35.5 percent). The commission/Te Hiringa Mahara's chief executive, Karen Orsborn, said their distress was driven by factors like online harm and the global environment. "It's the world that young people live in." There had also been an increase in staff, thanks to focused attention on growing numbers and increasing diversity, Orsborn said. "So by the time they do access services they're in a crisis, but there aren't enough services to meet that particular crisis so the burden becomes a whānau burden, and sometimes within all cultures - not just
Māori - whānau are actually the reason why our tangata are where they

are." Hine Moeke-Murray is chief executive of Te Kupenga Net Trust,
based in Gisborne, a kaupapa Maori organisation providing peer support and advocacy in mental health and addictions. She said a huge part of the issue was that many Māori did not meet the criteria for intervention. "It's no longer intervention, it's no longer prevention we are doing critical response to our whānau because they couldn't get through the doors in the first place." Without stable funding and strong relationships with clinical services it's very difficult to achieve better outcomes for whānau Māori, she said. "When we talk about intervention our whānau can come to a community organisation absolutely, if they need further clinical intervention because they may need some specialist care and they don't meet the criteria of that service where to from there? Where to from there? They get bounced back into the community and when something goes wrong it's the community organisation that's blamed." Services were jumping through hoops to meet the political outcomes the government of the day required, which created huge pressures on services as well, she said. "If there's no services out there that can meet the needs of our babies, all of our people, then how do we change the system because it is system driven." Koha said there were pockets of funding going out to Māori services, but not enough to make positive long-term outcomes. The system was still not meeting the needs of rangatahi, she said. "We have a rangatahi portion within our contract but we don't have a clinical [portion], so what I've had to do is employ clinicians out of some of our little bit of surplus that we have. We're not contracted to do it but we need to do it because I'm finding that that's a gap." Minister acknowledges inequitable mental health outcomes In a statement to RNZ, Minister for Mental Health Matt Doocey acknowledged Māori had inequitable mental health outcomes, particularly in suicide rates. "That is why when I launched the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, this had multiple specific actions that were for Māori, to acknowledge those inequities. "I am committed to working with community groups and Health NZ to ensure we are improving outcomes for all New
Zealanders, including Māori. That is where the mental health and
addiction targets come in. I have been very clear that we are not just
celebrating when we reach the targets at a national level. What is most
important is getting into the data and ensuring that all groups are
reaching the targets. This includes Māori. If there's a region and group
not meeting the target, I expect additional focus to be put into that

area." "We have invested additional funding, whether it be through the Innovation Fund or the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, for Māori, and I committed to continuing to work with our community organisations to get more funding out the door where needed. The commission's report noted seclusion - otherwise known as solitary confinement - was often a traumatising experience and the Ministry of Health reported that Māori in adult in-patient services were 6.6 times more likely to be secluded than non-Māori. Doocey said seclusion was an issue he had been closely looking at and one he cared strongly about addressing, including for Māori. "Each individual case is a clinical decision, and I expect that the appropriate processes and assessments are followed. "The Mental Health Bill currently before Parliament seeks to further reduce the use of seclusion. This includes requiring the person in charge of a service to report annually to the Director-General on the steps taken to eliminate the placement of people under compulsory care in seclusion. "The Bill as it currently stands will limit the use of seclusion and strengthen safeguards. It also prohibits the use of seclusion for people under the age of 18. I am committed to the goal of getting to zero seclusion overtime." Sign up for Ngā Pitopito Kōrero, a daily newsletter curated by our editors and delivered straight to your inbox every

16.fileDescription: Rural New Zealand faces a critical healthcare crisis with patients dying from preventable causes due to inadequate medical services and severe resource constraints. Despite rural communities producing 80% of New Zealand's export earnings, they experience significantly higher mortality rates, limited access to healthcare facilities, and acute doctor shortages. Surgeon Vanessa Blair highlights systemic failures within the healthcare system, including cases of misdiagnosis and preventable deaths at rural hospitals lacking adequate staffing levels. Research demonstrates that rural residents experience twice the preventable disease mortality compared to urban counterparts, elevated suicide rates, and poor access to specialist services. Rural hospitals such as Taupō operate at approximately half their required staffing levels, exacerbating the healthcare equity gap. While the government has introduced workforce initiatives including accommodation allowances, locum funding, and relocation programs to attract healthcare professionals to rural areas, healthcare experts argue these measures are insufficient without substantial increases in central government funding and systemic healthcare reforms.

chunkHighlights.text: The network's chairperson Dr Fiona Bolden said many of those statistics were worst for Māori living in the most remote areas. "Māori living under 30 years old were twice as likely to die from a preventable disease as Māori the same age living in a city." Non-Māori men aged 30 to 44 were 1.8 times more likely to die from preventable causes compared with their peers living in urban areas. Preventable causes included suicide - "there's scant access to specialist mental health support in the regions" - as well as workplace accidents and road crashes. Both primary care and hospital services in the regions needed a big injection of cash from central government, Bolden said. "They're not going to have a rural health service without putting more money into it. And a 4 percent rise in capitation funding [to GPs] is not going to address any of the issues." The sector was also anxiously awaiting the release of the Health Workforce Plan to deal with regional inequities, she said. Improving rural health a government "priority" Minister of Health Shane Reti said improving rural health was "an integral part of improving all health in New Zealand". The government inherited "long-standing" problems with the health workforce, but was tackling them head-on through an additional 25 medical school places and working with Waikato University on its proposal for a third medical school, he said. 17.fileDescription: A University of Otago study published in the New Zealand Medical Journal reveals that mental health patients in New Zealand face significant barriers to primary healthcare access. The research found that 26.8% of mental health patients were unable to secure a GP appointment in the past year, compared to 19.6% of the general population. Lead researcher Ruth Cunningham attributes these disparities to deep-rooted systemic issues including stigma, healthcare system pressures, and cognitive biases among providers. The study highlights that disparities are even more pronounced for Māori with mental health conditions, who are 7.7% more likely to report difficulties accessing GP appointments. Cunningham emphasizes the need for healthcare professionals to address their biases, increase workforce diversity with greater Māori and Pasifika representation, and maintain kindness and respect in patient care despite system stress.

ByRayssa Almeida - Reporter
2024-11-29 06:28:35+13:00

Mental health patients
in New Zealand face significantly worse
experiences in primary healthcare compared to those without mental
health conditions, according to a national study conducted by the University of Otago. The study, published in the New Zealand Medical Journal, analysed responses from a Health Quality and Safety Commission survey that asked about people's experiences with general practice services. The findings revealed critical barriers to accessing care, with 26.8 percent of mental health patients unable to secure a GP appointment in the past year, compared to 19.6 percent of the general population. Deep-rooted systemic issues Ruth Cunningham Lead researcher Ruth Cunningham said the disparities reflected deep-rooted systemic issues, including stigma and the pressures on the healthcare system itself. "When the system is under stress... our cognitive biases come through, and we're even more likely to treat people differently because of those biases," she said. "In those cases... providers [need to] think about the experience that people with mental health conditions are having [at the doctor.. but [it] can become harder when the system is under stress." Cunningham emphasised the importance of medical professionals being aware of their biases and how these affect patient care. "The way in which a diagnosis of mental health conditions, problematic substance or addiction, can get in the way of providing high-quality care is not something that is often talked about, but is a very important issue." Stigma also discourages patients from seeking care, Cunningham noted. "Experiences of stigma and discrimination... understandably [lead people to] disconnect from the provider or they simply don't go back." Connection and representation The study highlighted that disparities were even more significant for Māori with mental health conditions, who consistently reported greater challenges in accessing care, feeling respected, and having their concerns heard by healthcare providers. For instance, Māori with mental health conditions were 7.7 percent more likely than non-Māori to report difficulties in
securing a GP appointment within the past year. Cunningham pointed to

the need for a more diverse healthcare workforce to improve patient-provider relationships. "For Māori, the difference in care was exacerbated... even more adverse experiences of care," she said. "This is all about connection and relationships... and increasing Māori and Pasifika healthcare workforce representation. The patient needs to connect to their providers and, if that doesn't happen, they might not come back to seek treatment." Despite the disparities, Cunningham said there were positive developments within the healthcare system. "But we must continue to listen, address biases, and ensure care meets everyone's needs. Even in a stressed system, treating people with kindness and respect remains essential." Related

18.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines health inequalities and social determinants of health in New Zealand, focusing on disparities among ethnic groups. It explores how socio-economic status, ethnicity, employment, housing, education, and environmental conditions shape health outcomes. Significant health disparities exist between Māori and Pākehā populations, with Māori experiencing lower life expectancy (73-77 years vs 80-84 years in 2012-14), and an 8-year gap between least and most deprived areas for males. Major health challenges include cancer (30% of deaths in 2015), cardiovascular diseases, tobacco use, poor nutrition, and obesity. Tobacco remains the leading preventable cause of death, with Māori adults 2.5 times more likely to smoke. Healthcare access is limited by cost, with 25-33% deferring doctor visits due to expense. The document traces New Zealand's health services evolution from fee-based systems (pre-1940s) to subsidized services (post-1938) and the 21st-century primary health organization model. It discusses culturally responsive healthcare approaches for Māori and Pacific populations, including decorated clinics and traditional healer referrals. While Asian populations showed better health outcomes, they faced language barriers. Government policy and district health boards made reducing inequalities a statutory obligation, though targeted public health initiatives have not reached all eligible populations.

chunkHighlights.text: Health disparities between Māori and Pākehā were written about from the 19th century. Health researchers published major reports on social inequalities in health from the 1980s. Activity in this field increased in the 1990s and 2000s. Reducing inequalities was a major part of government health policy and a statutory obligation of district health boards in the early 21st century.

19.fileDescription:
This comprehensive document provides an overview of public health in New Zealand, covering disease prevention, health promotion, and population-level health inequalities from the 19th century to present. It traces the evolution of public health infrastructure, including the Department of Public Health (established 1900) and its transformation into the Ministry of Health, with major reforms in 1993 and the 2000s emphasizing district health boards.

Key areas covered include environmental health (sewerage, water treatment, housing standards, air pollution control), vaccination programs, tobacco control, and mental health services. The document details major public health initiatives including clean air efforts, smoking restrictions (1980s campaigns to 2019 restrictions on smoking in cars with children), immunization history against smallpox, diphtheria, polio, and measles, nutrition programs, and water fluoridation.

Significant attention is given to health disparities among Māori and Pacific Island populations, who experience disproportionately high disease and premature mortality rates. The document examines evidence of health inequalities linked to socio-economic status and government responses including district health boards with statutory obligations to reduce inequalities. Additional topics include tobacco control as a public health success story, cancer screening programmes, mental health with 20% prevalence in 12 months and 47% lifetime prevalence, water safety issues (Queenstown 1984, Havelock North 2016), and the 2017 Healthy Homes Guarantee Act addressing housing standards.

Despite Māori having the lowest life expectancy at birth, there has been a 3.1 year increase from the 2005-2007 to 2022-2024 periods, taking it to 75.8 years. Over the same time frame, life expectancy at birth for people who are Pākehā or other ethnicities each increased by 1.5 and 1.6 years. Regional trends The 2022-2024 data suggested that regional trends have remained consistent since data was first obtained for the 1990-1992 period. The Tasman region was estimated to have the highest life expectancy at birth for both males and females, 82.8 and 85.7 years, respectively. retrieved_chunks.text: Life expectancy, mortality and ethnicity Life expectancy for Māori improved dramatically over the 20th century, and the considerable gap between Māori and Pākehā life expectancy narrowed rapidly after the Second World War. Non-Māori life expectancy increased rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s, but the increases for Māori were small. However, the gap narrowed in the early 21st century. In 2012-14 life expectancy at birth was 83.9 years for non-Māori women, 80.3 for non-Māori men, 77.1 for Māori women and 73 for Māori men. Life expectancy at birth was 78.7 years for Pasifika females and 74.5 years for Pasifika males. In the early 21st century Māori had the highest all-age mortality rates, followed by Pacific people. The gap in mortality rates between these two groups and Europeans and others (mainly Asians) widened in the 1980s and 1990s. This was probably related to the economic restructuring of the time, which had a big impact on Māori and Pasifika employment and income. The gap narrowed from the late 1990s to the early 2000s, a time when the economy recovered and health policies began to address health inequalities. The Asian population (which included a large proportion of recent migrants) had the lowest mortality rate over this period. This reflected the good health of most migrants.

4.document_title: Otago Region: Comprehensive History, Geography, Economy, and Culture in New Zealand
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of Otago, a geographically diverse region in New Zealand's South Island covering 36,000 square kilometers with a 2013 population of 202,467. The region features varied landscapes including Central Otago's inland ranges, Southern Alps peaks, coastal lowlands, and distinctive geological formations shaped by schist uplifted over 2 million years. Historically, Māori arrived around 1250-1300, establishing tribes including Waitaha, Ngāti Māmoe, and Ngāi Tahu before hunting moa and later subsisting on coastal resources and pounamu. Scottish settlers arrived from 1848, founding Dunedin as a major center, with 12,000 immigrants arriving in the 1850s establishing a distinctly Scottish-Presbyterian character. The region's economic development was shaped by wool farming (1850s), gold discoveries near the Tuapeka River in 1861 (peak production of 17,400 kilograms in 1863), and refrigerated meat exports (1882). By 1880, Dunedin was New Zealand's largest and wealthiest city. The region's economy evolved from pastoral farming and gold mining to diversified agriculture including wool, refrigerated meat, orcharding, and sawmilling. Contemporary employment patterns show agriculture dominates Central Otago and Clutha (33% of workforce), hospitality drives Queenstown Lakes (30%), and education/health sectors dominate Dunedin (30%). Culturally, Otago boasts a rich literary tradition featuring poets like Thomas Bracken and Charles Brasch, visual artists including Colin McCahon and Ralph Hōtere, and the distinctive "Dunedin sound" music scene. The region excelled in rugby during the 1930s-1940s and produced Olympic champions. Today, Dunedin remains a center for education and medicine with a stable population of 112,000, while Queenstown and Wānaka are growing tourist destinations offering adventure sports like bungy jumping and skiing.
