13.fileDescription: This article examines New Zealand's 50-year experiment with alcohol prohibition and restricted drinking hours. Beginning in 1917 during World War I, the government implemented a 6pm closing time for bars as a compromise to full prohibition, intended to keep workers sober and productive. The policy, meant to be temporary, became permanent in 1918 and remained until 1967. During this period, men would rush to pubs at 5pm to consume as much alcohol as possible within the one-hour window, leading to widespread intoxication and social problems through the Great Depression and World War II. The article notes that returning servicemen exposed to European moderate drinking culture and international tourists contributed to changing attitudes. The 6pm closing was finally repealed on October 9, 1967, following a nationwide referendum. The piece reflects on New Zealand's historical puritanical attitudes toward hedonism and excess, contrasting them with modern perspectives on drug policy liberalization.

chunkHighlights.text: To its supporters, the failure of the 2020 referendum on the proposed Cannabis Legalisation and Control Bill would have seemed typical of stodgy old New Zealand. The idea of liberalising drug laws was too much for a country which still has a parochial suspicion of hedonism and excess.

14.fileDescription: Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick has launched an online platform seeking public feedback on cannabis regulation, five years after New Zealand narrowly rejected cannabis legalization in a referendum. Swarbrick argues that courts and police resources continue to be wasted enforcing cannabis prohibition, citing 26 imprisonments for cannabis offences and 3 for cannabis use alone in the past year. The platform aims to capture diverse regulatory ideas that emerged during the referendum debate but lacked a formal policy forum. While legalization remains the Greens' official position, the feedback will inform future policy development. This initiative follows a major Drug Foundation report recommending decriminalization of all drug use and a complete overhaul of the Misuse of Drugs Act, which the Foundation describes as a "colossal failure" since its introduction 50 years ago.

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick is asking for public feedback on
what good cannabis regulation looks like. It's been five years since the country narrowly voted against legalising cannabis in a referendum on the drug policy. Swarbrick said courts and police resources were still being wasted enforcing cannabis prohibition. "In the past year alone, 26 people have been imprisoned for cannabis offences as their most serious charge and three imprisoned just for cannabis use. "After 50 years of the war on drugs, it's clear that the drugs are winning." She's launched an online platform on Wednesday for members of the public to give feedback on what they think good regulation looks like. "I think one of the things that I found the most interesting about the unfortunate binary that comes about when you have a referendum on the table is that there were many people who had a lot of ideas about what they thought that sensible regulation could look like, but there wasn't any forum for those to be put into the policy platform." The co-leader said it was still the party's position that cannabis should be legalised, though the feedback received through the portal would "inform" its positions going forward. Swarbrick said while people often wanted to talk to her about the cost of living, housing, homelessness and the environment, she was still frequently "hit up" about cannabis legalisation. chunkHighlights.text: New report recommends decriminali sation of illicit drugs

A new report from the New Zealand Drug Foundation is calling for the total decriminalisation of illicit drugs. They say running drug users through the criminal justice system has exacerbated addiction, overdoses and deaths, and it was time to change New Zealand's fifty-year-old Misuse of Drugs Act to focus on a health-support response. But in 2020, New Zealanders rejected decriminalising cannabis at the polling booth - is there the appetite for such a huge, cultural change to be made? 16.filePath: pdf/Green MP Kahurangi Carter's overdose bill passes first hurdle.pdf
16.fileDescription: Green MP Kahurangi Carter's member's bill passed its first reading on Wednesday night, advancing legislation designed to prevent low-level drug prosecutions against those who call for help during suspected overdoses or bad drug reactions. The bill amends the Misuse of Drugs Act, Bail Act, and Parole Act to protect individuals from charges for personal possession, drug utensils, or parole breaches when seeking emergency assistance. Supported by Labour, ACT, and Te Pāti Māori, the bill was opposed only by National and New Zealand First. The legislation was motivated by cases like Jacob Gunnell's death in 2022, where witnesses hesitated to call emergency services due to fear of prosecution. The New Zealand Drug Foundation reports that three people die weekly from preventable overdoses, and removing prosecution fears could save lives. The bill now proceeds to the Health Select Committee for further consideration.

chunkHighlights.text: Green MP Kahurangi Carter's overdose bill passes first hurdle

ByLillian Hanly - Political reporter
2026-04-30 04:50:10+12:00

A member's bill by Green MP Kahurangi Carter passed its first hurdle on
Wednesday night. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/morningr eport/audio/2019032982/drug-overdose-assistance-protection-bill-passe s-first-reading The mother of a young man who fell to his death while on drugs says legislation now going through Parliament could save lives, and politicians had the "power to make a difference". A member's bill by Green MP Kahurangi Carter passed its first hurdle on Wednesday night. The legislation would prevent low-level drug prosecutions against those who call in suspected overdoses or bad drug reactions. Shelley O'Dwyer's son Jacob Gunnell died in 2022 after a negative reaction to LSD and a police statement told her emergency services were not called. She told RNZ she believes if those with him at the time knew they would not "get in trouble" and called for help, "he could still be with us". "How would you feel if you had to live for the rest of your life knowing that you should have actually rang an ambulance and now that person's passed away," O'Dwyer said. The New Zealand Drug Foundation has long called for change in this area, and executive director Sarah Helm said the law change could make a "big difference". "New Zealand loses three people every week to completely preventable, unintentional overdose, and that is a huge number of people," she told RNZ. Helm said currently people hesitate or fail to ring 111 or call for help in the event of an overdose or acute drug harm situation. "We know from coronial cases that people do hesitate and that that causes death." The law change would "remove that fear of prosecution that stops people from calling for help", Helm said. She said this was one of the "key planks" to prevent overdose, and currently there were not enough interventions to do so. "We can expect to see, unfortunately, more overdose fatalities over the coming years because of the increase of the potency and volatility of the drug market. "So every intervention we can get in place will help to protect New Zealand from that," Helm said. The bill passed its first reading on Wednesday night, with only National and New Zealand First opposed.

Green MP, "She's going to get the support of the ACT party on first
reading to send this to the select committee." ACT's Todd Stephenson. Carter's bill makes narrow amendments to the Misuse of Drugs Act, the Bail Act and the Parole Act. It specifies someone calling for help during a suspected overdose would not be charged for low level offences such as personal possession or use of drugs, possession of drug utensils, or a breach of parole conditions relating to drug use The Bill does not protect drug dealing, violent offending or Crimes Act offences and it preserves accountability for serious criminal behaviour. Ultimately - it is designed to stop people from hesitating if they are in doubt. Carter, speaking first during the debate, said normally when someone calls an ambulance to save a life, "they're considered a hero". "When someone is trying to help their friend experiencing an overdose - that should remain the case." Labour's Camilla Belich spoke in support, referencing evidence by the NZ Drug Foundation highlighting witnesses hesitancy to call for help as a contributing factor in drug deaths. She said that evidence showed there was a "need" for the Bill. "This is not about providing avenues for people to avoid arrest in cases of serious crime," Belich added. Labour's Camilla Belich. Speaking for ACT, Stephenson said under the current settings it was "sometimes unclear" if you reach out for help what the consequences were. He said he wanted to make sure that when something does go wrong, people do not hesistate in calling emergency services, "because if you can get help quickly, drug overdoses can be attended to and people can actually survive". "It does actually matter how quickly people get medical attention." He emphasised it was not a "soft on crime" bill. inequity." Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara. New Zealand First's Casey

seek help. "I think it is a very sad indictment on our society that we have

17.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines cannabis policy, enforcement, and use in New Zealand through multiple interconnected perspectives. It profiles individuals like Steve Wilson, a chronic pain sufferer using cannabis to manage central sensitization syndrome, and Kate Kennedy, whose cannabis use led to psychotic episodes, illustrating the tension between medicinal necessity and health risks. The document analyzes New Zealand's evolving cannabis landscape: nearly half of adults have tried cannabis, with 79% supporting its use for pain relief and 82% for terminal illness, yet the country maintains strict prohibition under a 40-year-old Misuse of Drugs Act. Police enforcement efforts are substantial—spending $90 million annually on cannabis enforcement with operations like Operation Dee seizing 132,000 plants and arresting 572 people. Treasury analysis projects potential tax revenue of $150 million annually from legal cannabis sales, while enforcement costs reach $109 million for courts and justice. The document explores the "entourage effect" theory, international public health guidelines recommending moderate consumption, and the disproportionate impact of enforcement on Māori communities. It presents cannabis simultaneously as a medical breakthrough for chronic pain management, an engine of gang economy, and a potential tax revenue source, while questioning New Zealand's prohibition approach compared to international law changes.

18.fileDescription: The Harm Reduction Coalition and drug policy advocates are calling for radical reform of New Zealand's Misuse of Drugs Act, marking 50 years since its enactment. Researchers, including Dr. Fiona Hutton and Dr. Julian Buchanan, argue that decades of drug prohibition have failed to reduce drug use or criminal trade. They advocate for repealing the current act and establishing new legislation that treats drugs as a health issue under the Ministry of Health rather than the justice system, with differentiated regulations based on drug-specific harms. Evidence from Portugal's decriminalization success is cited. However, the government has rejected liberalizing drug laws, instead announcing a $30 million methamphetamine crackdown with increased police enforcement and a media campaign. Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey emphasizes a health-led response balancing enforcement, prevention, and treatment, with $246 million invested in addiction services.

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] “We are everywhere” By Vaughan Yarwood The fight to decriminalise homosexuality. If there were such a thing as a social seismograph—a piece of tech that recorded the collisions and ruptures caused by deep seated movement in New Zealand society—it would have been off the charts in the 1980s. Shock after shock brought a usually restrained public out onto streets, playing fields and harbours. There was the Springbok rugby tour of 1981, French nuclear tests in the Pacific, and, in 1985, the Homosexual Law Reform Bill. Homosexuality had long been considered immoral and unnatural in Britain and its colonies, and buggery was punishable by death. In 1893, following changes in English law, New Zealand extended prohibitions to include any sexual activity between men and replaced the death penalty with flogging and imprisonment for life with hard labour. Consent was no defence. (Sex between women has never been illegal in this country.) It wasn’t until almost 70 years later that attempts were made to repeal the legislation, or at least reduce its severity. In 1959, Attorney General Rex Mason tried unsuccessfully to soften the sanctions on some homosexual activities—spurred, some say, by the suicide of a gay acquaintance. # The Foreshore and Seabed Debate: Arguments For and Against

The question of who owns — or has rights over — Aotearoa New Zealand's foreshore and seabed has been one of the most contentious constitutional and Treaty issues of the past three decades. The debate has spanned multiple pieces of legislation, sparked mass protest, and divided political parties. Here's a breakdown of the key arguments on both sides.

## Background

The controversy began in earnest when eight iwi of the upper South Island applied to the Māori Land Court in 1997 to have the foreshore and seabed of the Marlborough Sounds determined as Māori customary land, after failing to be awarded rights for mussel farming. [[1]](cite://1/1) This prompted the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, which reserved both the foreshore and seabed for the Crown. [[1]](cite://1/2) That law was later replaced by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, which restored iwi's ability to seek customary rights and title in court. [[1]](cite://1/3) Most recently, the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill passed its third reading in Parliament in October 2025, tightening the test for customary marine title (CMT). [[2]](cite://2/1)

## Arguments *For* the Legislation (Government's Position)

**Restoring Parliament's original intent**
The government's central argument, advanced by justice minister Paul Goldsmith, was that courts — particularly the Court of Appeal in a 2023 ruling — had interpreted the requirements for CMT in a way that "materially reduced their intended effect." [[2]](cite://2/2) The Supreme Court itself later confirmed the Court of Appeal had taken an "unduly narrow" approach. [[3]](cite://3/1)

**Balancing interests of all New Zealanders**
Goldsmith argued that "everybody in New Zealand has an interest in what goes on in the coastline," and the government was attempting to get that balance right. [[4]](cite://4/1) The 2011 Act was described as recognising Māori rights *while* managing the interests of all New Zealanders. [[5]](cite://5/1)

**Concern over scale of title awards**
Goldsmith cited cases decided since the Supreme Court ruling where "almost 100 percent of the coastline and those areas" were granted CMT, arguing the test still didn't achieve the balance the legislation set out to achieve. [[4]](cite://4/2)

**Parliament's constitutional supremacy**
Law dean Geoff McClay noted that, constitutionally, Parliament *is* supreme and does have the authority to amend legislation when it disagrees with how courts have interpreted it — which is what occurred here. [[2]](cite://2/3)

**Support from Hobson's Pledge**
Hobson's Pledge leader Don Brash supported the bill, saying the courts had reinterpreted Parliament's intent, and that his preference would be to return to the 2004 Act where the Crown owned the foreshore and seabed on behalf of all New Zealanders. [[6]](cite://6/1)

## Arguments *Against* the Legislation

**A form of raupatu (confiscation)**
Critics, including Green MP Hūhana Lyndon and Ngātiwai rangatira Aperahama Edwards, described the amendments as the "biggest raupatu" (confiscation/theft) Māori had faced. [[7]](cite://7/1)[[5]](cite://5/2) Te Pāti Māori MP Tākuta Ferris noted his party was *formed* in direct response to the 2004 Foreshore and Seabed Act and that the 2025 amendments were ripping off even the partial remedy provided in 2011. [[5]](cite://5/3)

**Retrospective application is constitutionally troubling**
Law expert McClay highlighted that retrospectively changing the rules on cases already filed — requiring them to be reheard under a stricter test — breaks a longstanding convention that cases should be decided under the law in place when they were filed. [[2]](cite://2/4) Labour MP Ginny Andersen said the bill "rewrites [Parliament's] intention, narrows it, and applies new rules retrospectively, overturning the work of the courts and reopening wounds." [[2]](cite://2/5)

**Based on a false premise about public access**
Victoria University law lecturer Luke Fitzmaurice Brown argued the bill was "based on the racist myth" that upholding Māori coastal rights would prevent people from accessing public beaches. CMT cannot be sold and has no effect on public access, fishing, or other recreational activities. [[6]](cite://6/2)

**Harmful to Māori-Crown relations**
Former attorney general and Treaty negotiations minister Chris Finlayson — himself a National MP — said the changes would be "extremely harmful" to race relations in New Zealand and did not restore Parliament's original intent. [[5]](cite://5/4)[[8]](cite://8/1)

**'Mean spirited' and punitive**
Veteran Māori lawyer Annette Sykes described the changes as "punitive" and "mean spirited," arguing the retrospective nature was "a breach of good faith" that penalised claimants who had spent years and considerable resources building their cases. [[8]](cite://8/2)

**Waitangi Tribunal opposition**
The Waitangi Tribunal recommended the Crown halt all efforts to amend the Takutai Moana Act, finding failings in the government's handling of the process, including introducing funding changes without consultation and leaving claimants in the lurch. [[9]](cite://9/1)[[10]](cite://10/1)

**Undermining indigenous property rights**
The broader Māori argument rests on the principle that before European law was imposed, Māori practised their own laws and customs which could not be entirely overruled by later legislation — a foundation for all customary title claims. [[11]](cite://11/1)

## Where Things Stand

The Amendment Bill passed its final reading on 22 October 2025 with support from the three coalition government parties. [[12]](cite://12/1) Opposition parties — Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori — have indicated their opposition, with some promising to repeal the changes. [[13]](cite://13/1) The legislation remains deeply contested, touching on constitutional convention, Treaty obligations, and what it means to share a coastline in a bicultural nation.

Would you like to explore the history of Māori protest movements that have emerged in response to these legislative battles, including the famous 2004 hīkoi?

## Sources

[2] [Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill Passes Third Reading](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/thehouse/576781/a-question-of-intent-takutai-moana-bill-passes-third-reading)
[3] [Supreme Court allows appeal of customary marine title judgment](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/535465/supreme-court-allows-appeal-of-customary-marine-title-judgment)
[4] [Government Forges Ahead with Foreshore and Seabed Law Despite Supreme Court Ruling](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/569058/government-forges-ahead-with-foreshore-and-seabed-law)
[5] [Ngātiwai Rangatira Speaks Out After Ejection from Foreshore and Seabed Debate](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/575505/ko-wai-hoki-ratou-ngatiwai-rangatira-speaks-out-after-ejection-from-foreshore-and-seabed-debate)
[6] [Changes to Customary Marine Title: Government Bill Criticized as 'Deeply Reckless'](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/532363/changes-to-customary-marine-title-deeply-reckless-law-expert)
[7] [Man removed from Parliament's gallery during foreshore and seabed debate](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/575439/man-removed-from-parliament-s-gallery-during-foreshore-and-seabed-debate)

1.document_title: Māori Land Rights, Indigenous Law, and Colonial Legislation in New Zealand: A Historical and Legal Analysis
1.document_summary:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

2.text:
[Page 13] For many years there was a legal argument that New Zealand courts had incorrectly interpreted Māori rights to the seabed and foreshore. This was tested when Ngāti Apa took a case arguing that Māori could have customary rights to both. Ultimately the Court of Appeal ruled that the Māori Land Court was able to decide on these rights. Before Ngāti Apa could have their day in court, the Labour government moved to overturn the Court of Appeal decision by statute. This led to a foreshore and seabed protest hīkoi in 2004.

2.document_title: Ngā rōpū tautohetohe – Māori Protest Movements: Land Rights, Cultural Activism, and Anti-Apartheid Resistance in New Zealand
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of Māori protest movements in New Zealand from the 19th century through the 2010s. It chronicles historic land rights protests including Hōne Heke Pōkai's flagpole cutting (1844-45), Parihaka land protests (1880s), the 1975 hīkoi led by Whina Cooper, the 506-day Bastion Point occupation (1977-78), Raglan golf course protests, and the Ihumātao occupation (2016-2020). The document details cultural rights campaigns including the 1972 Māori language petition leading to Māori Language Day, the He Taua confrontation against mock hakas (1979), and the establishment of the tino rangatiratanga flag. It covers Waitangi Day protests beginning with Ngā Tamatoa's 1971 activism and the significant 1984 hīkoi. The document addresses Māori opposition to apartheid South Africa, particularly the 1981 Springbok tour protests. Key government policies protested include the 1961 Hunn Report, the 1995 fiscal envelope, and the 2004 Foreshore and Seabed Act. Major outcomes include the establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), land returns through treaty settlements, the formation of the Māori Party, and the repeal of the Foreshore and Seabed Act through the Marine and Coastal Area Act 2011.

3.document_title: Kāwanatanga: Māori Governance, Colonial Authority, and Modern Challenges in New Zealand
3.document_summary: This document explores kāwanatanga, the Māori concept of governance and state authority, tracing its evolution from the 19th century to contemporary times. It begins with the 1835 Declaration of Independence by northern chiefs asserting sovereign power, followed by the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi where a critical translation discrepancy emerged—"kāwanatanga" was translated as "absolute sovereignty" in English, potentially misrepresenting chiefs' understanding. The document details colonial government strategies to assert kāwanatanga over Māori, including military interventions by governors like FitzRoy, Gore Browne, and Grey to suppress resistance over land ownership and the Māori King movement. Key mechanisms of colonial control included the Native Land Court (1865) which converted collective tribal land ownership to individual titles facilitating European acquisition, four Māori parliamentary seats (1867) that incorporated Māori into colonial governance while limiting influence, and co-option of chiefs through councils. Despite these controls, Māori maintained nationalist movements like Kīngitanga and Kotahitanga. From the 1970s onwards, the Waitangi Tribunal investigated Treaty breaches, leading to policy shifts including Māori language revitalization, treaty settlements, and a bicultural framework. Modern challenges persist, particularly regarding Māori rights and the 2004 foreshore and seabed legislation claiming Crown ownership, which prompted over 30,000 Māori and supporters to march on Parliament. This was replaced in 2011 by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, generating further controversy regarding the balance between Crown authority and Māori interests.

This in turn prompted the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, which regulated title to the foreshore and the seabed, effectively reserving both for the Crown. The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 restored iwi ’s ability to seek customary rights and title in court.

4.document_title: Marlborough Region: Comprehensive Geography, History, Geology, and Economic Development
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's Marlborough region across multiple dimensions. Geographically, the rectangular region in the north-east South Island features the Marlborough Sounds, Kaikōura ranges, and Wairau plain, with a sunny climate and major towns of Blenheim and Picton. Geologically, the Alpine Fault marks where Pacific and Australian tectonic plates collide, causing significant seismic activity including the 1848 magnitude 7.5 earthquake and 2016 magnitude 7.8 earthquake. Rock formations exceed 200 million years old. Historically, Māori settled coastal areas following 13th-century Polynesian settlement at Wairau Bar, with European exploration beginning with Abel Tasman (1642-43) and James Cook (1770), followed by whaling (1830s-1840s) and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Economic development evolved from pastoral farming and extractive industries (sawmilling, gold rushes, flax harvesting) to modern sectors including aquaculture (green-lipped mussels, salmon, abalone), wine production (Sauvignon blanc since 1973), and tourism. Key infrastructure includes the 1962 Wellington-Picton ferry and 1965 Cook Strait power cable. As of 2013, the region had 46,968 residents (85.2% European, 11.4% Māori), with 17.3% employed in agriculture versus 5.7% nationally. The region maintains rich cultural heritage with notable literary figures and sporting traditions dating to the 1850s-1860s.

7.document_title: Māori Land Tenure and Customary Rights Systems
7.document_summary: This document explores the traditional Māori system of land tenure and property rights known as "take whenua." Land was historically held communally by tribal groups (hapū) with individual and family use rights for specific purposes. Key principles included discovery (whenua kite hou), ancestral rights (take tupuna), conquest (take raupatu), and gifting (take tuku). Mana whenua refers to tribal authority over land and water bodies. Continuous occupation (ahi kā), symbolized by keeping fires burning, was essential to maintain land rights. The principle of ringa kaha meant victors had to actively defend conquered lands. Abandonment caused rights to diminish from ahi kā to ahi tere to ahi mataotao. Land transfers included conditions confirmed through ceremonies and taonga (treasures). The Native Land Court, established in 1865, resolved disputes but often simplified Māori customs, preferring conquest-based claims. By 1847, Chief Justice William Martin noted Māori had appropriated all valuable land through these customary systems. The system was fluid and accommodated changing tribal relationships, with disputed lands arising from migration and inter-tribal marriage.

8.document_title: New Zealand Aquaculture: Industry Overview, Farming Practices, and Regulatory Framework
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth analysis of New Zealand's aquaculture industry, covering its development, major farming practices, and regulatory landscape. The industry, valued at $280 million by 2001, primarily focuses on three export species: green-lipped mussels, quinnat salmon, and Pacific oysters. Green-lipped mussels are cultivated using the Japanese longline system, becoming New Zealand's second most important seafood export by 2000, sold to over 60 countries. Salmon farming evolved through three methods: ocean ranching (1976), sea-cage ranching (1983) in Big Glory Bay and Marlborough Sounds, and freshwater farming in South Island hydroelectric canals, producing 8,500 tonnes in 2001 with 65% exported. Pacific oysters, cultivated starting in 1970, reached 3,500 tonnes annually by 2001 and generated $13.6 million in exports. Additional species include pāua shellfish, scallops, and sea horses. The industry operates under a dual licensing system managed by regional councils and the Ministry of Fisheries, with a government moratorium on marine farm expansion by 2002. Key challenges include regional concentration, toxic algal blooms, and tensions between farmers and Māori groups regarding seabed ownership. Despite these challenges, the industry has strong future prospects for diversifying into high-value species such as pāua, kingfish, and crayfish.

11.document_title: Māori Land Court: Historical Evolution and Legislative Development from Treaty of Waitangi to Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the complete history and evolution of the Māori Land Court (Te Kōti Whenua) and Māori land tenure in New Zealand from the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) through 1993. The document covers three major periods: (1) The transformation from communal tribal land ownership to individual titles following the Native Lands Act 1862, which established courts to issue legal titles and introduced the 10-owner rule, resulting in massive land alienation—by the early 20th century, only 2 million of 27 million hectares remained in Māori ownership; (2) The legislative evolution from 1873-1909, including the abolition of the 10-owner rule under the Native Lands Act 1873, which inadvertently created fragmented titles with numerous owners, and the passage of approximately 560 acts dealing with Māori land, despite protective measures like the "taihoa" policy, over 800,000 hectares were sold; (3) The transformation from 1920-1993, where by 1920 only 19 acres per Māori remained, prompting the court to shift from land acquisition to land development support, culminating in the Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993—the first Māori land legislation referencing the Treaty of Waitangi and emphasizing land retention and development. The court's primary objectives evolved from facilitating land transfers to retaining Māori land ownership and promoting effective land use, while maintaining jurisdiction over marae governance and cultural matters.

New Zealand's evolution from a British colony to an independent nation is traced through the establishment of self-government in 1856, adoption of the Statute of Westminster in 1947, and the Constitution Act of 1986. The document covers state sector governance including 38 departments/ministries, Crown entities, and state-owned enterprises. 14.document_title: Rātana Church: History, Organization, and Legacy in New Zealand
14.document_summary: This document explores the Rātana Church, a major Māori spiritual and political movement founded by Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana (1873-). Following a divine vision in 1918, Rātana became a renowned healer, attracting thousands to Rātana Pā near Whanganui. He established Te Haahi Rātana in 1925, blending Christian theology with Māori spiritual elements symbolized by the five-pointed star and crescent moon. Rātana combined spiritual leadership with political activism, championing Māori rights and Treaty of Waitangi grievances. In 1924, he led a delegation to London with a 45,000-signature petition to King George V. By 1936, the church allied with the Labour Party, securing all four Māori Parliamentary seats by 1943—a dominance lasting 50 years. Organizationally, the church is governed by the Kōmiti Haahi Matua and a synod meeting annually at Easter, with 127 parishes and 160 registered apostles in New Zealand plus an Australian branch. Annual January birthday celebrations at Rātana Pā attract thousands and serve as both religious and political forums, featuring robed groups, seven brass bands, and choirs. By 2018, the church had over 40,000 members in New Zealand and thousands in Australia, making it the largest Māori denomination.

15.document_title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to Modern Legal Recognition
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

From the 1970s onwards, New Zealand underwent bicultural and multicultural transformation, highlighted by the 1981 Springbok rugby tour, the Waitangi Tribunal's establishment (1975), Māori cultural renaissance and language revitalization, and the emergence of significant Pasifika and Asian populations.

17.document_title: Anti-Racism Activism and Treaty of Waitangi in New Zealand: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to the 21st Century
17.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of racism and anti-racism activism in New Zealand from the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) through the early 21st century. It examines how systemic racism persisted through discrimination in housing, employment, sports, and institutions despite the Treaty's promise of equal rights for Māori. The document details key anti-racism movements including the Citizens' All Black Tour Association (1959), Citizens Association for Racial Equality (1964), HART (1969), and Māori-led organizations like Ngā Tamatoa and the Polynesian Panthers. 18.document_title: New Zealand Lakes: Formation, Ecology, Management, and Māori Land Rights
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's 775 lakes (at least 0.5 km long), covering their formation, ecology, management, and Māori land rights. Lake Taupō is the largest at 623 km², while Lake Hauroko is the deepest at 462 meters. Lakes form through diverse processes: 38% by glaciers (South Island), 16% by rivers, 15% by dunes, 8% artificially, and others by volcanoes, landslides, and coastal barriers. Glacial lakes like Tekapo display distinctive turquoise colors. The document details lake ecosystems including water level dynamics, seiches (20-55 minute oscillations), seasonal turnover, and food chains based on phytoplankton. Native fauna includes fish species, freshwater crayfish, and waterfowl such as ducks, grebes, and introduced species like black swans and Canada geese. Environmental challenges include nutrient overload from agricultural runoff and sewage causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion, particularly affecting lakes near Rotorua and Te Waihora since the 1950s. Recreational uses include boating, fishing, waterskiing, and game-bird hunting, managed by Fish and Game New Zealand. The document explores complex legal ownership of lake beds under the Treaty of Waitangi, highlighting the 1992 Crown return of Lake Taupō's bed to Ngāti Tūwharetoa and the 2006 agreement for Rotorua lakes. Water use is regulated under the Resource Management Act 1991 by regional and unitary councils with sustainability goals.

19.document_title: Northland Region, New Zealand: Comprehensive Geography, History, Society, and Development
19.document_summary:
This comprehensive document provides an in-depth examination of Northland, New Zealand's northernmost region spanning 330 kilometres from Auckland to Cape Rēinga with 1,700 kilometres of coastline. The region features unique landscapes including sand dunes, harbours, and bays, with geological formations of greywacke blocks and ancient volcanic rocks. Northland's temperate, moist climate earns it the nickname "the winterless north" (summers 22-26°C, winters 14-17°C).

The natural environment is characterized by unique flora including pōhutukawa trees and kauri forests, and fauna such as North Island brown kiwi, kōkako, and rare birds. However, only 14% of native forest remains due to human activity and kauri dieback disease.

With a population of 151,692 (2013), Northland has 32.4% Māori representation, predominantly the Ngāpuhi tribe—the country's largest tribal group. Historically significant as New Zealand's birthplace, Northland was the first landing place for Māori voyagers around 1300 CE and site of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi. The region experienced major transformations through European contact (1769), the Musket Wars (1819-1820s), and systematic land purchases that resulted in Māori retaining less than 20% of northern lands by 1908.

Economically, Northland evolved from gum digging (1870-1935) to diversified industries including dairy farming (22.6% of NZ's dairy cows by 1960), horticulture, forestry, mining, manufacturing, oil refining at Marsden Point (closed 2022), fishing, and aquaculture (35% of NZ's Pacific oysters). Infrastructure includes 6,600km of roads, three commercial airports, and major ports at Whangārei and Marsden Point.

Socially, Northland faces challenges including high unemployment (9.7% in 2013), low incomes, and socioeconomic deprivation (43% in most deprived category). Health disparities persist with Māori life expectancy 9 years lower than non-Māori. The region boasts vibrant cultural contributions from renowned artists like Colin McCahon and Friedensreich Hundertwasser, and notable authors including William Satchell and Jane Mander. Livestock statistics for 2012 show Northland accounting for 9.7% of national livestock numbers.

20.document_title: Māori Organisations: Evolution, Activism, and Cultural Development in New Zealand
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori organisations from the 19th century through the modern era. It covers traditional tribal structures (whānau, hapū, iwi) and pan-tribal organisations formed in response to land alienation, including the United Tribes of New Zealand (1835), the Kīngitanga (King Movement), and Kotahitanga movements. The document details post-WWII developments including rapid urbanisation (80% rural in 1950 to 80% urban by 1980), support organisations like the Māori Women's Welfare League (1951) and New Zealand Māori Council (1962), and major protest movements including the 1975 land march, 1977-78 Bastion Point occupation, and 1984 hīkoi to Waitangi. Educational initiatives are extensively covered, including te reo activism, kōhanga reo, kura kaupapa Māori, and tertiary institutions like Te Wānanga o Raukawa and Te Wānanga o Aotearoa. From the 1970s onwards, the document documents cultural institutions including Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori (1987), iwi radio stations (1989-1994), and Māori Television (2004), alongside urban marae, health services, sports organisations, and business entities. The Waitangi Tribunal's establishment in 1975 and subsequent claims led to significant settlements and Māori-led institutions, with major tribal holdings now controlling billions in assets.

[Page 17] Political appetite—for blue carbon, at least—is not a problem here. New Zealand First’s coalition agreement with the National Party promises to “progress work to recognise other forms of carbon sequestration, including blue carbon”. The Ministry for the Environment is already investigating including blue carbon in New Zealand’s greenhouse gas inventory and our Emissions Trading Scheme. Elizabeth Macpherson, a professor of law at the University of Canterbury, plans to spend the next five years mapping the legal and policy context of blue carbon schemes. Our coastlines and oceans are subject to interlocking local, national, and international laws, property rights and customary rights, she says. Throw in unresolved Treaty of Waitangi claims and evolving court decisions. “It gets super complex really quickly.” Her research, in partnership with Ngāi Tahu, will have a particular focus on how rangatiratanga might be embedded in blue carbon legislation and action. Macpherson—a former Treaty lawyer—knows that any exploration of blue carbon risks opening old wounds, especially those inflicted during the bitter fight over rights to the foreshore and seabed 20 years ago. “It’s extremely important that we don’t repeat any of the historical mistakes that we’ve made in terms of overriding Māori rights, interests and authority,” she says. The prospect of using blue carbon schemes to pay to restore areas of coast is promising, she says, but would have to be set up with care and foresight. “This has to be right for our place.”

21.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
21.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

22.document_title: Marine Reserves and Ocean Conservation in New Zealand: From Local Protection to Global Models
22.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's pioneering role in marine conservation through marine reserves and no-take zones. It chronicles Bill Ballantine's groundbreaking work establishing the first marine reserve at Goat Island Bay in 1977, which demonstrated dramatic ecological recovery despite initial opposition. Key case studies include the Whangarei Harbour Marine Reserve created through a 14-year campaign by Kamo High School students, and Fiordland's community-based protection model involving commercial fishers, tourism operators, Māori, and conservationists. The collection highlights marine reserves as "underwater stud farms" enabling ecosystem restoration through spillover effects and larval export, and as "wet libraries" serving as scientific benchmarks for ocean health. New Zealand's 31 no-take zones covering 8% of coastal waters represent 40 years of conservation experience inspiring global initiatives. Evidence demonstrates marine protection is essential for fisheries sustainability, with fish biomass increasing significantly inside reserves and adjacent areas. The documents emphasize addressing shifting baseline syndrome, strategic ecosystem-based reserve networks, and the need for increased ocean protection (20-50% no-take zones) to prevent fish stock collapse and preserve marine biodiversity.

23.document_title: The Queen Elizabeth II National Trust: Private Land Conservation and Heritage Protection in New Zealand
23.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection chronicles the Queen Elizabeth II National Trust's 25-26 year mission to protect New Zealand's natural and cultural heritage through private land covenants. Founded in 1977 by Waikato farmers Gordon and Celia Stephenson, the QEII Trust has enabled nearly 1,700 landowners to establish permanent protection agreements on over 70,000-75,000 hectares of land. The collection features multiple case studies demonstrating the covenant system's success, including Arthur Cowan's native forest restoration, the Perry and Harwood families' multi-covenant properties, and specialized conservation efforts protecting kiwi birds at Aroha Island, white-flippered penguins at Flea Bay, and paleontological sites with dinosaur fossils. The covenants protect diverse ecosystems including native bush, wetlands, archaeological sites, and wildlife habitats while allowing landowners to retain property ownership and engage in sustainable land use and ecotourism. Unlike overseas programs reliant on financial incentives, the QEII Trust operates on voluntary participation driven by conservation values, with a remarkable 98% compliance rate. The system has evolved from a grassroots initiative to mainstream conservation practice, with government funding reaching $3 million by 2003. Public access provisions enable community recreation while protecting sensitive ecosystems. The trust's collaborative, farmer-led governance approach treats conservation as shared responsibility rather than confrontational activism, creating a "quilt" of protected biodiversity across New Zealand's 16 million hectares of private rural land.

24.document_title: A Link to the Tropics: Ancient Submerged Islands and New Zealand's Geological Heritage
24.document_summary: A 2002 scientific cruise off New Zealand's Northland coast discovered evidence of ancient submerged islands that may have formed a land bridge for organisms reaching New Zealand. Led by Rick Herzer from the Institute of Geological and Nuclear Sciences, the expedition used seismic profiling and rock dredging to study the Northland Plateau. Key findings include flat-topped seamounts with erosion patterns indicating former land surfaces, shallow-water limestone with lagoon fossils, and rare high-grade schist and granite samples. Isotope analysis suggests these rocks underwent significant uplift (over 10 km) between 23-21 million years ago. The discovery supports the theory of an ancient archipelago extending from New Caledonia to Northland, which may have facilitated plant and animal migration to New Zealand. This challenges conventional understanding of New Zealand's evolutionary history, suggesting ongoing fauna and flora migration occurred after the country reemerged from the sea, with major implications for understanding the nation's biological development.

25.document_title: Submarine Frontier: New Zealand's Continental Shelf Project and Maritime Expansion
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's Continental Shelf Project and strategic maritime expansion. New Zealand possesses the world's fifth-largest Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) covering 4 million km², vastly exceeding its land area. The country has transitioned from agriculture-based to a diverse economy incorporating multibillion-dollar fishing, aquaculture, marine engineering, and ecotourism industries. The decade-long Continental Shelf Project (NZCSP), initiated in 1996, determined the outer edge of the continental shelf under UNCLOS Article 76, allowing coastal states to claim extended continental shelves beyond 200 nautical miles if geological linkage to their landmass can be demonstrated. The project involved comprehensive data collection from the Royal New Zealand Navy, GNS Science, and NIWA, employing multi-beam sonar, seismic-reflection geophysics, and sea-floor sampling across five contiguous areas including the Lord Howe Rise, Three Kings Ridge, and Chatham Rise. New Zealand's tectonically active margin, characterized by ridges, plateaux, and seamounts formed by plate collision, positions it advantageously to claim 1-2 million km² of extended continental shelf beyond the 200 nm EEZ. This extension grants sovereign economic rights over seabed resources including hydrocarbons, minerals, and sedentary organisms valuable for pharmaceutical research. New Zealand has negotiated maritime boundaries with Australia (treaty signed 2004) and continues negotiations with Fiji and Tonga.

26.text:
[Page 15] Another positive development has been the extension of marine protection to the open ocean. In 2007 the New Zealand government created a network of protected areas spanning 1.2 million square kilometres of the nation’s deep sea—30 per cent of the EEZ. The 17 benthic protection areas (BPAs) that make up the network are off limits to bottom trawling and dredging, in recognition of the destructiveness of these forms of fishing. (Scraping the seabed to catch fish has been likened to clearcutting the forest to catch deer.) Nearly half of New Zealand’s 250 seamounts—undersea islands that are likely bristling with undiscovered species—gain some protection under this measure, though midwater and surface organisms do not: fishing at these depths remains acceptable in the BPAs. Critics of the new network, however, say it is of marginal conservation relevance. Most of the BPAs are beyond current trawlable depth (about a thousand metres), so protection is being conferred on environments that are not under threat. Currently trawled areas of biodiversity importance, by contrast, have been largely excluded from the network. In exchange for giving up areas of seabed that were not going to be fished anyway, the fishing industry gained a political reprieve: the government agreed to delay establishment of further MPAs in the EEZ until at least 2013—a decision made without public consultation, notes Ballantine, and with no reason given.

27.document_title: Poor Knights Islands: Marine Conservation, Underwater Exploration, and Ecotourism
27.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the Poor Knights Islands off New Zealand's Northland coast, recognized by Jacques Cousteau as one of the world's top 10 dive spots. It chronicles the 25-year struggle to establish full marine protection, from the initial 1981 marine reserve designation with only 5% no-take zones to complete protection achieved in 1998 following a High Court judicial review. The islands occupy a unique oceanographic intersection between temperate and subtropical waters, featuring distinctive underwater architecture including arches, caves, and Rikoriko, the world's largest sea cave. Geologically, the islands are eroded remnants of a volcano that erupted 2-10 million years ago. The document details exceptional marine biodiversity resulting from proximity to the warm East Auckland Current, which delivers tropical organisms to the region. Pioneering 1960s-70s divers including Bill Palmer (who identified 13 new mollusk species) and Kelly Tarlton conducted early underwater expeditions at depths up to 60m, discovering remarkable species such as diadema urchins, paper nautilus, giant salps, and Sandager's wrasses. Post-protection research demonstrates significant ecological recovery: snapper abundance increased 14-fold between 1999-2001, with other species rebounding including kingfish and bronze whalers. The reserve exemplifies successful compromise between conservation and commercial interests, generating approximately 10 million dollars locally through ecotourism while supporting ongoing research on stingray populations and sustainable tourism levels.

28.document_title: Sea Change: Marine Management and Conservation in Aotearoa New Zealand
28.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's marine resource management, conservation, and governance challenges. 30.text:
[Page 26] In 2003, the Pew Oceans Commission wrote that two things are necessary to solve the ocean’s problems: better awareness and better governance. Better awareness crashed into public consciousness in 2011, when the container ship Rena struck a reef and disgorged its oil and contents into the Bay of Plenty. Incredibly, three years later, that toxic chalice is still languishing in the bay. It’s not going anywhere until the Environment Court hears the owner’s request to leave it there. Better awareness comes in quieter ways, too, as people abandon the “inexhaustibility hypothesis”—the mistaken idea that the ocean is so vast and bountiful nothing humans can do will seriously deplete it. Better governance, in New Zealand’s case, means developing an integrated oceans policy and reforming the country’s scattershot marine legislation. “There are 18 main statutes, 14 agencies, and six government strategies for marine management and planning in New Zealand,” notes a 2012 report by Monterey marine policy specialist Michael McGinnis. Lack of integration makes it expensive and uncertain for commercial enterprises to operate in the marine area and for the government to plan and manage. “It has led to messy, poor decision making,” Gary Taylor tells me when I visit the Environmental Defence Society’s offices on Auckland’s North Shore. Kids, a beach, some noisy gulls—there may be no more idyllic New Zealand summer scene. But the idyll is threatened—from without, in the form of exotic invaders and climate impacts, and from within, with rising levels of sediments, nutrients and contaminants pouring off the land. The sea has never been as impervious to human impact as we had thought. Increasingly, our footprint leaves its mark, and the tides cannot erase it. How lightly can we tread to sustain our encircling seas? One of the reasons for ad hoc marine governance, says Taylor, is that for a long time not much was happening in the marine realm except fishing. Now, with a surge of interest in the economic possibilities of the Exclusive Economic Zone, the need for strategic planning and environmental management has become urgent. “This is brought home quite clearly in the Chatham Rock Phosphate application to mine over an area of benthic reserve,” says Taylor. “They’re able to do that because the protected status of that area is not recognised in the EEZ Act. It’s in the Fisheries Act. So that’s an example of two pieces of legislation governing the same place.”

40.text: Milford Sound: A vertical, seemingly never-ending wall plummets into unseen depths in Greenstone Bay on the southern side of Milford Sound, where a surface layer of water stained dark with tannins encourages various deepwater organisms to live near the surface. These include large black coral trees, gorgonian fans and brachiopods—living fossils that are virtually unchanged from those that appeared 500 million years ago in the early Cambrian and are normally only found in the deep polar regions of the world. A red hydracoral (Errina novaezelandiae), this one found in a sand pocket at 16 m on a rocky ledge of Greenstone Bay, looks like a good place to forage to a hungry gastropod. The fiord is 16 km long and connects to the Tasman Sea at St Anne Point, where girdled and scarlet wrasse abound.

42.text:
[Page 1] 'Ko wai hoki rātou?': Ngātiwai rangatira speaks out after ejection from foreshore and seabed debate ByTnatanahira Māori news journalist 2025 10 10 07:26:34+13:00 Iwi leader speaks out after ejection from Parliament during tense foreshore debate Aperahama Edwards was removed from Parliament's gallery on Thursday for interrupting a debate on proposed changes to the law governing the foreshore and seabed. File picture. Ngātiwai rangatira Aperahama Edwards says the government has no authority to push through a law that would make it harder for Māori to win customary marine title to the foreshore and seabed. Edwards, chair of the Ngātiwai Trust Board, was removed from Parliament's gallery on Thursday for interrupting a debate on proposed changes to the law governing the foreshore and seabed. The government is forging ahead with plans to make it harder for Māori to get customary marine title (CMT), with Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith saying the changes would restore the legislation to its "original intent". That's despite objections from former Attorney General and National MP Chris Finlayson, who says the changes would not restore Parliament's "original intent" and be "extremely harmful" to race relations in New Zealand. Edwards was removed after calling out after a speech by ACT's Todd Stephenson who was speaking in support of the amendments. "What we want to make sure is that actually the intention of this house is restored," Stephenson said, before the interjection. Edwards has been a staunch opponent to the proposed changes and was a claimaint in an urgent Waitangi Tribunal inquiry, who recommended the Crown halt all efforts to amend the law. Speaking to RNZ, Edwards said he was in Wellington to attend a conference commemorating 50 years since the formation of the Waitangi Tribunal. "We knew that the second reading was coming up but we weren't sure of the time, and while we were down there we were alerted that it had been brought forward. "We thought we'd shoot back. I promised myself we were just going to listen," said. He said the debate was a "brazen unmasking of the underlying drivers" behind the push to reset the test. "There were points articulated that I don't believe have been articulated in that fashion before and I found that quite disturbing. "The whole thing is just ludicrous and it's offensive and, by and large, it's the biggest raupatu (confiscation/theft) that Te Ao Māori have faced." Edwards said Ngātiwai would never accept the government excercising an authority they do not believe they have. "Ko wai hoki rātou? Who do they think they are?" he said. The debate Speaking on behalf of Paul Goldsmith at the debate, Simon Watts said Marine and Coastal Area Act was established in 2011 to recognise Māori rights and manage the interests of all New Zealanders. Watts said the Supreme Court's decision to overturn a previous ruling by the Court of Appeal which effectively made it easier for Māori to get CMT showed the government was right to be concerned. "The bill provides the necessary clarification because it goes further than the Supreme Court in crucial ways, including more tightly defining what exclusive use in occupation means, requiring the courts to base any inferences on firm physical evidence, not on cultural association alone, and placing the burden of proof more squarely on applicants," he said. If the amendments are made, cases that are still live before the courts or undetermined would need to meet the higher threshold set by the government's new legislation. "In the government's view, retrospectively applying the amendment test is necessary to have as many applicants as possible decided under a test that appropriately captures Parliament's original intent," Watts said. He said the government had approved $15 million to help with rehearing costs. Labour's Peeni Henare blasted the government's approach, comparing it to the recent pay equity changes. "Now we're saying not only are we going to change the rules while everyone's playing the game, but we're going to push you all back to the start line. Why does this sound familiar to our people in the House here? That's what they did on equity pay equity," he said. "For anybody who's been through the process of proving either customary title or any kaupapa through a settlement, the proof of burden rests with the iwi, rests with the hapū, rests with the whānau, rests with the claimants. I can say to this House that that proof of burden is extremely high, and it takes years and years for that evidence to be built and for that case to be brought in front of the court, he said. Te Pāti Māori MP Tākuta Ferris pointed out that the reason his party was formed was in response to the controversial Foreshore and Seabed Act, which gave ownership of the coastline to the Crown except parts privately owned. That legislation was later replaced by the Marine and Coastal Areas (Takutai Moana) Act in 2011. Ferris said that was just a "band aid". "We get to this government, the Luxon led National government, and they don't like the band aid that was put on in 2011. They're ripping it off and taking everything with it. "We're proving a right that we didn't have to prove, because it was there in 2004 and an arrogant government took it away that's all this is, and here we are having to deal with it again," he said. Green MP and former Ngātiwai Trust Board chief executive Hūhana Lyndon said the government were "tearing up" Māori Crown relations at a time the nation should be celebrating. "We should be celebrating 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal, Oriini Kaipara coming into the House... but instead we're here fighting against a legislation that is the biggest raupatu against iwi Māori in the history of Aotearoa, because this is an uncaring government." "This government cares more about the property rights of Pākehā than the Māori. Why can't Māori have property rights?" she asked. The debate is set to resume at Parliament's next sitting day. In August, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith indicated to RNZ he wanted the law change to pass before October. 44.document_title: Marine and Coastal Rights Law Changes Not Justifiable, Former United Future Leader Says
44.document_summary: Former MPs who supported the 2011 Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act are criticizing the coalition government's proposed amendments to toughen customary rights tests for Māori. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon claims the changes restore Parliament's original intent following a 2023 Court of Appeal ruling that made it easier for groups to win customary title. However, former Attorney-General Chris Finlayson and former United Future leader Peter Dunne argue the amendments are unjustifiable and would undermine the original legislation's purpose. The changes would require continuous exclusive use and ownership since 1840, raising the already high bar for proving customary connection. Dunne contends the Supreme Court has already clarified the original intent and reopening this issue risks reigniting historical wounds around foreshore and seabed rights that sparked the formation of Te Pāti Māori.

45.text:
[Page 1] Government forges ahead with foreshore and seabed law ByCraig Mcculloch Acting Political Editor 2025 08 05 14:33:37+12:00 Government forges ahead with foreshore and seabed law despite Supreme Court ruling Paul Goldsmith has welcomed Cabinet's move to press ahead with the law change. The government is forging ahead with plans to change the law governing New Zealand's foreshore and seabed, despite a Supreme Court ruling last year that appeared to undercut the rationale for the change. The proposed legislation stems from a clause in National's coalition deal with NZ First, which promised to revisit the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act. That commitment was driven by fears that a 2023 Court of Appeal decision could have made it significantly easier for Māori groups to win recognition of customary rights over parts of the coastline. The government introduced a bill to Parliament last year to prevent that, but it hit pause in December after the Supreme Court effectively overturned the earlier ruling. At the time, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith welcomed the development and said ministers would take time to reassess their plans. On Tuesday, Goldsmith confirmed to RNZ that Cabinet had agreed to press ahead with the law change regardless and to pass it before October. "Everybody in New Zealand has an interest in what goes on in the coastline, and we're trying our best to get that balance right." Goldsmith said he was not convinced that last year's Supreme Court ruling had set a high enough test for judging whether customary rights should be granted. "We've had a couple of cases that have been decided since then which have shown almost 100 percent of the coastline and those areas being granted customary marine title which confirmed to us that the Supreme Court test still didn't achieve the balance that we think the legislation set out to achieve." Asked whether he expected an upswell of protest, Goldsmith said that had been an earlier concern but: "time will tell". "There's been a wide variety of views, some in favour, some against, but we think this is the right thing to do." The legislation was one of the key objections raised by Ngāpuhi leaders last year when they walked out on a meeting with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon in protest. More than 200 applications for customary marine title are making their way through the courts. Under the amendment bill, any court decisions issued after 25 July 2024, will need to be reconsidered. That would appear to cover seven cases, involving various iwi from around the country. "I understand their frustration over that," Goldsmith said. "But we believe it is very important to get this right, because it affects the whole of New Zealand." Goldsmith said the government had set aside about $15 million to cover the additional legal costs. The Marine and Coastal Area Act was originally passed by the National led government in 2011, replacing the controversial Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, which had extinguished Māori customary rights in favour of Crown ownership. The 2004 law introduced by Helen Clark's Labour government provoked widespread protest and led to the creation of the Māori Party, now known as Te Pāti Māori. National's 2011 replacement declared that no one owned the foreshore and seabed but allowed Māori groups to seek recognition of their rights or "Customary Marine Title" through the courts or in direct negotiations with the Crown. Customary title recognises exclusive Māori rights to parts of the foreshore and seabed, provided certain legal tests are met, including proving continuous and "exclusive" use of the area since 1840 without substantial interruption. The 2023 Court of Appeal ruling, however, declared that groups only needed to show they had enough control over the area that they could keep others from using it, and that situations where the law itself had prevented them from doing so could be ignored. The Supreme Court subsequently overturned that and said the Court of Appeal had taken an unduly narrow approach in its interpretation. 46.document_title: Opposition Promises to Repeal Marine and Coastal Rights Law Changes
46.document_summary: The New Zealand coalition government has passed significant changes to the Marine and Coastal Area Act (MACA), which opposition parties have pledged to repeal if re-elected. Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith defended the changes as restoring the legislation's original intent by tightening the test for Māori to secure customary marine titles, requiring firmer physical evidence and placing greater burden of proof on applicants. The government allocated $15 million to support Māori groups with court costs. Opposition parties, including Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori, strongly criticized the bill, arguing it diminishes Māori rights and continues a legacy of treating Māori as second-class citizens. The changes override court decisions made after July 24, 2024, including a Supreme Court ruling that had made it easier for groups to win customary title.

49.document_title: Seabed Miner Slows Fast Track with 'Cynical' Response
49.document_summary: Australian company Trans-Tasman Resources has delayed its fast-track bid to mine the South Taranaki Bight seabed by failing to provide required information to officials. An expert panel of five specialists has been appointed to review the application under the Fast-Track Approvals Act. Panel convener Jennifer Caldwell criticized the company's "cynical" approach, noting their responses provided little assistance. The company proposed a 76-day timeline, but the panel will now take 130 working days, delivering a verdict in March 2026. Trans-Tasman Resources plans to extract 50 million tonnes of seabed annually for 20+ years, returning 45 million tonnes of sediment. The proposal has faced decade-long opposition from iwi authorities, local councils, and environmental groups over cultural and environmental concerns. The company's engagement with local Māori has been criticized, with the managing director stating they would work with iwi "whether they want us or not."

Customary marine title In 2011, the then National government introduced the Takutai Moana Act to replace the controversial Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004. Section 58 of the 2011 act set out the statutory test Māori groups must meet for recognition of their coastal rights, this is known as customary marine title (CMT). If CMT was granted, Māori could give or refuse permission for certain activities that required resource consent. Those rights applied from the high tide mark and up to 12 nautical miles out to sea. On 18 October 2023, just four days after the general election, the Court of Appeal issued a judgment determining how the courts should interpret section 58. In response to that decision, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith announced plans in July to amend section 58 in order "to make clear Parliament's original intent." In a private meeting with fisheries industry representatives, Goldsmith speculated a law change would reduce the area subject to CMT from 100 percent to 5 percent. He later defended those comments, saying they were part of "free flowing discussion" and not based on any analysis. In his letter to ministers Judge Miharo Armstrong, the head of the tribunal panel, said the Crown had failed to demonstrate how it had arrived at its understanding of "Parliament's original intent". Claimants also alleged funding for applications for CMT under the act had been mismanaged, which the tribunal said would be addressed in the next stage of the inquiry. Lawyers representing the Crown at the urgent inquiry said the amendment bill was expected to be tabled next week on Monday. 51.document_title: Waitangi Tribunal Finds Failings in Government's Handling of Marine and Coastal Area Act Changes
51.document_summary: The Waitangi Tribunal has found that government changes to the Marine and Coastal Area Act (Takutai Moana Act 2011) are characterized by blind adherence to political commitments at the expense of Māori whānau, hapū, and iwi. The tribunal's urgent inquiry report found the government dismissed official advice, failed to consult with Māori, and breached Treaty principles by not demonstrating "Parliament's original intent" before seeking amendments. The government consulted commercial fishing interests while excluding Māori, and proposed retrospective amendments would force iwi to rehear cases and create financial burdens. The tribunal recommended the Crown halt amendment efforts and engage meaningfully with Māori, focusing on resource consent permissions rather than disrupting customary marine title awards.

[Page 1] ByTnatanahira Māori news journalist, Pokere Paewai Māori issues reporter 2024 12 02 19:22:57+13:00 Supreme Court allows appeal of customary marine title judgment The Supreme Court says the decision taken by the Court of Appeal relating to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act in October was "unduly narrow". The Supreme Court has released its judgment on an appeal that made it easier for Māori to gain customary marine title under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act. In its judgement, the Supreme Court said the major decision by the Court of Appeal last October was "unduly narrow" and the court would hear the Attorney General's appeal so the court could "state the appropriate section 58 test afresh reflecting the text, purpose and legislative history of MACA". Under the act, common marine and coastal area cannot be owned, and public fishing, navigation and access rights within this area are protected. However, iwi, hapū and whānau groups can apply to have their customary rights recognised. Section 58 of the act sets out the test to obtain a customary marine title (CMT) in the common marine and coastal area, previously referred to as the foreshore and seabed. Last October a Court of Appeal decision found groups only needed to show they had enough control over the area that they could keep others from using it, and situations where the law itself had prevented them from doing so could be ignored. The government confirmed in July they would legislate around the Court of Appeal's decision with Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith saying at the time they would amend section 58 of the act to "make clear Parliament's original intent". It meant those seeking Customary Marine Title would again need to prove they have had continuous exclusive use and ownership of the area since 1840. In its ruling, the Supreme Court said it was concerned the three stage test did not adequately address MACA's "reconciliatory purpose" and stated the act's purpose was to recognise the rights of Māori under the Treaty of Waitangi and long held rights of other New Zealanders. Issues The Supreme Court identified four key issues around the interpretation of section 58 which formed the basis of its judgement. Among them were: Who "holds" the relevant area "in accordance with tikanga" Who has exclusively used and occupied the area "from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption"
