55.document_title: George Stoddart Whitmore: Military Commander, Colonial Administrator, and Māori War Historian
55.document_summary: George Stoddart Whitmore (1829-1903) was a British military officer and colonial administrator who played a pivotal role in New Zealand's conflicts with Māori forces. Born in Malta to a military family, he served in South Africa and the Crimean War before arriving in New Zealand in 1861. Whitmore became substantively involved in the New Zealand Wars from 1866, leading seven distinct campaigns as commander of colonial forces. His military strategy exploited European advantages in transportation and logistics, converting the Armed Constabulary into an effective counter-insurgency force. He demonstrated exceptional military ability, particularly in campaigns against Te Kooti and Tītokowaru. Whitmore held significant political positions including colonial secretary and was appointed major general in 1886, the first New Zealander to achieve that rank. He authored "The last Māori war in New Zealand under the self-reliant policy" (1902), a partisan yet well-written historical work. Despite his military accomplishments, Whitmore was widely disliked for his harsh methods and arrogance, maintaining distance from subordinates and holding contemptuous views toward the Māori.

57.document_title: Tītokowaru: A Māori Leader's Life, Legacy, and Historical Memory
57.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the life and enduring legacy of Tītokowaru (born c. 1823), a prominent Māori leader of Ngāti Ruanui in South Taranaki. Born as Riwha and descended from notable chiefs, Tītokowaru initially embraced Christianity as a Methodist convert around 1842, advocating for peace. However, between 1850-1854, he shifted toward Māori nationalism and opposition to land-selling. After losing his right eye at Te Mōrere in 1864, he succeeded Te Ua Haumēne as a spiritual leader, developing a syncretic religion blending Pai Mārire, Christianity, and traditional Māori beliefs. From 1867-1868, Tītokowaru orchestrated a remarkable peace campaign through meetings and envoys, successfully uniting fractious Māori factions. His military genius emerged during the 1868-1869 war against colonial forces, where he achieved significant victories at Te Ngutu-o-te-manu and Moturoa despite facing overwhelming odds of 12-to-1. At his peak, he controlled an 80-mile territory and commanded 1,000 followers. After 1869, he transitioned to peaceful resistance and non-violent activism alongside Te Whiti, orchestrating campaigns against land confiscation until his death in 1888. The document addresses how Tītokowaru's War has become a forgotten chapter in New Zealand history, with Pākehā society selectively forgetting this period. His prophetic legacy establishes him as arguably New Zealand's greatest general and an influential peacemaker.

58.text:
[Page 9] small force of colonial troops and 'friendly' Māori, captured a Māori supply depot at the rear of the pā , which the Māori promptly evacuated. This was hailed, not least by Grey, as a famous victory. In the later 1860s the British government determined to withdraw imperial troops from the colonies, and force them to accept responsibility for their own internal security. So numerous were the victories of Te Kooti , Tītokowaru and other Māori generals in 1868, however, that the government and the settlers were extremely alarmed. With the support of his ministers, Grey constantly evaded carrying out instructions to finalise the return of the regiments, which had commenced in 1865 and 1866. In the end the British government had little alternative but to terminate the appointment of so headstrong a governor in 1868. Grey soon went to England, where he failed in an attempt to enter Parliament as a Gladstonian Liberal. He then returned to New Zealand, where he lived in his splendid home on Kawau Island, in the Hauraki Gulf. From there he emerged in 1874 to lead the fight against Julius Vogel 's proposal to abolish the provincial governments set up under the 1852 Constitution. In 1875 Grey was elected superintendent of Auckland province and also to Parliament for Auckland City West. He fought vigorously in Parliament and in public to save the provinces, but without success. The Atkinson government persisted with abolition, but soon lost on a vote of no confidence over its lack of other policies. In October 1877 Grey became premier. His cabinet included some conservatives, as well as radicals such as John Ballance and Robert Stout . As he did not have a safe majority in the House, Grey asked for a dissolution, which was refused by the governor, Lord Normanby. Grey now stumped the country, stirring up considerable enthusiasm for radical causes, such as 'one man one vote'. However, in 1878 the country ran into a severe depression, which led to much unemployment. The next year the government lost a division in the House, and then failed to win a majority in the ensuing election. After the defection of four Auckland members, Grey resigned in October 1879. Grey's ministry had introduced one or two important measures, such as Stout's Trade Union Act, but it was not a success. Within the cabinet there were deep divisions. One problem was the New Zealand Agricultural Company, in which Stout was deeply involved. Grey believed that Stout had brought the government into disrepute by his association with a speculative land enterprise. He became extremely hostile to this company and its promoters, who included Julius Vogel as well as Stout and Grey's own former treasurer, William Larnach . He attacked it relentlessly. Nevertheless, when Stout later became premier in 1884 Grey hoped that he might be invited to join the government. He was not and was embittered by the alliance of Stout with Vogel in this administration.

59.document_title: Te Tuhi, Wiremu Pātara: A Māori Leader and Editor of Te Hokioi
59.document_summary: Te Tuhi (Wiremu Pātara) was a prominent Ngāti Mahuta leader and second cousin of Māori King Tāwhiao. Born in Waikato, he served as editor, warrior, secretary and adviser to the King. In 1861, he became editor of Te Hokioi e Rere Atu Nā, a newspaper that promoted the King movement and argued for a Treaty of Waitangi interpretation limiting colonial government sovereignty over Māori. The newspaper ceased publication when war began in July 1863. Te Tuhi fought in the Waikato campaign and went into exile with Tāwhiao until 1881. He later accompanied the King to England in 1884 and represented him at various conferences. Admired for his shrewdness and good nature by both Māori and Pākehā, Te Tuhi died at Māngere on 2 July 1910, aged 85-86.

[Page 1] In the 1850s, when the King movement rose to prominence as an attempt to consolidate Māori authority and halt land sales, Ngāpora's inclination was initially against an intertribal Māori kingship. However, when Te Wherowhero was installed as King and returned to live in Waikato, Ngāpora remained at Māngere to act as the King movement's representative to the governor. In 1861, when Sir George Grey returned to New Zealand as governor, Ngāpora arranged for leaders of the King movement to meet him. At the meeting Rewi Maniapoto insisted on recognition of the Māori King's independence, which Grey would not grant. In 1863 the dispute over sovereignty moved towards war. Ngāpora warned the governor that war parties were gathering to attack the government outpost of Te Ia (Havelock, near Mercer), and that there were plans for a surprise attack on Auckland. In July 1863 Māori north of the Mangatawhiri River were required to give an oath of allegiance to Queen Victoria, or leave for Waikato. Ngāpora considered this requirement to be insulting, and refused the oath. Soldiers looted Māori property and an atmosphere of open hostility developed. Disillusioned, Ngāpora returned to Waikato. Meanwhile, on 12 July, Lieutenant General Duncan Cameron and British troops had crossed the Mangatawhiri River to invade Waikato. Although he did not take part in the fighting in Waikato, after the war and the confiscation of Waikato land Ngāpora went into exile in the King Country with Te Wherowhero's son, Tāwhiao .

60.document_summary: Ngāpora (Tāmati) was a 19th-century Māori leader from Ngāti Mahuta who played a significant role in Waikato politics and the King movement. Born early in the 1800s, he participated in tribal conflicts and later became a Christian lay preacher and government assessor. Initially skeptical of intertribal kingship, he became a key adviser to King Te Wherowhero and later his successor Tāwhiao, whose wife was Ngāpora's daughter. During the 1860s Waikato Wars, he warned governors of military threats but ultimately refused an oath of allegiance and went into exile in the King Country. He remained influential within the King movement, advocating for full restoration of confiscated lands and opposing peace settlements he deemed inadequate. Ngāpora died in 1885 at approximately 80 years old, having maintained his position as a trusted counselor to the Māori King until his death.

chunkHighlights.text:
The New Zealand Wars were a series of mid-19th-century battles
between some iwi and government forces (which included British and colonial troops) and their Māori allies, who were sometimes known as kūpapa . Northland In March 1845, Ngāpuhi led by Hōne Heke Pōkai and Te Ruki Kawiti attacked Kororāreka (Russell). Their forces fought British troops and other Ngāpuhi led by Tāmati Wāka Nene until January 1846. Read more about the Northern war Wellington In July 1846 Governor George Grey arrested Ngāti Toa rangatira Te Rauparaha, who he accused of supporting attacks on settlers in Hutt Valley. Government forces pursued Ngāti Toa and their allies into the hills behind Pāuatahanui. Whanganui Tensions between Whanganui Māori and settlers were heightened in 1846–47 by the arrival of British troops, the wounding of a chief and the hanging of Māori who killed four Europeans. Upriver Māori attacked Whanganui town, but after a battle at St John’s Wood peace was agreed. Read more about the Wellington and Whanganui wars Taranaki Many Taranaki Māori opposed land sales, and fighting began in 1860 over a disputed land purchase at Waitara. The British army and Pākehā settlers fought local Māori until March 1861. In 1865 there were battles in South Taranaki, and in 1866 Major-General Trevor Chute led troops around Mt Taranaki, destroying Māori villages. Read more about the North Taranaki war Waikato Waikato was the home of the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement). The government wanted to punish the king's followers who had fought in Taranaki, and to make Waikato land available to settlers. Troops invaded in July 1863. Fighting continued until April 1864, when the Kīngitanga and its supporters withdrew into what became known as the King Country. Read more about the Waikato War Tauranga British troops were sent to Tauranga in 1864. Rāwiri Puhirake and Ngaī te Rangi repelled a British attack on Pukehinahina (Gate Pā ) but were later defeated at Te Ranga. Read more about Gate Pā, Tauranga Prophetic movements Māori prophetic movements emerged to resist land loss. Some tribes which opposed these movements formed alliances with the settler government. The
British government began to withdraw its troops. In 1864 supporters of
the Pai Mārire faith attacked British forces in Taranaki and were

defeated on Moutoa Island in the Whanganui River by Māori from down-river. Pai Mārire spread to the East Coast, where its supporters were defeated by local Māori and Pākehā forces. Read more about Pai Mārire, South Taranaki and Whanganui Tītokowaru Ngā Ruahine leader Riwha Tītokowaru wanted to stop the confiscation of Māori land in South Taranaki. He fought government troops and Whanganui Māori in 1868–69. Read more about Tītokowaru's war Te Kooti Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Tūruki (Rongowhakaata) was imprisoned on the Chatham Islands, where he developed the Ringatū faith. In July 1868 he escaped and returned to Poverty Bay with 297 followers. He fled inland and was pursued by Pākehā and Māori forces for nearly four years. A total of about 1 million hectares was initially taken from iwi which had fought against the Crown, although some land was later returned. Public awareness of the history of the wars has changed over the decades, particularly as new history books and television series have been released. The 150th anniversary of the Taranaki and Waikato wars saw revived interest in understanding and marking the wars and their long-term impact on the nation's history. Zealand Wars
New Zealand Wars overview

The New Zealand Wars were a series of mid-19th-century campaigns involving some iwi Māori and government forces, which included British and colonial troops and their Māori allies. The two major periods of conflict were the mid-1840s and the 1860s.
Naming the wars

Though ‘New Zealand Wars’ is the most common collective name for these campaigns, a number of others have been used. Originally Europeans called them the Māori wars. This echoed the tendency of the British to name wars after their enemies – as in Boer War and Zulu War. In the late 1960s thought was given to renaming the wars. One popular

suggestion was land wars, due to the importance of land in the disputes. Another was Anglo–Māori wars to indicate the two major groups involved. Other less common suggestions included New Zealand civil wars and sovereignty wars. Māori names for the wars have included Ngā pakanga o Aotearoa (the New Zealand Wars) and Te riri Pākehā (the white man’s anger).

fileAuthor: Claudia Orange, with contributions from multiple historians
2.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

ByClaudia Orange

What is te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi)? Te Tiriti o Waitangi
(the Treaty of Waitangi) was a written agreement made in 1840 between the British Crown (the monarch) and more than 500 Māori chiefs. After that, New Zealand became a colony of Britain and Māori became British subjects. However, Māori and Europeans had different understandings and expectations of te tiriti. Drafting and signing te tiriti Te tiriti was drafted in English and then translated into Māori by missionary Henry Williams and his son Edward. It was presented to around 500 Māori at Waitangi on 5 February 1840 and there was much debate. The next day, 6 February, more than 40 chiefs signed te tiriti. Copies of te tiriti were taken around the country, and many more chiefs signed. Most Māori signed the te reo tiriti. Reasons why chiefs signed te tiriti included wanting controls on sales of Māori land to Europeans, and on European settlers. They also wanted to trade with Europeans, and believed the new relationship with Britain would stop fighting between tribes. Those who did not sign te tiriti were concerned they would lose their independence and power, and wanted to settle their own disputes. Some chiefs never had the opportunity to sign it, as it was not taken to all regions. What did te tiriti say? The meaning of the English treaty was not exactly the same as the meaning of the Māori tiriti. Article One: in Māori it gave Queen Victoria governance over the land, while in English it gave her sovereignty over the land – a stronger term. Article Two: Te tiriti guaranteed chiefs ‘te tino rangatiratanga ’ – chieftainship over their lands, villages and treasured things. It also gave the Crown the right to deal with Māori in buying land. The English-language treaty gave chiefs ‘exclusive and undisturbed possession’ of lands, forests, fisheries and other property. It also gave the Crown an exclusive right to deal with Māori over buying land. Article Three: both versions gave Māori the queen’s protection and the rights of British subjects. Te tiriti in the 19th century Even though not all chiefs signed te tiriti, the British government decided it placed all Māori under British authority. It did not take long for conflicts to arise between Māori and European settlers who wanted more
land. The government often ignored the protections te tiriti was
supposed to give Māori. In 1858 some iwi (tribes) chose Waikato rangatira

3.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines Kotahitanga, the Māori political movements aimed at unifying Māori people on a non-tribal basis throughout New Zealand history. It traces the evolution from early movements including the 1834 Flag of the United Tribes and 1835 Declaration of Independence, through the foundational Treaty of Waitangi (1840), to the emergence of the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement) in 1858 under Pōtatau Te Wherowhero. The document details various unification pathways including religious movements such as Pai Mārire and the Rātana church, as well as multiple Māori parliaments that operated from the 1870s through the 1920s. It covers the formal Paremata Māori (Māori Parliament) established in 1892 and the Kīngitanga's Kauhanganui parliament. Twentieth-century developments include the Māori War Effort Organisation, Māori political parties (Mana Motuhake, Te Pāti Māori), the Māori Women's Welfare League, and the New Zealand Māori Council. The document also addresses protest movements of the 1970s-1980s advocating for land rights, language preservation, and human rights. Additionally, it discusses pan-Māori organizations providing health and social services to urban communities, such as the Manukau Urban Māori Authority (MUMA) and Te Whānau o Waipareira Trust in Auckland, demonstrating how Kotahitanga principles extend to contemporary community service provision regardless of tribal affiliation.

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history of racism and anti-racism activism in New Zealand from the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) through the early 21st century. It examines how systemic racism persisted through discrimination in housing, employment, sports, and institutions despite the Treaty's promise of equal rights for Māori. The document details key anti-racism movements including the Citizens' All Black Tour Association (1959), Citizens Association for Racial Equality (1964), HART (1969), and Māori-led organizations like Ngā Tamatoa and the Polynesian Panthers. A significant focus is the All Blacks' exclusion of Māori players from tours to apartheid South Africa starting in 1928, and the pivotal 1981 Springbok tour protests. The document highlights institutional responses including the Office of the Race Relations Conciliator (1971), Human Rights Commission (1977), and the Waitangi Tribunal (1985). It addresses institutional racism within judicial, education, health, and social welfare systems, and describes how the Treaty gained constitutional significance from the 1980s onward, with the Tribunal's expanded authority embedding treaty principles into over 30 legislative pieces affecting constitutional, economic, land, language, health, education, and justice matters.

5.fileDescription:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

chunkHighlights.text:
The Treaty of Waitangi In the early 19th century Māori still lived
according to a complex system of customary laws. The British began trying to introduce their own laws to Māori with the Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between rangatira (chiefs) and the British Crown. Some of the laws that followed took aspects of Māori custom into account, but the British lawmakers saw this as a temporary step and anticipated a time when Māori would be fully integrated into their society. Laws and land Māori did not see land as a commodity to be bought and sold by individuals, but as something over which groups could hold communal rights of guardianship, occupation and use. These rights were gained by various means including discovery, conquest and gift. They were maintained by continual occupation over generations. Colonial legislation clashed with and overrode that system. New laws declared that the government had the right to take any land that was not needed by Māori, and that Māori could sell or lease land only to the Crown. The government backed up its laws with military force, and the New Zealand wars began. The government passed laws allowing it to confiscate the land of Māori believed to be ‘in rebellion’. A century of law-making From 1862 the government passed laws ruling that Māori lands could only be held by individual owners, not collectively by iwi (tribes) or hapū (sub-tribes). This resulted in further Māori land loss. Native Land Courts were set up to investigate and decide on titles to Māori land. The court hearings were often time-consuming and expensive. Right into the 20th century, the government made laws that impeded Māori land ownership. Beginning to make amends In the 1970s a wave of Māori protest actions drew public attention to land-related grievances. The Waitangi Tribunal was formed in 1975 to investigate breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi. Since then, Māori have made further gains. In the 1990s environmental legislation began to take account of Māori historical, spiritual and
cultural concerns. The importance of the Māori relationship to land was
acknowledged in Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document collection examines 150 years of the Treaty of Waitangi's history and its impact on New Zealand law, governance, and Māori rights. Beginning with the treaty's signing on February 6, 1840, between British Governor William Hobson and Māori chiefs, the narrative explores critical discrepancies between English and Māori versions that created fundamentally different understandings of sovereignty and land rights. The document traces systematic treaty breaches from the colonial era through the 1980s, including Governor FitzRoy's abandonment of land purchase monopolies and widespread land confiscations. Key case studies include the Kaituna River pollution crisis, Waitara disputes, Waiuku Block confiscations, and the Ngati Whatua's struggle for Orakei land rights. The establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975 marked a turning point, providing mechanisms for Māori to seek redress and establishing the treaty's legal force through landmark decisions like the 1987 Court of Appeal ruling. The tribunal evolved from adjudicating rights to facilitating stakeholder dialogue, achieving practical remedies including the 1983 Fisheries Act restoration of Māori fishing rights and the Bastion Point settlement. Throughout, the narrative emphasizes that broken colonial promises continue to undermine Māori rights and wellbeing, while the tribunal's collaborative approach offers innovative solutions for resolving historical injustices.

8.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces New Zealand's transformation from a British Crown colony to a fully independent sovereign nation through constitutional developments spanning 1840 to 2003. Key milestones include the 1852 Constitution Act establishing provincial governments and bicameral parliament, the 1876 abolition of provincial governments, the 1907 granting of Dominion status, and the 1947 adoption of the Statute of Westminster confirming full constitutional autonomy. The document details the evolution of responsible government through Governor Thomas Gore Browne's 1856 establishment of "double government," where ministers answered to parliament on colonial matters while the governor retained imperial authority. Democratic achievements include the property-based franchise extended to miners (1860), Māori parliamentary representation through four seats (1867), and women's suffrage (1893). New Zealand's path to independence was marked by peaceful, incremental constitutional steps rather than revolutionary change, including the establishment of New Zealand citizenship (1948), abolition of the upper house (1951), creation of a separate royal title (1953, revised 1974), and establishment of the Supreme Court as the final court of appeal replacing the British Privy Council (2003). Despite these achievements, New Zealand maintained the shared monarch as head of state and retained Commonwealth ties, with ongoing discussions about becoming a republic.

chunkHighlights.text: New Zealand wars

But it was too late. A dispute over a seemingly minor piece of land at Waitara, in Taranaki, in 1860 became the spark for the decade-long New Zealand wars. While it was supplying military reinforcements, the British government was reluctant to relinquish control of Māori affairs. A further move came in 1861 after Sir George Grey returned for a second term as governor. A new ministry headed by William Fox deplored the system of double government, and Grey agreed to consult ministers in this as in other matters and to give greater responsibility to the General Assembly. But the big shift came when the British government found backing settler aggression more and more distasteful and expensive, and announced that imperial garrisons would be removed from self-governing colonies. British battalions could only be retained if they were paid for by the colony.

9.fileDescription: Robert FitzRoy (1805-1865) was a distinguished British naval officer and polymath whose career spanned naval exploration, colonial governance, and meteorological innovation. Born into aristocracy, he entered the Royal Navy in 1819 and achieved exceptional academic results at naval college. FitzRoy commanded HMS Beagle during two surveying voyages (1828-1836) along South American coasts, carrying naturalist Charles Darwin on the second voyage. His surveying work earned him a Royal Geographical Society gold medal in 1837. In 1843, he was appointed Governor of New Zealand, succeeding William Hobson. Facing a bankrupt colony and inter-racial tensions, FitzRoy pursued justice-based policies treating Māori land claims as legal rights. He issued debentures to address fiscal crises and waived pre-emption rights on Māori land. During the Bay of Islands conflict sparked by chief Hōne Heke in 1844, FitzRoy maintained government credibility despite limited military resources. Recalled in 1845 for issuing debentures without authorization, he returned to England where he defended his administration. Subsequently holding various naval positions, FitzRoy's most significant later contribution came in 1854 when he headed Britain's first weather office at the Board of Trade, virtually inventing the term "forecasting" and creating the FitzRoy barometer. Despite his considerable achievements in naval surveying and meteorology, FitzRoy struggled with mental health issues and took his own life in 1865. His legacy encompasses fair governance in New Zealand, excellence in naval exploration, and foundational contributions to modern meteorology.

chunkHighlights.text: FitzRoy was then called on to deal with New Zealand's first racial war, sparked off by the Bay of Islands chief Hōne Heke . Its causes were not of FitzRoy's making, arising rather from economic failure and the diminished importance of the Far North after the removal of the government to Auckland. The first overt act of significance was the cutting down of the flagstaff on Maiki Hill above Kororāreka on 8 July 1844. The war that followed was between Heke and his followers and the government, and between Heke and other Ngāpuhi, of whom Wāka Nene and Patuone were the most important. The military engagements spread over 18 months and were concluded by FitzRoy's successor, Grey, on 23 January 1846. 11.fileDescription: Sir George Grey (1812-1898) was a prominent 19th-century British colonial governor and scholar. Born in Lisbon to a military family, he received military training at Sandhurst and served in Ireland before embarking on colonial service. His early career included unsuccessful expeditions in Western Australia (1837-39) and service as resident magistrate at King George Sound. As governor of South Australia (1840-1845), he balanced budgets while expanding cultivation and exports, implementing Aboriginal assimilation policies. His most significant tenure was as governor of New Zealand (1845-1853), where he effectively managed Māori affairs, acquiring nearly 33 million acres through negotiated purchases while maintaining peace for over a decade. He promoted Māori education, appointed magistrates, and built hospitals. Grey was knighted in 1848 and enjoyed considerable influence among Māori chiefs. As governor of the Cape Colony (1853-1861), he addressed race relations through frontier wars, missionary efforts, and European settlement policies, managing the 1857 Xhosa cattle-killing crisis. Returning to New Zealand as governor (1861-1868), he implemented controversial indirect rule policies and pursued military campaigns in Taranaki and Waikato, resulting in significant land confiscation. His dismissal in 1868 led to a political career as premier (1877-1879), where he advocated for radical reforms including universal male suffrage and Pacific expansion. Beyond politics, Grey was an accomplished naturalist, manuscript collector, and scholar of Māori language and culture, establishing important libraries in Cape Town and Auckland. He opposed Australian federation at the 1891 Federal Convention and championed democratic reforms throughout his career. After leaving New Zealand in 1894, Grey returned to England where he died in 1898 and was buried in St Paul's Cathedral.

chunkHighlights.text:
In 1845 Grey was appointed governor of New Zealand, where he faced
even greater difficulties than in South Australia. The government was so short of funds that the first governor, William Hobson , had drawn unauthorised bills on the British Treasury and his successor, Robert FitzRoy , had, contrary to instructions, issued government debentures, a form of paper money. Even more serious, in several districts of the North Island, there had been violent disputes between settlers and Māori, especially over land claims. In Wellington, Nelson and Taranaki there had been conflict over disputed New Zealand Company land purchases. In Nelson the settlers tried to occupy the Wairau district in the face of opposition from Ngāti Toa. Twenty-two settlers and at least four Māori were killed when an armed party stupidly attempted to arrest the formidable chiefs Te Rauparaha and Te Rangihaeata . In the far north Hōne Heke and his ally, Kawiti , had risen in revolt against British authority. Heke feared that the Europeans would take all their land. He was responsible for cutting down the British flag on four occasions; on the last, both sides sacked Kororāreka (Russell). Fortunately for the British most of Ngāpuhi sided with the government. Even so, the British
had suffered a disastrous defeat at Ōhaeawai.

12.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand government policy toward Māori from pre-1840 through the 2000s. It covers early British intervention, the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, and the establishment of protectors of aborigines. Key developments include the Kīngitanga movement in 1858, the creation of the Native Department, Māori Affairs Department, and Te Puni Kōkiri. The document details Māori governance structures including rūnanga (tribal councils) and their limited recognition through the Māori Councils Act 1900. Significant policy shifts include the controversial 1953 and 1967 Acts affecting land ownership, the establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975, and the Māori renaissance of the 1970s-2000s marked by Kōhanga Reo language initiatives. It addresses the "Closing the Gaps" policy introduced in 1999 and Te Puni Kōkiri's "Māori Potential Approach." Throughout this period, government policies oscillated between recognizing Māori authority and assimilationist approaches, consistently prioritizing land acquisition over Māori interests and self-determination (tino rangatiratanga).

13.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores the poukai tradition, the travelling court of the Maori King Tuheitia, which celebrates 150 years of the Kingitanga movement. Originating as solace for Waikato Maori during 19th-century land confiscations, poukai gatherings unite Maori communities to feast, grieve, share news, and bring concerns to the King. The document details a 2008 poukai at Te Tokonganuianoho Marae in Te Kuiti, describing the elaborate feasts, ceremonial welcomes, formal speeches, and substantive discussions on topics including land grants, tribal relations, and economics. It traces the historical context: King Tawhiao established poukai after the 1863 British invasion of Waikato and subsequent raupatu (land seizure) that displaced thousands. The tradition represents resilience and mana, serving bereaved families and the destitute post-war. The poukai operates independently under Maori leadership with minimal external influence, running from 10am to 4pm to accommodate travelers. Participants reconnect with whanau (family), share kai (food), and maintain cultural traditions passed down through generations, emphasizing Maori sovereignty, identity, and manaaki (hospitality). The document includes historical perspectives from 1882 when Kerry-Nicholls visited King Tawhiao to discuss raupatu settlement, highlighting the King's determination to maintain Maori sovereignty and traditions.

chunkHighlights.text: The british never warmed to the idea, or for that matter the reality, of a Maori king. Christopher William Richmond, who would become Minister for Native Affairs in August 1858, visited Waikato in mid-1857. He wrote, in the patronising tones typical of the day, “The native question is in an interesting state. Those aspirations for the maintenance of a separate nationality, which I [described] in ’55 as the secret cause of the opposi- tion to land sales, have lately taken the shape of an agitation for a Maori King… I hear in it the voice of a people crying out to be governed—a people weary of anarchy and desiring guidance in the right way. I believe it is a movement which we may take possession of and turn to great uses but which if neglected will become dangerous.”

But there was as much chance of the British taking possession of the Kingitanga as there was of Maori taking possession of Queen Victoria’s court, and within a year of Richmond’s letter, Maori anointed their first king—Potatau Te Wherowhero. When he died just two years later, his son Matutaera took the reign. (Te Ua Haumene, prophet of Pai Marire, gave him the name Tawhiao in 1864.) In July 1863, British troops invaded Waikato—partly in an attempt to crush “the King Movement”—and within 10 months, they had spent £300,000, lost 700 lives, killed 1000 Maori, and driven King Tawhiao into what the British called the King Country—largely the district of Ngati Maniapoto. Although they didn’t break the Kingitanga, Maori did suffer significantly, particularly due to the loss of their lands. Under the New Zealand Settlement Act 1863, Waikato had 1.2 million acres confiscated. Maori called it raupatu—seized land. It was the combined effect of the wars and raupatu on Maori that convinced King Tawhiao to establish the poukai tradition, a series of gatherings aimed at bringing together and feeding those who had been driven from their land.

14.fileDescription: This comprehensive document collection examines 150 years of the Treaty of Waitangi's history and its impact on New Zealand law, governance, and Māori rights. Beginning with the treaty's signing on February 6, 1840, between British Governor William Hobson and Māori chiefs, the narrative explores critical discrepancies between English and Māori versions that created fundamentally different understandings of sovereignty and land rights. The document traces systematic treaty breaches from the colonial era through the 1980s, including Governor FitzRoy's abandonment of land purchase monopolies and widespread land confiscations. Key case studies include the Kaituna River pollution crisis, Waitara disputes, Waiuku Block confiscations, and the Ngati Whatua's struggle for Orakei land rights. The establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975 marked a turning point, providing mechanisms for Māori to seek redress and establishing the treaty's legal force through landmark decisions like the 1987 Court of Appeal ruling. The tribunal evolved from adjudicating rights to facilitating stakeholder dialogue, achieving practical remedies including the 1983 Fisheries Act restoration of Māori fishing rights and the Bastion Point settlement. Throughout, the narrative emphasizes that broken colonial promises continue to undermine Māori rights and wellbeing, while the tribunal's collaborative approach offers innovative solutions for resolving historical injustices.

chunkHighlights.text: The Manukau people are part of the Waikato-Tainui confederation, and as more and more settlers arrived in Auckland the pressure to expand south into the Waikato became intense. But Waikato people did not want to sell, and by 1858 the tribes in the Maori King movement were united in their resolve to resist land sales to British settlers.

15.fileDescription: Ngāpora (Tāmati) was a 19th-century Māori leader from Ngāti Mahuta who played a significant role in Waikato politics and the King movement. Born early in the 1800s, he participated in tribal conflicts and later became a Christian lay preacher and government assessor. Initially skeptical of intertribal kingship, he became a key adviser to King Te Wherowhero and later his successor Tāwhiao, whose wife was Ngāpora's daughter. During the 1860s Waikato Wars, he warned governors of military threats but ultimately refused an oath of allegiance and went into exile in the King Country. He remained influential within the King movement, advocating for full restoration of confiscated lands and opposing peace settlements he deemed inadequate. Ngāpora died in 1885 at approximately 80 years old, having maintained his position as a trusted counselor to the Māori King until his death.

chunkHighlights.text: In the 1850s, when the King movement rose to prominence as an attempt to consolidate Māori authority and halt land sales, Ngāpora's inclination was initially against an intertribal Māori kingship. However, when Te Wherowhero was installed as King and returned to live in Waikato, Ngāpora remained at Māngere to act as the King movement's representative to the governor. In 1861, when Sir George Grey returned to New Zealand as governor, Ngāpora arranged for leaders of the King movement to meet him. At the meeting Rewi Maniapoto insisted on recognition of the Māori King's independence, which Grey would not

grant. In 1863 the dispute over sovereignty moved towards war. Ngāpora warned the governor that war parties were gathering to attack the government outpost of Te Ia (Havelock, near Mercer), and that there were plans for a surprise attack on Auckland. In July 1863 Māori north of the Mangatawhiri River were required to give an oath of allegiance to Queen Victoria, or leave for Waikato. Ngāpora considered this requirement to be insulting, and refused the oath. Soldiers looted Māori property and an atmosphere of open hostility developed. Disillusioned, Ngāpora returned to Waikato. Meanwhile, on 12 July, Lieutenant General Duncan Cameron and British troops had crossed the Mangatawhiri River to invade Waikato. Although he did not take part in the fighting in Waikato, after the war and the confiscation of Waikato land Ngāpora went into exile in the King Country with Te Wherowhero's son, Tāwhiao .

16.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

chunkHighlights.text: Conflict

In the north of the South Island and the far north and south of the North Island, the mid-1840s saw violence break out between Māori and Pākehā as Māori sought to hold on to their land and local authority. In the 1860s the conflict became more severe as Pākehā settlers, mostly British, sought land to sustain a growing population. While Māori exhibited remarkable inventiveness and tenacity during the wars , they eventually lost millions of acres of land . This was partly the result of confiscation, and partly the influence of new government institutions such as the Native Land Court . This was set up to facilitate the sale of land by assigning land titles to named individuals.

17.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of the British Empire into the modern Commonwealth, with emphasis on New Zealand's journey from colonial dependency to independent nation. It covers the empire's expansion from North America through Asia, Africa, and the Pacific, including New Zealand's annexation in 1840 and the emergence of self-governing dominions through responsible government principles. The 1926 Imperial Conference and 1931 Statute of Westminster established dominions as autonomous communities equal in status within the Commonwealth. Key topics include imperial trade networks with New Zealand's economic dependence on Britain for wool, meat, and dairy exports until the 1970s, military cooperation in the South African War and World Wars, and colonial administration of Western Samoa. The document examines post-World War II decolonization, when the empire transformed into a Commonwealth of over 54 independent nations by the early 2000s, predominantly Asian and African. New Zealand played a significant role in this evolution, hosting Commonwealth Games and CHOGMs while shifting strategic alignment from Britain to the United States during the Cold War.

chunkHighlights.text: War and empire

War was a recurrent feature of empire, enlarging or reducing Britain’s
colonial holdings. It was also a local concern during New Zealand’s first 100 years – British troops fought in the New Zealand wars and the Royal Navy provided external security. Imperial troops in New Zealand Once established, the elected New Zealand government handled all internal matters except those concerned with Māori. The British government, sick of settler land-grabbing, wanted out. In the early 1860s Britain moved to reduce its expenditure on the internal security of self-governing colonies. At this point the New Zealand wars started. The colonial government was dependent on imperial troops. Numbers reached a peak of 18,000 in 1864, and their withdrawal was delayed for several years. Despite New Zealand’s pleas, the last regiment left in February 1870, prompting a furious reaction – the mother country was seen by some as abandoning the colony. External security The question of how New Zealand would be defended against an outside attack was raised by Premier William Fox in December 1870. The solution was a strategy known as the Jervois Doctrine or ‘blue water school’. Te Tiriti o Waitangi – the Treaty of Waitangi ByClaudia Orange What is te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi)? Te Tiriti o Waitangi
(the Treaty of Waitangi) was a written agreement made in 1840 between the British Crown (the monarch) and more than 500 Māori chiefs. After that, New Zealand became a colony of Britain and Māori became British subjects. However, Māori and Europeans had different understandings and expectations of te tiriti. Drafting and signing te tiriti Te tiriti was drafted in English and then translated into Māori by missionary Henry Williams and his son Edward. It was presented to around 500 Māori at Waitangi on 5 February 1840 and there was much debate. The next day, 6 February, more than 40 chiefs signed te tiriti. Copies of te tiriti were taken around the country, and many more chiefs signed. Most Māori signed the te reo tiriti. Reasons why chiefs signed te tiriti included wanting controls on sales of Māori land to Europeans, and on European settlers. They also wanted to trade with Europeans, and believed the new relationship with Britain would stop fighting between tribes. Those who did not sign te tiriti were concerned they would lose their independence and power, and wanted to settle their own disputes. Some chiefs never had the opportunity to sign it, as it was not taken to all regions. What did te tiriti say? The meaning of the English treaty was not exactly the same as the meaning of the Māori tiriti. Article One: in Māori it gave Queen Victoria governance over the land, while in English it gave her sovereignty over the land – a stronger term. Article Two: Te tiriti guaranteed chiefs ‘te tino rangatiratanga ’ – chieftainship over their lands, villages and treasured things. It also gave the Crown the right to deal with Māori in buying land. The English-language treaty gave chiefs ‘exclusive and undisturbed possession’ of lands, forests, fisheries and other property. It also gave the Crown an exclusive right to deal with Māori over bu…

retrieved_chunks.text: Anti-racism and Treaty of Waitangi activism ByRobert Consedine Treaty of Waitangi When the Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840 there was a worldwide movement to abolish slavery. People had seen the negative effect of colonisation on the indigenous people of countries like Australia. Colonists believed the Treaty of Waitangi was fair because it offered Māori the rights of British citizens. The signing of the Treaty made it easier for settlers to acquire land. While many of them only mixed socially with other settlers , some male colonists consolidated their position by marrying Māori women and accessing land as whānau or kin . These Pākehā were often key ‘go-betweens’, connecting settlers and Māori . At the same time, t he children of Māori and Pākeha settlers were defined as ‘half castes’ and white settlers often saw themselves and their culture or ‘ civilisation ’ as superior to Māori culture . Racism, the belief that some people we re superior to others on the basis of their ethnic origins , existed alongside recognition in the Treaty of Māori as British citizens and official encouragement of marriage between Māori and settlers . From the late 1840s chiefs protested to Queen Victoria about breaches of the treaty. Those Pākehā who sided with Māori were known as ‘ philo -Māori’ .

The Treaty of Waitangi In the early 19th century Māori still lived
according to a complex system of customary laws. The British began trying to introduce their own laws to Māori with the Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between rangatira (chiefs) and the British Crown. Some of the laws that followed took aspects of Māori custom into account, but the British lawmakers saw this as a temporary step and anticipated a time when Māori would be fully integrated into their society. Laws and land Māori did not see land as a commodity to be bought and sold by individuals, but as something over which groups could hold communal rights of guardianship, occupation and use. These rights were gained by various means including discovery, conquest and gift. They were maintained by continual occupation over generations. Colonial legislation clashed with and overrode that system. New laws declared that the government had the right to take any land that was not needed by Māori, and that Māori could sell or lease land only to the Crown. The government backed up its laws with military force, and the New Zealand wars began. The government passed laws allowing it to confiscate the land of Māori believed to be ‘in rebellion’. A century of law-making From 1862 the government passed laws ruling that Māori lands could only be held by individual owners, not collectively by iwi (tribes) or hapū (sub-tribes). This resulted in further Māori land loss. Native Land Courts were set up to investigate and decide on titles to Māori land. The court hearings were often time-consuming and expensive. Right into the 20th century, the government made laws that impeded Māori land ownership. Beginning to make amends In the 1970s a wave of Māori protest actions drew public attention to land-related grievances. The Waitangi Tribunal was formed in 1975 to investigate breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi. Since then, Māori have made further gains. A precursor to the wars was the 1843 Wairau incident, in which Nelson settlers clashed with Ngāti Toa at Tuamarino (now known as Tuamarina) over a land dispute. The 1840s wars began with fighting between Ngāpuhi and government forces at Kororāreka (Russell) in 1845. A series of battles were fought in the Bay of Islands until early 1846. Later that year there was fighting between government forces and Māori in Wellington, and there were skirmishes in Whanganui in 1847.

Auckland needed the broader base that more farming would provide, but the unroaded clay of the North Auckland peninsula still baffled would-be farmers. What Auckland had to acquire were the broad, sweet acres of the Waikato and Waipa valleys. But they were occupied by the obdurate Kingites. Twenty years beforehand, the Maori had been promised that they could hold on to as much of their land as they wanted, and in the early 1860s the Waikato, King Country and Taranaki Maori were united in agreeing that this was exactly what they were going to do. This, to many rich, pro-war Auckland merchants, smelled strongly of rebellion.

While it was supplying military reinforcements, the British government was reluctant to relinquish control of Māori affairs. A further move came in 1861 after Sir George Grey returned for a second term as governor. A new ministry headed by William Fox deplored the system of double government, and Grey agreed to consult ministers in this as in other matters and to give greater responsibility to the General Assembly. But the big shift came when the British government found backing settler aggression more and more distasteful and expensive, and announced that imperial garrisons would be removed from self-governing colonies. British battalions could only be retained if they were paid for by the colony.

retrieved_chunks.text: The british never warmed to the idea, or for that matter the reality, of a Maori king. Christopher William Richmond, who would become Minister for Native Affairs in August 1858, visited Waikato in mid-1857. He wrote, in the patronising tones typical of the day, “The native question is in an interesting state. Those aspirations for the maintenance of a separate nationality, which I [described] in ’55 as the secret cause of the opposi- tion to land sales, have lately taken the shape of an agitation for a Maori King… I hear in it the voice of a people crying out to be governed—a people weary of anarchy and desiring guidance in the right way. I believe it is a movement which we may take possession of and turn to great uses but which if neglected will become dangerous.” But there was as much chance of the British taking possession of the Kingitanga as there was of Maori taking possession of Queen Victoria’s court, and within a year of Richmond’s letter, Maori anointed their first king—Potatau Te Wherowhero. When he died just two years later, his son Matutaera took the reign. (Te Ua Haumene, prophet of Pai Marire, gave him the name Tawhiao in 1864.) In July 1863, British troops invaded Waikato—partly in an attempt to crush “the King Movement”—and within 10 months, they had spent £300,000, lost 700 lives, killed 1000 Maori, and driven King Tawhiao into what the British called the King Country—largely the district of Ngati Maniapoto. Although they didn’t break the Kingitanga, Maori did suffer significantly, particularly due to the loss of their lands. Under the New Zealand Settlement Act 1863, Waikato had 1.2 million acres confiscated. Maori called it raupatu—seized land. It was the combined effect of the wars and raupatu on Maori that convinced King Tawhiao to establish the poukai tradition, a series of gatherings aimed at bringing together and feeding those who had been driven from their land.

retrieved_chunks.text: In the 1850s, when the King movement rose to prominence as an attempt to consolidate Māori authority and halt land sales, Ngāpora's inclination was initially against an intertribal Māori kingship. However, when Te Wherowhero was installed as King and returned to live in Waikato, Ngāpora remained at Māngere to act as the King movement's representative to the governor. In 1861, when Sir George Grey returned to New Zealand as governor, Ngāpora arranged for leaders of the King movement to meet him. At the meeting Rewi Maniapoto insisted on recognition of the Māori King's independence, which Grey would not grant. In 1863 the dispute over sovereignty moved towards war. Ngāpora warned the governor that war parties were gathering to attack the government outpost of Te Ia (Havelock, near Mercer), and that there were plans for a surprise attack on Auckland. In July 1863 Māori north of the Mangatawhiri River were required to give an oath of allegiance to Queen Victoria, or leave for Waikato. Ngāpora considered this requirement to be insulting, and refused the oath. Soldiers looted Māori property and an atmosphere of open hostility developed. Disillusioned, Ngāpora returned to Waikato. Meanwhile, on 12 July, Lieutenant General Duncan Cameron and British troops had crossed the Mangatawhiri River to invade Waikato. Although he did not take part in the fighting in Waikato, after the war and the confiscation of Waikato land Ngāpora went into exile in the King Country with Te Wherowhero's son, Tāwhiao .

In the 1860s the conflict became more severe as Pākehā settlers, mostly British, sought land to sustain a growing population. While Māori exhibited remarkable inventiveness and tenacity during the wars , they eventually lost millions of acres of land . This was partly the result of confiscation, and partly the influence of new government institutions such as the Native Land Court . This was set up to facilitate the sale of land by assigning land titles to named individuals.

High profile cases investigated by the tribunal included one brought by the tribe Te Āti Awa, who did not want the Taranaki synthetic fuel plant to discharge its outfall into the sea near a reef where they gathered shellfish. The tribunal recommended that the Māori language be made an official language of New Zealand, which occurred in 1987. A casebook system was adopted all the claims in a single area were researched together. Some people criticised the tribunal and thought the past should be forgotten. The government tried to limit the amount of compensation in 1994, but Māori opposed this. Tribunal enquiries identified matters which were undisputed, so hearings could focus on issues on which the Crown and claimants disagreed. [Page 3] In 1845 Grey was appointed governor of New Zealand, where he faced even greater difficulties than in South Australia. The government was so short of funds that the first governor, William Hobson , had drawn unauthorised bills on the British Treasury and his successor, Robert FitzRoy , had, contrary to instructions, issued government debentures, a form of paper money. Even more serious, in several districts of the North Island, there had been violent disputes between settlers and Māori, especially over land claims. In Wellington, Nelson and Taranaki there had been conflict over disputed New Zealand Company land purchases. In Nelson the settlers tried to occupy the Wairau district in the face of opposition from Ngāti Toa. Twenty two settlers and at least four Māori were killed when an armed party stupidly attempted to arrest the formidable chiefs Te Rauparaha and Te Rangihaeata . In the far north Hōne Heke and his ally, Kawiti , had risen in revolt against British authority. Heke feared that the Europeans would take all their land. He was responsible for cutting down the British flag on four occasions; on the last, both sides sacked Kororāreka (Russell). Fortunately for the British most of Ngāpuhi sided with the government. Even so, the British had suffered a disastrous defeat at Ōhaeawai.
{}
retrieved_chunks.title: Sir George Grey: Colonial Governor, Scholar, and Political Reformer

retrieved_chunks.text:
[Page 4] FitzRoy was then called on to deal with New Zealand's first racial war, sparked off by the Bay of Islands chief Hōne Heke . Its causes were not of FitzRoy's making, arising rather from economic failure and the diminished importance of the Far North after the removal of the government to Auckland. The first overt act of significance was the cutting down of the flagstaff on Maiki Hill above Kororāreka on 8 July 1844. The war that followed was between Heke and his followers and the government, and between Heke and other Ngāpuhi, of whom Wāka Nene and Patuone were the most important. The military engagements spread over 18 months and were concluded by FitzRoy's successor, Grey, on 23 January 1846. FitzRoy, with insufficient funds to pay a militia, and whose first call for troops from New South Wales was regarded as totally unjustifiable by the Colonial Office, maintained the credibility of his government (outside New Zealand Company
{}
retrieved_chunks.title: Robert FitzRoy: Naval Officer, Explorer, Governor of New Zealand, and Pioneer of Meteorology

[Page 1] Te Ānaua and his brother Te Māwae were among the leaders of the Wanganui tribes in the tribal wars of the early nineteenth century. In 1819 or 1820 he fought at Pūrua, near the mouth of the Wanganui River, against the expedition of northern, musket armed tribes led by Tūwhare, Patuone and Nene . When the Amiowhenua northern war expedition of 1821 22 attacked Wanganui, Te Ānaua fought against it at Mangawere, where two of his brothers were killed. He ambushed a section of the war party at Mangatoa and pursued it as far as Taupō.

[Page 6] With his aristocratic heritage and military background, Bernard Fergusson is often considered New Zealand’s last truly British governor general. His term in office marked another step in the country’s gradual transition away from imperial Britain towards a more independent identity. His strong and highly visible support for Māori language and culture was unique for a vice regal representative at the time and foreshadowed a shift in Pākehā attitudes towards Māori that would gradually gain currency in the decades following his departure.

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 3] From 1866 Whitmore at last became substantively involved in the New Zealand wars, leading the colonial forces in no fewer than seven distinct campaigns. As lieutenant colonel he led the Napier militia against an incursive Hauhau force, almost annihilating it at Ōmarunui on 12 October 1866. In July and August 1868 he organised the pursuit of Te Kooti inland from Poverty Bay. Despite difficult terrain, freezing weather and refractory troops, his own column caught Te Kooti at Ruakituri on 8 August, only to be defeated. Whitmore had been appointed commandant of the New Zealand Constabulary Force in early 1868. His rank was equivalent to lieutenant colonel. He fought his first two campaigns as a commander of local volunteers. In September the colonial forces met disaster in South Taranaki at the hands of Tītokowaru , and in the crisis Whitmore was promoted full colonel on 21 October 1868 and placed in charge of the main army, 1,000 strong. Hereafter he was, in effect, commander in chief. Within two weeks Whitmore had restored order among the mutinous troops, but even so he was severely defeated by Tītokowaru at the hard fought battle of Moturoa on 7 November. Leaving strong forces to contend with Tītokowaru, Whitmore then transferred his best troops to the East Coast and overcame great obstacles to take Te Kooti's stronghold of Ngātapa on 5 January 1869 with great slaughter, although Te Kooti himself escaped. Returning west, he led an army of 2,000 men against Tītokowaru's new pā , Tauranga ika, but the decisive clash was averted when in early February 1869 the Māori forces disbanded because of internal dissension. Until early April Whitmore mounted a vigorous but unsuccessful pursuit of Tītokowaru through inland Taranaki. Whitmore's last and most difficult campaign was an ambitious invasion of Te Kooti's sanctuary, the Urewera district, from 4 to 18 May. Although Te Kooti again escaped, Whitmore undermined him by proving that the Urewera was not inviolable. Wh…

[Page 10] Tītokowaru is arguably the best general New Zealand has ever produced, but his career as prophet, peacemaker, and leader of non violent resistance was longer and at least as significant. In the former career, he has been overshadowed by Te Kooti; in the latter, by Te Whiti. Neither of these leaders should be belittled, but it must be said that posterity has erred in this judgement. It exists because Tītokowaru's War is a dark secret of New Zealand history, forgotten by the Pākehā as a child forgets a nightmare. Such selective memory almost falsified Tītokowaru's prophecy: I shall not die, I shall not die, When death itself is dead, I shall be alive.
{}

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 9] small force of colonial troops and 'friendly' Māori, captured a Māori supply depot at the rear of the pā , which the Māori promptly evacuated. This was hailed, not least by Grey, as a famous victory. In the later 1860s the British government determined to withdraw imperial troops from the colonies, and force them to accept responsibility for their own internal security. So numerous were the victories of Te Kooti , Tītokowaru and other Māori generals in 1868, however, that the government and the settlers were extremely alarmed. With the support of his ministers, Grey constantly evaded carrying out instructions to finalise the return of the regiments, which had commenced in 1865 and 1866. In the end the British government had little alternative but to terminate the appointment of so headstrong a governor in 1868. Grey soon went to England, where he failed in an attempt to enter Parliament as a Gladstonian Liberal. He then returned to New Zealand, where he lived in his splendid home on Kawau Island, in the Hauraki Gulf. From there he emerged in 1874 to lead the fight against Julius Vogel 's proposal to abolish the provincial governments set up under the 1852 Constitution. In 1875 Grey was elected superintendent of Auckland province and also to Parliament for Auckland City West. He fought vigorously in Parliament and in public to save the provinces, but without success. The Atkinson government persisted with abolition, but soon lost on a vote of no confidence over its lack of other policies. In October 1877 Grey became premier. His cabinet included some conservatives, as well as radicals such as John Ballance and Robert Stout . As he did not have a safe majority in the House, Grey asked for a dissolution, which was refused by the governor, Lord Normanby. Grey now stumped the country, stirring up considerable enthusiasm for radical causes, such as 'one man one vote'. However, in 1878 the country ran into a severe depression, which led to much unemployment. The…

[Page 2] War began, however, on 12 July 1863, when Lieutenant General Duncan Cameron and British troops crossed the Mangatāwhiri River. Te Hokioi ceased publication and the press was abandoned. (It is now in the Te Awamutu Museum.) Pātara Te Tuhi fought against the British all through the campaign in Waikato, and went into exile with Tāwhiao in 1864. The King and his followers remained in isolation in the King Country for nearly 20 years. In May 1878 Pātara Te Tuhi spoke at a meeting at Hikurangi, near Kāwhia, at which Grey, now premier, was present. He told Grey that the King movement was reluctant to begin negotiations

retrieved_chunks.text:
[Page 1] In the 1850s, when the King movement rose to prominence as an attempt to consolidate Māori authority and halt land sales, Ngāpora's inclination was initially against an intertribal Māori kingship. However, when Te Wherowhero was installed as King and returned to live in Waikato, Ngāpora remained at Māngere to act as the King movement's representative to the governor. In 1861, when Sir George Grey returned to New Zealand as governor, Ngāpora arranged for leaders of the King movement to meet him. At the meeting Rewi Maniapoto insisted on recognition of the Māori King's independence, which Grey would not grant. In 1863 the dispute over sovereignty moved towards war. Ngāpora warned the governor that war parties were gathering to attack the government outpost of Te Ia (Havelock, near Mercer), and that there were plans for a surprise attack on Auckland. In July 1863 Māori north of the Mangatawhiri River were required to give an oath of allegiance to Queen Victoria, or leave for Waikato. Ngāpora considered this requirement to be insulting, and refused the oath. Soldiers looted Māori property and an atmosphere of open hostility developed. Disillusioned, Ngāpora returned to Waikato. Meanwhile, on 12 July, Lieutenant General Duncan Cameron and British troops had crossed the Mangatawhiri River to invade Waikato. Although he did not take part in the fighting in Waikato, after the war and the confiscation of Waikato land Ngāpora went into exile in the King Country with Te Wherowhero's son, Tāwhiao .
{}

## The War in Ukraine: Where Things Stand

The conflict between Russia and Ukraine is now in its fifth year, having begun with Russia's full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022. Based on the most recent search results available, here is a picture of how the war has unfolded across several key phases.

### Peace Talks and Diplomatic Pressure

As of early 2026, the war was grinding towards its fourth anniversary with peace talks underway but no breakthrough achieved. Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said it was 'not fair' that he was being asked to compromise more than Russian president Vladimir Putin. The key sticking points in negotiations include territory, who would monitor a ceasefire, and the fate of a key nuclear power plant. [[1]](cite://1/1)

By late 2025, Ukrainian officials were still discussing an end to the war while Russia continued attacking targets across Ukraine. [[2]](cite://2/1)

### The Frontlines in Eastern Ukraine

Russia has been making steady, if slow, gains in eastern Ukraine — particularly in the Donetsk region — throughout 2024 and into 2025. Ukraine's army chief described the situation as facing 'one of the most powerful Russian offensives' since the start of the full-scale invasion. [[3]](cite://3/1)

In August 2025, Russian forces made a sudden thrust near the mining town of Dobropillia, advancing up to 10 kilometres in two prongs, as part of their drive to take full control of Ukraine's Donetsk region. This came as US president Donald Trump and Putin prepared to meet in Alaska to discuss a possible deal. [[4]](cite://4/1)

### Ukrainian Offensives Inside Russia

In a bold strategic move, Ukraine launched a surprise offensive into the Russian border region of Kursk on 6 August 2024, capturing over two dozen towns and villages — the most significant cross-border attack on Russian soil since World War II. [[5]](cite://5/1) At its peak, Ukrainian troops advanced up to 30 kilometres inside Russia. [[6]](cite://6/1)

However, by early 2025, Russia had largely pushed back, with open-source maps showing Ukrainian forces in Kursk almost surrounded. [[7]](cite://7/1) Putin visited Kursk in a show of confidence that Russia would soon reclaim it entirely. [[8]](cite://8/1)

### Civilian Casualties and Attacks on Infrastructure

The human cost has been severe. The United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission reported that June 2025 saw the highest monthly civilian casualties in three years, with 232 people killed. A Russian drone attack also struck a maternity hospital in Kharkiv, injuring several women. [[9]](cite://9/1)

Russia has continued striking deep into Ukrainian territory, including attacks on energy infrastructure, civilian buildings, and cities. [[10]](cite://10/1)

### The Broader Picture

- NATO estimates casualties on both sides have exceeded one million. [[11]](cite://11/1)
- Nearly four million people have been displaced. [[11]](cite://11/2)
- The US, under Trump, suspended military aid and intelligence sharing in early 2025, prompting Russia to launch massive ballistic missile and drone strikes. European leaders responded by developing a ceasefire plan that would involve European and NATO peacekeepers on the ground. [[12]](cite://12/1)
- Zelensky has consistently resisted ceding Ukrainian territory, insisting any peace deal must be a just one. [[4]](cite://4/2)

From a New Zealand perspective, RNZ has been following this conflict closely since its beginning, reflecting the broader concern among democratic nations about the war's implications for international law and sovereignty.

Would you like to explore what New Zealand's government has said or done in response to the war in Ukraine?
