[Page 1] Ukraine outnumbered, outgunned, ground down by relentless Russia 2024 02 22 10:11:31+13:00 By Max Hunder, Reuters A BM 21 Grad multiple rocket launcher fires towards Russian positions on the frontline near Bakhmut, Donetsk region, on 23 April, 2023. As the Ukraine war enters its third year, the infantry of 59th Brigade are confronting a bleak reality: they're running out of soldiers and ammunition to resist their Russian invaders. One platoon commander who goes by his call sign "Tygr" estimated that just 60 70 percent of the several thousand men in the brigade at the start of the conflict were still serving. The rest had been killed, wounded or signed off for reasons such as old age or illness. Heavy casualties at the hands of Russian forces have been compounded by dreadful conditions on the eastern front, with frozen soil turning into thick mud in unseasonably warm temperatures, playing havoc with soldiers' health. "The weather is rain, snow, rain, snow. People get ill with simple flu or angina as a result. They're out of action for some time, and there is nobody to replace them," said a company commander in the brigade with the call sign "Limuzyn". "The most immediate problem in every unit is lack of people." On the cusp of the second anniversary of its 24 February invasion, Vladimir Putin's Russia is in the ascendancy in a conflict that combines attritional trench combat reminiscent of World War I with high tech drone warfare that's sending tens of thousands of machines into the skies above. Moscow has made small gains in recent months and claimed a major victory at the weekend when it took control of Avdiivka in the hotly contested eastern Donetsk region. A spokesperson for 3rd Separate Assault Brigade, one of the units that tried to hold the town, said the defenders were outnumbered seven to one. Reuters spoke to more than 20 soldiers and commanders in infantry, drone and artillery units on different sections of the 1000 km frontlines in eastern and southern Ukraine. While still motivated to fight Russian occupation, they spoke of the challenges of holding off a larger and better supplied enemy as military support from the West slows despite pleas for more from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. Ukrainian servicemen prepare for combat a Bradley fighting vehicle, not far away from Avdiivka, Donetsk region on 11 February, 2024. Another commander in the 59th Brigade, who only gave his first name Hryhoriy, described relentless attacks from groups of five to seven Russian soldiers who would push forward up to 10 times a day in what he called "meat assaults" highly costly to the Russians but also a major threat to his troops. "When one or two defensive positions are fighting off these assaults all day, the guys get tired," Hryhoriy said as he and his exhausted men were afforded a brief rotation away from the frontlines near the Russian occupied eastern city of Donetsk. "Weapons break, and if there is no possibility of bringing them more ammunition or changing their weapons, then you understand what this leads to." Russia's defence ministry didn't respond to a request for comment on the state of play on the frontlines. Ukrainian Deputy Defence Minister Ivan Havryliuk told Reuters that Ukraine had been forced onto the defensive by a lack of artillery ammunition and rockets, and that Kyiv was expecting Russia to intensify its assaults on several fronts. "If there are further delays to the necessary military aid, the situation on the front could become even more difficult for us," he said in a written response. Wanted: Fighters and ammo Kyiv relies heavily on money and equipment from abroad to fund its war effort, but with US$61 billion (NZ$98.8bn) in US aid held up by political bickering in Washington it is looking more exposed than at any time since the start of the invasion. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky (2nd L) visiting the advanced checkpoint of the 110th Separate Mechanized Brigade in the town of Avdiivka, Donetsk region, on 29 December, 2023. A soldier serving in a GRAD rocket artillery unit, whose call sign is "Skorpion", said that his launcher, which uses Soviet designed ammunition held by few of Ukraine's allies, was now operating at about 30 percent of maximum capacity. "It became like this recently," he said. "There aren't as many foreign munitions." Artillery shells are also in short supply as a result of Western countries' inability to keep up the pace of shipments for a drawn out war. On top of the US supply pause, the EU has conceded it will miss its target to supply a million shells to Ukraine by March by nearly half. Michael Kofman, a senior fellow and Russian military specialist at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, a Washington based think tank, estimated that Russia's artillery was firing at five times the rate of Ukraine's, a figure that Hryhoriy of the 59th Brigade also gave. "Ukraine is not getting a sufficient amount of artillery ammunition to meet its minimum defensive needs, and this is not a sustainable situation moving forward," Kofman added. Moscow now controls almost a fifth of Ukrainian territory including the Crimea peninsula it annexed in 2014, even if the frontlines of the war have largely stagnated in the last 14 months. Ukrainian officials have said their armed forces number about 800,000, while in December Putin ordered Russia's forces to be increased by 170,000 troops to 1.3 million. Beyond personnel, Moscow's defence spending dwarfs that of Ukraine. In 2024 it earmarked $109 billion for the sector, more than twice Ukraine's equivalent target of $43.8 billion. A new law aimed at mobilising 450 500,000 more Ukrainians is slowly making its way through parliament, but for some soldiers fighting now, significant reinforcements seem a distant hope. Ukrainian Defence Minister Rustem Umerov recently referred to Ukraine's artillery ammunition deficit as "critical" in a letter to the European Union, urging its national leaders to do more to bolster supplies. His letter said Ukraine's "absolute critical daily minimum requirement" was 6000 artillery shells, but his forces were able to fire just 2000 a day, the Financial Times reported. Drone war on massive scale Conventional warplanes are a relatively rare sight over the frontlines, largely because air defences act as a deterrent. Yet a different battle is raging in the skies, with both sides striving for the upper hand in drone technology. Drones or unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are cheap to produce and can surveil enemy movements and drop ordnance with pinpoint accuracy. Kyiv has overseen a boom in drone production and innovation and is developing advanced, long range UAVs, while Moscow has more than matched its rival with huge investments of its own, allowed it to nullify Ukraine's early advantage. The scale is astonishing. On the Ukrainian side alone, more than 300,000 drones were ordered from producers last year and more than 100,000 sent to the front, digital minister Mykhailo Fedorov told Reuters. A strong focus now is on light, nimble FPV drones, where operators, or pilots, get a first person view from an onboard camera. President Zelenskiy has set a target for Ukraine to produce one million FPV drones this year in light of the battlefield advantages delivered by the technology. Limuzyn, the company commander in the 59th Brigade, said Russia's widespread use of drones had made it difficult for Ukrainian troops to establish or strengthen fortified positions. "Our guys start to do something, a drone sees them, and a second drone arrives to drop something onto them." Drones have also forced the Russians to move valuable vehicles and weapons systems back by several

Ukraine's artillery fires at one-fifth the rate of Russia's, with a critical daily minimum requirement of 6,000 shells but only 2,000 available. Western military aid delays, particularly $61 billion in US funding held up by political disputes, have left Ukraine increasingly exposed. Russian forces employ relentless "meat assaults" with groups attacking up to 10 times daily, while electronic warfare systems escalate the technological arms race in the skies.

16.text:
[Page 1] Ukraine could face defeat in 2024. Here's how that might look 2024 04 13 20:54:48+12:00 By Frank Gardner, BBC security correspondent The former commander of Britain's Joint Forces Command has warned that Ukraine could face defeat by Russia in 2024. General Sir Richard Barrons has told the BBC there is "a serious risk" of Ukraine losing the war this year. The reason, he says, is "because Ukraine may come to feel it can't win". "And when it gets to that point, why will people want to fight and die any longer, just to defend the indefensible?" Ukraine was not yet at that point. But its forces were running critically low on ammunition, troops and air defences. Its much heralded counter offensive last year failed to dislodge the Russians from ground they had seized and now Moscow was gearing up for a summer offensive. So what will that look like and what are its likely strategic objectives? "The shape of the Russian offensive that's going to come is pretty clear," Gen Barrons said. "We are seeing Russia batter away at the front line, employing a 5 to 1 advantage in artillery, ammunition, and a surplus of people reinforced by the use of newish weapons." These include the FAB glide bomb, an adapted Soviet era "dumb bomb" fitted with fins, GPS guidance and 1500kg of high explosive, that is wreaking havoc on Ukrainian defences. "At some point this summer," said Barrons, "we expect to see a major Russian offensive, with the intent of doing more than smash forward with small gains to perhaps try and break through the Ukrainian lines. "And if that happens we would run the risk of Russian forces breaking through and then exploiting into areas of Ukraine where the Ukrainian armed forces cannot stop them." But where? Last year the Russians knew exactly where Ukraine was likely to attack from the direction of Zaporizhzhia south towards the Sea of Azov. They planned accordingly and successfully blunted Ukraine's advance. Now the boot was on the other foot as Russia masses its troops and keeps Kyiv guessing where it is going to attack next. "One of the challenges the Ukrainians have," said Dr Jack Watling, senior research fellow in land warfare at the Whitehall thinktank the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), "is that the Russians can choose where they commit their forces. "It's a very long front line and the Ukrainians need to be able to defend all of it." Which, of course, they can't. "The Ukrainian military will lose ground," said Dr Watling. "The question is: how much and which population centres are going to be affected?" It was quite possible that Russia's General Staff have yet to go firm on which direction to designate as their main effort. But it was possible to broadly break down their various options into three broad locations. Kharkiv "Kharkiv," said Dr Watling, "is certainly vulnerable." As Ukraine's second city, situated perilously close to the Russian border, Kharkiv was a tempting goal for Moscow. It was currently being pummelled daily with Russian missile strikes, with Ukraine unable to field sufficient air defences to ward off the lethal mix of drones, cruise and ballistic missiles aimed in its direction. "I think the offensive this year will have breaking out of the Donbas as its first objective," said Barrons, "and their eye will be on Kharkiv which is 29 kilometres or so from the Russian border, a major prize." Could Ukraine still function as a viable entity if Kharkiv were to fall? Yes, say analysts, but it would be a catastrophic blow to both its morale and its economy. The Donbas The area of eastern Ukraine known collectively as the Donbas has been at war since 2014, when Moscow backed separatists declared themselves "people's republics". In 2022 Russia illegally annexed the two Donbas oblasts, or provinces, of Donetsk and Luhansk. This was where most of the fighting on land has been taking place over the past 18 months. Ukraine has, controversially, expended enormous efforts, in both manpower and resources, in trying to hold on to first the town of Bakhmut, and then Avdiivka. It has lost both, as well as some of its best fighting troops, in the attempt. Kyiv has countered that its resistance has inflicted disproportionately high casualties on the Russians. That's true, with the battlefield in these places being dubbed "the meat grinder". But Moscow has plenty more troops to thrown into the fight and Ukraine doesn't. This week the Commander of US Forces in Europe, General Christopher Cavoli, warned that unless the US rushes significantly more weapons and ammunition to Ukraine then its forces will be outgunned on the battlefield by 10 to 1. Mass matters. The Russian army's tactics, leadership and equipment may be inferior to Ukraine's, but it has such superiority in numbers, especially artillery, that if it does nothing else this year, its default option will be to keep pushing Ukraine's forces back in a westward direction, taking village after village. Zaporizhzhia This, too, was a tempting prize for Moscow. The southern Ukrainian city of more than 700,000 (in peacetime) sits dangerously close to the Russian front lines. It was also something of a thorn in Russia's side given that it is the capital of an oblast of the same name that Russia has illegally annexed, and yet the city is still living freely in Ukrainian hands. But the formidable defences that Russia built south of Zaporizhzhia last year, in the correct expectation of a Ukrainian attack, would now complicate a Russian advance from there. The so called Surovikin Line, consisting of triple layers of defences, was laced with the largest, most densely packed minefield in the world. Russia could partially dismantle this but its preparations would likely be detected. Russia's strategic objective this year may not even be territorial. It could simply be to crush Ukraine's fighting spirit and convince its Western backers that this war was a lost cause. Dr Jack Watling believes the Russian objective is "to try to generate a sense of hopelessness. "This [Russian] offensive will not decisively end the conflict, irrespective of how it goes for either side." Gen Barrons was also sceptical that, despite the dire situation Ukraine now finds itself in, Russia will automatically drive home its advantage with a decisive advance. "I think the most likely outcome is that Russia will have made gains, but will not have managed to break through. "It will not have forces that are big enough or good enough to punch all the way through to the river [Dnipro]... But the war will have turned in Russia's favour." One thing was certain: Russia's President Putin has no intention of giving up on his assault on Ukraine. He's like a poker player gambling all his chips on a win. He's counting on the West failing to supply Ukraine with the sufficient means to defend itself. Despite all the Nato summits, all the conferences and all the stirring speeches, there is a chance he may be right. This story was first published by the BBC. Related
{}

17.text:
[Page 1] Ukrainian troops have pressed 30km into Russia, Moscow says By Matt Murphy, BBC News Ukrainian servicemen sit on a self propelled artillery 2S7 Pion while being carried by a military truck, in the Sumy region, near the border with Russia, on August 11, 2024, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Ukrainian troops have advanced up to 30km inside Russia, in what has become the the deepest and most significant incursion since Moscow began its full scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Russia's defence ministry said its forces had engaged Ukrainian troops near the villages of Tolpino and Obshchy Kolodez, as the offensive in the Kursk region entered a sixth day. Foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova accused Kyiv of "intimidating the peaceful population of Russia". President Volodymyr Zelensky, who directly acknowledged the attack for the first time in an address on Saturday night, said 2000 cross border attacks had been launched by Russia from Kursk this summer. "Artillery, mortars, drones. We also record missile strikes, and each such strike deserves a fair response," Zelensky told the country in his nightly address from Kyiv. A senior Ukrainian official told the AFP news agency that thousands of troops were engaged in the operation, far more than the small incursion initially reported by Russian border guards. While Ukrainian backed sabotage groups have launched intermittent cross border incursions, the Kursk offensive marks the biggest co ordinated attack on Russian territory by Kyiv's conventional forces. "We are on the offensive. The aim is to stretch the positions of the enemy, to inflict maximum losses and to destabilise the situation in Russia as they are unable to protect their own border," the official said. Russia's defence ministry said on Sunday that its forces had "foiled attempts by enemy mobile groups with armoured vehicles to break through deep into Russian territory". But in an apparent admission that Kyiv's forces have now advanced deep into the Kursk border region, the defence ministry reported engaging Ukrainian troops near the villages of Tolpino and Obshchy Kolodez which are about 25km and 30km from the Russia Ukraine border. Footage circulating online and verified by the BBC also appeared to show a Russian strike near the village of Levshinka, around 25km from the border. Ukrainian troops have claimed to have captured a number of settlements in the Kursk region. In Guevo, a village about 3km inside Russia, soldiers filmed themselves removing the Russian flag from an administrative building. Clips have also emerged of Ukrainian troops seizing administrative buildings Sverdlikovo and Poroz, while intense fighting has been reported in Sudzha a town of about 5000 people. Ukrainian troops have already filmed themselves outside Sudzha at a major gas facility involved in the transit of natural gas from Russia to the EU via Ukraine, which has continued despite the war. [Page 1] Russian forces make sudden thrust in eastern Ukraine, open source data shows 2025 08 12 23:23:57+12:00 By Andrew Osborn, Reuters Russian forces have made a sudden thrust into eastern Ukraine near the mining town of Dobropillia in a move that may be designed to increase the pressure on Ukraine to cede land as the United States and Russian presidents prepare to meet. Ukraine's authoritative DeepState war map showed on Tuesday that Russian forces had quickly advanced up to 10 kilometres north in two prongs in recent days, part of their drive to take full control of Ukraine's Donetsk region. DeepState said they had advanced near three villages on a section of the frontline associated with the two key Ukrainian strongholds of Pokrovsk and Kostyantynivka. US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are expected to discuss a possible deal to end the war in Ukraine when they meet in Alaska on Friday. Unconfirmed media reports say Putin has told Trump he wants Ukraine to hand over the part of the Donetsk region that Russia does not control. There was no immediate comment on the battlefield development from Moscow. Ukrainian military spokesperson Viktor Trehubov said only small groups were penetrating defensive lines, and this did not amount to a breakthrough. Pasi Paroinen, a military analyst with the Finland based Black Bird Group, said the situation had escalated rapidly, with Russian forces infiltrating past Ukrainian lines to a depth of roughly 17km during the past three days. "Forwardmost Russian units have reportedly reached the Dobropillia Kramatorsk road T0514 and Russian infiltration groups have also been reported near Dobropillia proper," he wrote on X. Tatarigami_UA, a former Ukrainian army officer whose Frontelligence Insight analysis tracks the conflict, posted: "In both 2014 and 2015, Russia launched major offensives ahead of negotiations to gain leverage. The current situation is serious, but far from the collapse some suggest." Sergei Markov, a former Kremlin adviser, said the Russians had been able to advance due to what he called "a partial collapse in the front" due to Ukraine's shortage of soldiers. He said, without citing evidence, that Ukraine had redeployed elite forces to try to thwart the advance. Russia's Interfax news agency and Ukrainian war bloggers reported the same. "This breakthrough is like a gift to Putin and Trump during the negotiations," Markov added, suggesting it could increase pressure on Kyiv to cede some land to prevent the Russian army eventually taking the rest of Donetsk by force. To do that, though, Russian forces would first need to take control of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka and Kostiantynivka four places Russian military analysts call "fortress cities". Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly pushed back against the idea of ceding territory to Russia, saying any peace deal must be a just one. Yuri Podolyak, a pro Russian military blogger, said Russia had yet to commit substantial forces to exploit the breach and try to secure an operational breakthrough. Bohdan Krotevych, former chief of staff of Ukraine's Azov brigade and a National Guard lieutenant colonel, took to X late on Monday to warn Zelenskiy of the threat, saying the frontline in the area was "a complete mess". "The line of combat engagement as a fixed line does not actually exist," he said. Reuters Related

fileAuthor: Andrew Osborn and Anastasiia Malenko, Reuters
5.fileDescription: Ukrainian forces that launched a surprise offensive into Russia's Kursk region in August 2024 are now nearly surrounded by Russian counteroffensive operations. Open source maps show approximately three-quarters of the Ukrainian force is almost completely encircled, connected to the main force by a narrow 1km corridor less than 500 meters wide at its narrowest point. Russian forces have advanced significantly, cutting off supply lines and threatening to completely encircle the Ukrainian contingent. Military analysts warn that Ukrainian forces face a difficult choice: attempt to hold the bridgehead for political leverage in peace negotiations or risk a dangerous retreat under constant drone and artillery fire. The situation represents a major reversal for Ukraine, which had hoped to use its Kursk presence as a bargaining chip in talks with Moscow. The deterioration comes amid US pressure for a ceasefire and suspended intelligence sharing with Kyiv.

"There are constant strikes on concentrations of Ukrainian Armed Forces, but the enemy still has serious offensive potential for this direction and has not abandoned plans for further breakthroughs, including in new areas of the front," it said. One of the Russian blogs, Rybar, said Russia had moved reinforcements to Belgorod from Goptarovka in the Kursk region. Emil Kastehelmi, a military analyst with the Finnish-based Black Bird Group, said Ukrainian forces had penetrated the first Russian defences and advanced most likely to a depth of three to four kilometres. But he said it was unlikely they could stage a serious breakthrough and threaten any important Russian logistical routes or cities. "The Ukrainians can, in theory, take some more villages from the border area, but that's not what a breakthrough means - it'd be a small tactical success, but there's very little to be achieved in the Demidovka direction at operational or strategic level," he told Reuters. "There's no proper element of surprise, and the Russian presence in the area is strong enough to at least conduct mostly successful defensive operations." In Kursk, the Russian Defence Ministry said on Friday its forces had recaptured the village of Gogolevka, one of only a handful of settlements still held by Ukraine out of around 100 that it seized last August. Ukraine's General Staff said its military had stopped 18 Russian assaults in the Kursk region over the past day. Open source mapping from Deep State, an authoritative Ukrainian military blogging resource, showed Russian forces in control of some but not all of Gogolevka, and indicated Kyiv's troops still controlled just under 80 sq km of Kursk. President
Vladimir Putin visited Kursk this month in a sign of increasing confidence
that Russia will shortly win it back, depriving Ukraine of a bargaining
chip in future peace talks. - Reuters Related

11.fileDescription: Nearly three years after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the conflict has resulted in over one million casualties on both sides and displaced nearly four million people. Russian forces have gradually expanded territorial control in eastern Ukraine, though Ukrainian forces have slowed their advances and conducted counter-offensives into Russian territory. This comprehensive analysis examines the current state of the conflict, military developments, humanitarian impact, and future geopolitical implications.

chunkHighlights.text: Ukraine war nearly 3 years on - where to from here?

2024-12-16 10:06:05+13:00
It's nearly three years since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. Nato estimates casualties on both sides have exceeded one million and the United Nations says nearly four million people have been displaced. Russian forces have slowly expanded the amount of territory they control over the last year, mostly in the east of Ukraine. But Ukrainian forces have made those advances as slow and difficult as possible and even staged a counter-offensive into Russian territory. Meanwhile there is uncertainty over what a Trump presidency will mean for US support for Ukraine, and how Russia's withdrawal from Syria could change things. James Waterhouse has been covering the war for the BBC since the beginning of the conflict.

response.response_text:
# Māori — Tangata Whenua, People of the Land

Māori are the indigenous people of New Zealand, known as *tangata whenua* — the people of the land. Their deep connection to this country is central to New Zealand's identity, history, and culture. [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

## Origins and Early Settlement

The ancestors of Māori arrived by waka (canoe) from Pacific islands before 1300 CE, settling first along the coast where they hunted seals and moa, grew food, and gradually moved into the forests. [[3]](cite://3/1) They lived in small tribal groups with a rich oral culture, strong traditions of warfare, and profound reverence for their ancestors and the gods of the natural world. [[3]](cite://3/2)[[4]](cite://4/1)

Māori tribes also carry a wealth of narratives about people and beings who existed long before the arrival of Polynesian settlers — collective knowledge that remains central to the experience and identity of *tangata whenua* today. [[5]](cite://5/1)

The bond between Māori and the land is captured in the expression *"Ko au, ko te whenua, ko te whenua, ko au"* — "I am the land and the land is me." [[6]](cite://6/1)

## Traditional Society

Pre-European Māori society was oral and organised around three core units: *whānau* (family), *hapū* (sub-tribe), and *iwi* (tribe). [[7]](cite://7/1)[[8]](cite://8/1) Society was also stratified into social rankings — *rangatira* (leaders), *tūtūā* (commoners), and *taurekareka* or *mōkai* (slaves) — with rank and leadership based on seniority of descent from founding ancestors. [[9]](cite://9/1)

Whakapapa (genealogy) was, and remains, central to Māori tradition. When Māori introduce themselves, they often reference the mountains, lakes, or rivers important to their tribe, grounding their identity firmly in the land. [[10]](cite://10/1)[[11]](cite://11/1)

Kin relationships underpin many social customs. *Hapū* hold rights over particular *marae* (communal gathering places), hosting gatherings, weddings, and funerals. *Kaumātua* and *kuia* (male and female elders) hold an honoured place in communities. [[12]](cite://12/1)

## The Arrival of Europeans and the Treaty of Waitangi

The arrival of Europeans from the early 1800s transformed Māori communities significantly. Missionaries arrived, many Māori converted to Christianity, and trade — particularly in pigs and potatoes — expanded rapidly. [[3]](cite://3/3)

In 1840, Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi) was signed between the British Crown and more than 500 Māori chiefs. [[13]](cite://13/1) However, the English and Māori versions of the treaty carried different meanings — the English version gave the Crown *sovereignty*, while the Māori version guaranteed *tino rangatiratanga* (chieftainship) over their lands, villages, and treasured possessions. [[13]](cite://13/2)[[14]](cite://14/1) This difference in understanding eventually led to conflict, land loss, and a long process of reinterpretation that continues today. [[15]](cite://15/1)

Following the New Zealand Wars of the 1840s and 1860s, Māori lost vast amounts of land through confiscation and sale. [[3]](cite://3/4)[[16]](cite://16/1)

## Revival and the 20th Century

In the first half of the 20th century, important leaders such as Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi worked to improve Māori wellbeing and revive the culture, renewing interest in the language and arts such as carving and weaving. [[3]](cite://3/5)

After the Second World War, many Māori moved to cities for work — a major shift from the rural, tribally centred life of previous generations. [[8]](cite://8/2) In the 1970s and 1980s, political activism intensified, with significant events including:

- A land march down the North Island to Parliament in 1975
- The creation of the Waitangi Tribunal (1975) to examine alleged breaches of the Treaty
- The occupation of Bastion Point in Auckland by protesters in 1977–78 [[3]](cite://3/6)

## Treaty Settlements

The Waitangi Tribunal was set up in 1975 to hear claims about Crown breaches of the treaty, and from 1985 could consider historic claims back to 1840. [[16]](cite://16/2) Settlement negotiations led to landmark agreements — including the Sealord fisheries agreement ($170 million) in 1992, and the Waikato Tainui settlement ($170 million) in 1995. Some settlements also included formal Crown apologies and cultural redress such as the restoration of Māori place names — for example, Aoraki/Mt Cook. [[16]](cite://16/3)

## Māori Today

By 2019, nearly 800,000 Māori people were living in New Zealand, with most in cities. The cultural landscape includes *kōhanga reo* (preschool language nests), Māori-language schools, two Māori television channels, 21 radio stations, and 29 members of Parliament who identified as Māori. [[3]](cite://3/7)

Te reo Māori became an official language of New Zealand in 1987, and a national target of one million te reo speakers by 2040 has been set. [[17]](cite://17/1) The language's revitalisation has been driven by the *kōhanga reo* generation — young, fluent speakers who, in the words of Māori Language Commission chair Rawinia Higgins, "don't know what it means to not have te reo Māori." [[18]](cite://18/1)

From protest to celebration, Māori culture, identity, and language continue to grow and assert their place at the heart of Aotearoa New Zealand. [[18]](cite://18/2)[[19]](cite://19/1)

Would you like to explore a particular aspect of Māori culture or history in more depth — such as te reo Māori, the Treaty settlement process, or traditional society?

4.document_title: Te Ao Mārama: Traditional Māori Worldview, Cosmology, and Spiritual Concepts
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the traditional Māori worldview and understanding of nature (Te Ao Mārama), presenting a holistic indigenous philosophy centered on interconnectedness and spiritual principles. It explains how Māori people viewed all elements of nature—birds, fish, people, wind, and sun—as an interconnected family linked through genealogies (whakapapa). The creation story describes how earth mother Papatūānuku and sky father Ranginui produced 70 children who became gods of different natural domains. Key concepts include whakapapa (genealogies explaining relationships between all things), Te Kore (a realm of unlimited potential and ultimate reality), and the cycle of light (Te Ao) and darkness (Te Pō) representing birth and death. Three interconnected spiritual concepts are examined: mana (extraordinary power and essence), tapu (sacred restrictions and disciplines), and mauri (life force energy binding all physical things). The document explores tangata whenua (people of the land), where identity is defined through geographical and ancestral connections, and discusses taniwha as spiritual guardians. It emphasizes how orators use speech to guide people from darkness into light, mirroring Tāne's separation of earth and sky, and highlights the practical and spiritual functions of oral traditions in transmitting knowledge while maintaining respect toward other species.

5.document_title: Māori: History, Culture, and Contemporary Society in New Zealand
5.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

6.text:
[Page 1] Welcome and hospitality Māori rituals for greeting visitors date from before Europeans arrived in New Zealand, and had a practical function. The women of a settlement would call out to approaching strangers, asking them to identify themselves and their intentions. Warriors would then challenge them in the wero ceremony. After this, once it was known that the visitors came in peace, they could enter and were welcomed and fed. Today the rituals include the karanga (call), wero , whaikōrero (speeches) and hongi (pressing of noses). The manuhiri (visitors) are then invited to eat and drink with their hosts. They can respond by giving a koha in the past, a gift of food or precious objects, but today usually money. Kinship, families and marae Kin relationships are very important and underpin many customs. Speeches often begin with the speaker’s whakapapa (genealogy), which may relate to the group addressed or the issue discussed. Most Māori, even if they live in the city, retain links with their tribal area and return there for events. Hapū (sub tribes) have rights over particular marae , and are known as tangata whenua (people of the land) of those marae . They can host gatherings, weddings and funerals, and must maintain the marae and its reputation. Kaumātua and kuia (male and female elders) have an honoured place in Māori communities. Tangi and birth In Māori tradition, when someone dies, their spirit leaves their body and travels to a sacred place at the northern tip of New Zealand. Their whānau (family) gathers at a tangihanga to be supported by the wider whānau and community. Tangi are usually held on the marae most closely associated with the deceased. Mourners stay with the family and the tūpāpaku (corpse) for several days. Urupā (cemeteries) are extremely tapu (sacred). When a baby is born, Māori traditionally bury the whenua (placenta) on land associated with one or both of the parents. Some Pākehā also now follow this custom. Māori social customs today Some customs have been adapted to non traditional situations. For instance, many marae in cities or outside New Zealand are multi tribal, so tribal traditions have to be adapted. Māori ceremonies are also used in non Māori settings, such as the opening of the Te Māori exhibition in New York in 1984. Welcome and hospitality Greeting visitors

7.document_title: King Country: A Comprehensive Regional Profile - Geography, History, Culture, and Development
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of the King Country region in New Zealand's western North Island. It encompasses geography and geology, featuring volcanic landscapes shaped by Mt Ruapehu and the Taupō Volcanic Zone, limestone karst formations, major rivers (Mōkau, Waipā, Whanganui), and diverse ecosystems including native forests and protected areas like Pureora Forest Park and Tongariro National Park. The region's rich Māori heritage is traced from the arrival of the Tainui waka and establishment of Ngāti Maniapoto as the dominant iwi, through the Kīngitanga (King movement) led by Pōtatau Te Wherowhero and his son Tāwhiao, to the struggle for land autonomy through Te Rohe Pōtae. European contact began in the late 1820s with missionaries and traders, followed by settlement from the 1880s after the opening of the region. Economic development includes pastoral farming, forestry, coal and ironsand mining, and the transformative North Island main trunk railway (completed 1908). Population peaked at 38,916 in 1961 before declining to 25,938 by 2013. Key tourism attractions include Waitomo Caves with glow-worm displays, Mt Ruapehu ski fields, and river cruises. Agriculture remains the dominant industry at 24.5%.

8.text:
[Page 3] Māori and history Although a country with a short human past, New Zealand has a rich tradition of telling its history. The Māori way of thinking has been described as walking forward into the future, while looking back into the past. Whakapapa (genealogy) has a central place in Māori tradition, and the carvings of meeting houses usually portray historical figures and past incidents. In oratory on the marae speakers constantly draw upon historical precedent. The founding waka (canoes) and historical battles are often referenced.

8.document_title: History and Historians: The Development of Historical Recording and Study in New Zealand (1890s-2000s)
8.document_summary: This document traces the evolution of historical recording and study in New Zealand from pre-1900 through the 2000s. It contrasts Māori traditional methods of recording history through carvings, oratory, and waiata with European approaches. Before 1900, New Zealand history was left to amateurs while universities focused on British history, with the first full history published in 1859 by A.S. Thomson. The early 20th century saw amateur historians document local histories and pioneer stories, while the Polynesian Society (founded 1892) worked to preserve Māori culture. From 1940-1970, academic historians emerged with new perspectives on colonial history and race relations. This comprehensive document examines sexuality in New Zealand across multiple dimensions and life stages. It contrasts traditional Māori attitudes—which accepted same-sex relationships and multiple partners—with European settler influences that introduced monogamous heterosexual ideals and criminalized homosexuality. Key legal milestones include decriminalization of male homosexuality (1986) and sex work (2003).

The document presents research on young people's sexuality, showing 25% of high school students have experienced sexual intercourse, with most relationships lasting 6-12 months. Young men value emotional connections alongside sex, while young women increasingly express sexuality in traditionally masculine ways. Contraception use is moderate at 58% consistent use, and teen birth rates have declined significantly since the 1970s.

Sexuality education has evolved from early 1900s "sex hygiene" focused on purity to modern comprehensive approaches covering physical, social, emotional, and spiritual dimensions. However, LGBTQ+ identities remain underrepresented in curricula. Approximately 4% of secondary students identify as attracted to their own or multiple genders, experiencing higher bullying rates and lower safety perceptions than heterosexual peers.

The document defines sexuality as comprising three interconnected aspects: sexual orientation, identity, and behavior, which may not align and can change over time. It explores adult sexual relationships and evolving attitudes toward women's sexual pleasure. Finally, it addresses sexuality across the lifespan, challenging stereotypes about aging by showing people over 60 report high satisfaction with intimate relationships (94%). It advocates for sexual citizenship rights for people with disabilities, highlighting barriers including limited sexuality education and vulnerability to sexual abuse.

15.document_title: Māori Education in New Zealand: Historical Development from Traditional Mātauranga to Contemporary Kaupapa Māori Initiatives
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori education in New Zealand from traditional times through contemporary developments. Traditional Māori education involved tohunga conducting rituals and whare wānanga (houses of learning) for chiefly classes. Missionaries arrived in 1816, establishing European-style schools, with the Native Schools system (1867-1969) making schooling compulsory from 1894, though it suppressed Māori language and suffered from inadequate resources. Church boarding schools like Te Aute College provided academic education, producing early Māori university graduates including Āpirana Ngata and Te Rangihīroa. From the 1980s, Kaupapa Māori education emerged as a grassroots movement, including kōhanga reo (Māori language preschools), kura kaupapa Māori (Māori-immersion schools), and wānanga (tertiary institutions), which revitalized te reo Māori from near extinction. Recent developments show Māori students in Māori-language schools performing better than English-medium counterparts. The 21st-century Ka hikitia strategy represents a shift toward recognizing diverse learning styles and supporting Māori success across all education levels.

16.text:
[Page 2] The largest group in Māori society was tūtūā (commoners). Terms referring to commoners were considered pejorative, but the dividing line between this group and rangatira was not sharp all members of a hapū or iwi could trace their descent from a common ancestor who was a recognised rangatira . The genealogical connections through male and female lines to founding ancestors meant that even those quite junior in rank were able to show they descended from important rangatira , and ultimately from the founding ancestors of hapū and iwi . Ethnographer Elsdon Best once wryly observed that he had yet to meet any Māori who admitted to being tūtūā. Māori society was described as democratic. Commoners did not act subserviently to rangatira . 17.document_title: Family Violence in New Zealand: Comprehensive Analysis of History, Legislation, and Contemporary Responses
17.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines family violence in New Zealand, covering its definition, historical evolution, and contemporary responses. Family violence encompasses physical, sexual, emotional, and psychological abuse, including threats and isolation. Historically, domestic violence was tolerated, particularly in the 19th century when women had limited legal protections. The women's movement of the 1970s catalyzed significant change, establishing rape crisis centres and women's refuges starting in 1974. Key legislative milestones include the Domestic Protection Act 1982, criminalization of marital rape in 1985, the Domestic Violence Act 1995, and the Family Violence Act 2018, which incorporated 53 recommended changes. Police data shows 178,000 family violence investigations in 2022/23, with men predominantly identified as perpetrators. Family violence disproportionately affects Māori, LGBT+ individuals, disabled persons, and those in financial difficulty. The document emphasizes that family violence involves psychological, economic, and emotional control beyond physical violence, with profound impacts including trauma and depression. Support services include women's refuges and Shine, while prevention campaigns such as "Family Violence: It's not OK" and the White Ribbon Campaign promote behavior change and perpetrator accountability.

[Page 8] Māori society before European contact was stratified into three social rankings: the rangatira or kāhui ariki (leaders), tūtūā (commoners), and taurekareka or mōkai (slaves). Rank and leadership were based on seniority of descent from founding ancestors. Rangatira normally traced tuakana (senior) descent lines from the founding ancestors, while tūtūā were from teina (junior) lines. The same principle applied at the whānau level: the mātāmua or tuakana (first born male and female) held the highest rank and were senior to all junior siblings of the same sex.

18.document_title: Māori Social Organisation: Tribal Structure, Hierarchy, and Evolution Through Colonisation and Urbanisation
18.document_summary: This document examines the structure and evolution of Māori tribal society in New Zealand. It explains the hierarchical organization of iwi (tribes) and hapū (clans), with whānau (extended families) as the basic social unit comprising 20-30 people across three to four generations. Tribal groups formed through waka (canoe) ancestry, resource pressure, migration, and conflict, with names derived from founding ancestors and clan prefixes like Ngāti or Te Uri. Traditional Māori society was stratified into three ranks: rangatira/kāhui-ariki (leaders), tūtūā (commoners), and taurekareka/mōkai (slaves), with special roles for tohunga (learned experts). European contact from the early 19th century disrupted traditional tribal functions through trade, musket wars, land confiscation, and colonisation. The document traces significant transformation during the 19th and 20th centuries, including the shift from hapū to iwi as the primary political unit, establishment of tribal trust boards after 1945 to address Treaty of Waitangi grievances, and urbanization's dramatic impact—with urban Māori population rising from 17% in 1936 to 80% by 1986. While urbanization has weakened some tribal connections, modern tribal organizations and reconnection programs continue to maintain cultural identity and links to ancestral lands.

[Page 9] New housing for Māori paid no attention to Māori tikanga (cultural values and traditions) because of the state’s aim of assimilating Māori into Pākehā society. This meant notions of keeping noa (non sacred or ordinary) and tapu (sacred) separate were sometimes violated, such as having a washing machine next to the kitchen sink. Many Māori nonetheless adapted their homes to allow the practice of tikanga . For instance, before the creation of urban marae , bodies were sometimes laid out in garages for tangihanga .

19.document_title: Māori Housing in New Zealand: Historical Evolution, Challenges, and Contemporary Solutions
19.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori housing from pre-colonial times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Traditionally, Māori lived in family-based kāinga (villages) with rectangular wharepuni (sleeping houses) constructed from natural materials. European settlers introduced European-style housing from the early 1800s, though most Māori initially maintained traditional dwellings. From the late 1800s, poor sanitary conditions—including inadequate water, sewerage, and overcrowding—led to disease outbreaks, prompting government intervention that resulted in the demolition of 1,256 houses and construction of 2,103 cottages by 1909. The 1918 influenza epidemic devastated Māori communities and prompted new housing initiatives including the Native Housing Act 1935. Post-WWII urbanization saw Māori migrate to cities like Auckland and Wellington, facing discrimination from landlords and living in overcrowded subdivided apartments. State housing policies effectively excluded Māori through discriminatory practices until 1944, while housing designs ignored Māori cultural values (tikanga), contributing to assimilation policies. By the 1980s-90s, Māori home ownership remained significantly lower than the general population (29-49% vs. 50-73%). Persistent problems in the early 21st century included substandard, cold, damp housing; overcrowding (23% of Māori in 2006 vs. 4% for Europeans); and poor health outcomes. Modern solutions emerged through iwi-led initiatives including papakāinga schemes, rural housing programs, and the government's Whānau Ora scheme (2010), which combines housing with health, education, and legal support, representing a shift toward Māori self-determination.

20.document_title: Hōkakatanga – Māori Sexualities and Takatāpui: Cultural Identity and Diversity in Aotearoa
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the history, cultural significance, and contemporary reclamation of sexuality and sexual diversity within Māori society. It demonstrates that traditional Māori culture was historically open and accepting of sexual diversity, including same-sex relationships, as evidenced through traditional stories, carvings, and songs depicting explicit sexuality and same-sex attraction, such as the relationship between Tūtānekai and Tiki. The text traces how European colonization and missionary influence imposed Victorian moral codes, leading to the censorship and removal of sexual references from Māori cultural artifacts and traditions. The document highlights the contemporary reclamation and significance of the term "takatāpui" among Māori people in the 21st century, which encompasses gay, lesbian, transgender, bisexual, and intersexual identities while acknowledging both sexual and cultural dimensions. It emphasizes that transgender people hold revered positions within Māori society as knowledge keepers and valued community members. The text discusses cultural initiatives like the 2004 television series and annual Hui Takatapui gatherings, and stresses the importance of protecting transgender rights and ensuring access to Māori culture, language, and tikanga. 21.text:
[Page 1] Te Tiriti o Waitangi the Treaty of Waitangi ByClaudia Orange What is te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi)? Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi) was a written agreement made in 1840 between the British Crown (the monarch) and more than 500 Māori chiefs. After that, New Zealand became a colony of Britain and Māori became British subjects. However, Māori and Europeans had different understandings and expectations of te tiriti. Drafting and signing te tiriti Te tiriti was drafted in English and then translated into Māori by missionary Henry Williams and his son Edward. It was presented to around 500 Māori at Waitangi on 5 February 1840 and there was much debate. The next day, 6 February, more than 40 chiefs signed te tiriti. Copies of te tiriti were taken around the country, and many more chiefs signed. Most Māori signed the te reo tiriti. Reasons why chiefs signed te tiriti included wanting controls on sales of Māori land to Europeans, and on European settlers. They also wanted to trade with Europeans, and believed the new relationship with Britain would stop fighting between tribes. Those who did not sign te tiriti were concerned they would lose their independence and power, and wanted to settle their own disputes. Some chiefs never had the opportunity to sign it, as it was not taken to all regions. What did te tiriti say? The meaning of the English treaty was not exactly the same as the meaning of the Māori tiriti. Article One: in Māori it gave Queen Victoria governance over the land, while in English it gave her sovereignty over the land a stronger term. Article Two: Te tiriti guaranteed chiefs ‘te tino rangatiratanga ’ chieftainship over their lands, villages and treasured things. It also gave the Crown the right to deal with Māori in buying land. The English language treaty gave chiefs ‘exclusive and undisturbed possession’ of lands, forests, fisheries and other property. It also gave the Crown an exclusive right to deal with Māori over buying land. Article Three: both versions gave Māori the queen’s protection and the rights of British subjects. Te tiriti in the 19th century Even though not all chiefs signed te tiriti, the British government decided it placed all Māori under British authority. It did not take long for conflicts to arise between Māori and European settlers who wanted more land. The government often ignored the protections te tiriti was supposed to give Māori. In 1858 some iwi (tribes) chose Waikato rangatira

21.document_title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to Modern Legal Recognition
21.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

The English version of the treaty stated that sovereignty was ceded to the Queen of England. [Page 1] Te Tiriti o Waitangi / the Treaty of Waitangi Te Tiriti o Waitangi / the Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840 between Māori rangatira and the British Crown. The Waitangi Tribunal was established by the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975. This was the first law to refer to the principles of the treaty. These principles were not defined in the legislation. But through court cases, new laws, Waitangi Tribunal findings and a 1989 government statement, the meaning of the principles of the treaty in contemporary New Zealand society has continued to be outlined. The treaty text itself is not law. Instead, the intentions and goals of the treaty are taken into account through the principles of the Treaty. Some people have suggested that this is a better idea because: The English and te reo Māori versions do not have exactly the same meaning and this may lead to uncertainty about which version to use. The treaty focuses on the issues relevant at the time it was signed and it is better to think about the spirit of the agreement and how it can be implemented today. It could diminish the mana of the treaty to make it law it should sit above the law. Principles Treaty principles are always evolving to suit changing beliefs and circumstances. They include: The treaty set up a partnership, and the partners have a duty to act reasonably and in good faith. The Crown has freedom to govern. The Crown has a duty to actively protect Māori interests. The Crown has a duty to remedy past treaty breaches. Māori retain rangatiratanga over their resources and taonga and have all the rights and privileges of citizenship. The Crown has a duty to consult with Māori. The needs of both Māori and the wider community must be met, which will require compromise. The Crown cannot avoid its obligations under the treaty by conferring authority on some other body. The treaty can be adapted to meet new circumstances. The management of resources and other taonga according to Māori culture as part of tino rangatiratanga . Taonga include all valued resources and intangible cultural assets. What are the treaty principles? Te Tiriti o Waitangi / the Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between Māori and the British Crown, is not itself law, but since 1975 many New Zealand laws have referred to the principles of the treaty. The first to do so was the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal. The act says that Māori can bring a claim to the tribunal about a Crown policy or practice (amongst other things) which was or is ‘inconsistent with the principles of the Treaty’. Since the 1975 act there have been many other official references to treaty principles, all attempting to define the meaning of the Treaty of Waitangi in contemporary New Zealand society. Treaty principles have been referred to in: court cases new laws Waitangi Tribunal findings a 1989 government statement. No final and complete list There is no final and complete list of treaty principles. Instead, official documents have referred to treaty principles in general terms, without including the actual treaty text, because the English and Māori versions of the treaty are not direct translations of each other, so difficulties arise in interpretation. In 1983 the Waitangi Tribunal said, ‘The spirit of the Treaty transcends the sum total of its component written words and puts literal or narrow interpretations out of place.’ 1

25.document_title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to Modern Legal Recognition
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

26.text:
[Page 1] Te Tiriti o Waitangi, signed between Māori and the British Crown in 1840, promised Māori could continue to own their lands, forests and fisheries for as long as they wished. However, tribes lost many resources through: government purchase of Māori land for low prices that left Māori with inadequate land reserves confiscation of land following the New Zealand wars the consequences of Native Land Court operations. Māori sought compensation for these and many other breaches of the treaty. Early settlements In the early 20th century two commissions of inquiry into the treatment of Māori found the Crown had acted unfairly. In the mid 20th century some compensation was finally paid to Taranaki, Ngāi Tahu and Waikato Maniapoto. However, these were tiny sums of money compared to the value of what had been taken from the tribes. After Māori moved to urban areas stronger protests about treaty breaches began, part of a Māori political and cultural renaissance. Tribunal and negotiations The Waitangi Tribunal was set up in 1975 to hear claims about Crown breaches of the treaty. From 1985 the tribunal could hear claims relating to breaches dating back to 1840, and it issued reports on these claims. In 1989 a Treaty of Waitangi policy unit was set up in the Department of Justice to advise the government on treaty policy, and negotiations began with claimants on their historical claims. The first treaty claim settlement, concerning the Waitomo Caves, was signed in 1989. In 1992 the Sealord agreement settled claims over commercial fisheries it was worth $170 million. Another large settlement involving a number of tribes was the ‘Treelords’ deal in 2008, which included almost $200 million of forest land. Some tribes found the time and expense of treaty claims too much, and decided to bypass the tribunal and negotiate directly with the government. The Waikato Tainui confederation of tribes, the first to do this, agreed to a settlement worth $170 million in 1995. The Ngāi Tahu tribe negotiated with the government after a claim to the tribunal was heard. They received a settlement worth $170 million in 1998. Some settlements included formal apologies from the Crown, and some involved cultural redress such as the restoration of Māori place names for example, Aoraki/Mt Cook. By 2010, 26 final settlements had been written into law. Settlement process As the settlement process speeded up, treaty claims developed a distinct process. The Crown sought to: identify treaty breaches identify those affected by them find their spokespeople negotiate a deed of settlement which outlined the settlement, often including land, money and an apology. Some people were critical of the treaty settlement process, calling it a ‘gravy train’ which unfairly benefited a few. In 1994 the government tried to cap the total value of settlements at $1 billion, but Māori strongly opposed this. By the early 2000s most people accepted the idea of treaty settlements. The process was seen as an example to the world of how to resolve historic grievances.

26.document_title: Treaty of Waitangi Settlement Process: Historical Development and Implementation
26.document_summary: This document outlines the Treaty of Waitangi settlement process in New Zealand, tracing its evolution from early 20th-century commissions of inquiry through 2011. It explains how Māori lost lands through government purchases, confiscation, and Native Land Court operations despite the 1840 treaty promising continued ownership. The Waitangi Tribunal was established in 1975, expanding in 1985 to address historical grievances dating back to 1840. The Treaty of Waitangi Policy Unit (TOWPU) was created in 1989 to coordinate settlement negotiations. Major settlements include the 1989 Waitomo Caves transfer, 1992 Sealord fisheries agreement ($170 million), 1995 Waikato-Tainui settlement ($170 million with Queen Elizabeth II's formal apology—the first to an indigenous people), and 1998 Ngāi Tahu settlement ($170 million addressing 34.5 million acres). By December 2011, 44 deeds of settlement had been signed. The settlement process developed a formal structure identifying breaches, affected parties, and negotiating deeds including land, money, and apologies. Despite controversies over conservation land and negotiation levels, treaty settlements became mainstream political practice and are internationally regarded as an efficient reconciliation model for addressing historical indigenous grievances.

[Page 3] Treaty of Waitangi Hobson and his advisers drew up the Treaty of Waitangi to obtain the voluntary transfer of sovereignty by Māori. The treaty was first signed on 6 February 1840. Its Māori language version promised Māori some degree of control over their resources and customs. However, the English language version indicated that the Crown’s sovereignty would not be shared. These differing understandings eventually led to warfare and a long process of reinterpretation and compensation.

27.document_title: Government Policy and Māori: A Comprehensive History from Pre-1840 to the 2000s
27.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand government policy toward Māori from pre-1840 through the 2000s. It covers early British intervention, the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, and the establishment of protectors of aborigines. Key developments include the Kīngitanga movement in 1858, the creation of the Native Department, Māori Affairs Department, and Te Puni Kōkiri. The document details Māori governance structures including rūnanga (tribal councils) and their limited recognition through the Māori Councils Act 1900. Significant policy shifts include the controversial 1953 and 1967 Acts affecting land ownership, the establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975, and the Māori renaissance of the 1970s-2000s marked by Kōhanga Reo language initiatives. It addresses the "Closing the Gaps" policy introduced in 1999 and Te Puni Kōkiri's "Māori Potential Approach." Throughout this period, government policies oscillated between recognizing Māori authority and assimilationist approaches, consistently prioritizing land acquisition over Māori interests and self-determination (tino rangatiratanga).

28.text:
[Page 10] On 28 April 1840, 61 Muriwhenua chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi at Kaitāia. Lieutenant Governor William Hobson assured them that the treaty would control Pākehā settlers and protect Māori lands and interests. Nōpera Pana kareao encapsulated Māori understanding of the treaty based on these promises, saying, ‘Ko te atarau o te whenua i riro i a te kuini, ko te tinana o te whenua i waiho ki ngā Māori’ (The shadow of the land will go to the Queen [of England], but the substance of the land will remain with us). One year later he reversed his opinion, saying that the substance of the land had gone to the Queen and that Māori retained only the shadow.

28.document_title: Muriwhenua Tribes: Comprehensive History, Genealogy, Treaty Settlements, and Contemporary Demographics
28.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of the Muriwhenua people, a collective of six iwi (tribes) in New Zealand's Far North region: Ngāti Kurī, Ngāi Takoto, Te Pātū, Ngāti Kahu, Te Aupōuri, and Te Rarawa. The territory extends from the Maungataniwha Range to Cape Rēinga. The document traces genealogical descent from various Pacific canoes and explores key historical figures including navigator Kupe, Chief Tūmatahina, and the sacred significance of Cape Rēinga. It details the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi signed by 61 Muriwhenua chiefs, subsequent land dispossession (approximately 204,000 hectares by 1890), and modern treaty settlements with financial redress ranging from $21-34 million. The document covers significant political activism including Whina Cooper's 1975 Māori land march and Waitangi Tribunal claims. Census data from 1991-2013 shows over 40,000 Muriwhenua people by 2013, with fewer than 12,000 remaining in Northland due to urban migration to Auckland since 1950.

29.text:
[Page 1] From bicultural to monocultural Before te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi) was signed in 1840, Māori and most British settlers lived within their own cultures. So called Pākehā Māori (Pākehā who lived in Māori communities) were among the first bicultural people, comfortable in both groups. After the treaty was signed, the settler population grew rapidly to outnumber Māori. British traditions and culture became dominant, and Māori were expected to adopt Pākehā ways. Honouring the treaty From the 1970s Māori protested more strongly about issues such as land loss and breaches of the treaty. In 1975 the government set up the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate contemporary breaches, and from 1985 the tribunal could consider historic claims going back to 1840. State sector biculturalism In the 1980s the government began to acknowledge that the treaty was New Zealand’s founding document. Government agencies began to recognise the languages, cultures, and traditions of both Pākehā and Māori, and some government reports advocated biculturalism. By the 2000s most government agencies had Māori as well as English names, and pōwhiri and whakatau (welcome ceremonies) were often performed at official functions. Debates The idea of biculturalism is debated. Some people think New Zealand should be a multicultural society that officially recognises the cultures of many different peoples, not just those of Māori and Pākehā . Others think that biculturalism doesn’t go far enough in supporting Māori culture and self determination. They argue for Māori institutions under Māori authority, such as a Māori justice system or a Māori house of Parliament.

29.document_title: Biculturalism in New Zealand: Development, Debates, and Evolution
29.document_summary: This document traces New Zealand's bicultural journey from pre-1840 coexistence through monoculturalism to the modern bicultural framework. It examines the historical context of early bicultural individuals like Pākehā-Māori, the Treaty of Waitangi's signing in 1840, and subsequent British cultural dominance through assimilation policies. The pivotal shift from the 1970s onward saw Māori protests against land loss and treaty breaches, prompting government action including the establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975. The 1980s marked a turning point when the government acknowledged the treaty as New Zealand's founding document, leading to significant state-sector reforms. Government agencies adopted bicultural policies: te reo Māori became official in 1987, departments adopted Māori names, and cultural practices like pōwhiri were incorporated into official functions. The document explores ongoing debates and criticisms of biculturalism, including arguments that it hasn't sufficiently protected Māori tino rangatiratanga (self-determination). It presents competing frameworks such as multiculturalism, bi-nationalism, and differentiated citizenship, with advocates like Moana Jackson and Whatarangi Winiata proposing more substantial reforms. While biculturalism secured Māori political voice in the 1980s-1990s, critics argue it positioned Māori as junior partners. The document notes that although "biculturalism" terminology is less common today, discussions about appropriate Māori-non-Māori relationships continue to evolve.

[Page 16] Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi) was largely ignored by European New Zealanders in the early 20th century, but it came to public attention in 1932. In that year the governor general, Lord Bledisloe , and his wife gifted to the nation James Busby’s house at Waitangi, outside which te tiriti had been signed, and land around it. A great hui at Te Tii marae in 1934 marked this gift. It also marked the 100th anniversary of the selection by northern rangatira of the United Tribes’ flag as the flag of an independent New Zealand.

31.document_title: On Patrimony
31.document_summary: Kennedy Warne reflects on a nine-day trek through the Olivine Wilderness Area in Mt Aspiring National Park, exploring the concept of patrimony—the heritage and natural legacy that shapes national identity. Drawing on Māori kaumatua Hori Parata's insight that "the land made us Māori," Warne argues that New Zealand's patrimony extends beyond architectural heritage to encompass the natural world as a fundamental shaper of identity. He contrasts New Zealand's narrow heritage focus with France's comprehensive patrimony concept, warning against weakening environmental protections through Resource Management Act reforms that prioritize economic growth. Warne contends that wilderness and natural landscapes are essential to understanding what it means to be Kiwi, and that the upcoming RMA debate will test what this generation truly values.

32.text:
[Page 1] Names were on my mind when I visited kaumatua Nuki Aldridge as I roamed Whangaroa Harbour in the Far North earlier this year. I had been wondering if there was a name that could be used fairly, accurately and without prejudice for all the people who identify as belonging to this country—to Aotearoa, to New Zealand. Was there a word that could overcome the limitations of existing names? “New Zealander”, while practical, feels inadequate. A name bestowed through happenstance, it doesn’t give adequate recognition to the indigenous people. “Aotearoan?” Too hard to say, with its six syllables; I can’t see it catching on. “How about Kiwi?” I asked Aldridge. He said that, especially for people his age, using that word for people was offensive. “The biggest insult you can put on a tangata Māori is to call him something you can eat,” he said. “It’s a hell of an insult. It means you can eat me.” Aldridge has given a lot of thought to names and identity—including the naming of his own people. “We’ve been led down the path of being called Pacific Islanders, Polynesians, New Zealanders, Māori and now Kiwi,” he said. “We’re not any of those, if you come down to a real identity.” Even Māori? Even Māori, a word traditionally applied to objects (denoting common, normal, ordinary, local), repurposed in the term “tangata Māori” to distinguish locals from foreign visitors. (The “tangata” part was eventually dropped, leaving “Māori” as the default term for the indigenous people.) “Who are you then, if not Māori?” I asked. “What word do you always hear in our korero going back to the beginnings of time?” Aldridge replied. “Let me give you a hint: Hawaiki nui, Hawaiki roa, Hawaiki pamamao. [Great Hawaiki, long Hawaiki, far distant Hawaiki.] We’re Hawaikians.” This made sense. Where do the souls of the tangata whenua go on death? Home to Hawaiki, as if completing a migratory circle—one that began in ancient times and is completed by each individual, if they care to believe it. Waitangi Wood joined the conversation, adding that for tangata whenua it is hapu that is the primary marker of identity, not a pan iwi term like “Māori”. “In the first instance, I’m not Māori,” she said. “I can choose from my whakapapa who I want to be. In most instances I’m Ngāti Rua. That’s who I am.”

32.document_title: Flags, Names and Identities
32.document_summary: This essay explores the relationship between names, identity, and national belonging in New Zealand. Through conversations with kaumatua Nuki Aldridge and Waitangi Wood, the author examines why finding a single inclusive name for all New Zealanders is problematic. The discussion reveals that terms like "Kiwi," "New Zealander," and even "Māori" have limitations and contested meanings. Aldridge proposes "Hawaikians" as a more authentic identity rooted in indigenous tradition, while Wood emphasizes that hapū (sub-tribe) is the primary identity marker for tangata whenua. The author concludes that rather than seeking a unified name, it's more appropriate to acknowledge distinct identities: Pākehā for European New Zealanders and Māori/iwi-specific names for indigenous peoples. Embracing these distinct names honors indigenous primacy and creates a more respectful relationship based on mutual recognition.

33.document_title: Back for the Gold: A Modern Expedition Retracing Barrington's 1864 Journey Through New Zealand's Olivine Wilderness
33.document_summary: This narrative documents a modern wilderness expedition through New Zealand's Olivine Wilderness Area, retracing the 1864 journey of three 19th-century gold prospectors—Antoine Simonin, James Farrell, and Alphonse Barrington. Led by landscape architect Mick Abbott and contemporary trekkers, the expedition uses historical sources including Barrington's published diary and modern technology to locate gold abandoned during his survival crossing. The narrative interweaves multiple themes: the physical demands of wilderness travel through treacherous terrain including the Cascade Gorge and Pyke River crossings; the contrast between modern comforts and 19th-century hardships; geological features of the Red Hills Range and olivine's carbon sequestration potential; and philosophical reflections on wilderness definition. Central to the work is an examination of New Zealand's relationship with wilderness and resource management, contrasting Māori sustainable stewardship practices—exemplified through pounamu (jade) as taonga (treasure)—with Pākehā extractive colonial approaches. The expedition reveals that true value lies not in material wealth but in experiential exploration and sustainable relationships with land, questioning whether Pākehā can move beyond destructive resource extraction toward nurturing land relationships.

34.text:
[Page 10] It isn’t just the oral stories, but other aspects of Maori culture, too, that have an impact on visitors. Napier says people view the whare runanga (meeting house) in the Waitangi Treaty Grounds, with its tukutuku (decorative panels) and carved poupou (pillars representing human ancestors), as a kind of temple. New Zealanders, observes Napier, usually stand with their heads bowed. “Culturally, that’s very significant to me. They feel the ambience of spirituality in this building and they humble themselves.” Most international visitors “are in awe. They can’t believe it.” Maori stories connect. They’re passed down from generation to gen eration, just as they’re told to visitors staying with tangata whenua on marae, in wharenui, in the mountains, in the bush, on the rivers and on the sea. No one can tell these stories like tangata whenua, for only tangata whenua have a direct link with the land. The closest visitors can get to the land is to hear stories from someone like Mihaka, who “talks like a proud Maori because I am one” [Chapter Break]
