65.text:
[Page 1] Indo Fijians 'struggling for identity' in Aotearoa voice concerns about ethnicity classification ByLydia Lewis RNZ Pacific Journalist 2024 11 01 11:58:19+13:00 Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says that as far as Fiji is concerned, Fijians of Indian descent are Fijian. While Fiji is part of the Pacific, Indo Fijians are not classified as Pacific peoples in New Zealand; instead, they are listed under Indian and Asian on the Stats NZ website. "The 'Fijian Indian' ethnic group is currently classified under 'Asian,' in the subcategory 'Indian', along with other diasporic Indian ethnic groups," Stats NZ told RNZ Pacific. "This has been the case since 2005 and is in line with an ethnographic profile that includes people with a common language, customs, and traditions. "Stats NZ is aware of concerns some have about this classification, and it is an ongoing point of discussion with stakeholders." The Fijian Indian community in Aotearoa has long opposed this and raised the issue again at a community event Rabuka attended in Auckland's Māngere ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Samoa last month. "As far as Fiji is concerned, [Indo Fijians] are Fijians," he said. When asked what his message to New Zealand on the issue would be, he said: "I cannot; that is a matter of sovereignty, the sovereign decision by the government of New Zealand. What they call people is their sovereign right. As far as we are concerned, we hope that they will be treated as Fijians." More than 60,000 people were transferred from all parts of British India to work in Fiji between 1879 and 1916 as indentured labourers. Today, they make up over 32 percent of the total population, according to Fiji Bureau of Statistics' 2017 Population Census. Now many, like Sangam community NZ leader and former Nadi Mayor Salesh Mudaliar, say they are more Fijian than Indian. "If you do a DNA or do a blood test, we are more of Fijian than anything else. We are not Indian," Mudaliar said. The indenture labourers, who came to be known as the Girmitiyas, as they were bound by a girmit a Hindi pronunciation of the English word "agreement". RNZ Pacific had approached the Viti Council e Aotearoa for their views on the issue. However, they refused to comment, saying that its chair "has opted out of this interview." "Topic itself is misleading bordering on disinformation [and] misinformation from an Indigenous Fijian perspective and overly sensitive plus short notice." 'Struggling for identity' "We are Pacific Islanders. If you come from Tonga or Samoa, you are a Pacific Islander," Mudaliar said. "When [Indo Fijians] come from Fiji, we are not. We are not a migrant to Fiji. We have been there for [over 140] years." "The community is still struggling for its identity here in New Zealand…we are still not [looked after]. He said they have tried to lobby the New Zealand government for their status but without success. "Now it is the National government, and no one seems to be listening to us in understanding the situation. "If we can have an open discussion on this, coming to the same table, and knowing what our problem is, then it would be really appreciated." Lifting quality of data Stats NZ said it is aware of the need to lift the quality of ethnicity data across the government data system. "Public consultation in 2019 determined a need for an in depth review of the Ethnicity Standard," the data agency said. In 2021, Stats NZ undertook a large scoping exercise with government agencies, researchers, iwi Māori, and community groups to help establish the scope of the review. Stats NZ subsequently stood up an expert working group to progress the review. "This review is still underway, and Stats NZ will be conducting further consultation, so we will have more to say in due course," it said. "Classifying ethnicity and ethnic identity is extremely complex, and it is important Stats NZ takes the time to consult extensively and ensure we get this right," the agency added. This week, Fijians celebrate the Hindu festival of lights, Diwali. The nation observes a public holiday to mark the day, and Fijians of all backgrounds get involved. Prime Minister Rabuka's message is for all Fijians to be kind to each other. "Act in accordance with the spirit of Diwali and show kindness to those who are going through difficulties," he told local reporters outside parliament on Thursday. "It is a good time for us to abstain from using bad language against each other on social media." Related

65.document_summary: Indo-Fijians in New Zealand are challenging their ethnic classification, which currently places them under "Asian/Indian" rather than "Pacific Islander" on Stats NZ records. Despite Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka affirming that Indo-Fijians are Fijians, New Zealand's classification system has remained unchanged since 2005. The Indo-Fijian community, descendants of indentured laborers (Girmitiyas) brought to Fiji between 1879-1916 who now comprise over 32% of Fiji's population, argues they should be recognized as Pacific Islanders. Community leaders like Salesh Mudaliar emphasize their deep roots in Fiji and Pacific identity rather than Indian heritage. Stats NZ acknowledges ongoing concerns and is conducting a comprehensive ethnicity standard review with stakeholder consultation to address data quality issues.

67.document_summary: Former Black Ferns sevens player Shiray Kaka, an Olympic gold medalist from the Tokyo Games, shares her personal journey of learning the Samoan language and reconnecting with her cultural heritage during Samoa Language Week. Born to a Māori mother and Samoan father from Moata'a village, Kaka grew up largely disconnected from both cultures. Motivated by the arrival of her baby boy and encouragement from her grandmother, she has committed to attending weekly Samoan lessons to ensure she can pass on cultural knowledge and language to the next generation. The article highlights Kaka's emphasis on the importance of learning language, understanding aganuu (cultural customs), and maintaining meaningful connection to her people and roots. Additionally, Kaka expresses her interest in representing Samoa's rugby team in the future and offers practical advice to others embarking on their own language learning journeys, encouraging consistency and full embrace of their cultural identity.

[Page 1] The Cook Islands secretary of culture Emile Kairua says people in his country are getting complacent about the use of Māori. Cook Islands Māori Language Week started on Sunday in New Zealand and will run until Saturday. Kairua said the language is at risk at the source. "Here in the homeland, we're complacent," he told RNZ Pacific. "People have stopped using it in their everyday lives. Even my children, I must admit, don't speak Cook Islands Māori. They understand it, thankfully, but they can't speak it." Kairua said he thinks Cook Islands Māori is stronger in Aotearoa because that is where a lot of the language teachers are living. "We haven't done a welfare audit of the language in Aotearoa [but] I would imagine that it's a lot stronger, purely because a lot of our teachers, a lot of our orators, are living in Aotearoa. https://www.rnz.co. nz/international/programmes/datelinepacific/audio/2018998039/cook isl anders reflect on nation s 60th milestone "I guess being away from the source, being away from home, there is a feeling of homesickness, so that you do tend to grab onto to what you're missing." He said it was "critical" that Cook Islanders "wake up and appreciate the importance of our language and make sure that it's not a dying part of our identity". "A race without a language they don't have an identity. So as Cook Islanders, either first, second or third generation, we need to hold on to this." Ministry of Pacific Peoples secretary Gerardine Clifford Lidstone said there is power in our language it anchors identity and builds belonging. The theme of the week, ''Ātui'ia au ki te vaka o tōku matakeinanga', translates to 'connect me to the offerings of my people'. The Cook Islands Māori community is the third largest Pacific group in Aotearoa New Zealand. UNESCO lists te reo Māori Kūki 'Airani as one of the most endangered Pacific languages supported through the Pacific Language Week series. [Page 1] A growing youthful population of Māori and Pasifika is the future of Aotearoa New Zealand, a former Pacific peoples minister says. https://w ww.rnz.co.nz/international/programmes/datelinepacific/audio/20189405 14/nz census shows an increase in pacific population Stats NZ data from the latest census has revealed an increase in Pacific population groups from 8.1 in 2018 to 8.9 percent in 2023. It also showed the median age for Pacific people is 25. The former minister and community leader Aupito William Sio said the data is a confirmation. "I have always known for a very long time that we are a very fast growing population which paints a picture that Pasifika as well as Māori are the future of New Zealand," he said. The Pasifika population has grown rapidly, about twice the rate of New Zealand's population, according to 2006 2023 census data. Pacific people now make up 442,632 people compared to 381,642 in 2018. The New Zealand population has grown to nearly five million in total. The matter of Indo Fijians/Fijian Indians claiming Pacific Islander in the census as their ethnicity must also be considered, Fiji Girmit NZ president Krish Naidu said, noting what has been a long standing issue. "They do have a Fijian passport. I will always include them but there is a different matter when it comes to Fijian. They are divided and it is a matter," Sio said. RNZ Pacific asked the Minister for Pacific Peoples Dr Shane Reti on whether Indo Fijians were included in Ministry of Pacific Peoples as Pacific people. In a statement, his office said: "The Ministry for Pacific Peoples is undertaking ongoing policy work to better understand this issue." During this month's Girmit celebrations in Auckland, Prime Minister Chris Luxon did not address the issue despite "clarity" being directly called from this coalition government being called for by the Girmit community. Under the coalition government there is no Pacific representation in Parliament. Budget and tax cuts Meanwhile, around 5000 public sector roles have been axed by the coalition government's priority to make national tax cuts. Over 60 jobs from the Ministry for Pacific Peoples are included in this, but 31 roles were already vacant. "The job cuts at the moment is causing uncertainty, it is causing a real sense of low morale within the public sector workforce," Sio said. "It's tough times for many facing redundancies." RNZ Pacific has spoken to one public sector worker who did not wish to be named. They had already lost "two jobs in one year." After the elections, they wanted to "create change" and help their community by working within the public sector. Despite many of their colleagues leaving because they did not align with the values of New Zealand new coalition leaders, they said staying in good faith has resulted in her job being on the line. The public sector worker said it was a "disappointing" outcome. Sio said he felt "suspicious about New Zealand's upcoming budget" and was unaware of Pacific community leaders being invited to any pre or post budget events. Following last year's scrutiny over a pre budget breakfast blowout, the Ministry of Pacific Peoples was criticised by ACT leader David Seymour for "overspending" taxpayer money. Opposition's deputy leader of Labour and spokesperson for Pacific peoples Carmel Sepuloni has been approached for comment. [Page 1] 'You're not a nobody': Auckland student embraces Solomon Islands heritage ByTiana Haxton Journalist, Coco Lance RNZ Pacific Digital Journalist 2025 11 28 13:40:23+13:00 Feature A student from St Pauls primary school in Auckland says his Solomon Islands heritage is his identity. Solomon Islands Pidgin Language Week is being celebrated across New Zealand, under the theme "Protektim langguis an kalsa blong yumi Protect our language and culture." To mark the occasion, the Solomon Islands Auckland Wantok Association Inc visited Bruce Satchell's primary school to share a cultural showcase with his classmates. Eleven year old Satchell is proud to hail from seven different cultures, including the Solomon Islands. He said learning about his indigenous heritage is how he connects to his identity. "It's really important because I get to know my family history and my indigenous part of my life. It's just very important to know where you're from, and like, you're not a nobody. So like a somebody, yeah." Satchell's cousins were amongst the performers sharing traditional Solomon Islands dances for the students of St Pauls primary. For the sixth grader, sharing his culture makes him feel proud of who he is. "Well, today was like, magical, seeing everyone like perform and give their best. Yeah, it was really good... I feel powerful and proud and glad to be here." The chair of the Auckland Wantok Association said it is vital to encourage young ones to connect with their heritage. Florie Dausabea was proud to support Bruce in sharing his Solomon Islands culture with his peers. "It reinforces and reaffirms who he is, his identity and his culture and custom. And I think that is very important. It is the essence of why we celebrate Solomon Islands language week." St Pauls primary caters to students between five and eleven years old. With a roll of 470, the school hosts a diverse spread of cultures. Principal Mary Zellman said it is vital the school takes every opportunity to celebrate everyone's heritage. "I really feel very strongly that we need to celebrate different people's cultures and have pride in our own cultures by celebrating everybody's cultures." "It's really important that we know who we are and where we come from, and that needs to be, that has to be acknowledged, because we're all human beings, We're all Special. We're all unique." Deputy principal Angelina Brayne echoed her sentiments, saying they want to foster cultural pride amongst all their students. This was something she saw in action as former students were amongst the performers on stage. "It was a privilege, an absolute honor, and to see our past pupils, also to be part of the cultural group and to go on from St Paul's School and to be proud of who they are, strong and their identity. That's what we want for all our tamariki." The Deo sisters have fond memories of their time at St Pauls primary. They said the teachers always encouraged them to be proud of their heritage. Ebony Deo was excited to return to embrace and show off their culture. "I'm very happy to show my culture to… my past teachers as well, to see like, how well I've done and how proud I am." Her elder sister Jolenna said being able to encourage the young students to embrace their indigenous languages is vital. "I think it's fundamental. I think it's incredibly important. I think language tells you a lot about who you are and the people that you come from, and gives you a sense of belonging... so language, to me, is like at the core of a lot of our culture." Solomon Islands is a predominantly Melanesian nation that has more than 70 indigenous languages and dialects on Melanesian and Polynesian origin. In this culturally diverse context, Pidgin has a unifying effect in that it is spoken by Solomon Islanders throughout the country. This year is only the second edition of the Solomon Islands Pidgin Language week runs through until Satruday. It is the last event on the Ministry of Pacific Peoples New Zealand language week series calendar. Related

2.fileDescription:
This comprehensive guide explores Auckland, New Zealand's largest metropolitan region with 1.42 million residents (one-third of the national population). The document covers Auckland's diverse geography featuring two harbours, 49 volcanic cones, and 1,613 kilometres of coastline. As a multicultural metropolis where Asians, Pacific Islanders, and Māori comprise 48% of residents, Auckland is the world's largest Polynesian city.

The guide traces Auckland's history from early Māori settlement through European colonization beginning in the 1820s, establishment as New Zealand's capital in 1840, the kauri timber industry boom (1870-1900), and transformation into a modern industrial and commercial center. It documents significant immigration waves including Irish settlers, post-WWII British immigrants, Māori rural-to-urban migration, Vietnamese refugees, and Asian migrants.

Geologically, Auckland features ancient greywacke basement rock and volcanic eruptions dating from 150,000 years ago to Rangitoto's eruption 600 years ago. The region's warm, moderately wet climate supports native vegetation including kauri forests and pōhutukawa trees, alongside over 600 introduced exotic species.

The document covers contemporary development as a primate city, urban sprawl, motorway development, and economic shifts from manufacturing to services. It details vibrant cultural institutions, sports venues like Eden Park, and the "City of Sails" sailing culture. The guide addresses government structure (unified council since 2010), education (558 schools plus tertiary institutions), healthcare development, and contemporary challenges including traffic congestion and housing affordability.

chunkHighlights.text: Auckland is the gateway for immigrants, and over one-third of its population were born overseas. Waves of immigrants have settled in particular areas, and helped shape local cultures. Europeans dominate rural areas, but in the central city over half of the population is Asian. West and South Auckland have large Pacific and Māori communities. Auckland’s openness to outside influences creates a buoyant culture.

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces Pacific Islander migration to New Zealand from the 1850s to 2018. Early arrivals included students brought by Anglican missionary George Selwyn in the 1850s, with approximately 200 Pacific Islanders in New Zealand by 1916. Migration patterns were influenced by colonial ties, with most Pacific peoples coming from nearby islands with British colonial histories including Samoa, Cook Islands, Tonga, Niue, Fiji, and Tokelau. From the 1970s onward, migration increased significantly, with communities forming primarily in Auckland. The document details specific groups including Kiribati people (arriving since the 1970s, reaching 3,225 by 2018) and Tuvaluans (growing from 900 in 1996 to 4,653 in 2018), many seeking work, education, health services, or fleeing environmental concerns. By 2018, over 9,600 people from other Pacific islands lived in New Zealand. The document also examines populations from French Polynesia (Tahitians with 1,737 by 2018), Papua New Guinea, and Solomon Islands, documenting their migration patterns, cultural practices, and integration into New Zealand society. Census data from 2006-2018 shows growth across multiple Pacific Islander ethnic groups. The document emphasizes cultural preservation through organizations, sports participation, and community networks, while addressing identity complexities faced by mixed-heritage individuals.

chunkHighlights.text: But there are many other Pacific islands, and in 2018 there were more than 9,600 people born in these islands living in New Zealand. Most numerous among other them were Kiribati people, Tuvaluans, Tahitians, Papua New Guineans and Solomon Islanders.

Initially, Pacific Islanders often came as students or visited on temporary work permits. From the 1970s more people settled, forming communities mainly in the Auckland area. Community life meant that they could continue to speak their language and maintain their customs.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines the systemic deportation and racial discrimination faced by Pasifika New Zealanders through the "dawn raids" of the 1970s-1980s. Initially encouraged to migrate for manufacturing jobs, Pacific Islanders faced targeted persecution when the economy declined. Despite comprising only one-third of overstayers, Pasifika people made up two-thirds of prosecutions. Police conducted racially-targeted raids on homes, workplaces, bars, and churches, detaining people based on appearance rather than legal status, affecting even New Zealand citizens and legal residents from Cook Islands, Tokelau, and Niue. The Polynesian Panthers emerged in 1971 as a resistance movement inspired by the American Black Panther Party. Founded by six young activists including Melani Anae, the Panthers fought racism through peaceful resistance, community programs, legal education, and counter-raids on politicians' homes. The piece highlights the Panthers' 50-year legacy and their continued advocacy efforts, including a 10,000-signature petition to the Immigration Minister and educational programs in schools. It documents current vulnerabilities faced by undocumented migrants and the government's formal apology announced for June 26, 2021. The Panthers continue their mission through community education, emphasizing that education remains the strongest form of protest against systemic injustice.

chunkHighlights.text: While Pasifika communities comprised a minority of migrants to New Zealand—eclipsed by migrants from Europe, North America and Australia—they were highly visible and easily scapegoated, much like the Chinese immigrants before them. “The myth was that Pasifika
people were stealing jobs,” says activist Alec Toleafoa. “That we were responsible for the violent crime, and that we were largely to blame for the country’s economic woes.”

For the Pasifika community, the crackdown on immigration status came as a surprise. Previously, the authorities hadn’t seemed to care about overstayers. “They were quite happy to waive the immigration documentation while things were going good,” says Toleafoa, “but once the economy busted, then they started to enforce immigration laws.”
Central Auckland suburbs such as Ponsonby and Grey Lynn were at the heart of the Pasifika diaspora. A marching group entertains crowds on Samoan Day at Grey Lynn Park on January 26, 1974.

5.fileTitle: Evicted from Aotearoa: The Dawn Raids, Polynesian Panthers, and Pasifika Immigration Injustice in New Zealand

The document details specific groups including Kiribati people (arriving since the 1970s, reaching 3,225 by 2018) and Tuvaluans (growing from 900 in 1996 to 4,653 in 2018), many seeking work, education, health services, or fleeing environmental concerns. By 2018, over 9,600 people from other Pacific islands lived in New Zealand. The document also examines populations from French Polynesia (Tahitians with 1,737 by 2018), Papua New Guinea, and Solomon Islands, documenting their migration patterns, cultural practices, and integration into New Zealand society. Census data from 2006-2018 shows growth across multiple Pacific Islander ethnic groups. The document emphasizes cultural preservation through organizations, sports participation, and community networks, while addressing identity complexities faced by mixed-heritage individuals.

chunkHighlights.text: In 2018 the six largest groups of Pacific peoples in New Zealand were Samoans, Tongans, Cook Islanders, Fijians, Niueans, and Tokelauans. However, there were also people from most of the other islands that pepper the world’s largest ocean.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's rapidly transforming society through ethnic diversity, urban development, and demographic shifts. Since the 1987 Immigration Act, New Zealand has become one of the most ethnically diverse nations with 213 ethnic groups. Auckland, hosting 40% of ethnic migrants, is now more diverse than Sydney, London, or Los Angeles, with Asian populations at 23% expected to overtake Maori as the largest ethnic minority by the 2020s. The document explores how diversity has manifested geographically through 'ethnoburbs' and ethnic precincts, exemplified by Northcote's transformation into an 80% Asian business district. New Zealand faces significant demographic challenges: single-person households have risen from one in ten to one in four, family structures have fundamentally shifted, and urban growth is heavily concentrated in major cities while many regional areas face permanent decline. Examples include Waiouru declining from 1,647 to 738 residents between 2001-2013, and Ruapehu District declining 12% since 2006. Rising income inequality grew faster than most OECD countries between 1985-2008, with the top 10% earning nine times more than the bottom 10%. Urban spatial segregation is increasing, with wealthy residents moving to city centers while lower-income populations are pushed to peripheries, creating housing affordability crises. The analysis contrasts compact urban intensification versus greenfield sprawl approaches. New Zealand's attitudes toward Asian immigration have warmed significantly since the 1990s, though challenges including stereotyping and workplace discrimination persist. Resilience across New Zealand's diverse communities will be essential for navigating the future.

chunkHighlights.text: Although, again, what does it mean to be from the ‘Pacific Islands’? In 2001, Pacific studies lecturer Melani Anae wrote: “There’s no generic ‘Pacific community’ but rather Pacific peoples, who align themselves variously, and at different times, along ethnic, geographic, church, family, school, age/gender, youth/elders, island born/NZ born, or occupational lines, or a mix of these.”

8.fileDescription: This comprehensive historical document traces the evolution of New Zealand national identity from European contact through the early 21st century. The work examines how the term "New Zealander" shifted from referring to Māori in early colonial periods to European settlers, then evolved into a complex multicultural identity. Key developments include: the emergence of distinct identity through cultural markers like the All Blacks rugby team's 1905 victory and Edmund Hillary's Everest climb; the impact of World Wars I and II on national consciousness; the development of Pākehā culture characterized by beach culture, bush appreciation, and rugby traditions; and transformation from bicultural to multicultural society through immigration from Pacific Islands, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. The document explores how environmental factors, compulsory education, the 1890 Liberal government's reformist policies (women's suffrage, land reform), and nation-building efforts shaped national identity. It examines Māori integration and separate nationalism, the role of military service and sporting achievements in establishing national character, and how social movements including feminism, biculturalism, and recognition of Māori sovereignty transformed New Zealand identity. By the 21st century, "New Zealandness" had become multifaceted, shaped by geography, Māori heritage, British colonization, and recent immigration.

chunkHighlights.text: As the numbers of non-British people increased, their cultural differences became more evident. In South Auckland, Pacific Islanders congregated and evolved a distinctive New Zealand Pacific culture which was more than the sum of their different cultures. Large Asian communities who had originally been settled throughout the country came together in areas with their own schools and styles of housing.

9.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines Tongan migration to New Zealand and community development from the 1960s onwards. By 2018, over 82,000 Tongans lived in New Zealand, with two-thirds born there, making them the second-largest Pacific ethnic group, primarily settled in Auckland's Ōtara and Māngere. Despite socio-economic challenges including lower median incomes ($21,000 vs $40,000 nationally), overcrowded housing, and lower employment rates, Tongans maintain strong cultural identity through churches, language, and family traditions rooted in anga faka-Tonga. The document explores how Tongan culture blends traditional values of respect, obedience, and reciprocal sharing with Christian beliefs introduced by Methodist missionaries in the 1820s. It identifies three distinct Tongan groups: those maintaining traditional anga faka-Tonga, New Zealand-born Tongans with decreasing language knowledge, and those identifying with broader Pacific Islander identity. Language preservation challenges are evident, with Tongan-speaking population declining from 63% (1996) to 40% (2018). The document highlights the emergence of Pasifika Aotearoa—a new cultural identity blending Pacific traditions with Afro-American influences, hip-hop, and reggae. Success measures are rooted in family obligations and community contributions, with cultural contributions through music, sports, and arts enriching New Zealand society.

chunkHighlights.text: Pacific Islanders with a broader ethnic identity in New Zealand call themselves PIs, Polys, or New Zealand-borns. They have developed new music, fashion, customs and ways of speaking. This distinctive identity is sometimes referred to as Pasifika Aotearoa.

Some young PIs are heavily influenced by Afro-American youth culture in their dress, slang, body language and music, especially hip hop and rhythm and blues. Rastafarianism is another significant influence, notable in young PIs’ dreadlocks and adapted reggae sounds. PIs in South Auckland are making cultural contributions through the Ōtara market and the Secondary Schools Cultural Festival.

Despite South Auckland’s reputation for social problems, lyrics by Pasifika Aotearoa music groups such as the OMC (Ōtara Millionaires’ Club) often praise areas of South Auckland with a strongly Pacific identity. The highly successful annual Pasifika Festival at Western Springs is contributing to the spectacle and strengthening of this identity.

10.fileDescription:
This comprehensive guide explores Auckland, New Zealand's largest metropolitan region with 1.42 million residents (one-third of the national population). The document covers Auckland's diverse geography featuring two harbours, 49 volcanic cones, and 1,613 kilometres of coastline. As a multicultural metropolis where Asians, Pacific Islanders, and Māori comprise 48% of residents, Auckland is the world's largest Polynesian city.

The guide traces Auckland's history from early Māori settlement through European colonization beginning in the 1820s, establishment as New Zealand's capital in 1840, the kauri timber industry boom (1870-1900), and transformation into a modern industrial and commercial center. It documents significant immigration waves including Irish settlers, post-WWII British immigrants, Māori rural-to-urban migration, Vietnamese refugees, and Asian migrants.

Geologically, Auckland features ancient greywacke basement rock and volcanic eruptions dating from 150,000 years ago to Rangitoto's eruption 600 years ago. The region's warm, moderately wet climate supports native vegetation including kauri forests and pōhutukawa trees, alongside over 600 introduced exotic species.

The document covers contemporary development as a primate city, urban sprawl, motorway development, and economic shifts from manufacturing to services. It details vibrant cultural institutions, sports venues like Eden Park, and the "City of Sails" sailing culture. The guide addresses government structure (unified council since 2010), education (558 schools plus tertiary institutions), healthcare development, and contemporary challenges including traffic congestion and housing affordability.

chunkHighlights.text: The region’s music scene is distinctive for its strong hip-hop culture, first channelled through American Samoa in the 1980s and revitalised by second- and third-generation Pacific Islanders in central and South Auckland. The movement has embraced graffiti, rap, clothing, and community programmes. Hip-hop artists such as Che Fu and Nesian Mystik and the recording label Dawn Raid have influenced mainstream popular music.

11.fileDescription: This document explores the rich landscape of cultural dance in New Zealand from the 19th century through the 2000s. It traces how immigrant communities brought diverse dance traditions including Pacific Island dances (tamure, lakalaka, siva), European styles (Scottish reels, Irish dancing, English folk dancing, Polish, Greek), and Asian forms (Balinese legong, Indian bharata natyam and kathak, Chinese lion and dragon dances). European folk dancing was initially dominant but expanded beyond English and Scottish traditions from the 1980s onward. Major cultural events like the Pasifika Festival and Polyfest emerged as among the largest dance festivals in Oceania. Key figures including Prime Minister Peter Fraser, teacher Rae Storey, and dancers Liong Xi and Vivek Kinra promoted these diverse forms. Organizations such as Dance Aotearoa New Zealand (DANZ) and Pacific Dance New Zealand (PDNZ) provided crucial support. By the 21st century, New Zealand's cultural dance scene had become highly diverse with multiple forms taught across schools and cultural centers. Different dance forms increasingly influenced each other and were performed at the same festivals, breaking down traditional boundaries. While cultural dance attracted large audiences and generated economic value, infrastructure remained limited with most events relying on volunteers.

chunkHighlights.text: Pacific dance

Pacific Island immigrants after the Second World War brought their dance styles with them to New Zealand. At first these dances were performed at family, community and school events. By the 2000s the Pacific dance community (especially in Auckland) was so large and active that it attracted visitors from around the Pacific. Auckland’s Pasifika Festival and Polyfest drew huge audiences. Pacific Dance New Zealand ran dance classes and the Pacific Dance Fono.

13.fileDescription: Auckland's Pasifika Festival is taking place at Western Springs on March 8-9, 2025, featuring diverse cultural performances, poetry, dance, and workshops celebrating Pacific Island communities. The festival, which runs 9am-6pm Saturday and 10am-4pm Sunday with free entry, showcases authenticity in cultural exchange and food offerings. Political leaders including opposition leader Chris Hipkins and Green Party MP Teanau Tuiono attended, emphasizing the importance of celebrating Pasifika communities as integral to Aotearoa's identity. ByChristina Persico, Coco Lance - RNZ Pacific Digital Journalist
2025-03-08 15:09:02+13:00

Auckland's Pasifika Festival is under way at Western Springs with a raft
of sound and colour. Events on offer on Saturday included poetry, Zumba, a guide-to-life workshop and multiple performances, including an afternoon show from Fijian R&B group the LeftOvas, who opened for Six60 earlier this month. Aansan Yen, who has Chinese heritage but was born and raised in the Netherlands, said she was intrigued by and interested in Pasific Island cultures. "I love to see the dance, the artistry, and I also feel a strong connection to the ocean," she said. https://www.r nz.co.nz/national/programmes/saturday/audio/2018978001/live-from-th e-pasifika-festival "It's important to celebrate unity, tradition, community - all the things that make life important for me." Political leaders also made an appearance, and the leader of the opposition Chris Hipkins said the festival was a chance to connect with different Pasifika communities in one place. "Pasifika communities make up such a big part of Aotearoa's overall culture and identity. We are of the Pacific," he said. "I think political leaders have got a really important job in bringing the community together. That means celebrating our differences." Pasifika Festival runs from 9am to 6pm on Saturday 8 March and 10am to 4pm on Sunday 9 March. The festival was cancelled in 2019 following the Christchurch mosque attacks, then again in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic. In 2023 the festival went ahead but took a very different tone, held just weeks after storms devastated much of Auckland. Major Events from Tātaki Auckland Unlimited's festival director and group manager Jep Savali said Pasifika Festival is now on a "growth curve". Authenticity had become an important topic in discussions with the Pasifika Village Charitable Trust, which advised on the cultural integrity of the festival. "In our feedback to each other about how we can be better, where we can once again grow this festival, authenticity is really important. Authenticity of food offering, authenticity in terms of the cultural exchange, in terms of the performances." Green Party MP Teanau Tuiono also used the weekend to
announce a petition asking the government to extend visa-free travel to

visitors from Pacific Island nations. Tuiono said Pasifika Festival would show Aotearoa New Zealand was a Pacific nation "by the rich cultural expression and coming together of peoples". Pasifika Festival runs from 9am to 6pm on Saturday 8 March and 10am to 4pm on Sunday 9 March. Entry is free. Related

fileAuthor: Eleisha Foon - RNZ Pacific Senior Journalist
14.fileDescription: Latest census data reveals that Pacific and Māori populations are growing rapidly and represent the future of Aotearoa New Zealand. The Pacific population increased from 8.1% in 2018 to 8.9% in 2023, with 442,632 people now comprising this demographic. The median age for Pacific people is 25, indicating a youthful population. Former Pacific peoples minister Aupito William Sio confirms this growth trajectory. However, the article highlights concerns including the unresolved status of Indo-Fijians claiming Pacific Islander ethnicity, lack of Pacific representation in Parliament under the coalition government, and significant job cuts affecting the Ministry for Pacific Peoples (60 jobs, 31 already vacant) due to budget priorities and tax cuts. Public sector workers report low morale and uncertainty amid redundancies.

chunkHighlights.text:
A growing youthful population of Māori and Pasifika is the future of
Aotearoa New Zealand, a former Pacific peoples minister says. https://w
ww.rnz.co.nz/international/programmes/datelinepacific/audio/20189405 14/nz-census-shows-an-increase-in-pacific-population Stats NZ data from the latest census has revealed an increase in Pacific population groups from 8.1 in 2018 to 8.9 percent in 2023. It also showed the median age for Pacific people is 25. The former minister and community leader Aupito William Sio said the data is a confirmation. "I have always known for a very long time that we are a very fast growing population which paints a picture that Pasifika as well as Māori are the future of New Zealand," he said. The Pasifika population has grown rapidly, about twice the rate of New Zealand's population, according to 2006-2023 census data. Pacific people now make up 442,632 people compared to 381,642 in 2018. The New Zealand population has grown to nearly five million in total. The matter of Indo-Fijians/Fijian-Indians claiming Pacific Islander in the census as their ethnicity must also be considered, Fiji Girmit NZ president Krish Naidu said, noting what has been a long-standing issue. "They do have a Fijian passport. I will always include them but there is a different matter when it comes to Fijian. They are divided and it is a matter," Sio said. RNZ Pacific asked the Minister for Pacific Peoples Dr Shane Reti on whether Indo-Fijians were included in Ministry of Pacific Peoples as Pacific people. In a statement, his office said: "The Ministry for Pacific Peoples is undertaking ongoing policy work to better understand this issue." During this month's Girmit celebrations in Auckland, Prime Minister Chris Luxon did not address the issue despite "clarity" being directly called from this coalition government being called for by the Girmit community. Under the coalition government there is no Pacific representation in Parliament. Budget and tax cuts Meanwhile, around 5000 public sector roles have been axed by the coalition government's priority to make national tax cuts. Over 60 jobs from the Ministry for Pacific Peoples are included in
this, but 31 roles were already vacant. "The job cuts at the moment is

causing uncertainty, it is causing a real sense of low morale within the public sector workforce," Sio said. "It's tough times for many facing redundancies." RNZ Pacific has spoken to one public sector worker who did not wish to be named. They had already lost "two jobs in one year." After the elections, they wanted to "create change" and help their community by working within the public sector. Despite many of their colleagues leaving because they did not align with the values of New Zealand new coalition leaders, they said staying in good faith has resulted in her job being on the line. The public sector worker said it was a "disappointing" outcome. Sio said he felt "suspicious about New Zealand's upcoming budget" and was unaware of Pacific community leaders being invited to any pre or post budget events. Following last year's scrutiny over a pre-budget breakfast blowout, the Ministry of Pacific Peoples was criticised by ACT leader David Seymour for "overspending" taxpayer money. Opposition's deputy leader of Labour and spokesperson for Pacific peoples Carmel Sepuloni has been approached for comment. Related

response.response_text:
## Kia Ora — Aotearoa's Beloved Greeting

The most widely used te reo Māori greeting is **'kia ora'**, which functions as a general hello. It's beautifully versatile — both Māori and Pākehā New Zealanders use it in everyday life, and it's increasingly common across all settings, from casual encounters to formal occasions. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

When saying farewell, you'd say **'ka kite'** or **'ka kite anō'** — the te reo equivalent of 'see you' or 'see you again'. [[1]](cite://1/2) Another greeting worth knowing is **'tēnā koe'**, which is also used as a way of acknowledging the person in front of you. [[2]](cite://2/1)

## Physical Greetings

Beyond words, Māori greeting customs involve a physical element that carries deep cultural meaning. The **hongi** — the ceremonial pressing of noses — is one of the most distinctive and ancient of these customs. [[3]](cite://3/1)

![embed-2](embed://2)

In a formal Māori context, you would shake hands *and* hongi (press noses briefly) when meeting someone. [[4]](cite://4/1) The hongi connects back to the mythological figure of Tāne Mahuta, who breathed life into the first woman, Hineahuone ('woman formed of earth'), through the nose — making the sharing of breath a deeply symbolic act of peace and connection. [[3]](cite://3/2)

## A Language of Welcome

The phrase **'haere mai'** — meaning 'welcome' — is also a cornerstone of Māori greeting tradition, historically called out to approaching visitors to invite them in. [[5]](cite://5/1)[[6]](cite://6/1) Formal welcomes, known as **pōwhiri**, can include the karanga (a ceremonial call by women), whaikōrero (formal speeches), and the hongi, all following a pattern that dates back to before European arrival in Aotearoa. [[7]](cite://7/1)[[3]](cite://3/3)

The Māori Language Commission (Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori) encourages all New Zealanders — Māori and non-Māori alike — to embrace simple greetings like 'kia ora' and 'tēnā koe' as a meaningful way to support and celebrate te reo Māori. As their tumu whakahaere (chief executive) Ngahiwi Apanui Barr put it, "whether it's speaking Māori every day... or just using greetings like kia ora or tēnā koe, it all adds up to te reo Māori surviving and being valued." [[2]](cite://2/2)

Would you like to know more about the pōwhiri ceremony and what to expect if you're welcomed onto a marae?

## Sources

[1] [New Zealand Manners and Social Etiquette: Historical Evolution and Modern Practice](https://teara.govt.nz/en/manners-and-social-behaviour)
[2] [Te Wiki o Te Reo Māori 2024: Te Taura Whiri's Dream for Nationwide Show of Love for Māori Language](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/526116/te-wiki-o-te-reo-maori-2024-te-taura-whiri-s-dream-for-nationwide-show-of-love-for-maori-language)
[3] [Māori Manners, Social Behaviour, and Cultural Customs: From Traditional Practices to Modern Adaptation](https://teara.govt.nz/en/maori-manners-and-social-behaviour-nga-mahi-tika)
[4] [New Zealand Manners and Social Etiquette: Historical Evolution and Modern Practice](https://teara.govt.nz/en/manners-and-social-behaviour)
[5] [Māori Manners, Social Behaviour, and Cultural Customs: From Traditional Practices to Modern Adaptation](https://teara.govt.nz/en/maori-manners-and-social-behaviour-nga-mahi-tika)
[6] [Welcoming the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall and York](https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/the-man-who-drew-wellington/)
[7] [Māori Manners, Social Behaviour, and Cultural Customs: From Traditional Practices to Modern Adaptation](https://teara.govt.nz/en/maori-manners-and-social-behaviour-nga-mahi-tika)

1.text:
[Page 1] ByRawinia Higgins rāua ko Basil Keane Te reo Māori is the language of the Māori people of New Zealand. It was made an official language of New Zealand in 1987. In 2018, around 21% of Māori and 4% of the total population could speak te reo Māori . Māori is a Polynesian language, part of the Austronesian language family. There are three major dialects eastern North Island, western North Island and South Island Māori. Pākehā encounter te reo The first Europeans in New Zealand had to learn Māori to communicate. Some married Māori women and had children who were bilingual. Māori was not a written language before Europeans arrived. Early spelling was varied, but became more standardised from the 1820s. Missionary William Williams published a Māori dictionary in 1844. Writing in Māori became important as Pākehā tried to buy Māori land. Missionaries translated the Bible for their converts. English spreads As European settlement increased, there were more English speakers. Māori communities mostly continued to speak Māori. In the later 19th century laws specially affecting Māori were translated into Māori, and interpreters were appointed to Parliament. Missionary schools had operated in Māori, but from 1847 children had to be taught in English. In the 19th century traditional oral literature was written down and Māori language newspapers were published. Language decline By the early 20th century more Māori spoke English as well as Māori. Over the 20th century the education system promoted English, many Māori men died in the world wars, and urban migration increased contact with Pākehā . English became the main language spoken in Māori homes, and many Māori saw it as the language of success and advancement. New initiatives In the later 20th century Māori studies courses were set up in universities. Some students became aware of issues such as land rights and language loss. In 1972 over 30,000 people signed a petition asking for te reo Māori to be taught in schools. In the 1970s some high schools began teaching te reo Māori . From 1982 kōhanga reo (pre school language learning nests) were set up. Kura kaupapa and wharekura (Māori language schools) also opened. Māori language radio stations began broadcasting in 1987. Māori Television (Whakaata Māori) was set up in 2004 and its Te Reo channel began transmitting in 2008. The Māori language The Māori language is known as te reo Māori or simply te reo (the language). It is the language of the Māori people of New Zealand. Te reo Māori is an official language in New Zealand, along with New Zealand Sign Language. It was made official in 1987.

1.document_title: Te Reo Māori: History, Decline, and Revitalisation in New Zealand
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of te reo Māori (the Māori language) from first European contact in 1769 through modern revitalisation efforts. Te reo Māori, a Polynesian language within the Austronesian family, became the official language of New Zealand in 1987. The document details the language's three major dialects and its evolution through early European contact, missionary involvement, and the development of written Māori from the 1820s onward. It chronicles the systematic decline following the Education Ordinance 1847, which mandated English-only education, leading to significant speaker population reduction by the 20th century due to urbanisation, world wars, and assimilationist policies. The revitalisation movement began in the 1970s, including the 1972 te reo petition (30,000 signatures), establishment of Māori Language Week, and the landmark 1984 Māori Language Claim (WAI 11). Key initiatives include kōhanga reo (language immersion centres) established in 1982, kura kaupapa (immersion schools), wharekura (secondary schools), and Te Ataarangi adult learning programmes. The Māori Language Act 1987 established Māori as an official language and created Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori. Broadcasting played a crucial role through Te Upoko o Te Ika radio station (1987), Te Māngai Pāho funding agency (1993), and Māori Television (2004). As of 2018, approximately 21% of Māori and 4% of the total population speak the language.

2.text:
[Page 6] Revival of te reo Māori has been a vital part of biculturalism in recent years. The number of New Zealanders who can speak more than a few words and phrases in te reo is growing. It is now not unusual to hear towns and cities being referred to by both their Māori and English names, and many people refer to New Zealand as Aotearoa.

2.document_title: Biculturalism in New Zealand: Development, Debates, and Evolution
2.document_summary: This document traces New Zealand's bicultural journey from pre-1840 coexistence through monoculturalism to the modern bicultural framework. It examines the historical context of early bicultural individuals like Pākehā-Māori, the Treaty of Waitangi's signing in 1840, and subsequent British cultural dominance through assimilation policies. The pivotal shift from the 1970s onward saw Māori protests against land loss and treaty breaches, prompting government action including the establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975. The 1980s marked a turning point when the government acknowledged the treaty as New Zealand's founding document, leading to significant state-sector reforms. Government agencies adopted bicultural policies: te reo Māori became official in 1987, departments adopted Māori names, and cultural practices like pōwhiri were incorporated into official functions. The document explores ongoing debates and criticisms of biculturalism, including arguments that it hasn't sufficiently protected Māori tino rangatiratanga (self-determination). It presents competing frameworks such as multiculturalism, bi-nationalism, and differentiated citizenship, with advocates like Moana Jackson and Whatarangi Winiata proposing more substantial reforms. While biculturalism secured Māori political voice in the 1980s-1990s, critics argue it positioned Māori as junior partners. The document notes that although "biculturalism" terminology is less common today, discussions about appropriate Māori-non-Māori relationships continue to evolve.

3.document_title: Māori Radio – Reo Irirangi: History and Development of Māori Language Broadcasting in New Zealand
3.document_summary: This document traces the history of Māori language radio broadcasting in New Zealand from 1928 to 2020. It covers early broadcasts including the first Māori-language programme in 1940, pioneering broadcasters like Wiremu Parker and Ted Nēpia, and the establishment of the Māori Programmes Section in 1964. The evolution progressed from pronunciation programmes to music broadcasts featuring showbands and the iconic 1984 hit 'Poi e'. The document chronicles iwi radio station development beginning in 1987, with Māori language advocates agitating for greater representation during a language crisis period. Key milestones include Te Reo o Aotearoa's launch in 1978, experimental FM stations like Te Reo o Pōneke in the early 1980s, and the first permanent Māori radio station in 1988. Government support through New Zealand on Air (1990) and Te Māngai Pāho (1993) enabled regional iwi radio expansion. By 2020, 21 iwi stations operated nationwide, fulfilling the vision of an indigenous-language broadcasting network serving Māori communities.

5.document_title: Radio Broadcasting in New Zealand: A Comprehensive History from 1921 to 2013
5.document_summary: This comprehensive history traces the evolution of radio broadcasting in New Zealand from 1921 to 2013. It begins with the first radio broadcast by physics professor Robert Jack in 1921 and early enthusiast-run stations, progressing through government control via the 1935 New Zealand Broadcasting Service (NZBS). The "golden age" (1936-1960) featured iconic personalities like Aunt Daisy and Phil Shone. Radio ownership surged from 53,407 licensed radios in 1930 to 317,509 by 1939, making New Zealand third globally in radio density. Television's introduction in 1960 and pirate stations like Radio Hauraki (1966) prompted significant changes. The Broadcasting Authority (1968) liberalized standards, leading to private radio licensing (1970) and FM authorization (1982). Deregulation (1989-1996) increased competition to nearly 300 stations by 1999, with two overseas-owned companies dominating 80% of commercial radio by 2013. The document covers public broadcasting through Radio New Zealand (RNZ), NZ On Air's promotion of local content, Māori radio stations (from 1987, with 21 iwi stations by 1994), minority community stations, and student radio, reflecting New Zealand's transformation from state monopoly to a diverse, deregulated broadcasting landscape.

[Page 15] Formal salutations are relatively straightforward: ‘Hello’ or ‘Good morning’ (or afternoon or evening) in greeting, and ‘Goodbye’ in farewell, accompanied by some pleasantry such as ‘Nice to meet you’ is always acceptable. Informal greetings are much more various and include ‘Hi’, ‘How are you?’, ‘Gidday’ and ‘How’s it going?’ Informal farewells include ‘Cheers’, ‘See you’, ‘See you later’, ‘Spot you later’, or simply ‘Later.’ It is increasingly common for both Māori and Pākehā New Zealanders to say ‘Kia ora’ in greeting and ‘Ka kite’ or ‘Ka kite anō’ in farewell.

6.document_title: New Zealand Manners and Social Etiquette: Historical Evolution and Modern Practice
6.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of manners and social etiquette in New Zealand from the 1800s through the 2000s. It examines how settlers brought formal English manners tied to class systems, which gradually transformed into New Zealand's distinctive informal, egalitarian approach to social behavior. Key historical developments include the relaxation of Victorian formality in the colonial context, the rise of working-class respect and equality, and the shift in the meaning of "gentleman" from wealth and status to courtesy regardless of class. The document addresses cross-cultural awareness, particularly regarding Māori protocols and the Māori renaissance from the 1970s onward, which increased understanding of marae etiquette among Pākehā New Zealanders. It discusses cultural misunderstandings in communication, such as eye contact differences between Pākehā and Māori/Samoan cultures. The text examines how manners changed from the 1970s onward, influenced by youth activism, feminism, and international exposure, leading to more casual dress codes. Rather than declining, manners have evolved to address modern contexts, including new etiquette for digital communication, social media, and cell phone use. The document concludes with practical guidance on contemporary New Zealand social conduct, including face-to-face interactions, public behavior, dining customs, greetings (including the hongi in formal Māori situations), and courteous conduct in various social and professional settings.

7.text:
[Page 2] The richness of te reo Many early missionaries to New Zealand had studied languages such as Greek and Latin, and readily appreciated the regular grammar and complex vocabulary of Māori. Missionary William Yate wrote, ‘The language is peculiarly soft and sweet, and in the longest speeches not a harsh sound ever strikes the ear … the language of New Zealand is remarkably rich, admits of a very varied phraseology, abounds in terms of peculiar nicety, and is capable of being reduced to the most precise grammatical principles.’ 1 French Catholic missionary Louis Servant also wrote a detailed and valuable account of early Māori society, published in English translation in 1973 as Customs and habits of the New Zealanders. Another CMS missionary (and later bishop), William Williams, published the first substantial Māori to English dictionary in 1844. Later editions were produced by his son and grandson, also Anglican bishops. The first professional teacher of Māori studies was probably Wiremu Te Rangikāheke, a mission educated scholar from the Ngāti Rangiwewehi tribe of Rotorua. From 1849 he worked closely with Governor George Grey, teaching him Māori language and customs. At times Te Rangikāheke was paid £36 a year, plus accommodation for himself and his family. He produced a large number of Māori language manuscripts on most aspects of Māori culture, and contributed to Grey's manuscripts of songs and proverbs, including Ko nga moteatea, me nga hakirara o nga Maori (1853), and Ko nga mahinga a nga tupuna Maori (1854), and its English translation, Polynesian mythology (1855).

7.document_title: Māori Studies in New Zealand: Historical Development and Institutional Expansion Across Universities
7.document_summary: This document traces the history and development of Māori studies as an academic discipline in New Zealand from its early origins through institutional expansion. It begins with early missionaries like Thomas Kendall who formally studied Māori language and culture starting in 1820, followed by the establishment of the Polynesian Society in 1892 with prominent Māori scholars including Apirana Ngata, Māui Pōmare, and Te Rangi Hīroa. Apirana Ngata, the first Māori university graduate (1893), pioneered university-level Māori studies and established the Māori Ethnological Research Board in 1923. The document details the systematic expansion of Māori studies across New Zealand universities: University of Auckland (1951) with Bruce Biggs' appointment as the first Māori language lecturer, Victoria University of Wellington (mid-1960s) under Joan Metge with innovative immersion-based language teaching methods developed by Koro Dewes, University of Canterbury (1974) with Te Awaroa Nēpia, Massey University, University of Waikato (1972), University of Otago (1983), and Lincoln University (1995). Key figures include Mākereti Papakura, the first Māori ethnologist, Hirini Mead who established the first university marae Te Herenga Waka in 1986, Hugh Kāwharu, and Mason Durie. The document emphasizes the transition from missionary-led linguistic studies to institutionalized academic programs and the distinction between university-based Māori studies and traditional tribal wānanga.

9.document_title: Māori and Television – Whakaata: A Comprehensive History of Indigenous Broadcasting in New Zealand
9.document_summary: This document traces the evolution of Māori representation and broadcasting in New Zealand television from the 1960s to 2024. In the early decades, Māori appeared primarily as guest performers, with the Howard Morrison Quartet featured in the first 1960 broadcast. The 1970s saw a Māori consciousness movement advocating for te reo Māori in schools, increasing pressure for more Māori television content. Key programmes like Tangata whenua (1974) demonstrated innovative Māori storytelling approaches. The 1980s-1990s marked significant growth in Māori production, including Ray Waru's Koha (1980), Te karere (1983), and Waka huia (1987). The Māori Language Act of 1987 made te reo an official language. The establishment of Aotearoa Television Network (1996-1997) was a significant milestone. In 2004, the government-subsidised Māori Television Service launched with bilingual programming, expanding to a second te reo Māori channel in 2008. By 2022, it was renamed Whakaata Māori, representing the evolution from Māori as guest performers to having their own indigenous broadcasting voice. The document examines bilingual programming, funding challenges, audience composition, and the tension between language revitalization and audience growth.

10.text:
[Page 11] Printer and missionary William Colenso was one of the first colonists to use te reo Māori fluently, and he introduced many Māori words into New Zealand English. From as early as 1843 he commonly interspersed Māori and English, using terms such as kapai (good) and anglicising others, such as tangiing (crying). He took care to explain the various meanings associated with Māori vocabulary, showing that the term Māori itself meant ubiquitous and common, and not merely indigenous, especially when applied to flora and fauna. He distinguished, therefore, a native tree from a Māori tree. The early use of the term Māori for common or ubiquitous in Māori English compounds often caused confusion. Māori clearing, Māori pass and Māori track pertained to Māori use or origin but Māori cabbage and Māori parsnip meant these plants were common and grew wild.

11.document_title: Māori Manners, Social Behaviour, and Cultural Customs: From Traditional Practices to Modern Adaptation
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori social customs and cultural practices that have endured through centuries of change. It covers welcome rituals including karanga (call), wero (challenge), whaikōrero (speeches), and hongi (nose pressing), which served practical peacekeeping functions. The text explains kinship, whakapapa (genealogy), and the marae as cultural centers. It details customs surrounding death through tangi (funeral ceremonies) where whānau gather to support the wairua (spirit), as well as birth traditions like placenta burial. The document emphasizes marae-based practices, cemetery customs, and the honored status of elders. It demonstrates how traditional customs have adapted to modern urban settings and are increasingly adopted by non-Māori New Zealanders, reflecting a thriving national culture.

12.text:
[Page 1] Welcome and hospitality Māori rituals for greeting visitors date from before Europeans arrived in New Zealand, and had a practical function. The women of a settlement would call out to approaching strangers, asking them to identify themselves and their intentions. Warriors would then challenge them in the wero ceremony. After this, once it was known that the visitors came in peace, they could enter and were welcomed and fed. Today the rituals include the karanga (call), wero , whaikōrero (speeches) and hongi (pressing of noses). The manuhiri (visitors) are then invited to eat and drink with their hosts. They can respond by giving a koha in the past, a gift of food or precious objects, but today usually money. Kinship, families and marae Kin relationships are very important and underpin many customs. Speeches often begin with the speaker’s whakapapa (genealogy), which may relate to the group addressed or the issue discussed. Most Māori, even if they live in the city, retain links with their tribal area and return there for events. Hapū (sub tribes) have rights over particular marae , and are known as tangata whenua (people of the land) of those marae . They can host gatherings, weddings and funerals, and must maintain the marae and its reputation. Kaumātua and kuia (male and female elders) have an honoured place in Māori communities. Tangi and birth In Māori tradition, when someone dies, their spirit leaves their body and travels to a sacred place at the northern tip of New Zealand. Their whānau (family) gathers at a tangihanga to be supported by the wider whānau and community. Tangi are usually held on the marae most closely associated with the deceased. Mourners stay with the family and the tūpāpaku (corpse) for several days. Urupā (cemeteries) are extremely tapu (sacred). When a baby is born, Māori traditionally bury the whenua (placenta) on land associated with one or both of the parents. Some Pākehā also now follow this custom. Māori social customs today Some customs have been adapted to non traditional situations. For instance, many marae in cities or outside New Zealand are multi tribal, so tribal traditions have to be adapted. Māori ceremonies are also used in non Māori settings, such as the opening of the Te Māori exhibition in New York in 1984. Welcome and hospitality Greeting visitors

13.text:
[Page 2] As with other Māori customs, the rituals of encounter have changed over time and vary from region to region, but they follow the same basic pattern the karanga (call) by the women, the wero , the whaikōrero (formal speeches) by representatives of both hosts and visitors, and finally the hongi (ceremonial pressing of noses), to confirm that the two groups are meeting in peace. The Māori custom of pressing noses in greeting is very ancient and refers to the mythological figure of Tāne Mahuta, who shaped a figure from earth and breathed life into it through the nose to create Hineahuone, the ‘woman formed of earth’.

14.text:
[Page 1] Humour in traditional stories Humour features in traditional Māori myths and stories. One example is the story of Kahungunu, ancestor of Ngāti Kahungunu iwi , who wanted to marry Rongomaiwahine. He caused a fight between her and her husband by farting. The couple blamed each other for the bad smell. Humour in speech making and song Humour is often used in whaikōrero (speeches), partly to hold the audience’s attention. Sometimes speeches at tangihanga are funny. Many traditional songs have comic elements. Māori humour in the 20th century In the early 20th century most Pākehā had little to do with Māori, who mostly lived in rural areas. A stereotype of the simple minded but good natured Māori developed in some Pākehā books and cartoons. Despite its racist overtones, this stereotype was an influence on the routines of Māori show bands, which were popular during the 1950s and 1960s. Some well known performers came out of the show bands, including singer Howard Morrison and comedian Billy T. James. Other well known Māori comedians who emerged in the later 20th century included Mike King and Pio Terei. Māori humour in the 2000s It is common for Māori to tell jokes and funny stories to each other while working in kāuta the cooking house at marae , where food is prepared. In the early 2000s Te kāuta , hosted by Kingi Biddle, aimed to recreate this atmosphere in a Māori language television chat show. Humour also features in literature and art, for example in the artworks of Michael Parekowhai. One study of humour in the workplace has shown that Māori humour is different to Pākehā humour, in both content and style.

14.document_title: Māori Humor: Cultural Traditions, Contemporary Expression, and Artistic Subversion
14.document_summary: This document explores Māori humor (te whakakata) across multiple dimensions—from traditional cultural practices to contemporary artistic expression. It traces the evolution through traditional myths and legends featuring trickster characters like Māui and Kahungunu, whaikōrero (speeches), and traditional songs with comic elements. In the 20th century, Māori humor was influenced by racist stereotypes in Pākehā media, shaping Māori show bands of the 1950s-60s with performers like Howard Morrison and Billy T. James. From the 1960s onward, Māori comedians developed more authentic humor reflecting the contrast between traditional and modern culture. The document analyzes sculptor Michael Parekowhai's culturally subversive artworks—including white elephants, guitars referencing Māori performers, and hand-carved grand pianos—demonstrating how humor serves as a critical tool in contemporary art. A key insight is that Māori humor differs distinctly from Pākehā humor, relying heavily on physical expression, body language, and performance similar to the haka. Throughout all contexts, humor serves essential purposes: entertaining, holding attention, defusing conflict, and maintaining social bonds. In the 2000s, humor remains integral to Māori social gatherings, exemplified by television programs like Te kāuta.

15.text:
[Page 16] Face to face It is usual to shake hands with both men and women when meeting formally, but is not necessary in casual situations. In a formal Māori situation, shake hands and hongi (press noses briefly). Sometimes, women will kiss the person they are greeting on the cheek. When in doubt, do as others do. It is considered impolite to dominate the conversation, boast about your accomplishments, interrupt constantly, talk about what you or others earn, or make critical comments about New Zealand or New Zealanders. Treat everyone you meet with the same courtesy, using ‘Please’ when making requests and saying ‘Thank you’ for any service, whether or not you are paying for it.

15.document_title: New Zealand Manners and Social Etiquette: Historical Evolution and Modern Practice
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of manners and social etiquette in New Zealand from the 1800s through the 2000s. It examines how settlers brought formal English manners tied to class systems, which gradually transformed into New Zealand's distinctive informal, egalitarian approach to social behavior. Key historical developments include the relaxation of Victorian formality in the colonial context, the rise of working-class respect and equality, and the shift in the meaning of "gentleman" from wealth and status to courtesy regardless of class. The document addresses cross-cultural awareness, particularly regarding Māori protocols and the Māori renaissance from the 1970s onward, which increased understanding of marae etiquette among Pākehā New Zealanders. It discusses cultural misunderstandings in communication, such as eye contact differences between Pākehā and Māori/Samoan cultures. The text examines how manners changed from the 1970s onward, influenced by youth activism, feminism, and international exposure, leading to more casual dress codes. Rather than declining, manners have evolved to address modern contexts, including new etiquette for digital communication, social media, and cell phone use. The document concludes with practical guidance on contemporary New Zealand social conduct, including face-to-face interactions, public behavior, dining customs, greetings (including the hongi in formal Māori situations), and courteous conduct in various social and professional settings.

16.text:
[Page 3] While the order of speeches is largely dictated by pāeke and tau utuutu, there are some tribal variations. Te Āti Awa tribes hongi (press noses briefly) and harirū (shake hands) with visitors as soon as they are welcomed. In Whanganui, while the pāeke style is generally followed, visitors in a party at a tangihanga are expected to speak first. In Northland, at a tangihanga , a speaker will often poroporoaki (bid farewell) to the deceased at the end of the karanga (when visitors are called onto the marae ). This can cause consternation when done outside Northland as hosts feel that the speakers are changing local protocol.

16.document_title: Te Kawa o te Marae: Comprehensive Guide to Māori Meeting House Protocols, Etiquette, and Cultural Practices
16.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth exploration of te kawa o te marae, the protocols and practices governing conduct on the marae (Māori meeting house). It covers the complete pōwhiri (welcome ceremony) process, including key roles such as kaikaranga (callers) and kaikōrero (speakers), typically held by respected elders. The document details two main speech order systems: pāeke (hosts speak first, then guests) and tau utuutu (alternating speakers), and describes the full pōwhiri sequence including ritual challenges (wero), karanga (calling), speeches, waiata (songs), koha (monetary gifts), hongi and harirū (greetings), hākari (feast), and poroporoaki (farewells). It explains the mythological foundations of marae layout, where the marae ātea represents Tūmatauenga (god of war) allowing forceful speeches, while the wharenui represents Rongo (god of peace) requiring peaceful discourse. The document provides practical etiquette guidelines for visitors, including dress codes, behavior during ceremonies, dining protocols, and conduct within the wharenui. It covers specific protocols for tangihanga (funeral ceremonies), hygiene practices, and restrictions on photography and recording. Tribal variations are noted, particularly regarding gender roles and speech protocols. The document emphasizes Māori language preservation on the marae.

17.text:
[Page 3] Large and important welcomes (known as pōwhiri ) may include extra elements such as laments to the dead, traditional songs and chants, and wero ceremonies that are deliberately confrontational and even alarming to outsiders. However, not all such ceremonies are so dramatic. Many are low key and informal. Whether large or small, the pōwhiri ends with an invitation to the manuhiri (visitors) to mingle with their hosts, the tangata whenua , and to eat and drink with them. They are no longer potentially threatening strangers, but guests to be cared for as long as they remain in the hosts’ territory. Providing plentiful food to guests is central to Māori custom.

18.document_title: New Zealand English: Language Evolution, Māori Influence, and Contemporary Usage
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the distinctive characteristics and evolution of English language in New Zealand. It traces New Zealand English from its origins with British explorers and early European settlers through systematic scholarly study beginning in the late 20th century. The text examines how New Zealand English has been shaped by local culture, geography, indigenous Māori language influence, and unique historical experiences. Key topics include word formation methods such as informal shortening with '-ie' or '-o' suffixes, compounding, and borrowing from other English varieties. The document details significant Māori language influence, particularly during the Māori renaissance of the 1970s, tracing early borrowing from Māori material culture and William Colenso's pioneering work in the 1840s, through decline during European dominance, to resurgence following language revitalization efforts. It highlights how new words emerge from politics (Rogernomics, ACC), sports (black-water rafting, zorbing), conservation (kiwi crèche, mainland island), farming (gypsy day, calfetaria), and weather terminology. The document provides examples of unique New Zealand vocabulary (bach, jandals, haka) and multi-meaning words like 'crook' and 'unit', while documenting contemporary phenomena such as "nek minnit" slang and earthquake-related terminology from the 2010-2011 Canterbury earthquakes.

19.document_title: Māori Radio – Reo Irirangi: History and Development of Māori Language Broadcasting in New Zealand
19.document_summary: This document traces the history of Māori language radio broadcasting in New Zealand from 1928 to 2020. It covers early broadcasts including the first Māori-language programme in 1940, pioneering broadcasters like Wiremu Parker and Ted Nēpia, and the establishment of the Māori Programmes Section in 1964. The evolution progressed from pronunciation programmes to music broadcasts featuring showbands and the iconic 1984 hit 'Poi e'. The document chronicles iwi radio station development beginning in 1987, with Māori language advocates agitating for greater representation during a language crisis period. Key milestones include Te Reo o Aotearoa's launch in 1978, experimental FM stations like Te Reo o Pōneke in the early 1980s, and the first permanent Māori radio station in 1988. Government support through New Zealand on Air (1990) and Te Māngai Pāho (1993) enabled regional iwi radio expansion. By 2020, 21 iwi stations operated nationwide, fulfilling the vision of an indigenous-language broadcasting network serving Māori communities.
