retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] Common origins Ngāti Whātua consist of four tribes whose lands stretch from the Hokianga down to Auckland. They share a common ancestor called Tuputupuwhenua or Tumutumuwhenua. They also share a common ancestral canoe, Māhuhu ki te rangi . Some say that the captain of the canoe, Rongomai, was drowned when the canoe capsized, then eaten by trevally fish. To this day, his descendants do not eat trevally. Tribes The four Ngāti Whātua tribes are: Te Roroa, whose name recalls a saying about the bravery of an ancestor, Manumanu II. His enemies said of him, ‘Te hei! Te roroa o te tangata , rite tonu ki te kahikatea!’ (Behold! That man is as tall as a white pine!) Te Roroa live in an area known for huge trees; the Waipoua kauri forest is in their territory. Te Uri o Hau and Te Taoū, from Kaipara Harbour. Both tribes are descended from Haumoewhārangi, who was killed in a dispute over kūmara (sweet potato) gardens. Ngāti Whātua o Ōrākei, which conquered the Auckland area in the 1740s. Their leader, Tūperiri, established a pā (fortified village) on One Tree Hill. Warfare In 1807 Ngāti Whātua defeated Ngāpuhi in battle at Moremonui. So many Ngāpuhi people were killed and left on the beach that the battle became known as Te Kai a te karoro ‘food for seagulls’. However, in the 1820s Ngāti Whātua suffered heavy defeats. Was there a word that could overcome the limitations of existing names? “New Zealander”, while practical, feels inadequate. A name bestowed through happenstance, it doesn’t give adequate recognition to the indigenous people. “Aotearoan?” Too hard to say, with its six syllables; I can’t see it catching on. “How about Kiwi?” I asked Aldridge. [Page 1] Te Whatanui Te Whatanui, sometimes known as Te Whata, Toheāpare, or Toheata, was the son of Tihao of Ngāti Huia and Ngāti Parewahawaha, two hapū of Ngāti Raukawa. His mother was Pareraukawa, elder sister of Hape or Hape ki tūārangi of Ngāti Raukawa and Ngāti Huia. Hape died at Maungatautari, the heartland of Ngāti Raukawa ancestral territory, which stretched eastwards from Maungatautari towards the Pātetere plateau, about the turn of the nineteenth century, when Te Whatanui was still young. Hape's own sons were also young, and Te Whatanui and the other hereditary chiefs of Ngāti Raukawa made no protest when Te Rauparaha , a contemporary of Te Whatanui and belonging to Ngāti Huia through his mother, claimed the succession to Hape's mana , and later married his widow. Effective leadership devolved on Te Whatanui and other chiefs; Te Whatanui was to be regarded as the leading chief of Ngāti Raukawa. Ngati Raukawa were increasingly threatened as the wars between Waikato and the Kāwhia tribes continued in the early nineteenth century. After Te Rauparaha had led the first migration of his people to Taranaki about 1821, he returned to attempt to recruit allies to join him in the resettlement of his people on the Kapiti coast. He turned to Ngāti Raukawa first, but Te Whatanui and other chiefs refused his invitation. However, when Te Rauparaha carried the same invitation to Te Waru of Ngāi Te Rangi, at Tauranga, to other chiefs, and finally to Ngāti Whakaue, at Rotorua, Te Whatanui went with him. There, perhaps late in 1821, Te Whatanui urged Ngāti Whakaue and Tūhourangi to kill any Ngāpuhi they might meet, because Whetūroa, his nephew, had been killed that year by Ngāpuhi, at Te Tōtara, in the Thames district. His wishes were heeded, and the killing of many Ngāpuhi by Ngāti Whakaue and Tūhourangi led to the mass Ngāpuhi attack on Mokoia in 1823.
{}

He defended the mission against a threat from other local Māori, built the first church at Whāingaroa, and on church instructions discarded eight of his nine wives. In 1837 he helped to obtain the release of slaves brought back to Waikato from the Taranaki raids. In 1840 he tried to interpose himself in a fight between Ngāti Tūwharetoa and the people of Waitōtara at Pātoka pā . He urged peace, but as he knelt to pray, Ngāti Tūwharetoa shot two of the assembled warriors.

retrieved_chunks.text:
[Page 3] About 1824 Ngāti Apa leaders joined Muaūpoko, Rangitāne and other tribes of the lower North Island, and relatives from the South Island, in a surprise attack on Ngāti Toa at Kapiti. Against overwhelming odds Ngāti Toa defeated their attackers at the battle known as Waiorua. One of the many Ngāti Apa captives, Te Rangimairehau, begged for mercy on the grounds of his relationship to Te Rangihaeata through Te Pikinga, but the alliance had reached its lowest point, and the supplicant was put to death. After Waiorua, Te Rauparaha and Te Rangihaeata killed Ngāti Apa leaders Te Rangihaukū and Koupeka at Te Awamate. Six months later Ngāti Toa attacked another pā , Te Poutū; this time Ngāti Apa were the victors. After this disaster Te Rangihaeata sent Te Pikinga to her people to make peace. By the end of the 1820s peace had been restored between Ngāti Apa and Ngāti Toa. In 1834 a great battle was fought between Ngāti Raukawa and Te Āti Awa at Haowhenua, a pā near Ōtaki. The outcome was inconclusive, but Ngāti Raukawa suffered the greater loss. They had been supported in the battle by Ngāti Apa, and afterwards abandoned Ōtaki for a period, moving into Ngāti Apa territory between the Manawatū and Rangitīkei rivers. It was the marriage between Te Pikinga and Te Rangihaeata which inclined the latter's Ngāti Raukawa relatives to treat their hosts with consideration; some skirmishes were fought, but on the whole relations were peaceful. In 1868, by which time both Te Rangihaeata and Te Pikinga had died, Ngāti Apa were able to claim equal rights with Ngāti Raukawa to the territory they shared. It was the status of Te Pikinga in her marriage that had preserved the lands of her people.
{}

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] When someone finds out I'm from Dannevirke the conversation usually goes something like this. Rando: "Oh so you're from Northland?" Me: "No you're thinking of Dargaville." R: "Canterbury?" M: "That's Darfield." R: "Oh..." Growing up, my Dad even had a shirt he wore while barbecuing that read 'Dannevirke? Where the hell is Dannevirke?' So where the hell is Dannevirke? If you've ever driven State Highway 2 from Wellington to Napier then you've gone through it. Maybe you stopped for a coffee, but more likely you noticed the giant Viking at the entrance of town proudly declaring 'Welcome' as you enter and 'Farvel' as you leave. Why Vikings? Well many of the first Pākehā settlers in the region came from Scandinavia and they named the new town after a Viking Age fortification now part of modern day Germany (literally the 'Danes Work'). Those settlers came over to clear the vast forest that covered the area, which was known variously as the 40, 70 or 90 Mile Bush. In Māori, this primeval forest is known as Te Tapere Nui o Whātonga and it was a home and pantry for the people of Rangitāne for centuries. Today, outside of a few scattered pockets of rugged bush, very little of it remains. The area along the upper reaches of the Manawatū river, around the present day town of Dannevirke, is known as Tamaki Nui ā Rua. My ancestors of Ngāti Mutuahi and Ngāti Te Rangiwhakaewa hapū made their kāinga along the river or in clearings in the vast forest. Today, Tamaki Nui ā Rua Dannevirke is a rural service town between the Ruahine and Puketoi ranges surrounded by dairy farms on almost every side. Its population of around 6000 people rarely fluctuates. Like most kids growing up in rural towns, I thought it was the most boring place on earth. Our only location of interest then was the KFC (widely rumoured to be the smallest one in the southern hemisphere). But as I got older I came to realise just how lucky I am to have grown up on my own whenua. Many Māori grow up disconnected…

Racialised debates following the March 2019 mosque massacre spurred historian Michael Belgrave to write Becoming Aotearoa our first major national history volume in 20 years. At the time, people tried to pass off New Zealand history as simply a story about white supremacy, Belgrave tells RNZ's Saturday Morning, when the truth was far more complicated. Instead, the Massey University professor explores Aotearoa's complicated evolution as a globalised country where two peoples tangata whenua and migrants together built an open, liberal society based on sometimes frayed social contracts. ## Tonga and Samoa: A Tale of Two Cultures

Both Tonga and Samoa are deeply rooted Pacific Island cultures with rich traditions, and while they share some broad similarities — strong Christian faith, reverence for family, and a proud sense of identity — each has its own distinct cultural framework.

## The Heart of Tongan Culture: *Anga Faka Tonga*

At the core of Tongan identity is *anga faka Tonga* — literally 'the Tongan way'. This encompasses values of sharing, respect, and obedience, all of which are upheld especially within the extended family. [[1]](cite://1/1)

A particularly distinctive Tongan tradition is the cultural authority held by a father's sisters over their nieces and nephews. This role is considered deeply honourable, even if younger Tongans raised outside Tonga sometimes find it confusing at first. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Tongan culture also observes very strict gender roles. Girls are raised to be home-oriented and submissive, while boys are reared to be independent and mobile. Interestingly, while men hold more political power, women are ranked *higher* in social standing within the community. [[3]](cite://3/1)

Tongan dance traditions are also richly ceremonial. Before performing, young unmarried women traditionally have their bodies oiled with coconut oil — often sent from family in Tonga, perfumed with local leaves. A further tradition sees audiences show appreciation by pressing bank notes onto the oiled skin of performers. [[4]](cite://4/1)

## The Heart of Samoan Culture: *Fa'asamoa*

Samoan identity is anchored in the concept of *fa'asamoa* — the Samoan way — which encompasses a web of values and traditions: [[5]](cite://5/1)

- **Aiga** (family) — the central pillar of Samoan life [[6]](cite://6/1)
- **Tautala Samoa** — the Samoan language [[5]](cite://5/2)
- **Gafa** — genealogies [[5]](cite://5/3)
- **Matai** — the chiefly system [[5]](cite://5/4)
- **Lotu** — the church [[5]](cite://5/5)
- **Fa'alavelave** — ceremonial and family obligations [[5]](cite://5/6)

Associated values include *alofa* (love), *tautua* (service), *fa'aaloalo* (respect), *feagaiga* (a covenant between siblings and others), and *usita'i* (discipline). [[5]](cite://5/7)

Within the *aiga*, young people are expected to serve and respect their elders, and in return receive love, protection, honour, and support. [[6]](cite://6/2) Generosity is not optional — family, church, and village all make constant demands on individuals, and one's social standing is closely tied to how much one gives. [[7]](cite://7/1)

Sunday is treated as a day of enforced rest in Samoa — reserved for eating, sleeping, and church — with activities like sport or even swimming off the table. [[8]](cite://8/1)

## Shared Threads

Both cultures share some striking commonalities:

- **Christianity** plays a central role in both Tongan and Samoan community life, with large and prominent churches being a feature of both cultures. [[9]](cite://9/1)[[10]](cite://10/1)
- **Extended family** is the bedrock of both societies, with obligations extending across generations and across the globe. [[1]](cite://1/2)[[11]](cite://11/1)
- **Respect for elders** is a core value in both traditions, with younger generations expected to serve and defer to those older. [[1]](cite://1/3)[[6]](cite://6/3)

## Identity in a Changing World

Both communities, particularly those living in New Zealand, are navigating how to carry their traditions into new environments. Tongan New Zealanders have emerged in several broad types — those raised fully in *anga faka Tonga*, those born in New Zealand with decreasing language fluency, and very few who have fully assimilated. [[12]](cite://12/1) Similarly, for Samoans, *fa'asamoa* remains constant even as its expression shifts — with the *aiga* (family) described as 'a permanent fixture' even as friendships and other ties come and go. [[11]](cite://11/2)

Both cultures have also shown a remarkable ability to enrich New Zealand society through sport, music, art, and community leadership. [[13]](cite://13/1)[[10]](cite://10/2)

Would you like to explore how either of these communities has maintained their cultural traditions while living in New Zealand?

1.document_title: Tongans in New Zealand: Migration, Culture, Identity, and Community Development
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines Tongan migration to New Zealand and community development from the 1960s onwards. By 2018, over 82,000 Tongans lived in New Zealand, with two-thirds born there, making them the second-largest Pacific ethnic group, primarily settled in Auckland's Ōtara and Māngere. Despite socio-economic challenges including lower median incomes ($21,000 vs $40,000 nationally), overcrowded housing, and lower employment rates, Tongans maintain strong cultural identity through churches, language, and family traditions rooted in anga faka-Tonga. The document explores how Tongan culture blends traditional values of respect, obedience, and reciprocal sharing with Christian beliefs introduced by Methodist missionaries in the 1820s. It identifies three distinct Tongan groups: those maintaining traditional anga faka-Tonga, New Zealand-born Tongans with decreasing language knowledge, and those identifying with broader Pacific Islander identity. Language preservation challenges are evident, with Tongan-speaking population declining from 63% (1996) to 40% (2018). The document highlights the emergence of Pasifika Aotearoa—a new cultural identity blending Pacific traditions with Afro-American influences, hip-hop, and reggae. Success measures are rooted in family obligations and community contributions, with cultural contributions through music, sports, and arts enriching New Zealand society.

2.text:
[Page 2] Who are the Tongans? Tongans are the original inhabitants of the Tonga Islands in the South Pacific. According to archaeological and linguistic research, they are the descendants of people who left Fiji and other parts of Melanesia to settle West Polynesia, including Tonga, some 3,000 or more years ago.

[Page 7] Matters of gender Tongan culture recognises only very strict gender roles. Girls are brought up to be submissive and to stay at home, whereas boys are reared to be independent and mobile. As adults, men have more political power, but women are ranked higher in the community. The terms fakaleitī (like a lady) and fakatangata (like a man) are the Tongan words for gay people. When they are not in sexual relationships, these people are usually ignored, but as sexual beings they can face discrimination within the community.

4.text:
[Page 8] Tonga is a dispersed community, and Tongan identities are evolving in response to the new environments. Three main types of Tongans have emerged. The first are those who have been raised in anga faka Tonga (the Tongan way), and still maintain their language. The second are those who were born in New Zealand and have decreasing knowledge of the language and anga faka Tonga. Interestingly, many New Zealand born Tongans understand the language but cannot speak it. They acquire sufficient Tongan to incorporate values of anga faka Tonga, but are not able to transmit the language to the next generation. However, very few have become wholly assimilated to a non Tongan way of life. When people are asked to state their ethnicity, the vast majority call themselves Tongan.

8.document_title: Tokelauans in New Zealand: Immigration, Community, and Cultural Identity
8.document_summary: This document traces Tokelauan migration to New Zealand from 1951 onwards, beginning with 10 arrivals and accelerating through government assistance programs, particularly the Tokelau Islands Resettlement Scheme (1966-1976) which facilitated over 500 relocations. By 2013, 7,175 Tokelauans lived in New Zealand compared to 1,383 on the islands, with major communities in Porirua-Hutt Valley (49%) and Auckland (27%). The document explores religious practices (83% belonged to religious groups in 2013), sports and cultural events including the biennial Easter festival initiated in 1979, and traditional arts such as wood carving, mat making, and vaka building. Language preservation shows decline, with only 32% speaking the language in 2013 (down from 44% in 2001), though those born in Tokelau remain twice as likely to be fluent. Census data reveals ethnic identity growth from 6,822 (2006) to 8,676 (2018), while residents born in Tokelau decreased from 1,662 (2001) to 1,251 (2018). The narrative highlights how Tokelauans maintained cultural identity through community associations and traditional practices despite culture shock, illustrating the tension between modernization and cultural continuity in the diaspora.

9.document_title: Māori Manners, Social Behaviour, and Cultural Customs: From Traditional Practices to Modern Adaptation
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori social customs and cultural practices that have endured through centuries of change. It covers welcome rituals including karanga (call), wero (challenge), whaikōrero (speeches), and hongi (nose pressing), which served practical peacekeeping functions. The text explains kinship, whakapapa (genealogy), and the marae as cultural centers. It details customs surrounding death through tangi (funeral ceremonies) where whānau gather to support the wairua (spirit), as well as birth traditions like placenta burial. The document emphasizes marae-based practices, cemetery customs, and the honored status of elders. It demonstrates how traditional customs have adapted to modern urban settings and are increasingly adopted by non-Māori New Zealanders, reflecting a thriving national culture.

10.text:
[Page 9] For some New Zealand borns, an understanding of custom serves as a stepping stone to new forms of expression. The operatic tenor Ben Makisi has moved from his knowledge of Tongan musical notation to explore European classical music. Tongan styles of sport, especially in netball and rugby, have influenced the games in New Zealand. All Black Jonah Lomu became a national icon. Tongan born Filipe Tohi brings Tongan elements to his sculpture and lashing. The new Pasifika Aotearoa identity has flourished and now includes a proliferating music culture, an eclectic fashion industry, and pan Pacific churches.
{}

11.document_title: Samoans in New Zealand: History, Migration, Culture, Identity, and Contributions
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the Samoan experience in New Zealand across historical, cultural, and social dimensions. It covers Samoa's geography, Samoan migration beginning in the 1950s, and New Zealand's colonial administration of Western Samoa (1914-1962). Key historical events include the 1918 influenza outbreak killing over 20% of the population, the independence movement (Mau) culminating in Samoa's 1962 independence, and the discriminatory "Dawn Raids" of the 1970s, for which New Zealand formally apologized in 2021. As of 2018, 182,721 Samoans lived in New Zealand, predominantly in Auckland. The document explores immigration schemes including the Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) program, economic indicators, and remittances (16% of Samoa's economy in 2019). Central to the analysis is fa'asamoa (Samoan culture) encompassing family (aiga), language, genealogy, and church traditions, alongside the identity paradox faced by New Zealand-born Samoans. It highlights significant Samoan contributions across academia, politics, sports, arts, and business, featuring notable figures such as Albert Wendt, Pacific MPs, accomplished athletes, and influential artists. The document also addresses the special relationship between Samoans and Māori, collaborative activism, language preservation efforts, and the role of Samoan churches as cultural centers.

12.text:
[Page 13] However, Samoans in New Zealand have distinctive experiences and values which they do not share with other Pacific Islanders. Differences of culture and language outweigh the commonality of the New Zealand experience. In the end, the bedrock of fa‘asamoa (Samoan culture) is aiga (family); friends and acquaintances come and go, but the aiga remains as a permanent fixture. PI identity is a phenomenon of young people. When they mature and have their own children, Samoans tend to return to their ethnic identity. For those of mixed ethnicity, Samoan identity is passed on to younger generations by the stories and instructions of their mothers or grandmothers, or by fathers who have been influenced markedly by their mothers.
{}

13.text:
[Page 9] Fa‘asamoa Samoan culture The concept of fa‘asamoa is essential to Samoan identity, and consists of a number of values and traditions: aiga (family) tautala Samoa (Samoan language) gafa (genealogies) matai (chiefly system) lotu (church) fa‘alavelave (ceremonial and other family obligations). There are also the associated values of alofa (love), tautua (service), fa‘aaloalo (respect), feagaiga (a covenant between sibilings and others) and usita‘i (discipline). The fa‘asamoa practised in Samoa may differ from that in New Zealand. Not every Samoan has the same understanding of the concept. What remains constant is maintaining the family and links with the homeland. Money, prayers, support, food, material goods, and even relatives themselves, circulate within families around the world wherever Samoan people live and work. Fa‘asamoa in New Zealand In 1998 one New Zealand born Samoan described what it means to follow fa‘asamoa: ‘The fa‘asamoa is: go to church, be a good Samoan, and that means to try your best at education, and looking after family, and go to family functions, plus that we've got to look after them when they're old.’
{}

The ‘va’ between Samoans and tangata whenua Māori and Pacific peoples share a special relationship, which can be expressed by the Samoan word va (social and sacred/spiritual spaces of relationships). Kinships and relationships can be traced through similarities of history and culture. This kinship connection is shown in the banter of Māori kaumatua (elders) on marae , when visitors from the Pacific are sometimes recognised as tuakana (older siblings), which acknowledges this ancient connection, or as teina (younger siblings), which acknowledges that Māori are tangata whenua of Aotearoa and those from the Pacific are manuhiri (visitors). Many Samoans worked alongside Māori activist groups to promote Māori rights, fight racial discrimination, and confront injustices. In the 1970s, the Polynesian Panthers stood alongside Ngā Tamatoa in the fight to establish te reo Māori as an official language of Aotearoa, on the Māori Land March, and at the Bastion Point protest. 19.text:
[Page 1] Homeland Samoans came to New Zealand from two islands in Samoa: Upolu and Savai‘i. They are hilly, with palm trees and attractive beaches along the coastlines. Samoa is a very Christian country, and there are many large and beautiful churches. Migrations New Zealand ruled Western Samoa from 1914 to 1962. In the 1960s and 1970s, large numbers of Samoans came to New Zealand for jobs, many travelling on temporary visas. In the mid 1970s, the police came into the homes of some who had overstayed their visas, and many were sent back to Samoa. The New Zealand government formally apologised for these events in 2021. Samoans continue to come to New Zealand for work and to join their families. Two thirds of New Zealand’s Samoans live in the ‘Pacific capital’, Auckland. Frequent travel between Samoa and New Zealand has kept families living in both countries closely connected. Culture Samoans brought to New Zealand their strong beliefs in Christianity and the importance of aiga (family). Their traditions are that children should respect, serve and obey their elders. Samoans work hard to maintain contact with family members across the seas. Some younger Samoans born in New Zealand cities have found it difficult to accept these rules. Unable to speak Samoan, they have found enjoyment and support in an urban culture with distinctive dancing, music, language and clothing. With other young Pacific Islanders they have made a new PI (Pacific Island) identity. Contributions Many Samoans have been highly successful in New Zealand and made significant contributions to their new home. They include playwrights and novelists, artists, sportspeople, and musicians ranging from hip hop to classical. In all these fields, Samoans have greatly enriched New Zealand life.

As children frolic, its waters rinse away the grime of the day. Later, adults will seek out its coolness, washing together and talking as the sun sets. 21.document_title: Samoa: A Comprehensive Exploration of Culture, Tradition, and Modernity
21.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection presents an in-depth exploration of Samoa through multiple perspectives. It examines the contradictions between Samoa's idyllic image and complex realities of fa'a Samoa, including tensions between traditional matai authority and individual freedoms, and high emigration rates to New Zealand. The collection covers Samoa's colonial history, including the 1918 influenza epidemic and the Mau independence movement, alongside contemporary journalism challenging corruption. Village governance through the fono system is analyzed, exploring how traditional authority maintains social order while restricting individual expression and contributing to high suicide rates. Religious dimensions include Christianity, Mormonism, and Baha'i, alongside cultural elements like traditional tattooing (pe'a), siapo cloth-making, and the role of fa'afafine in society. Environmental challenges include cyclone recovery and conservation efforts, while economic realities involve low wages, tourism, remittances, and aid dependence. A critical comparison between Western Samoa and American Samoa reveals how modernization and American individualism have paradoxically improved mental health outcomes while challenging cultural preservation. The work explores the fundamental paradox of Samoan society: communal values and cultural pride coexisting with oppressive social controls, limited economic opportunities, and psychological stress.

22.text:
[Page 25] The survival and strength of Samoa’s culture isn’t just attractive to tourists. Anthropologists, for one, love highly structured societies like Sa moa because they allow them to fill books with complex diagrams and spend years in tropical climes. Above all, they feel instinctively at home in a society ruled by a rigid pecking order with all manner of snits and quarrels about status. It reminds them so much of university life. Even the smallest villages support grand wedding cake churches and rugby fields. But these youths, practising for the Vailima (a brand of beer) Cup, won’t be training, or even enjoying a swim, on Sunday. It is a day of enforced rest: for eating, sleeping and going to church (above).

24.document_title: The Pacific Way
24.document_summary: Profile of Emeline Afeaki-Mafile'o, a first-generation New Zealand social entrepreneur of Tongan, Samoan and Māori descent. She founded Affirming Works, a mentoring agency specializing in Pasifika youth that has served 5,000 high schoolers across South Auckland. She established Pacific Advance Senior School (PASS) in Otahuhu for struggling students and co-founded Fofola Consulting, contributing to government policy on youth strategy, gang prevention, and family violence. Afeaki-Mafile'o also acquired and manages Tonga's entire coffee industry (100% of production) across 10 cooperative farms employing 80 people, using profits to fund community work. Her approach emphasizes bridging cultural gaps, amplifying local community knowledge, and transitioning from dependency models to social entrepreneurship, positioning herself as a bridge between Pacific and New Zealand cultures.

[Page 2] In 1976, at the first festival, six school groups took part. This year there were 135 teams, representing six different races. “Everyone gets a feel for each other’s culture here,” Tumama Faumui explains. “We learn what others respect, and what they expect.” [chapter break] It is a tongan tradition for young unmarried women to have their bodies oiled before they dance. The coconut oil being applied to Mere Latu’s arms and shoulders has been sent here by her grandmother in Tonga. Perfumed with leaves from Tonga’s trees, the oil looks good and smells nice, but has a more practical purpose, too: bank notes stick to it. It is another Tongan tradition to give money in appreciation of a good performance, and in a recent church charity concert Mere was almost literally clothed in notes—$2500 in all—from the admiring audience. Thirty minutes before her item for St Mary’s College, the attention Mere is receiving from her mother and aunt also helps to massage away stage jitters. With the fear of forgetting lines, fumbling complicated actions, letting team mates down, tension is high behind the scenes at the festival. It shows on the strained faces of the Indian team from Epsom Girls’ Grammar School (top), getting their stage directions just before they go on. “Someone’s always crying because it’s their first time,” says A J Paul (above), being comforted by a hug from her Westlake Girls’ High School classmate Arnia Dolan. [chapter break] When you’re transplanted to another country, you leave the flowers and trees and grasses of your home—the vital elements of your traditional food and clothing. Instead, you borrow from your new surroundings, sometimes with dramatic results. The costume design is traditional, but the boldly coloured raffia materials of the St Paul’s College Tongan group (left) are unmistakably 1990s New Zealand. More and more, however, festival costumes are returning to traditional roots, as Liston College’s Samoan team uniform shows (above). The costume of their fuataimi, or conductor, Kelly Seamanu, particularly echoes older times with its feathers, pearls and teeth of shark and wild pig. Sonie of the other island groups fly in fresh flowers from the Pacific, at a huge cost in money and effort. On the eve of the festival their families must work through the night to assemble such perishable costumes. The teams also display another form of cross cultural borrowing. Billy Matakitoga (middle, left) is a Niuean in his school’s Tongan team, which also includes two Samoans and two Cook Islanders. Within each school, it’s not uncommon for the students to move from one group to another, or to belong to more than one. Their heritage is not the critical factor, their keenness is. “This generation is the one which will lead the way to a better understanding between cultures in Auckland,” says one school principal.

25.document_title: Strictly Barefoot: Auckland's Polynesian Cultural Festival
25.document_summary: This article documents Auckland's Secondary Schools Maori and Pacific Islands Cultural Festival, one of the city's largest cultural events attracting over 100,000 spectators. The festival, now in its 18th year, features 135 teams representing six different races, showcasing traditional performances from Polynesian students. The article highlights the festival's significance for Auckland, which hosts more Polynesian people than many Pacific islands themselves—including 11,000 Niueans (vs. 2,000 on Niue) and 22,000 Cook Islanders (vs. 17,000 in the Cooks). Through personal stories and performance details, it explores how students express cultural pride, adapt traditional costumes using modern materials, and compete with dedication. The festival serves as a platform for cross-cultural understanding, with students often performing in groups outside their own heritage based on keenness rather than ancestry. Performances range from traditional dances to contemporary pieces addressing modern challenges faced by immigrant families.

26.document_title: Art and the Spirit: Māori Spirituality, Cultural Resilience, and Artistic Legacy
26.document_summary: This comprehensive work explores the profound connection between Māori spirituality (taha wairua) and artistic creation. Māori settlers brought supernatural beings and spiritual guidance to Aotearoa, where abundant natural resources—stone, wood, bone, shell, and fibre—enabled flourishing creative expression. Taonga (treasures) are living entities embodying ancestors and concepts, not mere objects. Every artifact reflects beauty and spiritual significance while maintaining connection to Papatuanuku (Mother Earth). Design forms reference natural sources, creating a spiral cycle returning materials to their origins. The work also explores Māori artistic resilience despite centuries of cultural devastation including land confiscation, disease, and language loss. Despite these hardships, Māori communities maintained ancestral art forms through dedicated individuals and tohunga (experts). Traditional fibre arts, garment manufacture, and architectural practices survived, while new art forms emerged through Māori-European cultural interaction. The sacred relationship between people and taonga conveys memories and promises, representing resilience and survival of spirit with optimism about cultural legacy for future generations.

The article highlights the festival's significance for Auckland, which hosts more Polynesian people than many Pacific islands themselves—including 11,000 Niueans (vs. 2,000 on Niue) and 22,000 Cook Islanders (vs. 17,000 in the Cooks). Through personal stories and performance details, it explores how students express cultural pride, adapt traditional costumes using modern materials, and compete with dedication. The festival serves as a platform for cross-cultural understanding, with students often performing in groups outside their own heritage based on keenness rather than ancestry. Performances range from traditional dances to contemporary pieces addressing modern challenges faced by immigrant families.

[Page 1] ByMary Afemata 2025 03 04 07:57:38+13:00 Auckland's Pasifika Festival, one of the largest and most vibrant celebrations of Pacific Island cultures, returns to Western Springs this weekend. The festival, in its 32nd year, will showcase the heartbeat of the Pacific through food, music, dance, and more. Alf Filipaina, Manukau ward councillor, fondly recalls the festival's early days and attending with his Samoan perspective. "I remember when they started the Pasifika Festival at Western Springs, way back in the day, the first one," he said. "You look and see your Samoan side of who you are performing, with the songs they sing and the performances." Filipaina also emphasised the importance of experiencing other Pacific cultures. He points to Polyfest, another key event, as an example of celebrating cultural richness through its eight diverse villages. "Watching our leaders of the future perform at Polyfest it's amazing. And it's not just about your own culture, but about learning something from other people's cultures too. That's why I love it." The festival's food is a major drawcard for the community, he says. "People should definitely try the food. Honestly, I eat too much of it, especially the panikeke. Oh, the banana one it's shocking, but we love our food." The two day celebration is family friendly event. Festival goers can expect to experience the richness of Pacific culture, language, and identity through over 1,000 performers from 11 Pacific countries including Aotearoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, Hawai'i, Niue, Samoa, Tokelau, and Tonga. The event will feature live music, dance, arts and crafts, traditional food, and hands on cultural experiences. Performances include youth showcases like Gafoa Le Ata from Kōwhai Intermediate, routines by The Royal Family Dance Crew, and soulful music by Samoan artist Vaniah Toloa. Pacific drumming and choir performances will also fill the festival with powerful rhythms. There will also be a Q&A with Miki Magasiva, director of film Tinā, and a performance by the rising R&B Fijian group LeftOvas LiveBand, who recently featured as the opening act for SIX60 after winning the Moana Music Open Mic Competition. A range of interactive workshops and cultural experiences include Mophead Storytelling with Dr. Selina Tusitala Marsh, traditional wood carving with Jim Stretton, and a live mural art collaboration with John Crouch and Jim To'o Stretton. While Filipaina has made it known that his favourite is the banana panikeke, those attending Pasifika can indulge in a variety of authentic Pacific dishes including Tongan 'ota ika, Fijian kokoda, and Niuean takihi. The festival will also feature island style barbecues, traditional hangi and umu feasts. Pasifika Vibes at MOTAT will offer ukulele lessons, children's activities, and live cultural performances. Plan ahead for travel Public transport is recommended, with trains and buses running. Although some bus routes will be diverted due to road closures. Use the AT Mobile app or visit AT.govt.nz/journeyplanner to plan your trip. Bike racks are available at Gate A for secure bike parking. Essentials for a comfortable day at Pasifika An empty water bottle is recommended, as free refill stations will be available throughout the event. Sun protection is essential and comfortable shoes are advised. Reusable bags are useful for carrying arts, crafts, and any festival finds. Do not bring Leave alcohol, smoking, and vaping at home, as they are not permitted at the festival. Dogs are not allowed, except for service dogs, and commercial photography equipment should also be left at home. Pasifika runs from 9am to 6pm on Saturday, 8 March, and 10am to 4pm on Sunday, 9 March. For more details on the programme, site map and history, click here. 40.document_title: Create Pathways Supporting Academic and Cultural Success of Pasifika - Project
40.document_summary: Pasifika researchers through NZCER's Te Pae Tawhiti Programme have conducted a comprehensive study exploring how to support academic and cultural success of Pasifika learners in Aotearoa New Zealand. The research, guided by Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles and Whakatere Tōmua (Wayfinding), identified four core values critical to Pasifika student success: belonging, whānau (family), respect, and enactment of culture. The study emphasizes that whānau involvement in school life, encouragement of academic perseverance, practical support, and curriculum integration are essential characteristics supporting educational success. Whānau serve as "wayfinders," navigating their children through the education system while balancing cultural values with educational goals to help tamariki thrive in both worlds.

[Page 1] Pasifika Festival 2025: A weekend celebrating culture, food, performance and song ByCoco Lance RNZ Pacific Digital Journalist 2025 03 10 09:18:09+13:00 Pasifika Festival ran at Auckland's Western Springs over the weekend bringing with it singing, dancing, food and activities. The annual event showcased Pasifika culture with food, performance and song, and a gathering of people from 11 different island nations. Many people wore traditional dress, and there were multiple generations in attendance. htt ps://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/morningreport/audio/2018978 175/pasifika fest held at auckland s western springs The festival started in the 1990s, but faced cancellations in recent years. In 2019, it was cancelled in the wake of the Christchurch mosque attacks, then again in 2020 due to the Covid 19 pandemic. It did run in 2023, but with a different tone as it followed shortly after the Auckland Anniversary weekend flooding. This year, rain dampened Saturday afternoon, and some festivalgoers mentioned the 2024 version was bigger. Festival Director Jep Savali said the event was evolving since its inception more than 30 years ago, and was growing again post Covid and the anniversary floods. "We are on a positive growth curve, and with that we are rebuilding, we're reenergising and reamplifying the community, this festival, and its reach within Tāmaki Makaurau so that it one day will reach its hay day, but in a different sense, in a sense that we're much more evolved, much more inclusive." One attendee hailed all the way from the Netherlands. Aansan Yeh said despite her east Asian heritage, she was drawn to the Pacific Islands. "I came to the Pasifika Festival because I'm really intrigued and interested in all Pacific Island cultures. "I love to see the dance; the artistry and I also feel a string connection to the ocean. I think it's really important because it brings people together and it's important to celebrate beauty, tradition, community all the things that make life important for me." Gina, leader of the Tuvalu dance group, said these events united the community and the group's cultural attire was made collaboratively by the women in her village. She was wearing a titi tao, she said "all the ladies of our whenua made them for us." Jep Savali added it would not be long until Pasifika Festival 2026 was on the brain. "There is approximately about eight months' worth of planning that goes into this festival. "There's a small team that goes in behind it but very importantly we connect with the community via the village cultural advisory group who are made up of community leaders within the eleven islands that are represented here at Pasifika." But Summer festivals are not over in Aotearoa, by a long shot Womad kicks off in New Plymouth on Friday, and Polyfest begins 2 April. [Page 1] ByTiana Haxton Journalist 2024 02 15 10:13:27+13:00 Wellington's Pacific community came together to honour their rich cultural heritage at the Wellington Pasifika Festival over the weekend. ht tps://www.rnz.co.nz/international/programmes/datelinepacific/audio/201 8925900/wellington s pacific community honour their cultural heritage at annual festival Wellington's Pacific community honour their cultural heritage With sights, sounds, and flavours evoking the essence of the Pacific, participants embarked on a journey through the diverse island nations of Te Moana Nui O Kiva. Drawing in a crowd of over 15,000 people annually, the event holds significant importance in preserving cultural ties to their homelands. "It's incredibly important so that we can make sure our identity is solid," Brienela Tauira Kisona, the Mistress of Ceremonies, said. "We do that by surrounding ourselves with people that identify with the same cultures, to ensure that we are continuing our Pacific traditions and cultures." Representatives from Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia showcased their crafts, cuisine, and captivating performances, highlighting the significance of the festival. Solomon Islands community vice president Selwyn Teho said the event provides an opportunity for all. "It's a day where we come and share our cultures with other Pacific countries too and then we share it with the whole Wellington community." Teho also emphasised the importance of youth involvement in cultural preservation, expressing pride in seeing different generations unite on stage. "Seeing our new generation and the older generation together on the stage is just really amazing" he said, adding: "It means a lot to us." Echoing similar sentiments, the Porirua Samoana Methodist Youth Group said having family support at cultural events was special. Vaioleni Aiono led a team of first time performers on stage while their parents cheered them on from the audience. "It's very special especially for our young girls who are first time performing so they do get stage fright and so its good to have our mums and dads here to support our young kids while we celebrate our culture with everyone here," Aiono said. PMN radio personality Susnation Seta, alongside Cook Islands champion dancer Caroline Bishop, engaged attendees in traditional dance forms of Ura Kuki Airani. Seta expressed gratitude for the opportunity to share Pasifika heritage. "The crowd and the atmosphere was absolutely amazing. It is an absolute honour to be celebrating Pasifika excellence at a festival like this." Another special guest was international opera tenor, Benjamin Fifita Makisi. The Wellington born Samoan Tongan singer has returned from Europe and has been enjoying performing at community events back home. He said performing Polynesian songs overseas is always well received and he was proud to bring the experience to his hometown. "It was really nice to come and showcase it (Opera) back home," Makisi said. "Events like this is a really good way to outreach to the community and to our own people." Saturday's resounding success underscores the enduring vibrancy and value of Pacific Island heritage in Aotearoa. The Wellington Pasifika Festival yet again left attendees eagerly anticipating next year's event. Events on offer on Saturday included poetry, Zumba, a guide to life workshop and multiple performances, including an afternoon show from Fijian R&B group the LeftOvas, who opened for Six60 earlier this month. Aansan Yen, who has Chinese heritage but was born and raised in the Netherlands, said she was intrigued by and interested in Pasific Island cultures. Political leaders also made an appearance, and the leader of the opposition Chris Hipkins said the festival was a chance to connect with different Pasifika communities in one place. "Pasifika communities make up such a big part of Aotearoa's overall culture and identity. We are of the Pacific," he said. "I think political leaders have got a really important job in bringing the community together. That means celebrating our differences." 46.text:
[Page 1] Thousands are expected to gather at Western Springs over the weekend as the Pasifika Festival returns to Auckland for its 33rd year. The festival celebrates Pacific food, music and culture in a city home to more than 275,000 Pacific people. It is one of the city's largest publicly funded cultural events, and free to the public. This year's festival features eight cultural villages representing 11 Pacific communities, including Samoa, Tonga, Fiji, Niue, Tuvalu, the Cook Islands and Aotearoa. 1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines Tongan migration to New Zealand and community development from the 1960s onwards. By 2018, over 82,000 Tongans lived in New Zealand, with two-thirds born there, making them the second-largest Pacific ethnic group, primarily settled in Auckland's Ōtara and Māngere. Despite socio-economic challenges including lower median incomes ($21,000 vs $40,000 nationally), overcrowded housing, and lower employment rates, Tongans maintain strong cultural identity through churches, language, and family traditions rooted in anga faka-Tonga. It identifies three distinct Tongan groups: those maintaining traditional anga faka-Tonga, New Zealand-born Tongans with decreasing language knowledge, and those identifying with broader Pacific Islander identity. Language preservation challenges are evident, with Tongan-speaking population declining from 63% (1996) to 40% (2018). The document highlights the emergence of Pasifika Aotearoa—a new cultural identity blending Pacific traditions with Afro-American influences, hip-hop, and reggae. Success measures are rooted in family obligations and community contributions, with cultural contributions through music, sports, and arts enriching New Zealand society.

chunkHighlights.text: Tongan identity

People gathering at large Methodist churches, women making tapa cloth, and children attending Tongan preschools show the Tongan community’s determination to keep alive their culture in New Zealand. 2.fileDescription: Profile of Emeline Afeaki-Mafile'o, a first-generation New Zealand social entrepreneur of Tongan, Samoan and Māori descent. She founded Affirming Works, a mentoring agency specializing in Pasifika youth that has served 5,000 high schoolers across South Auckland. She established Pacific Advance Senior School (PASS) in Otahuhu for struggling students and co-founded Fofola Consulting, contributing to government policy on youth strategy, gang prevention, and family violence. Afeaki-Mafile'o also acquired and manages Tonga's entire coffee industry (100% of production) across 10 cooperative farms employing 80 people, using profits to fund community work. Her approach emphasizes bridging cultural gaps, amplifying local community knowledge, and transitioning from dependency models to social entrepreneurship, positioning herself as a bridge between Pacific and New Zealand cultures.

chunkHighlights.text: Afeaki-Mafile’o describes meeting a girl who was furious at her controlling aunt; she didn’t understand that in Tonga, her father’s sisters wield a special cultural authority over her. “I had to explain her auntie’s role in Tongan culture, and how honourable that was. chunkHighlights.text: Matters of gender

Tongan culture recognises only very strict gender roles. Girls are brought up to be submissive and to stay at home, whereas boys are reared to be independent and mobile. As adults, men have more political power, but women are ranked higher in the community. The terms fakaleitī (like a lady) and fakatangata (like a man) are the Tongan words for gay people. When they are not in sexual relationships, these people are usually ignored, but as sexual beings they can face discrimination within the community.

4.fileDescription: This article documents Auckland's Secondary Schools Maori and Pacific Islands Cultural Festival, one of the city's largest cultural events attracting over 100,000 spectators. The festival, now in its 18th year, features 135 teams representing six different races, showcasing traditional performances from Polynesian students. The article highlights the festival's significance for Auckland, which hosts more Polynesian people than many Pacific islands themselves—including 11,000 Niueans (vs. 2,000 on Niue) and 22,000 Cook Islanders (vs. 17,000 in the Cooks). Through personal stories and performance details, it explores how students express cultural pride, adapt traditional costumes using modern materials, and compete with dedication. The festival serves as a platform for cross-cultural understanding, with students often performing in groups outside their own heritage based on keenness rather than ancestry. Performances range from traditional dances to contemporary pieces addressing modern challenges faced by immigrant families.

chunkHighlights.text: In 1976, at the first festival, six school groups took part. This year there were 135 teams, representing six different races.
“Everyone gets a feel for each other’s culture here,” Tumama Faumui explains. “We learn what others respect, and what they expect.”
[chapter-break]

It is a tongan tradition for young unmarried women to have their bodies oiled before they dance. The coconut oil being applied to Mere Latu’s arms and shoulders has been sent here by her grandmother in Tonga. Perfumed with leaves from Tonga’s trees, the oil looks good and smells nice, but has a more practical purpose, too: bank notes stick to it. It is another Tongan tradition to give money in appreciation of a good performance, and in a recent church charity concert Mere was almost literally clothed in notes—$2500 in all—from the admiring audience.

Thirty minutes before her item for St Mary’s College, the attention Mere is receiving from her mother and aunt also helps to massage away stage jitters. With the fear of forgetting lines, fumbling complicated actions, letting team mates down, tension is high behind the scenes at the festival. It shows on the strained faces of the Indian team from Epsom Girls’ Grammar School (top), getting their stage directions just before they go on.
“Someone’s always crying because it’s their first time,” says A J Paul (above), being comforted by a hug from her Westlake Girls’ High School classmate Arnia Dolan.
[chapter-break]

When you’re transplanted to another country, you leave the flowers and trees and grasses of your home—the vital elements of your traditional food and clothing. Instead, you borrow from your new surroundings, sometimes with dramatic results.
The costume design is traditional, but the boldly coloured raffia materials of the St Paul’s College Tongan group (left) are unmistakably 1990s New Zealand.

More and more, however, festival costumes are returning to traditional roots, as Liston College’s Samoan team uniform shows (above). The costume of their fuataimi, or conductor, Kelly Seamanu, particularly echoes older times with its feathers, pearls and teeth of shark and wild pig.

Sonie of the other island groups fly in fresh flowers from the Pacific, at a huge cost in money and effort. On the eve of the festival their families must work through the night to assemble such perishable costumes.

The teams also display another form of cross-cultural borrowing. Billy Matakitoga (middle, left) is a Niuean in his school’s Tongan team, which also includes two Samoans and two Cook Islanders. Within each school, it’s not uncommon for the students to move from one group to another, or to belong to more than one. Their heritage is not the critical factor, their keenness is.
“This generation is the one which will lead the way to a better understanding between cultures in Auckland,” says one school principal.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines the Samoan experience in New Zealand across historical, cultural, and social dimensions. It covers Samoa's geography, Samoan migration beginning in the 1950s, and New Zealand's colonial administration of Western Samoa (1914-1962). Key historical events include the 1918 influenza outbreak killing over 20% of the population, the independence movement (Mau) culminating in Samoa's 1962 independence, and the discriminatory "Dawn Raids" of the 1970s, for which New Zealand formally apologized in 2021. As of 2018, 182,721 Samoans lived in New Zealand, predominantly in Auckland. The document explores immigration schemes including the Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) program, economic indicators, and remittances (16% of Samoa's economy in 2019). Central to the analysis is fa'asamoa (Samoan culture) encompassing family (aiga), language, genealogy, and church traditions, alongside the identity paradox faced by New Zealand-born Samoans. It highlights significant Samoan contributions across academia, politics, sports, arts, and business, featuring notable figures such as Albert Wendt, Pacific MPs, accomplished athletes, and influential artists. The document also addresses the special relationship between Samoans and Māori, collaborative activism, language preservation efforts, and the role of Samoan churches as cultural centers.

chunkHighlights.text: Fa‘asamoa – Samoan culture
The concept of fa‘asamoa is essential to Samoan identity, and consists of a number of values and traditions:
aiga (family)
tautala Samoa (Samoan language)
gafa (genealogies)
matai (chiefly system)
lotu (church)
fa‘alavelave (ceremonial and other family obligations).
There are also the associated values of alofa (love), tautua (service), fa‘aaloalo (respect), feagaiga (a covenant between sibilings and others)
and usita‘i (discipline).

The fa‘asamoa practised in Samoa may differ from that in New Zealand. Not every Samoan has the same understanding of the concept. What remains constant is maintaining the family and links with the homeland. Money, prayers, support, food, material goods, and even relatives themselves, circulate within families around the world – wherever Samoan people live and work.
Fa‘asamoa in New Zealand
In 1998 one New Zealand-born Samoan described what it means to follow fa‘asamoa:

‘The fa‘asamoa is: go to church, be a good Samoan, and that means to try your best at education, and looking after family, and go to family functions, plus that we've got to look after them when they're old.’

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document collection presents an in-depth exploration of Samoa through multiple perspectives. It examines the contradictions between Samoa's idyllic image and complex realities of fa'a Samoa, including tensions between traditional matai authority and individual freedoms, and high emigration rates to New Zealand. The collection covers Samoa's colonial history, including the 1918 influenza epidemic and the Mau independence movement, alongside contemporary journalism challenging corruption. Village governance through the fono system is analyzed, exploring how traditional authority maintains social order while restricting individual expression and contributing to high suicide rates. Religious dimensions include Christianity, Mormonism, and Baha'i, alongside cultural elements like traditional tattooing (pe'a), siapo cloth-making, and the role of fa'afafine in society. Environmental challenges include cyclone recovery and conservation efforts, while economic realities involve low wages, tourism, remittances, and aid dependence. A critical comparison between Western Samoa and American Samoa reveals how modernization and American individualism have paradoxically improved mental health outcomes while challenging cultural preservation. The work explores the fundamental paradox of Samoan society: communal values and cultural pride coexisting with oppressive social controls, limited economic opportunities, and psychological stress.

chunkHighlights.text:
Homeland Samoans came to New Zealand from two islands in Samoa:
Upolu and Savai‘i. They are hilly, with palm trees and attractive beaches along the coastlines. Samoa is a very Christian country, and there are many large and beautiful churches. Migrations New Zealand ruled Western Samoa from 1914 to 1962. In the 1960s and 1970s, large numbers of Samoans came to New Zealand for jobs, many travelling on temporary visas. In the mid-1970s, the police came into the homes of some who had overstayed their visas, and many were sent back to Samoa. The New Zealand government formally apologised for these events in 2021. Samoans continue to come to New Zealand for work and to join their families. Two-thirds of New Zealand’s Samoans live in the ‘Pacific capital’, Auckland. Frequent travel between Samoa and New Zealand has kept families living in both countries closely connected. Culture Samoans brought to New Zealand their strong beliefs in Christianity and the importance of aiga (family). Their traditions are that children should respect, serve and obey their elders. Samoans work hard to maintain contact with family members across the seas. Some younger Samoans born in New Zealand cities have found it difficult to accept these rules. Unable to speak Samoan, they have found enjoyment and support in an urban culture with distinctive dancing, music, language and clothing. With other young Pacific Islanders they have made a new PI (Pacific Island) identity. Contributions Many Samoans have been highly successful in New Zealand and made significant contributions to their new home. They include playwrights and novelists, artists, sportspeople, and musicians ranging from hip hop to classical. In all
these fields, Samoans have greatly enriched New Zealand life.

The document highlights the emergence of Pasifika Aotearoa—a new cultural identity blending Pacific traditions with Afro-American influences, hip-hop, and reggae. Success measures are rooted in family obligations and community contributions, with cultural contributions through music, sports, and arts enriching New Zealand society.

chunkHighlights.text: For some New Zealand-borns, an understanding of custom serves as a stepping stone to new forms of expression. The operatic tenor Ben Makisi has moved from his knowledge of Tongan musical notation to explore European classical music. Tongan styles of sport, especially in netball and rugby, have influenced the games in New Zealand. All Black Jonah Lomu became a national icon. Tongan-born Filipe Tohi brings Tongan elements to his sculpture and lashing.
The new Pasifika Aotearoa identity has flourished and now includes a proliferating music culture, an eclectic fashion industry, and pan-Pacific churches.

retrieved_chunks.text: Matters of gender Tongan culture recognises only very strict gender roles. Girls are brought up to be submissive and to stay at home, whereas boys are reared to be independent and mobile. As adults, men have more political power, but women are ranked higher in the community. The terms fakaleitī (like a lady) and fakatangata (like a man) are the Tongan words for gay people. When they are not in sexual relationships, these people are usually ignored, but as sexual beings they can face discrimination within the community.

retrieved_chunks.text: Fa‘asamoa – Samoan culture The concept of fa‘asamoa is essential to Samoan identity, and consists of a number of values and traditions: aiga (family) tautala Samoa (Samoan language) gafa (genealogies) matai (chiefly system) lotu (church) fa‘alavelave (ceremonial and other family obligations). There are also the associated values of alofa (love), tautua (service), fa‘aaloalo (respect), feagaiga (a covenant between sibilings and others) and usita‘i (discipline). The fa‘asamoa practised in Samoa may differ from that in New Zealand. Not every Samoan has the same understanding of the concept. What remains constant is maintaining the family and links with the homeland. Money, prayers, support, food, material goods, and even relatives themselves, circulate within families around the world – wherever Samoan people live and work. Fa‘asamoa in New Zealand In 1998 one New Zealand-born Samoan described what it means to follow fa‘asamoa: ‘The fa‘asamoa is: go to church, be a good Samoan, and that means to try your best at education, and looking after family, and go to family functions, plus that we've got to look after them when they're old.’

retrieved_chunks.text: The central element in Samoan culture is the aiga (family). Within the family, giving and receiving tautua (service), fa‘aaloalo (respect) and alofa (love) are crucial in social relations. Young people are expected to serve and show respect to elders, and can expect in return to receive love, protection, honour, a name to be proud of, and support when this is needed.

retrieved_chunks.text: Migration Tongans come from a scattered group of islands in the South Pacific. They have brought a strong Christian faith and a deep loyalty to their extended family. In the 1960s they began to arrive as factory workers, and large numbers settled in the 1970s and 1980s. By 2018 there were over 80,000 Tongans in New Zealand, and two-thirds of them had been born there.
retrieved_chunks.title: Tongans.pdf

retrieved_chunks.text:
Homeland Samoans came to New Zealand from two islands in Samoa:
Upolu and Savai‘i. They are hilly, with palm trees and attractive beaches along the coastlines. Samoa is a very Christian country, and there are many large and beautiful churches. Migrations New Zealand ruled Western Samoa from 1914 to 1962. In the 1960s and 1970s, large numbers of Samoans came to New Zealand for jobs, many travelling on temporary visas. In the mid-1970s, the police came into the homes of some who had overstayed their visas, and many were sent back to Samoa. The New Zealand government formally apologised for these events in 2021. Samoans continue to come to New Zealand for work and to join their families. Two-thirds of New Zealand’s Samoans live in the ‘Pacific capital’, Auckland. Frequent travel between Samoa and New Zealand has kept families living in both countries closely connected. Culture Samoans brought to New Zealand their strong beliefs in Christianity and the importance of aiga (family). Their traditions are that children should respect, serve and obey their elders. Samoans work hard to maintain contact with family members across the seas. Some younger Samoans born in New Zealand cities have found it difficult to accept these rules. Unable to speak Samoan, they have found enjoyment and support in an urban culture with distinctive dancing, music, language and clothing. With other young Pacific Islanders they have made a new PI (Pacific Island) identity. Contributions Many Samoans have been highly successful in New Zealand and made significant contributions to their new home. They include playwrights and novelists, artists, sportspeople, and musicians ranging from hip hop to classical. In all
these fields, Samoans have greatly enriched New Zealand life.
retrieved_chunks.title: Samoans.pdf

retrieved_chunks.text: However, Samoans in New Zealand have distinctive experiences and values which they do not share with other Pacific Islanders. Differences of culture and language outweigh the commonality of the New Zealand experience. In the end, the bedrock of fa‘asamoa (Samoan culture) is aiga (family); friends and acquaintances come and go, but the aiga remains as a permanent fixture. PI identity is a phenomenon of young people. When they mature and have their own children, Samoans tend to return to their ethnic identity. For those of mixed ethnicity, Samoan identity is passed on to younger generations by the stories and instructions of their mothers or grandmothers, or by fathers who have been influenced markedly by their mothers.
retrieved_chunks.title: Samoans.pdf

retrieved_chunks.text: Tonga is a dispersed community, and Tongan identities are evolving in response to the new environments. Three main types of Tongans have emerged. The first are those who have been raised in anga faka-Tonga (the Tongan way), and still maintain their language. The second are those who were born in New Zealand and have decreasing knowledge of the language and anga faka-Tonga. Interestingly, many New Zealand-born Tongans understand the language but cannot speak it. They acquire sufficient Tongan to incorporate values of anga faka-Tonga, but are not able to transmit the language to the next generation. However, very few have become wholly assimilated to a non-Tongan way of life. When people are asked to state their ethnicity, the vast majority call themselves Tongan.

[Page 11] Because of Samoan culture’s strong base in the Christian church, fa’afāfine in modern Samoa can be marginalised. However, fa’afāfine beauty pageants are very popular. These draw on the tradition of gaining social recognition through entertainment, while also providing a way to raise funds for community organisations such as those combating HIV/AIDS or running the local rest home.

retrieved_chunks.text:
[Page 8] members. Although some were in prisons, hospitals or unemployed, others were going to church in large numbers, sending millions of dollars in remittances to their families back home, and graduating in increasing numbers from New Zealand universities. In 2018, 7.9% of Samoans aged 15 and over had a tertiary qualification or equivalent, compared to 5.7% in 2006. Samoans also featured among the country’s top sportspeople, and participated increasingly in the entertainment, education and business sectors. It was also clear that success did not necessarily come at the price of losing island culture. The ‘va’ between Samoans and tangata whenua Māori and Pacific peoples share a special relationship, which can be expressed by the Samoan word va (social and sacred/spiritual spaces of relationships). Kinships and relationships can be traced through similarities of history and culture. This kinship connection is shown in the banter of Māori kaumatua (elders) on marae , when visitors from the Pacific are sometimes recognised as tuakana (older siblings), which acknowledges this ancient connection, or as teina (younger siblings), which acknowledges that Māori are tangata whenua of Aotearoa and those from the Pacific are manuhiri (visitors). Many Samoans worked alongside Māori activist groups to promote Māori rights, fight racial discrimination, and confront injustices. In the 1970s, the Polynesian Panthers stood alongside Ngā Tamatoa in the fight to establish te reo Māori as an official language of Aotearoa, on the Māori Land March, and at the Bastion Point protest. In 2019 2020, Pacific people were involved in the Ihumātao land dispute in Māngere, Auckland.
{}

[Page 1] Who are the Samoans? Samoans are the original inhabitants of the Samoa Islands, which lie north of New Zealand between latitude 13° and 15° south. The two large islands are Upolu and Savai‘i, and the only other inhabited islands are Manono and Apolima. About 80 km south east is Tutuila, the principal island of the smaller territory of American Samoa.

[Page 11] In traditional Samoan contexts, preference for feminine tasks by a child thought to be a boy will usually be recognised at an early age. After being acknowledged as fa’afafine, the child is likely to transition including wearing women’s clothing, dancing the siva (a traditional dance usually performed wearing a feathered headdress), and fulfilling feminine roles within the village. Fa’afāfine are accepted as women in many contexts, but they may also undertake masculine tasks or fulfil men’s roles. Fa’afāfine often remain in their family homes and care for their parents.

[Page 7] The Samoan church in New Zealand Samoan churches proliferated in New Zealand cities. They took on the role of villages, and provided a platform for strong Samoan identity. # Māori and the New Zealand Justice System

The relationship between Māori and the justice system in Aotearoa New Zealand is one of the country's most significant and complex social issues — spanning centuries of legal history, deep structural inequities, and ongoing debate about how to create a fairer system for all New Zealanders.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## From Tikanga to British Law

Before 1840, the law of the land was tikanga Māori — the customs and methods of governance by which Māori society was ordered. This system was built around concepts such as mana (status, either inherited or acquired), tapu (sacred prohibition), rahui (a form of tapu restricting access to certain food sources), utu (repayment for another's actions), and muru (a ritual seizure of property as compensation for an offence). [[1]](cite://1/1)

When the Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840, British law arrived in force. In practice, however, it only applied in areas of significant Pākehā settlement; elsewhere, Māori traditional systems of governance continued to predominate. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Māori customary law is still recognised in New Zealand today, provided certain criteria are met: the custom must be longstanding, have continued without interruption, be reasonable, be certain in its terms, and must not have been displaced by Parliament through clear statutory wording. [[3]](cite://3/1)

## Specialist Courts and Institutions

The New Zealand court system includes several institutions specifically designed to address Māori needs and rights.

The Māori Land Court is the oldest specialist court in the country, having dealt with the alienation of Māori land since 1865 — when it was called the Native Land Court. It rules on issues of multiple ownership of Māori land, with appeals going to the Māori Appellate Court. [[4]](cite://4/1)

The Waitangi Tribunal, established in 1975, is a unique institution where Māori can bring complaints about breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi. From 1985, it was empowered to investigate breaches dating back to 1840. It makes recommendations to the government, and on the basis of its findings, the Crown has undertaken a range of treaty settlements since the late 1980s — including the restoration of fisheries to Māori ownership in 1992. [[3]](cite://3/2)[[5]](cite://5/1)

## Māori Over-Representation in Prison

Perhaps the most confronting dimension of this topic is the dramatic over-representation of Māori in the prison system. In the 19th century, very few Māori were imprisoned — usually less than 3% of the total prison population. [[2]](cite://2/2) That began to change in the early 20th century, with Māori urbanisation — accelerated by the Second World War — a clear contributing factor. By 1945, Māori made up 21% of prison admissions while representing just 6% of the total population. [[6]](cite://6/1)

By 1971, Māori were 40% of the prison population while forming around 10% of the country's total population. Since 1980, Māori have consistently made up about half of all prisoners. [[7]](cite://7/1)

More recent data paints an even starker picture. A 2025 study found Māori were overrepresented at every stage of the criminal justice system — 37% of people proceeded against by police, 45% of those convicted, and over half of the prison population at 52%, despite Māori making up only 17.8% of the population. In women's prisons, the proportion rises to 61–63%. [[8]](cite://8/1)

The same research found Māori were being *undercounted* in prison data by around 6% — roughly 405 people — because Corrections was not following national ethnicity recording protocols. Lead researcher Paula King said this affected resource allocation and government policy decisions: "If you're invisibilising Māori, you can't monitor Crown actions or inactions, or accurately assess the impact of policies." [[8]](cite://8/2)

## Sentencing Disparities

The inequities don't stop at the prison gate. A 2025 study examining first-time drink-driving cases found that, despite having similar alcohol levels at the time of offending, 9.9% of Māori offenders received a community-based sentence compared with just 3.3% of NZ Europeans. Even after controlling for offence characteristics and a range of demographic and socioeconomic factors, Māori remained *twice as likely* as NZ Europeans to receive a community-based sentence — a more severe outcome than a fine. [[9]](cite://9/1)

Separate analysis from the Understanding Policing Delivery programme found systemic bias at the policing stage: when all other factors were held constant, Māori were 11% more likely to be prosecuted than Pākehā. [[9]](cite://9/2)

## Contributing Factors

The reasons behind the high rates of Māori imprisonment are widely acknowledged to be complex. They include the larger proportion of Māori in lower socioeconomic groups, a younger age profile in the Māori population, higher rates of unemployment, the ongoing effects of urbanisation, and the influence of gang culture. Some critics argue the justice system disadvantages Māori at every stage — from arrest through to sentencing. [[7]](cite://7/2)

Those released from prison face dire outcomes. The mortality rate of people released from prison is three times that of the general population, with the first month after release the most dangerous. Mortality is worse for wāhine Māori (Māori women). The research also found that only 76% of Māori released from prison were enrolled with a Primary Health Organisation, leaving a quarter without access to subsidised care. [[8]](cite://8/3)

## Responses and Reforms

Several initiatives have sought to address these realities. The Department of Corrections runs Māori Focus Units, open to medium and minimum security prisoners, which aim to change behaviour through a greater understanding of tikanga Māori. The department also has a policy of consulting with Māori community groups and recruiting more Māori staff. [[10]](cite://10/1)

At a community level, marae-based programmes — such as those run by Tūhoe Hauora in Tāneatua — have proved successful for rangatahi (young people) who come into conflict with the law, using tikanga-based approaches to build self-worth and a sense of direction. [[11]](cite://11/1)

However, critics — including nurses working inside prisons — raised concerns in 2024 when the coalition government moved to remove Te Tiriti o Waitangi provisions from the Corrections Amendment Bill. Those provisions had compelled the Department of Corrections to improve outcomes for Māori and maintain obligations around healthcare and rehabilitation programmes. The New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) called the move "deeply shameful." [[12]](cite://12/1)

Meanwhile, sentencing reforms passed in 2025 — which cap the discounts judges can apply for mitigating factors — have drawn criticism for their likely disproportionate impact on Māori, given Māori already make up the majority of the prison population. The Ministry of Justice's own regulatory impact statement noted that the changes rested on inadequate consultation, *particularly with Māori*. [[13]](cite://13/1)

The debate continues about the right path forward, with researchers, community leaders, and whānau (families) consistently pointing to the need for kaupapa Māori (Māori-centred) approaches, secure housing, employment pathways, and sustained community support after release. As one researcher put it: "We're trying to break cycles of harm for future generations, to create a world our mokopuna (grandchildren) can live well in." [[8]](cite://8/4)

---

New Zealand’s legal system was founded on British law, but it has evolved into a separate system. International law and treaties have influenced New Zealand law, especially since the 1960s. Common law New Zealand has common law, which means judges make legal decisions based on previous judges’ decisions as well as on statutes (written law) passed by Parliament. Criminal law Criminal law is one of two broad parts of New Zealand law (the other being civil law). For something to be a crime in New Zealand it must be outlawed in a statute. Verdicts for serious criminal offences can be decided on by a jury 12 members of the public who have been selected randomly. New Zealand removed the death penalty for murder in 1961, and for treason in 1989. Civil law The other part of New Zealand law is civil law. This deals with disputes between individuals or organisations. Courts New Zealand courts are, in order of importance: Supreme Court Court of Appeal High Court Courts Martial Appeal Authority District Court other specialist courts, including the Family Court, Environment Court, Māori Land Court, Employment Court and Youth Court. There are also various tribunals which deal with particular areas of law. Alternative dispute methods such as mediation are increasingly used. Judges New Zealand has around 200 judges who decide on court cases. Judges are independent from the government, which is important for a fair justice system. The head of New Zealand’s judiciary (judges) is the chief justice, who presides over the Supreme Court. The legal profession In the early 2000s there were more than 11,000 practising lawyers in New Zealand. Most were both barristers (who work in courts) and solicitors (who give legal advice). The Waitangi Tribunal plays a crucial role in addressing Māori grievances.
