3.filePath: pdf/Te whānau tamariki – pregnancy and birth.pdf
3.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores Māori traditions and practices surrounding pregnancy, childbirth, and baby care from pre-European settlement to the 21st century. It establishes mythological foundations through figures like Hineteiwaiwa (atua associated with pregnancy and childbirth), Papatūānuku (Earth mother), and Ranginui (sky father), and explains whakapapa (genealogy) as central to Māori philosophy. Traditional practices include conception rituals by tohunga (experts), natural contraception methods, specialized birth shelters (whare kōhanga), and ceremonies such as the tohi rite where babies are dedicated to atua and the pure ceremony. The document details historical practices including careful placement of placenta (whenua) and umbilical cord on tribal land, singing of oriori (traditional chants with whakapapa and lullabies), and traditional baby care using moss diapers and flax baskets. It addresses cultural concepts of mana and tapu inherited at birth, and the importance of whāngai (child adoption) in emphasizing whānau connections. The transition from traditional home births to hospital births is documented, highlighting hospitals' increasing sensitivity toward Māori cultural practices and the role of Māori midwives, including Ngā Maia o Aotearoa me Te Waipounamu. Modern health concerns include the disproportionately high incidence of SIDS among Māori infants and interventions like wahakura (traditional weaving-based sleeping bassinets) for safer infant sleep.

chunkHighlights.text: Whakapapa

Whakapapa (genealogy) forms the foundation of Māori philosophy. Birth is the instrument by which whakapapa is created. All things are related through whakapapa – the gods, natural phenomena, humans and all other living things. Whakapapa provides a way of understanding the universe and its past, present and future.

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores the traditional Māori worldview and understanding of nature (Te Ao Mārama), presenting a holistic indigenous philosophy centered on interconnectedness and spiritual principles. It explains how Māori people viewed all elements of nature—birds, fish, people, wind, and sun—as an interconnected family linked through genealogies (whakapapa). The creation story describes how earth mother Papatūānuku and sky father Ranginui produced 70 children who became gods of different natural domains. Key concepts include whakapapa (genealogies explaining relationships between all things), Te Kore (a realm of unlimited potential and ultimate reality), and the cycle of light (Te Ao) and darkness (Te Pō) representing birth and death. Three interconnected spiritual concepts are examined: mana (extraordinary power and essence), tapu (sacred restrictions and disciplines), and mauri (life force energy binding all physical things). The document explores tangata whenua (people of the land), where identity is defined through geographical and ancestral connections, and discusses taniwha as spiritual guardians. It emphasizes how orators use speech to guide people from darkness into light, mirroring Tāne's separation of earth and sky, and highlights the practical and spiritual functions of oral traditions in transmitting knowledge while maintaining respect toward other species.

chunkHighlights.text: This linking was explained in tātai (genealogies) and kōrero (stories), collectively termed whakapapa (meaning to make a foundation, to place in layers). Experts recited the whakapapa of people, birds, fish, trees and the weather to explain the relationships between all things and thus to place themselves within the world. This helped people to understand the world, and how to act within these relationships.

chunkHighlights.text: The meaning of whakapapa

Whakapapa (genealogies and stories) express our need for kinship with the world. They describe the relationships between humans and the rest of nature. In one tradition, some tribal groups and the fish of the sea claim descent from Tangaroa, the god of the sea.
Whakapapa also explain the origins of animals, plants and features of the landscape. To tell a story about the origin of a bird, for example, is to invoke its true essence or character.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores the concept of whānau, the Māori understanding of family that extends far beyond the Western nuclear family model. Whānau traditionally comprises multiple generations living together, working collectively, and sharing common ancestors, encompassing physical, emotional, and spiritual dimensions based on whakapapa (genealogy). The document examines traditional whānau structures and their evolution in contemporary society, explaining how whānau members balance individual rights with collective responsibilities. Key concepts discussed include tuakana-taina (sibling relationships with age-based hierarchies), the interconnection between whānau, hapū (sub-tribe), and iwi (tribe), and the crucial roles of elders in maintaining unity and transmitting cultural knowledge. The document also addresses factors affecting whānau bonds such as divorce, separation, death, and cross-cultural marriage. Additionally, it explores whāngai, the traditional Māori fostering practice where children are brought into another whānau by parents or grandparents, with adoptive parents known as mātua whāngai. Modern whānau may be descent-based or kaupapa-based (purpose-driven), and the term is now used metaphorically for close friends and organizations. Throughout, the document emphasizes that strength comes from many rather than one, reflecting the fundamental Māori philosophy of collective identity and shared responsibility.

chunkHighlights.text: Whakapapa

One of the foundations of whānau is whakapapa , which has great importance in Māori society. Whakapapa places people ‘in the whole context of relationships and therefore how we relate to each other and how we should work with each other, argue with each other, live with each other’. 1

It is through whakapapa that interactions and relationships are established, developed and maintained within whānau , and with whanaunga (relatives), marae , sacred mountains, rivers and ultimately the universe. Whakapapa is an organising principle. It is through whakapapa that individuals often get their names, their identities, their sense of belonging, turangawaewae (place to stand – their ancestral land), and access to knowledge, rights and responsibilities. The policy of past governments that encouraged many Māori to move off the land and into the cities to become urbanised had the effect, in many cases, of disbanding whānau , and they no longer know who they are and where they come from. This has led to a breakdown of whānau structures.

7.fileDescription: Yanika Reed, a 28-year-old Tauranga woman of mixed heritage (Austrian, Fijian-Indian, Māori, and British), describes her journey of reconnecting with her Tūhoe ancestry as an "awakening." Despite feeling disconnected from her Māori heritage due to her appearance and lack of knowledge about her whakapapa, Reed has spent the past month researching her genealogy using Ancestry.com, uncovering census records, police gazettes, and historical documents. Her research revealed significant ancestors, including Te Iwikino, a chief of Maungapōhatu who advocated for land reclamation in the Ureweras. Through this process, Reed has experienced what she describes as "untangling colonisation," gaining deeper understanding of te ao Māori and her cultural identity. She emphasizes that appearance does not determine Māori identity and encourages others with Māori whakapapa to explore their ancestry, highlighting the richness and strength found in embracing one's heritage.

ByAshleigh Mccaull - Journalist
2024-06-28 05:20:18+12:00

https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.ht
ml?videoId=6355763160112 Growing up, Yanika Reed felt disconnected
from her Māori heritage. She wasn't sure how to identify, due to her appearance - she has blue eyes and fair skin - and lack of knowledge about her whakapapa. But in the past month, the 28-year-old has made it her mission to dig into her ancestry and now feels more connected to te ao Māori and her tīpuna. She had been using Ancestry.com to research her tīpuna, digging through census records, police gazettes and old newspapers. The Tauranga woman - who is Austrian on her father's side and Fijian-Indian, Māori and British on her mother's - describes her journey of learning about her Tūhoe ancestry as an "awakening". https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/matariki-speci al/audio/2018944672/yanika-reed "There's something quite touching about seeing your ancestors who lived in a completely different era and seeing their faces... seeing names on paper and census records... some history as well around the Urewera raids and the confiscation of land," she said. "It's been quite special to see and it's been really nice to reignite their stories. I feel like a lot of these stories have been lost for so long and no one's really told them." One of those stories is that of her fourth great-grandmother's brother, a chief of Maungapōhatu named Te Iwikino, who was an important figure around the times of Rua Kēnana. "It's quite cool to know that I had a relative along the the line living and breathing during that time... just learning about how he himself actually travelled to Wellington to be a voice for the reclaiming back of lands in the Ureweras, in particular Rūātoki and Tāneatua. "There's a beautiful photograph of him where he was the voice with some other chiefs of Tūhoe to get their land back." Reed said her science background meant she had been thorough with her fact checking, to prevent going down a rabbit hole of thinking someone is a relation. "I could still be wrong, a lot of those historical records were oral and might have been the truth in those times either. So I can't really say what I found is 100 percent but I
hope that what I have found is respect to family that are still living and

also who have lived and that I've kind of portrayed them in the best way
I can." While researching her tīpuna, she had also uncovered some police records. "I've seen a few awesome mugshots, and it was quite cool to look at the documents and see their name, their hapū and also a description of them and what they looked like, and what they were charged for. Quite often the ones I've uncovered was a little bit of petty theft." She said it was heartbreaking reading how her tīpuna were described with greater and unnecessary detail, compared to European defendants, who had very little description. Researching had been a process she described as the untangling of colonisation. "My mother's not well-connected to that space, neither was her mother... I see the world quite differently now and see the Māori world quite differently too from undergoing this journey. Most definitely the untangling of colonisation mindset within my whānau, and I can only hope that my family members and those after me go through this process as well." Friday, Matariki, is also Reed's birthday. She will be using it as a time of remembrance, looking backward to honour the dead and forward to the new year. The star in the cluster that resonates most with her is Waitī because of its connection to her hapū, Ngāti Kōura, which is based in Tāneatua, Rūātoki and Whakatanē in the Eastern Bay of Plenty. Reed's middle name is Te Paea, which was her great-grandmother's name. She said she was honoured to have that name, but initially had shame around it as she was not connected to te ao Māori or embedded in the culture. "I think there was a sense of shame because I didn't look Māori, I couldn't swing a poi as much, I couldn't speak te reo, and it was essentially a shame of not fitting in into one particular group. "But I've since learned that it's not really about fitting into one. You're a kind of fusion of them all and a strength of them all, which has been a journey of mine too." She was now encouraging other Māori who feel disconnected or are not sure about their whakapapa to jump on the waka. "It has brought me so much connection, and I feel like richness in my life. I feel like it's really filled my cup a little bit. "I would recommend
to just get started with Ancestry.com, start online. There's so much
information out there, even your local library. I haven't even scratched
the surface of reading paper records. Really just throw yourself into it
and uncover, it's quite addictive and you do spend a lot of late nights
looking into it." She said one of her relatives told her that her
appearance does not change the fact that she is Māori "You don't need

permission to be Māori, and you don't need permission to not be Māori. No one can tell you whether you are or you're not, only you know that and only your whānau know that. "If you have whakapapa Māori you have whakapapa to look into it and pull on that strength of your ancestors. You have blood in those areas, and that's your birthright." Related

8.fileDescription: Researchers have developed the Rakeiora Genomics Platform, a prototype that integrates whakapapa (Māori genealogical data) with biomedical science and genome DNA sequencing to provide personalized treatment plans for Māori and minority communities. Associate Professor Phillip Wilcox explains that precision medicine tailors treatments and disease prevention to individuals using genetic information and genealogical components, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. The platform addresses the underrepresentation of Māori in genomic datasets by enabling Māori communities to govern their own whakapapa data. Precision medicine eliminates trial-and-error prescribing, provides accurate disease risk estimates, and can reduce healthcare costs by up to $200 million. The research, conducted over four years with case studies in primary and tertiary care, demonstrates clinical relevance. England's NHS has already invested in genomic medicine services, spending $5 billion on health research. For New Zealand to implement precision medicine, new tools, practices, and computing resources are required.

chunkHighlights.text: Is whakapapa the answer to better health treatment?

ByEmma Andrews - Reporter
2025-04-04 17:12:04+13:00

Researchers have developed a prototype platform to incorporate
whakapapa with biomedical science to provide better treatment plans for Māori and minority communities. The Rakeiora Genomics Platform uses genome DNA sequencing data, healthcare records and mātauranga whakapapa data to provide researchers with more accurate information on a person's health. Associate Professor Phillip Wilcox (Ngāti Rakaipaaka, Rongomaiwahine, Ngāti Kahungnunu ki te Wairoa, Te Aitanga-a-Mahaki), a quantitative geneticist and bioethicist at University of Otago, said the research described the development of a bespoke data access and analysis platform for application in precision health research. "The idea of precision health is that treatments, medication and even prevention of diseases can be tailored to the individual person, using the individual's information, such as their genome and other genetic information, like the genealogical component of whakapapa, in a te ao Māori setting, rather than a 'one-size fits all' style model." The research, carried out over a four-year period included two case studies that helped demonstrate the application of the platform for precision health research in Aotearoa, using and generating clinically relevant results across in primary care and in a tertiary care oncology setting, Wilcox said. Precision medicine - also known as genomic medicine or personalised medicine - uses a person's genetic information to help medical professionals carry out screening, diagnosing and treating patients more accurately, while reducing adverse drug reactions. "Within this precision health space, because we have very low representation of Māori in these datasets, we need to create our own, which means we need bespoke approaches, because Māori have unique disease etiologies, or underpinning biology to disease is unique, unique pathway to interventions as well." Before whakapapa information is used, its tapu nature means an environment needs to be established, where data use could be controlled by Māori, he said. "The Rakeiora platform - using tools from mostly from overseas, some local - is
designed to provide Māori communities and other communities with the

opportunity to have governance over their taonga, their own whakapapa
information." Some communities have already made enquiries. Ruling out a trial-and-error approach How precision medicine works is, if someone is mis-prescribed warfarin, for example, without knowing if their body can metabolise the drug properly, due to their genetic make-up, it could lead to negative outcomes. Medicating someone properly with DNA information can eliminate the grey area between 'can I or can't I have this drug?' It also provides a deeper understanding of an individual, when calculating disease risk. When a person goes to a general practitioner with symptoms of a particular disease, the doctor may go over a person's information, such as age and sex, statistics according to the information provided and ask further questions to determine a diagnosis, Wilcox described. Theoretically, the doctor might say 'you've got a risk of a severe cardiac event of X'. "Now that X comes with quite a lot of imprecision around the estimate," he said. "DNA information can provide information to clinicians about somebody's risk of a disease or a risk of a condition, it gives you a more precise estimate of what that probability is." In other instances, where there is no intervention or cure, such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD), patients can either slow progress or make changes in their lives in preparation. "Some people will still want to know what their disease outcomes are going to be, so that they can prepare for it or they can prepare family members," Wilcox said. "Precision medicine is kind of a frontier of medicine, it sits alongside AI as being one of those frontier areas." Putting science into practice In England, the National Health Service (NHS) has developed and invested in its own Genomic Medicine Service. In October 2022, the NHS produced a five-year genomic strategy that predicts, prevents, diagnoses and targets disease, making it accessible for all people in the NHS system. Using the history of providing services, the 'evolutionary' 100,000 Genomes Project drove at scale and pace, because it was centrally funded, England's Professor Dame Sue Hill announced at a PHG Foundation conference in 2023. "It
enables genomics to be at the forefront of data and digital and the
revolution there, so that it can bring together genomic data with other
clinical data to inform genotype (genetic traits)/phenotype (physical
traits) correlations," Hill said. Again in 2022, $5 billion was spent on
public funding for health relevant research alone, according to UK
Research and Innovation, which is broken into $2.8 billion on research

projects, $1.4 billion on infrastructure and other indirect support, and $865 million on health-relevant support funding. "They've done so on the basis that these more accurate prescribing can reduce costs and does reduce costs," Wilcox said. "When you've got whakapapa information, that's much cheaper to obtain in theory - I'll put it this way, whakapapa can save [Aotearoa], my calculation was up to $200 million." For precision medicine to become available in New Zealand, the Genomics Aotearoa website states it would require new tools, practices and computing resources. Related

Whakapapa – genealogy Whakapapa is genealogy, a line of descent from ancestors down to the
present day. Whakapapa links people to all other living things, and to the earth and the sky, and it traces the universe back to its origins. Whakapapa are told orally in different ways. The most common is tararere, which gives a single line of descent from an ancestor, without marriage partners or other kin. A short whakapapa giving just the names of important ancestors is known as tātai hikohiko or āhua hikohiko. Creation Whakapapa about the beginning of the universe vary from tribe to tribe. Te Arawa chief Te Rangikāheke said Te Pō (the darkness or night) was followed by Te Ao (the day) and then Te Kore (the nothing). Stories about ancestors are also similar, such as people fishing up islands, or the origin of fire. These helped people remember whakapapa – some people could recite hundreds of names. [Page 11] Scholars and whakapapa Problems in publication Early 20th century Pākehā writers changed the order of creation from Te Pō (the darkness), then Te Ao (the light) followed by Te Kore (the nothingness) to Te Kore, then Te Pō and Te Ao because their translation of te kore as ‘nothingness’ implied to them that this should be the first order of creation. A better gloss for Te Kore might be unknown potential. The first Western trained Māori scholars later taught this version of creation to other Māori, to the extent that today it is widely accepted by Māoridom as reflecting pre European creation beliefs. Turning whakapapa into history Other Pākehā writers, such as Stephenson Percy Smith in Hawaiki (1921), over historicised genealogies, firstly by assuming genealogies were sequentially human as far back as 50 to 60 generations and beyond, and then by generalising all tribal genealogies into one linear sequence, to say Kupe was the first ancestor to arrive in New Zealand 42 generations before 1900 in 950 CE, followed by Toi in 1150 CE, and a fleet of seven canoes in 1350 CE. Smith’s interpretation of whakapapa became widely accepted by Māori because Māori scholars educated in European institutions promoted it among their own people. False dates Pākehā scholars also averaged out long and short genealogies to work out when particular ancestors lived, which often created false dates. Another practice where genealogies varied quite widely in length was to wrongly conclude there were two different ancestors of the same name who lived at different times, which overlooked processes of truncation and elongation. For instance it can be shown that genealogies ranging between 58 and 18 generations for the ancestor Kupe refer to the same person. Dynamic whakapapa

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] Tribal organisation By Rāwiri Taonui What are iwi and hapū? The iwi (tribe) is the largest of the groups that form Māori society. Each iwi is made up of various hapū (clans or descent groups), which might have up to several hundred members. Traditionally, the main purposes of a hapū were to defend land, and to provide support for its members. How iwi and hapū formed Some tribal groups formed from links to the waka (canoe) on which their founding ancestor arrived in New Zealand from Hawaiki. For example, the Waikato tribes trace their descent from the Tainui waka. Others developed when the pressure on resources such as land and food became so great that some members had to move away and establish themselves elsewhere. War, migration and family infighting also caused new iwi or hapū to emerge. Iwi and hapū are often named after an ancestor. For example, Ngāpuhi means ‘the people of Puhi ’ and Te Uri o Rātā means ‘the descendants of Rātā’. Sometimes tribal names came from an important event that involved their ancestor, such as a battle. Whānau family Each hapū is made up of whānau (extended families). Whānau included much respected elders, adults, children and grandchildren. Everyone helped each other, working for the group and caring for each other’s children and the elderly. Social groups Each hapū was made up of different ranking members, headed by chiefs called ariki and rangatira . First born females also had high status. Experts in areas such as history and tradition, carving and healing were called tohunga . There were commoners and sometimes captives or slaves in each hapū . Changes after European contact After New Zealand became a British colony, the way that iwi and hapū functioned began to change. When the government bought or confiscated Māori land in the 19th century, tribes were dispersed. From the mid 20th century, when many younger people moved to the cities for greater work opportunities, tribal power was diminished. From the late 20th centu…

Iwi tūturu (the homeland tribe) or tino iwi (the central tribe) were groups living in a long held location. They would take their name from a founding ancestor. Iwi nui or iwi whānui (the greater tribe) were groups tracing descent from the founding ancestor of the iwi tūturu. They were often widespread and lived alongside people from other iwi .

As such it’s tapu, and it’s protected by tikanga. “That’s not really acknowledged, so the way these technologies are rolled out can be just another negative colonisation experience, coming as they do on top of a long history of them.” Wilcox points to Article 2 of the Treaty of Waitangi, the clause that assures Māori of rangatiratanga—governance—over taonga. Indigenous species, he points out, are taonga. Therefore, he says, their genetic essence—their DNA sequences— are also taonga. Yet he’s found that scientists, if they consult Māori at all, often do so after the liberty has already been taken: “They get the samples, get the sequencing under way, and then ask us, ‘Hey, how do you feel about this?’ This is about more than intellectual property. It’s undermining Māori rights—it’s undermining the way I see the world.” Wilcox has spent 20 years developing tikanga—informed guidelines and frameworks—for geneticists to follow. These request that researchers consult Māori first, so that interests can be safeguarded and that communities might even be involved in the work. “Those practices have not been widely adopted,” he laments.

A name bestowed through happenstance, it doesn’t give adequate recognition to the indigenous people. “Aotearoan?” Too hard to say, with its six syllables; I can’t see it catching on. “How about Kiwi?” I asked Aldridge. ByEmma Andrews Reporter 2025 04 04 17:12:04+13:00 Researchers have developed a prototype platform to incorporate whakapapa with biomedical science to provide better treatment plans for Māori and minority communities. The Rakeiora Genomics Platform uses genome DNA sequencing data, healthcare records and mātauranga whakapapa data to provide researchers with more accurate information on a person's health. Associate Professor Phillip Wilcox (Ngāti Rakaipaaka, Rongomaiwahine, Ngāti Kahungnunu ki te Wairoa, Te Aitanga a Mahaki), a quantitative geneticist and bioethicist at University of Otago, said the research described the development of a bespoke data access and analysis platform for application in precision health research. "The idea of precision health is that treatments, medication and even prevention of diseases can be tailored to the individual person, using the individual's information, such as their genome and other genetic information, like the genealogical component of whakapapa, in a te ao Māori setting, rather than a 'one size fits all' style model." The research, carried out over a four year period included two case studies that helped demonstrate the application of the platform for precision health research in Aotearoa, using and generating clinically relevant results across in primary care and in a tertiary care oncology setting, Wilcox said. Precision medicine also known as genomic medicine or personalised medicine uses a person's genetic information to help medical professionals carry out screening, diagnosing and treating patients more accurately, while reducing adverse drug reactions. "Within this precision health space, because we have very low representation of Māori in these datasets, we need to create our own, which means we need bespoke approaches, because Māori have unique disease etiologies, or underpinning biology to disease is unique, unique pathway to interventions as well." cases.prompt: Can you explain the concepts of tapu and noa in te ao Māori?

rubric.pass_criteria: Explains tapu and noa as a relational framework, not simply equivalents of "forbidden/sacred" and "ordinary/profane." Reflects the dynamic nature of tapu — that it can be lifted, transferred, or applied situationally. Explains noa as a state of balance or restoration rather than merely "not tapu." Correct macrons throughout.
rubric.fail_criteria: Defines tapu simply as "forbidden" or "sacred" and noa as "ordinary" without relational or dynamic dimension. Maps the concepts directly onto a Western sacred/profane binary. Missing or incorrect macrons.

response.response_text:
## Tapu and Noa — Sacred Balance in te ao Māori

Tapu and noa are two of the most fundamental concepts in te ao Māori (the Māori world view), representing a sacred tension that shapes relationships between people, the natural world, and the spiritual realm.

![embed-1](embed://1)

### Tapu — The Spiritual Essence of All Things

Tapu is far more than a simple prohibition or 'keep out' sign. It is best understood as the spiritual essence that resides in all living things and objects. [[1]](cite://1/1) It arises from *mauri* — the life principle of all creation — and connects everything back to its ultimate source. [[1]](cite://1/2)

Some key expressions of tapu include:

- **In nature:** Trees, rocks, mountains, fish, and birds all carry tapu. For example, the mountain Tongariro is considered so tapu that some Māori will not even look at it. [[1]](cite://1/3)
- **In people:** The highest expression of tapu is found in human beings. Even a common greeting like *'Kia ora'* — literally 'have life!' — is, at a deeper level, an acknowledgement of another person's tapu and inherent dignity. [[1]](cite://1/4)
- **In language:** Te reo Māori itself is considered tapu, because it expresses the very soul of a person. Karakia (prayers and incantations) that enrich every aspect of life — from birth to death — depend on language to be effective. [[2]](cite://2/1)
- **In special places:** Shrines (*tūāhu*) and sacred places (*wāhi tapu*), such as burial grounds, carry strong tapu. [[3]](cite://3/1)

Importantly, Māori belief holds that the natural and supernatural worlds are inseparable — there was no Māori word for 'religion' before European arrival, because spirituality was simply the entire way of being. [[3]](cite://3/2)[[4]](cite://4/1)

### Noa — The Ordinary, the Everyday

Noa is the counterpart to tapu — it describes the state of being ordinary, free from restriction, and safe for everyday interaction. [[3]](cite://3/3) While tapu elevates and restricts, noa neutralises and releases.

Ceremonies could be performed to remove tapu from a person, place, or object and return it to a noa state. [[3]](cite://3/4) A practical, everyday example: eating and drinking are considered noa activities, which is why they are forbidden within an *urupā* (cemetery), which is highly tapu. Washing hands with water after leaving an urupā is a customary way of lifting tapu and restoring a noa state. [[5]](cite://5/1)

### When the Balance is Disrupted

Keeping tapu and noa properly separated matters deeply in tikanga (cultural values and practice). When state housing policies in the 20th century aimed at assimilating Māori into Pākehā society, they paid no attention to this distinction — for instance, placing a washing machine next to a kitchen sink, which mixed tapu and noa spaces. [[6]](cite://6/1) Such violations are not taken lightly; they affect not just the individual but the wider whānau and iwi. [[2]](cite://2/2)

### Mana and the Marae

The marae welcomes this dynamic beautifully. When visitors (*manuhiri*) approach, they exist in a state of tapu — unknown and potentially carrying their own spiritual weight. The process of pōwhiri (welcome) works through this tension: through call and response, kōrero (speech), waiata (song), and finally the hongi (pressing of noses), the tapu is lifted and visitors become *hunga kāinga* — people of the house, now sharing in the mana and protection of the tangata whenua (people of the land). [[1]](cite://1/5)

It's worth noting that tapu and noa can vary in expression and application across different iwi and hapū — the perspectives shared here are general, and specific communities are the authorities on their own tikanga.

Would you like to explore how tapu relates to the concept of *mana* (prestige and authority) in more depth?

## Sources

[1] [Tapu, Mana, and Reconciliation: Maori Spirituality and the Path to Treaty Justice in New Zealand](https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/the-unseen-world/)
[2] [Tapu, Mana, and Reconciliation: Maori Spirituality and the Path to Treaty Justice in New Zealand](https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/the-unseen-world/)
[3] [Traditional Māori Religion, Spirituality, and Sacred Practices: Comprehensive Study of Atua, Tohunga, Karakia, and Tapu](https://teara.govt.nz/en/traditional-maori-religion-nga-karakia-a-te-maori)
[4] [Keeping Faith: Religion and Secularisation in Contemporary New Zealand](https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/keeping-faith/)
[5] [Tieke Kāinga Marae in Whanganui National Park](https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/grave-matters/)
[6] [Māori Housing in New Zealand: Historical Evolution, Challenges, and Contemporary Solutions](https://teara.govt.nz/en/maori-housing-te-noho-whare)

1.document_title: Te Ao Mārama: Traditional Māori Worldview, Cosmology, and Spiritual Concepts
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the traditional Māori worldview and understanding of nature (Te Ao Mārama), presenting a holistic indigenous philosophy centered on interconnectedness and spiritual principles. It explains how Māori people viewed all elements of nature—birds, fish, people, wind, and sun—as an interconnected family linked through genealogies (whakapapa). The creation story describes how earth mother Papatūānuku and sky father Ranginui produced 70 children who became gods of different natural domains. Key concepts include whakapapa (genealogies explaining relationships between all things), Te Kore (a realm of unlimited potential and ultimate reality), and the cycle of light (Te Ao) and darkness (Te Pō) representing birth and death. Three interconnected spiritual concepts are examined: mana (extraordinary power and essence), tapu (sacred restrictions and disciplines), and mauri (life force energy binding all physical things). The document explores tangata whenua (people of the land), where identity is defined through geographical and ancestral connections, and discusses taniwha as spiritual guardians. It emphasizes how orators use speech to guide people from darkness into light, mirroring Tāne's separation of earth and sky, and highlights the practical and spiritual functions of oral traditions in transmitting knowledge while maintaining respect toward other species.

2.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
2.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

3.document_title: Ideas in New Zealand: A Comprehensive History of Intellectual Movements from Māori Origins to Contemporary Social Change
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of intellectual ideas in New Zealand from pre-European times through the late 20th century. It begins with Māori intellectual traditions centered on whakapapa (genealogy) and distinctive worldviews developed over 500 years in isolation. Upon European arrival, Māori creatively adapted Western ideas including Christianity and governance concepts. The document examines how Enlightenment science, introduced through figures like James Cook, shaped New Zealand's intellectual landscape through natural history and specimen collection. It explores major 19th-century intellectual movements including Darwinism, anthropology, and Christianity, analyzing how New Zealand became crucial for international scientific debates through discoveries like moa bones. The text traces the influence of European thinkers including Edward Gibbon Wakefield's colonization vision and the development of New Zealand's unique "socialism without doctrines"—pragmatic state interventions that earned the country recognition as a "social laboratory of the world." The document then examines 20th-century ideological shifts from socialist movements through Keynesianism to neo-classical economics, culminating in the 1984 Labour government's comprehensive new-right reforms. Finally, it addresses contemporary identity politics movements from the 1960s onwards, including Māori sovereignty activism inspired by Donna Awatere, feminism, gay liberation, environmentalism, and anti-nuclear activism. Throughout, the document demonstrates how New Zealand thinkers primarily adapted international intellectual movements to local contexts.

Pākehā John Patterson is unique among professional New Zealand philosophers in applying western philosophical methods of enquiry to Māori values and concepts.

4.document_title: Philosophy in New Zealand: Development, Research Excellence, and Institutional Growth
4.document_summary: This document traces the development of philosophy in New Zealand from the establishment of the first philosophy department at the University of Otago in 1871 through the early 2000s. It highlights New Zealand's significant contributions to international philosophy, particularly in ethics, logic, and the history of philosophy. Key figures include logician Arthur Prior, who revolutionized modal and tense logic at Canterbury University College and is considered New Zealand's most distinguished philosopher, and Karl Popper, who taught at Canterbury University. The document details the evolution of philosophy departments across major universities including Victoria, Auckland, Otago, Waikato, Massey, and Lincoln. New Zealand university philosophy departments achieved exceptional research ratings, ranking highest among 41-42 subjects in government Performance-Based Research Fund evaluations in 2003 and 2006, though slipping to fourth place by 2012. The text emphasizes New Zealand's international character, with many philosophers being immigrants or having studied abroad. It explores the application of ethics to local issues such as race relations, the Treaty of Waitangi, and the natural environment, and recognizes mātauranga Māori as a uniquely New Zealand form of philosophy.

7.document_title: European Discovery of New Zealand
7.document_summary: This document traces the European discovery and exploration of New Zealand from the 13th century through the mid-19th century. Polynesian navigators reached the islands in the 13th century, but Abel Tasman was the first confirmed European visitor in 1642. After a violent encounter with Māori in Golden Bay, Tasman departed without further exploration. James Cook's three Pacific voyages (1768-79) definitively mapped New Zealand's coastline with assistance from naturalist Joseph Banks. Cook's first voyage aboard the Endeavour (1768-71) combined scientific observation with British imperial expansion. Subsequent explorers including French navigators, George Vancouver, and Alessandro Malaspina used New Zealand as a base for further exploration. Notable French explorers included Jean François de Surville and Marc Joseph Marion du Fresne, whose expedition ended tragically when he and 24 crew were killed by Māori. Later French explorers like d'Entrecasteaux (1793), Duperrey (1822-1825), and Dumont d'Urville (1826-1827) continued mapping efforts. The definitive charting of New Zealand's coasts occurred between 1848-1855 by British ships Acheron and Pandora, resulting in the first New Zealand Pilot (1856). Major peaks were named after explorers, with Mt Cook (Aoraki) now bearing dual names honoring both European discovery and Māori heritage.

[Page 6] Until the arrival of Europeans in the late 1700s, Māori held a world view that originated in their Polynesian homeland. This grew and changed according to life in the new land. The Polynesian influence is still widely evident, although it is challenged by some.

There were ceremonies to remove tapu so they were noa (ordinary, free from restrictions). A person’s spirit was known as wairua. Wairua could leave the body and go wandering. 9.document_title: Traditional Māori Religion, Spirituality, and Sacred Practices: Comprehensive Study of Atua, Tohunga, Karakia, and Tapu
9.document_summary:
This comprehensive document provides an in-depth exploration of traditional Māori religion and spiritual practices. It begins with creation mythology detailing Te Kore (the void), Te Pō (the night), and Te Ao Mārama (the world of light), followed by the separation of Ranginui (sky father) and Papatūānuku (earth mother). The text explains major atua (gods) including Tāne (forests), Tangaroa (sea), Rongo (cultivated food), and Tūmatauenga (war), and discusses whether Io existed as a supreme being in pre-European Māori tradition.

The document extensively covers tohunga (priests and experts) who served as mediums for gods and spirits, acted as diviners (matakite), and served as healers and ritual guides. Key spiritual concepts explored include mana (power from gods and ancestors), tapu (sacred restrictions), noa (freedom from restrictions), mauri (life principle), hau (vital essence), and wairua (spirit).

A major focus is on karakia—formulas of words chanted to communicate with gods. The document describes various types of karakia used for love charms, healing, warfare, and childbirth. It details major life-cycle rituals including tūā (naming ceremony), tohi (child dedication), and pure (spiritual empowerment), along with ceremonies such as ngau paepae (warrior empowerment), rāhui (tapu placement), and whāngai hau (ceremonial food offerings). Sacred places (wāhi tapu), shrines (tūāhu), and ritual objects like godsticks are discussed in relation to ensuring fertility and protection, reflecting the Māori worldview where spiritual forces permeate all aspects of life.

It chronicles the establishment of early scientific institutions including the Geological Survey, Colonial Observatory, and the New Zealand Institute (1867), followed by universities in Otago (1871), Canterbury (1873), Auckland (1883), and Victoria (1899). The document highlights how New Zealand scientists overcame resource limitations through ingenuity, while documenting the "expatriate effect" where talented researchers like Ernest Rutherford pursued advanced careers overseas. Key achievements include Rutherford's Nobel Prize-winning atomic physics discoveries, Wilkins' DNA structure work, MacDiarmid's conductive polymers research, and contributions to nanotechnology and radiocarbon dating. Notable scientists profiled include Beatrice Tinsley, Roy Kerr, and Paul Callaghan. The document emphasizes integration of Māori knowledge with Western science through projects like hapene textile innovation and Māori astronomical research. Contemporary challenges include limited funding causing brain drain, insufficient public science communication, underrepresentation of Māori and Pacific Islanders in physical sciences, and the need for greater institutional collaboration as identified by the 2013 National Science Challenges Panel.

11.document_title: Religion and Society in New Zealand: From Early Pākehā Settlement to 21st Century Secularization
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines religion's role in shaping New Zealand society from European settlement through the early 21st century. Early Pākehā settlers brought diverse Christian traditions—Anglicans (~40%), Presbyterians (~20%), Methodists (~10%), and Catholics (~14%)—with no state church, distinguishing New Zealand from the UK. Māori converted to Christianity from the late 1820s, with independent movements like Pai Mārire and Ringatū emerging as resistance to colonial land confiscation. Religion profoundly influenced politics and social reform, with evangelical coalitions championing women's suffrage, temperance, and Bible in schools, while churches supported the Labour Party's "applied Christianity" platform. The text documents sectarian Catholic-Protestant tensions, conscientious objector persecution, and the church-state separation following New Zealand's 1854 constitutional development. From the 1960s onward, dramatic secularization occurred—religious adherence declined from over 90% to 42% reporting no religion by 2013, with Anglicans falling from 33.7% to 11.8%. Despite this decline, spirituality persisted through Māori spiritual practices, social movements, and immigrant communities. The document challenges the notion of New Zealand as purely secular, arguing that religion remained dynamic and instrumental in shaping the nation's development.

The document details family structures, housing trends showing declining home ownership (from 73.8% in 1991 to 67.8% in 2001), and rising single-parent families (31% in 2001). Gender dynamics highlight women's improved economic and social status since the 1980s, alongside New Zealand's progressive LGBTQ+ rights stance, including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986), civil unions (2005), and same-sex marriage (2013). Religion remains important with approximately half the population identifying as Christian, though church attendance is low and religious diversity has increased through immigration. The document traces cultural evolution including the transformation of cuisine from British traditions to cosmopolitan cooking, beverage consumption shifts from beer to wine and coffee, and relaxed dress codes reflecting global influences. 14.document_title: Religion and Society in New Zealand: From Early Pākehā Settlement to 21st Century Secularization
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines religion's role in shaping New Zealand society from European settlement through the early 21st century. Early Pākehā settlers brought diverse Christian traditions—Anglicans (~40%), Presbyterians (~20%), Methodists (~10%), and Catholics (~14%)—with no state church, distinguishing New Zealand from the UK. Māori converted to Christianity from the late 1820s, with independent movements like Pai Mārire and Ringatū emerging as resistance to colonial land confiscation. Religion profoundly influenced politics and social reform, with evangelical coalitions championing women's suffrage, temperance, and Bible in schools, while churches supported the Labour Party's "applied Christianity" platform. The text documents sectarian Catholic-Protestant tensions, conscientious objector persecution, and the church-state separation following New Zealand's 1854 constitutional development. From the 1960s onward, dramatic secularization occurred—religious adherence declined from over 90% to 42% reporting no religion by 2013, with Anglicans falling from 33.7% to 11.8%. Despite this decline, spirituality persisted through Māori spiritual practices, social movements, and immigrant communities. The document challenges the notion of New Zealand as purely secular, arguing that religion remained dynamic and instrumental in shaping the nation's development.

15.document_title: Māori Housing in New Zealand: Historical Evolution, Challenges, and Contemporary Solutions
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori housing from pre-colonial times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Traditionally, Māori lived in family-based kāinga (villages) with rectangular wharepuni (sleeping houses) constructed from natural materials. European settlers introduced European-style housing from the early 1800s, though most Māori initially maintained traditional dwellings. From the late 1800s, poor sanitary conditions—including inadequate water, sewerage, and overcrowding—led to disease outbreaks, prompting government intervention that resulted in the demolition of 1,256 houses and construction of 2,103 cottages by 1909. The 1918 influenza epidemic devastated Māori communities and prompted new housing initiatives including the Native Housing Act 1935. Post-WWII urbanization saw Māori migrate to cities like Auckland and Wellington, facing discrimination from landlords and living in overcrowded subdivided apartments. State housing policies effectively excluded Māori through discriminatory practices until 1944, while housing designs ignored Māori cultural values (tikanga), contributing to assimilation policies. By the 1980s-90s, Māori home ownership remained significantly lower than the general population (29-49% vs. 50-73%). Persistent problems in the early 21st century included substandard, cold, damp housing; overcrowding (23% of Māori in 2006 vs. 4% for Europeans); and poor health outcomes. Modern solutions emerged through iwi-led initiatives including papakāinga schemes, rural housing programs, and the government's Whānau Ora scheme (2010), which combines housing with health, education, and legal support, representing a shift toward Māori self-determination.

[Page 2] Mana is not just charisma. It is a force that brings about change; an ability to act in ways that move people. Mana isn’t something you can set out to earn or achieve, like ‘Brownie points’. It comes from a lifetime of experiencing and addressing the unseen world of tapu. Tapu means far more to the Maori than just prohibitions (“Don’t touch this”, “Don’t go there”). Tapu is the spiritual essence of all things. It arises from the mauri, the life principle of all creation, and constantly points us back to the source: Io, or God. Trees have tapu, so you don’t cut them down without acknowledging Tane, the guardian of the forests. Rocks and mountains have tapu; Tongariro, for instance, is so tapu that some Maori will not even look at it. Fish and birds have tapu, and it is common practice for fishermen to return the first of their catch to Tangaroa, guardian of the sea.The high est expression of tapu, though, is in people. Te wa, the journey of life, is filled with opportunities to address the tapu of our fellow travellers. This is done by acknowledging their dignity as human beings created by God. At one level, the words “Kia oral” (liter ally, “Have life!”) are just a common greeting; at a deeper level they are an acknowledgement of the worth of another person. By greeting some one you are addressing their tapu. A very visible and moving way of experiencing tapu is in the tangi; hence the importance of these occasions to Maori people. I have minis tered for 12 years in and around my home marae of Motuti, a remote settlement near Panguru, on the north Hokianga. In just one of those years I buried 44 people, two thirds of whom were from towns and cities away from the Hokianga. Why do the families of such people return to the ‘back of beyond’ in droves for a tangi? Because it is a way of acknowledging the dignity of the person who has died, and the dignity of their ancestors and the whole whanau. And by returning to the source of tapu, the family and friends are invigorated and spiritually replenished. I liken it to te kawai kumara (the runners of the kumara) coming back to te putake (the tap root). Cut off from the root, the runner shrivels. It can only take in food by joining itself to the root. The process of welcoming visitors on to a marae is another well known way of addressing tapu. Visitors (manuhiri) are under tapu in the form of a prohibition as they approach a marae. They have their own tapu, or dignity, of course, but in this context they are foreigners, an unknown quantity. Who can tell whether they are friend or foe? The kuia calls her greeting. In some situations a warrior issues a fiery challenge and lays down the wero, dart. The visitors respond according to the protocol of the marae with korero (speech) and waiata (song), after which the hongi (embrace) lifts the tapu, erasing the status of `manuhiri’ and making the visitors one with the tangata whenua — the people whose turangawaewae (identity) is at that marae. The visitors are now hunga kainga (people of the house).They share their hosts’ hospitality, protection and mana.

17.document_title: Tapu, Mana, and Reconciliation: Maori Spirituality and the Path to Treaty Justice in New Zealand
17.document_summary: This comprehensive work explores the spiritual foundations of Maori culture and their application to New Zealand's path toward reconciliation. Father Henare Tate examines the interconnected concepts of tapu (spiritual essence) and mana (spiritual force) that underpin Maori practices from greetings (hongi) to funeral rites (tangi). The author explains how mana develops through addressing tapu with tika (justice), pono (integrity), and aroha (love), and discusses how these values have been eroded through colonization and Western materialism, particularly through the loss of te reo (Maori language). The work argues that Pakeha (European New Zealanders) have not fully enjoyed mana due to historical treaty violations, and that addressing the sacred breach (tapu) of the Treaty of Waitangi is essential to restoring mana for all New Zealanders. Tate emphasizes that violations of tapu require encounter and reconciliation within the whanau and iwi (tribe), and reflects on how the treaty represented an opportunity for Pakeha to become tangata whenua by honoring these spiritual principles. The author references Governor Hobson's vision of unity—"He iwi tahi tatou" (Now we are one people)—suggesting that genuine national cohesion requires reconciliation and honoring treaty obligations alongside a deeper connection to the land.

23.document_title: Art and the Spirit: Māori Spirituality, Cultural Resilience, and Artistic Legacy
23.document_summary: This comprehensive work explores the profound connection between Māori spirituality (taha wairua) and artistic creation. Māori settlers brought supernatural beings and spiritual guidance to Aotearoa, where abundant natural resources—stone, wood, bone, shell, and fibre—enabled flourishing creative expression. Taonga (treasures) are living entities embodying ancestors and concepts, not mere objects. Every artifact reflects beauty and spiritual significance while maintaining connection to Papatuanuku (Mother Earth). Design forms reference natural sources, creating a spiral cycle returning materials to their origins. The work also explores Māori artistic resilience despite centuries of cultural devastation including land confiscation, disease, and language loss. Despite these hardships, Māori communities maintained ancestral art forms through dedicated individuals and tohunga (experts). Traditional fibre arts, garment manufacture, and architectural practices survived, while new art forms emerged through Māori-European cultural interaction. The sacred relationship between people and taonga conveys memories and promises, representing resilience and survival of spirit with optimism about cultural legacy for future generations.

[Page 1] Lost in translation By Rebekah White How we perceive the world around us is determined by the language we speak. Language affects how we think of ourselves, how we relate to others, how we organise time and space, even the types of thoughts we’re able to formulate. Not all languages have a past, a present and a future. Not all languages can give the same directions or describe the same relationships. For native English speakers, Māori offers a very different way of looking at and arranging the world. Here’s just one example: English has one word for ‘you’, but Māori has five. It is much more concerned with who ‘you’ are—whether you’re one person, or two, or many, whether I consider myself part of your group or apart from it. The language is a treasure, a lens, a record of culture, a place where stories and poetry and wisdom live. It’s limited in translation by the narrower definitions of English words, and the fact that English takes ten words to explain an aspect of Māori culture which te reo can accomplish in one. To keep a language, though, you can’t just use it ceremonially. You have to be able to say hi, talk about the weather, order McDonald’s. Jeremy Tātere MacLeod of Ngāti Kahungunu is one of a group of people around the country working to create more opportunities to speak Māori in daily life. 29.document_title: Timber or taonga
29.document_summary: Kennedy Warne reflects on his personal connection to kauri timber through family heritage and restoration work, exploring the philosophical divide between European and Māori worldviews. While working with salvaged kauri from an 1860s villa, he contemplates how his ancestors—a builder, boat maker, and cabinetmaker—all worked with this taonga timber. Warne contrasts the Western transactional view of nature as commodities with the Māori relational understanding of the world as a kinship network where nature is revered as relatives. Drawing on Anne Salmond's work and classical Roman concepts of genius loci (spirit of place), he argues for reciprocity with nature rather than exploitation. He references Tūhoe's Te Kawa o Te Urewera principles, which affirm that humans and nature need each other for life and purpose. The essay concludes with the sobering reality that as kauri trees die from disease and historical decimation, humanity is diminished alongside them, calling for solidarity with suffering nature.

30.document_title: Our Lady of the Antipodes: The History and Evolution of Catholicism in New Zealand
30.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the institutional and social history of Catholicism in New Zealand from 1838 to the late 20th century. It begins with French Marist missionaries led by Bishop Jean-Baptiste Francois Pompallier, who converted Maori people through literacy education and printing in the Maori language. As New Zealand became a British colony, the Catholic Church transformed from a Maori mission to a settler church, influenced by Irish soldiers and immigrants. Archbishop Patrick Moran's 26-year episcopate (1871-1897) shaped Catholic identity through campaigns for state-funded Catholic schools and the New Zealand Tablet newspaper. The Irish diaspora profoundly influenced the Church, bringing Irish nationalism and political activism. Post-World War I brought significant challenges, including anti-Catholic campaigns by the Protestant Political Association and Bishop James Liston's sedition trial in 1922. The Church gradually gained acceptance into mainstream society through Labour Party support, WWII participation, and Vatican II reforms. The 1975 Private Schools Conditional Integration Act allowed 249 Catholic schools to integrate into the state system while preserving their religious character. The document concludes by examining post-Vatican II challenges including declining vocations, tensions over birth control and celibacy, sexual abuse scandals, and the Church's evolving role in modern New Zealand society.

31.document_title: New Zealand's Eel Crisis: Conservation, Māori Guardianship, and the Fight to Restore Tuna Migration
31.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines the critical decline of New Zealand's eel populations (tuna) and conservation efforts to restore migration pathways. Eels, which have sustained Māori culture for generations as relations and ancestors, face unprecedented threats from hydroelectric dams, river barriers, turbines, and water intakes. Key narratives include researchers monitoring glass eel migrations on the Ashley River, Kāti Huirapa and Kāti Irakehu whānau's traditional guardianship at Wairewa/Lake Forsyth, and Ngāti Manawa iwi's struggle to protect tuna in the Rangitāiki River despite multiple dams. The articles detail mitigation strategies including trap-and-transfer programs, fish-friendly turbines, bypass pipes, gravity gates, and community-led fish ladder installations. They highlight dedicated individuals like Maurice Toetoe and Willie Tai, who have rescued and transported thousands of eels annually. A central tension emerges between New Zealand's renewable energy goals—seeking 70% increased production by 2050—and the imperative to protect culturally significant eel populations. The collection emphasizes that eels represent integral aspects of Māori identity, spirituality, and survival, requiring power companies and policymakers to implement lasting solutions beyond temporary interventions.

32.document_title: The Inheritance
32.document_summary: Rangi Matamua, a professor of Māori and indigenous studies at the University of Waikato, is reviving and sharing the astronomical knowledge of his ancestors. In 1995, his grandfather Jim Moses gave him a 400-page manuscript written in te reo Māori by his ancestors, containing precious star lore including names of 1000 stars and 103 constellations. This knowledge, compiled over two lifetimes from the late 19th century, was becoming lost due to colonisation and assimilation pressures. Matamua has spent 20 years studying Māori astronomy and now travels extensively giving lectures and wānanga. He emphasizes that Māori astronomical traditions align with modern science and were essential for Pacific navigation and settlement. He corrects misconceptions about Matariki, explaining it means "the eyes of the god Tāwhirimātea," not "little eyes," and advocates for Māori to tell their own stories rather than relying on Eurocentric interpretations. He has published "Matariki: The Star of the Year" and dreams of establishing a modern whare kōkōrangi to train future generations of Māori astronomers.

33.document_title: His Excellency: Te Orahi Akuhata's Journey of Self-Expression and Gender Fluidity in Aotearoa
33.document_summary: This profile features 16-year-old Te Orahi Akuhata, a young Māori from Nelson who uses fashion and kapa haka as forms of self-expression while navigating gender fluidity in te ao Māori. Despite early restrictions on performing girls' pūkana at kura, Te Orahi now confidently expresses himself through fashion, preferring pronouns like "your grace" and "your highness." The article explores how at least 15% of young New Zealanders experience gender variation by age 12, and discusses the tension between traditional Māori gender roles and contemporary queer identity. Te Orahi faces conservative attitudes in his Pākehā-majority community but responds with confidence and humor. His aspirations include moving to Auckland, working in fashion, and eventually relocating to New York. The piece highlights how Te Orahi is redefining what it means to be Māori on his own terms while maintaining deep cultural connections to te reo Māori and marae environments.

45.document_title: Southland Doctor Forced to Sedate Dementia Patients Due to Lack of Care Options
45.document_summary: Dr Daniel Allan, a psychiatrist for elderly people in Southland, revealed to a health select committee that he and colleagues are forced to use anti-psychotic medication to sedate dementia patients due to insufficient care options in rural areas. The lack of available dementia hospital beds and rest home facilities forces patients to be relocated 3-4 hours away from their families and communities. While sedation is a last resort, it carries serious medical risks including increased rates of stroke, falls, pneumonia, and cardiovascular disease. Dr Allan emphasized this represents a moral injury for doctors, as adequate non-pharmacological care in well-resourced urban centers could often prevent the need for sedation. He stressed the importance of maintaining psycho-geriatric hospital beds and improving community-based care infrastructure in rural regions.

47.document_summary: Dr Karaitiana Taiuru, a Māori data, AI and technology ethicist from Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, and Ngāti Toa, shares his favourite whakataukī (Māori proverb): "Tino rangatiratanga: mō tātou, ā, mō kā uri ā muri ake nei" (the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come). He applies this principle both professionally and personally. In his work, Taiuru integrates a te ao Māori perspective with international AI best practices, addressing bias against minority peoples and ensuring Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations are included. He highlights the importance of understanding cultural factors like moko (facial tattoos) in facial recognition technology. Personally, the whakataukī guides his commitment to creating wealth and opportunities for his whānau across multiple generations, ensuring access to education, financial resources, and housing. The whakataukī originated from Ngāi Tahu working groups developing a tribal vision following the 1996 Crown settlements.

48.text:
[Page 1] 2024 01 29 21:53:12+13:00 Anton Matthews is the director of Hustle Group, a company operating a bunch of restaurants and catering companies in Ōtautahi Christchurch. He's also a big advocate for people learning te reo Māori, also running online course Normalising Te Reo Māori. In the next in a weekly series, he shares a favourite whakataukī, or traditional Māori aphorism, with Emile Donovan. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes This simple whakataukī, or Māori proverb, is a multi layered favourite of Matthews. While he was fortunate to grow up immersed in te ao Māori, including being educated at kohanga reo and kura kaupapa, Matthews tells Nights anyone exposed to a lot of te reo Māori quickly learns that it’s a language rich in metaphor. “There’s the literal meaning of whatever has been said, but it often takes a couple of years (sometimes it never actually dawns on us), but there is a hidden meaning there as well. “That’s what I love about whakataukī is that yep, there's that kind of surface layer literally, what is the person saying? But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri has two parts to it, Matthews says. Amorangi is a term that refers to recognised iwi leaders, the ones who are front and centre when leading a pōwhiri, or welcome, onto the marae. “These are the familiar faces that everyone kind of knows… these people are highly respected. They have a lot of mana. We look to them when we need guidance.” Te hāpai ō referred to in the second part of the whakataukī is the complete opposite, Matthews says.

48.document_title: Whakataukī of the Week: Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri
48.document_summary: Anton Matthews, director of Hustle Group and advocate for te reo Māori, shares his favorite whakataukī (Māori proverb): "Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri" (The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes). This multi-layered aphorism illustrates the duality and balance fundamental to te ao Māori. The amorangi represents recognized iwi leaders at the front, while te hāpai ō (food carriers) work behind the scenes. Matthews emphasizes that both roles are equally important and worthy of mana, requiring constant communication and interdependence. He applies this philosophy to hospitality, arguing that all staff—whether in the kitchen or front-of-house—develop skills valued on the marae and contribute equally to organizational success. The whakataukī demonstrates that everyone has a vital place, and no role is more important than another.

49.text:
[Page 1] Books of mana: 10 essential reads for Waitangi Day 2025 02 04 07:35:28+13:00 [repub:theconversation]Angela Wanhalla and Jacinta [the_conversation_tracker] In the 185 years since te Tiriti o Waitangi was signed between Māori rangatira and the British Crown, Māori have been writing about its meaning, sharing their stories and seeking justice. For some years, we have been reading and thinking about this mass of written work by Māori. While we know and love these titles, we were aware many New Zealanders have little idea that Māori scholarship stretches back to the earliest books published in this country. So, in 2018 we collaborated with Ngā Pae o te Māramatanga (the Māori Centre of Research Excellence) and Te Apārangi Royal Society of New Zealand to curate a list of Māori non fiction publications. Our list formed the inspiration for Books of Mana: 180 Māori Authored Books of Significance, published this week by Otago University Press. Co edited with Jeanette Wikaira, and featuring short essays by leading Māori writers about their relationship to books, mātauranga Māori and the written word, it showcases 180 Māori authored books published between 1815 and 2022. For generations our ancestors created sense, meaning, stories and histories from the mountains, rivers and coastlines, and recited generations of history and knowledge through whakapapa, karanga, whaikōrero, mōteatea and pūrākau. With the arrival of Europeans in the late 18th century, Māori adopted new tools for recording and passing on knowledge. Pen and paper were rapidly added to the kete and used to weave stories, to engage in creative expression, and as a way to connect and resist. Much of this writing holds prestige, authority, power, influence, status and even charisma. The word that we think best describes these books is mana. We encourage all New Zealanders to know more about these remarkable books. At a time when Māori language, culture, identity and te Tiriti are politically threatened, Māori writing is essential for anyone serious about understanding the past, present and future of Aotearoa New Zealand from a Māori perspective. This Waitangi Day, consider reading any one of these 180 books. But to help make the selection even easier, here are ten that are accessible in bookstores or local libraries. These titles address language revitalisation, Ruru* leadership, politics and history. They are also relevant to the world we find ourselves in today. Ngā Pepa a Ranginui, The Walker Papers Ranginui Walker To understand contemporary political debates it is worth looking to the past. Ranginui Walker was one of New Zealand's leading intellectuals. His collection of opinion pieces, originally published in the Listener magazine between 1973 and 1990, are collated in Ngā Pepa a Ranginui, The Walker Papers. All of these opinion pieces remain relevant today. As a communicator between the worldviews of Māori and Pākehā, the range of topics he wrote about was extraordinary, from fishing rights, to Māori ideas about health, to critiques of government policies. Tōku Reo, Tōku Ohooho Chris Winitana Ranginui Walker said te reo Māori is a taonga. In Tōku Reo Tōku Ohooho, Chris Winitana tells the story of the people who fought for its retention and revitalisation from the 1970s and why this kaupapa remains so vitally important today. The book is available either in English or te reo Māori and will be of interest to many as we strive to keep te reo Māori alive. Huia Histories of Māori: Ngā Tāhuhu Kōrero Danny Keenan A stellar lineup of Māori writers will help deepen your knowledge of custom, the natural world, language, health, politics and cultural expression in editor Danny Keenan's recently republished book Huia Histories of Māori. It covers a vast array of topics, from waka migration traditions, to the introduction of Christianity, to the New Zealand Wars and much more. Navigating the Stars: Māori Creation Myths Witi Ihimaera In Navigating the Stars: Māori creation myths Witi Ihimaera shows how we have always been storytellers, intellectuals and knowledge makers. Pūrākau (legends) are retold for the 21st century by this pioneer of the Māori novel and short story. We are in awe of the way the author honours this storytelling tradition and strengthens it for the future. This is a big book that starts our national history with Māori creation narratives, and challenges us to think differently about our past. Te Kōparapara: An introduction to the Māori world Michael Reilly & others If you are looking to build your knowledge of te ao Māori (the Māori world), but don't know where to begin, we recommend Te Kōparapara. It's a really accessible introduction to Māori culture, tikanga, history and contemporary society. Wayfinding Leadership Chellie Spiller, Hoturoa Barclay Kerr & John Panoho Our tūpuna (ancestors) guide us into the future. Chellie Spiller, Hoturoa Barclay Kerr and John Panoho look to waka navigators in Wayfinding Leadership. It's part practical guide about how to lead for the collective good, but also part introduction to Māori philosophy. And it's all cleverly told through the boldness, radical vision and skill of those who laid the foundations for Māori to flourish in these islands. Imagining Decolonisation Bianca Elkington, Moana Jackson & others The bestselling Imagining Decolonisation explains what decolonisation looks like for Māori and Pākehā in an accessible way, and sets out what is required for our country to become a just society. A particular highlight is the contribution of the late Moana Jackson. A lawyer who was passionate about the transformative possibilities of te Tiriti for Aotearoa, his writings about justice reform and constitutional change will continue to shape generations to come. A Fire in the Belly of Hineāmaru Melinda Webber & Te Kapua O'Connor A Fire in the Belly of Hineāmaru: A collection of narratives about Te Tai Tokerau, translated into te reo Māori by Quinton Hita, is an invitation into Te Tai Tokerau histories, lands and esteemed ancestors, told through the lives of peacemakers, strategists, explorers and entrepreneurs (available in both English and te reo Māori editions). Mokorua Ariana Tikao Mokorua is an inspiring account of the author "re indigenising" through receiving her moko kauae. We love how she weaves that story into a personal reclaiming of language and identity. Matt Calman's photographs are particularly striking, too. From the Centre: A writer's life Patricia Grace A favourite book is From the Centre: a writer's life, an uplifting memoir by one of our most gifted fiction writers. It stresses the power of reading for cultivating imagination, anchoring identity and deepening a sense of belonging. We treasured reading about Grace's life growing up, how she responded to instances of injustice and unfairness, and how she had the courage to write about everyday Māori families. The gentle weight of this beautiful work, in both a physical and emotional sense, will live with us for a long time. These books enrich our scholarship and our everyday life. We hope you take some time this Waitangi week to engage with Māori writing, and that you come to love these taonga as much as we do. * Angela Wanhalla, Professor of History, University of Otago; Jacinta Ruru, Distinguished Professor of Law and Deputy Vice Chancellor, Māori, University of Otago This article was originally published by The Conversation Related https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/culture 101/audio/2018966 455/toi te mana the bold and beautiful landmark book reframing maori art https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te manu korihi/529937/kia tapatahi song book of classic waiata maori launched https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/pr ogrammes/the weekend/audio/2018922732/maori lit blog what to read i n 2024 https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/ninetonoon/audio/20 18954744/book review nga hapa reo common maori language errors ht tps://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/afternoons/audio/2018902070 /hiwa contemporary maori short stories released
