3.document_title: Traditional Māori Games, Sports, and Cultural Practices: A Comprehensive Overview
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the rich heritage of traditional Māori games, sports, and cultural practices (ngā tākaro), which were integral to Māori society as entertainment, education, ritual practices, and community bonding. The document covers athletics including wrestling (mamau), boxing (mekemeke), running (omaoma), and jumping (pekepeke); water sports encompassing swimming (kauhoe), diving (kōkiri), surfing (whakaheke ngaru), and canoe racing (whakatere waka); physical games such as swings (moari, tārere), pīoi, piu, and hiding games; stick and string games including tī rākau and whai; word and hand games (kai, tī ringaringa); and other pastimes like kite-flying, puppet manipulation, spinning tops, and stilts. The document includes cultural narratives such as Te Houtaewa's legendary run and Hinepoupou's swim, along with board games like Mū tōrere. It explains mythological origins through figures like Miru and Raukatauri, and describes the role of these activities in community gatherings and warrior training. The document chronicles the suppression of these traditions by missionaries from the 1820s, leading to their decline through the 19th century. However, since the mid-20th century, there has been a significant revival of traditional games, with modern adaptations like fire poi and glow poi gaining international recognition, and team sports such as kī-o-Rahi and tapuae becoming increasingly popular. Contemporary developments include waka ama, which emerged in the mid-1980s and gained international prominence following the 1990 International Polynesian Canoe Federation World Sprints Championship.

4.text:
[Page 1] Welcome and hospitality Māori rituals for greeting visitors date from before Europeans arrived in New Zealand, and had a practical function. The women of a settlement would call out to approaching strangers, asking them to identify themselves and their intentions. Warriors would then challenge them in the wero ceremony. After this, once it was known that the visitors came in peace, they could enter and were welcomed and fed. Today the rituals include the karanga (call), wero , whaikōrero (speeches) and hongi (pressing of noses). The manuhiri (visitors) are then invited to eat and drink with their hosts. They can respond by giving a koha in the past, a gift of food or precious objects, but today usually money. Kinship, families and marae Kin relationships are very important and underpin many customs. Speeches often begin with the speaker’s whakapapa (genealogy), which may relate to the group addressed or the issue discussed. Most Māori, even if they live in the city, retain links with their tribal area and return there for events. Hapū (sub tribes) have rights over particular marae , and are known as tangata whenua (people of the land) of those marae . They can host gatherings, weddings and funerals, and must maintain the marae and its reputation. Kaumātua and kuia (male and female elders) have an honoured place in Māori communities. Tangi and birth In Māori tradition, when someone dies, their spirit leaves their body and travels to a sacred place at the northern tip of New Zealand. Their whānau (family) gathers at a tangihanga to be supported by the wider whānau and community. Tangi are usually held on the marae most closely associated with the deceased. Mourners stay with the family and the tūpāpaku (corpse) for several days. Urupā (cemeteries) are extremely tapu (sacred). When a baby is born, Māori traditionally bury the whenua (placenta) on land associated with one or both of the parents. Some Pākehā also now follow this custom. Māori social customs today Some customs have been adapted to non traditional situations. For instance, many marae in cities or outside New Zealand are multi tribal, so tribal traditions have to be adapted. Māori ceremonies are also used in non Māori settings, such as the opening of the Te Māori exhibition in New York in 1984. Welcome and hospitality Greeting visitors

5.document_title: Matariki – Te Tau Hou Māori
5.document_summary: Matariki is the Māori name for the Pleiades star cluster, marking the Māori New Year when it rises in midwinter. Derived from 'Ngā Mata o te Ariki Tāwhirimātea' (The eyes of the god Tāwhirimātea), it heralds seasonal changes and traditionally served as a time to acknowledge the dead, reflect, give thanks for harvests, and share bounty with family. Tohunga kōkōrangi (astronomy experts) observed the stars to predict weather and harvests. The Matariki period involved three key practices: remembering the deceased through ceremonies like 'whāngai i te hautapu' (feeding the stars), celebrating with feasting and dancing, and planning for the year ahead. The nine stars each hold significance: Matariki (well-being), Waitī (fresh water), Waitā (ocean), Tupuānuku (ground food), Tupuārangi (sky food), Waipunarangi (rain), Ururangi (winds), Pōhutukawa (the deceased), and Hiwa-i-te-rangi (dreams). Celebrations declined after European arrival but were revived in the 2000s, with the first modern public celebrations beginning in 2000. Since 2022, Matariki became an official public holiday observed on a Friday in late June or July. Different iwi celebrate at different times and recognize varying numbers of stars. Puanga (Rigel) serves as an alternative new year marker for western North Island iwi.

Marae dining halls A late 20th century description of a hākari at a marae reflects a common pattern for hākari inside the wharenui or dining hall. The local ladies put great effort into arranging the tables so that they look hospitable and plentiful. 12.document_title: Māori Housing in New Zealand: Historical Evolution, Challenges, and Contemporary Solutions
12.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori housing from pre-colonial times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Traditionally, Māori lived in family-based kāinga (villages) with rectangular wharepuni (sleeping houses) constructed from natural materials. European settlers introduced European-style housing from the early 1800s, though most Māori initially maintained traditional dwellings. From the late 1800s, poor sanitary conditions—including inadequate water, sewerage, and overcrowding—led to disease outbreaks, prompting government intervention that resulted in the demolition of 1,256 houses and construction of 2,103 cottages by 1909. The 1918 influenza epidemic devastated Māori communities and prompted new housing initiatives including the Native Housing Act 1935. Post-WWII urbanization saw Māori migrate to cities like Auckland and Wellington, facing discrimination from landlords and living in overcrowded subdivided apartments. State housing policies effectively excluded Māori through discriminatory practices until 1944, while housing designs ignored Māori cultural values (tikanga), contributing to assimilation policies. By the 1980s-90s, Māori home ownership remained significantly lower than the general population (29-49% vs. 50-73%). Persistent problems in the early 21st century included substandard, cold, damp housing; overcrowding (23% of Māori in 2006 vs. 4% for Europeans); and poor health outcomes. Modern solutions emerged through iwi-led initiatives including papakāinga schemes, rural housing programs, and the government's Whānau Ora scheme (2010), which combines housing with health, education, and legal support, representing a shift toward Māori self-determination.

13.text:

They were the venues for tangihanga (ceremonies of mourning) and gatherings to mark significant occasions such as birthdays and marriages. Some purpose built halls such as the Auckland Māori Community Centre provided a gathering place, but were not really suitable for the demands of a tangihanga , or the full expression of Māori culture and hospitality. Many Māori had firmly planted their roots in the city, but they still needed a tūrangawaewae a place to stand and express their cultural identity.

13.document_title: Urban Māori Migration, Identity, and Community Development in New Zealand Cities
13.document_summary: This document traces Māori migration from rural tribal areas to urban centers in New Zealand, particularly from the 1940s onwards. Before WWII, over 80% of Māori lived in rural areas; by 2013, 84% lived in urban areas. Post-war economic growth and labor demand prompted this mass urbanization. Urban Māori faced significant challenges including discrimination in housing and employment, unemployment, and cultural identity loss for city-born children. In response, communities established cultural clubs like Ngāti Pōneke Young Māori Club, political groups like Ngā Tamatoa, and tribal affiliate groups. Urban marae emerged as cultural centers and pan-tribal meeting grounds, including Hoani Waititi marae in Auckland and Ngā Hau E Whā in Christchurch. These institutions recreated traditional structures in urban settings, including alternative burial sites like Waikumete cemetery's Urupā. By the 1980s, urban Māori authorities such as Te Whānau o Waipareira Trust emerged as separate entities to address community needs independently of traditional tribal structures, fundamentally reshaping Māori society and establishing "urban Māori" as a distinct identity.

14.document_title: Tangihanga: Māori Death Customs, Ceremonies, and Funeral Practices
14.document_summary: Tangihanga is the enduring and most significant Māori ceremony for mourning the dead, encompassing comprehensive funeral and mourning practices central to maintaining Māori cultural identity. The ceremony involves traditional body preparation (tūpāpaku), including wrapping and placement in waka tūpāpaku, display on a marae, and traditional speeches (whaikōrero), calls (karanga), and chants (apakura). The ceremony typically lasts three days and concludes with burial at a cemetery (urupā). Key elements include the roles of whānau pani (bereaved family), the significance of pare kawakawa (greenery wreaths), and the hākari (feast) which symbolically welcomes the bereaved back to the living. Traditional practices include body preparation with red ochre, bone retrieval and hiding, and the removal of tapu (spiritual restriction) from the deceased's home. Mythologically, death originates from Hine-nui-te-pō, the goddess of death, after the demigod Māui failed to overcome mortality. The tangihanga serves to honor the deceased's mana, maintain cultural connections through whakapapa (genealogy), and reinforce the importance of relationships and life within Māori traditions. Modern tangihanga practices have adapted to urban settings and cultural changes, including casket displays and family participation in eating after visitors depart, though they remain closest to pre-European forms.

15.document_title: Family Violence in New Zealand: Comprehensive Analysis of History, Legislation, and Contemporary Responses
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines family violence in New Zealand, covering its definition, historical evolution, and contemporary responses. Family violence encompasses physical, sexual, emotional, and psychological abuse, including threats and isolation. Historically, domestic violence was tolerated, particularly in the 19th century when women had limited legal protections. The women's movement of the 1970s catalyzed significant change, establishing rape crisis centres and women's refuges starting in 1974. Key legislative milestones include the Domestic Protection Act 1982, criminalization of marital rape in 1985, the Domestic Violence Act 1995, and the Family Violence Act 2018, which incorporated 53 recommended changes. Police data shows 178,000 family violence investigations in 2022/23, with men predominantly identified as perpetrators. Family violence disproportionately affects Māori, LGBT+ individuals, disabled persons, and those in financial difficulty. The document emphasizes that family violence involves psychological, economic, and emotional control beyond physical violence, with profound impacts including trauma and depression. Support services include women's refuges and Shine, while prevention campaigns such as "Family Violence: It's not OK" and the White Ribbon Campaign promote behavior change and perpetrator accountability.

16.document_title: Men's Clubs, Fraternal Societies, and Social Organizations in New Zealand: A Comprehensive History
16.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of male-dominated social organizations in New Zealand from the 1840s to the early 21st century, including gentlemen's clubs, workingmen's clubs, Freemasonry, friendly societies, and service clubs. Gentlemen's clubs emerged starting with the Pickwick Club in 1840, featuring exclusive male-only membership, modern facilities, libraries, and dining rooms rooted in 18th-century London traditions. Workingmen's clubs developed as alternatives to pubs, emphasizing self-improvement and affordable recreation for working-class men. Freemasonry established its first New Zealand meeting in 1837 and grew to over 180 active lodges with 4,800 members by 2022. Friendly societies provided mutual aid and financial support during sickness or death, with membership peaking at 113,709 by 1938 before declining after the 1938 Social Security Act. Service clubs including Rotary, Lions, and Jaycees emphasized community-focused fraternal socializing. All organizations initially maintained strict male-only policies but gradually admitted women from the 1960s-1990s due to feminist pressure and changing social attitudes. Declining membership resulted from changing work patterns, alternative leisure activities, and evolving social values.

17.text:
[Page 7] Adapting traditional practices for modern times The application of old customs to new times and a changing society is a complex and contentious process. However, Māori custom has proved to be both resilient and adaptable. Public debate and the resolution of disagreement are central features of Māori society, and customs concerning the marae and whaikōrero (speechmaking) are designed to assist decision making. On the marae decisions are customarily reached by consensus, and this is another custom which is proving applicable and valuable in wider New Zealand society. Professor Hirini Mead describes a number of Māori customs which are both traditional and applicable to very different present day circumstances. One is the development of urban marae , which are often non tribal or multi tribal and may require imaginative revisions of traditional protocols. Another is the use of formal Māori ceremonies in non Māori settings, such as the opening of the Te Māori art exhibition at the New York Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1984. Most cultures have borrowed customs from other cultures and adapted their own customs to suit changing circumstances. The persistence and adaptation of Māori custom within Māori society, and its selective adoption by non Māori, is an indication of a thriving, confident and tolerant national culture.

[Page 1] Leisure in traditional Māori society ngā mahi a te rēhia ByRoss Calman In the early years of Māori settlement there would have been more leisure than later: the human population was low and food was plentiful. But within 200 years of human arrival, moa were extinct and so were some seal populations. Māori had to travel to find food, and store food for later. Increasing competition for food led to war, which reduced the time available for leisure. Age and class Children and the elderly had fewer daily tasks, so they had more leisure time. Children’s leisure activities also helped them learn. Teens and young adults took part in romantic activities such as wooing and composing romantic ditties. Rangatira (chiefs) were involved in food production and war, so had no more time for leisure than tūtūa (commoners). Social aspects Work was done in daylight. At night especially in winter people gathered for conversation, stories and indoor games. Some hākari (feasts) were linked to ritual and politics, but others were a chance to socialise and take part in leisure activities. The rising of the star Whānui (Vega) was associated with the kūmara harvest festival a time of feasting, haka , poi, taonga puoro (music) and tākaro (games). The rising of Matariki (the Pleiades) marked the new year a time for celebration and arts such as dancing and singing. Te whare tapere Te whare tapere (the house of entertainment) included kōrero pūrākau (story telling), waiata (songs), haka , poi, music and games. Stories were told to pass on knowledge and for entertainment. There were waiata for every occasion, and they were rich with history, tradition and metaphor. Haka and poi took place at most gatherings. Musical instruments were part of many rituals and were also played to entertain. Sports and games Sports and games were played at most social gatherings. The marae was the venue for kaipara (athletics and martial arts). In summer, water sports such as swimming, diving and surfing were popular. On winter evenings and in bad weather, people played games like tī ringaringa (hand games), whai (string patterns) and karetao (puppets). Children played with toys made from natural materials.

18.document_title: Traditional Māori Leisure, Entertainment, and Cultural Practices: A Comprehensive Study
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores leisure activities, entertainment practices, and cultural traditions in traditional Māori society. It examines how work-leisure balance was shaped by resource availability, environmental changes, and warfare throughout pre-European New Zealand. Early settlement offered abundant leisure due to plentiful food, but moa extinction and seal depletion forced sustainable harvesting practices and increased competition for mahinga kai (food sources). Age and social class influenced leisure availability, with children and elderly enjoying more free time. Leisure was primarily communal and evening-based, featuring storytelling, games, and indoor entertainment. Traditional pastimes included waiata (songs), haka, poi, taonga puoro (musical instruments), tākaro (games), and sports such as kaipara (athletics), swimming, and diving. Major festivals included the kūmara harvest festival marked by Whānui (Vega) and the Matariki new year festival in June. Hākari (feasts) served ritual, political, and social functions. Te whare tapere (the house of entertainment) encompassed cultural expression and knowledge transmission. Traditional children's toys were crafted from natural materials such as harakeke (flax) and raupō (bulrush), including tētere (flax trumpets) and toparere (flax leaf gliders). Entertainment and leisure activities were integral to Māori society, transmitting knowledge, history, cultural values, and warfare skills across generations.

19.document_title: Tangihanga: Māori Death Customs, Ceremonies, and Funeral Practices
19.document_summary: Tangihanga is the enduring and most significant Māori ceremony for mourning the dead, encompassing comprehensive funeral and mourning practices central to maintaining Māori cultural identity. The ceremony involves traditional body preparation (tūpāpaku), including wrapping and placement in waka tūpāpaku, display on a marae, and traditional speeches (whaikōrero), calls (karanga), and chants (apakura). The ceremony typically lasts three days and concludes with burial at a cemetery (urupā). Key elements include the roles of whānau pani (bereaved family), the significance of pare kawakawa (greenery wreaths), and the hākari (feast) which symbolically welcomes the bereaved back to the living. Traditional practices include body preparation with red ochre, bone retrieval and hiding, and the removal of tapu (spiritual restriction) from the deceased's home. Mythologically, death originates from Hine-nui-te-pō, the goddess of death, after the demigod Māui failed to overcome mortality. The tangihanga serves to honor the deceased's mana, maintain cultural connections through whakapapa (genealogy), and reinforce the importance of relationships and life within Māori traditions. Modern tangihanga practices have adapted to urban settings and cultural changes, including casket displays and family participation in eating after visitors depart, though they remain closest to pre-European forms.

30.document_title: Rotorua Anzac Day: Dawn Service and Civic Memorial Commemoration
30.document_summary: Rotorua's 2025 Anzac Day commemorations begin with a dawn service at Ōhinemutu at 5:45am led by Te Arawa Māori Returned Services League, followed by a civic memorial service and parade at 8:50am. The event honors those who served in the Australia New Zealand Army Corps, particularly remembering the Gallipoli campaign's 2,779 New Zealand casualties. Key speakers include pioneering Māori air force pilot Angela Swann-Cronin, youth representatives Patience Lister and Harrison Roberts-Brake, and Mayor Tania Tapsell. Swann-Cronin, the first Māori woman air force pilot, will share a message of aroha (compassion) and honor her ancestor Hēnare Kōhere who died at the Somme in 1916. The service includes prayers, hymns, wreath-laying, performances by the City of Rotorua Highland Pipe Band, and a tribute to Sir Robert Gillies of the 28th Māori Battalion. Approximately 1,000 attendees are expected, with the service live-streamed on council's YouTube.

33.document_title: New Zealand Politics 2024: Year in Review - Government, Policy Reform, and Political Leadership
33.document_summary: A comprehensive review of New Zealand's political landscape throughout 2024, documenting the coalition government's first year in power. The document chronicles major political events including nationwide Māori mobilisation and protests over the Treaty Principles Bill, the Hīkoi moo Te Tiriti protest with tens of thousands attending, and significant policy developments such as the crime crackdown, gang patch ban, and Fast-Track legislation. Key personnel changes include Darleen Tana's removal from parliament, James Shaw stepping down as Green co-leader with Chlöe Swarbrick taking over, and Andrew Coster's departure from the police force. The government faced criticism over accommodation allowances, prison bed commitments, disability funding cuts, and the reversal of the oil and gas exploration ban. Notable incidents include former Green MP Golriz Ghahraman's resignation over shoplifting charges, Minister Andrew Bayly's conduct complaint, and the death of Kiingi Tuheitia in September. The year also saw significant media industry upheaval with Newshub closure and TVNZ cuts. Despite various challenges and opposition party disputes, the government achieved most of its Quarter 4 objectives, with the Fast-Track legislation ultimately passing into law amid parliamentary protest.

36.document_title: Māori Queen Launches Two Economic Initiatives During Her First National Address
36.document_summary: Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po delivered her first royal address as head of the Kiingitanga movement on the one-year anniversary of her father's passing. She emphasized that being Māori is not defined by conflict or protest, but through daily practices like speaking te reo Māori, environmental stewardship, learning history, and choosing Māori names. She highlighted kotahitanga (solidarity) as central to Māori identity and launched two economic initiatives: Ōhanga Ki Te Ao, a summit to develop economic opportunities for Māori with global partners, and Tahua Kotahitanga, a capital fund with seed funding from iwi entities to unlock investment opportunities. These initiatives represent her commitment to advancing her father's vision of Māori self-determination and economic independence.

Whakataukī (Māori proverbs) are a fun and powerful way to help rangatahi develop their own voices and find grounding in the "continuum of whakapapa", Dr Hinemoa Elder says. The child psychiatrist and author weaves observations from her professional life into the new book Dear Moko a child centred reshaping of her beloved 2020 whakataukī collection. https://www.rnz.co.nz/nation professional life into the new book Dear Moko a child centred reshaping of her beloved 2020 whakataukī collection. https://www.rnz.co.nz/nation al/programmes/saturday/audio/2018961498/hinemoa elder dear moko The idea that children should be "seen and not heard" first introduced to Aotearoa by Pākehā settlers is one that Elder challenges in Dear Moko. Although this "older, more colonised" message about the place of young people still prevails in New Zealand culture, it is critical that whānau seek to understand young people's actual lived experience, she says, as they did in generations past. "I'm constantly trying to tune into a tūpuna [ancestral] voice in thinking about their struggles and trying to retain at least some of the older kōrero." Most young people are just trying to please their families, she says, and are "exquisitely attuned" to how their whānau receives them. "I'm often saying to parents 'Hey, our teenagers, our rangatahi get a bit of a bad rap but actually they're very caring because they've been keeping their pain private in order to protect your feelings and they pay a big price for that'." An illustration from Dear Moko. "I'm really quite shocked about the degree of complexity and the amount of difficulty that our whānau are trying to absorb themselves without professional help at all. "We need to make sure that rural communities are better resourced with mental health services and these services are functioning as well as looking at prevention." [Page 1] 'What's good for Māori is good for workers' iwi and unions unite in solidarity ByLayla Bailey Mcdowell Māori News Journalist, Pokere Paewai Māori issues reporter 2025 10 28 19:29:56+13:00 Unions and Māori have united in solidarity against government policy, coming together for Rā Whakamana a nationwide day of action calling to reaffirm the tino rangatiratanga of tangata whenua and protect the rights and wellbeing of all workers. The mobilisation coincided with the 190th anniversary of He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni (the Declaration of Independence of the United Tribes of New Zealand) and the first Labour Day demonstrations in 1890. https://www.rnz.co.nz/ news/te manu korihi/577073/hundreds gather across aotearoa calling o n government to honour te tiriti Despite the harsh weather which cancelled events in South Auckland and Tauranga, hundreds gathered in central Tāmaki Makaurau, braving the rain and heavy winds. Crowds, including representatives from iwi, the PSA, E Tū, and the New Zealand Nurses Organisation, as well as politicians, gathered at Okahu Bay to mark the beginning of the hīkoi, where they were welcomed by leaders of Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei. The hīkoi travelled from Okahu Bay to the Ports of Auckland through driving rain and wind. Community Activist and leader of Kaiāwhina Tāmaki Bianca Ranson told RNZ the kaupapa is about creating kotahitanga in the face of government policies she describes as "attacks on Māori, workers and communities. "For the first time, iwi and unions are uniting on this really significant day 190 years since the signing of He Whakaputanga. "Rā Whakamana is about recognising the mana of our wāhine, our workers, our rangatahi and tangata whenua, and coming together to create kotahitanga, strength and unity against this government and the attacks that are happening across all fronts," she said. Tāmaki Kaiāwhina is an Auckland based community security or marshalling service working to keep people safe during protests. Ranson said they have supported over 200 kaupapa over the last two years, and Rā Whakamana was "the most inspiring." "Because as this develops and grows, the strength of iwi, tangata whenua, hapū, whānau coming together, united with workers, is massive." Ranson said the message from those activating was clear. "We absolutely and completely reject all of the attacks against Te Tiriti, against workers, and against hapū, whānau and iwi. "[This] is a united stand against this government and all of the attacks against pay equity, against workers, against wāhine, and also against us as tangata whenua, the Regulatory Standards Bill, and everything that we've seen so far, even with the MACA Bill." She said those activating across the motu are affirming their tino rangatiratanga and mana motuhake as they "continue to fight for Te Tiriti justice and constitutional transformation. "That is the hope and aspiration for all of us for our future and for the future of Aotearoa. "We need to see this as a one term government, because we will not tolerate any of this happening to our people, to our workers any longer." Also in attendance were Te Pāti Māori MPs Tākuta Ferris, Mariameno Kapa Kingi, and Tāmaki Makaurau MP Oriini Kaipara, who addressed the crowd at the end of the hīkoi. "We're activating for not only our workers' rights, but our whānau rights mums, nanas, grandads, sons, nephews, nieces," she said. "We all deserve what is owed to us, and that is guaranteed by Te Tiriti. We shouldn't have to be begging for what's right." Kaipara told RNZ the day marked an historic moment in the collaboration between iwi and the union movement. "It's the first time iwi leaders have come out in full support of union activations right across Aotearoa. "Here in Tāmaki we have hundreds, if not thousands, of whānau living in vulnerable conditions and many of them are the workers impacted by this government and previous governments who haven't honoured the agreements." Kaipara said many workers are "fatigued, over it, undervalued and leaving in droves. "Today is about everyday citizens raising their voices to say, that's enough. "Our people need better pay, better working conditions, and to be honoured and recognised with proper support systems wrapped around them. The Tāmaki Makaurau activation ended with karakia and the waiata Ngā Iwi E. Meanwhile, around 300 people attended the activation in central Wellington. The crowd were treated to music from the Brass Razoo Solidarity Band and waiata by students from Te Ara Whānui Kura Kaupapa Māori. E Tū co President Muriel Tunoho told RNZ it is a chance to take a collective stand against the government. "There [is] strength in numbers and strength in voices coming together for this one kaupapa, and that one kaupapa has to be about getting rid of this government." E tū members are particularly concerned by the government's changes to pay equity claims, she said. "Job protection and job security in itself I think is all at risk under this government. I think this government has shown us that workers rights and tangata whenua rights are not their priority." Council of Trade Unions President Richard Wagstaff told the crowd that unions and Māori have very strong shared interests. "We often say what's good for Māori is good for workers and what's good for workers is good for Māori. Unfortunately what's bad for workers is what's bad for Māori." Patient Voice Aotearoa chairperson Malcolm Mulholland was there encouraging people to sign the Buller Declaration, a petition signed by more than 50,000 people urging the government to address a "state of crisis" in New Zealand's health system. The declaration will be delivered to Parliament of November 18th, he said. Iwi and unions are often advocating for the same cause, he said. "I think a lot of the unions advocate for Māori workers and a lot of the iwi clearly advocate for our people and there is obviously big synergies between the two, so having that relationship is important and having them come together is equally so." 39.document_title: Together for Te Tiriti: Lush Joins Fight Against Treaty Principles Bill
39.document_summary: Cosmetics company Lush Aotearoa has launched a campaign against the Treaty Principles Bill, calling it a direct threat to Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Ahead of Waitangi Day, the company encourages customers to sign the Ngāti Whakaue petition opposing the bill. Lush has released a limited-edition soap called "Together for Te Tiriti" with a fresh lemon fragrance, priced at $13 to represent Te Tiriti's three principles: protection, partnership, and participation. One hundred percent of profits go to ActionStation to fund Te Tiriti justice work. The campaign has received overwhelming public support, with petition signatures skyrocketing. Lush advocacy executive Jessielee Pearce emphasizes that the bill seeks to remove tino rangatiratanga from Māori law and that Te Tiriti is essential for achieving equity. She calls on other businesses to recognize their responsibility as tangata Tiriti and engage with Te Tiriti and tangata whenua. Lush has committed to dual-language signage and fostering a workplace culture that embraces tikanga Māori.

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores the rich heritage of traditional Māori games, sports, and cultural practices (ngā tākaro), which were integral to Māori society as entertainment, education, ritual practices, and community bonding. The document covers athletics including wrestling (mamau), boxing (mekemeke), running (omaoma), and jumping (pekepeke); water sports encompassing swimming (kauhoe), diving (kōkiri), surfing (whakaheke ngaru), and canoe racing (whakatere waka); physical games such as swings (moari, tārere), pīoi, piu, and hiding games; stick and string games including tī rākau and whai; word and hand games (kai, tī ringaringa); and other pastimes like kite-flying, puppet manipulation, spinning tops, and stilts. The document includes cultural narratives such as Te Houtaewa's legendary run and Hinepoupou's swim, along with board games like Mū tōrere. It explains mythological origins through figures like Miru and Raukatauri, and describes the role of these activities in community gatherings and warrior training. The document chronicles the suppression of these traditions by missionaries from the 1820s, leading to their decline through the 19th century. However, since the mid-20th century, there has been a significant revival of traditional games, with modern adaptations like fire poi and glow poi gaining international recognition, and team sports such as kī-o-Rahi and tapuae becoming increasingly popular. Contemporary developments include waka ama, which emerged in the mid-1980s and gained international prominence following the 1990 International Polynesian Canoe Federation World Sprints Championship.

2.fileDescription:
This comprehensive document provides an in-depth exploration of traditional Māori religion and spiritual practices. It begins with creation mythology detailing Te Kore (the void), Te Pō (the night), and Te Ao Mārama (the world of light), followed by the separation of Ranginui (sky father) and Papatūānuku (earth mother). The text explains major atua (gods) including Tāne (forests), Tangaroa (sea), Rongo (cultivated food), and Tūmatauenga (war), and discusses whether Io existed as a supreme being in pre-European Māori tradition.

The document extensively covers tohunga (priests and experts) who served as mediums for gods and spirits, acted as diviners (matakite), and served as healers and ritual guides. Key spiritual concepts explored include mana (power from gods and ancestors), tapu (sacred restrictions), noa (freedom from restrictions), mauri (life principle), hau (vital essence), and wairua (spirit).

A major focus is on karakia—formulas of words chanted to communicate with gods. The document describes various types of karakia used for love charms, healing, warfare, and childbirth. It details major life-cycle rituals including tūā (naming ceremony), tohi (child dedication), and pure (spiritual empowerment), along with ceremonies such as ngau paepae (warrior empowerment), rāhui (tapu placement), and whāngai hau (ceremonial food offerings). Sacred places (wāhi tapu), shrines (tūāhu), and ritual objects like godsticks are discussed in relation to ensuring fertility and protection, reflecting the Māori worldview where spiritual forces permeate all aspects of life.

3.fileDescription: Kaumātua are respected elders in Māori society who serve as vital storehouses of tribal knowledge, genealogy, and traditions. They hold multiple roles including guardians of tikanga (Māori customs), leaders of whānau (family) and rūnanga (tribal councils), nurturers of children, and dispute resolvers. Traditionally, kaumātua raised grandchildren, arranged marriages, and provided guidance on ceremonial and daily matters, transmitting cultural knowledge through storytelling, waiata (songs), and mentorship. The document explores their significance in traditional Māori stories (Māui, Tāwhaki, Toi) where they appear as knowledge keepers and nurturers. While life expectancy changes have affected the age threshold for kaumātua status (historically 30s-40s, now typically mid-60s+), their role remains vital. In modern times, urbanization in the 20th century caused cultural dislocation and threatened knowledge transmission. Contemporary solutions include community initiatives such as Te Arataki Manu Kōrero o Tainui and kaumātua flats, which preserve cultural knowledge, maintain elders' active participation in community life, and sustain their leadership roles. Despite challenges, kaumātua remain essential to Māori cultural identity and tribal mana (prestige).

chunkHighlights.text: Dial-a-kaumātua

From the mid-1980s it became popular for many public institutions to call on kaumātua to perform Māori ceremonial rites such as karakia , blessings and pōwhiri (welcoming ceremonies) as part of their drive to become, or at least to appear, more bicultural and responsive to Māori.
Some question the cultural integrity of such performances, particularly where they have been perceived as tokenistic. Some have cynically referred to this activity as ‘Dial-a-kaumātua’.

In some communities a younger generation has been forced to step forward, to perform certain ceremonial roles in place of their kaumātua . In others, tribes have sought to build the capacity of their elders. Te Arataki Manu Kōrero o Tainui, instigated by the late senior Ngāti Maniapoto kaumātua Tui Adams, brought together Tainui elders to improve their knowledge of Tainui tikanga (customs) and history and to ensure the continuity of Tainui traditions and identity.

Kaumātua remain important to the cultural strength of Māori tribes and as cultural symbols of Māori identity. Mason Durie said: ‘The standing of a tribe, its mana … relates more to the visible presence and authority of its elders … it is the older generation who carry the status, tradition and integrity of their people.’ 3

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores Māori social customs and cultural practices that have endured through centuries of change. It covers welcome rituals including karanga (call), wero (challenge), whaikōrero (speeches), and hongi (nose pressing), which served practical peacekeeping functions. The text explains kinship, whakapapa (genealogy), and the marae as cultural centers. It details customs surrounding death through tangi (funeral ceremonies) where whānau gather to support the wairua (spirit), as well as birth traditions like placenta burial. The document emphasizes marae-based practices, cemetery customs, and the honored status of elders. It demonstrates how traditional customs have adapted to modern urban settings and are increasingly adopted by non-Māori New Zealanders, reflecting a thriving national culture.

chunkHighlights.text: Adapting traditional practices for modern times

The application of old customs to new times and a changing society is a complex and contentious process. However, Māori custom has proved to be both resilient and adaptable. Public debate and the resolution of disagreement are central features of Māori society, and customs concerning the marae and whaikōrero (speechmaking) are designed to assist decision-making. On the marae decisions are customarily reached by consensus, and this is another custom which is proving applicable and valuable in wider New Zealand society.

Professor Hirini Mead describes a number of Māori customs which are both traditional and applicable to very different present-day circumstances. One is the development of urban marae , which are often non-tribal or multi-tribal and may require imaginative revisions of traditional protocols. Another is the use of formal Māori ceremonies in non-Māori settings, such as the opening of the Te Māori art exhibition at the New York Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1984.

Most cultures have borrowed customs from other cultures and adapted their own customs to suit changing circumstances. The persistence and adaptation of Māori custom within Māori society, and its selective adoption by non-Māori, is an indication of a thriving, confident and tolerant national culture.

Does not treat Cook Island Māori as a subset or variant of NZ Māori. Notes shared Polynesian heritage while affirming distinct identities and languages.

response.response_text:
## Two Peoples, One Whakapapa (Genealogy)

Cook Island Māori and New Zealand Māori are distinct peoples with separate cultural identities, languages, and histories — yet they share deep ancestral roots that connect them across the Pacific.

## Origins and Shared Ancestry

The two groups are closely related by whakapapa. It is likely that some ancestors of New Zealand Māori arrived from the Cook Islands around 700 years ago. [[1]](cite://1/1) Oral traditions from Aitutaki in the Cook Islands even claim that the famous Tainui waka (canoe) stopped there on its voyage from Ra'iatea to New Zealand, and Cook Islanders rekindled links with the Tainui iwi (tribe) in the 1990s. [[2]](cite://2/1) The two peoples share place names, and even family names — for example, Paikea, which originated with a family from Mauke who settled near East Cape in New Zealand. [[2]](cite://2/2)

There is, however, a touch of friendly sibling rivalry in this relationship. As one journalist has noted, "there is a bit of stick between Cook Islands Maori and New Zealand Maori. One group maintains they kicked the other out a thousand years ago … The voyagers claim those who stayed behind were the slack ones!" [[1]](cite://1/2)

## Different Homelands, Different Status

A key distinction is that New Zealand Māori are the *tangata whenua* — the people of the land — and are recognised as the original inhabitants of Aotearoa New Zealand. [[3]](cite://3/1) Their history in New Zealand includes a rich oral culture, centuries of settlement, the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, land wars, and a long struggle for cultural and political recognition. [[4]](cite://4/1)

Cook Island Māori, by contrast, are a Pacific community who originate from the Cook Islands — a self-governing nation in free association with New Zealand. Cook Islanders hold New Zealand citizenship but come from a separate homeland with its own governance. [[5]](cite://5/1)

## Language: Related but Distinct

Both peoples speak Māori languages that fall under the same Tahitic branch of the Austronesian language family, which means the dialects of the Cook Islands are *very* similar to te reo Māori. [[2]](cite://2/3)[[6]](cite://6/1) However, they are separate languages. Cook Islands Māori (te reo Māori Kūki 'Airani) has several island dialects, with Rarotongan emerging as the dominant form. [[7]](cite://7/1)

Sadly, both languages face pressure. Among Cook Islanders living in New Zealand, only 18% could hold an everyday conversation in Cook Islands Māori by 2001, and by 2018 that figure had dropped further to just 10%. [[8]](cite://8/1) Language nests (*punanga reo*) and school programmes have been introduced to help revive it. [[8]](cite://8/2) UNESCO lists te reo Māori Kūki 'Airani as one of the most endangered Pacific languages. [[9]](cite://9/1)

## Culture and Community

While New Zealand Māori culture is organised around iwi (tribes) and hapū (sub-tribes) with a strong focus on land, Cook Island Māori culture centres on the *kopu tangata* — the extended family — as a powerful unifying force. [[10]](cite://10/1) Cook Island cultural traditions such as embroidering *tīvaevae* (colourful quilts), the ritual of cutting a boy's hair at adolescence, and energetic dance and drumming performances remain important expressions of identity. [[10]](cite://10/2)

Today, Cook Island Māori are the third largest Pacific community in Aotearoa New Zealand [[9]](cite://9/2), and around 90,000 people identify as both Māori and Pacific — a reflection of just how intertwined these communities have become. [[11]](cite://11/1)

---

1.document_title: Cook Islanders: Migration, Settlement, and Cultural Identity in New Zealand
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the migration history and settlement patterns of Cook Islanders in New Zealand from the early 20th century through 2018. Beginning with small numbers of soldiers and students in the 1920s-1930s, migration accelerated significantly after WWII as young people sought better wages and urban opportunities. By 1976, over 12,000 Cook Islanders had settled in New Zealand, eventually reaching 61,000 by 2013 and over 80,000 by 2018—outnumbering those remaining on the islands. Early migrants concentrated in major cities including Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch, working in factory, domestic, canning, and timber mill jobs. Chain migration became prevalent from the 1960s onward as established residents sponsored family members. Economic factors, including limited agricultural export opportunities and job losses in the 1990s, drove continued emigration. The kopu tangata (extended family) remains central to Cook Islander identity, with communities maintaining strong connections through enua associations, churches, and cultural institutions. Religion provided crucial welfare and guidance. Cultural practices including traditional dance, music, tīvaevae (quilting), and language preservation are vital to their heritage. Language preservation faces challenges, with only 10% able to converse in Cook Islands Māori by 2018, though initiatives like punana reo aim to reverse this decline.

2.text:
[Page 2] Traditionally people sought guidance in the church. In New Zealand the church also became a place for them to meet and chat in their own language Cook Islands Māori. Even so, by the early 2000s (when 70% of the country’s Cook Islanders were New Zealand born), only 18% could speak their mother tongue. Preschool ‘language nests’ and teaching in some schools are helping to save it. Other customs are flourishing: embroidering tīvaevae, the colourful quilts; the ritual of cutting a boy’s hair at adolescence; energetic dance and drumming performances. The kopu tangata (extended family) remains a powerful unifying force.
{}

6.document_title: Translation and Interpreting in New Zealand: History, Development, and Modern Multilingual Services
6.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of English-Māori translation and interpreting in New Zealand from 1769 to the early 21st century. It begins with Tupaia, a Tahitian chief who interpreted for James Cook's voyage, and covers early missionary translations of Christian texts. A major focus is the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), whose overnight translation by Reverend Henry Williams raised critical questions about accuracy and the meaning of "tino rangatiratanga." The document details how translation services evolved from essential survival tools for early European settlers to formal institutional roles in courts, government, and Parliament. Key figures include Pei Te Hurinui Jones, a prolific translator of English literature into Māori. The narrative covers the first use of Māori in Parliament from 1868, the decline of translation services in the 20th century, and Māori's declaration as an official language in 1985-1987. Modern developments include the 1990 Nga tangata taumata rau translation project, the establishment of full-time Parliamentary interpreters by 1999, the 2013 bilingual Mokomoko Act, and the licensing of interpreters through Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori. The document also discusses translation services in education, digital platforms, literary translation initiatives like Gecko Press, and the expansion of New Zealand Sign Language interpreting services. This work represents significant recognition within the publishing and literary community.

7.text:
[Page 8] By 2001 only 18% of Cook Islanders in New Zealand were able to hold an everyday conversation in Cook Islands Māori, and by 2018 this figure had fallen further, to 10%. Initiatives such as punana reo (‘language nests’ for young children), and learning materials provided in some schools give hope for saving the language. A language curriculum for New Zealand schools was launched in 2004.

8.document_title: Te Reo Māori: History, Decline, and Revitalisation in New Zealand
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of te reo Māori (the Māori language) from first European contact in 1769 through modern revitalisation efforts. Te reo Māori, a Polynesian language within the Austronesian family, became the official language of New Zealand in 1987. The document details the language's three major dialects and its evolution through early European contact, missionary involvement, and the development of written Māori from the 1820s onward. It chronicles the systematic decline following the Education Ordinance 1847, which mandated English-only education, leading to significant speaker population reduction by the 20th century due to urbanisation, world wars, and assimilationist policies. The revitalisation movement began in the 1970s, including the 1972 te reo petition (30,000 signatures), establishment of Māori Language Week, and the landmark 1984 Māori Language Claim (WAI 11). Key initiatives include kōhanga reo (language immersion centres) established in 1982, kura kaupapa (immersion schools), wharekura (secondary schools), and Te Ataarangi adult learning programmes. The Māori Language Act 1987 established Māori as an official language and created Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori. Broadcasting played a crucial role through Te Upoko o Te Ika radio station (1987), Te Māngai Pāho funding agency (1993), and Māori Television (2004). As of 2018, approximately 21% of Māori and 4% of the total population speak the language.

9.text:
[Page 3] As the country’s original inhabitants, Māori are tangata whenua (the people of the land). Māori culture is a key element of the New Zealand identity . Māori differences from Pākehā are evident in social customs such as tangi (funerals).

9.document_title: New Zealand Society: A Comprehensive Overview of Population, Culture, Health, Education, and Modern Life
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's society across multiple dimensions. It covers the nation's diverse population of over 5 million people, including 67% of European descent, significant Māori (565,329), Pacific Islander, and Asian communities. Demographic trends reveal an aging population, declining birth rates, and increasing ethnic diversity concentrated primarily in the North Island, particularly Auckland. The document details family structures, housing trends showing declining home ownership (from 73.8% in 1991 to 67.8% in 2001), and rising single-parent families (31% in 2001). Gender dynamics highlight women's improved economic and social status since the 1980s, alongside New Zealand's progressive LGBTQ+ rights stance, including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986), civil unions (2005), and same-sex marriage (2013). Health outcomes have improved significantly since the 1950s, with life expectancy at 76 years for men and 81 for women (2000), though Māori populations experience lower life expectancy and higher mortality rates. The education system provides free, compulsory state schooling from ages 6-16, with special initiatives like kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa Māori for language preservation. Religion remains important with approximately half the population identifying as Christian, though church attendance is low and religious diversity has increased through immigration. The document traces cultural evolution including the transformation of cuisine from British traditions to cosmopolitan cooking, beverage consumption shifts from beer to wine and coffee, and relaxed dress codes reflecting global influences. Throughout, it highlights both multicultural achievements and persistent socioeconomic disparities faced by Māori communities.

[Page 5] Traditional culture Pre European Māori culture was oral, and based on small autonomous sub tribes living in valleys, harbours and other localities. Tribal histories are rich with stories of armed conflict, and New Zealand’s many sculpted hills and ridges the relics of fortifications are evidence of the importance of warfare in traditional Māori society.

10.document_title: Māori: History, Culture, and Contemporary Society in New Zealand
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

12.document_title: Te Ao Mārama: Traditional Māori Worldview, Cosmology, and Spiritual Concepts
12.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the traditional Māori worldview and understanding of nature (Te Ao Mārama), presenting a holistic indigenous philosophy centered on interconnectedness and spiritual principles. It explains how Māori people viewed all elements of nature—birds, fish, people, wind, and sun—as an interconnected family linked through genealogies (whakapapa). The creation story describes how earth mother Papatūānuku and sky father Ranginui produced 70 children who became gods of different natural domains. Key concepts include whakapapa (genealogies explaining relationships between all things), Te Kore (a realm of unlimited potential and ultimate reality), and the cycle of light (Te Ao) and darkness (Te Pō) representing birth and death. Three interconnected spiritual concepts are examined: mana (extraordinary power and essence), tapu (sacred restrictions and disciplines), and mauri (life force energy binding all physical things). The document explores tangata whenua (people of the land), where identity is defined through geographical and ancestral connections, and discusses taniwha as spiritual guardians. It emphasizes how orators use speech to guide people from darkness into light, mirroring Tāne's separation of earth and sky, and highlights the practical and spiritual functions of oral traditions in transmitting knowledge while maintaining respect toward other species.

[Page 4] Until the mid 20th century the Māori population was largely rural. Between 1951 and 1971 the proportion of Māori living in cities rose from 20% to 58%. By 2001 Māori were as likely to be living in cities and larger towns as the rest of the population. When Māori and Pākehā began living in closer proximity, the belief that the country had ‘the best race relations in the world’ was tested. A race relations conciliator was first appointed in 1971 to help combat racial discrimination . Pacific Islanders In 2001 about half the 231,800 Pacific Islanders in New Zealand were Samoan . The next largest groups were Cook Island Māori (52,600) and Tongan (40,700). Many more Cook Island Māori, Niueans and Tokelauans live in New Zealand than on their home islands. More than half the Pacific Islanders who live in New Zealand were born there. The population is young and concentrated in the Auckland region. Asians Between 1991 and 2001, the proportion of Asians in New Zealand almost doubled. By 2001, Asians made up 6.6% of the population. Chinese formed the largest group, followed by Indians . Within these two communities there are families that have been in the country for several generations. In 2006 three quarters of New Zealand’s Asians lived in the Auckland region. They have sometimes borne the brunt of anti immigrant sentiment, exploited by some politicians. However, New Zealand society has generally welcomed the newcomers. Languages Most New Zealanders speak only English . But a revival of the Māori language , combined with increasing numbers of immigrants, meant that in the 2000s more than half a million New Zealanders spoke at least one other language. In 2006 Māori was spoken by about 157,000 people. One in four Māori spoke the language, and conscious efforts had been made to keep it alive. The most common language after English and Māori was Samoan, spoken by more than 80,000 people. Other languages with large numbers of speakers included Tongan, Hindi, French and the Chinese dialects of Cantonese and Mandarin.

Throughout, it highlights both multicultural achievements and persistent socioeconomic disparities faced by Māori communities.

15.text:
[Page 1] Tribal organisation By Rāwiri Taonui What are iwi and hapū? The iwi (tribe) is the largest of the groups that form Māori society. Each iwi is made up of various hapū (clans or descent groups), which might have up to several hundred members. Traditionally, the main purposes of a hapū were to defend land, and to provide support for its members. How iwi and hapū formed Some tribal groups formed from links to the waka (canoe) on which their founding ancestor arrived in New Zealand from Hawaiki. For example, the Waikato tribes trace their descent from the Tainui waka. Others developed when the pressure on resources such as land and food became so great that some members had to move away and establish themselves elsewhere. War, migration and family infighting also caused new iwi or hapū to emerge. Iwi and hapū are often named after an ancestor. For example, Ngāpuhi means ‘the people of Puhi ’ and Te Uri o Rātā means ‘the descendants of Rātā’. Sometimes tribal names came from an important event that involved their ancestor, such as a battle. Whānau family Each hapū is made up of whānau (extended families). Whānau included much respected elders, adults, children and grandchildren. Everyone helped each other, working for the group and caring for each other’s children and the elderly. Social groups Each hapū was made up of different ranking members, headed by chiefs called ariki and rangatira . First born females also had high status. Experts in areas such as history and tradition, carving and healing were called tohunga . There were commoners and sometimes captives or slaves in each hapū . Changes after European contact After New Zealand became a British colony, the way that iwi and hapū functioned began to change. When the government bought or confiscated Māori land in the 19th century, tribes were dispersed. From the mid 20th century, when many younger people moved to the cities for greater work opportunities, tribal power was diminished. From the late 20th century, however, tribal organisations have worked to reconnect people with their tribal origins.

15.document_title: Māori Social Organisation: Tribal Structure, Hierarchy, and Evolution Through Colonisation and Urbanisation
15.document_summary: This document examines the structure and evolution of Māori tribal society in New Zealand. It explains the hierarchical organization of iwi (tribes) and hapū (clans), with whānau (extended families) as the basic social unit comprising 20-30 people across three to four generations. Tribal groups formed through waka (canoe) ancestry, resource pressure, migration, and conflict, with names derived from founding ancestors and clan prefixes like Ngāti or Te Uri. Traditional Māori society was stratified into three ranks: rangatira/kāhui-ariki (leaders), tūtūā (commoners), and taurekareka/mōkai (slaves), with special roles for tohunga (learned experts). European contact from the early 19th century disrupted traditional tribal functions through trade, musket wars, land confiscation, and colonisation. The document traces significant transformation during the 19th and 20th centuries, including the shift from hapū to iwi as the primary political unit, establishment of tribal trust boards after 1945 to address Treaty of Waitangi grievances, and urbanization's dramatic impact—with urban Māori population rising from 17% in 1936 to 80% by 1986. While urbanization has weakened some tribal connections, modern tribal organizations and reconnection programs continue to maintain cultural identity and links to ancestral lands.

16.text:
[Page 4] Connection with iwi and hapū Although Māori in the 2000s are a highly urbanised people, most retain some links with their original tribal territories and return there for ceremonial and social events. 16.document_title: Māori Manners, Social Behaviour, and Cultural Customs: From Traditional Practices to Modern Adaptation
16.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori social customs and cultural practices that have endured through centuries of change. It covers welcome rituals including karanga (call), wero (challenge), whaikōrero (speeches), and hongi (nose pressing), which served practical peacekeeping functions. The text explains kinship, whakapapa (genealogy), and the marae as cultural centers. It details customs surrounding death through tangi (funeral ceremonies) where whānau gather to support the wairua (spirit), as well as birth traditions like placenta burial. The document emphasizes marae-based practices, cemetery customs, and the honored status of elders. It demonstrates how traditional customs have adapted to modern urban settings and are increasingly adopted by non-Māori New Zealanders, reflecting a thriving national culture.

17.text:
[Page 1] The significance of iwi and hapū Iwi The largest political grouping in pre European Māori society was the iwi (tribe). This usually consisted of several related hapū (clans or descent groups). The hapū of an iwi might sometimes fight each other, but would unite to defend tribal territory against other tribes. Iwi tūturu (the homeland tribe) or tino iwi (the central tribe) were groups living in a long held location. They would take their name from a founding ancestor. Iwi nui or iwi whānui (the greater tribe) were groups tracing descent from the founding ancestor of the iwi tūturu. They were often widespread and lived alongside people from other iwi .

18.text:
[Page 2] Early regional arts and culture Iwi regional cultures The cultural life of 19th century Māori varied for iwi and hapū living in different parts of the country. Cultural practices such as weaving, carving and singing waiata were diverse in form, reflecting local traditions, histories and landscapes. Whakairo (carving) reflected distinct whakapapa (genealogy). Some regional distinctions of style can also be observed. A ‘serpentine’ style is associated with northern iwi such as Te Rarawa, Ngāpuhi and Te Roroa, while eastern iwi such as Ngāti Porou were known for square style carvings.

18.document_title: Regional Cultural and Creative Life in New Zealand: From the 19th Century to the 2000s
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of regional cultural and creative life in New Zealand from the 19th century through the 2000s. It examines how Māori communities maintained distinct cultural practices including waiata singing, weaving, and carving styles that varied by iwi and region, while European settlements established cultural institutions such as choral societies, museums, and libraries. Dunedin emerged as the most vibrant cultural center due to Scottish settlers and gold wealth, producing notable figures like Thomas Morland Hocken and William Mathew Hodgkins. Other regions developed distinctive cultural scenes: Rotorua fostered Māori culture and early film; Christchurch became a literary hub with the Caxton Press; Wellington attracted writers and developed post-WWII coffee house culture; Auckland became a fashion capital and avant-garde center. The document highlights literary revolutions in the 1930s with publications like Phoenix and Tomorrow, and traces the emergence of distinctive musical genres from the late 1970s onward, including punk in Auckland, the Dunedin sound indie-pop, hip hop in South Auckland, and heavy metal in Waikato. Major cultural events and festivals are examined, including WOMAD in New Plymouth, Art Deco Weekend in Napier, and Polyfest in Auckland. Provincial artistic clusters in Nelson, Whanganui, Taranaki, and Dunedin developed distinct artistic traditions, with Wellington's thriving arts scene and film industry presence highlighted as significant cultural contributions.

19.text:
[Page 1] Linking the people to the land Many Māori traditions tell of the Polynesian settlers from Hawaiki, who reached the coast in canoes about 700 years ago. But there are also myths and legends of earlier beings, such as the first human to be created. Through these stories, tribes can trace a long relationship with the land, and with the different regions they live in. Hineahuone In tradition, Ranginui (the sky father) and Papatūānuku (the earth mother) were the parents of Tāne. Tāne made the first woman from the soil, naming her Hineahuone. One story says ‘the arms, the body, the limbs, the thighs, these all took shape and the skeleton was complete’. With Tāne she had a daughter, Hinetītama, later known as Hine nui te pō, who is seen in the dawn and in the setting sun. It is said that all human beings are descended from these ancestors. Māui The trickster demigod Māui is said to have dragged the North Island from the ocean, using the jawbone of his grandmother as a hook. The Māori name for the island is Te Ika a Māui (Māui’s fish). The many other stories about Māui tell of the theft of fire, the capture of the sun and the pursuit of immortality. Ancestors from the natural world Māori people believed that they were related to the natural world the earth, the birds, the trees. The Ngāi Tūhoe tribe believe that their ancestor was Hine pūkohu rangi, the maiden of the mist that swirled around the Urewera mountains. Patupaiarehe and tūrehu There are many accounts of mysterious people who were already in New Zealand when Polynesian voyagers arrived by canoe. It is said that they lived high in the mountains, and could be heard calling to each other. Two of these groups were known as the patupaiarehe and the tūrehu. Kupe In many traditions, Kupe was the first Polynesian to discover New Zealand. He chased a great octopus across the ocean in his canoe, and finally killed it at Cook Strait. Kupe explored the country and named many places, such as Pari Whero (Red Rocks), on the Wellington coast. Toitehuatahi In some traditions the ancestor Toitehuatahi arrived from Hawaiki, and in others he was born in New Zealand. Tribes are proud to claim they are descended from Toi, and the Ngāti Awa people say his village overlooked the Bay of Plenty, near present day Whakatāne.

19.document_title: Māori Origins, Ancestors, and Tribal Narratives: Creation Mythology, Kupe, Toi, and the Connection Between People and Land
19.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori tribal traditions, creation mythology, and ancestral narratives that form the foundation of Māori cultural identity and connection to Aotearoa New Zealand. It presents a genealogical framework beginning with creation stories featuring Hineahuone, the first human created from earth by Tāne, and the demigod Māui who legendarily fished up the North Island. The text examines pre-canoe narratives of mysterious beings like patupaiarehe and tūrehu, and early explorers and ancestors including Kupe and Toitehuatahi (Toi). Central to the narratives is Kupe, credited as the first Polynesian discoverer of New Zealand, whose journey pursued a giant octopus and resulted in naming locations across the islands, with his wife Kuramārōtini naming Aotearoa ('long white cloud'). The document also emphasizes Toi's significance as an early ancestor recognized as tangata whenua (people of the land), with strong associations to the Whakatāne district and influence among Ngāti Awa, Mataatua, and Ngāi Tūhoe peoples. These interconnected narratives illustrate an organic worldview where earth, sea, and sky possess mana and human qualities, enabling Māori to identify with natural elements. The traditions establish deep connections between Māori tribes and the land, forming the basis for tribal identity, tenure, ancestral authority, and the spiritual relationship between Māori people and their environment across generations.

20.text:
[Page 1] Early settlement The ancestors of Māori arrived on canoes from Pacific islands before 1300 CE. Settling first on the coast, they hunted seals and moas. They also began to grow food, and some moved to the forests. They lived in small tribal groups, with a rich culture of spoken stories, and strong traditions of warfare. Their ancestors, and the gods of the natural world, were very important. Europeans arrive The arrival of Europeans from the early 1800s had a major effect on these early communities. Among the newcomers were missionaries, and many Māori became Christians. They learnt to read and write and began trading, especially in pigs and potatoes. The Treaty of Waitangi signed in 1840 established British law and government, but it could not prevent warfare in the 1840s and 1860s as Māori defended their lands and local authority. After the wars Māori lost land through confiscation and sale, mostly to British settlers. Revival In the first half of the 20th century important leaders such as Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi worked to make life better for Māori and to revive the culture. There was a new interest in the language, and in arts such as carving and weaving. After the Second World War many Māori moved to the cities in search of jobs. In the 1970s and 1980s groups protested about their rights to land, and helped promote the language and culture. Important events were a march down the North Island to Parliament in 1975, the creation of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975 to look at claimed breaches of the Treaty, and the occupation of Bastion Point in Auckland by protesters in 1977 78. Māori today In 2019 there were nearly 800,000 Māori people, with most living in cities. There were kōhanga reo (preschool language nests) and schools using the Māori language, two Māori television channels and 21 radio stations, 29 members of Parliament who identified as Māori, and many creative projects in film, music and art. 20.document_title: Māori: History, Culture, and Contemporary Society in New Zealand
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

21.text:

Descended from a people who lived on small Pacific islands, where land was at a premium and their lives often depended on what they could find in the ocean, they now had extensive space and resources. 21.document_title: Waka: Māori and Moriori Canoes, Cultural Heritage, and Maritime Traditions
21.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores waka (canoes), essential vessels in Māori and Moriori culture and maritime history. It traces waka from their Polynesian origins as double-hulled voyaging canoes that carried the first settlers to Aotearoa (New Zealand) over a month-long journey, to their evolution into specialized single-hulled vessels adapted to New Zealand's abundant large forests. The text describes major waka types including waka taua (war canoes up to 30 metres, holding 100 people), waka tētē (fishing and trading canoes), waka tīwai (river canoes), waka tangata (educational canoes), and mōkihi (rafts), with regional variations such as East Coast and South Island mōkihi rafts, and Moriori waka from the Chatham Islands including waka pūhara, waka rimu, waka pahī, and waka rā. The document details construction methods, including tree selection, carving, and ceremonial practices, and explains how waka design changed as Māori adapted to New Zealand's resources and geography. It covers essential waka equipment including paddles (hoe), sails (rā), poling poles (toko), anchors (punga), and bailers, with detailed descriptions of bailing systems such as puna wai or tāinga ā wai designated areas and intricately carved bailers known as tatā, tīheru, and tā wai. The document emphasizes waka's cultural significance in Māori genealogy and mythology, connecting ancestors to the ancestral homeland of Hawaiki through legendary voyages by Māui and Kupe.

32.document_summary: Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown affirmed the nation's commitment to its special relationship with New Zealand during the 60th anniversary of self-governance in free association. Brown emphasized there is no strategic shift to reject the relationship, describing it as grounded in enduring kinship. He acknowledged current tensions as temporary challenges, comparing the relationship to steel that cannot be broken. The celebration featured cultural performances and speeches about the nation's future. Notable absences included New Zealand PM Christopher Luxon and Foreign Minister Winston Peters, with Governor-General Dame Cindy Kiro representing New Zealand. Citizens expressed desires for economic independence, cultural preservation, and improved healthcare. Tensions stem from New Zealand pausing $20 million in development funding over concerns about Cook Islands' agreements with China.
