The need for cohesive action led to the founding of the second New Zealand Labour Party in 1916. McCombs helped to draft its constitution and programme. He was also its first president but, objecting to the party's approach to prohibition, resigned his membership a year later. He rejoined the party in 1918 and served as deputy chairman from 1919 until 1923. In 1919 he tied the vote for its parliamentary leadership. When lots were drawn the post went to the more militant Harry Holland , with whom McCombs had clashed in 1917. The antagonism between the two men continued but McCombs's frequent challenges to Holland's leadership were unsuccessful.

23.document_title: James McCombs: New Zealand Labour Politician and Social Reformer
23.document_summary: James McCombs (1873-1933) was a pioneering New Zealand Labour politician and social reformer. Born in Ireland and emigrated to New Zealand in 1876, he became involved in socialist and prohibitionist movements before entering politics. Elected to Parliament in the 1913 Lyttelton by-election, McCombs served as the first president of the second New Zealand Labour Party (founded 1916) and later as deputy chairman. Throughout his 20-year parliamentary career, he championed prohibition, opposed conscription, advocated for proportional representation, and was notably progressive on women's rights, including efforts to enable women's election to Parliament and appointment as justices of the peace. Known for his debating skills and financial expertise, he opposed deflationary depression policies and advocated for central planning. He remained in opposition throughout his career and died in 1933, succeeded in his parliamentary seat by his wife Elizabeth.

24.document_title: Michael Joseph Savage: Life, Political Career, and Legacy as New Zealand's Social Security Pioneer
24.document_summary: Michael Joseph Savage (1872-1940) was an Irish-Australian-born New Zealand Labour politician who became the nation's first Labour Prime Minister. Born in Victoria, Australia, Savage emigrated to New Zealand in 1907 and became active in unionism and socialist movements in Auckland. Elected to Parliament in 1919 representing Auckland West, he became Labour leader in 1933. His advocacy for pensions, free healthcare, and workers' rights resonated during the Great Depression. Labour won the 1935 election with 55 of 80 seats, implementing progressive legislation including state house construction and Reserve Bank nationalization. At the 1937 Imperial Conference, Savage criticized Britain's appeasement policies. In 1938, despite terminal colon cancer, he championed the Social Security Bill, introducing universal free healthcare and pensions termed "applied Christianity." Labour's vote share increased from 46% to 56%. Savage died on March 27, 1940, leaving a legacy that fundamentally shaped New Zealand's social welfare system for generations.

25.document_title: Ernest John Bartlett Allen: A Biography
25.document_summary: Ernest John Bartlett Allen (1884-1945) was a British-born socialist activist and intellectual who became a leading figure in industrial unionism and revolutionary socialism. Born in Berkshire, he studied European languages at Oxford and joined the Social Democratic Federation before moving to the Socialist Labour Party, where he championed industrial unionism as the path to revolution. He founded the Advocates of Industrial Unionism and edited the Industrialist, publishing influential works on revolutionary tactics. In 1910, he joined Tom Mann's Industrial Syndicalist Education League. Relocating to New Zealand in 1912, Allen became assistant editor of the Māoriland Worker and later its editor. Initially supporting WWI and conscription, he lost his position but continued writing on socialist strategy. In 1922, he published "Labour and politics," arguing for constitutional methods suited to New Zealand's unique circumstances. Allen worked various jobs including driver and clerical worker, and lectured at the Auckland Rationalist Association until his death in 1945.

26.document_title: John Kendrick Archer: Baptist Minister and Labour Party Leader
26.document_summary: John Kendrick Archer (1865-1949) was a prominent Baptist minister and New Zealand Labour Party leader. Born in Leicestershire, England, he was ordained in 1891 and served as a pastor in northern England before immigrating to New Zealand in 1908. Influenced by Baptist preacher John Clifford and committed to Christian socialism, Archer became a powerful advocate for social justice and workers' rights. In New Zealand, he held significant positions including president of the Baptist Union (1916-1918), mayor of Christchurch (1925-1931), and Labour Party president (1928-1929). Though unsuccessful in four parliamentary campaigns, he was appointed to the Legislative Council in 1937. Archer was known for his uncompromising moral stance, blending religious conviction with political activism, and remained active in church and community work until his death.

27.document_title: William Edward Parry: New Zealand Labour Leader and Politician
27.document_summary: William Edward Parry (1878-1952) was a prominent New Zealand labour leader and politician. Born in Orange, New South Wales, he migrated to New Zealand in 1906 and became deeply involved in union activities at Waihī goldmines, serving as president of the Waihī Amalgamated Miners' and Workers' Union (1909-1912). A co-founder of the New Zealand Federation of Labour, Parry was imprisoned for four months during the 1912 Waihī strike and participated in the 1913 waterfront strikes. He joined the Labour Party in 1916 and was elected MP for Auckland Central in 1919. As a close ally of Michael Joseph Savage, Parry served in Savage's first cabinet in 1935 as minister of internal affairs until 1949, overseeing pensions and social security. An advocate for physical fitness and health education, he was responsible for the Physical Welfare and Recreation Act 1937. Parry represented Auckland Central until 1946, then Arch Hill until his retirement in 1951. Though not an innovative policy maker, he was respected for his administrative abilities and remained a significant figure in New Zealand's labour movement.

28.document_summary: Richard Eddy (1882-1955) was a prominent New Zealand labour union organiser and leader. Born in North Canterbury, he worked on farms before becoming involved in rural trade unionism. After moving to Waimate, he joined the local labour movement and became secretary of the Waimate Workers' Union in 1912. As a strong advocate of the 'One Big Union' movement, he helped organise farmhands and Māori shearers across the South Island. In 1935, he re-entered union work to rebuild the New Zealand Workers' Union during the depression, becoming its president in 1936. He served as vice president of the New Zealand Federation of Labour (1937-1943) and was elected to the Legislative Council (1941-1950). During WWII, he acted as a vital link between the Labour Party and union movement, serving on various government councils and committees. He retired as union president in 1946 but continued as chief industrial officer until 1950.

29.document_title: Richard John Seddon: Life, Political Rise, Leadership, and Legacy as New Zealand's Premier
29.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical account traces Richard John Seddon's life from his birth in Lancashire, England in 1845 through his rise to prominence as New Zealand's Premier. Beginning as an unruly student interested in mechanical drawing, Seddon was apprenticed as an engineer and eventually emigrated to New Zealand in 1863, where he prospected for gold and worked at railway workshops. After settling on the West Coast and establishing businesses including a hotel and store at Kūmara, he married Louisa Spotswood in 1869 and became a miners' advocate and local politician. Elected to Parliament in 1879 for Hokitika, he represented mining constituencies and became known for his focus on West Coast issues. By the late 1880s, he had risen to prominence as a leading mining authority and opposition figure. Seddon became Premier in 1893, outmaneuvering rival Robert Stout following John Ballance's death. His populist style and mastery of parliamentary procedure enabled him to centralize power, earning the nickname "King Dick" for his autocratic governance. As Premier, he held multiple portfolios including labour, colonial treasurer, education, and immigration, implementing key reforms such as the Old-age Pensions Act 1898, Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1894, and Workers' Dwellings Act 1905. Known for his imposing physical presence and carefully cultivated public image, Seddon excelled at crowd management and maintaining public sympathy while consolidating Liberal reforms. He pursued imperialist expansion in the Pacific, notably annexing the Cook Islands in 1901, and maintained strict party discipline. His health declined from 1897 onwards, yet he remained in power until his death on June 10, 1906, aboard the Oswestry Grange while returning from Australia. His legacy encompasses humanitarianism, imperialism, and populist prime-ministerial leadership in New Zealand.

30.document_title: Māwhete: A Māori Political Leader, Legislative Councillor, and Labour Party Advocate
30.document_summary: William Arthur Moffatt (Māwhete), born 1880 in Tiakitahuna, was a prominent Māori political leader and advocate of Ngāti Hineaute descent with connections to multiple iwi. Working as an interpreter and land agent before entering politics, Māwhete stood unsuccessfully for the Western Māori seat in 1914 and 1922, then became the Labour Party's candidate in 1925, losing to Māui Pōmare. He played a crucial liaison role between Labour and the Rātana movement, organizing conferences and establishing Māori Labour committees. Appointed to the Legislative Council in 1936, he served until 1950 as the sole Māori member, championing Treaty of Waitangi rights, Māori welfare, and equal treatment. Throughout his over 30-year political career driven by Labour's principle of racial equality, Māwhete advocated for Māori interests in land, housing, health, and education, and participated in wartime Māori recruitment efforts. However, his efforts yielded mixed results, as the government abandoned policies he had helped develop and independent Māori political power was curtailed. Appointed OBE in 1959, he died in Palmerston North on 24 July 1961.

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history and development of New Zealand's Labour Party from its founding in 1916 through the early 2020s. Founded by left-wing organisations and trade unions, the party evolved from a union-based socialist movement to a broad-based social democratic party. The Labour Party achieved significant electoral success in 1935, winning 53 of 80 seats and forming the first Labour government (1935-1949), which introduced major social reforms including state housing, free health services, and government control of banks and broadcasting. Subsequent Labour governments served in 1957-60, 1972-75, 1984-90, 1999-2008, and 2017-2023. The 1984 Labour government under David Lange dramatically shifted toward neo-liberalism and "Rogernomics," privatizing state assets. Later governments under Helen Clark (1999-2008) and Jacinda Ardern (2017-23) retreated from neo-liberalism and governed under proportional representation and coalition arrangements. The party abandoned its explicit socialist objective in 1951, adopting social democratic principles. By the early 21st century, Labour evolved into a "catch-all" party drawing support across occupational, ethnic, gender, and educational groups. Women have been integral to the party since its inception, with notable figures including Elizabeth McCombs, Mabel Howard, Helen Clark, and Jacinda Ardern as prime ministers. The document outlines the party's organisational structure, including local branches, 11 affiliated unions, 72 electorate committees, six geographic regions, and national bodies for candidate selection and policy development.

chunkHighlights.text: In the first decades of the 20th century, industries grew strongly in New Zealand’s main cities and union membership also increased. The Labour Party was formed in this period as the political wing of the union movement, and was set up and financed by trade unions. Many union leaders adopted the ideas of Marxists and syndicalists, which had the revolutionary aim of overthrowing capitalism and abolishing the

wage-earning system. Their aims were expressed in Labour’s 1916 policy objective, which called for ‘the socialisation of the means of production, distribution and exchange’. 1 This meant state ownership and control of all major parts of the economy.
Party of the unions

Labour therefore began as a narrowly based sectional party. Its founding focus was on the needs of wage workers, who soon guaranteed the party a secure base in the poorer urban, milling and mining electorates. The party’s members were mostly the members of unions affiliated to the party (known as affiliate members). Individual members belonging to local party branches (general members) were at first a minority.
Widening appeal

To become a governing party, Labour had to widen its appeal to include other sections of the population. It began to do this in the 1920s and 1930s by shaping its policies to the specific problems of those times. The poverty and insecurity that spread through the community during the depression years made this transition easier.

3.fileDescription: James McCombs (1873-1933) was a pioneering New Zealand Labour politician and social reformer. Born in Ireland and emigrated to New Zealand in 1876, he became involved in socialist and prohibitionist movements before entering politics. Elected to Parliament in the 1913 Lyttelton by-election, McCombs served as the first president of the second New Zealand Labour Party (founded 1916) and later as deputy chairman. Throughout his 20-year parliamentary career, he championed prohibition, opposed conscription, advocated for proportional representation, and was notably progressive on women's rights, including efforts to enable women's election to Parliament and appointment as justices of the peace. Known for his debating skills and financial expertise, he opposed deflationary depression policies and advocated for central planning. He remained in opposition throughout his career and died in 1933, succeeded in his parliamentary seat by his wife Elizabeth.

chunkHighlights.text: With the formation of the National government by the Reform and Liberal parties in 1915, McCombs and four other members affiliated to the labour movement became the official opposition. The need for cohesive action led to the founding of the second New Zealand Labour Party in 1916. McCombs helped to draft its constitution and programme. He was also its first president but, objecting to the party's approach to prohibition, resigned his membership a year later. He rejoined the party in 1918 and served as deputy chairman from 1919 until 1923. In 1919 he tied the vote for its parliamentary leadership. When lots were drawn the post went to the more militant Harry Holland , with whom McCombs had clashed in 1917. The antagonism between the two men continued but McCombs's frequent challenges to Holland's leadership were unsuccessful.

4.fileDescription: Michael Joseph Savage (1872-1940) was an Irish-Australian-born New Zealand Labour politician who became the nation's first Labour Prime Minister. Born in Victoria, Australia, Savage emigrated to New Zealand in 1907 and became active in unionism and socialist movements in Auckland. Elected to Parliament in 1919 representing Auckland West, he became Labour leader in 1933. His advocacy for pensions, free healthcare, and workers' rights resonated during the Great Depression. Labour won the 1935 election with 55 of 80 seats, implementing progressive legislation including state house construction and Reserve Bank nationalization. At the 1937 Imperial Conference, Savage criticized Britain's appeasement policies. In 1938, despite terminal colon cancer, he championed the Social Security Bill, introducing universal free healthcare and pensions termed "applied Christianity." Labour's vote share increased from 46% to 56%. Savage died on March 27, 1940, leaving a legacy that fundamentally shaped New Zealand's social welfare system for generations.

5.fileDescription: John Kendrick Archer (1865-1949) was a prominent Baptist minister and New Zealand Labour Party leader. Born in Leicestershire, England, he was ordained in 1891 and served as a pastor in northern England before immigrating to New Zealand in 1908. Influenced by Baptist preacher John Clifford and committed to Christian socialism, Archer became a powerful advocate for social justice and workers' rights. In New Zealand, he held significant positions including president of the Baptist Union (1916-1918), mayor of Christchurch (1925-1931), and Labour Party president (1928-1929). Though unsuccessful in four parliamentary campaigns, he was appointed to the Legislative Council in 1937. Archer was known for his uncompromising moral stance, blending religious conviction with political activism, and remained active in church and community work until his death.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces New Zealand's historical trajectory from Māori settlement around 1250-1300 CE through the early 21st century. It covers Polynesian settlement and tribal societies, European discovery by Abel Tasman (1642) and James Cook (1769-70), and early European interaction through sealers, whalers, and traders. From 1814, missionaries introduced Christianity and European farming techniques. The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) established British sovereignty while guaranteeing Māori rights, though interpretation differences complicated implementation. European settlement escalated through the New Zealand Company, the 1852 Constitution Act, and land conflicts resulting in the Taranaki Wars and Waikato campaign with large-scale land confiscation. Economic development progressed through wool production, gold discoveries, Julius Vogel's public works program, and the frozen-meat industry. Politically, the Liberal Party's 1890 victory established a "family farm" economy, women's suffrage followed in 1893, and the First World War established the Anzac tradition. Labour's 1935 victory under Michael Joseph Savage introduced welfare reforms, while Labour's 1984 economic liberalization transformed the nation. From the 1970s onwards, New Zealand underwent bicultural and multicultural transformation, highlighted by the 1981 Springbok rugby tour, the Waitangi Tribunal's establishment (1975), Māori cultural renaissance and language revitalization, and the emergence of significant Pasifika and Asian populations.

chunkHighlights.text: Organised labour flexed its muscles in the 1890 maritime strike, and in the Waihī and waterside strikes of 1912–13. Setbacks on the industrial front turned the labour movement towards political action. The Labour Party , founded in 1916, made uneven gains through the 1920s, then was swept into power under Michael Joseph Savage in 1935 by an electorate disillusioned with how the conservative coalition government had handled the depression. When Savage died in 1940, Peter Fraser became prime minister .
Labour in power

In power, the Labour Party, aided by an economic recovery already under way when it was elected, revived the economy further by pragmatic rather than doctrinaire socialist policies. The Reserve Bank was taken over by the state in 1936, spending on public works increased, and a state housing programme began. The Social Security Act 1938 dramatically extended the welfare state.

7.fileDescription: James Thorn (1882-1956) was a prominent New Zealand labour activist and politician. Born in Christchurch to a butcher's family, Thorn initially worked as a moulder before serving in South Africa, where witnessing civilian casualties transformed him into a pacifist. Influenced by labour advocate Jack McCullough, he became deeply involved in labour organizing, serving as secretary of the metalworkers' union and helping organize agricultural labourers in Canterbury. He stood for Parliament in 1905 and 1908 with the Political Labour League before spending four years in Britain as a socialist propagandist. Arrested for anti-conscription activism during WWI, Thorn married Margaret Anderson in 1917 and spent the 1920s as editor of the Maoriland Worker and Labour Party official. He finally won parliamentary election in 1935 as member for Thames, serving 11 years with particular interest in collective security and the United Nations. After losing his seat in 1946, he served as High Commissioner to Canada and participated in drafting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. He died in 1956.

response.response_text:
## The Tohunga Suppression Act 1907

The Tohunga Suppression Act 1907 was a piece of New Zealand legislation that made it an offence to practise as a tohunga — a traditional Māori healer or spiritual expert. It remains one of the more controversial laws of the colonial era, touching on health policy, Māori cultural identity, and the enduring tensions between Western and traditional knowledge systems.

## Background: Why Was It Passed?

By the early 20th century, the tradition of the tohunga had already been weakened by colonisation. European diseases had proved difficult for tohunga to treat, which undermined confidence in traditional healing, and the whare wānanga (schools of higher learning) that had trained tohunga began to close. [[1]](cite://1/1)

Into this vacuum stepped a new type of practitioner — described as 'second class tohunga' — who lacked proper education and authority, and who were seen to exploit the superstitions of a people caught between two cultures, travelling from pā to pā (village to village) claiming to cure all manner of illness. By the early 1900s, these figures were regarded as a threat by both Pākehā and Māori authorities. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Health officials and police also lodged complaints that tohunga were endangering rather than enhancing Māori health — for example, by bathing the sick in cold water and administering alcohol. [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1)

## Who Drove the Legislation?

The Act grew out of concern over the practices of self-appointed tohunga, and was supported by a number of influential Māori figures. [[5]](cite://5/1)

- The Te Aute College Students' Association was particularly critical, believing tohunga could harm patients and hinder Māori progress. [[5]](cite://5/2)
- Prominent Māori doctors Māui Pōmare and Te Rangi Hīroa (Sir Peter Buck) spoke out against tohunga practices. Pōmare strongly supported the Act's introduction, driven by what he saw as preventable Māori deaths. [[5]](cite://5/3)[[4]](cite://4/2)
- The bill was presented to Parliament by Māori member of parliament James Carroll and was supported by all four Māori MPs. For Carroll, the Act reflected his impatience with what he considered regressive Māori attitudes. [[5]](cite://5/4)[[6]](cite://6/1)
- A health official named James Mason was also instrumental in the Act's passage, following his return to New Zealand in 1906. [[7]](cite://7/1)

## What Did the Act Say?

The Act's preamble stated that any person who gathered Māori around them by practising on their superstition or credulity, or who misled any Māori by professing to possess supernatural powers in the treatment of disease, foretelling of future events, or otherwise, was liable on conviction to a fine of up to £25 or imprisonment for up to six months. [[5]](cite://5/5)

## Rua Kēnana and Political Motivations

The Act has been seen by some as primarily directed at the Ngāi Tūhoe prophet Rua Kēnana, who had established an independent settlement at Maungapōhatu in the Urewera from 1907. Carroll regarded Rua as a charlatan who was drawing the Tūhoe people into isolation, and local police had been watching Rua since May 1906 on suspicion of acting as a tohunga. [[5]](cite://5/6)[[8]](cite://8/1)[[6]](cite://6/2)

Despite this, Rua was never actually charged under the Act. [[8]](cite://8/2)

## Enforcement — and Its Limits

In practice, the Act was rarely used. Few prosecutions were brought and even fewer convictions secured. Its main practical effect was to drive tohunga underground rather than eliminate the practice altogether. [[5]](cite://5/7)[[9]](cite://9/1)[[10]](cite://10/1)

The case of the tohunga Hikapuhi illustrates this well — she faced years of complaints and investigations, yet when Apirana Ngata urged in July 1909 that she be prosecuted under the Act, Carroll's response in May 1910 was simply 'No action'. [[11]](cite://11/1)

## Treaty of Waitangi Concerns

The Act has also been viewed as a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi), as it challenged traditional Māori wisdom — considered one of the taonga (treasures) that Māori were promised under the second article of the Treaty. [[5]](cite://5/8)

## Repeal and Legacy

The Tohunga Suppression Act was repealed in 1962. [[12]](cite://12/1)[[5]](cite://5/9) Twenty years later, health authorities began showing a willingness to accept traditional healing practices as complementary to Western medicine — even recognising tohunga and incorporating their work into the mainstream health system. [[12]](cite://12/2)

While the Act was not an outright assault on all aspects of traditional healing, it reinforced a broader cultural message that 'tohungaism' was undesirable — a message that sat uneasily alongside the promise of the Treaty and the enduring value Māori placed in their traditional knowledge. [[9]](cite://9/2)[[13]](cite://13/1)

---

Would you like to explore more about the revival of traditional Māori healing practices and rongoā (Māori medicine) in the decades after the Act was repealed?

1.document_title: Primary Health Care in New Zealand: A Comprehensive History from 1867 to the Early 21st Century
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of primary health care and the medical profession in New Zealand from 1867 to the early 21st century. It documents the transformation from family doctors, nurses, and midwives delivering care in the 1800s, through professionalization and self-regulation (Medical Practitioners' Act 1867, nursing registration 1901, midwifery registration 1911), to the modern primary health care system. Key developments include district nursing services, Plunket (1907), and the 1941 agreement maintaining fee-for-service payments with government subsidies. The document examines challenges of a two-tiered system with free hospital care but expensive GP visits, and traces reform efforts from the 1970s onwards, including midwife autonomy re-establishment (1990), alternative practitioners' emergence, and patient rights activism. Major reforms in the 1990s-2000s introduced contractual arrangements with GPs, independent practitioner associations (IPAs), and primary health organisations (PHOs) based on population-based funding with higher subsidies for disadvantaged populations. The 2015 zero-fee GP visits scheme for children under 13 represents the latest access initiative. The document also details Māori health care practices combining natural medicines and spiritual healing with European medicine.

2.text:
[Page 13] Māori still retained many of their traditional ideas about health. Officials in the health sector gradually developed a greater understanding of Māori approaches to health and sickness, and government policies showed a greater acceptance of these approaches and their value for health care. Tohunga still practised in many Māori communities, and Pākehā were increasingly willing to view their work more positively. The Tohunga Suppression Act was repealed in 1962. Twenty years later the health authorities began to show a willingness to accept traditional healing practices as complementary to Western medicine, and even to recognise tohunga and incorporate their work into the mainstream health system.

2.document_title: Te Hauora Māori: A Comprehensive History of Māori Health in New Zealand from Pre-European Times to the 20th Century
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

The Tohunga Suppression Act was presented by Māori MP James Carroll and supported by the four Māori members of parliament. It was passed in 1907. The preamble read: Every person who gathers Maoris around him by practising on their superstition or credulity, or who misleads or attempts to mislead any Maori by professing or pretending to possess supernatural powers in the treatment or cure of any disease, or in the foretelling of future events, or otherwise, is liable on summary conviction before a Magistrate to a fine not exceeding twenty five pounds or to imprisonment for a period not exceeding six months. The Act has also been viewed as a breach of the Treaty of Waitangi, as it challenged traditional Māori wisdom considered to be one of the taonga (treasures) that Māori were promised under the second article of the Treaty.

3.document_title: Rongoā: Traditional Māori Healing Practices, Medicinal Plants, and Cultural Revival
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores rongoā, the traditional Māori healing system encompassing herbal remedies, physical therapies, and spiritual healing practices. It details how Māori classified illnesses into mate atua (supernatural diseases caused by broken tapu and malevolent spirits) and mate tangata (physical ailments), with tohunga (priests) treating each through specialized methods including exorcism, purificatory rites, and herbal treatments. The document catalogs over 200 medicinal plants used in traditional Māori medicine, with detailed applications for key species including harakeke (flax), kawakawa (pepper tree), mānuka, kōwhai, kūmarahou, rātā, koromiko, tētēaweka, and rimu. It examines the historical impact of European colonization, which introduced new illnesses that traditional healers could not cure, leading to declining faith in rongoā and the 1907 Tohunga Suppression Act that criminalized traditional practitioners. The document discusses how this act was repealed in 1962 and how rongoā experienced significant revival from the late 20th century due to resurgence of Māori culture, loss of confidence in Western medicine, and demand for spiritual dimensions in healing. Modern rongoā practitioners differ from traditional tohunga, with variable informal training and eclectic practices that often incorporate Western and other medical systems. The establishment of Ngā Ringa Whakahaere o te Iwi Māori in 1993 marks an important institutional development for Māori healers.

6.document_title: Māori Land Rights, Indigenous Law, and Colonial Legislation in New Zealand: A Historical and Legal Analysis
6.document_summary:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

7.text:
[Page 12] Healers unite Ngā Ringa Whakahaere o te Iwi Māori, a national body of Māori healers, was set up in 1993. It aims to be an authoritative and unified voice for traditional Māori healing, and to uphold, promote, protect and sustain its practice. It is the only legally constituted body that speaks for a large number of healers.

8.document_title: Te Hauora Māori: A Comprehensive History of Māori Health in New Zealand from Pre-European Times to the 20th Century
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

9.document_title: Māori Land Rights, Indigenous Law, and Colonial Legislation in New Zealand: A Historical and Legal Analysis
9.document_summary:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

10.text:
[Page 12] Modern healers Today’s healers differ significantly from the tohunga of old times. Training is highly variable, usually informal, and often less tribally bound than the rigorous education of the whare wānanga (house of higher learning). Many modern healers work in urban clinics, some alongside mainstream health professionals. They experiment, incorporating knowledge and practices from Western and other medical systems. As a result their work is idiosyncratic, with no standard system of diagnosis or consensus about treatments. Despite this, many healers are recognised as having knowledge and ability that has been passed down from their whānau , hapū or iwi .

10.document_title: Rongoā: Traditional Māori Healing Practices, Medicinal Plants, and Cultural Revival
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores rongoā, the traditional Māori healing system encompassing herbal remedies, physical therapies, and spiritual healing practices. It details how Māori classified illnesses into mate atua (supernatural diseases caused by broken tapu and malevolent spirits) and mate tangata (physical ailments), with tohunga (priests) treating each through specialized methods including exorcism, purificatory rites, and herbal treatments. The document catalogs over 200 medicinal plants used in traditional Māori medicine, with detailed applications for key species including harakeke (flax), kawakawa (pepper tree), mānuka, kōwhai, kūmarahou, rātā, koromiko, tētēaweka, and rimu. It examines the historical impact of European colonization, which introduced new illnesses that traditional healers could not cure, leading to declining faith in rongoā and the 1907 Tohunga Suppression Act that criminalized traditional practitioners. The document discusses how this act was repealed in 1962 and how rongoā experienced significant revival from the late 20th century due to resurgence of Māori culture, loss of confidence in Western medicine, and demand for spiritual dimensions in healing. Modern rongoā practitioners differ from traditional tohunga, with variable informal training and eclectic practices that often incorporate Western and other medical systems. The establishment of Ngā Ringa Whakahaere o te Iwi Māori in 1993 marks an important institutional development for Māori healers.

11.document_title: Traditional Māori Religion, Spirituality, and Sacred Practices: Comprehensive Study of Atua, Tohunga, Karakia, and Tapu
11.document_summary:
This comprehensive document provides an in-depth exploration of traditional Māori religion and spiritual practices. It begins with creation mythology detailing Te Kore (the void), Te Pō (the night), and Te Ao Mārama (the world of light), followed by the separation of Ranginui (sky father) and Papatūānuku (earth mother). The text explains major atua (gods) including Tāne (forests), Tangaroa (sea), Rongo (cultivated food), and Tūmatauenga (war), and discusses whether Io existed as a supreme being in pre-European Māori tradition.

The document extensively covers tohunga (priests and experts) who served as mediums for gods and spirits, acted as diviners (matakite), and served as healers and ritual guides. Key spiritual concepts explored include mana (power from gods and ancestors), tapu (sacred restrictions), noa (freedom from restrictions), mauri (life principle), hau (vital essence), and wairua (spirit).

A major focus is on karakia—formulas of words chanted to communicate with gods. The document describes various types of karakia used for love charms, healing, warfare, and childbirth. It details major life-cycle rituals including tūā (naming ceremony), tohi (child dedication), and pure (spiritual empowerment), along with ceremonies such as ngau paepae (warrior empowerment), rāhui (tapu placement), and whāngai hau (ceremonial food offerings). Sacred places (wāhi tapu), shrines (tūāhu), and ritual objects like godsticks are discussed in relation to ensuring fertility and protection, reflecting the Māori worldview where spiritual forces permeate all aspects of life.

12.text:
[Page 9] The impact of colonisation Colonisation by Europeans had a significant effect on traditional Māori healing. Tohunga had limited ability to combat the diseases brought by Europeans. Though Western medicine was also relatively ineffectual at the time, this failure still strongly affected Māori confidence in tohunga . Some Pākehā missionaries attributed the spread of disease to a lack of Christian faith. As their own healers appeared impotent, many Māori accepted this explanation and turned to Christianity. Over time, the whare wānanga (schools of higher learning) which had trained tohunga started to close. The tradition of the tohunga declined.

15.document_title: Fields of Plenty: The Revival of Herbal Medicine and Medicinal Herbs Industry in New Zealand
15.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores the resurgence of herbal medicine in New Zealand, examining its historical roots, contemporary revival, and industry development potential. The articles trace how traditional Māori medicine (rongoā) and European herbalism were marginalized through 20th-century legislation but have experienced renewed interest since the 1980s. Featured practitioners demonstrate practical applications of wild-crafting and garden-based healing traditions. New Zealand's excellent growing conditions support cultivation of high-value medicinal herbs such as arnica, mānuka, kumarahou, horopito, and St John's Wort, with successful local initiatives like Tairawhiti Pharmaceuticals and Forest Herbs Research. Key challenges include international certification requirements (GMP standards), regulatory frameworks, and intellectual property concerns regarding indigenous Māori plants following the Wai 262 claim. The collection emphasizes tensions between holistic plant-based healing and scientific validation, while addressing global threats to medicinal plant species and advocating for conservation efforts and "barefoot doctoring" using readily available garden herbs as primary healthcare. The government's recent agreement to regulate medical herbalism signals growing recognition of herbal medicine's role in sustainable healthcare.

16.text:

19.document_title: Tūhoe: Self-Determination, Cultural Identity, and the Struggle for Te Urewera
19.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the Tūhoe iwi (tribe) of New Zealand and their 150-year struggle toward self-determination and cultural restoration. It traces Tūhoe's resistance against colonial dominance, land confiscation, and systematic violence—including the 1916 arrest of Rua Kēnana and Te Kooti's legendary resistance. The narrative examines historical trauma from military raids and the 1921 repeal of the 1896 Urewera District Native Reserve Act that had granted them autonomy. Central to the document is Tūhoetanga—the essence of Tūhoe identity—and how the iwi maintains cultural continuity through traditional practices, tikanga programs, and intergenerational knowledge transmission despite 85% living away from their ancestral homeland. The text details Tūhoe's commitment to land rights and rejection of Crown offers excluding land return, culminating in the 2012 settlement including financial redress, control of Te Urewera National Park, and a pathway to self-governance. Through personal narratives and historical analysis, the document illustrates how Tūhoe pursues mana motuhake (self-determination) by reclaiming cultural practices, developing a 40-year blueprint for independence, and redefining ownership through mana whenua principles. The work demonstrates Tūhoe's resilience in maintaining traditions, rebuilding identity through wānanga and cultural programs, and navigating ongoing injustices while seeking existential healing and autonomy.

20.text:
[Page 4] Despite its popularity, however, herbalism and rongoā Māori had—and continue to have—their detractors. In 1907, Neil, then president of the fledgling New Zealand Association of Medical Herbalists (NZAMH), petitioned Parliament for legal status for herbalists. He was unsuccessful. According to one letter writer to the Evening Post, “The stewer of drugs is obsolete.” In 1939, faith healer turned herbalist Bill Anderton—a Labour MP for 25 years and grandfather of 1984 88 finance minister Roger Douglas—applied again for separate registration. A government compromise, whereby registered medical herbalists would be dependent on GP referral, was declined. According to former NZAMH president Joan Flynn, Anderton recognised that, while herbal medicine can be complementary to orthodox medicine, “it can also provide a complete alternative for many patients”.

On Savai`i he found that healers were using bark to treat hepatitis. “Hepatitis is viral, and I got interested because we don’t have anything to treat virals.” Cox discovered the active molecule appeared to have some promise for treating AIDS. Cox is not involved for the money. “I made sure the intellectual property rights and the patent belong to the Samoans.” Samoans place great value on natural medicine. Earlier I had watched a natural healer treat a young boy for an upset stomach. There was a power in her performance, a healing sense that lay in the ritual: the shaving and scraping of the root, the mortar and pestle percussion of boulder against hardwood as she pounded the fibre. This was no perfunctory prescription. The mixture released a faint ginger tang into the room. She scooped the crushed fibre into a square of linen, twisted it and wrung a milky fluid from the fibre into a cup. She called for the boy. He left the TV game show he had been watching and presented his tongue for a spoonful of mixture, immediately wincing at the taste. With a conjurer’s aplomb the healer whipped a ball of crushed root and leaf into his mouth, and plucked it out just as quickly. By now he’d had enough. With a firm hand she pinned him to the floor. 22.document_title: Samoa: A Comprehensive Exploration of Culture, Tradition, and Modernity
22.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection presents an in-depth exploration of Samoa through multiple perspectives. It examines the contradictions between Samoa's idyllic image and complex realities of fa'a Samoa, including tensions between traditional matai authority and individual freedoms, and high emigration rates to New Zealand. The collection covers Samoa's colonial history, including the 1918 influenza epidemic and the Mau independence movement, alongside contemporary journalism challenging corruption. Village governance through the fono system is analyzed, exploring how traditional authority maintains social order while restricting individual expression and contributing to high suicide rates. Religious dimensions include Christianity, Mormonism, and Baha'i, alongside cultural elements like traditional tattooing (pe'a), siapo cloth-making, and the role of fa'afafine in society. Environmental challenges include cyclone recovery and conservation efforts, while economic realities involve low wages, tourism, remittances, and aid dependence. A critical comparison between Western Samoa and American Samoa reveals how modernization and American individualism have paradoxically improved mental health outcomes while challenging cultural preservation. The work explores the fundamental paradox of Samoan society: communal values and cultural pride coexisting with oppressive social controls, limited economic opportunities, and psychological stress.

24.document_title: Fields of Plenty: The Revival of Herbal Medicine and Medicinal Herbs Industry in New Zealand
24.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores the resurgence of herbal medicine in New Zealand, examining its historical roots, contemporary revival, and industry development potential. The articles trace how traditional Māori medicine (rongoā) and European herbalism were marginalized through 20th-century legislation but have experienced renewed interest since the 1980s. Featured practitioners demonstrate practical applications of wild-crafting and garden-based healing traditions. New Zealand's excellent growing conditions support cultivation of high-value medicinal herbs such as arnica, mānuka, kumarahou, horopito, and St John's Wort, with successful local initiatives like Tairawhiti Pharmaceuticals and Forest Herbs Research. Key challenges include international certification requirements (GMP standards), regulatory frameworks, and intellectual property concerns regarding indigenous Māori plants following the Wai 262 claim. The collection emphasizes tensions between holistic plant-based healing and scientific validation, while addressing global threats to medicinal plant species and advocating for conservation efforts and "barefoot doctoring" using readily available garden herbs as primary healthcare. The government's recent agreement to regulate medical herbalism signals growing recognition of herbal medicine's role in sustainable healthcare.

33.document_title: Rua Kēnana Hepetipa: The Māori Spiritual Leader, Messiah, and Legacy of Maungapōhatu
33.document_summary: This document chronicles the life and spiritual leadership of Rua Kēnana Hepetipa, a pivotal Māori religious and political figure. Born to Ngāti Kahungunu and Tūhoe descent, Rua emerged as the claimed successor to Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Tūruki within two years of the latter's death in 1893. Following a supernatural revelation on Maungapōhatu mountain in 1905-1906, where he encountered the archangel Gabriel and was baptized as Hepetipa, Rua established the "City of God" at Maungapōhatu in 1907. His community, the Iharaira (Israelites), adopted Nazarite practices and constructed Hīona (Zion), a circular meeting house modeled after the Dome of the Rock. Through strategic marriages to twelve women, Rua linked the Tūhoe and Te Whakatōhea tribes. The community initially succeeded but declined due to harsh conditions and infrastructure challenges. A pivotal moment came with Rua's 1915 arrest for illicitly selling alcohol, politically motivated due to his pacifist stance during World War I. This led to the April 2, 1916 armed police expedition—the worst police-Māori clash of the century, with two Māori killed. Rua's subsequent Supreme Court trial, the longest in New Zealand's legal history until 1977, resulted in his conviction for resisting arrest and imprisonment. Released in 1918, Rua rebuilt Maungapōhatu and attempted to create an economically viable community, though it ultimately failed. Despite government surveillance and the Tohunga Suppression Act, Rua met Prime Minister Joseph Ward in 1908, advocating for equal laws for Māori and Pākehā. His legacy as a visionary leader for a dispossessed people endures in New Zealand's cultural imagination.

34.document_title: James Carroll: Bicultural Pioneer, Māori Political Leader, and Land Administrator in New Zealand
34.document_summary: James Carroll (Timi Kara, b. 1857) was a transformative bicultural figure in New Zealand history, born to an Irish father and Ngāti Kahungunu mother in Wairoa. Raised bilingually with Māori as his first language, Carroll pursued a pioneering career bridging European and Māori worlds. He served as interpreter to Parliament (1879-1883) before winning the Eastern Māori seat in 1887, later representing Waiapu (1893-1908) and Gisborne (1908-1919). As the first Māori to hold the Native Affairs portfolio (1899-1912), Carroll became pivotal in Māori land administration. Key achievements include securing the Urewera District Native Reserve Act 1896, establishing Māori Councils and Land Administration Acts (1900), and implementing the Native Land Act 1909. Carroll advocated for Māori economic empowerment and equality, opposing Crown pre-emption of land and supporting leasing arrangements. He championed land management committees and body corporate structures for Māori landowners while opposing separatist movements like Te Kotahitanga. Despite facing intense pressure from Pākehā opposition demanding land alienation, Carroll implemented land incorporations and enabled Māori farming development. Though unable to prevent significant Māori land loss, his diplomatic skills and unwavering commitment earned him respect from both Māori elders and the Pākehā establishment.

35.document_title: Tūtekohi Rangi: A Māori Faith Healer and the Tūtekohi Movement
35.document_summary: Tūtekohi Rangi (c. 1871-1956), also known as Wiremu Retimana Rangi or Richmond Rangi, was a Māori expert in lore and carving from Mangatuna on the East Coast. From the 1930s, he established a reputation as a faith healer and tohunga, leading the Tūtekohi movement—an unregistered Anglican offshoot featuring religious meetings that attracted 200-300 followers by 1949. The movement held meetings across five locations, drawing invalids with tuberculosis and other ailments seeking cures. Meetings lasted 4-8 weeks, disrupting employment, domestic life, and children's schooling, prompting concerns from health officials and police. Despite attempts to suppress the movement under the Tohunga Suppression Act 1907, neither government nor tribal authorities successfully intervened, partly due to Māori reluctance to oppose a tohunga. The movement likely ended with Tūtekohi's death on 21 February 1956.

36.document_title: James Malcolm Mason: Pioneer of New Zealand's Public Health System
36.document_summary: James Malcolm Mason (1864-1924) was a Scottish-born physician who became New Zealand's first chief health officer. After studying medicine in Edinburgh and Glasgow, he practiced in Portsmouth and Blyth before emigrating to New Zealand in 1895. Mason established the Ōtaki cottage hospital and gained prominence through his bacteriological expertise and public health advocacy. In 1900, he was appointed chief health officer following the Public Health Act 1900, which established one of the world's first national departments of public health. His tenure focused on preventive health, vaccination, sanitation, tuberculosis control, and Māori health. He edited the New Zealand Medical Journal, established tuberculosis sanatoriums, and influenced the creation of Plunket nurses. Despite recurring ill health, Mason served with distinction until 1909, later practicing privately and serving in WWI. He died in 1924, remembered for his far-sighted contributions to New Zealand's public health development.

He developed the technique of using a microscope to show people the micro organisms that inhabited impure water. He also had slides of the various microbes to show to sceptics. In a number of his reports Pōmare commented bitterly about the mortality that some of the new breed of tohunga caused; for example, by attempting to heal the sick by bathing them in cold water and administering alcohol. Although Pōmare believed that the decline in Māori numbers could be halted by the correct medical methods, he also saw that the nature of the Māori population was changing; a new population with European ancestry was emerging and he considered that they would have the best characteristics of both races. Unlike Apirana Ngata , who was concerned over the loss of Māori identity, Pōmare welcomed intermarriage and Māori acculturation. From 1902 to 1910 Pōmare reported to Parliament on his work in a series of exuberant reports in which he dealt not only with medical matters but also gave his opinion on a number of issues, including education and land tenure, at times earning rebukes from his superiors. 37.document_title: Māui Pōmare: Māori Leader, Health Reformer, and Political Pioneer
37.document_summary: Māui Wiremu Piti Naera Pōmare (1875/1876-1930) was a transformative Māori leader and New Zealand's first Māori health officer. Born in Taranaki to parents with connections to Ngāti Toa and Ngāti Mutunga, Pōmare was educated at Te Aute College and studied medicine in the United States, graduating MD from American Medical Missionary College in 1899. As Māori health officer from 1901, he pioneered health reform initiatives including sanitation improvements and village inspections. He organized the 1901 royal hui at Rotorua and supported the Tohunga Suppression Act. Elected to Parliament in 1911 representing the Western Māori seat, Pōmare served in various ministerial roles under William Massey's Reform Party. His major achievements include securing compulsory registration of Māori births and deaths (1913), negotiating the West Coast Settlement Reserves Amendment Act (1913) to address land confiscation grievances, and chairing Māori recruitment during WWI. As Cook Islands minister (1916-1928), he increased funding and improved services. As Health Minister (1923-1926), he launched a safe maternity campaign that dramatically reduced puerperal sepsis deaths through improved asepsis techniques and midwifery training. Collaborating with Ngata, Pōmare established a royal commission into land confiscations (1926), securing compensation for Taranaki and Waikato. He died of tuberculosis in 1930, leaving a legacy of bridging Māori and Pākehā worlds while advancing indigenous welfare.

38.document_title: Mārama Russell: A Māori Healer, Midwife and Seer
38.document_summary: Mārama Moetara Russell (c. 1875-1952) was a prominent Māori healer, midwife, and seer from Hokianga, New Zealand. Born into a respected Te Roroa and Ngāti Korokoro family with strong ancestral connections to Treaty of Waitangi signatories, she married Frederick George Russell in 1897 and had 14 children. From her mid-30s, Mārama practiced traditional Māori healing for 40 years, specializing in mate Māori (Māori illnesses) using natural remedies like flax, pirikahu plants, and tōtara splints. As a skilled midwife, she assisted with childbirth, infertility treatment, and gender determination. Her reputation as a seer extended to diagnosing illnesses before symptoms were described and commanding spirits. A committed Anglican who reconciled her faith with traditional beliefs, Mārama reinforced the Māori holistic worldview by restoring balance and wholeness, particularly addressing tapu violations and utu requirements. Her practice served as a counterpoint to tohunga makutu, and many Māori patients preferred her remedies to Pākehā medicine.

39.document_title: Hikapuhi: A Māori Healer and Her Legacy
39.document_summary: Hikapuhi (Te Hikapuhi Poihipi) was a prominent Māori healer born between 1860-1871 in Rotorua to parents of Ngāti Te Rangiunuora descent. She rose to prominence around 1905, calling herself a nurse rather than a tohunga, and traveled throughout New Zealand administering Three Star brandy as medicine accompanied by healing words. Though credited with miracles including curing blindness, her credibility suffered after a prominent chief died following her treatment. Government officials, including health officer Māui Pōmare, attempted to suppress her activities due to concerns about alcohol distribution, particularly to children. However, many Māori patients testified to her compassion and effectiveness, as she provided free medical care to those unable to afford European doctors. Despite petitions supporting her work and her acquittal by the Rongokako Council, official disapproval and the irresponsible actions of some followers undermined her practice. Her activities gradually ceased after 1913, and she died in Rotorua on 6 January 1934. Hikapuhi represented both a symbol of Māori spiritual healing and European establishment failure, providing essential healthcare to marginalized communities.

40.document_title: Bush, Alice Mary: Pioneer Paediatrician and Family Planning Advocate
40.document_summary: Alice Mary Bush (1914-1974) was a pioneering New Zealand paediatrician and family planning advocate. Born in Auckland, she earned her medical degree from the University of Otago in 1937 and became the first New Zealand woman to achieve fellowship in the Royal Australasian College of Physicians (1955) and the Royal College of Physicians of London (1970). Bush established a thriving private paediatric practice in Auckland and was instrumental in developing paediatric services in New Zealand, founding the Paediatric Society of New Zealand in 1947. She is best remembered for her advocacy work in family planning, serving as president of the New Zealand Family Planning Association and securing medical association approval for doctors to work in NZFPA clinics in 1961. Bush championed women's health and children's welfare, believing planned families supported social stability. She died in 1974 at age 59, leaving a legacy memorialized through the Alice Bush Family Planning Clinic and Memorial Prize.

Her work was undermined by the irresponsible actions of some of her disciples. The last mention of her working in Wairarapa was in 1913. When she visited Wellington in 1915 it is clear that her vogue was at an end. Her husband died in Ōhinemutu, Rotorua, on 13 June 1913. Hikapuhi may have returned to her Te Arawa kin at this time; she died in Rotorua on 6 January 1934. Hikapuhi's powers as a prophet and tohunga put her patients in touch with the Māori cosmogony, healed their spirit and gave them hope. Her achievement was summed up by A. L. D. Fraser in the course of condemning her: she 'went from town to town and from kāinga to kāinga , and as she wandered all through the colony her mana spread with her. She had a halo, a glamour of almost godlike attributes'. To Europeans and to the Māori establishment Hikapuhi was a nuisance and a symbol of their own failure; to many Māori she provided the only medical care they were likely to get.

41.document_title: Hikapuhi: A Māori Healer and Her Legacy
41.document_summary: Hikapuhi (Te Hikapuhi Poihipi) was a prominent Māori healer born between 1860-1871 in Rotorua to parents of Ngāti Te Rangiunuora descent. She rose to prominence around 1905, calling herself a nurse rather than a tohunga, and traveled throughout New Zealand administering Three Star brandy as medicine accompanied by healing words. Though credited with miracles including curing blindness, her credibility suffered after a prominent chief died following her treatment. Government officials, including health officer Māui Pōmare, attempted to suppress her activities due to concerns about alcohol distribution, particularly to children. However, many Māori patients testified to her compassion and effectiveness, as she provided free medical care to those unable to afford European doctors. Despite petitions supporting her work and her acquittal by the Rongokako Council, official disapproval and the irresponsible actions of some followers undermined her practice. Her activities gradually ceased after 1913, and she died in Rotorua on 6 January 1934. Hikapuhi represented both a symbol of Māori spiritual healing and European establishment failure, providing essential healthcare to marginalized communities.

[Page 7] Tomoana's greatest achievement as a member of Te Kotahitanga was to present to the native minister in June 1893 a draft Federated Māori Assembly Empowering Bill, and a petition listing Māori grievances. The bill asked for power over Māori to be delegated to Te Kotahitanga, subject only to the governor. In 1893 Tomoana took up the cause of Tūhoe who were resisting the survey of their land, and circulated a petition on their behalf throughout Hawke's Bay. This action led Premier Richard Seddon to release Tūhoe prisoners. In the 1898 session of the Kotahitanga parliament at Papawai, Wairarapa, the main item of business was discussion of Seddon's bill to set up Māori land boards, which threatened to further reduce Māori control of their land. Tomoana took, as always, a moderate line, accepting the bill as a basis for discussion where most others regarded it as a violation of the rules and procedures of the Māori parliament.

42.document_title: Hēnare Tomoana: Māori Chief, Political Leader, and Legacy of Self-Determination
42.document_summary: Hēnare Tomoana (c. 1820s-1830s) was a prominent Māori chief from Heretaunga, Hawke's Bay, descended from high-ranking lineages including Ngāti Hāwea. After converting to Christianity in 1852, he became involved in land transactions and military campaigns against Te Kooti (1868-1869). Lack of government compensation deepened his financial crisis, resulting in the loss of his Heretaunga block share by 1869. Disillusioned with government treatment, Tomoana emerged as a leading figure in the Hawke's Bay Repudiation movement from 1873, founding and editing Te Wānanga newspaper to educate Māori about land issues and European business practices. Elected to Parliament for Eastern Māori in 1879, he advocated for Māori land law reform and successfully introduced a bill establishing local Māori committees to adjudicate land titles, leading to the 1883 Native Committees Act. As a House member and senior chief, Tomoana became a principal figure in Te Kotahitanga, the movement for an independent Māori parliament, serving as Speaker of the Great Council. His major achievement was presenting a draft Federated Māori Assembly Empowering Bill to the native minister in 1893, seeking delegated power over Māori affairs. Known for his moderate approach balancing advocacy with pragmatism, Tomoana earned appointment to the Legislative Council in 1898, a position he held until his death in 1904. His legacy reflects a lifelong commitment to Māori self-governance and land rights protection.

43.document_title: Patient Safety Advocates Oppose Government Plans to Drop Therapeutic Products Act
43.document_summary: Patient safety advocates and legal experts express alarm over the government's plan to repeal the Therapeutic Products Act (TPA), which was signed into law in July 2024 and scheduled to take effect in 2026. The TPA would have modernized regulation of medicines, natural health products, and medical devices—bringing them under a unified regulatory framework similar to drugs. Critics, including Carmel Berry from Mesh Downunder and legal expert Dr. Laura Hardcastle, warn that scrapping the act will leave New Zealanders vulnerable to harm from inadequately regulated medical devices. They cite historical failures including surgical mesh implants, faulty pacemakers, and metal-on-metal joints that caused significant injury and cost ACC over $32.5 million in claims. The current 1981 Medicines Act is outdated and provides minimal pre-market assessment or mandatory reporting of adverse events. However, the Medical Technology Association argues the TPA represents regulatory overreach, claiming most medical devices already have overseas approvals and that harmonizing with international regulators like the US FDA and Australia's TGA is sufficient. Legal experts counter that the US FDA's 510(k) fast-track process has been criticized for insufficient rigor, allowing some devices to be licensed despite original models being withdrawn for ineffectiveness or harm.

A Waitangi Tribunal inquiry report has warned government that a repeal of Section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act could cause harm to children in care. Jackson said the National Party was instrumental to introducing Section 7AA and worked alongside Tariana Turia and the Māori Party to bring it together. "I give National credit for actually cobbling together that legislation and actually saying let's try and find who their parents were, lets try and find their whakapapa Māori because statistics tell us that once they know something about their history and their background they're better off for it." In an interview with Morning Report Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said he would not be commenting on the report and had not had a chance to read it. Jackson said the government had disrespected the Waitangi Tribunal and would be foolish to ignore the advice of such a knowledgeable panel of people. "It's sad the way they went after the tribunal. I see the tribunal as incredibly important part of our history and I don't like the disrespect that was shown to the tribunal particularly by David Seymour who thinks that his party has more mana than some of the most respected Māori leaders of this country who are on the tribunal" In its report the tribunal also asked the government to consider allowing time for a periodic review of the legislation which would provide a considered analysis of Section 7AA to the Minister for Children by 1 July next year. Tribunal claimants appealed a High Court decision last week which overturned a tribunal summons ordering the Minister for Children to provide evidence at the inquiry. [Page 1] Traditional Chinese medicine finding a place in New Zealand ByLiu Chen Journalist, RNZ (RNZ Chinese), RNZ Asia 2026 05 22 08:07:27+12:00 https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.ht ml?videoId=6395186517112 Auckland acupuncturist Selwyn Wong Doo still remembers a time when he was helping at his father's clinic wearing a school uniform. His father, William, opened the first Chinese medicine clinic in Auckland in 1939, eventually serving as the founding president of Acupuncture New Zealand. Wong Doo, 71, said his father was blindfolded and led to a monastery in China to learn his skills before practising in New Zealand. "I remember him saying that he got scared once and gave up acupuncture because one of his clients said he was doing witchcraft and had the police come and knock on his door," he said. Selwyn Wong Doo, 71, is a traditional Chinese medicine practitioner. His father stopped offering acupuncture treatment for a while, carrying on with Chinese herbs, massages and diet, before picking it up again in the 1960s. Acupuncture gained some prominence in North America in the early 1970s after The New York Times published a first hand experience of acupuncture and moxibustion in China in July 1971. That was just before US President Richard Nixon visited China in February 1972. "My Dad in those days had about a six months' waiting list of people wanting to come and see him because he would have been one of the very few around at that time," Wong Doo said. Selwyn Wong Doo's late father, William Naturally, Wong Doo picked up the skills and carried on the family practice. In 1977, a bill was introduced to Parliament to restrict the practice of acupuncture to registered medical doctors, physiotherapists or dentists, he said. While such professions typically didn't know about acupuncture, professional practitioners would not be able to continue to offer such services if the bill went through. In a bid to retain their roles, a small group of acupuncturists gathered in Auckland and started the New Zealand Register of Acupuncturists that same year. The organisation is now known as Acupuncture New Zealand. "I think a lot of people understand acupuncture now," Wong Doo said. Renjie Xi, vice president of Acupuncture New Zealand Traditional Chinese medicine has deep roots in New Zealand, with evidence of the practice dating back to gold fields in the 19th century, said Renjie Xi, vice president of Acupuncture New Zealand. Much of its modern history had been associated with Acupuncture New Zealand, he said, adding that the establishment of regulatory body Chinese Medicine Council in 2021 was something of a landmark for the profession. "Today, Chinese medicine is a fully regulated health profession under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act, with more than 1300 registered practitioners nationwide," Xi said. All practitioners must be registered with the council, hold an annual practicing certificate and demonstrate ongoing competence, he said. Acupuncture, herbal medicine and tuina (Chinese massage) were the most representative therapeutic techniques, which were also the most widely practised services in New Zealand, Xi said. Cupping, moxibustion, gua sha (scraping therapy) were common complimentary treatments, he said. Gordon Zheng with some traditional Chinese herbs Gordon Zheng's Beijing Chinese Medicine Clinic on Dominion Road in Auckland is a practice that offers a bit of everything. Having studied at an institute now known as the Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, he started one of the first few Chinese medicine clinics in Auckland in 1992. "We were the third in Auckland, I think," Zheng said. "I'd estimate that there are probably more than 200 clinics in Auckland now." Although his patients were predominantly Chinese at the beginning, these days Zheng has a mixture of patients from all ethnic backgrounds, with some using his services for more than 20 years. A patient being treated with acupuncture at Gordon Zheng's clinic. "Many conditions can be regulated with acupuncture," Zheng said. "For example, facial paralysis and strokes can both be treated with acupuncture, and even conditions such as hypertension and diabetes can be managed with it. Traditional Chinese medicine was an empirical science, he said. "It relies on doctors accumulating experience through long term clinical practice over many years," he said. Traditional Chinese medicine carried an element of risk if not handled well, he said. For example, he said, needles could be inserted too deep, or the toxicity of certain herbs unconsidered. Caren Chen explains the structure of a human knee joint. Operating on Auckland's North Shore for five years, Caren Chen's Happipuncture Clinic has gradually built a loyal client base. Chen trained for seven years at the Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, working at a hospital before coming to New Zealand. Traditional Chinese medicine was specifically tailored to an individual, and two people experiencing a headache could be given different herbs and acupuncture treatment, Chen said. "I think traditional Chinese medicine is more of a holistic view that combines heaven, Earth and humanity," she said. Chen believed the best care could be provided to patients when combining traditional Chinese medicine with Western medicine. As such, her clinic offers physiotherapy and massage services. Moxibustion at Caren Chen's clinic "For example, when treating patients with pain or neuromuscular issues, in addition to considering meridians and acupuncture points from a traditional Chinese medicine perspective, we also think about muscle anatomy and exercise science from a Western medical perspective," Chen said. "We can keep preserve the good parts of [Chinese medicine] traditions the essence of them while also continuing to learn from Western culture." Recognition of Chinese medicine appeared to have grown in New Zealand over the past decade, but there was a long way to go, Chen said. "I think more people in New Zealand are gradually becoming exposed to and accepting traditional Chinese medicine and acupuncture, and many are increasingly placing their trust in these treatments, I believe that is a positive thing," she said. "From the perspective of practitioners, we also hope to continue improving ourselves overall whether that's our professional skills, cultural understanding or English proficiency. "I think that is the only way traditional Chinese medicine can develop more successfully in Western countries." Chinese Medicine Council chair Paddy McBride Chinese Medicine Council chair Paddy McBride said awareness of the benefits of Chinese medicine was growing not only in New Zealand but globally. "Chinese medicine has a history of many thousands of years and has strong emphasis on staying well rather than waiting to seek treatment only when something has gone wrong," she said. "The Chinese Medicine Council of New Zealand would like all New Zealanders to know that the profession is regulated and that Chinese medicine is a safe, valid choice to meet their health care needs." McBride would like to see traditional Chinese medicine incorporated into and offered within the public health system, as it is in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan. "Currently practitioners are working in private practice, and the cost of treatment is beyond many who would greatly benefit from the different aspects of Chinese medicine." Caren Chen treats a patient with a massage. Jacqui Lunday, Health New Zealand's national chief for allied health, said the organisation recognised that cultural beliefs, traditions and practices could influence an individual's health experience and treatment preferences. "Practitioners are expected to demonstrate cultural competence as part of their core professional practice, which includes acknowledging and respecting culturally specific approaches, while ensuring care is delivered safely and aligns with recognised standards and best practice," Lunday said. A Ministry of Health spokesperson said traditional Chinese medicine was regulated similarly to other allied health professions such as physiotherapists, podiatrists and chiropractors. "While some allied health professional services are offered in the public health system (such as occupational therapy and speech language therapy), this does not routinely include traditional Chinese medicine," the spokesperson said. "Some traditional Chinese treatments, like acupuncture, can be funded by ACC." RELATED
