45.document_title: Traditional Chinese Medicine Finding a Place in New Zealand
45.document_summary: This article explores the growing establishment and recognition of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) in New Zealand. It traces the history from the first Chinese medicine clinic opened in Auckland in 1939 by William Wong Doo, through early challenges including police scrutiny and restrictive legislation in 1977. The article highlights how acupuncture gained prominence after media coverage in the early 1970s and how practitioners formed the New Zealand Register of Acupuncturists to protect their profession. Today, TCM is fully regulated under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act with over 1,300 registered practitioners. The article features interviews with practitioners like Selwyn Wong Doo, Gordon Zheng, and Caren Chen, who discuss TCM's holistic approach and integration with Western medicine. Key therapeutic techniques include acupuncture, herbal medicine, and tuina massage. While awareness and acceptance are growing, challenges remain including limited public health system integration and accessibility costs. The Chinese Medicine Council advocates for broader incorporation into public healthcare, similar to countries like China, South Korea, and Japan.

[Page 1] A group of midwives in Te Wai Pounamu are on a mission of reclamation, empowering wāhine and whānau by embedding te ao Māori into every part of their practice. Ōhua Midwives is a Māori led practice based in Ōtautahi founded by four wāhine who saw a deep need in their rohe for a midwifery service embedded in te ao Māori. In 2025, Ilah Marie (Ngāti Porou, Whakatōhea), Toni Wieser (Ngāti Toarangatira, Ngāpuhi), Kerianne Harmon Becks (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Porou), and Kenzie Nahona (Ngāti Porou, Te Āti Haunui a Pāpārangi) graduated from Ara Institute of Canterbury as part of a record breaking cohort: 10 Māori and two Pasifika midwives, the largest ever at the institute. Marie said during their studies, they saw a great need for a kaupapa Māori midwifery service. "On our placements, we realised there was no practice that was kaupapa Māori or te ao Māori driven," she said. "We all decided while we were there that when we come out we'll establish one, especially for whānau in the east [of the city] … we just wanted to plug the gaps in our communities." With Māori and Pasifika making up just 10 and 5 percent of all midwives respectively in Aotearoa, the group hope more wāhine from these communities pursue a career in midwifery. In te ao Māori, the Maramataka, the Māori lunar calendar, guides many aspects of life, including birth and fertility. Each moon phase holds meaning, influencing everything from planting kai to whānau planning, rest, and renewal. The name of their practice, Ōhua, was born from this mātauranga. While reading the pukapuka Wawata by Dr Hinemoa Elder, a page opened to the phase Ōhua, which was a tohu the group said. "Ōhua aligns with nurturing relationships and grounding oneself, making it significant for whānau to seek support and prepare spiritually and mentally. "By honouring this phase, we encourage whānau to stay present, value the collective journey, and appreciate the shared process of bringing new life into the world." The group explained that in its traditional context, Ōhua was linked to growth, nurturing and life force. "Making it favourable for planting and cultivating resources, deriving from 'Hua' which can be defined as fruit, be abundant, to bloom or blossom." Reclaiming traditional birthing practices Central to the kaupapa of Ōhua Midwives is the Māori health model Te Whare Tapa Whā. It recognises taha wairua, hinengaro, tinana and whānau grounded in whenua. Marie said they began every experience with māmā and whānau by acknowledging the tapu of te whare tangata. Te whare tangata, in te ao Māori, can be translated as 'house of humanity,' a women's womb or uterus. "We know that when we are even putting our hands on that space, we incorporate whānau, te ao, all of our natural resources, like muka," she said. Muka is a fibre made from harakeke (flax) and is used to tie the umbilical cord (pito) after birth. In te ao Māori, the placenta is known as whenua, which can also be translated to land in te reo. It holds massive significance and is a representation of the connection between the newborn pēpi and the land. Traditionally, the placenta would be buried in a location significant to the whānau, like their ancestral lands to not only honour and nourish Papatūānuku, the Earth Mother, but ground the pēpi to its whakapapa. The rōpū said they honour the whenua in their practice and help explain its significance to whānau, passing down mātauranga they may not have. "The placenta is whenua. It's significant. We hold it with our highest respect," Marie said. They encourage ipu whenua, a woven or crafted basket made from natural materials, which the placenta can be placed and buried in. "Talking to [whānau] about ways that we can follow tikanga in a modern time is important, because a lot of whānau are removed from their whenua," Marie said. "Even if whānau can't access their original whenua, planting in a pot is symbolic, connecting culture with practice." In replacement of plastic modernised tools, they use mātauranga Māori. "We cut the iho (umbilical cord) with pounamu cutters or kōhatu and use muka instead of plastic clamps. "We teach whānau to prepare it themselves, weave it, tie it... so they learn whakapapa and the reasons behind it." Centring whānau in every birth The midwives also stressed the importance of a whānau based care. "Whānau are from all different regions, iwi everywhere around Aotearoa, so it's important we are actually connecting with them and being led and guided by them and their tikanga as well, is really important," Wieser said. "In midwifery, usually there's just one set standard of care, but in te ao Māori, we really chime in on what the whānau needs are and how they were raised and what they were brought up doing. "Speaking with nannies, papas, wider whānau gives us a foundation to care for them in ways they recognise." They said their care model weaves professional practice with whānau connection. "Some of our whānau say they've never had friendship from previous midwives, so they're relieved to meet us and know we're real people. That connection matters," Harmon Becks said. The group also spoke about the importance of holding space for whānau during the birth, when appropriate, allowing them to lead. "We stand back, let papas or whānau members catch the pēpi. We're just the background, but we empower them to lead their own birth," Marie said. Honouring those who paved the way While Ōhua is new, the wāhine said they stand firmly within a longer lineage of Māori midwives who paved the way. Harmon Becks said they have been inspired by wānanga and rangahau (research) made available to them by wāhine like Kelly Tikao, who has done significant mahi in the midwifery space, upholding mātauranga Māori. "We're doing this loudly, but we aren't the first. If not for the Māori midwives who came before us… all four of us wouldn't be here," she said. The wānanga through Kelly Tikao, Ngā Maia and Te Ara ō Hine Tapu Ora enrichened their mātauranga (knowledge), they said. "During our degree, we went outside mainstream education. 99.9 percent of that learning is thanks to her mahi," Wieser said. Growing the kaupapa Looking ahead to the future of Ōhua, Harmon Becks said they are looking to expand their services across Aotearoa. "We're big dreamers, but we make it happen. "We're planning our own clinic, growing Ōhua beyond Ōtautahi. We can't wait to support Māori graduates building this mahi with us." They want to encourage more wāhine Māori to enter the midwifery space. "Every whānau needs their own midwife, so be one for your whānau," Wieser said. "Midwives are big ass hype girls. We celebrate the strength of māmā. We're here whispering, 'Girl, you got this, you're strong, you are all the things,'" Marie added. The group said education and guidance across the overall health system is vital, especially as Māori midwives remain underrepresented Waipounamu. "Even one more Māori midwife in hospital can make a in Te huge difference in how whānau experience their care." Related

[Page 1] How colonisation created the state care to prison pipeline 2024 07 23 19:07:31+12:00 By Dr Rawiri Waretini Karena* On 24 July, the Abuse in Care Royal Commission of Inquiry's final report will be made public by the government. Ahead of the report's public release, survivors share their hopes for the healing process ahead. First Person Abuse in care is a colonial story. When I walked into the prison yard for the first time as a teenager, having never been there before I already knew 80 percent of the men in there. We'd spent the last 11 years growing up together in state care. That's when I knew there was a pipeline to prison; a pipeline that has spent decades sweeping up and funnelling Māori children from state care to prison. We talk about fractured homes, fractured families, and fractured communities, but what is the whakapapa of how they became fractured? Look at it this way: if I sold you a car and I had cut the brakes, and you went off and drove it and you crashed, who is responsible? You for driving, or me for cutting the brakes? This acknowledges that whilst we are responsible for our actions, we are not responsible for the hidden mechanisms that operate within the environment we are born into, privileging one faction at the expense of the other. For me, it's clear the issue leads right back to legislative policies of successive governments. You can't separate abuse in state care from our history of colonisation and indigenous oppression. The stories of survivors of state care their stories are all part of the colonial story. Family violence, sexual violence and child abuse were not a traditional part of Māori culture prior to colonisation. This is captured in a proverb that states, "He Mareikura, he taonga tuku iho ki waenganui ko Ranginui rāua ko Papatūānuku. He tapu te wharetangata" our women are a sacred conduit between heaven and earth, because they hold the holy house of birthing. Māori families traditionally lived in communities where a child was loved and nurtured, so harming a child was tapu because when one harms a child, they also harm their whakapapa, leading to serious consequences, as whakapapa was also considered sacred. But when the British arrived, they brought with them the colonial tool of assimilation, targeting indigenous children because they were the better bet to be assimilated to Western views and Western ways of seeing things, by being coerced into upholding Western pedagogies. In Aotearoa, the British created Māori experiences of stolen generations through distributing assimilation policies via legislation, establishing the Native Department in 1861. In 1867, they implemented the Neglected and Criminal Children's Act, which Oranga Tamariki can whakapapa back to, as well as the Native Schools Act 1867, which established an education system designed to assimilate Māori into Pākehā society by requiring that only the English language can be written or spoken in schools. This was enforced through severe corporal punishment. As an analogy, if you take a stone and you drop it into a pond, it creates ripples. The Native Schools Act 1867 represents that stone. The first ripple made the Māori language illegal. The second ripple saw te reo Māori banned by the state. The third ripple saw legal justification for beating and abusing tama ariki for speaking their native language. The fourth ripple saw the status of tama ariki changed from taonga to the lower status as a commodity. This led to the fifth ripple, where tama ariki over generations began experiencing abuse, neglect, and death at the hands of their caregivers, who experienced harsh corporal punishment in schools as children, and then in turn applied the same form of discipline to their tama ariki, leading to the children ending up in state care. From 1950 to 1999, more than 200,000 children were subject to state care abuse, perpetuating a never nding systemic cycle of fractured homes, fractured families, and fractured communities without any intergenerational insights into the insidious systemic mechanisms that created the problem in the first place. When this report comes out, I really want to see the government be brave and explore this cause and effect. So far, the coalition has been really good at criticising crime rates, establishing boot camps and pointing the finger at gangs. But they've been really slow to identify contributing factors and the root causes that led to these outcomes. The royal commission has been operating since 2018. It's collected the lived experiences of thousands of survivors and hard evidence that support both survivors' stories and the recommendations made. They have all the information they need to make informed, evidence based decisions. We've been here before the Waitangi Tribunal and the remuneration process came about because there was finally, a recognition that the inalienable, inherited rights that Māori held previous to and recognised under Te Tiriti o Waitangi were breached over numerous generations, leading to intergenerational poverty, loss of cultural heritage, and a near extinction of te reo Māori, and that these breaches led to the privileging of pākehā at the expense of Māori. But this has been accompanied by a certain political intentionality that has enabled what I call "historical amnesia", to pervade the country, perpetuating ideas about Māori riding a gravy train, as opposed to acknowledging a history of invasion, war, genocide and the confiscation/ theft of trillions of dollars' worth of lands, resources, and assets. We can't let that happen again. We must unpack this narrative about state care and how it came about, and that is what the government is scared to do. I want to encourage them to be brave and open, so we never have to repeat it. But they do not know how. Yet Māori, do. Because we have done this before as well. In 1906, 95 percent of Māori could speak their native language. Eighty years later, only 5 percent could. We've gone from generations who lost their reo to future generations of fluent speakers. When I look at the damage done to Māori children in state care, assimilation sought to disconnect them from their native voice, and cultural heritage, controlling the way Māori children perceive themselves. Because a people alienated from their cultural heritage are like a tree without roots, blowing to and fro, for they are not grounded and anchored in their whakapapa, customs, and language, becoming vulnerable to the manipulations of those who do not have their best interests at heart. Part of the healing journey enables Māori children in state care to reconnect back to their cultural heritage, whilst our country as a catalyst for change, embraces working together as Te Tiriti partners honouring our history whilst simultaneously ensuring our futures, from a place of aroha, humility, and compassion to build the type of respectful race relations that would be the envy of the rest of the world. * Dr Rawiri Waretini Karena is from Ngāti Māhanga, Ngāti Māhuta, as well as Ngāti Kaahu, and Ngāti Hine. He spent more than a decade in state care before being convicted of murder and spending more than a decade in prison. Since his release, Waretini Karena has become an expert in intergenerational trauma and alternatives to violence. He graduated with a PhD Doctorate of Philosophy in Indigenous studies in 2014, and was a lecturer on the Masters and PhD Professional Doctorate Program at Te Whare Wānanga o Awanuiārangi. He is a national and internationally published editor and author lecturing at Wintec specialising in counselling social work and mental health. He has recently been a head of research at Tuu Oho Mai Services facilitating

47.document_title: How Colonisation Created the State Care to Prison Pipeline
47.document_summary: Dr Rawiri Waretini-Karena examines the systemic connection between colonial policies and the state care to prison pipeline affecting Māori children in Aotearoa New Zealand. He traces how British colonisation introduced assimilation policies, including the Native Schools Act 1867, which banned te reo Māori and justified corporal punishment. These policies created intergenerational trauma, fracturing families and communities. The author argues that abuse in state care is fundamentally a colonial story, with over 200,000 children subjected to state care abuse from 1950-1999. He calls for the government to acknowledge these root causes and work toward healing by reconnecting Māori children to their cultural heritage, language, and whakapapa, emphasizing that understanding this cause-and-effect relationship is essential to breaking the cycle.

[Page 3] and the pollen for other purposes. The law was framed as a fire safety measure, but Deidre Brown was doubtful. "There's been research suggesting the government was concerned Māori builders were undercutting the new settler builders, because Māori could build out of raupō," she said. "The ordinance was more about protecting newly arrived British carpenters." Savannah Brown said she read the original document at the National Archives and "touching it was profound". "Realising this single piece of paper marked the beginning of the decline of traditional Māori architecture." A Māori home of 1900 Two boys and a young man outside a raupō hut. The ripple effects of this legislation were quick, they said. Use of traditional materials dropped, hapū lost access to wetlands and forests, as land was taken or drained, and rangatahi (young people) moved away from their kāinga, taking labour and expertise with them. Through the early and mid 20th century, Māori home ownership declined sharply. Instead of homes being free to build and live in, and homelessness being "virtually unimaginable", whānau Māori found themselves at the "bottom of the housing heap", living in low quality accommodation in the cities. Government built state houses helped some whānau, but the designs reflected European nuclear families, rather than Māori communal life. "They just weren't built for the bigger Māori families," Deidre Brown said. "Six, maybe eight kids, lots of aunties and uncles coming in and out, bringing kai with them." Standard layouts placed bathrooms next to kitchens, breaching tikanga, and put houses at the front of sections, leaving little room for pōwhiri, visitors or tangihanga. Even hallways worked against whānau life. "It prevented the singing and storytelling that went on in a traditional whare moe." Later, Māori were excluded from government mortgage support for decades access began only in 1959. In the 2023 census, Māori home ownership had fallen to 27.5 percent, and, according to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development's latest insights report for June 2025, more than 60 percent of those experiencing homelessness identify as Māori. "When legislation stopped us building for ourselves, autonomy disappeared," Savannah Brown said. Iwi architects and researchers at MĀPIHI are creating housing that is both culturally grounded and affordable. Rebuilding autonomy Both researchers said Māori led solutions already existed and they may be the key. Te Māhurehure Marae in Auckland's Pt Chevalier and Ngāti Toa were among those creating papakāinga that wove housing into marae life, natural environments and cultural practice. "They've done away with front yards and back yards, [and] people are closely linked to their wharenui," Savannah Brown said. "They have kura kaupapa, a community vegetable garden [māra kai], and they're creating their own supply chain. In many ways, it's like what their ancestors had in the 19th century, but using modern technologies." Savannah Brown said capability within whānau was key, but smaller hapū often struggled, as rangatahi moved to cities. She also believed systems needed reform. One of her research areas was the possibility of a Māori building authority. "There are huge misunderstandings at council level around tikanga Māori and whenua Māori," she said. "Some processes become absurd… like marae having to seek resource consent from themselves." Both told RNZ that they hoped more Māori entered architecture to help shift the sector. "Housing sits at the centre of wellbeing," Deidre Brown said. "The more Māori we have in this sector, the better for our people." 50.document_title: Researchers Link Māori Housing Inequities to 180 Years of Restrictive Building Laws
50.document_summary: Researchers Professor Deidre Brown and Savannah Brown examine how 180 years of restrictive building legislation has perpetuated Māori housing inequities in New Zealand. The 1842 Raupō Houses Ordinance, which taxed and banned traditional raupō homes, marked a turning point that disrupted Māori self-determined housing practices. This legislation displaced Māori from traditional kāinga, eliminated access to building materials, and forced reliance on European-designed state housing unsuitable for whānau. Today, Māori home ownership stands at 27.5% and over 60% of homeless individuals identify as Māori. The researchers highlight that Māori-led solutions like papakāinga developments offer culturally grounded, sustainable alternatives. They advocate for restoring Māori autonomy through increased Māori representation in architecture, potential Māori building authorities, and systems reform to address colonial legislation's lasting impacts on housing outcomes.

[Page 1] Taulasea, or traditional healers, play a significant role in Samoan society, new study finds ByChristina Persico 2025 06 27 10:14:53+12:00 A new study has found traditional healers, or Taulasea, have a key role in Samoan society. The study was published in Kotuitui: New Zealand Journal of Social Sciences Online. Researchers interviewed 14 Taulasea three were from Aotearoa and the others from Samoa. They were aged between 44 and 94 years old and practiced a range of healing methods. The findings revealed four major themes: sacredness of the Taulasea knowledge and practice; Taulasea specialisation; Taulasea methods and approaches; and holistic views that impact health. Lead author Professor Riz Firestone from Massey University said Taulasea play a sacred, community centred role "rooted in spiritual duty rather than commerce". "Healers diagnose holistically, combining prayer, plant based medicines, massage and dietary advice, and they act as gatekeepers, referring severe cases to westernised medical care," she said. "Present day lifestyle habits that are modernised, reliant on processed foods and sedentary lifestyles contribute to surging diet related conditions like type 2 diabetes and malnutrition. Taulasea advocate a return to simple traditional diets." https://www.rnz.co.nz/international/programmes/dateli nepacific/audio/2018966384/unlocking the healing powers of samoa s p lants The study said traditional healers are often the first port of call for Samoans in need of care. "The healing practices of Taulasea are deeply rooted in a spiritual context, where their work is above mere employment and is perceived by them as a sacred duty," it said. "This sense of duty shapes how they conduct their practices, emphasising the role of service over financial remuneration. "Although it is difficult to validate the spiritual dimension of the Taulasea's work, as people continue to use their services as either a first port of call or simultaneously whilst seeking Westernised medicine, the perpetual use of traditional healing reinforces the value of their positionality in society." Taulasea also recognised shifts in practices due to the changing environment and conditions that people present to them, the study said. "The blend of traditional, cultural, spiritual, and scientific may provide a robust framework for addressing health issues and enhancing overall quality of life. "In some societies, there have been collaborative approaches, where Taulasea have played complementary role with Westernised doctors, but this has been largely regulatory towards traditional healers. "Nonetheless, both practitioners can coexist, but a model of care and the nature of the collaboration requires further consultation between the two." The study also noted recent research that showed there may be "subjective benefits" that patients reap from seeing a traditional healer, that "may not be quantifiable in a Western framework", and so the subjective benefits must be further explored to get a deeper understanding of their work and role. "As global standards are shifting to incorporate more indigenous and traditional knowledge, it would be important to acknowledge the Taulasea still have a significant role in current modern day systems, and this could be capitalised upon. "What is currently needed is a further understanding of why people continue to use Taulasea; and how a reciprocal model of care be informed and developed for use in the future, where Samoans (and all Pacific people) have access to the best of both traditional and Westernised healing practices." The study also said the Taluasea were strict on patient commitment and compliance. "From the Taulasea's perspective, this is a critical part of their service, because should the patient not comply, the consequences are detrimental to the Taulasea themselves or their family members. "They believe that the sickness or illness transfers to them and/or to their family members; whether people regard this as being superstitious, it is a commonly held view by the Taulasea in this study from generational knowledge passed down to them." The study did note its limitations, including a small, non random sample size, possible translation issues, and its reliance on narrative interviews without other forms of methodological triangulation, such as a observational data. 51.document_summary: A new study published in Kotuitui: New Zealand Journal of Social Sciences Online reveals that Taulasea (traditional Samoan healers) play a crucial, sacred role in Samoan society. Researchers interviewed 14 Taulasea aged 44-94 from Samoa and Aotearoa, identifying four major themes: sacredness of knowledge, specialization, healing methods, and holistic health views. Taulasea diagnose holistically using prayer, plant-based medicines, massage, and dietary advice, serving as gatekeepers who refer severe cases to Western medicine. [Page 1] Te Pāti Māori slams tabling of controversial Oranga Tamariki Bill during Parliament recess ByTnatanahira Māori news journalist 2024 05 13 20:50:16+12:00 Te Tai Tokerau MP Mariameno Kapa Kingi. Te Pāti Māori is "disgusted" by the tabling of the controversial Oranga Tamariki Amendment Bill while Parliament is in recess. The bill to repeal Section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 was introduced to Parliament on Monday, coinciding with a Court of Appeal judgment which found the Waitangi Tribunal was right to summons Children's Minister Karen Chhour to submit evidence as part of an urgent inquiry. Speaking to RNZ, Te Tai Tokerau MP Mariameno Kapa Kingi said she was not surprised but deeply disappointed at the pathway the minister had taken. It was a "terrible and sneaky" thing to introduce while Parliament was in recess, she said. "Why would one do that? What is the motive behind that?" She said the motive was clear: That "despite what the Tribunal or any other court is saying", the government was going to carry out its 100 day plan. "It's rubbish, it's disgusting and it's appalling. Again, just another disappointment Māori have to deal with." According to the Bill's explanatory note, the intention of the Bill was to "enable Oranga Tamariki Ministry for Children to renew its focus on the safety and wellbeing of children in care arrangements". It said the government was concerned the introduction section of 7AA has led the Oranga Tamariki to prioritise cultural factors over the safety and stability of children in long term care arrangements. "Concerns have been raised that Oranga Tamariki Ministry for Children has moved tamariki Māori from stable long term care arrangements and placed them with whānau, hapū, and iwi groups to which they whakapapa. "Concerned voices in this area have described these changes in placement as traumatic and argue that they should only occur in cases where there is risk to the safety of the child." Kapa Kingi, a former social worker, said in repealing section 7AA "They're showing their hand, they're showing their practice, they're showing that they believe they know better for mokopuna Māori. "This is not an accident, this is a deliberate plan. They care not for us in the way we need it, so we have to." Kapa Kingi said real change would come from whānau outside of Parliament not politicians. "Sixty thousand people marched to Waitangi. They didn't march to Waitangi to say 'Oh we think you're doing a really great job'. They marched to show resistance on the paepae," she said. RNZ has contacted Chhour for comment. Related

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores rongoā, the traditional Māori healing system encompassing herbal remedies, physical therapies, and spiritual healing practices. It details how Māori classified illnesses into mate atua (supernatural diseases caused by broken tapu and malevolent spirits) and mate tangata (physical ailments), with tohunga (priests) treating each through specialized methods including exorcism, purificatory rites, and herbal treatments. The document catalogs over 200 medicinal plants used in traditional Māori medicine, with detailed applications for key species including harakeke (flax), kawakawa (pepper tree), mānuka, kōwhai, kūmarahou, rātā, koromiko, tētēaweka, and rimu. It examines the historical impact of European colonization, which introduced new illnesses that traditional healers could not cure, leading to declining faith in rongoā and the 1907 Tohunga Suppression Act that criminalized traditional practitioners. The document discusses how this act was repealed in 1962 and how rongoā experienced significant revival from the late 20th century due to resurgence of Māori culture, loss of confidence in Western medicine, and demand for spiritual dimensions in healing. Modern rongoā practitioners differ from traditional tohunga, with variable informal training and eclectic practices that often incorporate Western and other medical systems. The establishment of Ngā Ringa Whakahaere o te Iwi Māori in 1993 marks an important institutional development for Māori healers.

chunkHighlights.text: The impact of colonisation

Colonisation by Europeans had a significant effect on traditional Māori healing. Tohunga had limited ability to combat the diseases brought by Europeans. Though Western medicine was also relatively ineffectual at the time, this failure still strongly affected Māori confidence in tohunga .

Some Pākehā missionaries attributed the spread of disease to a lack of Christian faith. As their own healers appeared impotent, many Māori accepted this explanation and turned to Christianity. Over time, the whare wānanga (schools of higher learning) which had trained tohunga started to close. The tradition of the tohunga declined.

3.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori health across multiple centuries, from pre-European times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Before European contact, Māori were generally fit and healthy with life expectancy around 28-30 years, relying on traditional healing practices involving tohunga (healers), rongoā rākau (plant medicines), and karakia (rituals). European arrival brought devastating diseases like measles, influenza, typhoid, and tuberculosis, causing significant population decline. Land confiscation, poor housing, and unsanitary conditions worsened health outcomes. From 1900 onwards, government health services expanded with the Public Health Department establishing a Māori section led by Dr Māui Pōmare. Despite vaccination campaigns and health education, tuberculosis, typhoid, and the 1918 influenza pandemic devastated Māori communities. The 1938 Social Security Act introduced free hospital admission and universal medical benefits. Post-WWII improvements included successful tuberculosis campaigns and declining infant mortality rates. However, significant health disparities persisted throughout the 20th century, with Māori mortality rates approximately twice that of non-Māori in 1960. Contributing factors included socioeconomic disparities in employment, income, education, and substandard housing. The government gradually adopted a bicultural approach to health, particularly after the 1984 Te Hui Whakaoranga workshop, promoting Māori participation in health planning and recognizing traditional healing practices alongside Western medicine.

4.fileDescription: Māui Wiremu Piti Naera Pōmare (1875/1876-1930) was a transformative Māori leader and New Zealand's first Māori health officer. Born in Taranaki to parents with connections to Ngāti Toa and Ngāti Mutunga, Pōmare was educated at Te Aute College and studied medicine in the United States, graduating MD from American Medical Missionary College in 1899. As Māori health officer from 1901, he pioneered health reform initiatives including sanitation improvements and village inspections. He organized the 1901 royal hui at Rotorua and supported the Tohunga Suppression Act. Elected to Parliament in 1911 representing the Western Māori seat, Pōmare served in various ministerial roles under William Massey's Reform Party. His major achievements include securing compulsory registration of Māori births and deaths (1913), negotiating the West Coast Settlement Reserves Amendment Act (1913) to address land confiscation grievances, and chairing Māori recruitment during WWI. As Cook Islands minister (1916-1928), he increased funding and improved services. As Health Minister (1923-1926), he launched a safe maternity campaign that dramatically reduced puerperal sepsis deaths through improved asepsis techniques and midwifery training. Collaborating with Ngata, Pōmare established a royal commission into land confiscations (1926), securing compensation for Taranaki and Waikato. He died of tuberculosis in 1930, leaving a legacy of bridging Māori and Pākehā worlds while advancing indigenous welfare.

He developed the technique of using a microscope to show people the micro-organisms that inhabited impure water. He also had slides of the various microbes to show to sceptics.

In a number of his reports Pōmare commented bitterly about the mortality that some of the new breed of tohunga caused; for example, by attempting to heal the sick by bathing them in cold water and administering alcohol. He strongly supported Carroll's introduction of the Tohunga Suppression Act in 1907.

Although Pōmare believed that the decline in Māori numbers could be halted by the correct medical methods, he also saw that the nature of the Māori population was changing; a new population with European ancestry was emerging and he considered that they would have the best characteristics of both races. Unlike Apirana Ngata , who was concerned over the loss of Māori identity, Pōmare welcomed intermarriage and Māori acculturation.

From 1902 to 1910 Pōmare reported to Parliament on his work in a series of exuberant reports in which he dealt not only with medical matters but also gave his opinion on a number of issues, including education and land tenure, at times earning rebukes from his superiors. These reports make it clear that he believed in the radical modernisation of Māori society even if this meant the loss of all Māori land. He considered that Māori should adopt a European lifestyle, become self-reliant and, above all, work.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores rongoā, the traditional Māori healing system encompassing herbal remedies, physical therapies, and spiritual healing practices. It details how Māori classified illnesses into mate atua (supernatural diseases caused by broken tapu and malevolent spirits) and mate tangata (physical ailments), with tohunga (priests) treating each through specialized methods including exorcism, purificatory rites, and herbal treatments. The document catalogs over 200 medicinal plants used in traditional Māori medicine, with detailed applications for key species including harakeke (flax), kawakawa (pepper tree), mānuka, kōwhai, kūmarahou, rātā, koromiko, tētēaweka, and rimu. It examines the historical impact of European colonization, which introduced new illnesses that traditional healers could not cure, leading to declining faith in rongoā and the 1907 Tohunga Suppression Act that criminalized traditional practitioners. The document discusses how this act was repealed in 1962 and how rongoā experienced significant revival from the late 20th century due to resurgence of Māori culture, loss of confidence in Western medicine, and demand for spiritual dimensions in healing. Modern rongoā practitioners differ from traditional tohunga, with variable informal training and eclectic practices that often incorporate Western and other medical systems. The establishment of Ngā Ringa Whakahaere o te Iwi Māori in 1993 marks an important institutional development for Māori healers.

chunkHighlights.text: The Tohunga Suppression Act

The Tohunga Suppression Act grew out of concern over the practices of some self-appointed tohunga . The influential Te Aute College Students’ Association was particularly critical, believing that tohunga might harm patients, and could hinder Māori progress. Tohunga also came under attack from the prominent Māori doctors Māui Pōmare and Te Rangi Hīroa (Sir Peter Buck).
The Tohunga Suppression Act was presented by Māori MP James Carroll and supported by the four Māori members of parliament. It was passed in 1907. The preamble read:

Every person who gathers Maoris around him by practising on their superstition or credulity, or who misleads or attempts to mislead any Maori by professing or pretending to possess supernatural powers in the

treatment or cure of any disease, or in the foretelling of future events, or otherwise, is liable on summary conviction before a Magistrate to a fine not exceeding twenty-five pounds or to imprisonment for a period not exceeding six months.
There were few prosecutions under the Act, and very few convictions – its main effect was to drive tohunga underground. In 1962, it was repealed.
The Act has been seen by some as an attempt to control the Ngāi Tūhoe prophet Rua Kēnana, who built an independent settlement at Maungapōhatu in the Urewera from 1907.

The Act has also been viewed as a breach of the Treaty of Waitangi, as it challenged traditional Māori wisdom – considered to be one of the taonga (treasures) that Māori were promised under the second article of the Treaty.

6.fileDescription: James Carroll (Timi Kara, b. 1857) was a transformative bicultural figure in New Zealand history, born to an Irish father and Ngāti Kahungunu mother in Wairoa. Raised bilingually with Māori as his first language, Carroll pursued a pioneering career bridging European and Māori worlds. He served as interpreter to Parliament (1879-1883) before winning the Eastern Māori seat in 1887, later representing Waiapu (1893-1908) and Gisborne (1908-1919). As the first Māori to hold the Native Affairs portfolio (1899-1912), Carroll became pivotal in Māori land administration. Key achievements include securing the Urewera District Native Reserve Act 1896, establishing Māori Councils and Land Administration Acts (1900), and implementing the Native Land Act 1909. Carroll advocated for Māori economic empowerment and equality, opposing Crown pre-emption of land and supporting leasing arrangements. He championed land management committees and body corporate structures for Māori landowners while opposing separatist movements like Te Kotahitanga. Despite facing intense pressure from Pākehā opposition demanding land alienation, Carroll implemented land incorporations and enabled Māori farming development. Though unable to prevent significant Māori land loss, his diplomatic skills and unwavering commitment earned him respect from both Māori elders and the Pākehā establishment.

chunkHighlights.text: The Tohunga Suppression Act 1907 reflected Carroll's impatience with what he considered regressive Māori attitudes. It was aimed at 'so called prophets' such as Rua Kēnana of Maungapōhatu. Carroll respected the Tūhoe people and took a legitimate pride in having protected Tūhoe land in 1895, but he wanted Tūhoe to 'improve themselves in the scale of civilisation' and it infuriated him that Rua, whom he regarded as a charlatan, could apparently draw them off into isolation again.

7.fileDescription: James Malcolm Mason (1864-1924) was a Scottish-born physician who became New Zealand's first chief health officer. After studying medicine in Edinburgh and Glasgow, he practiced in Portsmouth and Blyth before emigrating to New Zealand in 1895. Mason established the Ōtaki cottage hospital and gained prominence through his bacteriological expertise and public health advocacy. In 1900, he was appointed chief health officer following the Public Health Act 1900, which established one of the world's first national departments of public health. His tenure focused on preventive health, vaccination, sanitation, tuberculosis control, and Māori health. He edited the New Zealand Medical Journal, established tuberculosis sanatoriums, and influenced the creation of Plunket nurses. Despite recurring ill health, Mason served with distinction until 1909, later practicing privately and serving in WWI. He died in 1924, remembered for his far-sighted contributions to New Zealand's public health development.

8.fileDescription: This document chronicles the life and spiritual leadership of Rua Kēnana Hepetipa, a pivotal Māori religious and political figure. Born to Ngāti Kahungunu and Tūhoe descent, Rua emerged as the claimed successor to Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Tūruki within two years of the latter's death in 1893. Following a supernatural revelation on Maungapōhatu mountain in 1905-1906, where he encountered the archangel Gabriel and was baptized as Hepetipa, Rua established the "City of God" at Maungapōhatu in 1907. His community, the Iharaira (Israelites), adopted Nazarite practices and constructed Hīona (Zion), a circular meeting house modeled after the Dome of the Rock. Through strategic marriages to twelve women, Rua linked the Tūhoe and Te Whakatōhea tribes. The community initially succeeded but declined due to harsh conditions and infrastructure challenges. A pivotal moment came with Rua's 1915 arrest for illicitly selling alcohol, politically motivated due to his pacifist stance during World War I. This led to the April 2, 1916 armed police expedition—the worst police-Māori clash of the century, with two Māori killed. Rua's subsequent Supreme Court trial, the longest in New Zealand's legal history until 1977, resulted in his conviction for resisting arrest and imprisonment. Released in 1918, Rua rebuilt Maungapōhatu and attempted to create an economically viable community, though it ultimately failed. Despite government surveillance and the Tohunga Suppression Act, Rua met Prime Minister Joseph Ward in 1908, advocating for equal laws for Māori and Pākehā. His legacy as a visionary leader for a dispossessed people endures in New Zealand's cultural imagination.

The authorities had maintained a watch over Rua, encouraged by some high-standing Māori leaders, particularly James Carroll and Kererū. In 1907 the Tohunga Suppression Act had been passed, directed primarily at Rua. He was seen to be a disruptive influence because of his claims to be a spiritual healer, and because of his hostility to the native schools, which were teaching the children in English. The local police were instructed to watch Rua from May 1906 on the grounds that he was 'suspected of acting as a Tohunga '. He was harassed with the dog tax in 1907, but, despite Kererū's efforts, was never charged under the Tohunga Suppression Act.

10.fileDescription:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

11.fileDescription: Hikapuhi (Te Hikapuhi Poihipi) was a prominent Māori healer born between 1860-1871 in Rotorua to parents of Ngāti Te Rangiunuora descent. She rose to prominence around 1905, calling herself a nurse rather than a tohunga, and traveled throughout New Zealand administering Three Star brandy as medicine accompanied by healing words. Though credited with miracles including curing blindness, her credibility suffered after a prominent chief died following her treatment. Government officials, including health officer Māui Pōmare, attempted to suppress her activities due to concerns about alcohol distribution, particularly to children. However, many Māori patients testified to her compassion and effectiveness, as she provided free medical care to those unable to afford European doctors. Despite petitions supporting her work and her acquittal by the Rongokako Council, official disapproval and the irresponsible actions of some followers undermined her practice. Her activities gradually ceased after 1913, and she died in Rotorua on 6 January 1934. Hikapuhi represented both a symbol of Māori spiritual healing and European establishment failure, providing essential healthcare to marginalized communities.

chunkHighlights.text: the onus of action onto the Rongokako Council. But Te Tau did not want responsibility either. He suggested that it was the government's responsibility to remove Hikapuhi from his district. In 1909 the influential Wairarapa leader Hoani Parāone Tūnuiārangi alleged that 20 people had died under Hikapuhi's hands, and that she had provoked liquor consumption and quarrelling on visits to Gisborne and Wairoa. However, most of the complaints seemed to be against her followers. Hikapuhi herself had been investigated by the Rongokako Council and acquitted of any wrongdoing. Many Māori had signed a petition asking the Rongokako Council to authorise her work. In July 1909 Apirana Ngata urged that Hikapuhi should be prosecuted under the Tohunga Suppression Act 1907; Carroll's response in May 1910 was 'No action'.

Hikapuhi's activities gradually ceased. The weight of official disapproval had its effect, and her methods lost favour as the number of nurses working in Māori health was increasing. Her work was undermined by the irresponsible actions of some of her disciples. The last mention of her working in Wairarapa was in 1913. When she visited Wellington in 1915 it is clear that her vogue was at an end. Her husband died in Ōhinemutu, Rotorua, on 13 June 1913. Hikapuhi may have returned to her Te Arawa kin at this time; she died in Rotorua on 6 January 1934.

Hikapuhi's powers as a prophet and tohunga put her patients in touch with the Māori cosmogony, healed their spirit and gave them hope. Her achievement was summed up by A. L. D. Fraser in the course of condemning her: she 'went from town to town and from kāinga to kāinga , and as she wandered all through the colony her mana spread with her. She had a halo, a glamour of almost godlike attributes'. To Europeans and to the Māori establishment Hikapuhi was a nuisance and a symbol of their own failure; to many Māori she provided the only medical care they were likely to get.

13.fileDescription: This comprehensive collection explores the resurgence of herbal medicine in New Zealand, examining its historical roots, contemporary revival, and industry development potential. The articles trace how traditional Māori medicine (rongoā) and European herbalism were marginalized through 20th-century legislation but have experienced renewed interest since the 1980s. Featured practitioners demonstrate practical applications of wild-crafting and garden-based healing traditions. New Zealand's excellent growing conditions support cultivation of high-value medicinal herbs such as arnica, mānuka, kumarahou, horopito, and St John's Wort, with successful local initiatives like Tairawhiti Pharmaceuticals and Forest Herbs Research. Key challenges include international certification requirements (GMP standards), regulatory frameworks, and intellectual property concerns regarding indigenous Māori plants following the Wai 262 claim. The collection emphasizes tensions between holistic plant-based healing and scientific validation, while addressing global threats to medicinal plant species and advocating for conservation efforts and "barefoot doctoring" using readily available garden herbs as primary healthcare. The government's recent agreement to regulate medical herbalism signals growing recognition of herbal medicine's role in sustainable healthcare.

response.response_text:
## The Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004

The Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 was New Zealand legislation passed by Helen Clark's Labour government that effectively reserved ownership of the country's foreshore and seabed for the Crown. [[1]](cite://1/1) In doing so, it extinguished Māori customary rights over the coastline — and the controversy it sparked would reshape New Zealand politics for years to come.

## Background: How It Came About

The origins of the Act lie in a 1997 application by eight iwi of the upper South Island. Having failed to be awarded rights for mussel farming, they applied to the Māori Land Court to have the foreshore and seabed of the Marlborough Sounds recognised as Māori customary land. [[2]](cite://2/1)

This prompted a broader legal argument about whether Māori could hold customary rights to the seabed and foreshore. The iwi Ngāti Apa tested this in court, and the Court of Appeal ultimately ruled that the Māori Land Court *was* able to decide on such rights. [[3]](cite://3/1) Before Ngāti Apa could pursue their claim, however, the Labour government moved to overturn that Court of Appeal decision by passing the 2004 Act — effectively shutting down the avenue for Māori to seek customary title through the courts. [[3]](cite://3/2)

## Why Was It So Controversial?

The Act was deeply controversial for several interconnected reasons:

**It vested Crown ownership over Māori customary claims.** The legislation deemed the foreshore and seabed to be held by the Crown, overriding any potential Māori customary title. [[4]](cite://4/1) For many Māori, this was seen as a fundamental breach of the principles underpinning Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi), which had guaranteed chiefs' authority over their lands, fisheries, and treasured things. [[5]](cite://5/1)

**It overturned a court decision by statute.** Rather than allowing Māori to have their day in court, the government legislated to prevent the very possibility. As Tau Henare later reflected, "everybody has a right... to go to court to find out whether they are right or whether they are wrong." [[6]](cite://6/1) The move was seen as deeply unjust.

**It triggered one of New Zealand's largest ever hīkoi (protest marches).** More than 30,000 Māori and their Pākehā supporters marched on Parliament to challenge the legislation. [[4]](cite://4/2)[[6]](cite://6/2) The loss of Māori legal rights to the foreshore and seabed had galvanised a generation. [[7]](cite://7/1)

**It fractured the Labour-Māori political relationship and gave birth to a new party.** Tariana Turia, a sitting Labour MP, resigned from both the party and Parliament in protest at the Act. [[8]](cite://8/1) She forced a by-election in her electorate, was re-elected, and went on to co-found the Māori Party (later Te Pāti Māori) alongside Pita Sharples. [[9]](cite://9/1)[[10]](cite://10/1) In the founding co-leaders' view, the legislation violated Māori customary title over New Zealand's coastline. [[9]](cite://9/2) At the 2005 general election, Te Pāti Māori won four of Parliament's seven Māori seats. [[9]](cite://9/3)

Hone Harawira, who led the hīkoi opposing the Act, was subsequently elected as the Māori Party's MP for Te Tai Tokerau. [[8]](cite://8/2)

## What Replaced It?

The Act was repealed and replaced by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, passed by John Key's National government in partnership with the Māori Party. [[2]](cite://2/2)[[1]](cite://1/2) This restored iwi's ability to seek customary rights and title through the courts, declaring that no one owned the foreshore and seabed but allowing Māori groups to apply for Customary Marine Title (CMT). [[1]](cite://1/3) That legislation has itself remained contested, with ongoing legal and political battles over what threshold Māori must meet to establish their rights. [[11]](cite://11/1)[[12]](cite://12/1)

---

Would you like to explore the formation of the Māori Party in more depth, and how the foreshore and seabed issue shaped Māori politics over the following decade?

1.document_title: Māori Land Rights, Indigenous Law, and Colonial Legislation in New Zealand: A Historical and Legal Analysis
1.document_summary:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 restored iwi ’s ability to seek customary rights and title in court.

2.document_title: Marlborough Region: Comprehensive Geography, History, Geology, and Economic Development
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's Marlborough region across multiple dimensions. Geographically, the rectangular region in the north-east South Island features the Marlborough Sounds, Kaikōura ranges, and Wairau plain, with a sunny climate and major towns of Blenheim and Picton. Geologically, the Alpine Fault marks where Pacific and Australian tectonic plates collide, causing significant seismic activity including the 1848 magnitude 7.5 earthquake and 2016 magnitude 7.8 earthquake. Rock formations exceed 200 million years old. Historically, Māori settled coastal areas following 13th-century Polynesian settlement at Wairau Bar, with European exploration beginning with Abel Tasman (1642-43) and James Cook (1770), followed by whaling (1830s-1840s) and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Economic development evolved from pastoral farming and extractive industries (sawmilling, gold rushes, flax harvesting) to modern sectors including aquaculture (green-lipped mussels, salmon, abalone), wine production (Sauvignon blanc since 1973), and tourism. Key infrastructure includes the 1962 Wellington-Picton ferry and 1965 Cook Strait power cable. As of 2013, the region had 46,968 residents (85.2% European, 11.4% Māori), with 17.3% employed in agriculture versus 5.7% nationally. The region maintains rich cultural heritage with notable literary figures and sporting traditions dating to the 1850s-1860s.

3.document_title: New Zealand Aquaculture: Industry Overview, Farming Practices, and Regulatory Framework
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth analysis of New Zealand's aquaculture industry, covering its development, major farming practices, and regulatory landscape. The industry, valued at $280 million by 2001, primarily focuses on three export species: green-lipped mussels, quinnat salmon, and Pacific oysters. Green-lipped mussels are cultivated using the Japanese longline system, becoming New Zealand's second most important seafood export by 2000, sold to over 60 countries. Salmon farming evolved through three methods: ocean ranching (1976), sea-cage ranching (1983) in Big Glory Bay and Marlborough Sounds, and freshwater farming in South Island hydroelectric canals, producing 8,500 tonnes in 2001 with 65% exported. Pacific oysters, cultivated starting in 1970, reached 3,500 tonnes annually by 2001 and generated $13.6 million in exports. Additional species include pāua shellfish, scallops, and sea horses. The industry operates under a dual licensing system managed by regional councils and the Ministry of Fisheries, with a government moratorium on marine farm expansion by 2002. Key challenges include regional concentration, toxic algal blooms, and tensions between farmers and Māori groups regarding seabed ownership. Despite these challenges, the industry has strong future prospects for diversifying into high-value species such as pāua, kingfish, and crayfish.

In 2004 it passed legislation which deemed the ownership of the foreshore and seabed to be held by the Crown. More than 30,000 Māori and their Pākehā supporters marched on Parliament to challenge the legislation, which was replaced in 2011 by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act. This sparked further controversy.

4.document_title: Kāwanatanga: Māori Governance, Colonial Authority, and Modern Challenges in New Zealand
4.document_summary: This document explores kāwanatanga, the Māori concept of governance and state authority, tracing its evolution from the 19th century to contemporary times. It begins with the 1835 Declaration of Independence by northern chiefs asserting sovereign power, followed by the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi where a critical translation discrepancy emerged—"kāwanatanga" was translated as "absolute sovereignty" in English, potentially misrepresenting chiefs' understanding. The document details colonial government strategies to assert kāwanatanga over Māori, including military interventions by governors like FitzRoy, Gore Browne, and Grey to suppress resistance over land ownership and the Māori King movement. Key mechanisms of colonial control included the Native Land Court (1865) which converted collective tribal land ownership to individual titles facilitating European acquisition, four Māori parliamentary seats (1867) that incorporated Māori into colonial governance while limiting influence, and co-option of chiefs through councils. Despite these controls, Māori maintained nationalist movements like Kīngitanga and Kotahitanga. From the 1970s onwards, the Waitangi Tribunal investigated Treaty breaches, leading to policy shifts including Māori language revitalization, treaty settlements, and a bicultural framework. Modern challenges persist, particularly regarding Māori rights and the 2004 foreshore and seabed legislation claiming Crown ownership, which prompted over 30,000 Māori and supporters to march on Parliament. This was replaced in 2011 by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, generating further controversy regarding the balance between Crown authority and Māori interests.

5.text:

This was tested when Ngāti Apa took a case arguing that Māori could have customary rights to both. Ultimately the Court of Appeal ruled that the Māori Land Court was able to decide on these rights. Before Ngāti Apa could have their day in court, the Labour government moved to overturn the Court of Appeal decision by statute. This led to a foreshore and seabed protest hīkoi in 2004.

6.document_title: Te hī ika – Māori Fishing: Traditional Practices, Cultural Heritage, and Contemporary Fisheries Management
6.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores Māori fishing practices across traditional, historical, and contemporary contexts. It covers the spiritual significance of fishing in Māori tradition, including the god Tangaroa and legendary figures like Māui and Kupe. Traditional fishing methods included nets made from flax, hooks, lines, spears, and pots, with fishing being a tapu (sacred) activity involving specific rituals and karakia (incantations). Fishing grounds were carefully managed by tribes with expert knowledge of optimal fishing times and seasons, and fish were preserved through steaming and drying for tribal feasts.

Early European observers like Captain Cook and Joseph Banks noted Māori fishing expertise and the enormous scale of their operations, including nets up to 900 metres long. Large-scale tribal expeditions involved hundreds of people in canoes, with catches distributed among families and exchanged with inland tribes. In 1852, 1,792 canoes brought 45 tons of fish to Auckland, demonstrating the significance of Māori fishing to early European settlements.

Following European settlement, traditional fishing declined due to land loss, European commercial competition, and regulatory restrictions. The 1992 Sealord deal granted Māori 50% ownership of New Zealand's largest fishing company and 22% of total quota. The Māori Fisheries Act 2004 established governance structures including Te Ohu Kaimoana. Today, Māori control over a third of New Zealand's fishing industry, with many tribes operating successful seafood companies, balancing commercial operations with customary fishing and traditional food preparation.

7.text:
[Page 9] Water in New Zealand is protected by legislation, principally the Resource Management Act 1991. It provides a legal framework for using water, managing its quality, and balancing the needs of different groups who affect or use water. For example, fishers and swimmers want the lakes and rivers to be clear, while factory owners need to dispose of waste material. Regional councils throughout the country monitor water quality, and then decide how to manage land and effluent. In consultation with the local community, a council might decide to maintain high water quality in upland rivers and lakes for recreation and biodiversity, but allow some runoff and waste into lowland rivers and estuaries.

7.document_title: Water Quality in New Zealand: Comprehensive Assessment of Threats, Management Strategies, and Case Studies
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines water quality in New Zealand, addressing freshwater management and protection challenges. While New Zealand has high-quality freshwater by global standards, it faces significant threats from soil erosion, sewage, farm fertilizers, and algae growth. Major pollution sources include point sources (sewage pipes) and non-point sources (farm runoff), with contaminants encompassing sediments, organic matter, and dissolved chemicals like nitrate and phosphate. High nitrate levels pose particular health risks for infants. The document presents case studies of Lake Rotorua, Lake Taupō, and the Manawatū River, illustrating how human activities have degraded water quality. Management strategies outlined under the Resource Management Act 1991 include regional council monitoring, water-quality standards, and weed control methods. Key issues addressed include excessive nutrient levels causing algal blooms, invasive species like hornwort and didymo, and disease-causing organisms. Solutions involve multiple approaches: grass carp for vegetation control, restoring riparian shade, reducing nutrient inputs, improving farming practices, and implementing legislative protections. The document emphasizes voluntary farm management practices, including dairy farmer initiatives using effluent spraying and wetland treatment systems, a voluntary accord between Fonterra Co-operative Group and government entities to minimize dairying's environmental impact, and a Code of Practice for Fertiliser Use to mitigate agricultural harm.

8.document_title: Fiordland's Marine Ecosystem: Glacial Formations, Species Diversity, and Conservation Management
8.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's 14 fiords in the south-west of the South Island, examining their geological origins and unique marine ecosystems. Fiords are long, narrow sea inlets with steep sides carved by glaciers approximately 20,000 years ago. When glaciers melted, seawater filled these formations, creating distinctive ecosystems characterized by a layer of fresh water from heavy rainfall sitting above salt water, which reduces sunlight penetration and creates dark conditions similar to deep ocean environments. This enables "deep water emergence," allowing deep-water species to thrive at shallow depths.

The Fiordland marine ecosystem supports exceptionally diverse marine life including over 150 fish species such as the brotula fish, Jock Stewart fish, scorpion fish, and deep-water wavyline perch, along with sponges, corals, sea stars, sea urchins, and marine mammals including New Zealand fur seals and a resident pod of 60 bottlenose dolphins in Doubtful Sound. Life concentrates in distinct zones: the upper zone (0-15m) with hardy organisms like mussels and barnacles, the lower zone (15-40m) dominated by sponges and corals, and deep basins (40m+) with sparse life.

Conservation challenges include fragmented management due to jurisdictional gaps between terrestrial and marine authorities, commercial fishing targeting blue cod, crayfish, and pāua, and increasing tourism pressures. Conservation efforts began in 1995 with the Guardians of Fiordland Fisheries and Marine Environment, followed by the Fiordland Marine Management Act 2005, which established 928,000 hectares as a special management area with eight new marine reserves.

9.text:
[Page 8] As New Zealand’s population grows and spreads, producing more buildings and road networks, the risk from landslides increases. This is addressed by legislation that controls resource development (Resource Management Act 1991), building activity (Building Act 1991), and emergency management (Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002). The insurance scheme administered by the Earthquake Commission also helps to spread and mitigate the risk. Soil conservation and forestry techniques are employed to reduce landslides on productive land.

9.document_title: Landslides
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document explains landslides as natural processes affecting New Zealand and globally. It defines landslides as movements of earth and materials down slopes and coastlines, detailing causes including gravity, weak rock, steep slopes, deforestation, earthquakes, and heavy rainfall. The document classifies landslide types by movement patterns: falling, sliding, and flowing. New Zealand's main types include alpine landslides (rock avalanches reaching 200 km/h), low mountain landslides (gradual movements), and layered rock landslides. Additional coverage includes rotational landslides, creeping earthflows, regolith landslides (most widespread), and submarine landslides. Major historical events documented include the 13,000-year-old hard rock landslide in Fiordland forming Green Lake, the 1846 Waihī mud flow (55-60 deaths), the 1923 King Country rail crash (17 deaths), the 1929 Murchison earthquake-triggered slides (14 deaths), and the 1979 Abbotsford disaster (69 houses destroyed). Deforestation between 1880-1920 increased landslide activity sevenfold. Approximately 362 landslide-related deaths occurred between the 1840s and early 2000s. Protective measures include building codes, road warnings, land management practices, legislation, and engineering solutions such as the Clyde Dam stabilization project ($936 million).

10.document_title: Māori Land Rights, Indigenous Law, and Colonial Legislation in New Zealand: A Historical and Legal Analysis
10.document_summary:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

11.text:
[Page 3] Rights to bodies of water were shown by posts, which were placed in particular areas and were often given names. 11.document_title: Māori Land Tenure and Customary Rights Systems
11.document_summary: This document explores the traditional Māori system of land tenure and property rights known as "take whenua." Land was historically held communally by tribal groups (hapū) with individual and family use rights for specific purposes. Key principles included discovery (whenua kite hou), ancestral rights (take tupuna), conquest (take raupatu), and gifting (take tuku). Mana whenua refers to tribal authority over land and water bodies. Continuous occupation (ahi kā), symbolized by keeping fires burning, was essential to maintain land rights. The principle of ringa kaha meant victors had to actively defend conquered lands. Abandonment caused rights to diminish from ahi kā to ahi tere to ahi mataotao. Land transfers included conditions confirmed through ceremonies and taonga (treasures). The Native Land Court, established in 1865, resolved disputes but often simplified Māori customs, preferring conquest-based claims. By 1847, Chief Justice William Martin noted Māori had appropriated all valuable land through these customary systems. The system was fluid and accommodated changing tribal relationships, with disputed lands arising from migration and inter-tribal marriage.

12.text:
[Page 1] Te Tiriti o Waitangi, signed between Māori and the British Crown in 1840, promised Māori could continue to own their lands, forests and fisheries for as long as they wished. However, tribes lost many resources through: government purchase of Māori land for low prices that left Māori with inadequate land reserves confiscation of land following the New Zealand wars the consequences of Native Land Court operations. Māori sought compensation for these and many other breaches of the treaty. Early settlements In the early 20th century two commissions of inquiry into the treatment of Māori found the Crown had acted unfairly. In the mid 20th century some compensation was finally paid to Taranaki, Ngāi Tahu and Waikato Maniapoto. However, these were tiny sums of money compared to the value of what had been taken from the tribes. After Māori moved to urban areas stronger protests about treaty breaches began, part of a Māori political and cultural renaissance. Tribunal and negotiations The Waitangi Tribunal was set up in 1975 to hear claims about Crown breaches of the treaty. From 1985 the tribunal could hear claims relating to breaches dating back to 1840, and it issued reports on these claims. In 1989 a Treaty of Waitangi policy unit was set up in the Department of Justice to advise the government on treaty policy, and negotiations began with claimants on their historical claims. The first treaty claim settlement, concerning the Waitomo Caves, was signed in 1989. In 1992 the Sealord agreement settled claims over commercial fisheries it was worth $170 million. Another large settlement involving a number of tribes was the ‘Treelords’ deal in 2008, which included almost $200 million of forest land. Some tribes found the time and expense of treaty claims too much, and decided to bypass the tribunal and negotiate directly with the government. The Waikato Tainui confederation of tribes, the first to do this, agreed to a settlement worth $170 million in 1995. The Ngāi Tahu tribe negotiated with the government after a claim to the tribunal was heard. They received a settlement worth $170 million in 1998. Some settlements included formal apologies from the Crown, and some involved cultural redress such as the restoration of Māori place names for example, Aoraki/Mt Cook. By 2010, 26 final settlements had been written into law. Settlement process As the settlement process speeded up, treaty claims developed a distinct process. The Crown sought to: identify treaty breaches identify those affected by them find their spokespeople negotiate a deed of settlement which outlined the settlement, often including land, money and an apology. Some people were critical of the treaty settlement process, calling it a ‘gravy train’ which unfairly benefited a few. In 1994 the government tried to cap the total value of settlements at $1 billion, but Māori strongly opposed this. By the early 2000s most people accepted the idea of treaty settlements. The process was seen as an example to the world of how to resolve historic grievances.
{}

12.document_title: Treaty of Waitangi Settlement Process: Historical Development and Implementation
12.document_summary: This document outlines the Treaty of Waitangi settlement process in New Zealand, tracing its evolution from early 20th-century commissions of inquiry through 2011. It explains how Māori lost lands through government purchases, confiscation, and Native Land Court operations despite the 1840 treaty promising continued ownership. The Waitangi Tribunal was established in 1975, expanding in 1985 to address historical grievances dating back to 1840. The Treaty of Waitangi Policy Unit (TOWPU) was created in 1989 to coordinate settlement negotiations. Major settlements include the 1989 Waitomo Caves transfer, 1992 Sealord fisheries agreement ($170 million), 1995 Waikato-Tainui settlement ($170 million with Queen Elizabeth II's formal apology—the first to an indigenous people), and 1998 Ngāi Tahu settlement ($170 million addressing 34.5 million acres). By December 2011, 44 deeds of settlement had been signed. The settlement process developed a formal structure identifying breaches, affected parties, and negotiating deeds including land, money, and apologies. Despite controversies over conservation land and negotiation levels, treaty settlements became mainstream political practice and are internationally regarded as an efficient reconciliation model for addressing historical indigenous grievances.
