ByPokere Paewai - Māori issues reporter
2024-10-30 19:29:19+13:00

The changes to the Marine and Coastal Area Act would make it harder
for Māori to make customary claims on coastlines, a critic says. Changes
to Māori marine title have gone before the justice select committee, with one submitter saying the Bill is based on racist myth. The changes to the Marine and Coastal Area Act would make it harder for Māori to make customary claims on coastlines. Section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area Act 2011 requires an applicant group to prove they have exclusively used and occupied an area from 1840 to the present day, without substantial interruption, before they are granted Customary Marine Title (CMT). That threshold for CMT was eased after a decision by the Court of Appeal which found groups only needed to show they had enough control over the area that they could keep others from using it, and situations where the law itself had preventing them from doing so could be ignored - that decision is back before the Supreme Court on 4 November. Earlier this year, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith announced the government would introduce legislation to overturn the Court of Appeals decision - and amend section 58 "to make clear Parliament's original intent". This was supported by Hobson's Pledge leader Don Brash, who told the committee the courts had reinterpreted that intent. "We feel strongly supportive of this Bill as it intends to amend the original Marine and Coastal Area Act. Having said that if we had a choice we'd go back to the Foreshore and Seabed Act in 2004 where the Crown owns the foreshore and seabed on behalf of all New Zealanders, but that isn't on the table," he said. Victoria University law lecturer Luke Fitzmaurice-Brown said the Bill was based on the racist myth that upholding Māori coastal rights meant people would be unable to access public beaches. "That has never been true and the current law makes that very clear," he said. CMT cannot be sold and had no effect on public access, fishing or other recreational activities, but grants rights over resource consents, conservation, consultation rights over marine mammal watching and coastal policy, and ownership of various minerals
and protected objects. Fitzmaurice-Brown told the committee changes to

the law were "deeply reckless" and asked for the Bill to be withdrawn. "Through this Bill and other Bills this current government, you as many members of this committee, are unpicking the constitutional fabric of this country one thread at a time and in my view that is deeply reckless." Māori groups whose cases for CMT had already been decided in the courts - or had been decided and were under appeal - would remain unchanged However, cases that were still live before the courts or were undetermined would need to meet the higher threshold set by the government's new legislation. In September, the Waitangi Tribunal recommended the government halt its current efforts to amend the Marine and Coastal Area Act. 12.fileDescription: Former Attorney-General and National MP Chris Finlayson has strongly criticized the government's decision to amend the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, calling it "foolish" and "extremely harmful" to race relations. The proposed changes would toughen the test for Māori to obtain customary marine title, which recognizes exclusive Māori rights to foreshore and seabed areas. Finlayson argues the amendments undermine the original 2010 settlement between the National Party and Māori Party, contradicting the government's claim to restore original intent. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon defends the changes as necessary to achieve better balance for all New Zealanders. Labour and iwi leaders oppose the legislation, with the Waitangi Tribunal previously finding the changes reflect "blind adherence" to political commitments at Māori's expense.

ByTnatanahira - Māori news journalist
2025-08-06 06:03:04+12:00

Former Attorney-General and National MP Chris Finlayson. A former
Attorney-General and National MP has lashed out at the government over its decision to push on with controversial legislation that would make it harder for Māori to get customary marine title. Chris Finlayson is calling the move foolish and "extremely harmful" to race relations. But Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says it will see the law returned to its "original intention" and strike a better balance for the rights of all New Zealanders. The changes to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act would toughen the test for judging whether customary rights should be given. Customary title recognises exclusive Māori rights to parts of the foreshore and seabed, provided certain legal tests are met, including proving continuous and "exclusive" use of the area since 1840 without substantial interruption. A 2023 Court of Appeal ruling, however, declared that groups only needed to show they had enough control over the area that they could keep others from using it, and that situations where the law itself had prevented them from doing so could be ignored. The Supreme Court subsequently overturned that and the government put a pause on any amendments to the law. On Tuesday, Treaty Negotiations Minister Paul Goldsmith said after the discussing the ruling, Cabinet felt it still did not achieve the "balance" the government wanted and the test to win customary rights was still too low. His comment were echoed by Luxon who, speaking from Papua New Guinea, said the change would get the legislation back to its "original intention". "We obviously have looked at the Supreme Court decision pretty closely [and] think it's quite broad and able to be interpreted in quite a broad way," he said. "We think the best way to do [that] is actually to get legislation to put it back to its original intent, which struck the right balance." Chris Finlayson disputes that, and told RNZ the Supreme Court had already expressed "very well" what Parliament's intention back in
2010 was. "These amendments do not restore the original intention of

Parliament. They undermine them. Let there be no doubt about that at
all," he said. Finlayson was Attorney-General at the time the legislation was enacted in law in 2011, which replaced the controversial Foreshore and Seabed Act. "What they are doing by these foolish amendments is destroying the settlement that the National Party and the Māori Party reached in 2010." Finlayson said there was no justification for the move, which he said was "extremely harmful" to race relations in New Zealand. "Tangata whenua have a few wins in court, and it's ripped away from them by the government, which changes goal posts 15 years later. "I am very, very saddened by what they have done, and I think it's a very bad day for race relations in New Zealand. "I just can't believe that they're as foolish as they appear to be," he said. Labour Party Māori Crown-Relations spokesperson Peeni Henare said the changes would restrict the ability of Māori to test their rights in court. "In 2011, the National Party made much of their commitment to Māori 'having their day in court' and this proposed change takes that away again." Henare said the law, as it stands today, does not give Māori ownership rights like control over public access. "This action by the government does nothing to strengthen the Māori-Crown relationship, despite them saying they value iwi Māori. "The government needs to be straight up and admit they don't care about Māori. Their actions don't match their words," he said. The amendments prompted fierce backlash from iwi last year, including Ngāpuhi who walked out of an Iwi Chairs Forum meeting with the Prime Minister in protest of the legislation. It also drew the ire of Northland iwi Ngāti Wai, who said at the time they would not accept the Crown "exercising an authority we do not believe they possess". In September last year, The Waitangi Tribunal found the changes were characterised by a "blind adherence" to pre-existing political commitments at the expense of Māori. retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] Te Tiriti o Waitangi the Treaty of Waitangi ByClaudia Orange What is te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi)? Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi) was a written agreement made in 1840 between the British Crown (the monarch) and more than 500 Māori chiefs. After that, New Zealand became a colony of Britain and Māori became British subjects. However, Māori and Europeans had different understandings and expectations of te tiriti. Drafting and signing te tiriti Te tiriti was drafted in English and then translated into Māori by missionary Henry Williams and his son Edward. It was presented to around 500 Māori at Waitangi on 5 February 1840 and there was much debate. The next day, 6 February, more than 40 chiefs signed te tiriti. Copies of te tiriti were taken around the country, and many more chiefs signed. Most Māori signed the te reo tiriti. Reasons why chiefs signed te tiriti included wanting controls on sales of Māori land to Europeans, and on European settlers. They also wanted to trade with Europeans, and believed the new relationship with Britain would stop fighting between tribes. Those who did not sign te tiriti were concerned they would lose their independence and power, and wanted to settle their own disputes. Some chiefs never had the opportunity to sign it, as it was not taken to all regions. What did te tiriti say? The meaning of the English treaty was not exactly the same as the meaning of the Māori tiriti. Article One: in Māori it gave Queen Victoria governance over the land, while in English it gave her sovereignty over the land a stronger term. Article Two: Te tiriti guaranteed chiefs ‘te tino rangatiratanga ’ chieftainship over their lands, villages and treasured things. It also gave the Crown the right to deal with Māori in buying land. The English language treaty gave chiefs ‘exclusive and undisturbed possession’ of lands, forests, fisheries and other property. It also gave the Crown an exclusive right to deal with Māori over…

[Page 1] By Paul Meredith Tribal owners Traditionally, land was held by tribal groups but individuals or families could claim the right to use an area for a garden, catching birds or fish, cutting down a tree, or building a house. Sometimes there were disputes over who had rights to an area. Mana whenua Mana whenua means the authority of a tribe over land. It included rights not just to the land, but also the beds of lakes, rivers and the sea. Land rights principles Māori could claim land rights under a number of principles. Whenua kite hou means newly discovered land. The discoverer of an area had rights to it. Chiefs sometimes named areas after parts of their body. This made these places tapu (sacred), so no one else would dare to use them. People recited whakapapa (genealogies), to prove they were descended from the ancestors who had first discovered and lived in a place. Tribes sometimes conquered other tribes and moved onto their land. They had to be able to defend themselves in case the first group returned. Sometimes they intermarried with people from the conquered group so children of those marriages also had ancestral rights over the land. Tribes sometimes made gifts of land to other groups. Ahi kā continuous occupation To prove their rights to an area, Māori needed to show they had occupied it continually. This is known as ahi kā (lit fire), because people kept fires burning for cooking. If they left the land, the fire was seen as dying out, and they could lose their rights. Native Land Court The Native Land Court was set up in 1865 to decide on disputes over Māori land ownership. Māori had to argue their cases in court, and the Pākehā judges sometimes simplified and misunderstood Māori customs.

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] Following a major protest march by Māori in 1975, the government set up the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches of te Tiriti o Waitangi. At first the tribunal could only investigate claims of breaches since 10 October 1975. Developing the tribunal From 1985 the tribunal could investigate claims of breaches dating back to 1840. High profile cases investigated by the tribunal included one brought by the tribe Te Āti Awa, who did not want the Taranaki synthetic fuel plant to discharge its outfall into the sea near a reef where they gathered shellfish. A similar claim near Rotorua concerned the discharge of sewage into the Kaituna River, with its eel fishery. Both claims succeeded in protecting tribal food sources. The tribunal recommended that the Māori language be made an official language of New Zealand, which occurred in 1987. The tribunal recommended compensation for Ngāi Tahu for the loss of most of the South Island. Other important tribunal recommendations were for Ngāti Whātua’s Ōrākei claim, the Manukau Harbour claim and the Muriwhenua claim. Changes, 1988 onwards Claims to the tribunal began to pile up. A casebook system was adopted all the claims in a single area were researched together. Some people criticised the tribunal and thought the past should be forgotten. The government tried to limit the amount of compensation in 1994, but Māori opposed this. The Office of Treaty Settlements was set up to negotiate directly with claimants without waiting for a tribunal report, and also to negotiate with claimants who had tribunal reports. Tribunal enquiries identified matters which were undisputed, so hearings could focus on issues on which the Crown and claimants disagreed. Researching claims Research on claims was carried out by the tribunal, claimants and the Crown. Claims were classified as historical if they concerned Crown policies or actions before 1992. In the 1880s protesters from Parihaka, Taranaki, disrupted surveys of confiscated land. In the late 19th century Māori petitioned Parliament over land grievances, and some went to England to present these grievances to the monarch. In the 1890s Māori protesters obstructed Pākehā trying to open the spit across the mouth of Lake Ōnoke in Wairarapa. Our coastlines and oceans are subject to interlocking local, national, and international laws, property rights and customary rights, she says. Throw in unresolved Treaty of Waitangi claims and evolving court decisions. “It gets super complex really quickly.” Her research, in partnership with Ngāi Tahu, will have a particular focus on how rangatiratanga might be embedded in blue carbon legislation and action. retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 26] In 2003, the Pew Oceans Commission wrote that two things are necessary to solve the ocean’s problems: better awareness and better governance. Better awareness crashed into public consciousness in 2011, when the container ship Rena struck a reef and disgorged its oil and contents into the Bay of Plenty. Incredibly, three years later, that toxic chalice is still languishing in the bay. It’s not going anywhere until the Environment Court hears the owner’s request to leave it there. Better awareness comes in quieter ways, too, as people abandon the “inexhaustibility hypothesis”—the mistaken idea that the ocean is so vast and bountiful nothing humans can do will seriously deplete it. Better governance, in New Zealand’s case, means developing an integrated oceans policy and reforming the country’s scattershot marine legislation. “There are 18 main statutes, 14 agencies, and six government strategies for marine management and planning in New Zealand,” notes a 2012 report by Monterey marine policy specialist Michael McGinnis. Lack of integration makes it expensive and uncertain for commercial enterprises to operate in the marine area and for the government to plan and manage. “It has led to messy, poor decision making,” Gary Taylor tells me when I visit the Environmental Defence Society’s offices on Auckland’s North Shore. Kids, a beach, some noisy gulls—there may be no more idyllic New Zealand summer scene. But the idyll is threatened—from without, in the form of exotic invaders and climate impacts, and from within, with rising levels of sediments, nutrients and contaminants pouring off the land. The sea has never been as impervious to human impact as we had thought. Increasingly, our footprint leaves its mark, and the tides cannot erase it. How lightly can we tread to sustain our encircling seas? The government is forging ahead with plans to change the law governing New Zealand's foreshore and seabed, despite a Supreme Court ruling last year that appeared to undercut the rationale for the change. The proposed legislation stems from a clause in National's coalition deal with NZ First, which promised to revisit the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act. That commitment was driven by fears that a 2023 Court of Appeal decision could have made it significantly easier for Māori groups to win recognition of customary rights over parts of the coastline. The government introduced a bill to Parliament last year to prevent that, but it hit pause in December after the Supreme Court effectively overturned the earlier ruling. At the time, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith welcomed the development and said ministers would take time to reassess their plans. On Tuesday, Goldsmith confirmed to RNZ that Cabinet had agreed to press ahead with the law change regardless and to pass it before October. "Everybody in New Zealand has an interest in what goes on in the coastline, and we're trying our best to get that balance right." ## The 2016 Kaikōura Earthquake

At 12.02am on Monday 14 November 2016, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck central New Zealand, making it one of the most powerful — and complex — seismic events in the country's recorded history. [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

### A Remarkably Complex Rupture

What made this earthquake so scientifically extraordinary was its behaviour. At least 21 faults ruptured across 160 kilometres, with seismic energy leaping between them in ways that defied existing scientific models. [[3]](cite://3/1) Scientists had previously believed a fault could only trigger a neighbouring fault if they were less than about six kilometres apart — but the Kaikōura earthquake jumped across faults 15–20 kilometres apart. [[3]](cite://3/2) It is now considered one of the most complex earthquakes ever recorded. [[4]](cite://4/1)

One eyewitness, Scott Waterford, was literally astride the Kekerengu Fault as it ruptured. He described "the incredible noise" and watching trees lean over then right themselves, before the ground split open beneath his feet — his right leg going up and his left going down. The fault picked his house off its foundations and shunted it 10 metres away. [[4]](cite://4/2)

### Damage and Casualties

Two people lost their lives: one at Mt Lyford as a result of a heart attack, and another when a house collapsed in Kaikōura. [[2]](cite://2/2) Landslides cut off road and rail links to Kaikōura, stranding large numbers of visitors in the popular tourist town. [[2]](cite://2/3) State Highway 1 at Waipapa Bay was so badly mangled that the fault forced one section of road nearly four metres upward, while landslides blocked the road entirely around the headland — cutting locals off from schools and jobs. Repairing road and rail links was expected to take months, even years, and cost billions of dollars. [[5]](cite://5/1)

Beneath the sea, the earthquake unleashed a massive underwater landslide in the Kaikōura Canyon — a 1,200-metre-deep chasm south of the Kaikōura Peninsula. Around 50–60 metres of sediment roared down the canyon, scouring the sea floor to a depth of 20–30 metres and flowing at least 700 kilometres up the Hikurangi Trough. [[6]](cite://6/1)

### Tsunami

The earthquake also triggered the most significant local-source tsunami since 1947. [[3]](cite://3/3) Hundreds of people were evacuated from their homes to higher ground in Kaikōura and from low-lying suburbs of cities including Wellington and Christchurch. [[7]](cite://7/1) The maximum wave height onshore was 6–7 metres at Goose Bay, with 2.5-metre waves at Kaikōura and 1.6-metre waves reaching Wellington. [[8]](cite://8/1)[[9]](cite://9/1) At Little Pigeon Bay on Banks Peninsula, a three-metre wave shoved a holiday house off its foundations. [[8]](cite://8/2)

However, the tsunami's effects were dampened by a combination of low tide and coastal uplift along long stretches of the shoreline. [[8]](cite://8/3) There was also considerable confusion in the emergency response — in some areas, including Wellington, warning sirens weren't sounded until after the waves had already arrived. [[7]](cite://7/2)

## The 2016 Wellington Earthquake

The search results treat these as related but distinct events. The 2016 earthquake that affected Wellington was, in fact, the Kaikōura earthquake itself — but Wellington experienced it in a particularly significant way due to the unusual nature of the rupture.

Because the earthquake moved along at least five separate faults extending around 150 kilometres up the east coast of the South Island, its extraordinary release of energy was directed much closer to Wellington than to Kaikōura itself. [[10]](cite://10/1)

![embed-2](embed://2)

The earthquake necessitated the demolition of several modern office buildings erected on reclaimed land on Wellington's waterfront — a sobering outcome given that these were relatively new structures. [[11]](cite://11/1) The event reinforced long-standing warnings that Wellington faces significant seismic risk, with further large earthquakes considered not just likely but potentially overdue, meaning new buildings must be designed to survive such events and older buildings must be either strengthened or demolished. [[11]](cite://11/2)

The Kaikōura earthquake also challenged Wellington's tsunami preparedness. Warning sirens in some areas of the city weren't sounded until after the waves had arrived, exposing gaps in the city's civil defence response. [[7]](cite://7/3)

Would you like to explore more about what the Kaikōura earthquake revealed about Wellington's vulnerability to future seismic events?

1.document_title: Marlborough Region: Comprehensive Geographical and Historical Guide
1.document_summary: This comprehensive geographical and historical guide covers the Marlborough region of New Zealand's South Island. It encompasses key settlements including Picton, Blenheim, Kaikōura, and the Marlborough Sounds, along with notable geographical features such as D'Urville Island, Stephens Island, French Pass, and Tapuae-o-Uenuku mountain. The guide traces the region's history from early Māori settlement through European exploration and colonial development, including the Treaty of Waitangi signings (1840), the 1843 Wairau affray, and the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake. Major settlements are profiled with their populations and economic roles. The region's economy evolved from gold mining and sawmill operations to modern industries including dairy farming, viticulture, mussel farming, fishing, and tourism. Notable sites include Ship Cove, the Queen Charlotte Track, aviation heritage sites, and various Māori cultural landmarks reflecting the region's bicultural heritage and significance to Rangitāne iwi.

2.document_title: Canterbury Region: Comprehensive Geography, History, Culture, and Development
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of Canterbury, New Zealand's South Island region, covering geography, history, culture, economy, and governance. Geographically, Canterbury features vast plains, the Southern Alps, braided rivers, and Christchurch, the "garden city." The region's geology was shaped by volcanic activity (Banks Peninsula 15-12 million years ago) and glaciation, with significant seismic activity including devastating earthquakes in 2010-2011 (6.3 magnitude, 185 deaths) and 2016 (7.8 magnitude Kaikōura). Historically, Ngāi Tahu Māori settled the region 600-700 years ago, establishing centers like Kaiapoi. European settlement began with Captain Cook (1770) and intensified after the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), with the Canterbury Association organizing settlement from 1850. The region developed strong agricultural heritage, transitioning from large estates to family farms, with sheep farming dominant (3.15 million head by 1885, 11% of national flock in 2012), supplemented by wheat production (62.5% of national) and expanding dairy operations (115% increase 2002-2012). Major irrigation schemes, including the Rangitātā diversion race (1945) and Central Plains Water scheme (2015), enabled intensive farming. Industrial development centered on farm-related processing and manufacturing, maintaining 11% of national manufacturing employment by 2013. Tourism accounted for 8.4% of jobs in 2010 but was severely impacted by the 2011 earthquake, with recovery underway by 2014. Transport infrastructure evolved significantly with the Lyttelton rail tunnel (1867), road tunnel (1964), Ōtira tunnel (1923), and Christchurch airport (opened 1940, first international airport 1950). Culturally, Canterbury developed a rich artistic heritage with notable figures including Samuel Butler, Denis Glover, Allen Curnow, and Rita Angus. The region has a strong sporting tradition, including rugby (Crusaders), tennis (Anthony Wilding), and hosted the 1974 Commonwealth Games. Governance evolved from provincial abolition (1876) through the Canterbury Regional Council (1989) to the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority (CERA) post-2011. In 2013, Canterbury had 478,623 residents (11.3% of New Zealand's population), predominantly European (86.2%), with recovery efforts including the Christchurch Central Recovery Plan (July 2012) and ongoing reconstruction.

3.document_title: Tsunamis in New Zealand: Hazards, History, and Warning Systems
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines tsunamis as a significant natural hazard in New Zealand. It covers tsunami generation through sea floor movements from earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and landslides, and explains how these waves travel at high speeds in deep ocean before slowing and increasing in height near shallow water. New Zealand's vulnerability stems from its extensive coastline and location in the Pacific Ocean, where approximately 80% of global tsunamis occur. The document provides historical analysis of major tsunami events including the 1855 Wairarapa earthquake tsunami (magnitude 8.1-8.2), the 1868 Peru-Chile tsunami (magnitude 9.0) that devastated the Chatham Islands and Banks Peninsula, the 1947 Gisborne tsunamis, and the 1960 Chile tsunami (magnitude 9.5). Archaeological evidence indicates Māori settlements shifted from coastal to inland sites in the mid-15th century due to tsunami inundation. 19.document_title: What Kaikōura Taught Us
19.document_summary: The November 14 Kaikōura earthquake in New Zealand revealed unprecedented scientific discoveries about seismic activity. The event, now considered one of the most complex earthquakes ever recorded, ruptured at least 21 faults across 160 kilometres. Key findings include: seismic energy unexpectedly jumped between faults 15-20 kilometres apart (previously thought impossible beyond 6 km), an inland epicentre triggered a significant tsunami despite theoretical predictions, and evidence suggests the tectonic plate boundary itself may have ruptured. The earthquake unleashed massive underwater landslides in the Kaikōura Canyon, with 50-60 metres of sediment scoured down the chasm and flowing 700+ kilometres along the Hikurangi Trough. Remarkably, one resident witnessed the ground literally splitting beneath him as the Kekerengu Fault tore open. Scientists now have an unprecedented opportunity to study how marine life regenerates in the canyon's rich ecosystem following this catastrophic event.

20.text:
[Page 2] At least 21 faults ruptured across 160 kilometres, seismic energy leaping between them in unexpected ways. Scientists believed a fault could set off a neighbouring fault only if they were less than about six kilometres apart, but the Kaikōura earthquake jumped across faults 15 20 kilometres apart. Moreover, scientists didn’t think an earthquake with an epicentre so far inland could cause a tsunami. Yet the faults triggered the most significant local source tsunami since 1947. While its effects were dampened by the low tide and coastal uplift, tsunami wave evidence was found along 200 kilometres of coastline.

21.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the 2016 Kaikōura Earthquake (magnitude 7.8), one of New Zealand's most significant natural events. The earthquake ruptured at least nine interconnected faults across 120 kilometres of the Kaikōura coast, with displacements up to 12 metres on the Kekerengu Fault. Scientists including Russ Van Dissen and Tim Little investigated how seismic energy jumps between faults. The rupture extended from Culverden to Cook Strait, triggering over 8,000 aftershocks and unexpected surface breaks on previously thought-inactive faults like Papatea and Leader. The earthquake lifted 80 kilometres of coastline, with dramatic coastal uplift at Waipapa Bay where the Papatea Fault forced a 700-metre stretch of coastline 5.5 metres out of the sea. The event triggered approximately 100,000 landslides and caused significant landscape transformation. Marine geologists aboard the research vessel Tangaroa documented unprecedented underwater effects, including a 1.4-metre vertical slip on the Needles Fault. Using advanced drone technology and 3D mapping, researchers document fault interactions to improve New Zealand's National Seismic Hazard Model and enhance building codes. The research reveals complex plate tectonics shaped by the collision of the Australian and Pacific Plates, with the Marlborough fault system accommodating plate-boundary movement at three centimetres per year through periodic violent earthquakes.

24.document_title: What Kaikōura Taught Us About Wellington
24.document_summary: This article examines lessons from the magnitude-7.8 Kaikōura Earthquake of November 14, 2016, and its unexpected impacts on Wellington. Despite ground shaking below design code thresholds (0.6-0.8g vs. required 1.0g), approximately 40 Wellington buildings suffered severe damage, including modern structures like Statistics House (2005) and the Asteron Centre (2010). The article identifies three critical factors: the earthquake's unusually long duration (90 seconds), frequency characteristics (1-2 seconds) that resonated with 8-15-storey buildings causing amplified swaying, and liquefaction effects on reclaimed land creating a "bowl-of-jelly" amplification. These combined factors created a "perfect quake" scenario that current building codes fail to anticipate. The author argues that New Zealand's building codes rely on minimum one-in-500-year standards and should instead adopt advanced seismic technologies like base isolation, damping systems, and damage-resistant design. The article calls for a fundamental rethink of building standards, viewing structures as intergenerational assets rather than short-term investments, and designing buildings to endure 100+ years against nature's unpredictable forces.

26.document_title: The End of the Everywhere Bird: Red-Billed Gulls in Decline
26.document_summary: This article examines the dramatic decline of red-billed gulls (tarāpunga) in New Zealand, particularly at the Kaikōura colony, which has plummeted from 15,000-20,000 birds in the 1980s-90s to approximately 3,800 by December 2023. Researcher Jim Mills spent 55 years (1964-2017) monitoring and banding over 76,000 chicks, creating one of the world's largest avian databases. Red-billed gulls face multiple interconnected threats including predation by feral cats, disease, avian influenza, and critically, starvation due to changing ocean conditions. The gulls depend on krill upwellings off the Kaikōura coast, which require specific water temperature patterns; warm water intrusions prevent krill from reaching the surface. Birds have become smaller and lighter over decades—signs of chronic starvation—with only about half of breeding females attempting nesting. Wildlife rehabilitator Sabrina Luecht documents starving gulls at Project WellBird, warning of potential extinction within two to three decades. Mills' research contributed to the global "One-Third for the Birds" study, revealing that seabird breeding success declines when forage fish fall below one-third of historical maximums. While Otago's gull populations are increasing due to abundant krill, conservation efforts in Kaikōura include citizen science projects and predator control. The article emphasizes how these overlooked birds possess complex social structures and remarkable adaptability, yet remain vulnerable to environmental changes and human indifference.

27.text:
[Page 1] By Kate Evans Last year’s earthquake is now believed to be one of the most complex ever recorded. On November 14, two minutes after midnight, Scott Waterford had just gone to bed when the Kaikōura earthquake shook him out of it. Still in his undies, Waterford took shelter in a doorway. Then, as the shuddering intensified, he jumped off the veranda and ran into the paddock. “All I remember is the incredible noise, and because of the full moon I could see everything twisting and bending.” He saw trees lean over then stand back up, and power lines spark as they were ripped from his house. A minute or so after the shaking started, the ground split open. “I was standing there watching my house and trying not to fall over, and suddenly my right leg went up and my left leg went down. I was still swearing quite a lot.” Waterford was literally astride the Kekerengu Fault as it tore towards the sea. That’s when he started running. He sprinted across the paddocks to his boss’s house, leaping over a few fences on the way. Later, he discovered the fault had picked his house up off its foundations and shunted it 10 metres away. Scientists knew about this ‘lightning and thunder’ effect in theory, but only a couple of people have experienced it in person: first the shaking, then the land breaking. “The shaking moves faster than the fault unzips,” says Russ van Dissen, a GNS Science earthquake geologist who is an expert on the Kekerengu Fault. “Through instruments we know that this happens, that they travel at different speeds—but to have a person right at that place and see it with their own eyes is amazing.”

28.document_title: The 1855 Wairarapa Earthquake: Comprehensive Analysis of New Zealand's Largest Seismic Event
28.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the 1855 Wairarapa earthquake, one of New Zealand's most significant seismic events, which struck on January 23, 1855, near Wellington. With a magnitude of 8.0-8.2, the earthquake caused the Wairarapa Fault to rupture over 75-90 km, producing one of the world's largest horizontal displacements averaging 12 meters. The event resulted from the Pacific and Australian Plates colliding at 25 km depth, triggering over 250 aftershocks within 11 hours. The earthquake caused dramatic land uplift of up to six meters along the Wellington coast and Palliser Bay, exposing thousands of shellfish and stranding vessels. Physical effects included harbor water surges of approximately 2 meters, tsunamis reaching up to 9 meters in Palliser Bay, widespread ground fissures up to 5 meters deep, and massive landslides in the Rimutaka Range. Eyewitness accounts from residents and the British survey ship Pandora describe severe destruction with collapsed buildings and widespread damage across Wellington. The earthquake affected approximately 52,000 square kilometers, causing extensive infrastructure damage yet resulting in only 10 fatalities. The event significantly impacted Wellington's development and construction practices, with evidence suggesting a pattern of major seismic activity along the fault over 10,000 years.

[Page 1] 2024 01 08 22:09:13+13:00 By Kathryn Armstrong, BBC News A damaged car lies underneath a collapsed building in Shika town, Ishikawa Prefecture on 8 January. The death toll from Japan's devastating New Year's Day earthquake has risen to 161, authorities say. Efforts are continuing in attempts to find more than 100 people who remain missing a week later. But bad weather is hampering rescuers with heavy rain and snow triggering warnings of landslides and building collapses. The 7.6 magnitude earthquake struck the remote Noto peninsula toppling buildings and sparking a major fire. The majority of the deaths have happened in the hard hit cities of Wajima and Suzu. Meanwhile, the number of people missing has dropped from 195 to just over 100. The death toll has jumped from the 120 reported on Sunday. Police officers check a collapsed building in the city of Wajima, on 5 January. More than 2000 people are reportedly still cut off due to massive damage to roads. Several others are living in emergency shelters. The Japanese military has been handing out supplies including food, water and blankets for those who have had to vacate their homes. The defence ministry said in a statement on Sunday that it had sent nearly 6000 troops out to help with the relief mission. They added that they believe there are still people alive who need rescue and vowed to continue their lifesaving operations despite the ending of a critical 72 hour window to find survivors. A man walks past the ruins of a shopping district in the city of Wajima, on 4 January. Stories of miraculous recoveries have been emerging. A woman in her 90s was found alive under rubble five days after the earthquake hit, in Suzu. Those in the worst affected areas are being urged to keep their guard up as they continue to experience further quakes. As of early Monday local time, more than 1200 tremors had been recorded since New Year's Day, Japanese public broadcaster NHK reported. Japan is one of the most seismically active countries in the world, and activity has been increasing in the Noto area since the end of 2020. More than 500 small and medium earthquakes have hit there over the past three years. 43.document_title: Taiwan Rattled by 7.0-Magnitude Earthquake, No Major Damage Reported
43.document_summary: A 7.0 magnitude earthquake struck 32km off Taiwan's northeastern coastal city of Yilan on Saturday with a depth of 73km. The quake was felt across Taiwan and assigned an intensity-four category, indicating potential minor damage. Initial reports showed no major damage, though isolated cases included gas and water leakage and minor building damage. Over 3,000 homes in Yilan lost power temporarily, and TSMC evacuated staff from some northern facilities as a precaution. Authorities warned of potential aftershocks between 5.5-6.0 magnitude in the coming days. President Lai Ching-te assured the public that authorities had the situation under control. Taiwan's location near tectonic plate junctions makes it earthquake-prone, with historical precedent including a 2016 quake that killed over 100 people and a 1999 quake that killed over 2,000.

[Page 1] Fire fighters conduct a search for survivors in Suzu City, Ishikawa Prefecture three days after a major earthquake hit Japan on New Year's Day. Thousands of rescuers pressed on in their search for survivors of a New Year's Day quake that killed at least 77 people in Japan, hoping to save as many as they can within a three day survival window which ends on Thursday afternoon (early this evening NZT). "There's little time left until it's 72 hours since the quake," Masuhiro Izumiya, the mayor of hard hit Suzu city, said on Wednesday evening at a regional disaster response meeting. "We really need to muster all of our remaining strength to continue rescue efforts." Survival rates drop off 72 hours after the quake, according to emergency responders. Severed roads and the remote location of the worst hit areas have complicated rescue efforts. Nearly 600 tremors have hit the Noto peninsula since the main quake, raising fears of landslides and further damage to infrastructure. "Compared to other disasters the road situation into Wajima is very bad. I feel it's taking longer than usual for assistance to arrive," Shunsaku Kohriki, a medical worker, told Reuters in Wajima city. "I think realistically speaking the evacuees will have to live in really tough conditions for a while yet," he said. 100,000 houses without water The full extent of the damage and casualties remains unclear four days after the deadliest quake in Japan since at least 2016. mayor Izumiya says 90 percent of houses in Suzu may have collapsed. An aerial photo shows Nie Town in Suzu City, Ishikawa Prefecture isolated by landslides. Damage to roads and infrastructure has hampered post earthquake rescue efforts. All the deaths have been reported near the epicentre of the magnitude 7.6 quake in Ishikawa prefecture. More than 33,000 people have evacuated from their homes and about 100,000 houses have no water supply, officials in the area said. Around 30,000 households remained without power in Ishikawa, according to Hokuriku Electric. Mobile providers NTT Docomo, SoftBank, KDDI and Rakuten Mobile said connectivity was still patchy in some areas. An aerial photo shows a search conducted at collapsed houses in Suzu City, Ishikawa Prefecture. The city's mayor says 90 percent of houses there may have collapsed. As Japanese businesses return from the New Year holidays, manufacturers are also gauging the impact of the quake on their production lines. Display makers Japan Display and EIZO, as well as semiconductor firm Kokusai Electric said on Thursday they were repairing damaged factory facilities. 53.document_summary: The Wellington Region Emergency Management Office organized "The Long Walk Home" event on March 1, 2024, with over 300 participants walking 30km from central Wellington to Mana. The event aimed to raise awareness about the realities of getting home after a major earthquake. Emergency management officials estimate that approximately 80,000 people could need to walk home if a large earthquake struck during work hours, as roads and public transport would likely be unusable. The event was inspired by the 2013 Seddon earthquake, which forced many people to walk home when transportation systems were disrupted. Organizers emphasized the importance of earthquake preparedness and realistic planning for disaster scenarios.

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive geographical and historical guide covers the Marlborough region of New Zealand's South Island. It encompasses key settlements including Picton, Blenheim, Kaikōura, and the Marlborough Sounds, along with notable geographical features such as D'Urville Island, Stephens Island, French Pass, and Tapuae-o-Uenuku mountain. The guide traces the region's history from early Māori settlement through European exploration and colonial development, including the Treaty of Waitangi signings (1840), the 1843 Wairau affray, and the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake. Major settlements are profiled with their populations and economic roles. The region's economy evolved from gold mining and sawmill operations to modern industries including dairy farming, viticulture, mussel farming, fishing, and tourism. Notable sites include Ship Cove, the Queen Charlotte Track, aviation heritage sites, and various Māori cultural landmarks reflecting the region's bicultural heritage and significance to Rangitāne iwi.

2.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of Canterbury, New Zealand's South Island region, covering geography, history, culture, economy, and governance. Geographically, Canterbury features vast plains, the Southern Alps, braided rivers, and Christchurch, the "garden city." The region's geology was shaped by volcanic activity (Banks Peninsula 15-12 million years ago) and glaciation, with significant seismic activity including devastating earthquakes in 2010-2011 (6.3 magnitude, 185 deaths) and 2016 (7.8 magnitude Kaikōura). Historically, Ngāi Tahu Māori settled the region 600-700 years ago, establishing centers like Kaiapoi. European settlement began with Captain Cook (1770) and intensified after the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), with the Canterbury Association organizing settlement from 1850. The region developed strong agricultural heritage, transitioning from large estates to family farms, with sheep farming dominant (3.15 million head by 1885, 11% of national flock in 2012), supplemented by wheat production (62.5% of national) and expanding dairy operations (115% increase 2002-2012). Major irrigation schemes, including the Rangitātā diversion race (1945) and Central Plains Water scheme (2015), enabled intensive farming. Industrial development centered on farm-related processing and manufacturing, maintaining 11% of national manufacturing employment by 2013. Tourism accounted for 8.4% of jobs in 2010 but was severely impacted by the 2011 earthquake, with recovery underway by 2014. Transport infrastructure evolved significantly with the Lyttelton rail tunnel (1867), road tunnel (1964), Ōtira tunnel (1923), and Christchurch airport (opened 1940, first international airport 1950). Culturally, Canterbury developed a rich artistic heritage with notable figures including Samuel Butler, Denis Glover, Allen Curnow, and Rita Angus. The region has a strong sporting tradition, including rugby (Crusaders), tennis (Anthony Wilding), and hosted the 1974 Commonwealth Games. Governance evolved from provincial abolition (1876) through the Canterbury Regional Council (1989) to the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority (CERA) post-2011. In 2013, Canterbury had 478,623 residents (11.3% of New Zealand's population), predominantly European (86.2%), with recovery efforts including the Christchurch Central Recovery Plan (July 2012) and ongoing reconstruction.

chunkHighlights.text: In mid-2014 opinion was divided over the direction and pace of the rebuild. Tensions between the government and Christchurch City Council had hindered progress; some thought CCDU processes were scaring off developers, and thousands were still waiting for their homes to be rebuilt. On the other hand, the government’s relationship with the council was improving; about 10% of the rebuild had been completed, cordons had been lifted from the inner-city red zone and several large businesses had committed to moving back into the CBD.
The Kaikōura earthquake

At 12.02 a.m. on Monday 14 November 2016 a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck central New Zealand, causing significant damage to buildings and infrastructure in northern Canterbury and neighbouring Marlborough. Landslides cut off road and rail links to Kaikōura, stranding large numbers of visitors in the popular tourist town. Two people lost their lives: one at Mt Lyford as a result of a heart attack and another when a house collapsed in Kaikōura.

3.fileDescription: The November 14 Kaikōura earthquake in New Zealand revealed unprecedented scientific discoveries about seismic activity. The event, now considered one of the most complex earthquakes ever recorded, ruptured at least 21 faults across 160 kilometres. Key findings include: seismic energy unexpectedly jumped between faults 15-20 kilometres apart (previously thought impossible beyond 6 km), an inland epicentre triggered a significant tsunami despite theoretical predictions, and evidence suggests the tectonic plate boundary itself may have ruptured. The earthquake unleashed massive underwater landslides in the Kaikōura Canyon, with 50-60 metres of sediment scoured down the chasm and flowing 700+ kilometres along the Hikurangi Trough. Remarkably, one resident witnessed the ground literally splitting beneath him as the Kekerengu Fault tore open. Scientists now have an unprecedented opportunity to study how marine life regenerates in the canyon's rich ecosystem following this catastrophic event.

chunkHighlights.text:
By Kate Evans
Last year’s earthquake is now believed to be one of the most complex ever recorded.
On November 14, two minutes after midnight, Scott Waterford had just gone to bed when the Kaikōura earthquake shook him out of it.
Still in his undies, Waterford took shelter in a doorway. Then, as the shuddering intensified, he jumped off the veranda and ran into the paddock.
“All I remember is the incredible noise, and because of the full moon I could see everything twisting and bending.”
He saw trees lean over then stand back up, and power lines spark as they were ripped from his house.
A minute or so after the shaking started, the ground split open.
“I was standing there watching my house and trying not to fall over, and suddenly my right leg went up and my left leg went down. I was still swearing quite a lot.”
Waterford was literally astride the Kekerengu Fault as it tore towards the sea.

That’s when he started running. He sprinted across the paddocks to his boss’s house, leaping over a few fences on the way. Later, he discovered the fault had picked his house up off its foundations and shunted it 10 metres away.
Scientists knew about this ‘lightning and thunder’ effect in theory, but only a couple of people have experienced it in person: first the shaking,
then the land breaking.

“The shaking moves faster than the fault unzips,” says Russ van Dissen, a GNS Science earthquake geologist who is an expert on the Kekerengu Fault. “Through instruments we know that this happens, that they travel at different speeds—but to have a person right at that place and see it with their own eyes is amazing.”

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines the 2016 Kaikōura Earthquake (magnitude 7.8), one of New Zealand's most significant natural events. The earthquake ruptured at least nine interconnected faults across 120 kilometres of the Kaikōura coast, with displacements up to 12 metres on the Kekerengu Fault. Scientists including Russ Van Dissen and Tim Little investigated how seismic energy jumps between faults. The rupture extended from Culverden to Cook Strait, triggering over 8,000 aftershocks and unexpected surface breaks on previously thought-inactive faults like Papatea and Leader. The earthquake lifted 80 kilometres of coastline, with dramatic coastal uplift at Waipapa Bay where the Papatea Fault forced a 700-metre stretch of coastline 5.5 metres out of the sea. The event triggered approximately 100,000 landslides and caused significant landscape transformation. Marine geologists aboard the research vessel Tangaroa documented unprecedented underwater effects, including a 1.4-metre vertical slip on the Needles Fault. Using advanced drone technology and 3D mapping, researchers document fault interactions to improve New Zealand's National Seismic Hazard Model and enhance building codes. The research reveals complex plate tectonics shaped by the collision of the Australian and Pacific Plates, with the Marlborough fault system accommodating plate-boundary movement at three centimetres per year through periodic violent earthquakes.

In the Kaikōura Canyon, the 1200-metre-deep chasm that drops from south of the Kaikōura Peninsula into the Hikurangi Trough, the earthquake’s shaking unleashed around 50-60 metres of sediment. It roared down the chasm, gathering mud, then scoured the sea floor to a depth of 20-30 metres.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines tsunamis as a significant natural hazard in New Zealand. It covers tsunami generation through sea floor movements from earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and landslides, and explains how these waves travel at high speeds in deep ocean before slowing and increasing in height near shallow water. New Zealand's vulnerability stems from its extensive coastline and location in the Pacific Ocean, where approximately 80% of global tsunamis occur. The document provides historical analysis of major tsunami events including the 1855 Wairarapa earthquake tsunami (magnitude 8.1-8.2), the 1868 Peru-Chile tsunami (magnitude 9.0) that devastated the Chatham Islands and Banks Peninsula, the 1947 Gisborne tsunamis, and the 1960 Chile tsunami (magnitude 9.5). Archaeological evidence indicates Māori settlements shifted from coastal to inland sites in the mid-15th century due to tsunami inundation. The document details tsunami hazards including local earthquakes on submarine faults, the Hikurangi Trough subduction zone, landslides, and offshore volcanoes. Approximately a dozen tsunamis exceeding one meter strike New Zealand annually. New Zealand's dual warning system includes the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center for distant tsunamis (providing 12+ hours warning) and natural warning signs for local tsunamis (arriving within minutes). Key safety measures include tsunami gauge networks, evacuation zone maps, and public alert systems. The principle "If LONG or STRONG, GET GONE!" is emphasized for earthquake-triggered tsunamis. Only one official death from tsunamis has been recorded since European settlement.

chunkHighlights.text: The magnitude 7.8 Kaikōura earthquake sequence on 14 November 2016 triggered tsunami along the east coast of New Zealand. Hundreds of people were evacuated from their homes to higher ground in Kaikoura and from low lying suburbs of cities such as Wellington and Christchurch. However, conflicting reports meant that warning sirens in some areas, such as Wellington, weren’t sounded until after the waves had arrived. There was also confusion among the public over how to respond to the sirens.

10.filePath: pdf/What Kaikōura taught us about Wellington.pdf
10.fileDescription: This article examines lessons from the magnitude-7.8 Kaikōura Earthquake of November 14, 2016, and its unexpected impacts on Wellington. Despite ground shaking below design code thresholds (0.6-0.8g vs. required 1.0g), approximately 40 Wellington buildings suffered severe damage, including modern structures like Statistics House (2005) and the Asteron Centre (2010). The article identifies three critical factors: the earthquake's unusually long duration (90 seconds), frequency characteristics (1-2 seconds) that resonated with 8-15-storey buildings causing amplified swaying, and liquefaction effects on reclaimed land creating a "bowl-of-jelly" amplification. These combined factors created a "perfect quake" scenario that current building codes fail to anticipate. The author argues that New Zealand's building codes rely on minimum one-in-500-year standards and should instead adopt advanced seismic technologies like base isolation, damping systems, and damage-resistant design. The article calls for a fundamental rethink of building standards, viewing structures as intergenerational assets rather than short-term investments, and designing buildings to endure 100+ years against nature's unpredictable forces.

chunkHighlights.text: For Wellington, lessons of the magnitude-7.8 Kaikōura Earthquake on November 14 are beginning to emerge, albeit perplexingly. While the epicentre was in Kaikōura, the earthquake behaved unusually, moving along at least five separate faults and extending around 150 kilometres up the east coast of the South Island. That meant its extraordinary release of energy was much closer to Wellington than Kaikōura.

11.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth exploration of Wellington, New Zealand's capital city. It covers the region's geography, including Wellington city, Lower Hutt, Upper Hutt, Porirua, and the Kāpiti Coast with a 2013 population of 430,197. Wellington's distinctive physical characteristics include rugged terrain, a beautiful harbour, the famous Town Belt, and its location on three active earthquake faults along the Australian and Pacific tectonic plate boundary. Historically, the document traces Wellington's development from early Māori settlement through European contact beginning with Captain Cook's 1770 exploration and the New Zealand Company's colonization efforts. Wellington transformed from a chaotic early settlement (1840) to New Zealand's capital (1865) and financial hub, with significant growth driven by Julius Vogel's public works vision (1870-1876). The narrative covers industrialization, technological innovation including cable cars and aviation, and post-WWII developments including state housing and Porirua's creation. Wellington's evolution continued through the late 20th century with Pacific Island immigration in the 1960s, economic restructuring in the 1980s, and a successful rebrand as a cultural capital in the 1990s through film, IT, and biotechnology industries. Today, Wellington is established as New Zealand's arts capital, hosting the International Festival of the Arts and Wellington Film Festival, with world-class institutions like Te Papa Tongarewa museum and the City Gallery. The region features important conservation areas including Zealandia wildlife sanctuary and island sanctuaries. Demographics show 76% European residents, with significant Māori (12.7%), Asian (11.3%), and Pacific peoples (8.6%) populations.

chunkHighlights.text: About 1460 CE a massive earthquake, called Haowhenua (the land destroyer) by Māori, raised sections of Wellington’s coastline. The island of Motukairangi was suddenly joined to the mainland – today it is Miramar Peninsula.

The largest earthquake in recent times (magnitude 8.2) was in 1855. It raised the Wairarapa coastline by 3 metres, and land around Wellington by 1–2 metres. The quake brought benefits to the town – it drained Te Aro swamp, yielding new land. The Basin Reserve, intended as an inland dock, became a sports ground. Further afield, a new road was able to be built between Wellington and Petone on a rock platform raised from the sea.

In 1942 two strong quakes damaged city buildings and as a result, architectural ornamentation such as pediments was removed. Two more strong quakes occurred in 2013, and another in 2016 necessitated the demolition of several modern office buildings erected on reclaimed land on Wellington’s waterfront. Because further large earthquakes are likely – even overdue – new buildings are designed to survive. Older buildings must be either strengthened or demolished.

response.response_text:
## A Telling Silence: The Press and Māori Land in the 1880s

The attitude of New Zealand newspapers toward Māori land sales in the 1880s was, perhaps most damningly, one of **indifference**. The clearest window into this comes from the *New Zealand Herald* itself, which in 1883 acknowledged that the workings of the Native Land Court had 'been a scandal for many years past' — but went on to note that because 'the chief sufferers were Māori, nobody troubles themselves very much.' [[1]](cite://1/1)

That frank admission of public and press apathy is striking. It suggests that even when newspapers did report on the troubling mechanics of Māori land alienation, the expectation was that their Pākehā readership simply would not be moved to concern.

## What the Papers Did Report

When newspapers did cover the Native Land Court process, the *Herald*'s 1883 account painted a grim picture of what actually unfolded at court sittings:

- Māori landowners were kept waiting for months at a time near European towns while cases dragged on.
- Land buyers made cash advances to keep Māori claimants nearby, charging 'enormous interest.' [[1]](cite://1/2)
- The money, the paper observed, 'usually went for rum,' with the time spent in what it called 'debauchery.' [[1]](cite://1/3)
- The consequence was that, by the time a sitting concluded, Māori had 'entirely divested themselves of their land.' [[1]](cite://1/4)

This kind of reporting reflected a paternalistic and moralistic lens — documenting the social destruction without interrogating the structural system driving it. As a Native Land Court judge, Lewis, would later put it in 1891, 'the whole object was to enable alienation [sale] for settlement.' [[1]](cite://1/5)

## The Herald Under William Berry

There was some nuance within the press. Under editor William Berry, who led the *New Zealand Herald* from 1875 to 1903, the paper showed 'a distinct moderation in its earlier hostility towards Māori.' Berry had acquired knowledge of Māori history and demonstrated sympathy with issues affecting Māori. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Yet even this more considered editorial voice had its limits. The *Herald* under Berry supported the government's attack on Te Whiti's village at Parihaka in 1881, on the grounds that it would open up 'a fertile area of the country for European settlement.' [[2]](cite://2/2) The interests of Pākehā settlement consistently outweighed Māori land rights, even in the more sympathetic corners of the press.

## Māori Voices in the Press

Māori themselves were not passive in this media landscape. They wrote to newspapers — including the government press — to warn both Pākehā and fellow Māori about dishonest land sales, often providing genealogy and geographic boundaries to assert ownership and declaring that particular land 'would not be given up.' [[3]](cite://3/1) This was a deliberate, pragmatic use of the press as a tool of resistance and instruction.

## Fading from the Page

By the 1890s, 'the Māori question' had largely faded from the mainstream printed page, replaced by new preoccupations around women's rights and labour politics. [[4]](cite://4/1) The systemic dispossession that the *Herald* had itself called a scandal just years earlier quietly slipped out of the public conversation.

As author Ted Reynolds reflected decades later, the *Herald*'s own 1883 words still rang true: the suffering was real and documented — but because it was Māori suffering, it didn't prompt action. [[5]](cite://5/1)

1.document_title: Māori Newspapers and Magazines in New Zealand: A Comprehensive Historical Overview
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides a historical overview of Māori-language newspapers and magazines in New Zealand from 1842 onwards. The first Māori newspaper, Ko te Karere o Nui Tireni, was published by the government in 1842, followed by approximately 40 Māori newspapers through the early 1930s. These publications served distinct purposes: government newspapers taught Māori about Pākehā customs and laws; philanthropist and church-owned papers (Te Karere o Poneke, Te Korimako, Te Haeata) promoted temperance and Christianity; and Māori-owned papers (Te Hokioi, Te Wananga, Kotahitanga) gave voice to Māori perspectives on government, land issues, and political discourse. The newspapers contained news, editorials, letters, and advertisements, serving as invaluable historical records of Māori-Pākehā interactions and cultural traditions. Māori-led newspapers ceased as major publications after 1913. Māori magazines emerged later, with Te Ao Hou (1952-1975) being the first, published by the Department of Māori Affairs and supporting emerging writers like Witi Ihimaera and Patricia Grace. Subsequent publications included government magazines (Te Kaea, Tu Tangata, Kōkiri Paetae), language revitalization publications (Toi Te Kupu, He Muka), tribal magazines (Kia Hiwa Ra, Te Karaka), and pan-tribal publications (Mana). These publications reflect Māori oral traditions through poetic language and metaphors, while preserving the Māori language and documenting New Zealand history from a Māori perspective.

[Page 1] Magazines and periodicals ByBen Schrader Early publications Wellington’s first settlers brought books and periodicals to set up a public library. The first local periodical was the New Zealand Journal , published by the New Zealand Company from 1840 to 1852. It aimed to promote the company and its settlements, but included letters about colonial life. In the 1860s local imitations of the British humour magazine Punch were published. Other magazines included the New Zealand Magazine , which lasted for a year, and Zealandia , which concentrated on local content and produced 12 issues. Early literary magazines From 1893 the Triad focused on the arts, with Charles Baeyertz its colourful editor. From 1915 it was produced in Sydney. It closed in 1926. The New Zealand Illustrated Magazine , which aimed to foster New Zealand art and writing, ran from 1899 to 1905. The quarterly Art in New Zealand was published from 1928 to 1946. Popular magazines Popular magazines of the 1920s and 1930s included: the Mirror , a magazine for middle class women that covered royal tours and society weddings the New Zealand Woman’s Weekly , which was published from 1932 the New Zealand Listener , founded by the government in 1939 to publish radio listings. Later art and literary magazines Between 1930 and 1950 more attempts were made to set up arts and literary magazines. These often aimed to support nationalist writing and tell New Zealand stories. They included: Phoenix , which published just four issues but was an outlet for important writers Tomorrow , which was banned by the government because of its radical politics Landfall , which was founded in 1947 with Charles Brasch as editor. Literary magazines in the 2010s included Sport and New Zealand Books . Specialist magazines Special interest magazines have focused on diverse issues, including temperance ( White Ribbon ), the environment ( Forest and Bird ), farming ( New Zealand Farmer ), food and wine ( Cuisine ) and New Zealand music ( Rip It Up ). Te Ao Hou and Mana focused on Māori culture; Broadsheet was a feminist magazine, and Consumer explored consumer issues. The internet The rise of the internet in the early 2000s meant that some magazines lost readers. However, many publications set up websites. Some magazines were only produced online. Early ventures, 1840 to 1890 Magazines and journals have been part of New Zealand’s cultural landscape since the beginning of organised European settlement. The first settlers to Wellington carried with them a collection of books and periodicals for a public library to foster the colony’s intellectual life. Many settlers were avid readers of British and American periodicals, from the conservative Spectator , a weekly (published from 1828), to the radical quarterly Westminster Review (1823). Such periodicals carried analytical articles and commentary on the likes of literature, politics, culture, economy and the arts. This and their smaller format helped to distinguish them from daily and weekly newspapers. From 1840 there were occasional attempts to create local versions of foreign periodicals aimed at a New Zealand readership and publishing the work of local writers. A guiding aim for many of them was to encourage a New Zealand literature that spoke to New Zealand issues and concerns. While many of these ventures were short lived, new initiatives continued to form and seek an audience.

4.document_title: The History and Evolution of New Zealand Newspapers: From Colonial Press to Digital Era (1839-2000s)
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces New Zealand's newspaper industry from 1839 to the early 21st century, beginning with the New Zealand Gazette printed in London in 1839. It follows the evolution through the colonial period when hand-printed weekly papers served local communities. The 1860s gold rush and population growth, combined with improved printing technology and telegraph communication, made newspapers increasingly viable. By 1911, there were 64 daily papers, with major publications like the New Zealand Herald (1863) and Otago Daily Times (1861) establishing themselves as key outlets. The text examines journalism professionalization through the United Press Association (1879) and highlights editors and proprietors who leveraged newspapers for political influence. It covers technological advances from steam-powered presses to computerized typesetting, and addresses women's gradual expansion from social columns into serious reporting. The mid-20th century saw competition from radio and television reduce newspaper numbers, though offset printing and computers accelerated production. By 2007, most New Zealand papers were owned by two Australian companies (Fairfax and APN). Despite internet challenges and declining classified advertising, newspapers demonstrated resilience through localized distribution and essential community roles, with readership declining less than 5% by 2009.

They include Auckland’s New Zealand Herald (set up in 1863) and Wellington’s Evening Post (1865), which merged with its morning rival the Dominion to become the Dominion Post in 2002.

7.document_title: New Zealand's Relations with Asia: Historical Evolution from Colonial Era to Modern Economic Partnership
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces New Zealand's evolving relationship with Asia from the 1790s through the early 21st century. Early contacts began through sealing trade and Chinese gold mining in the 1860s-1880s, though Pākehā New Zealanders initially viewed Asia with suspicion and implemented restrictive immigration laws targeting Chinese, Japanese, and Indian nationals. British imperial connections significantly influenced New Zealand's perspective on Asian nations. Key historical events include the 1936 rugby tour to Japan, New Zealand's support for China during Japanese invasion (1931-1937), military involvement in WWII, and post-war occupation of Japan through Jayforce (1946-1949). During the Cold War, New Zealand formed strategic military alliances including ANZUS (1951) and SEATO (1954), participated in the Korean War and Vietnam War, and engaged in the Malaysian Emergency and Indonesian Confrontation. A pivotal shift occurred in the 1970s when Britain's entry into the European Economic Community forced New Zealand to diversify exports toward Asia. This economic reorientation accelerated with China's economic liberalization, culminating in New Zealand becoming the first developed nation to sign a free-trade agreement with China (2008). By 2018, China had become New Zealand's largest trading partner. The 1986 Immigration Policy Review marked a fundamental policy shift from favoring European immigration to actively recruiting Asian professionals. Asian residents increased from 33,834 (1986) to 251,130 (2006), with projections of approximately 700,000 Asian New Zealanders by 2026. Cultural integration deepened through Asian cuisine adoption, language study, and media representation. By 2002, New Zealand had diverse Asian media outlets and elected MPs of Asian descent. New Zealand expanded diplomatic engagement with multilateral Asian institutions including ASEAN, APEC, and the East Asia Summit, illustrating its transformation from a security-focused Cold War ally to an economically integrated Asia-Pacific nation.

[Page 1] Newspapers ByMark Derby Early newspapers New Zealand’s first newspaper, the New Zealand Gazette , was printed in London in 1839 by the New Zealand Company for settlers migrating to Wellington. Further issues were published in 1840 after they arrived, and newspapers were produced in other European settlements as they were established. A government paper was published at Russell, the capital, from June 1840. Production of newspapers was a long, slow process. Most appeared just once or twice a week. Transport was difficult, so each paper served only its local community. Overseas news was reprinted from three month old papers arriving from Europe by ship. Growth The gold rush and growing population in the 1860s made newspapers more viable. Several papers from this period are still published today, including the New Zealand Herald and the Evening Post (now the Dominion Post ). The Otago Daily Times was the first daily paper. Aspiring politicians, including Julius Vogel and John Ballance (both later premiers), started papers to further their political ambitions. Printing technology improved, making it quicker to produce papers. Illustrations were often included. The telegraph made it possible to report on national and international events. In 1879 the United Press Association (later the New Zealand Press Association) was set up to share news among the main papers. Early 20th century Newspapers grew in the early 20th century, and by 1911 there were 64 daily papers in New Zealand. Press agencies supplied international news, papers published poems, stories and essays, and some journalists became nationally or internationally known. An increasing number were women, but they were often confined to covering ‘women’s issues’.

[Page 12] Native Land Court The treaty’s promised protection of Māori land rights was ignored by successive governments. By 1860 almost the entire South Island had been alienated from Māori. The Native Land Court (later the Māori Land Court) converted iwi owned Māori land rights into Crown granted titles, making the land easier to sell. By the early 1890s around two thirds of the North Island had been alienated, and land loss continued through the late 19th and 20th centuries.

12.document_title: Kāwanatanga: Māori Governance, Colonial Authority, and Modern Challenges in New Zealand
12.document_summary: This document explores kāwanatanga, the Māori concept of governance and state authority, tracing its evolution from the 19th century to contemporary times. It begins with the 1835 Declaration of Independence by northern chiefs asserting sovereign power, followed by the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi where a critical translation discrepancy emerged—"kāwanatanga" was translated as "absolute sovereignty" in English, potentially misrepresenting chiefs' understanding. The document details colonial government strategies to assert kāwanatanga over Māori, including military interventions by governors like FitzRoy, Gore Browne, and Grey to suppress resistance over land ownership and the Māori King movement. Key mechanisms of colonial control included the Native Land Court (1865) which converted collective tribal land ownership to individual titles facilitating European acquisition, four Māori parliamentary seats (1867) that incorporated Māori into colonial governance while limiting influence, and co-option of chiefs through councils. Despite these controls, Māori maintained nationalist movements like Kīngitanga and Kotahitanga. From the 1970s onwards, the Waitangi Tribunal investigated Treaty breaches, leading to policy shifts including Māori language revitalization, treaty settlements, and a bicultural framework. Modern challenges persist, particularly regarding Māori rights and the 2004 foreshore and seabed legislation claiming Crown ownership, which prompted over 30,000 Māori and supporters to march on Parliament. This was replaced in 2011 by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, generating further controversy regarding the balance between Crown authority and Māori interests.

13.document_title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to Modern Legal Recognition
13.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

14.text:
[Page 5] Land confiscation Following the New Zealand wars of the 1860s, the Native Land Court was involved in the confiscation of Māori land. The courts were given specific powers to investigate the claims of ‘rebel’ and ‘non rebel’ landowners. Land owned by ‘rebels’ was deemed to be Crown land.

14.document_title: Māori Land Court: Historical Evolution and Legislative Development from Treaty of Waitangi to Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the complete history and evolution of the Māori Land Court (Te Kōti Whenua) and Māori land tenure in New Zealand from the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) through 1993. The document covers three major periods: (1) The transformation from communal tribal land ownership to individual titles following the Native Lands Act 1862, which established courts to issue legal titles and introduced the 10-owner rule, resulting in massive land alienation—by the early 20th century, only 2 million of 27 million hectares remained in Māori ownership; (2) The legislative evolution from 1873-1909, including the abolition of the 10-owner rule under the Native Lands Act 1873, which inadvertently created fragmented titles with numerous owners, and the passage of approximately 560 acts dealing with Māori land, despite protective measures like the "taihoa" policy, over 800,000 hectares were sold; (3) The transformation from 1920-1993, where by 1920 only 19 acres per Māori remained, prompting the court to shift from land acquisition to land development support, culminating in the Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993—the first Māori land legislation referencing the Treaty of Waitangi and emphasizing land retention and development. The court's primary objectives evolved from facilitating land transfers to retaining Māori land ownership and promoting effective land use, while maintaining jurisdiction over marae governance and cultural matters.

15.text:
[Page 2] Alienation of Māori land Māori lost land to the Crown and private owners through a wide variety of methods. The dominant acquirer, by purchase or otherwise, was the Crown, even after the first Native Lands Acts were passed in 1862 and 1865, setting up the Native Land Court to investigate Māori land titles. In the 2000s Māori land alienation is a central subject of investigation and reporting by the Waitangi Tribunal, and a major focus in the process of redressing historic grievances. Pre treaty transactions Early transactions Alienation of Māori land began before British sovereignty was proclaimed over New Zealand in 1840. Missionary organisations, private settlers and New South Wales land speculators all entered into various kinds of land transactions with Māori. For example, Te Rarawa chief Nōpera Pana kareao arranged with the Church Missionary Society for 1,000 acres (405 hectares) to be set aside at Kaitāia for the mission. There were numerous similar arrangements wherever missions were located.
