42.document_title: Te Awa-i-taia, Wiremu Nēra: A Māori Leader of Ngāti Māhanga
42.document_summary: Te Awa-i-taia (c. late 18th century - 1866) was a prominent leader of Ngāti Māhanga on the Waipā River. A skilled warrior renowned for his taiaha expertise, he participated in major Waikato campaigns against Te Rauparaha and Ngāti Ruanui in Taranaki. Converted to Christianity in 1833-1834, he was baptised as Wiremu Nēra in 1836 and became a conscientious convert, promoting Christianity among his people and building the first church at Whāingaroa. A staunch supporter of the Crown, he signed the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840 and opposed the Māori King movement, maintaining allegiance to Queen Victoria. He served as a government intermediary during the 1863 Waikato War, providing guides and support to British troops. Te Awa-i-taia also engaged in land sales to the Crown and attempted infrastructure development. He died at Raglan on 27 April 1866, succeeded by his nephew Hetaraka Nero.

43.text:
[Page 3] The authority of Te Rangihaeata and Te Rauparaha depended on their continued strength, and on their skills in reconciling conflicts among their migrant allies, and between them and allied local tribes. After Ngāti Raukawa's arrival in three migrations in the late 1820s, Te Rauparaha had permitted them to settle in the Ōtaki, Manawatū and Horowhenua areas. Te Rangihaeata, who, through his marriage with Te Pikinga, retained mana over the area north of the Rangitīkei River, gave certain hapū permission to occupy land there. Ngāti Apa later regarded Te Rangihaeata's mana as the most important factor preventing their enslavement by Ngāti Raukawa. In 1834 the balancing act was to fail; Te Āti Awa attacked Ngāti Raukawa at Haowhenua, Ōtaki, and a general war developed. Te Rangihaeata supported the Ngāti Raukawa side because of their links to him through his grandmother, Parekōwhatu. Other factions of Ngāti Toa, notably Te Hiko o te rangi and Ngāti Te Maunu, supported Te Āti Awa. Te Rangihaeata permitted another large group of Ngāti Raukawa to settle in the Rangitīkei area after Haowhenua. Following Haowhenua a group of Ngāti Tama came from Wairarapa to the Kapiti coast and camped at Paremata. Te Rangihaeata, Te Rauparaha, their Ngāti Kimihia followers, and a part of Ngāti Raukawa drove them to Ōmanga rau tāwhiri. After a year Ngāti Tama made an attempt to capture Mana Island itself. Te Rangihaeata forcibly expelled them to Ōhariu. Annoyed at their persistence, Te Rangihaeata said their leader, Te Kāeaea , must have dog's ears, since he was so obdurate; Te Kāeaea was henceforth known as Taringakurī. Te Rangihaeata was feared and disliked by the whaling communities living under his aegis. He exacted tribute in the form of numerous demands for the gifts he considered they owed him for his tolerance, demands which the whalers saw as extortion and bullying. Europeans who encountered him in the late 1830s or 1840s tended to regard him as Te Rauparaha's 'fighting general' or as his lieutenant. Te Rauparaha was credited with the greater cunning, but Te Rangihaeata was thought to be more ferocious. Te Rangihaeata's mother, Waitohi, died late in 1839. Te Rangihaeata erected a mausoleum to his mother's memory; it was later recorded in a painting by George French Angas . During the prolonged tangi held for her on Mana Island, Ngāti Raukawa irritation at Te Āti Awa re emerged, culminating in their attack on Waimea pā at the battle of Te Kūititanga, Waikanae. Once again Te Rangihaeata supported Ngāti Raukawa. In October 1839 the New Zealand Company ship Tory brought Colonel William Wakefield to the Kapiti coast to purchase land for European settlement. He induced Te Rangihaeata to sign, on 28 October 1839, a deed purporting to purchase all his rights and claims on both sides of Cook Strait. Te Rangihaeata intended to give Europeans the right to occupy certain specific areas such as Nelson. Later this deed and others were invalidated; they were inadequately translated or explained, and far too sweeping in their description of territories 'purchased'. On 19 June 1840 Te Rangihaeata signed the Treaty of Waitangi on board the Herald. He probably intended to do no more than accept a governor to rule over the turbulent whalers and keep the company settlers in check.
{}

43.document_title: Te Rangihaeata: A Ngāti Toa Leader and His Resistance to European Settlement
43.document_summary: Te Rangihaeata (born c. 1780s) was a prominent war leader of Ngāti Toa who shaped 19th-century New Zealand history. Born in Kāwhia, he rose to prominence through military campaigns alongside Te Rauparaha, participating in major war expeditions and establishing authority on the Kapiti coast (1821-1822). His life changed dramatically with European contact: he signed a land deed in 1839 and the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, misunderstanding the permanent alienation of land these entailed. Increasingly angry at European land purchases, he actively opposed surveying and settlement efforts, including blocking access to Porirua and burning surveyors' huts in Wairau. His wife Te Rongo was killed during an armed clash with European constables in June 1843. Following the Wairau incident, he opposed land sales in the Hutt Valley and faced military confrontations at Pāuatahanui under Governor Grey. Te Rangihaeata eventually retreated to the Poroutāwhao swamp, where he remained in relative isolation. He died in 1855, remembered as a significant Māori leader who fought to protect his people's land rights.

44.text:
[Page 4] Although the name of Taiaroa appears on the copy of the Treaty of Waitangi taken to the Otago region in June 1840, he did not sign. He played a leading role in South Island land sales to the Crown, and in February 1840 was one of a party of Ngāi Tahu leaders with whom Governor George Gipps tried unsuccessfully to negotiate a treaty. Although he professed friendship with the Pākehā he was generally cautious of settlement. However, the depopulation of the South Island's relatively small communities by disease, and the lessening of Ngāi Tahu control over their resources, was weakening the position of the tribe. In June 1844 Frederick Tuckett , a surveyor for the New Zealand Company, persuaded Taiaroa and other chiefs to sell the Otago block for £2,400. Taiaroa and several other Ngāi Tahu leaders later travelled to Wellington to protest that they had not received a 10th part of the Otago block, which had been promised as part of the sale agreement. In 1848 Taiaroa ceded his land rights in Canterbury and in 1853 he was a signatory to the Murihiku sale.
{}

44.document_title: Taiaroa, Te Mātenga: A Ngāi Tahu Leader of the South Island
44.document_summary: Taiaroa (Te Mātenga) was a prominent Ngāi Tahu leader born in the late 1790s at Waikākahi, who became influential from the 1830s-1860s at Ōtākou on the Otago Peninsula. He first encountered Europeans in 1823 when meeting Captain John Kent, subsequently encouraging trade and manufacturing dressed flax. During the mid-1820s, Taiaroa participated in Ngāi Tahu internecine warfare, warning relatives of attacks. He played a crucial role defending against Te Rauparaha's Ngāti Toa invasions (1829-1837), including the siege of Kaiapoi and the final victory at Tūtūrau. Though initially cautious of European settlement, Taiaroa engaged in significant land sales to the Crown and private buyers from 1838-1853, including the controversial Otago block sale in 1844. He attended major intertribal meetings, was baptized in 1859, and died in 1863 at Ōtākou, counseling his descendants to maintain peace with Europeans.

45.text:
[Page 3] Kawiti did not give his agreement to the treaty on 6 February when others signed at Waitangi, but his people still pressed him to sign. At a special meeting with Hobson, in May 1840, Kawiti reluctantly agreed to sign the treaty. (His name appears above the signatures of 6 February.) He expressed his reservations in the strongest terms, saying the Māori population was declining so fast that the Europeans were likely to get the land anyway. He did not want to 'sign away his land'.
{}

45.document_title: Kawiti: A Māori Warrior, Peacemaker, and His Enduring Legacy
45.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the life and legacy of Kawiti (Te Ruki), a renowned Ngāti Hine warrior and leader born in the 1770s in northern New Zealand. Known as "The Duke" by Europeans, Kawiti was a skilled military tactician who played crucial roles in major battles including Moremonui (1807-08), Te Ika-ā-ranganui (1825), the Girls' War (1830), and the Northern War (1845-46). He demonstrated exceptional military strategy at Puketutu and Ōhaeawai, and constructed the famous Ruapekapeka pā with underground bunkers. Beyond his warrior prowess, Kawiti earned recognition as a peacemaker and vigorously resisted British rule and the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840, fearing land dispossession. After peace negotiations in January 1846, he reconciled with rivals and settled at Waiōnui and Pākaraka. The document also recounts Kawiti's final words to his people, urging them to preserve ancestral treasures and resist when treaty promises are broken. His great-grandson Tāwai built a marae complex at Waiōmio Caves as a memorial to Kawiti, honoring four generations of leadership and cultural continuity within the whānau. Kawiti died in 1854 at approximately 80 years old, leaving a lasting legacy as both a formidable warrior and advocate for his people's sovereignty and territorial rights.

46.text:
[Page 4] Although Te Puni had signed the Treaty of Waitangi on 29 April 1840 at Port Nicholson, he does not seem to have thought well of the government, because they favoured chiefs he regarded as his inferiors. Also, officials doubted the validity of his land sales, which was damaging to his mana .
{}

46.document_title: Te Puni-kōkopu (Hōniana): A Māori Chief's Life and Legacy in Colonial New Zealand
46.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical account chronicles the life of Te Puni-kōkopu, known as Hōniana in his youth, a distinguished Māori chief of Ngāti Te Whiti and Ngāti Tāwhirikura hapū of Te Āti Awa. Born in Taranaki in the late eighteenth century, Te Puni acquired his name after escaping from Rewarewa pā by leaping into the Waiwhakaiho River. Initially overshadowed by his younger cousin Te Wharepōuri, he participated in various tribal conflicts and migrations, including the great overland migration of 1832 (Tama-te-uaua) to Waikanae and eventually to Wellington. As a crucial intermediary between Māori and European settlers, Te Puni welcomed the New Zealand Company settlement at Port Nicholson in 1839 and signed controversial land sale deeds with Colonel William Wakefield. From 1847 onwards, he served as an advisor to Governor Grey, receiving a pension and becoming an esquire during Grey's knighthood. He adopted European dress and lifestyle, becoming official visitor to Wellington Hospital in 1848, while maintaining his village's prosperity with livestock and crops. Though he supported the Crown, he opposed certain land purchases and protested inadequate consultation on various blocks. Disillusioned in his final years, Te Puni died on December 5, 1870, receiving a state funeral with government honors and a government-erected monument, leaving a complex legacy as a Māori leader who bridged indigenous and European cultures in 19th-century New Zealand.

47.text:
[Page 1] BySusana Suisuiki RNZ Pacific Journalist 2025 02 06 14:28:22+13:00 A Māori academic says that although New Zealand's founding document, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, is a partnership between Māori and the Crown, it is relevant for Pasifika people. Today, 6 February 2025, marks 185 years since the signing of the Te Tiriti (or Treaty of Waitangi in English) in Aotearoa. Huge crowds of people along with iwi (tribe) leaders, dignitaries and the politicians gathered in Waitangi. https://www.rnz.co. nz/international/programmes/datelinepacific/audio/2018973692/pasifika peoples need to be part of waitangi discussions "There's a deep history between Māori and Pasifika people," Professor Claire Charters (Ngāti Whakaue, Tūwharetoa, Ngā Puhi, Tainui) told RNZ Pacific Waves. She said like all people, including Pasifika, Te Tiriti o Waitangi "gives the authorisation for our tangata Te Tiriti peoples to come to Aotearoa/New Zealand." "It is the basic premise on which settlement was permitted into Aotearoa. "But I think the relationship between our Pasifika brothers and sisters is particulary unique and particulary close," Charters said. "While Pasifika peoples are also part of tangata Te Tiriti, they are part of us as Polynesians and Pasifika people," she said. Related https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/541081/waitangi day 2025 in pictur es https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/541047/the events around the c ountry for waitangi day https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/541042/wai tangi delivers education classrooms can t provide https://www.rnz.co.nz /news/national/541038/te matinitini ki waitangi thousands arrive at wait angi for many different reasons https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/in depth/54 0919/the day the maori queen came to waitangi

47.document_title: Māori Academic Says Te Tiriti o Waitangi Relevant for Pasifika People
47.document_summary: On the 185th anniversary of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (February 6, 2025), Māori academic Professor Claire Charters argues that while the founding document is a partnership between Māori and the Crown, it is also relevant for Pasifika people. Charters emphasizes the deep historical connection between Māori and Pasifika peoples, noting that Te Tiriti provides authorization for all people, including Pasifika, to settle in Aotearoa/New Zealand. She highlights that Pasifika peoples are part of the broader Polynesian and Pasifika community, making their relationship with the treaty particularly unique and close.

48.text:
[Page 1] 2024 05 14 16:18:58+12:00 [repub:theconversation] Olli Hellmann [the_conversation_tracker] https:/ /counter.theconversation.com/content/229469/count.gif?distributor=rep ublish lightbox advanced Younger respondents to a new survey were significantly more likely to recall the signing of the Treaty than older generations as a significant event in New Zealand's history. (file image) The stories Aotearoa New Zealand tells itself about the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi/the Treaty of Waitangi have evolved considerably over time. For many decades, starting with the 1940 centennial, state sponsored commemorations of the signing, the event was romanticised as a coming together of two peoples. Increasingly, these collective memories were challenged primarily by Māori activism, but also by the work of revisionist historians. As a result, today's official narratives acknowledge the Treaty was broken repeatedly, often violently, during European colonisation. And they also recognise the Crown's obligation to remedy past breaches. Some conservative politicians have seen this shift in collective remembering as an opportunity for political point scoring. They denounce recent reinterpretations of the Treaty as sowing social division and weakening national unity. For example, in his 2004 Orewa speech, then National leader Don Brash reviled the Treaty settlements process for creating "a racially divided state". In 2017, National Prime Minister Bill English claimed many New Zealanders "cringe" at Māori protests on Waitangi Day. Lately, ACT party leader David Seymour has attacked current interpretations of the Treaty as being "divisive". His Treaty Principles Bill aims to rewrite those principles, against loud opposition from Māori. But my new research, published recently in the journal Political Science, does not support claims the Treaty divides New Zealanders. In fact, the survey suggests quite the opposite: the Treaty provides a powerful symbol that promotes mutual understanding and reconciliation. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, centre, with ACT leader David Seymour, left, and NZ First leader Winston Peters arrive at the Treaty Grounds at Waitangi on 5 February, 2024. Our most important historical event The survey involved a broadly representative sample of more than 1000 people. The key question asked respondents to spontaneously name the most important event in the history of Aotearoa New Zealand. This may seem simple, but it is an effective way to tap into readily accessible and therefore meaningful memories. The Treaty of Waitangi was the most frequent response, among both Pākehā/European New Zealanders (38 percent) and Māori (59 percent). Younger respondents were significantly more likely to recall the signing of the Treaty than older generations. This possibly reflects efforts since the late 1990s to educate citizens on the Treaty and the role of the Waitangi Tribunal in redressing historical injustices. In fact, among those respondents born between 2000 and 2006, more than 70 percent identified the Treaty as the most important event in national history. Marchers on a hīkoi from Te Rerenga Wairua (Cape Reinga) arrive at the Treaty Grounds on Waitangi Day this year. Remembering the past matters The survey data make it possible to investigate how collective memories of the historical past shape what individuals think about politics and society in the present. In particular, we can compare two groups of respondents: those who recalled the Treaty of Waitangi as most important, and those who attached the greatest importance to Eurocentric historical events (such as the arrival of Captain Cook and European settlers, World War I, and women's suffrage). Participants were also prompted to rate their "warmth" towards other social groups. In addition, the survey included a range of questions about national identity and redress of historical wrongs against Māori. Analysis of the responses revealed four important findings.

48.document_title: Treaty of Waitangi Unites Rather Than Divides New Zealand, Survey Finds
48.document_summary: A new survey of over 1,000 New Zealanders challenges claims that the Treaty of Waitangi divides the nation, finding instead that it serves as a powerful symbol promoting mutual understanding and reconciliation. The Treaty was identified as the most important event in New Zealand history by 38% of Pākehā and 59% of Māori respondents, with younger generations (70%+ born 2000-2006) showing significantly higher recognition. Key findings reveal that Māori who prioritize the Treaty show warmth toward European New Zealanders, Treaty-focused respondents maintain strong national belonging, and Pākehā naming the Treaty support inclusive national identity and historical redress. The research contradicts conservative politicians' arguments that revisionist Treaty narratives create division, demonstrating instead that acknowledging Treaty breaches fosters bicultural belonging and commitment to reconciliation.

49.text:
[Page 3] The symbolic power of the Treaty When nations craft narratives about their historical origins be it revolutions, wars or the making of constitutions they tend to frame these stories positively. Aotearoa New Zealand is different. The Treaty of Waitangi often considered the nation's founding document includes in its more recent narratives an admission of guilt and an obligation to remedy past wrongs. Some politicians have taken aim at these narratives. They claim dwelling too much on historical breaches of the Treaty for example, through Waitangi Tribunal proceedings or Māori protest strains the social fabric. However, the recently published survey findings indicate such concerns are misplaced. Rather, narratives that foreground Treaty breaches help forge a bicultural sense of belonging and commitment to work through those breaches. The survey also finds the Treaty holds especially strong symbolic power among young people. This suggests electoral strategies that seek to undo decades of revisionist storytelling about the Treaty will likely lead to diminishing returns in the future. *Olli Hellmann is an associate professor of political science at the University of Waikato. 50.document_summary: Ngāti Hāua, a central North Island iwi, received a formal apology from the Crown and signed a historic deed of settlement after eight years of negotiations. Treaty Negotiations Minister Paul Goldsmith delivered the apology for Crown actions spanning over a century, including the execution of ancestors in 1846, warfare in the 1860s, and extensive land acquisition that left the iwi virtually landless. The settlement includes statutory pardons for two ancestors, return of 64 culturally significant sites, $6 million cultural revitalisation fund, and $20.4 million in financial redress. The Crown acknowledged breaches of te Tiriti o Waitangi and their role in socio-economic hardship including poor health, inadequate housing, and low educational outcomes. Iwi Trust chair Graham Bell emphasized this settlement represents a new beginning and resource for future prosperity.

52.document_title: The Treaty Principles Bill: Legislation, Principles, and Nationwide Protest Movement
52.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines the Treaty Principles Bill, a four-page legislation introduced to Parliament on November 7, 2024, which aims to codify the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi in law. The bill establishes three main principles: Executive and Parliamentary power to govern in the best interests of all; Crown recognition of Māori rights as agreed in historical treaty settlements; and equal rights for all before the law. All parties except ACT have committed to voting it down at second reading. The document covers the bill's controversial early introduction timing and the subsequent nationwide hikoi (march) protest movement, representing a significant Māori unity initiative with participants from the Far North and South Island marching to Parliament. The Waitangi Tribunal's report found the bill breaches partnership principles, lacks consultation with Māori, misinterprets the Treaty, and would effectively revoke Crown promises to Māori. ACT's David Seymour argues Parliament should define Treaty principles to ensure equal rights within a liberal democratic framework, while critics contend the bill advances assimilation and damages the Māori-Crown relationship. The hikoi demonstrates widespread political engagement and solidarity among Māori communities opposing the proposed legislation, with organizers emphasizing themes of Māori unity and collective action across different regions of New Zealand.

53.text:
[Page 1] 2024 02 02 09:44:32+13:00 [repub:theconversation] Paul Moon* [the_conversation_tracker] https://c ounter.theconversation.com/content/221973/count.gif?distributor=repu blish lightbox advanced no caption. Analysis: When it comes to grappling with the Treaty of Waitangi/Te Tiriti o Waitangi, one of the commonest responses is that it's a matter of interpretation. It seems to be a perfectly fair reaction, except that historical interpretation generally requires adherence to rules of evidence. It is not a licence to make any claims whatsoever about the Treaty, and then to assert their truth by appealing to the authority of personal interpretation. Yet since the 1970s we've been faced with the paradoxical situation of a growing body of Treaty scholarship that has led to less consensus about its meaning and purpose. It is therefore worthwhile to investigate some of the more common misconceptions about the Treaty that have accrued over recent decades. This will not lead to a definitive interpretation of the Treaty. But it might remove a few obstacles currently in the way of understanding it better. The Treaty or Te Tiriti? A common view persists that the English and Māori versions of the Treaty are fundamentally at odds with each other, especially over the central issue of sovereignty. But research over the past two decades on British colonial policy prior to 1840 has revealed that Britain wanted a treaty to enable it to extend its jurisdiction to its subjects living in New Zealand. It had no intention to govern Māori or usurp Māori sovereignty. On this critical point, the two versions are essentially in agreement. The Treaty is not a contract The principle of contra proferentem appropriated from contract law refers to ambiguous provisions that can be interpreted in a way that works against the drafter of the contract. However, there are several problems in applying this principle to the Treaty. Firstly, treaties are different legal instruments from contracts. This explains why there are correspondingly few examples of this principle being used in international law for interpreting treaties. Secondly, as there are no major material differences between the English and Māori versions of the Treaty when it comes to Māori retaining sovereignty, there is no need to apply such a principle. And thirdly, under international law, treaties are not to be interpreted in an adversarial manner, but in good faith (the principle of pacta sunt servanda). Thus, rather than the parties fighting over the Treaty's meaning, the requirement is for them to work with rather than against each other. Relationships evolve over time No rangatira (chief) ceded sovereignty over their own people through the Treaty. Nor was that Britain's intention hence Britain's recognition in August 1839 of hapū (kinship group) sovereignty and the guarantee in the Treaty that rangatiratanga (the powers of the chiefs) would be protected. Britain simply wanted jurisdiction over its own subjects in the colony. This is what is known as an "originalist" interpretation one that follows the Treaty's meaning as it was understood in 1840. This has several limitations: it precludes the emergence of Treaty principles; it wrongly presumes that all involved at the time of the Treaty's signing had an identical view on its meaning; and, crucially, it ignores all subsequent historical developments. Treaty relationships evolve over time in numerous ways. Originalist interpretations fail to take that into account. Questions of motive British motives for the Treaty were made explicit in 1839, yet in the following 185 years false motives have entered into the historical bloodstream, where they have continued circulating. What Britain wanted was the right to apply its laws to its people living in New Zealand. It also intended to "civilise" Māori (through creating the short lived Office of Protector of Aborigines) and protect Māori land from unethical purchases (the pre emption provision in Article Two of the Treaty). And Britain wanted to afford Māori the same rights as British subjects in cases where one group's actions impinged on the other's (as in the 1842 Maketū case, involving the conviction for murder and execution of a young Māori man). The Treaty was not a response to a French threat to New Zealand. And it was not an attempt to conquer Māori, nor to deceive them through subterfuge. Myths of a 'real' Treaty and 4th article Over the past two decades, some have alleged there is a "real" Treaty the so called "Littlewood Treaty" that has been concealed because it contains a different set of provisions. Such conspiratorial claims are easily dispelled. The text of the Littlewood Treaty is known and it is merely a handwritten copy of the actual Treaty. And, most obviously, it cannot be regarded as a treaty on the basis that no one signed it. Another popular myth is that there is a fourth article of the Treaty, which purportedly guarantees religious freedom. This article does not appear in either the Māori or English texts of the Treaty, and there is no evidence the signatories regarded it as a provision of the agreement. It is a suggestion that emerged in the 1990s, but lacks any evidential or legal basis. Finally, there is the argument that the Treaty supports the democratic process. In fact, the Treaty ushered in a non representative regime in the colony. It was the 1852 New Zealand Constitution Act that gave the country a democratic government a statute that incidentally made no reference to the Treaty's provisions. This list is not exhaustive. But in dispensing with areas of poor interpretation, we can improve the chances of a more informed and productive discussion about the Treaty. *Paul Moon is Professor of History, Auckland University of Technology This article was first published by The Conversation.
{}

The author clarifies that: (1) the English and Māori versions are essentially in agreement on sovereignty, contrary to popular belief; (2) the Treaty is not a contract and should not be interpreted using contract law principles; (3) Treaty relationships evolve over time beyond originalist interpretations; (4) Britain's motives were explicit in 1839—to extend jurisdiction over British subjects, "civilize" Māori, and protect Māori land—not to conquer or deceive; and (5) myths about a hidden "Littlewood Treaty," a fourth article guaranteeing religious freedom, and the Treaty supporting democracy lack evidential basis. 56.text:
[Page 1] To honour the Treaty: Māori and Pacific people unite 'like the in laws' to redefine New Zealand's multicultural future ByEleisha Foon RNZ Pacific Senior Journalist 2024 02 06 10:41:25+13:00 Pacific people across Aotearoa are engaging with Māori in new ways and uniting on how to honour the Treaty of Waitangi, while also considering whether a new constitution is needed for the multi cultural nation that New Zealand is today. Waitangi Day, held on 6 February, is one of the most important days on the calendar for Māori. https://www.rnz.co.nz/int ernational/programmes/datelinepacific/audio/2018924863/pacific deleg ates at waitangi stand in solidarity Pacific delegates at Waitangi 'stand in solidarity' Thousands of people are gathering on Waitangi treaty grounds where the country's founding document was signed on this day in 1840. For months, several Māori groups have spoken out against the reform agenda of the new centre right government, and Pacific leaders and young people have joined them in protests. For Maori and Pacific, Waitangi Day not only marks the history of the Treaty, but a significant cultural shift, Former Minister of Pacific People's, Aupito William Sio, said. He said it is a moment where there seems to be a call to action to acknowledge the past but to also unite in carving a path forward to create the future of New Zealand. The change in government has become some what of a cultural catalyst, sparking fresh dialogue lead by Kingitanga the Māori King Movement around creating a new constitution, with Pasifika alongside Pākehā, key partners in that conversation. "We really need to have a serious conversation about what it means to be a nation of Aotearoa New Zealand and what the treaty actually means for not just Māori but all New Zealanders," Sio said. "Politicians come and go, but it is people that remain" and it is the people who ultimately have the power to shape the future of Aotearoa, he said. Maori and Pacific: 'Walk in both cultural identities' The Pacific has a unique role to play in helping form a blueprint for the nation going forward, according to Sio. He said Pasifika were "like the in laws" to Māori, noting overall about 20 percent of the population had ancestry or genealogical connections to Māori. Political Commentator Thomas Wayne shared similar sentiments about the deep connections between Māori and Pasifika people. He said there was a growing cohort of Pacific people who are also Māori. "I have grandchildren who walk in both cultural identities and I get a sense of what is good for Māori is good for Pacific, Wayne said. "We understand there is a cultural, linguistic, genealogical vaka and relationship to the people of this land. "We just need to turn up. When someone in the family is facing a challenge they need to know that we stand with [Māori]. We need to show them we can do that." Sio urged Pasifika people to learn about Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the significance of the nation's founding document. "I want them to be confident about their world views and multi culturalism," he said. Related https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te manu korihi/508467/live updates waitang i day 2024 dawn service https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te manu korihi/508 462/waitangi 2024 thousands stand in unity to challenge government o n treaty principles

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

chunkHighlights.text: Te Tiriti o Waitangi – the Treaty of Waitangi
ByClaudia Orange

What is te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi)? Te Tiriti o Waitangi
(the Treaty of Waitangi) was a written agreement made in 1840 between the British Crown (the monarch) and more than 500 Māori chiefs. After that, New Zealand became a colony of Britain and Māori became British subjects. However, Māori and Europeans had different understandings and expectations of te tiriti. Drafting and signing te tiriti Te tiriti was drafted in English and then translated into Māori by missionary Henry Williams and his son Edward. It was presented to around 500 Māori at Waitangi on 5 February 1840 and there was much debate. The next day, 6 February, more than 40 chiefs signed te tiriti. Copies of te tiriti were taken around the country, and many more chiefs signed. Most Māori signed the te reo tiriti. Reasons why chiefs signed te tiriti included wanting controls on sales of Māori land to Europeans, and on European settlers. They also wanted to trade with Europeans, and believed the new relationship with Britain would stop fighting between tribes. Those who did not sign te tiriti were concerned they would lose their independence and power, and wanted to settle their own disputes. Some chiefs never had the opportunity to sign it, as it was not taken to all regions. What did te tiriti say? The meaning of the English treaty was not exactly the same as the meaning of the Māori tiriti. Article Two: Te tiriti guaranteed chiefs ‘te tino rangatiratanga ’ – chieftainship over their lands, villages and treasured things. It also gave the Crown the right to deal with Māori in buying land. The English-language treaty gave chiefs ‘exclusive and undisturbed possession’ of lands, forests, fisheries and other property. 3.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces Māori history from Polynesian origins to contemporary times. Māori ancestors arrived in New Zealand by canoe before 1300 CE, establishing communal societies governed by tapu and mana. European arrival from the 1600s-1800s brought Christianity, literacy, and the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), followed by land wars and population decline to under 50,000 by 1900. The 20th century witnessed cultural revival through leaders like Apirana Ngata and Te Puea Hērangi, with renewed focus on language, arts, and traditions. The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) addressed historical grievances and facilitated land claims settlements. By 2019, approximately 800,000 Māori lived primarily in urban centers with established educational institutions and political representation. Contemporary Māori society demonstrates remarkable achievements in media, business, and tourism while maintaining cultural adaptation through integration of European and modern elements. Challenges persist including higher disease rates, literacy concerns, housing disparities, and unemployment. Today, Māori culture continues evolving through language revitalization programs and prominent figures in arts, film, and politics.

chunkHighlights.text: In 1840, a treaty was signed by representatives of Queen Victoria of England and more than 500 Māori chiefs representing numerous tribes throughout the country. The effect of te Tiriti o Waitangi was to bring intertribal conflict to an end, and to provide a constitutional basis for the establishment of British law and government in New Zealand. The English version of the treaty stated that sovereignty was ceded to the Queen of England. However, the Māori version said that the treaty guaranteed ‘tino rangatiratanga ’ or chieftainship of New Zealand to Māori. The debate continues today.

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document collection examines 150 years of the Treaty of Waitangi's history and its impact on New Zealand law, governance, and Māori rights. Beginning with the treaty's signing on February 6, 1840, between British Governor William Hobson and Māori chiefs, the narrative explores critical discrepancies between English and Māori versions that created fundamentally different understandings of sovereignty and land rights. The document traces systematic treaty breaches from the colonial era through the 1980s, including Governor FitzRoy's abandonment of land purchase monopolies and widespread land confiscations. Key case studies include the Kaituna River pollution crisis, Waitara disputes, Waiuku Block confiscations, and the Ngati Whatua's struggle for Orakei land rights. The establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975 marked a turning point, providing mechanisms for Māori to seek redress and establishing the treaty's legal force through landmark decisions like the 1987 Court of Appeal ruling. The tribunal evolved from adjudicating rights to facilitating stakeholder dialogue, achieving practical remedies including the 1983 Fisheries Act restoration of Māori fishing rights and the Bastion Point settlement. Throughout, the narrative emphasizes that broken colonial promises continue to undermine Māori rights and wellbeing, while the tribunal's collaborative approach offers innovative solutions for resolving historical injustices.

chunkHighlights.text: He had 30 pigs, five tons of potatoes and half a ton of flour for the visiting chiefs, and gifts of tobacco which they could smoke while lis- tening to Hobson — who nearly missed the whole show because he had come ashore late and half-dressed, believing he had not been wanted until the next day — as he asked them to sign the Treaty of Waitangi, the piece of paper which today either angers, bores, frightens, puzzles, shames or gives hope to the country that is still trying to forget it or to come to terms with the promises that were exchanged on February 6, 1840.

After that first Waitangi Day, thetreaty was taken around the country and signed again at perhaps 49 other gatherings. It seems certain that the two sides left the signing ceremonies with sharply different ideas of what had been achieved. The British side believed they had gained sovereignty over a new colony. The Maori chiefs believed they had saved their country from being overrun by British settlers, and that the Queen now protected their status as chiefs over their own tribes.

The reason for the difference is that Maori and English texts of the treaty differ in what they say. The various English versions agree on one thing, that the Queen is to have sovereignty. However, in the Maori version the chiefs merely cede kawanatanga, the right to govern the country.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's relationship with the British royal family from 1840 to the early 21st century. It traces the Treaty of Waitangi's establishment of Queen Victoria as head of state and explores how royal popularity fluctuated from initial unpopularity in the 1880s to widespread enthusiasm by 1897, then declining interest from the 1970s onward. The document details constitutional roles, royal tours beginning in 1869, and Māori interactions with royalty. It chronicles major royal visits from 1927 onwards, including the Duke and Duchess of York, Queen Elizabeth II, Charles and Diana, and Prince William, documenting evolving public enthusiasm and how Māori maintained separate political relationships with the Crown. The document also examines republicanism in New Zealand from European settlement through the late 20th century, tracing early republican advocates and the revival of republicanism in the 1960s with organizations like the Republican Association of New Zealand and the New Zealand Republican Party. Despite active debate between republican and monarchist groups, general public opinion remained lukewarm toward republicanism, largely due to respect for Queen Elizabeth II and uncertainty about alternatives.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's unique constitutional structure comprising multiple laws, court judgments, government documents, and conventions rather than a single written document. It covers foundational concepts including the landmark case Fitzgerald v Muldoon (1976), which established that the Prime Minister cannot suspend laws. Key sources include UK statutes (Magna Carta, Bill of Rights Act 1689), NZ Parliament statutes (Constitution Act 1986, Electoral Act 1993), and constitutional conventions governing ministerial responsibility and caretaker protocols. The document details the executive, legislative, and independent judiciary structures with separation of powers. It examines New Zealand's constitutional evolution around two pillars: the Treaty of Waitangi (1840)—an agreement between the British Crown and Māori chiefs—and representative democracy, with voting rights extended to all adult males (1879) and women (1893). The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) reinterpreted the Treaty's meaning in the late 20th century. Mixed-member proportional representation (1996) fundamentally altered constitutional dynamics. The document traces executive power evolution from the 1930s-1990s, describing how reforms including the Official Information Act 1982 and Bill of Rights Act 1990 limited executive authority. New Zealand's constitution is notably flexible, changing through statute amendments and convention shifts, with citizens protected through complaint mechanisms including ombudsmen and human rights commissions. Parliament maintains supremacy stronger than other Westminster democracies.

7.fileDescription:
This document examines the complex relationship between Māori traditional law and British colonial legislation in New Zealand from pre-Treaty times to 2011. It traces how Māori operated under a sophisticated customary law system based on concepts like mana, tapu, rahui, and utu before the Treaty of Waitangi (1840). Traditional Māori land rights were based on ahi kā (occupation) and various take (rights), contrasting sharply with colonial land laws that clashed with Māori communal land concepts.

The analysis documents systematic land dispossession through key colonial legislation including the Land Claims Ordinance 1841, Native Land Purchase Ordinance 1846, New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, and Native Lands Acts 1862-1865. The Native Land Court individualized Māori land titles to facilitate European settlement, causing severe hardship through distant hearings, high costs, and lengthy delays. The 1.3 million hectares confiscated under the Settlements Act exemplifies the scale of dispossession.

From the 1970s onward, Māori protests prompted significant legislative reforms recognizing customary rights and treaty principles. Key reforms include the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993, Resource Management Act 1991, and landmark cases like Tom Te Weehi's 1986 fishing rights case. The document also addresses the intersection of Māori indigenous property rights with European marine law, demonstrating how Māori claims to traditional rights over marine areas are grounded in pre-existing legal traditions. By 2011, legislation increasingly incorporated Treaty of Waitangi principles and recognized Māori spiritual, cultural, and property rights.

chunkHighlights.text:
The Treaty of Waitangi In the early 19th century Māori still lived
according to a complex system of customary laws. The British began trying to introduce their own laws to Māori with the Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between rangatira (chiefs) and the British Crown. Some of the laws that followed took aspects of Māori custom into account, but the British lawmakers saw this as a temporary step and anticipated a time when Māori would be fully integrated into their society. Laws and land Māori did not see land as a commodity to be bought and sold by individuals, but as something over which groups could hold communal rights of guardianship, occupation and use. These rights were gained by various means including discovery, conquest and gift. They were maintained by continual occupation over generations. Colonial legislation clashed with and overrode that system. New laws declared that the government had the right to take any land that was not needed by Māori, and that Māori could sell or lease land only to the Crown. The government backed up its laws with military force, and the New Zealand wars began. The government passed laws allowing it to confiscate the land of Māori believed to be ‘in rebellion’. A century of law-making From 1862 the government passed laws ruling that Māori lands could only be held by individual owners, not collectively by iwi (tribes) or hapū (sub-tribes). This resulted in further Māori land loss. Native Land Courts were set up to investigate and decide on titles to Māori land. The court hearings were often time-consuming and expensive. Right into the 20th century, the government made laws that impeded Māori land ownership. Beginning to make amends In the 1970s a wave of Māori protest actions drew public attention to land-related grievances. The Waitangi Tribunal was formed in 1975 to investigate breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi. Since then, Māori have made further gains. In the 1990s environmental legislation began to take account of Māori historical, spiritual and
cultural concerns. The importance of the Māori relationship to land was
acknowledged in Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993.

8.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi (te Tiriti o Waitangi), signed in 1840 between Māori rangatira and the British Crown, and their integration into New Zealand law and governance. Rather than being law itself, the treaty's intentions are applied through evolving principles developed via court cases, legislation, and Waitangi Tribunal findings since 1975. Key principles include partnership and good faith between Crown and Māori, Crown's freedom to govern, active Crown protection of Māori interests, duty to remedy past breaches, Māori rangatiratanga over resources and taonga, Crown's duty to consult, and balancing community needs. The document details landmark cases like the 1987 Lands case and the Fisheries Act case where Te Rūnanga o Muriwhenua successfully challenged the quota management system, establishing the treaty as a "living instrument." It outlines treaty principles developed by the Waitangi Tribunal through the Ngāi Tahu report, including exchange, partnership, good faith, active Crown protection, fiduciary duty, options, consultation, and development. The document formally recognizes and affirms the rights of persons of Māori descent as Indigenous peoples under the Treaty, establishing legal acknowledgment of Indigenous rights and constitutional status of Māori people within the legal framework.

chunkHighlights.text:
Te Tiriti o Waitangi / the Treaty of Waitangi Te Tiriti o Waitangi / the
Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840 between Māori rangatira and the British Crown. The Waitangi Tribunal was established by the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975. This was the first law to refer to the principles of the treaty. These principles were not defined in the legislation. But through court cases, new laws, Waitangi Tribunal findings and a 1989 government statement, the meaning of the principles of the treaty in contemporary New Zealand society has continued to be outlined. The treaty text itself is not law. Instead, the intentions and goals of the treaty are taken into account through the principles of the Treaty. Some people have suggested that this is a better idea because: The English and te reo Māori versions do not have exactly the same meaning and this may lead to uncertainty about which version to use. The treaty focuses on the issues relevant at the time it was signed and it is better to think about the spirit of the agreement and how it can be implemented today. It could diminish the mana of the treaty to make it law – it should sit above the law. Principles Treaty principles are always evolving to suit changing beliefs and circumstances. They include: The treaty set up a partnership, and the partners have a duty to act reasonably and in good faith. The Crown has freedom to govern. The Crown has a duty to actively protect Māori interests. The Crown has a duty to remedy past treaty breaches. Māori retain rangatiratanga over their resources and taonga and have all the rights and privileges of citizenship. The Crown has a duty to consult with Māori. The needs of both Māori and the wider community must be met, which will require compromise. The Crown cannot avoid its obligations under the treaty by conferring authority on some other body. The treaty can be adapted to meet new circumstances. The management of resources and other taonga according to Māori culture as part of tino rangatiratanga .
Taonga include all valued resources and intangible cultural assets.
What are the treaty principles?

Te Tiriti o Waitangi / the Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between Māori and the British Crown, is not itself law, but since 1975 many New Zealand laws have referred to the principles of the treaty. The first to do so was the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal. The act says that Māori can bring a claim to the tribunal about a Crown policy or practice (amongst other things) which was or is ‘inconsistent with the principles of the Treaty’.

Since the 1975 act there have been many other official references to treaty principles, all attempting to define the meaning of the Treaty of Waitangi in contemporary New Zealand society. Treaty principles have been referred to in:
court cases
new laws
Waitangi Tribunal findings
a 1989 government statement.
No final and complete list

There is no final and complete list of treaty principles. Instead, official documents have referred to treaty principles in general terms, without including the actual treaty text, because the English and Māori versions of the treaty are not direct translations of each other, so difficulties arise in interpretation. In 1983 the Waitangi Tribunal said, ‘The spirit of the Treaty transcends the sum total of its component written words and puts literal or narrow interpretations out of place.’ 1

fileAuthor: Olli Hellmann, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Waikato
9.fileDescription: A new survey of over 1,000 New Zealanders challenges claims that the Treaty of Waitangi divides the nation, finding instead that it serves as a powerful symbol promoting mutual understanding and reconciliation. The Treaty was identified as the most important event in New Zealand history by 38% of Pākehā and 59% of Māori respondents, with younger generations (70%+ born 2000-2006) showing significantly higher recognition. Key findings reveal that Māori who prioritize the Treaty show warmth toward European New Zealanders, Treaty-focused respondents maintain strong national belonging, and Pākehā naming the Treaty support inclusive national identity and historical redress. The research contradicts conservative politicians' arguments that revisionist Treaty narratives create division, demonstrating instead that acknowledging Treaty breaches fosters bicultural belonging and commitment to reconciliation.

[repub:theconversation] Olli Hellmann [the_conversation_tracker] https:/

ublish-lightbox-advanced Younger respondents to a new survey were significantly more likely to recall the signing of the Treaty than older generations as a significant event in New Zealand's history. (file image) The stories Aotearoa New Zealand tells itself about the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi/the Treaty of Waitangi have evolved considerably over time. For many decades, starting with the 1940 centennial, state-sponsored commemorations of the signing, the event was romanticised as a coming together of two peoples. Increasingly, these collective memories were challenged - primarily by Māori activism, but also by the work of revisionist historians. As a result, today's official narratives acknowledge the Treaty was broken repeatedly, often violently, during European colonisation. And they also recognise the Crown's obligation to remedy past breaches. Some conservative politicians have seen this shift in collective remembering as an opportunity for political point scoring. They denounce recent reinterpretations of the Treaty as sowing social division and weakening national unity. For example, in his 2004 Orewa speech, then National leader Don Brash reviled the Treaty settlements process for creating "a racially divided state". In 2017, National Prime Minister Bill English claimed many New Zealanders "cringe" at Māori protests on Waitangi Day. Lately, ACT party leader David Seymour has attacked current interpretations of the Treaty as being "divisive". His Treaty Principles Bill aims to rewrite those principles, against loud opposition from Māori. But my new research, published recently in the journal Political Science, does not support claims the Treaty divides New Zealanders. In fact, the survey suggests quite the opposite: the Treaty provides a powerful symbol that promotes mutual understanding and reconciliation. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, centre, with ACT leader David Seymour, left, and NZ First leader Winston Peters arrive at the Treaty Grounds at Waitangi on 5 February, 2024. Our most important
historical event The survey involved a broadly representative sample of

more than 1000 people. The key question asked respondents to spontaneously name the most important event in the history of Aotearoa New Zealand. This may seem simple, but it is an effective way to tap into readily accessible - and therefore meaningful - memories. The Treaty of Waitangi was the most frequent response, among both Pākehā/European New Zealanders (38 percent) and Māori (59 percent). Younger respondents were significantly more likely to recall the signing of the Treaty than older generations. This possibly reflects efforts since the late 1990s to educate citizens on the Treaty and the role of the Waitangi Tribunal in redressing historical injustices. In fact, among those respondents born between 2000 and 2006, more than 70 percent identified the Treaty as the most important event in national history. Marchers on a hīkoi from Te Rerenga Wairua (Cape Reinga) arrive at the Treaty Grounds on Waitangi Day this year. Remembering the past matters The survey data make it possible to investigate how collective memories of the historical past shape what individuals think about politics and society in the present. In particular, we can compare two groups of respondents: those who recalled the Treaty of Waitangi as most important, and those who attached the greatest importance to Eurocentric historical events (such as the arrival of Captain Cook and European settlers, World War I, and women's suffrage). Participants were also prompted to rate their "warmth" towards other social groups. In addition, the survey included a range of questions about national identity and redress of historical wrongs against Māori. Analysis of the
responses revealed four important findings.

The Treaty was identified as the most important event in New Zealand history by 38% of Pākehā and 59% of Māori respondents, with younger generations (70%+ born 2000-2006) showing significantly higher recognition. Key findings reveal that Māori who prioritize the Treaty show warmth toward European New Zealanders, Treaty-focused respondents maintain strong national belonging, and Pākehā naming the Treaty support inclusive national identity and historical redress. chunkHighlights.text:
The symbolic power of the Treaty When nations craft narratives about their historical origins - be it revolutions, wars or the making of constitutions - they tend to frame these stories positively. Aotearoa New Zealand is different. The Treaty of Waitangi - often considered the nation's founding document - includes in its more recent narratives an admission of guilt and an obligation to remedy past wrongs. Some politicians have taken aim at these narratives. They claim dwelling too much on historical breaches of the Treaty - for example, through Waitangi Tribunal proceedings or Māori protest - strains the social fabric. However, the recently published survey findings indicate such concerns are misplaced. Rather, narratives that foreground Treaty breaches help forge a bicultural sense of belonging and commitment to work through those breaches. The survey also finds the Treaty holds especially strong symbolic power among young people. This suggests electoral strategies that seek to undo decades of revisionist storytelling about the Treaty will likely lead to diminishing returns in the future. *Olli Hellmann is an associate professor of political science at the University of
Waikato. Related

11.fileDescription: New Zealand's major political parties have taken stronger positions than ever before on whether Māori ceded sovereignty under the Treaty of Waitangi. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon stated that Māori ceded sovereignty and the Crown is sovereign, while Labour leader Chris Hipkins argues Parliament's sovereignty was taken, not ceded. The Greens and Te Pāti Māori support this view. ACT and NZ First see the debate as a distraction. A 2014 Waitangi Tribunal report found Māori did not cede sovereignty. Legal experts highlight translation differences between the English and te reo Māori versions of the Treaty, with the Māori text referring to tino rangatiratanga (self-determination) being guaranteed to Māori, which would be inconsistent with ceding sovereignty.

chunkHighlights.text: Waitangi Tribunal calls for Treaty Principles Bill to be abandoned
ACT interpretation of Treaty inaccurate and misleading - claimants

In 2014, a Waitangi Tribunal report found Māori did not cede sovereignty. The northern iwi who presented evidence for that report - Ngāti Hine and Ngāti Manu - have penned an open letter to Luxon warning his comments are misleading and they're deeply frustrated by his disregard for the truth. Professor Claire Charters from the University of Auckland and head lecturer Carwyn Jones from Te Wānanga o Raukawa point to the different translations of the Treaty of Waitangi as cause for confusion. Charters says the te reo Māori version will always take precedence in the law. Jones explains the English text speaks about sovereignty going to the British Crown, but the Māori text refers to tino rangatiratanga being guaranteed to Māori. "We often think about that as being self determination or independence, and that's an idea which is actually much more like sovereignty. So that's being retained by Māori. And so it would be inconsistent with that guarantee for Māori to have ceded sovereignty in Te Tiriti." The debate over tino rangatiratanga and sovereignty - and how they're asserted in Aotearoa - will only continue to evolve. In this week's Focus on Politics, Political Reporter Lillian Hanly closely examines the debate on whether Māori ceded sovereignty and the political parties' views on the matter. Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840 between Māori rangatira and the British Crown. The Waitangi Tribunal was established by the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975. ublish-lightbox-advanced Younger respondents to a new survey were significantly more likely to recall the signing of the Treaty than older generations as a significant event in New Zealand's history. (file image) The stories Aotearoa New Zealand tells itself about the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi/the Treaty of Waitangi have evolved considerably over time. For many decades, starting with the 1940 centennial, state-sponsored commemorations of the signing, the event was romanticised as a coming together of two peoples. Increasingly, these collective memories were challenged - primarily by Māori activism, but also by the work of revisionist historians. As a result, today's official narratives acknowledge the Treaty was broken repeatedly, often violently, during European colonisation. And they also recognise the Crown's obligation to remedy past breaches. Some conservative politicians have seen this shift in collective remembering as an opportunity for political point scoring. They denounce recent reinterpretations of the Treaty as sowing social division and weakening national unity. For example, in his 2004 Orewa speech, then National leader Don Brash reviled the Treaty settlements process for creating "a racially divided state". In 2017, National Prime Minister Bill English claimed many New Zealanders "cringe" at Māori protests on Waitangi Day. Lately, ACT party leader David Seymour has attacked current interpretations of the Treaty as being "divisive". His Treaty Principles Bill aims to rewrite those principles, against loud opposition from Māori. But my new research, published recently in the journal Political Science, does not support claims the Treaty divides New Zealanders. In fact, the survey suggests quite the opposite: the Treaty provides a powerful symbol that promotes mutual understanding…

The symbolic power of the Treaty When nations craft narratives about their historical origins - be it revolutions, wars or the making of constitutions - they tend to frame these stories positively. Aotearoa New Zealand is different. The Treaty of Waitangi - often considered the nation's founding document - includes in its more recent narratives an admission of guilt and an obligation to remedy past wrongs. Some politicians have taken aim at these narratives. They claim dwelling too much on historical breaches of the Treaty - for example, through Waitangi Tribunal proceedings or Māori protest - strains the social fabric. However, the recently published survey findings indicate such concerns are misplaced. Rather, narratives that foreground Treaty breaches help forge a bicultural sense of belonging and commitment to work through those breaches. The survey also finds the Treaty holds especially strong symbolic power among young people. This suggests electoral strategies that seek to undo decades of revisionist storytelling about the Treaty will likely lead to diminishing returns in the future. *Olli Hellmann is an associate professor of political science at the University of
Waikato. Related

[Page 7] The Waitangi Tribunal has also identified other treaty principles: In 1991 the Tribunal said, ‘The cession by Maori of sovereignty to the Crown was in exchange for the protection by the Crown of Maori rangatiratanga .’ 3 The principles of partnership and good faith relate closely to the principle of exchange. The treaty is a partnership between Māori and the Crown, which requires the partners to act toward each other ‘reasonably and with the utmost good faith’. 4 Active Crown protection of Māori interests means that the Crown cannot protect Māori by avoiding actions that breach the treaty. Instead, the Crown must act to protect Māori treaty rights, in order to honour the treaty. The tribunal has said that, ‘the word “guarantee” meant more than merely leaving the Maori people unhindered in their enjoyment of language and culture. It required active steps to be taken to ensure that the Maori people have and retain the full exclusive and undisturbed possession of their language and culture.’ 5 The Crown fiduciary duty developed in the 1990s when the Crown made decisions relating to assets such as radio broadcasting and energy. In this case, a fiduciary relationship is when a junior partner (Māori) trusts the more senior partner (the Crown) to act in their best interests. The tribunal has said, ‘Because the Crown is in the more powerful position as the government in this partnership, the Crown has a fiduciary obligation to protect Maori interests.’ 6 The principle of options means that Māori can pursue a direction based on personal choice. The tribunal has explained that the treaty protected traditional Māori rights and also gave Māori the rights of British subjects. As a result, Māori have the option to operate in one or other world, or to ‘walk in two worlds’. 7 Most importantly, Māori should choose this direction for themselves.

[Page 13] Something that is destined to be debated for years to come is the Treaty of Waitangi. So pivotal to the story of New Zealand is this document that Te Papa accords it a large open space in the centre of the museum, from which the nation’s founding agreement seems to emanate its own magnetic energy. Standing at the entrance to “Signs of a Nation,” I see a visitor pause to listen to quiet voices coming from a cluster of tall poles. “The treaty—it’s not just for Maori, it’s a bill of rights for us all.” “We can support a symphony orchestra, but a full time Maori culture group wouldn’t even be considered.” “Why should good honest Kiwi farmers be kicked off their land because of some cock up hundreds of years ago.” “The treaty is just a gravy train for the rich Maori elite.” “It’s only fair that as this place belonged to the Maori they have the right to say how it should be run.” The voices offer ordinary New Zealanders’ feelings about biculturalism, and this murmur of sound acts as a backdrop to the museum’s presentation of the treaty proper. Beyond the poles, fused in glass, a replica Treaty of Waitangi towers above the viewer. Standing seven metres high, it commands attention from every direction. Its tattered condition testifies to the neglect it suffered during its first 50 years of existence. Nearly lost in a fire in the government offices in Auckland just a year after it was signed, the document was locked away and forgotten. Rediscovered in 1908, it was found to have been chewed by rats and damaged by water. So much for the icon of nationhood.

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 3] In 1840 Lieutenant Governor William Hobson arrived at the Bay of Islands to negotiate an agreement with Māori chiefs so that British sovereignty could be extended to New Zealand. He presented to the assembled chiefs the document since known as the Treaty of Waitangi. There were two versions, one in Māori and the other in English. Those who signed the Māori version did so after considerable explanation and discussion, and in the belief that they understood the nature of the transaction. They believed that the treaty protected their rights, recognised their trusteeship of the land and gave them the rights and privileges of British subjects, in exchange for their allegiance to the Crown. Their rangatiratanga , they believed, was guaranteed. On 6 February 1840, after much debate, Heke became the first of the 45 influential northern chiefs to sign. After the signing of the treaty, discontent grew among many Māori. When the capital was shifted from the Bay of Islands to Auckland many economic benefits were lost. The introduction of customs duties forced up prices, and revenue from shipping levies now went to the government. The felling of kauri trees was banned for a time and under government control land sales tapered off. Heke was incensed to see his people suffer in the ensuing depression, and to see Māori methods of enforcing law and order displaced by British practices. [Page 3] The symbolic power of the Treaty When nations craft narratives about their historical origins be it revolutions, wars or the making of constitutions they tend to frame these stories positively. Aotearoa New Zealand is different. The Treaty of Waitangi often considered the nation's founding document includes in its more recent narratives an admission of guilt and an obligation to remedy past wrongs. Some politicians have taken aim at these narratives. They claim dwelling too much on historical breaches of the Treaty for example, through Waitangi Tribunal proceedings or Māori protest strains the social fabric. However, the recently published survey findings indicate such concerns are misplaced. Rather, narratives that foreground Treaty breaches help forge a bicultural sense of belonging and commitment to work through those breaches. The survey also finds the Treaty holds especially strong symbolic power among young people. This suggests electoral strategies that seek to undo decades of revisionist storytelling about the Treaty will likely lead to diminishing returns in the future. *Olli Hellmann is an associate professor of political science at the University of Waikato. # Nau mai, haere mai — Welcome to Aotearoa New Zealand!

Moving to New Zealand is a wonderful adventure, and understanding a bit about its history and culture will help you feel more at home. Here's an overview of what shapes this unique country.

## The First People — Māori, Tangata Whenua

The Māori are the indigenous people of New Zealand, known as **tangata whenua** — 'the people of the land' — and their culture is a cornerstone of New Zealand's identity. [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1)

The ancestors of Māori arrived by ocean-going waka (canoes) from east Polynesia, likely from islands such as Rarotonga or Raiatea, shortly before 1300 CE. [[3]](cite://3/1) In tradition, the explorer Kupe is said to have first discovered New Zealand, and his wife Kuramārōtini named it **Aotearoa** — meaning 'long white cloud' — the Māori name now used for the country alongside 'New Zealand'. [[4]](cite://4/1)

Māori have a rich oral tradition, and their sense of identity is deeply connected to the land — mountains, lakes, and rivers all hold profound cultural significance. [[5]](cite://5/1) **Whakapapa** (genealogy) sits at the heart of Māori tradition, with carvings on meeting houses, oratory on the **marae** (communal gathering place), and references to founding waka all forming part of how history is remembered and told. [[6]](cite://6/1)

## A Brief History

New Zealand's history, in brief:

- **Early Māori settlement:** Māori lived in tribal groups, gardening, fishing, carving, and weaving, with strong traditions of oral storytelling and, at times, warfare. [[7]](cite://7/1)
- **European arrival:** The Dutch explorer Abel Tasman was the first European to discover New Zealand, in 1642, followed by English navigator James Cook, who mapped the country in 1769–70. Missionaries, traders, and settlers followed. [[8]](cite://8/1)
- **The Treaty of Waitangi, 1840:** This is arguably the most important document in New Zealand history. Te Tiriti o Waitangi was a written agreement between the British Crown and more than 500 Māori chiefs. It established British governance, but came with promises to protect Māori land and rights. [[9]](cite://9/1) Importantly, the English and Māori versions of the treaty carried different meanings — a source of ongoing debate and significance to this day. [[10]](cite://10/1)
- **Land wars and loss:** Conflict over land broke out in the 1860s, and Māori lost significant territory through confiscation and sale. [[8]](cite://8/2)
- **Social progress:** New Zealand became the first country in the world to grant women the right to vote, in 1893. [[8]](cite://8/3)
- **Māori revival:** From the 1970s and 1980s, Māori began vigorously reviving their language and culture. Key moments included a march to Parliament in 1975 and the establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal that same year to investigate breaches of the Treaty. [[7]](cite://7/2)
- **A diverse nation:** Since the 1970s, New Zealand has welcomed many more ethnic communities from the Pacific Islands, Asia, and beyond — including, of course, the Philippines. [[8]](cite://8/4)

## The Treaty Today — A Living Document

Te Tiriti o Waitangi is not just a historical document; it continues to shape modern New Zealand law and society. Its principles — including partnership, the protection of Māori interests, and the duty to consult — are woven into many of the country's laws and institutions. [[11]](cite://11/1) The Treaty is sometimes described as a 'bill of rights for all New Zealanders'. [[12]](cite://12/1)

As of 2025, around 932,000 people — roughly 18 percent of New Zealand's population — identified as Māori, a growing community projected to exceed one million by 2033. [[13]](cite://13/1)

## Biculturalism and You

New Zealand considers itself a **bicultural** society, built on the relationship between Māori and Pākehā (New Zealanders of European descent). [[14]](cite://14/1) This means Māori culture, language (te reo Māori), and customs are present in everyday life — from place names and greetings to ceremonies and government institutions.

As a newcomer, you may encounter:

- **The hongi** — a greeting where noses are pressed together, connecting breath and life.
- **The marae** — a communal space central to Māori social and spiritual life, with its own protocols for visitors (manuhiri).
- **Tangihanga (tangi)** — Māori funerals, which are significant community events held on the marae. [[15]](cite://15/1)
- **Manaakitanga** — the spirit of hospitality, care, and generosity that Māori communities are known for extending to newcomers. [[16]](cite://16/1)

Many migrants find that Māori communities are particularly warm in welcoming new arrivals, sharing tikanga (cultural values and practices), stories, and support. [[16]](cite://16/2)

There's also a Māori academic perspective worth knowing: Te Tiriti o Waitangi is considered relevant not just to Māori and Pākehā, but to all people who come to live in Aotearoa — including Pasifika peoples with their own deep historical ties to Māori as fellow Polynesians. [[17]](cite://17/1)

1.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's society across multiple dimensions. It covers the nation's diverse population of over 5 million people, including 67% of European descent, significant Māori (565,329), Pacific Islander, and Asian communities. Demographic trends reveal an aging population, declining birth rates, and increasing ethnic diversity concentrated primarily in the North Island, particularly Auckland. The document details family structures, housing trends showing declining home ownership (from 73.8% in 1991 to 67.8% in 2001), and rising single-parent families (31% in 2001). Gender dynamics highlight women's improved economic and social status since the 1980s, alongside New Zealand's progressive LGBTQ+ rights stance, including decriminalization of homosexuality (1986), civil unions (2005), and same-sex marriage (2013). Health outcomes have improved significantly since the 1950s, with life expectancy at 76 years for men and 81 for women (2000), though Māori populations experience lower life expectancy and higher mortality rates. The education system provides free, compulsory state schooling from ages 6-16, with special initiatives like kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa Māori for language preservation. Religion remains important with approximately half the population identifying as Christian, though church attendance is low and religious diversity has increased through immigration. The document traces cultural evolution including the transformation of cuisine from British traditions to cosmopolitan cooking, beverage consumption shifts from beer to wine and coffee, and relaxed dress codes reflecting global influences. Throughout, it highlights both multicultural achievements and persistent socioeconomic disparities faced by Māori communities.

The traditions establish deep connections between Māori tribes and the land, forming the basis for tribal identity, tenure, ancestral authority, and the spiritual relationship between Māori people and their environment across generations.

The early 20th century saw amateur historians document local histories and pioneer stories, while the Polynesian Society (founded 1892) worked to preserve Māori culture. From 1940-1970, academic historians emerged with new perspectives on colonial history and race relations.
