response.response_text:
# The 1981 Springbok Tour: New Zealand's Closest Thing to Civil War

Few events in New Zealand history have cut as deep as the 1981 Springbok rugby tour — 56 days of conflict that pitted neighbour against neighbour, family against family, and forced the country to confront who it really was.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## Background: A Long and Troubled History

Rugby was the national game of both New Zealand and white South Africa, and the two countries had been competing fiercely since the 1920s. But South Africa's apartheid system — a formal policy of racial segregation established in 1948 that excluded Black and 'coloured' players from national sports teams — had long shadowed the relationship. [[1]](cite://1/1)

The tensions were not new. As far back as 1937, the Springboks had refused to play an all-Māori team. In 1960, 160,000 New Zealanders signed a petition opposing an All Blacks tour of South Africa. A Labour government cancelled a planned Springbok tour in 1973. But in 1975, the National Party made freedom of 'sporting contacts' an election issue and won a landslide victory. [[2]](cite://2/1)

When the Springbok team arrived on 19 July 1981 — the first tour since 1965 — the stage was already set for a reckoning. [[3]](cite://3/1)

## Two Sides of a Nation

At its core, the debate was about New Zealand's national identity. As one source put it, for some, rugby was the heart of New Zealand's identity — a country of strong outdoor men whose contests with South Africa were central to their world view. For others, New Zealand's identity was as an opponent of racism and a fighter for human rights, and sport had to reflect those values. [[4]](cite://4/1)

The division wasn't just ideological — it was geographical. Support for the tour was strongest in rural areas, while opposition was concentrated in cities. Long-standing prejudices resurfaced, with pro-tour supporters and anti-tour activists hurling insults across the divide. [[5]](cite://5/1)

Prime Minister Robert Muldoon, despite New Zealand being a party to the Commonwealth's Gleneagles Agreement against sporting contact with apartheid South Africa, refused to stop the tour. Many New Zealanders felt betrayed — not by the New Zealand Rugby Football Union, whose position had always been clear, but by a government that appeared to step back from a fundamental issue of integrity. [[6]](cite://6/1)[[7]](cite://7/1)

## The Protests: Unprecedented in New Zealand History

The opposition was massive and organised. In Auckland, the Mobilisation to Stop the Tour (MOST) was established; in Wellington, the Coalition to Oppose the Springbok Tour (COST). The umbrella group Halt All Racist Tours (HART) coordinated much of the national effort. [[8]](cite://8/1)[[9]](cite://9/1)

An estimated 65,000 people took to the streets in the first major mobilisation, and around 150,000 people turned out across the three-month tour — the biggest mass protest New Zealand had ever seen. [[6]](cite://6/2)[[10]](cite://10/1)

Māori activists played a significant role. The Patu Squad in Auckland, led by Ripeka Evans, Donna Awatere and Hone Harawira, had a core of around 100 members, mostly Māori, and represented a distinct strand of protest that connected opposition to apartheid with the fight against racism at home. [[11]](cite://11/1)

The churches were also involved. St Matthew's Anglican Church in Auckland hosted anti-tour meetings, and Archbishop Paul Reeves was prominent in opposing the tour. [[12]](cite://12/1)

![embed-2](embed://2)

## Violence and Chaos

Anti-tour campaigners blocked roads and invaded rugby grounds. Running street battles between protesters and supporters became commonplace, and police batoned protesters — with bloody results. [[3]](cite://3/2) In Wellington, protesters who pushed into a police line on Molesworth Street were heavily batoned. [[13]](cite://13/1)

The Hamilton test had to be cancelled after protesters occupied the field at Rugby Park, with red smoke from flares drifting across the ground as 18,000 fans looked on. A stolen plane — piloted by ex-fighter pilot Pat McQuarrie — circled overhead, and police commissioner Bob Walton called the game off in the interests of public safety. [[6]](cite://6/3)

The tour's most iconic moment came in the final test at Eden Park in Auckland, when a light plane flew over the ground dropping flour bombs, pamphlets and stink bombs onto the pitch, striking All Black prop Gary Knight. The match continued, with New Zealand winning 25–22 in injury time. [[14]](cite://14/1)

By the tour's end, more than 1,500 people had been charged with protest-related offences, and the tour had cost taxpayers $7.2 million (equivalent to $27.5 million in 2013 terms). [[2]](cite://2/2)[[8]](cite://8/2)

## The Legacy

The 1981 tour galvanised and strengthened New Zealand's anti-racist movement. After 1981, no more racially selected Springbok teams toured New Zealand, and in 1984 the Labour government banned South African sports teams from the country entirely. [[8]](cite://8/3)[[2]](cite://2/3)

The tour also sparked a broader national conversation. Attention turned to domestic race relations and to the need for New Zealanders to better understand Te Tiriti o Waitangi (the Treaty of Waitangi). [[15]](cite://15/1) Some New Zealanders with a conscience shifted their sporting allegiances, following the All Whites to the 1982 football World Cup, and New Zealand women began to challenge the dominance of male sports in the media. [[4]](cite://4/2)

In a remarkable full circle, South Africa's two votes are believed to have been critical in New Zealand winning the right to host the 2011 Rugby World Cup — with South African officials publicly thanking New Zealand protest leaders like John Minto and Trevor Richards for their role in helping end apartheid. [[16]](cite://16/1)

Would you like to know more about the role Māori activists played in the 1981 protests specifically?

[3] [Public Protest in New Zealand: Methods, History, and Democratic Engagement](https://teara.govt.nz/en/public-protest)

Labour and National governments adopted differing approaches to African decolonization, with controversial rugby tours in 1976 and 1981 causing international diplomatic crises. Migration patterns show white South African and Rhodesian populations in New Zealand increased from 2,685 in 1986 to 41,676 by 2006. Despite Africa's 1.2 billion people and 54 nations, New Zealand demonstrated a "very low level of ambition" in the continent, though Africa's UN voting strength became significant for New Zealand's Security Council aspirations.

14.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of government involvement in sport and physical education in New Zealand from the colonial period through 2012. It covers three interconnected areas: children's sport (Education Act 1877, KiwiSport 1988); adult sport and recreation (Physical Welfare and Recreation Act 1937, Hillary Commission 1987, regional sports trusts); and high-performance elite sport (New Zealand Sports Foundation, SPARC, Sport New Zealand). Government funding for elite sport rose from $6.2 million in 2001/2 to $81.7 million by 2012/13, with High Performance Sport New Zealand (HPSNZ) established in 2011. The document extensively addresses political dimensions of sport, including New Zealand's controversial sporting relations with apartheid South Africa (1921-1992), the 1981 Springbok tour protests, and boycotts of the 1980 Moscow Olympics. Major government investments include the 2011 Rugby World Cup ($26 million) and Eden Park's redevelopment ($190 million), demonstrating how sport became intertwined with national policy and international relations.

15.text:
[Page 8] First organised opposition to racist rugby New Zealand’s first organised nationwide opposition to racist sporting contacts was in 1959, when the Rugby Football Union accepted another invitation to send an all white team to South Africa. Many prominent New Zealanders formed the Citizens' All Black Tour Association (CABTA). Its chair was Rolland O’Regan, father of Tipene O’Regan, who later became a prominent leader of Ngāi Tahu. CABTA established more than 20 regional branches and mounted a vigorous campaign with the slogan, ‘No Maoris, no tour’. Around 160,000 New Zealanders signed an anti tour petition, and thousands around the country marched in protest. This was the biggest protest against racially selected sports teams in the world at that time. However, it did not persuade New Zealand’s government to intervene to stop the tour, which went ahead in 1960.

15.document_title: Anti-Racism Activism and Treaty of Waitangi in New Zealand: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to the 21st Century
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of racism and anti-racism activism in New Zealand from the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) through the early 21st century. It examines how systemic racism persisted through discrimination in housing, employment, sports, and institutions despite the Treaty's promise of equal rights for Māori. The document details key anti-racism movements including the Citizens' All Black Tour Association (1959), Citizens Association for Racial Equality (1964), HART (1969), and Māori-led organizations like Ngā Tamatoa and the Polynesian Panthers. A significant focus is the All Blacks' exclusion of Māori players from tours to apartheid South Africa starting in 1928, and the pivotal 1981 Springbok tour protests. The document highlights institutional responses including the Office of the Race Relations Conciliator (1971), Human Rights Commission (1977), and the Waitangi Tribunal (1985). It addresses institutional racism within judicial, education, health, and social welfare systems, and describes how the Treaty gained constitutional significance from the 1980s onward, with the Tribunal's expanded authority embedding treaty principles into over 30 legislative pieces affecting constitutional, economic, land, language, health, education, and justice matters.

16.text:
[Page 26] As late as 1975 a book entitled The New Zealanders featured an image of the All Black rugby forward Colin Meads carrying a sheep under each arm. But this stereotype was being challenged. The catalyst was the attempt to isolate South Africa for its apartheid policies. In 1973 Prime Minister Norman Kirk cancelled a proposed tour by South Africa’s Springbok rugby team, but a subsequent leader, Robert Muldoon, appealing to the ‘ordinary bloke’, determined that rugby would proceed and refused to stop the 1981 tour. The result was 56 days of conflict. At one level the argument was about playing sport with apartheid South Africa. At another level it was about what it meant to be a New Zealander: defined by feats on the rugby field, or an example to the world, a fighter for racial justice?

16.document_title: New Zealand Identity Formation: From Colonial Origins to Multicultural Nation
16.document_summary: This comprehensive historical document traces the evolution of New Zealand national identity from European contact through the early 21st century. The work examines how the term "New Zealander" shifted from referring to Māori in early colonial periods to European settlers, then evolved into a complex multicultural identity. Key developments include: the emergence of distinct identity through cultural markers like the All Blacks rugby team's 1905 victory and Edmund Hillary's Everest climb; the impact of World Wars I and II on national consciousness; the development of Pākehā culture characterized by beach culture, bush appreciation, and rugby traditions; and transformation from bicultural to multicultural society through immigration from Pacific Islands, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. The document explores how environmental factors, compulsory education, the 1890 Liberal government's reformist policies (women's suffrage, land reform), and nation-building efforts shaped national identity. It examines Māori integration and separate nationalism, the role of military service and sporting achievements in establishing national character, and how social movements including feminism, biculturalism, and recognition of Māori sovereignty transformed New Zealand identity. By the 21st century, "New Zealandness" had become multifaceted, shaped by geography, Māori heritage, British colonization, and recent immigration.

17.text:
[Page 4] Deputy Prime Minister Brian Talboys wrote a letter to the NZRFU in April 1980, emphasising the responsibilities of sports bodies and governments under the Gleneagles Agreement. But why did the Deputy Prime Minister rather than the Prime Minister himself deliver this heads up about responsibility? Why did the Talboys’ letter say “I am deeply concerned”, rather than, “The Government is deeply con cerned”? The NZRFU was on full alert for every sign, every inflection. In September 1980, it issued the invitation. History already showed a prime minister could stop an incoming Springbok tour. The Labour Prime Minister Norman Kirk had done exactly that in 1973. Kirk had asked—the word used in his final letter to the NZRFU was “required”—the union to defer the Springbok tour of that year, and the NZRFU had done so. Even Muldoon had shown a willingness to mix politics and sport. In 1980 he’d met the New Zealand Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association and hinted at the removal of financial grants if it did not support an American led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympic Games. The association complied. No such tough stances had yet been visited on the NZRFU, but the Springbok tour was still months away, so the nation waited. The more experienced anti apartheid heads operating out of Wellington wanted the issue to move along quietly, using international pressure, the Gleneagles Agreement and polls that had shown public opinion was trending against the tour. They didn’t want threats or civil disruption, but on that point there was a tactical split in the movement. Aucklanders John Minto and Dick Cuthbert were already workshopping civil disobedience classes, offering lessons in arms linking and in passive dropping, and active training for parachute jumps using aircraft. [Chapter Break] The first big mobilisation against the Springbok tour of 1981 brought an estimated 65,000 people onto the streets of New Zealand’s major cities. By the time of the second big mobilisation of June 3, the polls were running 32 per cent for and 51 per cent against the tour. The Prime Minister scheduled what was to be his first and last direct appeal to the NZRFU, to be televised live on July 6, 1981. The country tuned in. Most people expected a strong call to the NZRFU, but they reckoned without Muldoon’s stubbornness on the issue of sport and politics, and the importance to National of securing rugby mad provincial seats for the November 1981 election. Among those protesting the 1981 Springbok tour was Daniel Morgan Lynch, a Wellington schoolboy—one of about 80 anti apartheid demonstrators who marched to the South African Consulate in their school uniforms. The Prime Minster’s speech that night was best described as odd. It recalled the bond between South Africa and New Zealand—how the soldiers of each had fought and died together in WWII—and drifted on to its limp conclusion: “I say to them [the NZRFU], think well before you make a decision.” Having waited for months, many New Zealanders felt betrayed. Not by the NZRFU (its position was always clear) but by the Government, which had lost its footing on a basic issue of integrity—or so it seemed. It had lost footing internationally at Gleneagles, and internally with its choice to step back from fundamentally opposed forces within society. The Prime Minister had long ago targeted the New Zealand anti apartheid movement as a brittle enemy. That bias in the movement towards the intellect, towards morality, towards the idealism of the political left, didn’t seem to compare with the emotional power of rugby and the pro tour love of sport. [Sidebar 2] But the anti tour demands were now emotional too. From the distress that had built during the Soweto shootings of 1976. From patriotic pride wounded by the events of Montreal that same year, and the insults to African leaders before and since. From indignation, that the hard fought Gleneagles Agreement had been, apparently, slyly discarded. As the Springbok tourists arrived, emotions ran high throughout the country, among those both for and against the tour, and so high that the unspoken social contract that kept citizens generally at peace with one another fractured. [Chapter Break] July 25,1981. The protest group is huddled mid‑ field on Rugby Park, Hamilton, the second fixture of the Springbok tour. Red smoke drifts up from flares and the green field is cut into geometric lines by police in glinting riot gear. Around the protest group, in the terraces and the stand, on slopes that look as though they might avalanche, are 18,000 rugby fans. Radio news puts out a continuous commentary: “More police are coming out from under the stand. They’re equipped in their riot helmets. The visors on the helmet. Long batons slung at their hips. They’re moving in towards the demonstrators in a line.” Then television, primed to begin broadcast of the Springboks’ provincial match against Waikato, begins transmitting that smoky image of the entrenched group on the field. People vault suburban fences to tell their neighbours. Soon the nation is watching. Those who support the tour are repulsed into rage. Those who oppose it see, at last, a potent symbol of their dissent. As the on field group binds in a solid mass at the centre of Rugby Park, Hamilton, on July 25, 1981, the Rev Dr George Armstrong breaks away to address Red Squad police lined up on the northern 22 metre line. Soon after this photo was taken, police pushed Armstrong out through the main exit. Crowds there reached down to rip off his clerical collar, and fists rained on his head. On field the group is facing outwards and packed tightly for its own survival. There is the euphoric fulfilment of the chant when some genius leads a change from the reedy ANC freedom call, “Amandla!” to the full throated Kiwi call, “The Whole World’s Watching!” Well exactly. At 4 am in South Africa, something like half a million whites have awoken to the first live television coverage of the first Springbok rugby game abroad since the country was networked in 1976. All they see is a graphic display of the New Zealand anti apartheid movement. Communal energy infuses the on field group. This high profile Springboks v Waikato game is severely at risk. If police charge, the on field group looks sufficiently resolute to go down as a bloody fullstop to the tour. If the police prise people out of its linked arms mass, as they’re now doing, the clearance will take hours. There’s also a stolen plane on its way to the rugby ground, piloted by the ex fighter pilot Pat McQuarrie. Pat is staunch. He could also be mad enough. No one knows what Pat might do. The game was called off by Police Commissioner, Bob Walton, in the interests of public safety the situation deteriorated. The picture that perhaps best represented what happened at Hamilton that day was one that was snapped off a television screen news bulletin. It’s a fuzzy, murky image, but its very lack of clarity encompassed all the distortion and indecision, the fear, the defiance. The pelting as the protest group filed out of the ground, the hunting through the Hamilton streets, the violation of the sanctity of Red Cross ambulances and, as night came, the besieging and ransacking of houses. The mob.

17.document_title: Tainted Games: Sport and Politics in New Zealand - The 1981 Springbok Tour Protests and Anti-Apartheid Movement (1975-1985)
17.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the intersection of sport and politics in New Zealand from 1975 to 1985, with particular focus on the 1981 Springbok rugby tour protests and the anti-apartheid movement. It traces the 1976 Montreal Olympics boycott by 28 African nations protesting the All Blacks' tour of apartheid South Africa, and the subsequent Gleneagles Agreement (June 1977) committing Commonwealth nations to combat apartheid in sport. The document details Prime Minister Robert Muldoon's controversial decision to allow the Springbok tour despite 51% public opposition, sparking New Zealand's largest mass protest with approximately 150,000 participants over three months. Key events include the July 25 incident at Rugby Park in Hamilton where 18,000 clashed, resulting in game cancellation, and violent confrontations at Eden Park during the third test match with 270 injured civilians and 32 police officers. Led by activists like John Minto and Dick Cuthbert, protesters employed sophisticated tactics including cable-cutting and bridge blockades. The narrative demonstrates how these protests influenced international rugby politics, ultimately affecting South Africa's support for New Zealand's 2011 Rugby World Cup bid.

18.document_title: Rugby – Just a Game? The Cultural Significance, History, and Traditions of New Zealand Rugby
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores rugby's profound cultural significance in New Zealand and Wales, tracing its evolution from medieval England through modern times. It chronicles rugby's introduction to New Zealand in 1870 by Charles Monro and its thriving in harsh frontier conditions. Key historical events include the legendary 1905 All Blacks tour to Britain, the politically charged 1981 Springbok tour during apartheid, and the establishment of the Ranfurly Shield in 1902. The document examines rugby's role as a unifying force across diverse communities, from urban centers to remote villages, exploring grassroots culture including Golden Oldies rugby and family involvement. It analyzes the physical dimensions of the sport, particularly the front row's role in the scrum and legendary players like Colin Meads. The text emphasizes how rugby traditions pass through generations and questions whether modern professionalization and television influence threaten rugby's connection to pioneer heritage. Despite these concerns, rugby remains resilient and deeply woven into New Zealand and Welsh society, transcending its origins as merely a game to become a defining element of national identity.

23.document_title: A Bomb for 'Big Brother': Neil Roberts and the Wanganui Computer Bombing
23.document_summary: On November 18, 1982, 22-year-old Neil Roberts bombed Wairere House in Wanganui, New Zealand, home to the Wanganui Computer (National Law Enforcement System)—the country's first centralized electronic database containing personal information on all citizens. Roberts, who had participated in anti-government demonstrations, detonated approximately two kilograms of gelignite at the building's entrance, killing himself but leaving the computer system undamaged. The bombing was a protest against what many viewed as an Orwellian symbol of state surveillance and control. The computer, operational since 1976 and decommissioned in 2005, recorded driver's licenses, firearms licenses, vehicle registrations, and criminal records accessible nationwide. The incident reflects broader concerns about privacy and government surveillance that persist today, particularly regarding mass surveillance programs like the "Five Eyes" alliance.

24.text:
[Page 14] Keith Quinn (on a TV One blog) was the only New Zealand commentator who reported this. “The way I saw it,” he wrote, “Mr Stofile was publicly thanking Messrs John Minto and Trevor Richards and the rest of the New Zealand protest people for their role in changing rugby and life in South Africa 25 years ago.” A few days later, the South African President, Thabo Mbeki, confirmed it in the Government magazine ANC Today : “…we must mention the outstanding role played by the people of New Zealand in the campaign to isolate apartheid sport as we engaged in struggle for our liberation,” he wrote. “If only for this reason, it was good that SARU (the South African Rugby Union) supported the New Zealand bid.” The voting figures were secret, but leaked minutes from the Argentina Rugby Union’s general committee in January last year suggested the final vote was a close run 11 10. If that is correct, South Africa’s two votes were critical for New Zealand’s success in gaining the 2011 hosting rights. With that, the high intensity battle that began in 1975 to keep politics out of sport had come full circle. Three decades later, the political protests of 1981 had finally delivered New Zealand the sporting event dearest to its heart.

[Page 5] As the 1981 Springbok tour had divided the country, so the peace flotilla united it. Soon after Barry Keon had volunteered Tryptich , other boats and crews from around the country materialised. Dan and I secured a place aboard the single masted steel hulled yacht Chimera , from Greymouth. Chimera joined Joie, Kela and New Zealand Maid in a mini flotilla based in Wellington. Dennis Johnson, a non sailor with a knack for words, coordinated the fun draising for the capital’s little fleet. “There were some grotty aspects to the job,” he recalls. “Some of the media people wanted to corner the market and cut out other stations. This sort of commercial carry on really gave me the tomtits. I just about decked a few of them.” Despite such negatives, TV exposure really kicked off the fundraising campaign. People everywhere offered their support. Joie—here seen raising support—was one of four to sail from from Wellington. “Someone would ring up and say ‘I’m an artist. I want to paint all the boats, have an exhibition and donate all the proceedings to the flotilla.’ I would say, ‘Great, but can you organise this, mate, because we can’t.’ The Body Shop one day said, ‘We’ve collected $5000.’ It was really gratifying knowing people were swinging in behind us.”

26.document_title: Moruroa Protest: A Comprehensive Account of the 1995 Peace Flotilla Against French Nuclear Testing
26.document_summary:
This document collection chronicles the 1995 peace flotilla protest against French nuclear testing at Moruroa atoll in French Polynesia. France announced eight final underground nuclear tests before ratifying the UN's comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty, sparking widespread Pacific protests. Author Marty Taylor, an inexperienced sailor and filmmaker, joined the protest aboard the yacht Chimera to document the event, tracing French nuclear testing from 1966-1995, detailing 167 tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa atolls and examining environmental damage including porous geology and potential radioactive leakage.

In August 1995, a four-yacht flotilla led by coordinator Dennis Johnson sailed from Wellington, New Zealand to Moruroa, gaining public support through media exposure and donations. The journey proved treacherous, with severe storms featuring 65-75 knot winds and 12-16 meter swells. After 19 days at sea, the Wellington-based yachts regrouped near the test site, supported by the RNZN survey vessel Tui, engaging in strategic cat-and-mouse games with French naval forces around the 12-mile exclusion zone.

Key protest actions included a traditional piragua paddle to Moruroa by Tahitian independence activists and a Greenpeace mission to support indigenous Polynesians reclaiming their ancestral atoll. Journalists successfully captured and transmitted photographs of Polynesian islanders aboard the Vega vessel to Reuters, providing counter-evidence to French claims. Though the flotilla failed to stop the nuclear testing, the mission succeeded in bearing witness to events and amplifying a dissenting New Zealand voice on the international stage, demonstrating the grassroots nature of the anti-nuclear protest movement.

34.document_title: Sonja Margaret Loveday Davies: A Complete Biography
34.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical account chronicles the life of Sonja Margaret Loveday Davies (1923-2005), a pioneering New Zealand activist and union organizer. Born in Wallaceville, Davies overcame a difficult childhood marked by foster care and family instability to become a transformative figure in New Zealand's labor and peace movements. After working as a nurse and recovering from tuberculosis, she emerged as a community leader in Nelson, becoming the first woman elected to the Hospital Board (1956) and city council (1961). As a Labour Party activist, she championed women's rights and childcare, serving on the party's national executive from 1965. She founded the New Zealand Association for Child Care Centres and pioneered the Working Women's Charter, earning the first woman Federation of Labour executive seat. In November 1987, Davies entered Parliament as member for Pencarrow, focusing on early childhood education and peace promotion. She navigated Labour Party divisions and retained her seat in the 1990 election, opposing the National government's rescission of the Employment Equity Act. Her 1984 autobiography inspired the 1992 film "Bread and Roses." Despite personal tragedies, including her son Mark's death in 1978 and her daughter's death in 1994, Davies remained active until her death on 12 June 2005. She left a lasting legacy as a trailblazer for women in public life, recognized through the Sonja Davies Peace Award and a parliamentary plaque.

35.document_title: Rona Bailey: A Life of Radical Activism and Cultural Leadership in Twentieth-Century New Zealand
35.document_summary: Rona Bailey (1914-2005) was a prominent figure in New Zealand's radical left movement, serving as a communist activist, organizer of major protest movements, and pioneering leader in modern dance and physical education. Born in Whanganui, Bailey developed her political consciousness during studies in the United States (1937-1939) under modern dance pioneers. She was instrumental in the 1951 waterfront lockout resistance and became national secretary of the Society for Closer Relations with the USSR. Bailey was a central organizer of Wellington's anti-Vietnam War movement (1965-1976) and deeply involved in the anti-apartheid movement from the late 1940s, serving as treasurer of the National Anti-Apartheid Committee and participating in protests against the 1981 South African rugby tour. In theatre, she co-founded the QEII Arts Council Drama Training School (later Toi Whakaari) in 1970, serving as a movement tutor until 1988 and promoting biculturalism through Māori and Pasifika representation. She was a founding member of communist organizations including the Wellington Marxist-Leninist Organisation (1976) and engaged with Project Waitangi (1985) to educate Pākehā about the Treaty of Waitangi. Bailey died in Wellington on September 7, 2005, at age 90, leaving a legacy as a principled activist dedicated to integrating cultural expression with political activism.

36.document_title: Frank David Winter: Māori Advocate and Social Justice Champion
36.document_summary: Frank David Winter (1906-1976) was a prominent Māori advocate and social justice champion who dedicated his life to advancing Ngāi Tahu interests and workers' rights. Born in Waipukurau to a telegraph linesman's family with Ngāi Tahu heritage, Winter studied at Te Aute College and joined the Native Department in 1924. He married Perle Hera Rākapa Taiaroa, a pioneering Māori dental nurse, in 1931. Winter's most significant contribution was his 20-year tenure as chairman of the Ngāitahu Māori Trust Board (1956-1976), where he reformed administration, managed finances, and successfully lobbied for legislative amendments to extend the 1944 Ngāi Tahu settlement through the Māori Purposes Act 1973. He also served as assistant and deputy general secretary of the New Zealand Public Service Association, advocating for government superannuation and improved working conditions. He remained committed to Māori sovereignty and social justice until his death in Wellington.

37.document_title: Bruce Beetham and Social Credit: New Zealand's Third-Party Political Movement
37.document_summary: Bruce Craig Beetham (1936-1997) was a prominent New Zealand politician who led the Social Credit Political League from 1972 to 1981. Born in New Plymouth, he was a teacher and lecturer who transformed Social Credit from a marginal 1% party into a significant political force, with polling reaching over 30% by December 1980. Beetham won the Rangitīkei seat in a 1978 by-election, becoming only the second non-Labour/National member elected since 1946. At the 1978 general election, Social Credit achieved 16.1% of the vote, and in 1981 secured 20.7% but only two parliamentary seats, highlighting electoral system disproportionality. A controversial 1982 decision to support the Clyde dam project damaged the party's credibility. Following Labour's 1984 election victory, Social Credit's support collapsed to 7.6%, finishing fourth for the first time. The party rebranded as the New Zealand Democratic Party in 1985 but continued declining, losing parliamentary seats by 1987. Despite personal challenges and failed attempts to revive Social Credit, Beetham's leadership helped catalyze electoral reform and New Zealand's shift toward a multi-party system.

38.document_title: Ranginui Walker: Influential Māori Writer, Activist, Scholar and Public Intellectual
38.document_summary: Ranginui Joseph Isaac Walker (1932-2016) was a highly influential Māori writer, activist, scholar and public intellectual who played a pivotal role in the cultural and political renaissance of Māori during the 1970s and 1980s. Born in Lower Waiaua, Bay of Plenty, Walker was educated at Hato Petera and trained as a teacher before earning a BA and MA in anthropology from the University of Auckland. As a lecturer in Māori studies and sociology, he became a formidable public intellectual influenced by radical theorists including Paulo Freire, Ivan Illich, and Frantz Fanon. Walker served as secretary and later chair of the Auckland District Māori Council (1969-1989) and was instrumental in organizing the 1970 Young Māori Leaders Conference, which led to the formation of Ngā Tamatoa. He was instrumental in major Māori political movements including the 1979 haka party incident and opposition to the 1981 Springbok tour. Through regular columns in the New Zealand Listener (1973–90) and Metro magazine (1993–97), he provided authoritative perspectives on Māori issues and the Treaty of Waitangi. His seminal work "Ka whawhai tonu matou: Struggle without end" (1990) presented a comprehensive Māori historical perspective. Walker served as professor and head of Māori Studies at the University of Auckland (1986–1998) and was appointed to the Waitangi Tribunal in 2003. He received the Prime Minister's Award for literary achievement and left a lasting legacy in New Zealand scholarship and Māori advocacy.

Appointed auxiliary bishop in 1958, Delargey championed lay participation in the church and attended all four sessions of Vatican II. He became Bishop of Auckland in 1970, introducing parish councils and pastoral reforms. Elevated to Archbishop of Wellington in 1974 and cardinal in 1976, he was the first New Zealander to participate in papal elections. Delargey advocated for religious unity, racial harmony, human rights, and Catholic school integration into the state system. He died in 1979, leaving a legacy of progressive church leadership and social commitment.

41.document_title: Ben Couch: Māori Politician, Rugby Player, and Community Leader
41.document_summary: Ben Couch (1925-1996) was a prominent Māori politician, rugby player, and community leader in New Zealand. Born in Lyttelton to mixed Ngāi Tahu heritage, he became a skilled first five-eighth who toured with the All Blacks and Māori teams in the 1940s. After establishing himself as a builder and shearing contractor in Pirinoa, he entered politics as a National Party member, winning the Wairarapa seat in 1975—the second Māori to win a general seat. As Minister of Māori Affairs (1978-1984) and Minister of Police (1980-1984), he advocated for Māori self-sufficiency, cultural pride, and strong law enforcement. Known for his integrity, blunt honesty, and unwavering principles, Couch championed kōhanga reo language programs and worked to rehabilitate offenders through his labor force. After leaving Parliament, he devoted himself to refurbishing Tuhirangi marae and served as a Treaty of Waitanui Fisheries Commissioner until his death.

42.document_title: Robert David Muldoon: Life, Political Career, and Legacy in New Zealand
42.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical document traces Robert David Muldoon's complete life from his birth in Auckland on 25 September 1921 through his death on 5 August 1992. Born to James Henry Muldoon and Amie Rusha Browne, Muldoon overcame childhood hardships including his father's mental illness and a facial scar to become a prominent accountant and politician. He served in WWII across New Caledonia, Egypt, and Italy, and became the first overseas student to win the Leverhulme Prize. After joining the National Party in 1947, he won the Tāmaki seat in 1960 and gained recognition as a skilled debater. Appointed Minister of Finance in 1967, Muldoon served for 14 of the next 17 years, introducing innovative economic policies including "mini-budgets" and currency devaluation. He rose to Prime Minister (1975-1984), dominating government through his forceful personality and intelligence while facing severe economic challenges. His administration implemented the "Think Big" growth strategy and faced major controversies including the Springbok rugby tour and strained labor relations. Despite winning elections in 1978 and 1981, his government fell in 1984 when the National Party's vote split, allowing Labour under David Lange to win decisively. In his post-prime ministerial years, Muldoon remained politically active as foreign affairs spokesperson, chaired the Global Economic Action Institute (1988-1991), and hosted a popular weekly radio programme on Radio Pacific until his death. His legacy reflects both personal ambition and genuine concern for ordinary New Zealanders.

43.document_title: Hilda Phillips: A Critic of Māori Rights and the Anti-Treatyist Tradition in New Zealand
43.document_summary: This biographical and historical analysis examines Hilda Phillips (1922-2006), a prominent conservative critic of Māori land rights and autonomy campaigns in New Zealand. Born in Cape Town to a Jewish family, Phillips emigrated to New Zealand in 1952. When Māori protests intensified in the early 1970s, she became a vocal opponent of remedial legislation and Māori self-determination efforts. Publishing approximately 60 articles between 1974-1981, Phillips argued that special provisions for Māori violated meritocratic principles. Her arguments were heavily criticized by scholars like W.H. Oliver and Keith Sorrenson for unreliable evidence. After 1985, when the Waitangi Tribunal gained retrospective powers, Phillips renewed activism through public speaking and self-published materials like "Let the truth be known" (1988), aligning with the One New Zealand Foundation. In 1989, historian Harry Evison published a comprehensive rebuttal criticizing her arguments about Treaty claims and Māori land ownership as containing misinformation. After her husband Morris died in 1990, Phillips reduced her campaigning due to health issues. She continued publishing through the 1990s and deposited her archive at the Alexander Turnbull Library before her death in 2006. Her work pioneered the "anti-Treatyist" tradition—a body of writing that draws on limited evidence to discredit Māori grievances.

[Page 1] Analysis As we build towards the clash between the All Blacks and Springboks, the greatest rivalry in rugby had a somewhat inevitable reminder of its painful past. News came through over the past 48 hours of the intention by SA Rugby to formally apologise for the exclusion of Māori (and presumably Pasifika) players for being excluded from touring apartheid era South Africa. The proposal was put forward by SA Rugby president Mark Alexander, whose career was shaped by the fact that as a coloured player, he was restricted to a separate competition to white and native African players. Selection for the Springboks was impossible, even if they hadn't been banned from test matches during Alexander's career. There's a couple of issues though. The first being that while Alexander's invitation for the Māori All Blacks to tour South Africa next year was probably done with the best of intentions, the team has previously run into trouble due to the country's complete post apartheid course correction regarding selection and sporting contact. The other one is that both SA Rugby and NZ Rugby have actually already said sorry, 15 years ago and in a way that directly involved the Māori All Blacks. The reason why perhaps it's not so well remembered is that it was an event that both governing bodies were prodded into and ended up as a more of a political points scoring effort in the Beehive. 2010 marked a century of Māori representative sides in New Zealand, which included by a couple of rare fixtures against tier one opposition. The then NZ Māori team were due to face Ireland and England in June, however in May the old issue of sporting contact with South Africa was brought up by Green Party MP Keith Locke, a veteran protester from the 1981 tour. Then Prime Minister John Key was asked by Locke whether he would be apologising for the previous National led government's role in sanctioning the historic tours that excluded players. The issue had come to light when South Africa's Sport and Recreation Minster Reverend Makhenkesi Arnold Stofile sent a public letter of apology to Māori players who were left out of the 1928, 1949 and 1960 tours. This caught the NZRU (now NZ Rugby) unaware, given that their previous stance on the issue was that no apology was necessary, they said, on the advice of the Māori Rugby Board. However, this was disputed by board chairman Mike Eagle, who said: "At no stage were they against it; the timing just wasn't right in their opinion. The public reaction around this apology certainly created more harm than good and it could have escalated during the centenary year." But again this was contradicted by fellow board member Wayne Peters, who claimed that apologising to help people move on was "irresponsible". NZRU CEO Steve Tew eventually issued a statement saying: "It is even more complicated in South Africa where the very people who are apologising now were victims of the regime that they are apologising for. They had a degree of urgency because they had some political pressure from their government to get on and do it. "This has never been a straightforward issue. It's one of the most complex issues that our country has dealt with in my lifetime. Frankly, there's probably never any 100 percent right or wrong approach to it". A private apology was sent out, along with a media release, but nothing was formally said. There were official functions set up for the NZ Māori side's upcoming fixtures, however officials stayed tight lipped about actually making an apology at them. The release read: "Today, on behalf of the New Zealand Rugby Union, we wish to say sorry first and foremost to those Māori players who were not considered for selection for teams to tour South Africa or to play South Africa. We apologise to the families of those players and to the wider Māori community who were affected directly or indirectly by the decisions taken to not include Māori players for those teams and tours. "It was a period in which the respect of New Zealand Māori rugby was not upheld and that is deeply regretted." The South African Rugby Union followed suit, with president and Alexander's predecessor Oregan Hoskins calling a press conference to apologise as well: "As the current guardians of the game of rugby union it is therefore appropriate that we take this opportunity to apologise to those Māori players who may have been excluded from selection and to the offence this may have caused to the Māori community. "But, even more importantly, this is the opportunity to apologise on behalf of rugby to black South Africans who were denied the opportunity to represent not only their country but also their provinces throughout those long dark years because of the connivance of our predecessors in the systematic suppression of the majority." 45.document_title: The Issues with an Apology to Māori Rugby Players
45.document_summary: This analysis examines SA Rugby's recent proposal to formally apologize to Māori and Pasifika players excluded from touring apartheid-era South Africa. While SA Rugby president Mark Alexander's invitation appears well-intentioned, the article highlights two key issues: the Māori All Blacks' previous troubles with South Africa regarding post-apartheid selection policies, and the fact that both SA Rugby and NZ Rugby already apologized 15 years ago in 2010. That earlier apology emerged from political pressure following South Africa's Sport Minister's public letter and Green Party MP Keith Locke's questioning of then-PM John Key. Despite initial resistance from NZRU, both unions eventually issued private apologies and media releases acknowledging the exclusion of Māori players from 1928, 1949, and 1960 tours. The article underscores the complexity of addressing historical sporting injustices tied to apartheid and the political dimensions surrounding such reconciliation efforts.

46.text:
[Page 1] South Africa Rugby to apologise to Māori players excluded by apartheid ByNone Sports Journalist 2025 08 30 10:10:11+12:00 South Africa Rugby to apologise to Māori players excluded by apartheid South Africa Rugby president Mark Alexander has revealed that plans are in place to welcome the Māori All Blacks next year, as well as formally apologise for historic exclusion during the country's apartheid era. "We must also acknowledge that the injustice of apartheid extended beyond our borders. The Māori All Blacks a team rich in heritage and pride were denied the right to tour South Africa for decades, simply because they were not white. That exclusion was a stain on our history and it is long overdue that we confront it with humility and remorse," said Alexander this week, as reported by Cape Town based journalist Mark Keohane. "I am pleased to share that the South African Rugby Union is currently in discussion with our counterparts in New Zealand to host the Māori All Blacks for two matches on South African soil next season," said Alexander. "These games will not only be a celebration of rugby excellence they will be a moment of reckoning, of recognition and of reconciliation. We intend to use this occasion to formally apologise for the discrimination they endured and to honour those who were excluded and marginalised here at home." Alexander's remarks come one week out from the highly anticipated first test between the All Blacks and Springboks, but also as plans are being finalised for the All Blacks to tour South Africa in 2026. It will be their first full tour of any nation since their iconic series win over the Springboks in 1996. It is understood that the tour, which will be officially called 'The Greatest Rivalry', will involve the All Blacks playing three tests and five midweek games, with a fourth test to be held at Twickenham in London later in the year. In a statement, NZ Rugby did not mention any specific involvement of the Māori All Blacks in the 2026 tour but said that they are "excited to share more details about the All Blacks and Springboks tours in the coming weeks alongside the South African Rugby Union. As a part of this, we are exploring opportunities for the Black Ferns to be involved." Māori and Pasifika players were barred from touring South Africa with the All Blacks in 1949 and 1960, with the 1970 and 1976 cohort that included Sir Bryan Williams and Sid Going infamously given 'honorary white' status under the apartheid regime's laws. There had been an earlier pre apartheid tour in 1928, with Māori players excluded, however that was at the behest of the NZRFU (now NZ Rugby) for fear of upsetting the already deeply racially divided situation in South Africa at the time. A then New Zealand Māori side toured South Africa in 1994, the same year Nelson Mandela had been elected president and apartheid had been fully dismantled. The team's visit had been orchestrated by Alexander's predecessor Louis Luyt as a gesture of goodwill towards Mandela's new African National Congress government, amid escalating tensions at the time that saw South Africa on the brink of civil war. Mandela and Luyt then played pivotal roles in the following year's Rugby World Cup, which saw the Springboks defeat the All Blacks in the final. Related

The SARU will host the Māori All Blacks for two matches next season as a gesture of reconciliation. Māori and Pasifika players were barred from tours in 1949 and 1960, while later cohorts received 'honorary white' status. A Māori side toured in 1994 after apartheid's dismantling. The announcement coincides with upcoming All Blacks-Springboks tests and plans for the All Blacks' 2026 tour, called 'The Greatest Rivalry', featuring three tests and five midweek games.

All Blacks history says otherwise Protesters interrupt the New Zealand v South Africa Rugby Match at Eden Park in Auckland with flour bombs in reaction to apartheid, 12 September 1981. Analysis "Keep politics out of sport." It's the war cry of the more 'traditional' footy fan, but there is no hiding from the fact that the two are closely linked and have been since the All Black's inception. TJ Perenara caused a serious stir during the haka in Sunday's final test of the year against Italy, and Perenara's final outing in black. The outspoken halfback called "Toitū te tiriti o Waitangi" as he led Ka Mate, again prompting rhetoric about players needing to just play the game. But whether it's a prime minister using the side to promote themselves, players calling out social injustice, or the side simply embroiled in geopolitical scandals, politics and sport are rarely far apart. RNZ looks back at the history of when All Blacks and politics clashed. 1906 New Zealand Premier Richard Seddon leads the Originals off the ship as they arrive home to an adoring crowd. 1928 All Black legend George Nepia is left behind as All Blacks first tour racially segregated South Africa. 1960 Citizens' All Black Tour Association chase All Black plane as they depart for South Africa. 1970 Ken Gray retires instead of touring South Africa due to apartheid regime while Bob Burgess declines to even trial. 1975 National promise to strengthen sporting relations with South Africa. 1981 Peak of sport meets politics. Skipper Graham Mourie and Bruce Robertson both sat out the tour. Bob Burgess takes part in the nationwide protests. 1986 Cavaliers make rebel tour to South Africa. 1995 Josh Kronfeld writes "nuclear free" on his headgear in a match for Otago to protest nuclear testing in the Pacific. 2011 Prime Minister John Key stands with All Black's skipper Richie McCaw as he lifts the World Cup. 2014 Israel Dagg tweets in support of John Key during the election. 2015 Sonny Bill Williams Tweets photos of dead children to protests the Syrian crisis. 2016 Kane Hames writes "Standing Rock" on wrist to protest the North Dakota pipeline during Māori All Blacks match in US. 2018 Brad Weber and TJ Perenara both speak out against Israel Folau's homophobic tweets. 2018 19 Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern hands Bledisloe Cup to Kieran Reed. 2019 TJ Perenara writes "Ihumātao" on his wrist in support of the protests fighting housing development on the sacred site. 2024 TJ Perenara begins haka with a call to honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi. [Page 1] All Blacks vs Springboks: The memorable moments BySport 2025 09 05 06:32:44+12:00 From the 1976 Tour of South Africa to their two epic World Cup final contests, RNZ looks back at the most memorable moments between the All Blacks and Springboks. 1976 Tour of South Africa This series was memorable for a number of reasons. One it included five Māori members of the All Blacks tour squad as well as Samoan New Zealander Sir Bryan Williams. Those six players were given honorary 'white status' for the tour, as they did in 1970, as South Africa was still in its apartheid era, leading to protests both in New Zealand and throughout the world. Due to the decision to play in South Africa during the apartheid era, 25 African nations (29 countries in total world wide) boycotted the 1976 Montreal Olympics in protest of New Zealand's participation at the games. At the time the United Nations had called for a sporting embargo against South Africa due to its apartheid regime. As for the series itself, New Zealand played 22 matches in total, winning 18 and losing six. The matches weren't without controversy either, speaking to the Herald, All Blacks prop Billy Bush said he wasn't awarded a try by the ref in the final Test match because he was Māori. New Zealand lost the Test 15 14 and the four match Test series against South Africa three one as a result. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Az31E_EKEVk 1981 'flour bomb test' Much like the 1976 tour, South Africa's tour of New Zealand was incredibly polarising. New Zealand's love of rugby and opinion on politics divided families and caused mass protests throughout the country. Despite Prime Minister Robert Muldoon giving the tour the go ahead, it didn't stop the matches from being affected. The Test in Hamilton had to be cancelled while protests were held in Wellington and Christchurch on the respective game days. However, the most memorable moment on the field came in the final match when two men flew a plane over Eden Park, dropping 'flour bombs' onto the pitch, striking All Black prop Gary Knight. Despite the incident, the referees allowed the match to continue with New Zealand winning the Test in injury time 25 22. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rkZMIySG75c 1995 Rugby World Cup final Entering the final, both New Zealand and South Africa had gone through the tournament unbeaten. Despite the match being in South Africa, New Zealand went into the match as favourites following the side's demolition of England which included a four try spree by the late Jonah Lomu. The tournament itself was also incredibly influential for South Africa's public relations to the world in a post apartheid era with Nelson Mandela at the helm. Despite New Zealand's try scoring ability throughout the tournament, the match was tryless with only Andrew Mehrtens and Joel Stransky kicking each teams' points. On top of that, the match was the first in World Cup final history to go to extra time, with Stranksy famously kicking the drop goal to hand South Africa its first World Cup victory and hand New Zealand its first loss in a World Cup final. The match was marred by controversy here in New Zealand with claims of the All Blacks being poisoned before the match. Regardless of the claims, the way the South African backline, the late halfback Joost van der Westhuizen in particular, shut down Lomu was nothing short of extraordinary given the All Black wing's abilities at the time. For many South Africans, the most memorable moment of that day will always be Nelson Mandela, donning the Springboks number six jersey, handing over the Webb Ellis Trophy to South African captain Francois Pienaar. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9Wh4MPGp68A 1996 Tour of South Africa 1996 was a momentous year in rugby for a myriad of reasons. The sport had officially become professional, just a year after the aforementioned final in the Rainbow nation. At the time the All Blacks possessed one of the best backlines of any era, with the likes of Christian Cullen, Jonah Lomu, Jeff Wilson, Frank Bunce, Glen Osborne, Eric Rush, Andrew Mehrtens, Alama Ieremia, Scott McLeod, Carlos Spencer and Tabai Matson. Then there was the formidable forward pack; Ian Jones, Josh Kronfield, Craig Dowd, Norm Hewitt, Olo Brown, Zinzan Brooke, Robin Brooke, Todd Blackadder, Taine Randell and captain Sean Fitzpatrick to name a few. Coming into the tour, the All Blacks had already won the Tri Nations tournament for the year, but that elusive South African Tour victory still haunted them. The first match in Durban was like any other All Blacks Springboks Test match; physical and close. New Zealand won the match 23 19, outscoring the South Africans three tries to one. The second Test, much like the first, was another tight encounter. With just a minute left on the clock, a four point lead and victory just moments away, the All Blacks won a scrum on the left hand side of the South African 22. After winning the scrum and

[Page 1] Tom Newnham who challenged South Africa's apartheid system for 40 years honoured 2024 05 01 11:20:49+12:00 Tom Newnham pictured during a visit to a village in China in 1981 the same year as the Springbok tour of New Zealand. A New Zealand anti apartheid activist has been posthumously honoured for the decades he spent campaigning to cut ties with apartheid South Africa. Tom Newnham, who died in 2010, was awarded the Order of the Companions of O R Tambo for his tireless campaigning against apartheid. Starting with the 1960 All Blacks tour of South Africa, Newnham worked to change New Zealand's sporting contact with South Africa by organising speaking tours by prominent international anti apartheid activists. https: //www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/morningreport/audio/2018936471 /nzer tom newnham posthumously honoured for work against apartheid Newnham's son, Rewi Newnham, attended the ceremony in Pretoria and told Morning Report it was a tremendous ceremony. "These are the highest national awards bestowed upon not just South Africans, but international citizens as well who have supported South Africa over the years. "It was really quite humbling to be there representing my father, a few years after he passed away of course, so a lot of memories coming back. "Amongst the awardees were some very notable people in South Africa and internationally, many of whom have made huge sacrifices. "To see my father's award amongst that was really quite a humbling experience for me." Newnham said his father spent 40 years fighting the anti apartheid campaign, which ultimately triumphed when apartheid legislation was repealed in the early 1990s. "The sort of sacrifices he made were psychological. There was a lot of stuff that today would be called hate speech and hate mail and so on, that he suffered, some physical abuse as well. "But he stood up to that, and I guess in some ways he maybe thrived on it. He knew that he had to in order to get through this." Newnham also acknowledged the people who supported his father over the years, saying they should take a lot of credit for the award. 51.document_title: The Issues with an Apology to Māori Rugby Players
51.document_summary: This analysis examines SA Rugby's recent proposal to formally apologize to Māori and Pasifika players excluded from touring apartheid-era South Africa. While SA Rugby president Mark Alexander's invitation appears well-intentioned, the article highlights two key issues: the Māori All Blacks' previous troubles with South Africa regarding post-apartheid selection policies, and the fact that both SA Rugby and NZ Rugby already apologized 15 years ago in 2010. That earlier apology emerged from political pressure following South Africa's Sport Minister's public letter and Green Party MP Keith Locke's questioning of then-PM John Key. Despite initial resistance from NZRU, both unions eventually issued private apologies and media releases acknowledging the exclusion of Māori players from 1928, 1949, and 1960 tours. The article underscores the complexity of addressing historical sporting injustices tied to apartheid and the political dimensions surrounding such reconciliation efforts.

52.text:
[Page 1] https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.ht ml?videoId=6378447101112 All Blacks v Springboks Kick off: 7:05pm Saturday 6 September Eden Park, Auckland Live blog updates on RNZ Sport Grant Fox's experience of watching the All Blacks play the Springboks as a kid is something he says ignited "a dream inside me" to one day pull on the black jersey. One day out from the two sides meeting again in the most anticipated test match of the year, the former record points scorer and inaugural World Cup winner's memories of the rivalry were strong, rating the Springboks as the All Blacks' "greatest foe", especially considering the experience he had playing against them in 1992. "Ellis Park, intense," said Fox of the dramatic match that was the Springboks' first since readmission to test rugby after democratic elections had been held in South Africa. "We'd had a successful run through the provinces with the one test at the end of it all. We had a job to do and were up 27 10 with about 10 minutes to go. So we'd actually done a pretty good job. And then they came roaring back at us, and we won 27 24. I think the final score was. I mean, we were deserving winners, but we could have got pipped at the end of the game." The match had been hastily arranged during the 1992 season, which also marked 100 years since the formation of the New Zealand Rugby Union (now NZ Rugby) and saw the All Blacks jet off to South Africa after an intense series against the then world champion Wallabies. "South Africa had been an exile for a while. I don't want to re litigate all, all of that, but they will now back in the fold, and they are our greatest foe. They really are. As a kid growing up, I can remember watching Brian Williams on black and white TV playing in 1970. "He was my hero…that dream burned inside me…from a little kid, that's what I remember. I wanted to have the opportunity to play against our greatest foe, and we got that in 1992." Fox spoke at a new exhibition at the All Blacks Experience in Auckland called Jerseys Of Significance, which was funded by former White House advisor Chris Liddell and businessman Rob Morrison. It showcases a number of historically important All Black jerseys, including Jonah Lomu's 1995 World Cup jersey he wore in his iconic semi final performance against England, Richie McCaw's 2015 World Cup final jersey, George Nepia's 1924 Invincibles jersey, a 1905 Originals jersey belonging to Ernie Booth, and Anna Richards' 2002 Black Ferns World Cup winning jersey. Fox's contribution was his inaugural World Cup winning jersey, a classic All Black strip with a white collar and notably without the tournament branding that adorns team gear these days. "It's a privilege to have my jersey here and it really didn't belong to me I just filled it for a period of time. What's been created (at the All Blacks Experience) is something special…it's spine tingling. I;m choking up a bit talking about it now." The 63 year old, who these days is happy to have the limelight on professional golfer son Ryan, is proud to say he has one of the most extensive and unique jersey collections in New Zealand rugby. "I was lucky enough to play for NZ Schools, NZ Universities, NZ Colts, NZ Juniors and the All Blacks. So I've got that whole set of jerseys at home, every one of them. It's a little set I'm very proud of because I'm not sure too many people would have." Fox is keen for people to come along and see his jersey, along with all the others in the exhibition. "It's a very special experience and you don't have to love rugby to come here. You just need to come and understand a bit of the history of this country, because we're part of that history." Related

[Page 1] Wild facts about the first All Blacks Pumas v All Blacks Kick off: 9:10am Sunday 17 August Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes, Córdoba Live blog updates on RNZ The All Blacks return to action this weekend against the Pumas in Cordoba. While things have come a long way from training on the decks of ships, or making a mad dash from milking the cows to playing a test match, the age of professionalism was paved through over a century of amateur pioneers. The early days of the All Blacks were full of incredible tales. Though the team did not officially adopt the iconic name until 1905, the country has been selecting its best players to represent Aotearoa since 1884. Here are some of the most fascinating, quirky and tragic stories from New Zealand rugby's earliest characters. An All Black strawweight John Dumbell, an 1884 All Black who weighed just 50kg. An ironic surname considering he could have been curled by a few of today's All Blacks. All Black shot dead Alfred Cooke, who debuted in 1894, was killed in 1900. He was shot accidentally by a friend during a shooting expedition at Lake Ellesmere / Te Waihora, preventing him from seeing his brother debut for the All Blacks in 1903. Coast to coast Henry Butland traversed the Southern Alps on foot to get from Hokitika to Lyttleton for the 1893 tour of Australia. Took part in the Klondike Gold Rush and his son Jack founded Chesdale Cheese. The OG Barrett brothers The Bayley bunch had six brothers who played for Taranaki in the late nineteenth and early 20th centuries with Alfred and Walter making their debuts for New Zealand in 1893 and '94 respectively. Horse kills All Black James Lambie first played for New Zealand in 1893. In 1905 while travelling home on horseback after watching Taranaki play Great Britain, he was kicked in the head by his horse and died as a result. Boots and bulbs William Balch, who won a sole New Zealand cap in 1894, was also a noted authority on growing daffodils. Boy amongst men Joe Warbick, who played 21 matches for the 'Natives' and seven for New Zealand starting in 1884, was the youngest person to ever play provincial rugby at just 15. He would often play barefooted and could slot a droppie from halfway. Killed by the Waimangu Geyser eruption of 1903. The fraud forward James O'Donnell was selected for the first national side to tour Australia in 1884, but was arrested on a fugitive warrant at Clinton and returned to Invercargill to face fraud charges. A taboo romance In a 19th century Romeo and Juliet tale, David Gage and a Scottish Aristocrat fell in love during the 1888 89 'Natives' Tour, eventually forced to part ways due to interracial romance being forbidden in Scottish high society. The story was adapted into a three part mini series called 'Savage Play.' Boats 'n all Thomas Ryan, the first player to kick a conversion and a drop goal for New Zealand in 1884, was a renowned artist with three of his pieces in the collection of the Auckland Art Gallery. He also skippered a ship for 20 years which ran between Taupō and Tokaanu. Typhoid takes trailblazer Named the first captain of the All Blacks in 1884, William Millton died from typhoid at just 29. Original big bopper Timothy O'Connor was the heaviest All Black in the original 1884 side at a whopping 89kg. Swept away John Taiaroa, a member of the first new Zealand side in 1884, drowned on New Years Eve in 1907 after slipping off his boat in the Otago Harbour. His body was recovered two weeks later, ten miles away. All Black author Billy Stead, a member of the 1905 Originals tour to Britain, wrote 'The Complete Rugby Footballer,' published in 1906, widely regarded as one of the best rugby manuals ever written. Founder of the fern Thomas Ellison was the first captain of New Zealand in 1893, one of the first Māori lawyers in New Zealand, and was the man behind the iconic silver fern on black uniform. All Black hero In 1897, All Black Robert Oliphant was given a bravery award for saving a little girl from drowning in the Auckland Harbour. Mining death An All Black in 1894, John Swindley died in Sumatra in a mining accident in 1918. In the family A member of the first All Black team of 1884, Henry Robert's son Teddy, also a halfback, was a member of the All Blacks in 1913, making them the first father son duo to play for New Zealand. Edward and William Millton marked the first All Black brothers in 1884. A lucky escape In 1906, Fred Roberts was too ill to travel home with the All Blacks and stayed in San Francisco for several weeks. After surgery to remove his infected tonsils, he travelled back to New Zealand, narrowly missing the 1906 San Francisco earthquake which destroyed his hotel. Reporting from the field Ernie Booth was also a journalist at the same time he played for the All Blacks from 1905 07. Way to get the scoops! On field fatality In 1913 on a tour to Canada, a player on the Victoria team was carried from the field after suffering a big hit from an All Black. He died after the game and it was first thought this was due to concussion of the brain, but a medical investigation showed that he had suffered a heart attack. Tri code star Before there was Israel Folau, there was George Gillett who played for the All Blacks from 1905 08, and also represented the the New Zealand rugby league and Australian rules sides. 1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the history of racism and anti-racism activism in New Zealand from the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) through the early 21st century. It examines how systemic racism persisted through discrimination in housing, employment, sports, and institutions despite the Treaty's promise of equal rights for Māori. The document details key anti-racism movements including the Citizens' All Black Tour Association (1959), Citizens Association for Racial Equality (1964), HART (1969), and Māori-led organizations like Ngā Tamatoa and the Polynesian Panthers. chunkHighlights.text: In 1883 George Rusden, an Australian civil servant and historian, published a History of New Zealand , which set out a long list of violations of the Treaty of Waitangi.
First sporting contacts with South Africa
Rugby was the national game of both New Zealand and white South Africa, and the two countries competed fiercely on the field from the 1920s.

South Africa was ruled by a white minority which enforced rigid segregationist laws over the black majority. From 1948 a formal system of apartheid was established. Black and ‘coloured’ (mixed-race) players were excluded from the country’s national sports teams.
Pre-war rugby tours

The Springboks, South Africa’s national rugby team, first toured New Zealand in 1921. They played one close-fought match against a team of ‘New Zealand Natives’ (Māori) and a South African journalist reported that the Springboks were ‘frankly disgusted’ at playing against ‘a band of coloured men’. 1 On their next tour in 1937, the Springboks refused to play an all-Māori team, although several Māori were included in the All Blacks. Te Arawa tribe called for a sporting and cultural boycott of South Africa, and most Māori supported them. Some protested with banners announcing ‘Cash before Conscience’ – tours were lucrative.

The document details multiple protest methods including letters and petitions (such as the 1880s suffrage petitions and 1970 Save Manapōuri petition), public meetings and rallies, sit-ins and occupations (including the 1977-78 Bastion Point occupation and 2022 Parliament grounds occupation), pickets and boycotts, and protest marches. Notable historical examples include the 1975 Māori hikoi, 1981 Springbok tour protests, 1913 waterfront disputes, and 2019 climate strikes with 170,000 participants. The document emphasizes significant Māori activism and land rights protests such as Takaparawhā/Bastion Point, Pureora Forest, Moutoa Gardens, and Ihumātao. It also covers the evolution of protest tactics from counter-culture movements of the 1960s-70s to modern 'Occupy' movements and COVID-19 policy protests. While destructive protests are relatively rare in New Zealand, the document concludes that public protest remains an essential feature of participatory democracy, enabling responsive government and community engagement with politicians despite predictions of decline.

chunkHighlights.text: 1981 Springbok tour

Rugby supporters eagerly anticipated the first Springbok tour to New Zealand since 1965. Opponents associated the Springboks with the racist South African apartheid regime and urged the government to stop the tour. It refused and the team arrived on 19 July. Anti-tour campaigners tried to halt the tour’s progress by blocking roads and invading rugby grounds. Running street battles and violent clashes between tour opponents and supporters became commonplace. Struggling to control events, the police batoned protesters, with bloody results.

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the relationship between sport and national identity in New Zealand from the 1870s through the 2010s. It chronicles how sporting achievements have shaped New Zealand's national character and international image. The narrative progresses from early sporting heroes like Joe Scott and the racehorse Carbine in the 1880s, through the establishment of national sporting associations and rugby's emergence as the primary symbol of national pride. The All Blacks' triumphant 1905-06 tour of Britain and France marked a pivotal moment in establishing sporting nationalism. The document examines how individual athletes—including Tom Heeney, Phar Lap, Jack Lovelock, Edmund Hillary, Peter Snell, Valerie Adams, and Sarah Ulmer—contributed to national pride. The 1981 Springbok tour controversy revealed tensions about national values regarding apartheid. Television coverage transformed sports consumption and amplified sporting nationalism, while women athletes and lesser-known sports challenged rugby's dominance. Significant achievements include the 1987 and 2011 Rugby World Cup victories, Team New Zealand's 1995 America's Cup win, and the 2009 All Whites World Cup qualification. The analysis reveals sport has served as both a unifying force and a battleground for national identity debates, reflecting broader questions about New Zealand's values and place in the world.

chunkHighlights.text: Africa. Most African nations boycotted the Olympics in protest against New Zealand’s presence.
Bugger rugger

Many New Zealanders saw the 1981 Springbok tour as an argument about the place of rugby in the country’s identity. A 30-year-old mother wrote: ‘I have for years resented the dominance that rugby has in the homes, schools and society in general. It’s time that a few other values took over from bloody rugby.’ A 28-year-old said: ‘I disliked the macho aspect of rugby and resent the way it has dominated New Zealand culture. I was brought up in North Canterbury (Alec Wyllie country) and I detest the way rugby males relate to women.’ ‘Bugger rugger,’ wrote another. 1

Sport was becoming a cause for national embarrassment, and a fierce debate broke out which reached a peak during the 1981 Springbok tour of New Zealand. For some, rugby was the heart of New Zealand’s identity as a country of strong outdoor men. The contests with South Africa were central to this tradition and world view. Others argued that New Zealand had an identity as an opponent of racism and a fighter for human rights. Sport must accord with these values. For 56 days in the winter of 1981 New Zealanders argued with other New Zealanders about their national identity in the nation’s closest approach to civil war since the 1860s.
Rugby’s dominance reduced?

The argument had other consequences. In 1981 and 1982 many sporting Kiwis with a conscience shifted their interests to the ‘round game’ and followed the long journey of the New Zealand football team, the All Whites, to the world cup. And New Zealand women began to challenge the dominance of male sports in the media and in the national psychology.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's complex relationship with cities from the mid-19th century through the 2000s, exploring urbanization, cultural representations, and the persistent city-country divide. It traces the evolution from strong anti-urban sentiments among European settlers—who viewed cities as unhealthy threats to agrarian society—to rapid urbanization, with urban populations growing from nearly 40% in 1881 to over 50% by 1911. The document analyzes how New Zealand's four main urban centers (Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, and Dunedin) have been depicted across multiple media forms including literature, visual art, film, and television. Literary representations evolved from emphasizing urban alienation and social inequality in early works like John A. Lee's "Children of the Poor" to more nuanced explorations of suburban conformity and multicultural urban experiences. Visual artists similarly progressed from promotional colonial imagery to impressionist and expressionist styles celebrating urban dynamism. The document examines historical conflicts such as the 1913 waterfront strike and the 1981 South African rugby tour, which exposed deep geo-political divisions between liberal urban constituencies and conservative rural populations. Despite persistent anti-city rhetoric rooted in an "agrarian cult," cities ultimately became dominant centers of New Zealand society. The text concludes that while ongoing tensions exist between urban and rural communities, both recognize the importance of building bridges rather than deepening divisions.

chunkHighlights.text: Perhaps the most divisive city–country rift occurred during the 1981 South African rugby tour of New Zealand, opposed by anti-apartheid protesters. Support for the tour was strongest in country districts, and opposition to it centred in cities. Long-standing prejudices re-surfaced. Pro-tour supporters called anti-tour supporters ‘poofters’; anti-tour activists retaliated with taunts of ‘country bumpkin’, and ‘sheep-shaggers’.
