chunkHighlights.text: Tāwhirimātea (‘The eyes of the god Tāwhirimātea’) and refers to a large cluster of stars, known in some European traditions as the Pleiades. According to Māori tradition, the god of the wind, Tāwhirimātea, was so angry when his siblings separated their parents, Ranginui the sky father and Papatūānuku the earth mother, that he tore out his eyes and threw them into the heavens. The cycle of life and death Traditionally, Matariki was a time to acknowledge the dead and to release their spirits to become stars. It was also a time to reflect, to be thankful to the gods for the harvest, to feast and to share the bounty of the harvest with family and friends. Matariki revived Matariki, or Māori New Year, celebrations were once popular, but had largely stopped by the 1940s. In the 2000s, they were revived. Now, thousands of people take part in events to honour the beginning of the Māori New Year, and in whānau celebrations to remember those who have died and to plan for the year ahead. Since 2022, a public holiday marking Matariki has been held on a Friday in June or July each year.
Heralding the new year
Tirohia ake ngā whetu
Me ko Matariki e ārau ana
He tiki mai tahau i ngā mahara e kohi nei
Whakarerea ake e nā te roimata koua riringi
I gaze up to the stars
To the assembly of Matariki
Captured are my memories of you who have left me behind
Tears rippling
like springs in my eyes.

Matariki is a small cluster of stars also known as the Pleiades, in the Taurus constellation. In New Zealand it comes into view low on the north-eastern horizon, in the tail of the Milky Way, just before dawn in midwinter. This heralds the Māori New Year and the changing of the seasons.

Iwi celebrate Matariki at different times, some when the cluster is first seen in the dawn sky, others after the full moon rises or at the beginning of the next new moon. For some iwi the star cluster includes seven stars, while for others it has nine.
For all iwi , the importance of Matariki is expressed through proverbs and songs linking it with the bright star Whānui (Vega):
Ka puta Matariki ka rere Whānui.
Ko te tohu tēnā o te tau e!
Matariki reappears, Whānui starts its flight.
Being the sign of the [new] year!
Creation stories

Matariki is an abbreviation of ‘Ngā Mata o te Ariki Tāwhirimātea’ (‘The eyes of the god Tāwhirimātea’). According to Māori tradition, when Ranginui, the sky father, and Papatūānuku, the earth mother were separated by their offspring, one of their sons, god of the winds Tāwhirimātea, became angry, tearing out his eyes and hurling them into the heavens.

3.fileDescription: This article explores the Matariki star cluster through multiple cultural perspectives. In Aotearoa, Matariki represents the crushed eyes of Tāwhirimātea from Māori creation mythology. The article reviews a book by Rangi Matamua and Miriama Kamo that documents how various cultures interpret this constellation: Japan calls it Subaru ("united"), viewing the stars as sacred jewels used to bring the sun goddess Amaterasu out of a cave; other cultures know it as the Blossom Cluster, seven brothers, or sisters sharing a husband. The book features stunning watercolour illustrations by Isobel Joy Te Aho-White depicting Māori astronomical symbolism and the maramataka (lunar calendar), making it an iconic resource for children and readers exploring cultural astronomy and reflection.

chunkHighlights.text: The story of the Matariki constellation is the lesser-known continuation of the Māori creation myth, after Tāne pushed Ranginui and Papatūānuku apart to bring light into the world. Tāwhirimātea, god of the wind and weather, wanted his parents to stay together. He sought utu for their separation, attacking his siblings, the other atua, one by one. His stormy rage defeated them all, until he reached Tūmatauenga, the god of humanity and war. The devastation of this defeat led Tāwhirimātea to gouge out, crush, then fling his eyes at his father’s chest, their gleam forming the Matariki constellation.

chunkHighlights.text: Matariki: the star that signifies well-being, reflection, hope and the gathering of people; considered to be a female star which is the guardian of the other stars in the cluster. The name Matariki denotes both this individual star and the whole cluster.
Waitī: the star linked with fresh water and food that comes from fresh water.
Waitā: the star linked with the ocean and food that comes from it.
Tupuānuku: the star linked with food that grows in the ground.
Tupuārangi: the star linked with food that comes from the skies: fruits, berries, and birds.
Waipunarangi: the star linked with the rain.
Ururangi: the star that determines the winds for the year.
Pōhutukawa: the star associated with those who have died.
Hiwa-i-te-rangi: the star associated with dreams and aspirations for the coming year.

Others say Matariki is the mother surrounded by her six daughters, Tupuānuku, Tupuārangi, Waitī, Waitā, Waipunarangi and Ururangi. In one account Matariki and her daughters appear to assist the sun, Te Rā, whose winter journey from the north has left him weakened.
Matariki and Puanga
Matariki outside New Zealand

The Matariki cluster is of great significance for spiritual, environmental and cultural reasons throughout the Pacific. Many Pacific people use its progress across the skies to track passing time and changing seasons. It is known as Matariki in Cook Islands; as Mataliki in Tokelau, Niue, Tuvalu, Tonga, ‘Uvea and Futuna; as Matali’i in Samoa; as Matari’i in Tahiti; and as Makali’i in Hawai’i.

The Matariki stars have been the subjects of scientific observations and mythological stories in cultures throughout the world for thousands of years, including in the Middle East, Asia, Australia, Europe and North and South America.

According to Greek myth, the nine brightest stars of Pleiades are Pleione and Atlas and their seven daughters. While wandering through the woods one day, the daughters were spied by Orion, who gave chase. To save them from Orion’s dishonourable intentions, Zeus transformed them into stars and placed them in the sky. A number of ancient temples on the Acropolis in Athens face the direction where the Pleiades rise.

While all iwi celebrate the Māori New Year in June or July, some iwi in Whanganui, Taranaki, the Far North and the South Island refer to this period as Puanga rather than Matariki. In these parts of the country, the Matariki star cluster is hard to see clearly and so iwi place importance on
the star Puanga (Rigel), which is the next significant star closest to Matariki, and easier to see in twilight. Ngai Tahu in the South Island call the star Puaka.
There are also regions where the setting of the star Rehua (Antares) in winter denotes the change of seasons.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's public holidays from the mid-1800s to the 21st century. It covers the 12 statutory public holidays including New Year's Day, Waitangi Day (6 February), Easter, Anzac Day (25 April), King's Birthday, Matariki (Māori new year, added in 2022), Labour Day (fourth Monday in October), provincial anniversary days, Christmas Day, and Boxing Day. The Bank Holidays Act 1873 established the first public holidays, with Labour Day becoming the first statutory general holiday for all workers in 1899. The document details cultural heritage reflected in these holidays, including Christian traditions, Māori customs, and imperial history. Key holidays examined include Waitangi Day commemorating the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and Māori protests regarding treaty breaches; Anzac Day (25 April) marking the 1915 Gallipoli landing; and Matariki representing New Zealand's first public holiday recognizing te ao Māori. The text also covers provincial anniversary days, royal occasions, and the emergence of diverse cultural celebrations like Chinese New Year and Diwali, reflecting New Zealand's multicultural society. It notes "Mondayisation" of holidays, employee entitlements (time-and-a-half pay), shop trading restrictions, and the 2016 Shop Trading Hours Act amendment regarding Easter Sunday trading.

chunkHighlights.text: Matariki holiday – June or July

In June 2022, the nation celebrated Matariki as a public holiday for the first time. The day is the first holiday that recognised and celebrated te ao Māori (the Māori world). Matariki is an abbreviation of ‘Ngā mata o te ariki Tāwhirimātea’ (The eyes of the god Tāwhirimātea) and refers to a large cluster of stars, also known as the Pleiades, which rises in the early morning in midwinter. It marks the changing of the seasons and the beginning of the Māori New Year.

The government announced at the time the legislation was passed that it intended to ensure that mātauranga Maori was at the heart of celebrations of the public holiday. The day would be a time for remembrance, for celebrating the present and for looking to the future.

chunkHighlights.text: Māori traditionally greeted the first sightings of Matariki with expressions of grief for those who had died since its last appearance. A ceremony called ‘whāngai i te hautapu’ was held at this time to remember the dead. This also involved ‘feeding the stars’ with specially prepared foods.
In 1957 Rangihuna Pire, a kaumātua of Ngā Ruahine, recalled being taken as a child to watch for Matariki at Kaūpokonui in south Taranaki:

The old people might wait up several nights before the stars rose. They would make a small hāngī . When they saw the stars, they would weep and tell Matariki the names of those who had gone since the stars set, then the oven would be uncovered so the scent of the food would rise and strengthen the stars, for they were weak and cold.

fileAuthor: Ross Calman, Arthur Saunders Thomson, and various historical sources
7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document explores leisure activities, entertainment practices, and cultural traditions in traditional Māori society. It examines how work-leisure balance was shaped by resource availability, environmental changes, and warfare throughout pre-European New Zealand. Early settlement offered abundant leisure due to plentiful food, but moa extinction and seal depletion forced sustainable harvesting practices and increased competition for mahinga kai (food sources). Age and social class influenced leisure availability, with children and elderly enjoying more free time. Leisure was primarily communal and evening-based, featuring storytelling, games, and indoor entertainment. Traditional pastimes included waiata (songs), haka, poi, taonga puoro (musical instruments), tākaro (games), and sports such as kaipara (athletics), swimming, and diving. Major festivals included the kūmara harvest festival marked by Whānui (Vega) and the Matariki new year festival in June. Hākari (feasts) served ritual, political, and social functions. Te whare tapere (the house of entertainment) encompassed cultural expression and knowledge transmission. Traditional children's toys were crafted from natural materials such as harakeke (flax) and raupō (bulrush), including tētere (flax trumpets) and toparere (flax leaf gliders). Entertainment and leisure activities were integral to Māori society, transmitting knowledge, history, cultural values, and warfare skills across generations.

chunkHighlights.text: The appearance of Matariki ‘was marked by feasting and by what the Maori term “Nga mahi a te rehia” – the arts of pleasure, such as dancing, singing, the playing of many forms of games, and contests of many kinds.’ 5

chunkHighlights.text: Matariki atua ka eke mai i te rangi e roa,
E whāngainga iho ki te mata o te tau e roa e.
Divine Matariki come forth from the far-off heaven,
Bestow the first fruits of the year upon us.
Matariki was also a time for planning for the year ahead. If the stars were clear and bright, it signalled a favourable and productive season
ahead, and planting would begin in September. If the stars appeared hazy and closely bunched together, a cold winter was in store and planting was put off until October.
Modern Matariki

Matariki celebrations were popular before the arrival of Europeans in
New Zealand, and they continued into the 1900s. Gradually they dwindled, with the last elaborate traditional festivals recorded in the 1940s, although some iwi retained regional knowledge. Some new Māori faiths, such as Ringatū, incorporated aspects of traditional Matariki festivities into new customs. Revival At the beginning of the 21st century Māori began to revive the practice of celebrating Matariki as a time of remembrance, joy and peace. Iwi , hapu and whānau once again came together at Matariki to mourn family members, to share kai, wānanga (have discussions) and whakanui (celebrate) within their local community. Some hold traditional ceremonies at dawn to call out the names of people who have died since the last rising of Matariki, as a form of farewell, and to cook seasonal food. Iwi had a significant role in reviving interest in the celebration in the wider community. When Te Rangi Huata organised the first modern public Ngāti Kahungunu Matariki celebrations in Hastings in 2000, about 500 people joined him. Since then his work has grown, with major events each year in Wairoa, Napier, Hastings, Waipukurau and Masterton. These give thanks for the harvest and pray for a bountiful planting season, bringing the whole community together in doing so. In 2021, between 2,500 and 9,000 people attended Ngāti Kahungunu’s major events. Books by astronomy and mātauranga Māori expert Professor Rangi Matamua (Tūhoe) have helped to reinforce the special place Matariki had for Māori communities in the past, and its connection to Māori understandings of their natural and spiritual world. Events organised by local councils and institutions such as the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa (Te Papa), Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori (Māori Language Commission) and Te Wānanga o Aotearoa have also focused new attention on Matariki. Kapa haka festivals, star observations, fireworks, hangi, and concerts were held around the country. In 2017 the traditional fireworks night in Wellington, previously
held in November to mark Guy Fawkes Day, was shifted to July in order

to celebrate Matariki. The revival of Matariki also played a part in increasing the popularity of the traditional Māori kites (pākau). Hekenukumai Busby, an expert in traditional navigation, said that the ancestors of Māori, including the Polynesians of ancient history, welcomed Matariki by flying kites. Public holiday In 2020, the government announced its intention to establish a public holiday during Matariki that recognised and celebrated te ao Māori (the Māori world), which was celebrated for the first time in 2022. A Matariki Advisory Group was set up to advise ministers on when and how the new public holiday should be celebrated. The date of the Matariki public holiday shifts each year to align with the Māori lunar calendar. It is observed on a Friday, usually in late June or early July. The advisory group’s members were drawn from across the country to ensure that the mātauranga (knowledge) of various iwi was represented.

9.fileDescription: Matariki, the Māori New Year, is celebrated on Friday, June 20, 2025, and serves as an official public holiday since 2022, marking the first holiday recognizing Te Ao Māori. Unlike Easter or Christmas, trading restrictions don't apply, allowing shops and businesses to operate normally or close as they choose. Employees working on Matariki are entitled to time-and-a-half pay and an alternative day off. Hospitality businesses may add a 15% surcharge to cover employee costs, which must be clearly signaled. Matariki is named after a star cluster in Taurus (Pleiades) that rises in mid-winter, traditionally marking the end of harvest. The holiday date changes annually based on the Māori environmental calendar system, falling on the closest Friday to the Tangaroa lunar period during Pipiri month. Future dates through 2052 have been predetermined by the Matariki Advisory Committee.

chunkHighlights.text:
Matariki marks the Māori new year. Matariki celebrates the Māori New
Year and is a time for people to gather, honour the dead, celebrate the present and make plans for the future. This year, the public holiday falls on Friday 20 June. It became an official public holiday only in 2022, but it's already become one of our most meaningful days and the first holiday to recognise Te Ao Māori. It was the first new public holiday since Waitangi Day became a public holiday in 1974. The date of Matariki changes from year to year, but it will always fall in June or July. There will be plenty of Matariki events throughout Friday and the weekend, and RNZ will be featuring coverage throughout. Do I have to work? It's a non-working day just like any other public holiday - which means if you are asked to work on the day (as regularly rostered), you're entitled to time-and-a-half pay and an alternative day off. What's open? Trading restrictions don't apply to Matariki in the way they do on Easter holidays, Christmas or the first half of Anzac Day. Shops, restaurants, cafes and other businesses can be open as usual, but they can close if they wish - so it pays to check opening hours beforehand. Will there be surcharges? Hospitality businesses can add a 15 percent surcharge to their services to cover the costs of paying employees time-and-a-half. If a business does charge a surcharge, they must have clear signage communicating this to the customer. Customers can complain to the Commerce Commission if they feel they have been misled about surcharges. What is Matariki all about? Matariki is the name of a star cluster in the constellation of Taurus, commonly known as Pleiades. In mid-winter, the stars rise and herald in Te Mātahi o te Tau, the Māori New Year. The word 'Matariki' is an abbreviation of 'Ngā mata o te ariki o Tāwhirimātea' or 'the eyes of the god Tāwhirimātea'. Matariki was taken as a wife by Rehua and she gave birth to eight children, each star having a unique purpose and defined role in Te Ao Māori. Traditionally falling at the end of the harvest, the cluster's rise marked a time of abundant food and feasting. Today, people across Aotearoa gather to celebrate the day with plenty of kai, stargazing, and community gathering. Why does the

holiday date change each year? Matariki public holiday is observed on different dates each year. This is because Māori follow an environmental calendar system that considers the sun, the moon, various stars, and other ecological indicators to determine time. The Matariki public holiday dates fall on the closest Friday to the Tangaroa lunar period during the lunar month of Pipiri. Tangaroa is not a single phase of the moon but rather the last quarter period of the lunar calendar. Because of this, the dates to celebrate Matariki will differ from year to year. 10.fileDescription: Auckland will host the national Matariki ceremony for 2026 at Takaparawhau on July 10, hosted by Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei. The celebration will feature the theme "Matariki herenga waka - For Everyone," reflecting Auckland's role as a global city and the phrase "Tāmaki, a place where people moor their canoes." Professor Rangi Mātāmua, chief Matariki advisor, expects this to be the largest celebration yet, emphasizing themes of reflecting on the past, celebrating the present, and looking to the future. The event will be broadcast nationwide and include infrastructure improvements and technology like big screens. Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei aims to reconnect attendees with the taiao (environment) and traditional rituals, while Minister Paul Goldsmith noted growing international interest in New Zealand's Matariki traditions.

chunkHighlights.text: Matariki 2026 will be held at Takaparawhau in Auckland, hosted by Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei

ByTnatanahira - Māori news journalist
2025-12-08 10:26:40+13:00

Steam from the umu at Takaparawhau rises upward towards the stars,
as Kai is lifted from the ground during Matariki 2024. Tāmaki Makaurau, Auckland, is set to host the national Matariki ceremony for 2026. The hautapu ā-motu will be held at Takaparawhau on July 10 and hosted by mana whenua Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei. They are no strangers to holding hautapu, having previously hosted four of the largest Matariki gatherings in the country. The site at Takaparau will give attendees a pristine view of Auckland Harbour and the many islands and coastlines dotted through it. The celebration will be broadcast across Aotearoa New Zealand with a distinct theme - "Matariki herenga waka - For Everyone". Professor Rangi Mātāmua at the site set for the 2026 Matariki ceremony, Takaparawhau. Speaking to RNZ at the planned hautapu site, Professor Rangi Mātāmua - one of the architects of the Matariki public holiday and chief Matariki advisor - said the theme reflected Auckland's role as a global city. "If you consider the makeup of the region that Ngāti Whātua encompass, and the Tāmaki region, it is a home for people from across the globe, it's the biggest Polynesian community, in the world and it also has people here from across the globe, from all different ethnicities and cultures and backgrounds." "The phrase 'Tāmaki Herenga Waka' means, 'Tāmaki, a place where people moor their canoes'. We've taken that and massaged it a little bit to be' Matariki herenga waka'." he said. Mātāmua said the 2026 celebration would likely be the largest so far. "There's not really a template for doing something like this - establishing a national holiday - and I think it has been very successful because of the themes." "It's about reflecting on the past, celebrating the present, looking to the future but it's underpinned by sharing, being aware of the environment, celebrating who we are and the things that we value." Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei kaikōrero Kīngi Makoare. Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei kaikōrero Kīngi Makoare told RNZ the format his people use to host hautapu had proven
to be a success. "We're doing some infrastructure work at the moment

on the ground to make sure it's stable as possible through those winter
months so that we're able to host, utilising other things like technology, big screens." "Bringing our own whānau as well as the wider general public that are actually really excited to know more about Matariki and know how they can celebrate it in public and in their own homes is really, really exciting for us." he said. Makoare said Matariki served as an opportunity for his people to reconnect with the taiao, or environment - something that can be difficult in the country's largest city. "We have a kōrero here, 'Tāmaki Makaurau kainga ngā ika me ngā wheua katoa' essentially talking about the abundance that once was here in Tāmaki." "With the ongoing intensification and urbanization of Tāmaki Makaurau, that level of abundance has decreased dramatically." "Unfortunately, my generation doesn't know what that abundance looks like. The real focus [is] the reconnection with the taiao, reconnection with ourselves and reconnection with some of those rituals and ceremonies that have been handed down from our tūpuna." Makoare said. Speaking at the announcement this evening, Minister for Culture and Heritage Paul Goldsmith said more New Zealander were engaging with, and enjoying, Matariki ceremonies across the country. "That task of rebuilding, re-finding, understanding and reimagining in a modern world, an ancient tradition, I think that's been very interesting. "Also becoming more and more clear is that linked with the stars, there are many cultures that celebrate this passage of time in different ways and so I think that's becoming an interesting element to it, that more and more people from around the world have seen what we're doing here and become quite interested in it." he said. 11.fileDescription: Matariki is the Māori name for the Pleiades star cluster, marking the Māori New Year when it rises in midwinter. Derived from 'Ngā Mata o te Ariki Tāwhirimātea' (The eyes of the god Tāwhirimātea), it heralds seasonal changes and traditionally served as a time to acknowledge the dead, reflect, give thanks for harvests, and share bounty with family. Tohunga kōkōrangi (astronomy experts) observed the stars to predict weather and harvests. The Matariki period involved three key practices: remembering the deceased through ceremonies like 'whāngai i te hautapu' (feeding the stars), celebrating with feasting and dancing, and planning for the year ahead. The nine stars each hold significance: Matariki (well-being), Waitī (fresh water), Waitā (ocean), Tupuānuku (ground food), Tupuārangi (sky food), Waipunarangi (rain), Ururangi (winds), Pōhutukawa (the deceased), and Hiwa-i-te-rangi (dreams). Celebrations declined after European arrival but were revived in the 2000s, with the first modern public celebrations beginning in 2000. Since 2022, Matariki became an official public holiday observed on a Friday in late June or July. Different iwi celebrate at different times and recognize varying numbers of stars. Puanga (Rigel) serves as an alternative new year marker for western North Island iwi.

chunkHighlights.text: Matariki has given rise to a number of whakataukī (proverbs). ‘Matariki kāinga kore’ (homeless Matariki) refers to the star cluster’s constant travel – disappearing from the sky only once a year, when it pauses to rest in May when the moon wanes. The association of Matariki with crops has given rise to the saying: ‘Matariki ahunga nui’ (Matariki provider of plentiful food). Because it appears in the season when game has been caught and preserved, there is the saying: ‘Ka kitea a Matariki, kua maoka te hinu’ (When Matariki is seen, then game is preserved).

retrieved_chunks.text: The story of the Matariki constellation is the lesser-known continuation of the Māori creation myth, after Tāne pushed Ranginui and Papatūānuku apart to bring light into the world. Tāwhirimātea, god of the wind and weather, wanted his parents to stay together. He sought utu for their separation, attacking his siblings, the other atua, one by one. His stormy rage defeated them all, until he reached Tūmatauenga, the god of humanity and war. The devastation of this defeat led Tāwhirimātea to gouge out, crush, then fling his eyes at his father’s chest, their gleam forming the Matariki constellation.

Waitā: the star linked with the ocean and food that comes from it. Tupuānuku: the star linked with food that grows in the ground. Tupuārangi: the star linked with food that comes from the skies: fruits, berries, and birds. Waipunarangi: the star linked with the rain. Ururangi: the star that determines the winds for the year. Matariki and Puanga Matariki outside New Zealand The Matariki cluster is of great significance for spiritual, environmental and cultural reasons throughout the Pacific. Many Pacific people use its progress across the skies to track passing time and changing seasons. It is known as Matariki in Cook Islands; as Mataliki in Tokelau, Niue, Tuvalu, Tonga, ‘Uvea and Futuna; as Matali’i in Samoa; as Matari’i in Tahiti; and as Makali’i in Hawai’i. [Page 5] Matariki sets in the western sky during the lunar month of Haratua (mid May to early June). This is a tohu (sign) that the harvest season has come to an end. By this time, people should have completed their preparations for the cold months ahead. Matariki reappears in the skies in the lunar month of Te Tahi o Pipiri (late June or early July). For many iwi the return of the stars marks the beginning of the Māori New Year. The correct time for celebrations of the new year is determined by the position of both the stars and the moon. Therefore, although the stars may be visible in the sky, Matariki festivities should not commence until Tangaroa, the last quarter moon of the first month of the Māori year. This time usually comes a few days after the first rising of Matariki above the horizon.

Tāwhirimātea, god of the wind and weather, wanted his parents to stay together. He sought utu for their separation, attacking his siblings, the other atua, one by one. His stormy rage defeated them all, until he reached Tūmatauenga, the god of humanity and war. [Page 1] Record numbers have attended Matariki events since it became a national holiday, according to festival organisers. Auckland Council Matariki Festival lead Melz Huata Lucas (Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Tūwharetoa, Kāi Tahu, Ngāi Tahu) said the festival had grown as public awareness had increased. Matariki became an official public holiday in 2021, fulfilling a pre election promise made by the then Labour government. Huata Lucas estimated more than 200,000 people had attended Matariki events in the city centre alone each year since. "It is continuing to grow and definitely being noticed by staff on the ground." Bay of Plenty Matariki Festival organiser Jackie Sanders said she was expecting the largest turnout yet for the event and had had to add more dates for sold out events. She said more than 10,000 people attended the festival's events throughout the region in 2023. On Saturday, a pre dawn ceremony on Pukekohekohe Hill marked the start of Auckland's Matariki Festival. Ngāti Tamaoho, which is the festival's iwi partner for the next three years, led a karakia and pōwhiri at Ngā Hau e Whā Marae. Huata Lucas said more people were starting to get excited about Matariki and understand what it was about. "Māori have always celebrated Matariki as the start to the new year. It is a time to reflect on the year that has gone by and the people who have passed." She said people were also learning about Matariki from their children. "In schools, they are learning about what the stars represent and they can bring that home to their families." Huata Lucas said organisers had been able to expand the Auckland festival to more than 90 Matariki events taking place across the city, many of which are free. She encouraged people to check what events were happening in their area and establish traditions with their families. ## Ko wai te Pirimia o Aotearoa? | Who is the Prime Minister of New Zealand?

Ko **Christopher Luxon** te Pirimia o Aotearoa i tēnei wā — Christopher Luxon is the current prime minister of New Zealand, leading the National Party-led coalition government. [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1)

The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government, with key responsibilities including appointing ministers, leading cabinet meetings, acting as spokesperson for the government, and providing advice to the governor-general — who represents King Charles III as head of state. [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1)

Luxon has consistently led the preferred prime minister polls, though his position has been contested by Labour leader Chris Hipkins in more recent polling. [[5]](cite://5/1)

## He aha ngā mahi a te Pirimia? | What does the Prime Minister do?

The role has evolved significantly over time. Since 1906, every leader of New Zealand has been formally sworn in as prime minister — a title reserved for self-governing dominions. [[6]](cite://6/1) From 1996, prime ministers have typically led coalition or minority governments under the Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) electoral system, requiring them to manage governments made up of several parties with differing values. [[3]](cite://3/2)

He pātai anō — would you like to know more about the history of New Zealand's prime ministers and how the role has changed over time?

1.document_title: Premiers and Prime Ministers of New Zealand: Leadership Evolution, Political Systems, and Historical Development
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's political leadership from 1856 to 2023. It explains how the prime minister's role evolved from "colonial secretary" to "premier" and finally "prime minister" (formally adopted in 1906). Early leadership was unstable with 24 ministries between 1856-1891, but the Liberal Federation's 1891-1912 tenure marked the rise of organized political parties. The document examines how technological advances—from train travel and aviation to radio (1920s), television (1960), and the internet—reshaped the prime minister's role as government spokesperson. It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

2.text:
[Page 1] Premiers and prime ministers The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government. His or her main responsibilities are: appointing ministers and leading meetings of cabinet acting as the spokesperson for the government, within and outside of Parliament providing advice to the sovereign (the head of state) or the sovereign’s representative in New Zealand (the governor general). Leaders in the 19th century New Zealand was granted internal self government by Britain in 1856. Initially the leader of the country was known as the colonial secretary or premier, but in the early 20th century the term ‘prime minister’ was formally adopted. New Zealand’s leadership changed frequently in the first 40 years of self government. Different leaders each had their own ideas about what were the most important issues for a new nation. Members of Parliament in New Zealand did not belong to political parties at this time. The rise of the party The first political party to govern in New Zealand was the Liberal Federation, which held power from 1891 to 1912. The prime minister became the leader and public face of the governing party, and his public image became increasingly important. Modern leadership Changing technologies in the 20th century also influenced the prime minister’s role as a spokesperson for the government. Radio broadcasting, followed by television and later the internet connected prime ministers to the voting public. They had to become experts at communicating in the media. From 1996 prime ministers usually led coalition or minority governments under the mixed member proportional (MMP) electoral system. This meant prime ministers had to lead governments made up of several political parties with differing values. Lasting legacies? In the early 2000s there were four statues of former premiers and prime ministers in Wellington. Geographical features such as glaciers, mountains and rivers, and small towns, have also been named after leaders. The role of prime minister The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government.

4.document_title: New Zealand's Constitution: Comprehensive Overview of Sources, Conventions, and Democratic Framework
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's unique constitutional structure comprising multiple laws, court judgments, government documents, and conventions rather than a single written document. It covers foundational concepts including the landmark case Fitzgerald v Muldoon (1976), which established that the Prime Minister cannot suspend laws. Key sources include UK statutes (Magna Carta, Bill of Rights Act 1689), NZ Parliament statutes (Constitution Act 1986, Electoral Act 1993), and constitutional conventions governing ministerial responsibility and caretaker protocols. The document details the executive, legislative, and independent judiciary structures with separation of powers. It examines New Zealand's constitutional evolution around two pillars: the Treaty of Waitangi (1840)—an agreement between the British Crown and Māori chiefs—and representative democracy, with voting rights extended to all adult males (1879) and women (1893). The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) reinterpreted the Treaty's meaning in the late 20th century. Mixed-member proportional representation (1996) fundamentally altered constitutional dynamics. The document traces executive power evolution from the 1930s-1990s, describing how reforms including the Official Information Act 1982 and Bill of Rights Act 1990 limited executive authority. New Zealand's constitution is notably flexible, changing through statute amendments and convention shifts, with citizens protected through complaint mechanisms including ombudsmen and human rights commissions. Parliament maintains supremacy stronger than other Westminster democracies.

5.text:
[Page 3] Until 1 January 1951 New Zealand had an upper house, the Legislative Council. Premiers and prime ministers were usually from the House of Representatives (the lower house), but they governed from the council on five occasions: Frederick Whitaker (1863 64 and 1882 83), George Waterhouse (1872 73), Daniel Pollen (1875 76) and Sir Francis Henry Dillon Bell (1925). As legislative councillors were political appointees on life or seven year terms, these were the only unelected politicians to lead the country.

7.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of New Zealand's political system, constitutional development, and national identity. It covers New Zealand's parliamentary democracy structure with a mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system where citizens aged 18+ vote for both political parties and local MPs every three years. The document details the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), the founding document between British representatives and Māori chiefs, which established British authority while promising Māori land rights and cultural preservation, though it notes significant translation discrepancies between English and Māori versions. New Zealand's evolution from a British colony to an independent nation is traced through the establishment of self-government in 1856, adoption of the Statute of Westminster in 1947, and the Constitution Act of 1986. The parliamentary structure comprises 120 seats (65 general, 7 Māori, 48 party list), with the cabinet as the most powerful political body. The document covers state sector governance including 38 departments/ministries, Crown entities, and state-owned enterprises. The Waitangi Tribunal, created in 1975, addresses Māori grievances. 8.text:
[Page 1] New Zealand’s system of government New Zealand is a parliamentary democracy. The prime minister is the head of New Zealand’s government, which must have the support of the majority of members of Parliament. The country’s laws are made by Parliament, which is based on the British Westminster system. New Zealanders aged 18 and over can vote for members of Parliament (MPs). Elections are held every three years. Under the mixed member proportional system (MMP), New Zealanders cast two votes one for a political party, and one for a local MP. The number of seats each party gains in Parliament is decided by how much of the total party vote the party gets. New Zealand is fully independent, but it is also a constitutional monarchy: the head of state is King Charles III. He is represented in New Zealand by the governor general, who traditionally does what the government advises him or her to do. The Treaty of Waitangi The Treaty of Waitangi is the founding document of modern New Zealand. It is named after the place in the Bay of Islands where it was first signed on 6 February 1840. It was signed by William Hobson and other people representing the British Crown (Queen Victoria), and a large number of Māori chiefs. The chiefs agreed that the British should have some authority in New Zealand, and that European people could settle there. They understood that in turn they would keep their own lands and customs, and that the authority of the chiefs would remain. Promises made to Māori in the treaty were not always kept, and there is debate about what it means. The Waitangi Tribunal deals with claims from Māori tribes about their land and other issues to do with the treaty. Independence and nationhood Thousands of settlers, mostly from England, Scotland and Ireland, began to arrive in New Zealand in the 1840s, and they set up their own government in the 1850s. Over the next 150 years the country became less dependent on the British government. But there are still many signs of the historic link with Britain for example, the monarch’s head appears on New Zealand coins. New Zealand is a small independent country which plays an active role in the United Nations and the Commonwealth. It is a distinctive nation, with its own traditions and ways of life. It has its own flag, coat of arms, national anthem and national holidays. The origins of nationhood

8.document_title: New Zealand: Government, Constitutional System, and National Identity
8.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of New Zealand's political system, constitutional development, and national identity. It covers New Zealand's parliamentary democracy structure with a mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system where citizens aged 18+ vote for both political parties and local MPs every three years. The document details the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), the founding document between British representatives and Māori chiefs, which established British authority while promising Māori land rights and cultural preservation, though it notes significant translation discrepancies between English and Māori versions. New Zealand's evolution from a British colony to an independent nation is traced through the establishment of self-government in 1856, adoption of the Statute of Westminster in 1947, and the Constitution Act of 1986. The parliamentary structure comprises 120 seats (65 general, 7 Māori, 48 party list), with the cabinet as the most powerful political body. The document covers state sector governance including 38 departments/ministries, Crown entities, and state-owned enterprises. New Zealand's legal system hierarchy includes District Courts, High Court, Court of Appeal, and Supreme Court, with local government comprising 61 territorial councils and 11 regional councils. The Waitangi Tribunal, created in 1975, addresses Māori grievances. National identity elements include citizenship laws (1948), national symbols (kiwi bird, silver fern, pōhutukawa), and official languages (Māori since 1987, sign language since 2006). The document concludes with New Zealand's international relations, including ANZUS alliance with the United States, close ties with Australia, constitutional relationships with Pacific territories, and participation in the UN, Commonwealth, WTO, APEC, and CPTPP.

9.text:
[Page 12] In the early 21st century New Zealand led the world in terms of women holding leading political positions. There have been three women prime ministers: Jenny Shipley (1997 99), who led the National Party from 1997 to 2001; Helen Clark (1999 2008), the first woman to become prime minister following an election, who was leader of the Labour Party from 1993 to 2008; and Jacinda Ardern (2017 23}, who became leader of the Labour Party in August 2017 and prime minister less than three months later. In 2023 both Te Pāti Māori and the Green Party had Māori women, Debbie Ngarewa Packer and Marama Davidson respectively, as co leaders.

9.document_title: Women's Rights and Equality in New Zealand: A Comprehensive Historical Analysis from the 19th to 21st Century
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of women's rights and equality in New Zealand from the 19th century to the early 21st century across multiple domains. It examines how colonisation undermined Māori women's traditional power and how European settlers' gender ideologies shaped laws, property rights, education, and employment. Key legal milestones include the Married Women's Property Act (1884), women's suffrage in 1893 (first country globally), equal pay legislation (1960-1972), marital rape criminalization (1985), and the Human Rights Commission Act (1977). The document documents two major waves of feminist activism: the 1880s-1890s suffrage movement and the 1970s-1980s women's liberation movement. Progress is evident in women's increased parliamentary representation (60 of 120 MPs by 2022), three female prime ministers, and expanded access to education and employment. Women now comprise 61% of tertiary students and achieved academic parity with boys. However, persistent inequalities remain, including wage gaps (12% in 2016), underrepresentation in STEM fields and leadership roles, occupational segregation, and high rates of intimate partner violence. The document also examines women's roles in the arts, sports, religion, and cultural participation, highlighting both barriers overcome and ongoing disparities.

10.text:
[Page 7] Religion was politically divisive in the early 1900s when Sir Joseph Ward (a Catholic) and William Massey (Protestant) led the major parties, Liberal and Reform. Generally, though, it seldom raised political ripples in New Zealand. Because the Anglican Church is not an established (that is, official state) church in New Zealand, Frederick Weld, a Catholic, could become premier in 1864. Julius Vogel, who was Jewish, became premier in 1873. By contrast, in 2017 Britain had still not had a Catholic or Jewish prime minister. Non belief was also not a bar to office in New Zealand; colonial premiers Alfred Domett, Robert Stout and John Ballance were freethinkers.

10.document_title: Premiers and Prime Ministers of New Zealand: Leadership Evolution, Political Systems, and Historical Development
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's political leadership from 1856 to 2023. It explains how the prime minister's role evolved from "colonial secretary" to "premier" and finally "prime minister" (formally adopted in 1906). Early leadership was unstable with 24 ministries between 1856-1891, but the Liberal Federation's 1891-1912 tenure marked the rise of organized political parties. The document examines how technological advances—from train travel and aviation to radio (1920s), television (1960), and the internet—reshaped the prime minister's role as government spokesperson. It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

27.document_title: 'The prime minister is dying': 50 years since Norman Kirk's last public appearance
27.document_summary: This article commemorates the 50th anniversary of Norman Kirk's final public appearance on August 18, 1974, at St Peter's College in Palmerston North, New Zealand. Despite severe illness—including an enlarged heart, blood clot in his lungs, and liver problems—Kirk insisted on attending the school opening ceremony for his friend Joe Walding. His wife Ruth confided to the school's board chair that "the prime minister is dying." Kirk died 13 days later on August 31, 1974, aged 51, making him the first New Zealand prime minister to die in office since 1940. During his two-year tenure, Kirk's government recognized China, protested French nuclear testing, refused entry to a racially selected Springbok rugby team, and introduced a retirement savings scheme. The article features insights from his private secretary Margaret Hayward and reflects on how Kirk's death prompted massive public grief followed by rapid public amnesia as successor Bill Rowling took office.

29.document_title: How the Sound and Voices of Politics Have Changed from 1912 to 1990
29.document_summary: This article explores the evolution of political communication in New Zealand through audio recordings of fourteen Prime Ministers and a Speaker spanning from 1912 to 1990. The piece highlights how political speech, accents, tones, and presentation styles have transformed over nearly eight decades. Early leaders like William Massey and George Forbes employed formal, gentler speech patterns, while later politicians such as Rob Muldoon and David Lange adopted more modern, recognizably "Kiwi" accents and contemporary communication styles. The article notes that many early politicians were immigrants with strong accents, and that political communication has shifted from formal Empire-praising rhetoric to more direct, populist approaches. The audio compilation, curated with assistance from RNZ's audio historians, provides comparative insights into how New Zealand's political voices have evolved, reflecting broader changes in political culture and public communication.

Sir Don McKinnon has made a statement following Bolger's death. The document reports on this significant event in New Zealand's political history, capturing the tribute and reflections on Bolger's substantial contributions to New Zealand politics and governance.

1.fileDescription: The latest Taxpayers Union Curia poll shows New Zealand's coalition government retaining majority control with 63 seats despite Labour's recovery. National leads at 34.6% (42 seats), followed by Labour at 33.2% (41 seats), with smaller parties ACT (9.5%), Greens (9.1%), and NZ First (7.4%) completing the coalition. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's preferred PM rating improved to 24.5%, outpacing Labour's Chris Hipkins at 20%. However, public sentiment deteriorated significantly, with 46% believing the country is headed in the wrong direction versus 33.3% positive, representing a 10.3-point drop. The poll surveyed 1,000 eligible voters between April 30 and May 2, 2025, with a 3.1% margin of error.

chunkHighlights.text: National's Christopher Luxon has continued a steady recovery as preferred prime minister over Labour's Chris Hipkins. Labour has regained support lost the previous month in the latest Taxpayers Union Curia poll, with smaller gains for National. Those positions are reversed on the preferred prime minister stakes, with National's Christopher Luxon's recovery outpacing that of Labour's Chris Hipkins, while New Zealand First's Winston Peters has taken a tumble. The major parties' gains also came the expense of the others, with the exception of New Zealand First which held steady. Despite a four-seat improvement for Labour on the last survey in April bringing it just one seat shy of National, the coalition would, on these numbers, retain a majority with 63 seats to the opposition parties' 58. The key right-track-wrong-track metric will be disappointing for the governing parties, however, with New Zealanders' pessimism about the government's direction leading to a 10-point drop. fileAuthor: Gavin McLean, Manatū Taonga (Ministry for Culture and Heritage)
3.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's political leadership from 1856 to 2023. It explains how the prime minister's role evolved from "colonial secretary" to "premier" and finally "prime minister" (formally adopted in 1906). Early leadership was unstable with 24 ministries between 1856-1891, but the Liberal Federation's 1891-1912 tenure marked the rise of organized political parties. The document examines how technological advances—from train travel and aviation to radio (1920s), television (1960), and the internet—reshaped the prime minister's role as government spokesperson. It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

chunkHighlights.text: Premiers and prime ministers

The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among
those forming the government. His or her main responsibilities are: appointing ministers and leading meetings of cabinet acting as the spokesperson for the government, within and outside of Parliament providing advice to the sovereign (the head of state) or the sovereign’s representative in New Zealand (the governor-general). Leaders in the 19th century New Zealand was granted internal self-government by Britain in 1856. Initially the leader of the country was known as the colonial secretary or premier, but in the early 20th century the term ‘prime minister’ was formally adopted. New Zealand’s leadership changed frequently in the first 40 years of self-government. Different leaders each had their own ideas about what were the most important issues for a new nation. Members of Parliament in New Zealand did not belong to political parties at this time. The rise of the party The first political party to govern in New Zealand was the Liberal Federation, which held power from 1891 to 1912. The prime minister became the leader and public face of the governing party, and his public image became increasingly important. Modern leadership Changing technologies in the 20th century also influenced the prime minister’s role as a spokesperson for the government. Radio broadcasting, followed by television and later the internet connected prime ministers to the voting public. They had to become experts at communicating in the media. From 1996 prime ministers usually led coalition or minority governments under the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system. This meant prime ministers had to lead governments made up of several political parties with differing values. Lasting legacies? In the early 2000s there were four statues of former premiers and prime ministers in Wellington. Geographical features such as glaciers,
mountains and rivers, and small towns, have also been named after
leaders.
The role of prime minister
The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government.

4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of New Zealand's political system, constitutional development, and national identity. It covers New Zealand's parliamentary democracy structure with a mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system where citizens aged 18+ vote for both political parties and local MPs every three years. The document details the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), the founding document between British representatives and Māori chiefs, which established British authority while promising Māori land rights and cultural preservation, though it notes significant translation discrepancies between English and Māori versions. New Zealand's evolution from a British colony to an independent nation is traced through the establishment of self-government in 1856, adoption of the Statute of Westminster in 1947, and the Constitution Act of 1986. The parliamentary structure comprises 120 seats (65 general, 7 Māori, 48 party list), with the cabinet as the most powerful political body. The document covers state sector governance including 38 departments/ministries, Crown entities, and state-owned enterprises. New Zealand's legal system hierarchy includes District Courts, High Court, Court of Appeal, and Supreme Court, with local government comprising 61 territorial councils and 11 regional councils. The Waitangi Tribunal, created in 1975, addresses Māori grievances. National identity elements include citizenship laws (1948), national symbols (kiwi bird, silver fern, pōhutukawa), and official languages (Māori since 1987, sign language since 2006). The document concludes with New Zealand's international relations, including ANZUS alliance with the United States, close ties with Australia, constitutional relationships with Pacific territories, and participation in the UN, Commonwealth, WTO, APEC, and CPTPP.

chunkHighlights.text:
New Zealand’s system of government New Zealand is a parliamentary
democracy. The prime minister is the head of New Zealand’s government, which must have the support of the majority of members of Parliament. The country’s laws are made by Parliament, which is based on the British Westminster system. New Zealanders aged 18 and over can vote for members of Parliament (MPs). Elections are held every three years. Under the mixed-member proportional system (MMP), New Zealanders cast two votes – one for a political party, and one for a local MP. The number of seats each party gains in Parliament is decided by how much of the total party vote the party gets. New Zealand is fully independent, but it is also a constitutional monarchy: the head of state is King Charles III. He is represented in New Zealand by the governor-general, who traditionally does what the government advises him or her to do. The Treaty of Waitangi The Treaty of Waitangi is the founding document of modern New Zealand. It is named after the place in the Bay of Islands where it was first signed on 6 February 1840. It was signed by William Hobson and other people representing the British Crown (Queen Victoria), and a large number of Māori chiefs. The chiefs agreed that the British should have some authority in New Zealand, and that European people could settle there. They understood that in turn they would keep their own lands and customs, and that the authority of the chiefs would remain. Promises made to Māori in the treaty were not always kept, and there is debate about what it means. The Waitangi Tribunal deals with claims from Māori tribes about their land and other issues to do with the treaty. Independence and nationhood Thousands of settlers, mostly from England, Scotland and Ireland, began to arrive in New Zealand in the 1840s, and they set up their own government in the 1850s. Over the next 150 years the country became less dependent on the British government. But there are still many signs of the historic link with Britain – for example, the monarch’s head appears on New Zealand coins. New Zealand is a small independent country which plays an active
role in the United Nations and the Commonwealth. It is a distinctive
nation, with its own traditions and ways of life. It has its own flag, coat of
arms, national anthem and national holidays.

5.fileName: Labour has eight-point lead over National in latest poll.pdf
5.filePath: pdf/Labour has eight-point lead over National in latest poll.pdf
5.fileDescription: According to the latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll, Labour leads National by eight percentage points with 38% support compared to National's 30%. Labour leader Chris Hipkins is the preferred prime minister at 45%, ahead of Christopher Luxon at 39%. Labour's coalition partners (Greens at 8% and Te Pāti Māori at 2%) could potentially form a government with Labour, achieving a bare majority of 61 seats. National's coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First poll at 8% and 9% respectively. Neither the current coalition nor opposition has clear governing numbers.

chunkHighlights.text:
Labour leads National by eight points in latest poll Labour leader Chris Hipkins is preferred prime minister on 45 percent, while Christopher Luxon is at 39 percent, according to the latest poll. Labour has an eight-point lead over National in the latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll, but neither the coalition nor the opposition parties have the numbers to govern. Labour has 38 percent support in the poll, up four points since the last survey in October, compared to National on 30 percent, down one point. National's coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First are on 8 and 9 percent respectively. The Greens are registering 8 percent - down one - with Te Pāti Māori on two percent - also down one. On this result, Labour could potentially form a government with the support of the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, assuming Te Pāti Māori wins one electorate. They would have 61 seats between them - the barest majority. Labour leader Chris Hipkins is still the preferred prime minister on 45 percent, while Christopher Luxon is at 39 percent, although Luxon has gained 3 points since the last The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll in October. There have been three women prime ministers: Jenny Shipley (1997 99), who led the National Party from 1997 to 2001; Helen Clark (1999 2008), the first woman to become prime minister following an election, who was leader of the Labour Party from 1993 to 2008; and Jacinda Ardern (2017 23}, who became leader of the Labour Party in August 2017 and prime minister less than three months later. [Page 7] Religion was politically divisive in the early 1900s when Sir Joseph Ward (a Catholic) and William Massey (Protestant) led the major parties, Liberal and Reform. Generally, though, it seldom raised political ripples in New Zealand. Because the Anglican Church is not an established (that is, official state) church in New Zealand, Frederick Weld, a Catholic, could become premier in 1864. Julius Vogel, who was Jewish, became premier in 1873. By contrast, in 2017 Britain had still not had a Catholic or Jewish prime minister. Non belief was also not a bar to office in New Zealand; colonial premiers Alfred Domett, Robert Stout and John Ballance were freethinkers.

retrieved_chunks.text: This black-and-white portrait depicts an elderly Māori man wearing traditional attire, including a feathered headdress and a white sash. He holds a pipe in his mouth, a common practice among Māori people. The photograph bears the name stamp of photographer Alfred Burton, who acquired a collection of negatives from the original photographer, McGarrigle. McGarrigle’s Māori portraits often resemble contemporary photographs of Native Americans, though there is no evidence he visited the U.S. Photographers of that era commonly used a wardrobe of clothes and accessories for their subjects. Despite occasional deviations from historical accuracy, McGarrigle’s images never appear forced or imposed.

retrieved_chunks.text: The Royal Society of New Zealand Portrait Gallery commissioned expatriate New Zealand artist Juliet Kac to produce a portrait of Wilkins in commemoration of the 50th anniversary of the discovery of the structure of DNA. [Page 2] In 2023, 41 prime ministers had led New Zealand since the country was granted internal self government by Britain in 1856. However, not all used the title of ‘prime minister’. Early on ‘colonial secretary’ was used. From the 1860s ‘premier’ grew more common, alternating informally with ‘prime minister’ by the century’s end. Since 1906 every leader has been sworn in as prime minister. This title is reserved for self governing dominions, whereas Crown colonies and state governments have premiers.

1.document_title: Premiers and Prime Ministers of New Zealand: Leadership Evolution, Political Systems, and Historical Development
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's political leadership from 1856 to 2023. It explains how the prime minister's role evolved from "colonial secretary" to "premier" and finally "prime minister" (formally adopted in 1906). Early leadership was unstable with 24 ministries between 1856-1891, but the Liberal Federation's 1891-1912 tenure marked the rise of organized political parties. The document examines how technological advances—from train travel and aviation to radio (1920s), television (1960), and the internet—reshaped the prime minister's role as government spokesperson. It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

2.text:
[Page 1] Premiers and prime ministers The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government. His or her main responsibilities are: appointing ministers and leading meetings of cabinet acting as the spokesperson for the government, within and outside of Parliament providing advice to the sovereign (the head of state) or the sovereign’s representative in New Zealand (the governor general). Leaders in the 19th century New Zealand was granted internal self government by Britain in 1856. Initially the leader of the country was known as the colonial secretary or premier, but in the early 20th century the term ‘prime minister’ was formally adopted. New Zealand’s leadership changed frequently in the first 40 years of self government. Different leaders each had their own ideas about what were the most important issues for a new nation. Members of Parliament in New Zealand did not belong to political parties at this time. The rise of the party The first political party to govern in New Zealand was the Liberal Federation, which held power from 1891 to 1912. The prime minister became the leader and public face of the governing party, and his public image became increasingly important. Modern leadership Changing technologies in the 20th century also influenced the prime minister’s role as a spokesperson for the government. Radio broadcasting, followed by television and later the internet connected prime ministers to the voting public. They had to become experts at communicating in the media. From 1996 prime ministers usually led coalition or minority governments under the mixed member proportional (MMP) electoral system. This meant prime ministers had to lead governments made up of several political parties with differing values. Lasting legacies? In the early 2000s there were four statues of former premiers and prime ministers in Wellington. Geographical features such as glaciers, mountains and rivers, and small towns, have also been named after leaders. The role of prime minister The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government.
{}

[Page 3] Until 1 January 1951 New Zealand had an upper house, the Legislative Council. Premiers and prime ministers were usually from the House of Representatives (the lower house), but they governed from the council on five occasions: Frederick Whitaker (1863 64 and 1882 83), George Waterhouse (1872 73), Daniel Pollen (1875 76) and Sir Francis Henry Dillon Bell (1925). As legislative councillors were political appointees on life or seven year terms, these were the only unelected politicians to lead the country.

[Page 5] From 1840 New Zealand’s governors ruled autocratically (with absolute authority), advised by the Executive Council and Legislative Council and answerable to the authorities in London. In 1854, though the new Parliament was still only there to provide advice to the governor, politicians had already asked for self governance in domestic matters, rather than having to defer to Britain. That year, while awaiting the reply from London, the acting governor, Colonel Robert Wynyard, appointed politician James FitzGerald to his Executive Council. Thomas Forsaith succeeded FitzGerald in the role. However, neither the ‘FitzGerald ministry’ nor the ‘Forsaith ministry’ lasted long. Their leaders were not true premiers. New Zealand’s earliest genuine ministries, formed after Parliament became responsible (fully self governing for most internal policy) in 1856, were short lived. The first premier, Henry Sewell, was sworn in on 18 April 1856, but was gone by 20 May. His successor, William Fox, was replaced by Edward Stafford on 2 June. In all there were 24 ministries between 1856 and 1891. To many it is a blur of beards, names and dates, but power was transferred peacefully each time, showing that the fledgling democracy worked.
{}

[Page 7] The 1890 election introduced government by party for the first time, when new premier John Ballance established the Liberal Federation. Ballance died in 1893 and was succeeded by Richard Seddon (sometimes known as ‘King Dick’), who effortlessly dominated New Zealand politics for the next 13 years. There was little real parliamentary opposition until 1909, when William Massey welded together the Reform Party. Thereafter political power centred on parties and their leaders. Personality became increasingly important for political success. The charismatic Gordon Coates ensured victory for Reform in 1925, and Labour’s Michael Joseph Savage, with his genial, fatherly image, enjoyed mass adulation in the 1930s.

7.document_title: Colonial and Provincial Government in New Zealand: Evolution from 1840 to Modern Regional Administration
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's governmental structure from 1840 through the modern era. It begins with New Zealand's transition from New South Wales to a separate British crown colony in 1840 under appointed governors. The document details the initial provincial divisions and the pivotal 1852 Constitution Act, which established six provinces with elected superintendents and councils exercising significant autonomy over land sales revenue and customs duties. It covers the New Provinces Act 1858, the impact of the Waikato War (1863) on provincial finances, and centralization efforts including the capital relocation to Wellington in 1865. A critical turning point came in 1876 with the abolition of provincial governments, driven by financial pressures and Colonial Treasurer Julius Vogel's national public works program. The provinces were replaced with counties and road boards, marking a shift toward centralized administration. The document concludes by examining the 20th-century evolution from provinces to regions and the significant restructuring of health administration from hospital boards (1935) through area health boards (1983), crown health enterprises (1992), district health boards (2002), and finally to Te Whatu Ora Health New Zealand and Te Aka Whai Ora Māori Health Authority in 2022.

8.text:
[Page 7] Religion was politically divisive in the early 1900s when Sir Joseph Ward (a Catholic) and William Massey (Protestant) led the major parties, Liberal and Reform. Generally, though, it seldom raised political ripples in New Zealand. Because the Anglican Church is not an established (that is, official state) church in New Zealand, Frederick Weld, a Catholic, could become premier in 1864. Julius Vogel, who was Jewish, became premier in 1873. By contrast, in 2017 Britain had still not had a Catholic or Jewish prime minister. Non belief was also not a bar to office in New Zealand; colonial premiers Alfred Domett, Robert Stout and John Ballance were freethinkers.

[Page 8] Greater independence For a while New Zealand’s prime ministers opposed greater independence from Britain. New Zealand and Australia resisted the structural reforms towards independence pushed by other dominions at the 1926 and 1930 imperial conferences. The 1931 Statute of Westminster confirmed that dominions had exclusive power to make their laws. However, New Zealand did not adopt this statute until 1947, and then only as part of a political manoeuvre to make it constitutionally possible to abolish the Legislative Council. Increasingly, however, New Zealand began to act independently in foreign affairs. During the 1940s the prime minister’s profile rose as the country signed a number of international treaties. Prime Minister Peter Fraser established a New Zealand embassy in the United States and played an important role in setting up the United Nations.

It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

21.document_title: David Russell Lange: Life, Political Career, and Leadership as New Zealand Prime Minister
21.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical document traces David Russell Lange's life from his birth in Ōtāhuhu, Auckland in 1942 through his tenure as New Zealand's youngest 20th-century Prime Minister (1984-1989). Born to a medical practitioner father and Methodist mother, Lange studied law at the University of Auckland and practiced as a criminal defence counsel before joining the Labour Party in 1963. He won a by-election in Māngere in 1977 and became Labour leader in 1983. Following Labour's landslide victory in June 1984, he became Prime Minister at age 41. His government implemented radical economic reforms known as "Rogernomics" under Finance Minister Roger Douglas, including currency devaluation, GST introduction, and privatization of state assets. As Foreign Minister and PM, Lange became the public face of New Zealand's nuclear-free policy, controversially refusing USS Buchanan entry in 1985 and navigating the Rainbow Warrior bombing incident with France. His 1987 re-election increased Labour's majority, and he pursued education reforms emphasizing efficiency and equity. However, internal cabinet conflicts with Roger Douglas over economic reforms, particularly the proposed flat tax in 1988, weakened his position. Despite exceptional oratorical skills and inspirational rhetoric, Lange lacked interest in policy detail and struggled to build factional strength within cabinet. He resigned as party leader in August 1989, ceding power to former allies who had become adversaries. He died in 2005 at age 63 from heart failure.

22.document_title: Edward William Stafford: Colonial Premier of New Zealand - Political Career and Legacy
22.document_summary: Edward William Stafford (1819-1901) was a prominent Anglo-Irish politician who served as New Zealand's colonial premier for approximately nine years across two terms (1856-1861 and 1865-1872). Born in Edinburgh, he emigrated to New Zealand in 1843 and became the first superintendent of Nelson in 1853. Stafford championed responsible government, universal suffrage, and progressive policies including free secular education and public works programs. As premier, he navigated complex constitutional issues, provincial rivalries, and Māori affairs with pragmatic effectiveness. He managed expensive Māori wars (1865-1868), including the Pai Mārire uprising and campaigns by Tītokowaru and Te Kooti, while reducing war expenditure from £886,259 to £327,180 and increasing revenue to £1,058,029 through taxation increases. Stafford established four Māori electorates in 1867, advocated for railway construction, and opposed forced land confiscation. His final ministry (1872) was defeated over public works administration and Māori land return policies. Though personally unpopular due to retrenchment policies, he was recognized as an able administrator who strengthened ministerial representation during New Zealand's formative parliamentary era.

23.document_title: Bill Rowling: Life, Political Career, and Prime Ministerial Legacy in New Zealand
23.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical document traces Wallace Edward "Bill" Rowling's life and political career in New Zealand. Born in Motueka, Nelson in 1927, Rowling came from a politically active Labour family and became a teacher with economics degrees from Canterbury University. He entered Parliament in 1962 representing the Buller electorate and served on agricultural committees. As Labour Party president (1970-1972), he modernized the party organization, contributing to Labour's 1972 election victory. Appointed Finance Minister by Norman Kirk in 1972, Rowling advocated for overseas borrowing and economic stimulus during the oil crisis. Following Kirk's death in August 1974, Rowling became Prime Minister at age 46, the youngest since 1887. As PM, he maintained focus on domestic affairs, supported nuclear-free policies, and defended heavy borrowing to protect employment. After his 1975 election loss to Robert Muldoon, Rowling served six years as opposition leader despite defeats in 1978 and 1981 elections, facing leadership challenges from David Lange and Roger Douglas before stepping down in 1983. He later served as ambassador to the United States (1985-1988) during the ANZUS rift and opposed Lange's neo-liberal reforms. His legacy reflects quiet nationalism and commitment to New Zealand independence, culminating in his role developing Te Papa Tongarewa national museum. He received a knighthood in 1983 and died in 1995.

24.document_title: Francis Henry Dillon Bell: New Zealand Statesman and Lawyer
24.document_summary: Francis Henry Dillon Bell (1851-1936) was a prominent New Zealand lawyer, politician, and statesman. Born in Nelson, he was educated in England at Cambridge and called to the English Bar before returning to Wellington in 1875. Bell became a leading advocate in the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal, serving as Crown solicitor and helping establish law reporting in New Zealand. He was elected mayor of Wellington (1891, 1892, 1896) and served in Parliament from 1893-1896. After retiring from politics, he became recognized as leader of the New Zealand Bar and was appointed King's Counsel in 1907. Under Prime Minister William Massey, Bell held multiple ministerial portfolios and briefly served as Prime Minister in 1925, becoming New Zealand's first native-born PM. He was instrumental in drafting wartime legislation, managing Western Samoa's mandate, and reforming New Zealand's conveyancing system. Bell was appointed KCMG (1915), GCMG (1923), and Privy Counsellor (1926). Regarded as an outstanding lawyer and statesman, he exemplified a "tory radical" approach, balancing conservative principles with progressive social policies.
