25.document_title: George Robert Laking: New Zealand's Twentieth-Century Public Servant, Diplomat, and Law Reform Pioneer
25.document_summary: George Robert Laking (1912-2008) was a prominent New Zealand public servant and diplomat with a 40+ year career spanning government service, diplomacy, and law reform. Born in Auckland, he joined the Customs Department in 1929 and studied law at Victoria University College. During WWII, he worked in the Prime Minister's Department and was instrumental in establishing the Department of External Affairs. His diplomatic career included postings as counsellor in Washington (1949), deputy high commissioner in London (1958), ambassador to the EEC (1960), and ambassador to Washington (1961-1967). As secretary of Foreign Affairs and head of the Prime Minister's Department (1967-1972), he advised Prime Ministers on Cold War foreign policy, Vietnam withdrawal, and China recognition. After his diplomatic career, Laking established a second influential career in government accountability and law reform. As the first privacy commissioner for the Wanganui Computer Centre (1977-78) and later as chief ombudsman (1977-1984), he championed citizens' rights against state intrusion, particularly regarding police accountability and official information access. He significantly expanded the ombudsman's jurisdiction. Laking contributed substantially to law reform through the Public and Administrative Law Reform Committee (1980-85) and the Legislation Advisory Committee (1986-91), notably chairing a working party that modernized New Zealand's alcohol legislation in 1987. He also led the New Zealand Institute of International Affairs (1979-84) and served on the Human Rights Commission (1978-1984). Described as a courteous yet formidable personality with sardonic humor, Laking exemplified impartial public service, exercising significant behind-the-scenes influence on domestic and international policies. He received honors including appointment as a Companion of the Order of St Michael and St George (1969) and promotion to Knight (1985), passing away in Wellington on January 10, 2008, at age 95.

27.document_title: Sidney George Holland: New Zealand Prime Minister - Life, Leadership, and Political Legacy (1893-1961)
27.document_summary: Sidney George Holland (1893-1961) was a prominent New Zealand politician who served as Prime Minister from 1949 to 1957. Born in Canterbury to English parents, Holland worked in business before entering Parliament in 1935 as MP for Christchurch North. He became leader of the National Party in 1940 and led it to victory in 1949, ending 14 years of Labour rule. As Prime Minister, Holland abolished the Legislative Council and took a hard line against militant unions during the 1951 waterfront dispute. His government deregulated the economy by ending rationing and removing price controls while maintaining full employment and social security. New Zealand signed the ANZUS treaty in 1951 under his leadership. Holland introduced the PAYE taxation system and established the Tourist Hotel Corporation. By 1956, his health deteriorated significantly, and he announced his retirement on August 12, 1957, succeeded by Holyoake on September 20. He was knighted and made a minister without portfolio, retiring from Parliament in November 1957. Holland died in Wellington Hospital on August 5, 1961. His major contribution was establishing the National Party as a dominant force in New Zealand politics throughout the latter twentieth century.

28.document_title: Norman Eric Kirk: New Zealand's Labour Prime Minister - Political Biography and Legacy
28.document_summary: This biographical account traces Norman Eric Kirk's remarkable political journey from his working-class origins to becoming New Zealand's fourth Labour Prime Minister. Born in 1923 in Waimate, South Canterbury, Kirk rose from humble beginnings as a roof painter, railway worker, and boiler engineer to become a transformative political figure. After joining the Labour Party in 1943, he served as mayor of Kaiapoi from 1953, implementing progressive infrastructure reforms. Elected to Parliament in 1957 representing Lyttelton, Kirk distinguished himself as an excellent debater and advocate for constituents and the disadvantaged. He ascended through Labour ranks, becoming party vice president in 1963 and president in 1964, before defeating Arnold Nordmeyer on December 9, 1965, to become leader of the parliamentary Labour Party at age 42. His 1969 campaign slogan "Make things happen" emphasized planned economic development, though he narrowly lost to Keith Holyoake. Labour's 1972 electoral victory brought Kirk to the Prime Minister's office, where his government pursued activist policies including establishing diplomatic relations with China, opposing racial discrimination, and resisting nuclear testing. However, global economic slowdown, oil price increases, and rising inflation undermined his ambitious agenda. Kirk's health deteriorated following a grueling international tour and leg surgery in April 1974. Despite declining health, he continued working through mounting industrial unrest until his death from congestive cardiac failure on August 31, 1974, at age 51. Kirk left a lasting legacy as Labour's last passionate advocate for big government.

29.document_title: Robert Stout: Life, Political Career, Legal Legacy, and Educational Reform in New Zealand (1844-1930)
29.document_summary: Robert Stout (1844-1930) was born in Lerwick, Shetland, Scotland, and emigrated to Otago, New Zealand in 1863, becoming a prominent figure in Dunedin society. He served as attorney general and minister for lands and immigration (1878-1879) under Sir George Grey, championing land reform and state intervention. As premier (1884-1887) in alliance with Julius Vogel, Stout advocated for civil service reform, secondary education, and technical education. His most enduring legacy emerged through his appointment as Chief Justice (1899-1926), where he decided over 1,400 cases with liberal statutory interpretation. Throughout his career, Stout championed women's rights, including the Electoral Bill (1878) and the Married Women's Property Act (1884). He profoundly influenced New Zealand's university system, founding Victoria College and serving as Chancellor of the University of New Zealand (1903-1923). Appointed KCMG in 1886 and privy counsellor in 1921, Stout exemplified the rare intellectual politician who emphasized educating public opinion and moral development, making him a key architect of democratic New Zealand.

30.document_title: John Ross Marshall: New Zealand Politician, Legal Professional, and Prime Minister
30.document_summary: This biographical account chronicles the life and political career of John Ross Marshall (1912-1988), a prominent New Zealand politician and legal professional. Born in Wellington to Scottish parents, Marshall studied law at Victoria University College, earning his LLB in 1934 and LLM in 1935. He served in World War II as a major in the New Zealand Division, participating in campaigns across Fiji, Norfolk Island, New Caledonia, and Italy. Marshall entered Parliament in 1946, representing Mount Victoria (later Karori) for the National Party, serving until 1975. He held ministerial positions for 20 years, including 12 years as Deputy Prime Minister and nearly one year as Prime Minister (February 1972-December 1972). As Minister of Labour from 1968, Marshall navigated complex industrial disputes, deregistered the Seamen's Union during a 1971 strike, and introduced the Stabilisation of Remuneration Bill. His most significant achievement was establishing the Accident Compensation scheme, providing income-related compensation to injured workers regardless of fault. Marshall's key contributions included housing policy expansion, health and justice reforms, and the New Zealand-Australia Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). He was instrumental in negotiating favorable transition arrangements for New Zealand's butter, cheese, and lamb exports during Britain's applications to join the EEC. Known as 'Gentleman Jack' for his courteous demeanor and Christian principles, Marshall was knighted in 1974 and retired from Parliament in 1975, becoming a consultant, university fellow, and patron of charitable organizations.

36.document_summary: Former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern's upcoming memoir "A Different Kind of Power" will be published in early June 2025 by Penguin Random House New Zealand. The deeply personal memoir will explore Ardern's leadership style and her philosophy on kindness as a powerful force in politics. Ardern, who became the world's youngest female head of government at 37 in October 2017, will share insights into pivotal moments from her tenure, including the Christchurch mosque terror attacks (2019), the Whakaari White Island eruption (2019), and the Covid-19 pandemic (2020). She will also detail her decision to step down as Prime Minister. The memoir emphasizes Ardern's belief that kindness possesses strength and power, capable of giving people hope, changing minds, and transforming lives—challenging perceptions that kindness is merely sentimental or naive.

38.document_title: How the Sound and Voices of Politics Have Changed from 1912 to 1990
38.document_summary: This article explores the evolution of political communication in New Zealand through audio recordings of fourteen Prime Ministers and a Speaker spanning from 1912 to 1990. The piece highlights how political speech, accents, tones, and presentation styles have transformed over nearly eight decades. Early leaders like William Massey and George Forbes employed formal, gentler speech patterns, while later politicians such as Rob Muldoon and David Lange adopted more modern, recognizably "Kiwi" accents and contemporary communication styles. The article notes that many early politicians were immigrants with strong accents, and that political communication has shifted from formal Empire-praising rhetoric to more direct, populist approaches. The audio compilation, curated with assistance from RNZ's audio historians, provides comparative insights into how New Zealand's political voices have evolved, reflecting broader changes in political culture and public communication.

39.document_title: 'The prime minister is dying': 50 years since Norman Kirk's last public appearance
39.document_summary: This article commemorates the 50th anniversary of Norman Kirk's final public appearance on August 18, 1974, at St Peter's College in Palmerston North, New Zealand. Despite severe illness—including an enlarged heart, blood clot in his lungs, and liver problems—Kirk insisted on attending the school opening ceremony for his friend Joe Walding. His wife Ruth confided to the school's board chair that "the prime minister is dying." Kirk died 13 days later on August 31, 1974, aged 51, making him the first New Zealand prime minister to die in office since 1940. During his two-year tenure, Kirk's government recognized China, protested French nuclear testing, refused entry to a racially selected Springbok rugby team, and introduced a retirement savings scheme. The article features insights from his private secretary Margaret Hayward and reflects on how Kirk's death prompted massive public grief followed by rapid public amnesia as successor Bill Rowling took office.

[Page 3] Until 1 January 1951 New Zealand had an upper house, the Legislative Council. Premiers and prime ministers were usually from the House of Representatives (the lower house), but they governed from the council on five occasions: Frederick Whitaker (1863 64 and 1882 83), George Waterhouse (1872 73), Daniel Pollen (1875 76) and Sir Francis Henry Dillon Bell (1925). As legislative councillors were political appointees on life or seven year terms, these were the only unelected politicians to lead the country.

retrieved_chunks.text:
[Page 5] From 1840 New Zealand’s governors ruled autocratically (with absolute authority), advised by the Executive Council and Legislative Council and answerable to the authorities in London. In 1854, though the new Parliament was still only there to provide advice to the governor, politicians had already asked for self governance in domestic matters, rather than having to defer to Britain. That year, while awaiting the reply from London, the acting governor, Colonel Robert Wynyard, appointed politician James FitzGerald to his Executive Council. Thomas Forsaith succeeded FitzGerald in the role. However, neither the ‘FitzGerald ministry’ nor the ‘Forsaith ministry’ lasted long. Their leaders were not true premiers. New Zealand’s earliest genuine ministries, formed after Parliament became responsible (fully self governing for most internal policy) in 1856, were short lived. The first premier, Henry Sewell, was sworn in on 18 April 1856, but was gone by 20 May. His successor, William Fox, was replaced by Edward Stafford on 2 June. In all there were 24 ministries between 1856 and 1891. To many it is a blur of beards, names and dates, but power was transferred peacefully each time, showing that the fledgling democracy worked.
{}

[Page 7] The 1890 election introduced government by party for the first time, when new premier John Ballance established the Liberal Federation. Ballance died in 1893 and was succeeded by Richard Seddon (sometimes known as ‘King Dick’), who effortlessly dominated New Zealand politics for the next 13 years. There was little real parliamentary opposition until 1909, when William Massey welded together the Reform Party. Thereafter political power centred on parties and their leaders. Personality became increasingly important for political success. The charismatic Gordon Coates ensured victory for Reform in 1925, and Labour’s Michael Joseph Savage, with his genial, fatherly image, enjoyed mass adulation in the 1930s.

[Page 7] Religion was politically divisive in the early 1900s when Sir Joseph Ward (a Catholic) and William Massey (Protestant) led the major parties, Liberal and Reform. Generally, though, it seldom raised political ripples in New Zealand. Because the Anglican Church is not an established (that is, official state) church in New Zealand, Frederick Weld, a Catholic, could become premier in 1864. Julius Vogel, who was Jewish, became premier in 1873. By contrast, in 2017 Britain had still not had a Catholic or Jewish prime minister. Non belief was also not a bar to office in New Zealand; colonial premiers Alfred Domett, Robert Stout and John Ballance were freethinkers.

[Page 8] Greater independence For a while New Zealand’s prime ministers opposed greater independence from Britain. New Zealand and Australia resisted the structural reforms towards independence pushed by other dominions at the 1926 and 1930 imperial conferences. response.response_text:
## Climate Change: What the Science Says

The short answer is yes — climate change is real, and the scientific evidence strongly points to human activity as the primary driver. Here's what the research tells us.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The Evidence for Warming

The signs of a changing climate are measurable and widespread. In New Zealand alone, temperatures rose by about 0.7°C between 1920 and 2000, accompanied by fewer frosts, retreating glaciers and snowlines in the South Island, reduced alpine snow mass, and a sea level rise of 14–17 centimetres [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1). Globally, seas have been rising more rapidly since the late 19th century, a trend that's accelerating as oceans warm [[3]](cite://3/1).

In recent years, the pace of change has intensified. Between June 2023 and September 2024, global temperatures were unlike anything previously recorded, making both 2023 and 2024 the hottest years in history [[4]](cite://4/1). Each of the top 10 hottest years on record has occurred in the past decade, while the coldest 10 all occurred more than 100 years ago — a pattern that, as one climatologist put it, simply should not happen in a stable climate [[5]](cite://5/1).

## The Human Fingerprint

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) — a body of scientists sponsored by the United Nations — expresses "very high confidence" (defined as greater than 90 percent probability) that warming is being caused by human activity [[6]](cite://6/1).

The mechanism is well understood. Burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide (CO₂), which trap heat near the Earth's surface [[4]](cite://4/2). Ice cores drilled in Antarctica and Greenland show that CO₂ levels ranged between about 180 and 300 parts per million (ppm) over the past 650,000 years. By the mid-19th century, before industrialisation spread globally, CO₂ stood at around 280 ppm. With the burning of coal, oil, and gas, that figure had already reached 382 ppm by the mid-2000s — 36 percent above pre-industrial levels [[6]](cite://6/2). Scientists are unanimous that fossil fuel burning has largely driven long-term global warming [[4]](cite://4/3).

## What About Natural Variability?

It's true that natural processes — such as El Niño and La Niña weather patterns — do influence climate year to year, and scientists acknowledge this variability [[7]](cite://7/1). There are also genuine uncertainties in how precisely temperatures will rise; the IPCC estimates a global average increase of between 1.4°C and 5.8°C by century's end, with the wide range reflecting uncertainties in climate models and future emissions scenarios [[8]](cite://8/1)[[9]](cite://9/1).

However, scientists are clear that while natural variability explains some short-term fluctuations, it cannot account for the sustained, long-term warming trend we're observing. Beyond the next few decades, global warming caused mostly by human activity is expected to dominate [[7]](cite://7/2). A principal scientist at Earth Sciences New Zealand (formerly NIWA) noted in early 2026 that climate scientists have long warned we'd see more extreme weather — and it now appears we're living through it [[10]](cite://10/1).

## The Bottom Line

The debate you may have heard tends to be less about the science — which is robust and well-established — and more about the scale, timing, and policy responses. The core finding is clear: Earth is warming, the pace has accelerated since industrialisation, and human greenhouse gas emissions are the dominant cause [[6]](cite://6/3)[[4]](cite://4/4)[[5]](cite://5/2).

Would you like to explore what climate change means specifically for Aotearoa New Zealand — including projected temperature rises and sea level changes here at home?

1.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an integrated analysis of climate change, covering global climate systems, New Zealand-specific impacts, and future projections. It explains fundamental climate science, including the definition of climate as average weather over long periods and the role of solar radiation balance. The document details past climate variations, from glacial and interglacial periods to recent warming trends, emphasizing greenhouse gases as primary drivers of climate change. Atmospheric CO2 has risen from 280 ppm to 410 ppm since pre-industrial times, with the IPCC confirming that global warming is unequivocal and primarily caused by human activities since 1950. Assessment methods for understanding past climate include glacial ice cores, tree rings, sediment cores, and fossil pollens. New Zealand's climate history shows temperature increases of 1.1°C since 1909, with distinct rainfall pattern changes since 1930. The country's greenhouse gas emissions come mainly from agriculture (48%), energy sector (41%), and industrial processes (11%). Based on 2018 projections, New Zealand faces a temperature increase of 1.4°C by 2090, sea level rise of 46-105 cm by 2100, altered rainfall patterns, glacier reduction, and increased westerly winds. Agricultural impacts include potential crop relocation, increased droughts in eastern regions, northward spread of subtropical grasses, increased pests and diseases, and potential restrictions on kiwifruit production after 2050. The Paris Agreement aims to limit global temperature increase to under 2°C, with New Zealand committing to reduce emissions by 30% below 2005 levels by 2030.

2.text:
[Page 11] New Zealand climate changes There are a number of potential changes for New Zealand’s climate. In a 2018 study completed by the National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research for the Ministry for the Environment, the mid range estimate for projected New Zealand temperature change was an expected increase of 1.4°C by 2090 relative to the period 1986 2005. Other likely changes included a rise in sea level above 1990s levels of between 46 and 105 centimetres by 2100, increased rainfall in the south and west of the country coupled with a decrease in the north and east, a long term reduction in glacier length and ice thickness, and an increased westerly windflow across New Zealand.

[Page 6] In line with measurements worldwide, New Zealand temperatures rose substantially during the 20th century, increasing by about 0.7°C between 1920 and 2000. The warmest year (up to 2003) was 1998, closely followed by 1999. Climate change has produced other effects: fewer frosts, retreating glaciers and snowlines in the South Island, reduced alpine snow mass, and a rise in sea level of 14 17 centimetres.

3.document_title: New Zealand Climate: Comprehensive Overview of Regional Variations, Global Patterns, and Life Impacts
3.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth analysis of New Zealand's climate, defined as long-term weather patterns characterized by a temperate maritime climate. It details mean annual temperatures ranging from 10°C in the south to 16°C in the north, with at least 1,800 sunshine hours annually. Westerly winds and mountain ranges create distinct regional climate variations: the West Coast of the South Island is the wettest area receiving over 6,000mm of rainfall annually, while eastern regions are significantly drier, receiving as little as 400mm. Most areas receive 600-1,600mm of rainfall annually, with snow primarily in mountain areas. Temperature trends show a rise of approximately 0.7°C between 1920 and 2000, with 1998 being the warmest year recorded. Global climate patterns affecting New Zealand include the Antarctic Oscillation, El Niño–Southern Oscillation (with 3-7 year cycles), and the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation, which influence wind direction, temperature, and precipitation patterns. The document examines how New Zealand's climate significantly impacts three major areas of life: recreation (outdoor activities, gardening, sailing), health (extreme weather challenges, hospital admissions during cold periods), and the economy (agriculture production variations, renewable energy generation, and tourism activities).

8.text:
[Page 9] To accurately predict human induced changes in New Zealand’s climate, scientists need to know the global extent of greenhouse gas emissions, likely future changes in carbon dioxide concentrations, and the influence of New Zealand’s topography on local climate. Each of these factors comes with uncertainties. For example, gauging future emissions relies on anticipating human behaviour, including the success of constraints negotiated under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. Our understanding of the carbon cycle and of sources of non carbon dioxide greenhouse gases is also incomplete.

[Page 17] NIWA also carries out research on climate change and long term climate cycles, such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation that affects New Zealand’s weather patterns. In El Niño years, stronger westerly winds bring more rain to southern and western regions. By contrast, the La Niña pattern brings rainy conditions to the north east of the North Island. 10.document_title: Floods in New Zealand: Causes, History, Impacts, and Management Strategies
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines flooding in New Zealand, covering its causes, history, impacts, and management strategies. New Zealand experiences frequent floods due to weather systems, mountain ranges, and extensive river networks, averaging over 80 damaging floods between 1968-2017. Major historical events include the 1863 Central Otago floods (100+ deaths), 1938 Kōpuawhara Stream flash flood (21 deaths), 1984 Southland floods, Cyclone Bola 1988 ($90 million losses), 2004 Manawatū River floods ($400 million), and 2023 Cyclone Gabrielle ($10+ billion, 15 deaths). The document explains flood mechanisms including flash floods, debris flows, and landslide-triggered floods. Two-thirds of New Zealand's population lives in flood-prone areas, with human activities like deforestation and urbanization increasing risk. Flood management strategies include stopbanks, dams, floodgates, regional council monitoring, and NIWA forecasting. Historical legislation such as the River Boards Act 1884 and Resource Management Act 1991 established flood management frameworks. Climate change is expected to increase extreme rainfall frequency and intensity.

21.document_title: Carbon and Climate
21.document_summary: This article explores the relationship between carbon, atmospheric greenhouse gases, and climate change. It explains how carbon dioxide and other trace gases trap heat in Earth's atmosphere through the Greenhouse Effect, which is essential for maintaining temperatures suitable for life. The article discusses how atmospheric CO2 levels have increased since the Industrial Revolution due to fossil fuel combustion, documented through ice core analysis. It examines carbon removal through photosynthesis and forest planting as potential offsets, while noting complications such as methane emissions from livestock. The IPCC predicts global temperature increases of 1°C by 2025 and 3°C by century's end if emissions continue unchecked, causing sea level rise and climate disruptions. Regional climate prediction is complicated by phenomena like El Niño and atmospheric blocking, which create extreme weather patterns. Recent extreme weather events worldwide suggest climate is already changing, with previously rare events becoming more frequent.

22.text:
[Page 4] The most important greenhouse gas is water vapour, followed by carbon dioxide and methane. The burning of fossil fuels, such as coal and oil, has accelerated since the Industrial Revolution, greatly increasing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Bubbles of gas trapped in ice laid down hundreds of years ago in the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have been analysed and show a level of carbon dioxide of about 280 parts per million (ppm) before 1750. The level has now reached 360 ppm and is projected to reach between 540 and 970 ppm by the end of this century, depending on how much effort is make to cut back on the burning of fossil fuels worldwide.

22.document_title: Climate Change Through Time: Temperature Reconstruction and Historical Civilizational Impacts
22.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the relationship between Earth's past temperatures and their impact on human civilizations. The first section details scientific methods for reconstructing historical temperatures using proxy data techniques such as oxygen isotope ratios in ice cores, fossil pollen, tree rings, and lake sediments spanning hundreds of thousands of years. The IPCC reports a 0.6°C rise in global average temperature over the past century, with current warming showing no precedent in the past 1000 years. Atmospheric CO2 levels have risen from 280 ppm pre-1750 to 360 ppm currently, with levels not seen in 20 million years. Temperature projections indicate increases of 1.4-5.8°C by century's end with sea level rises of 9-88 cm. The second section explores the historical correlation between climate change and civilizational collapse, demonstrating how environmental disruptions—particularly droughts and temperature fluctuations—coincided with settlement abandonment around 1100 A.D., evidenced by a 10-meter drop in Lake Titicaca's water level. Historical examples include the Akkadian empire drought and Maya civilization decline. While acknowledging that climate change may not be the sole cause of societal disruption, the document argues that the increasing correlation between climate events and civilizational collapse suggests climate has played a significant historical role with crucial implications for predicting climate's future impact on society.

38.document_title: Greenhouse Plan Not Realistic, Places NZ Reputation at Risk - Experts
38.document_summary: New Zealand's draft emissions reduction plan faces significant criticism from climate experts for being unrealistic and unambitious. Released in July 2024, the government's plan relies heavily on tree-planting and carbon capture technology to meet greenhouse gas budgets toward net-zero emissions by 2050. However, experts including Massey University professor Ralph Sims argue the plan ignores decades of climate science advice, places too much faith in non-existent technologies, and will result in higher emissions. New Zealand is on track to meet its first emissions budget (2022-2025) and barely meet the second (2026-2030), but will miss the third (2031-2035) by approximately 17 million tonnes. Critics highlight that the government has cancelled climate policies including EV subsidies and oil/gas exploration bans, moving in the wrong direction. The plan lacks infrastructure development and regulatory measures needed for essential mitigation. New Zealand's international standing and Paris Agreement commitments are at risk, as the country has one of the highest per capita emissions globally and must purchase expensive international carbon credits.

[Page 1] Scientists struggle to explain record surge in global heat 2024 12 16 19:31:34+13:00 By Nick Perry for AFP The world has been getting hotter for decades but a sudden and extraordinary surge in heat has sent the climate deeper into uncharted territory and scientists are still trying to figure out why. Over the past two years, temperature records have been repeatedly shattered by a streak so persistent and puzzling it has tested the best available scientific predictions about how the climate functions. Scientists are unanimous that burning fossil fuels has largely driven long term global warming, and that natural climate variability can also influence temperatures one year to the next. But they are still debating what might have contributed to this particularly exceptional heat surge. Experts think changes in cloud patterns, airborne pollution, and Earth's ability to store carbon could be factors, but it would take another year or two for a clearer picture to emerge. "Warming in 2023 was head and shoulders above any other year, and 2024 will be as well," said Gavin Schmidt, director of the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies, in November. "I wish I knew why, but I don't," he added. "We're still in the process of assessing what happened and if we are seeing a shift in how the climate system operates." 'Uncharted territory' When burned, fossil fuels emit greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide that trap heat near the Earth's surface. As fossil fuel emissions have risen to record highs in 2023, average sea surface and air temperatures have curved upwards in a consistent, decades long warming trend. But in an unprecedented streak between June 2023 and September 2024, global temperatures were unlike anything seen before, said the World Meteorological Organization and sometimes by a considerable margin. The heat was so extreme it was enough to make 2023 and then 2024 the hottest years in history. "The record global warmth of the past two years has sent the planet well into uncharted territory," Richard Allan, a climate scientist from the UK's University of Reading, told AFP. What occurred was "at the limit of what we would expect based on existing climate models", Sonia Seneviratne, a climatologist from ETH Zurich in Switzerland, told AFP. "But the overall long term warming tendency is not unexpected" given the amount of fossil fuels being burned, she added. 'Difficult to explain' Scientists said that climate variability could go some way to explaining what happened. 2023 was preceded by a rare, three year La Niña phenomenon that had a strong cooling effect on the planet by pushing excess heat into the deep oceans. This energy was released back to the surface when an opposite, warming El Niño event took over in mid 2023, boosting global temperatures. But the heat has lingered even after El Niño peaked in January. Temperatures have not fallen as fast as they rose, and November was still the second warmest on record. "It is difficult to explain this at the moment," said Robert Vautard, a member of the UN's climate expert panel IPCC. "We lack a bit of perspective. "If temperatures do not drop more sharply in 2025, we will really have to ask ourselves questions about the cause," he told AFP. Jury out Scientists are looking for clues elsewhere. One theory is that a global shift to cleaner shipping fuels in 2020 accelerated warming by reducing sulphur emissions that make clouds more mirror like and reflective of sunlight. In December, another peer reviewed paper looked at whether a reduction in low lying clouds had let more heat reach Earth's surface. At the American Geophysical Union conference this month, Schmidt convened scientists to explore these theories and others, including whether solar cycles or volcanic activity offered any hints. There are concerns that without a more complete picture, scientists could be missing even more profound and transformational shifts in the climate. "We cannot exclude that some other factors also further amplified the temperatures... the verdict is still out," said Seneviratne. Scientists this year warned that Earth's carbon sinks such as the forests and oceans that suck CO2 from the atmosphere had suffered an "unprecedented weakening" in 2023. This month, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said the Arctic tundra, after locking away C02 for millennia, was becoming a net source of emissions. Oceans, which have acted as a massive carbon sink and climate regulator, were warming at a rate scientists "cannot fully explain", said Johan Rockstrom of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. "Could this be a first sign of a planet starting to show a loss of resilience? We cannot exclude it," he said last month. 42.document_title: Climate Change Scientists Accuse New Zealand Government of Ignoring Scientific Evidence on Methane Targets
42.document_summary: Twenty-six international climate scientists have written an open letter to New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon criticizing the government's plan to lower methane reduction targets. The scientists argue the proposed "no additional warming" approach ignores scientific evidence and would allow farming—New Zealand's largest emissions source—to maintain current high methane levels indefinitely. The government appointed its own scientific panel to justify lower targets, contradicting the independent Climate Change Commission's recommendation of 35-47% methane reductions by 2050. Prime Minister Luxon dismissed the scientists as "worthies" and defended New Zealand's record, while the Green Party warned the government is on a "climate denial bandwagon." Agricultural lobby groups support lower targets, but critics argue this sets a dangerous precedent that could exempt wealthy farming nations from climate responsibility.

43.document_title: NZ at Bottom of League Table for EV Chargers: Government Falling Short on Infrastructure Goals
43.document_summary: New Zealand ranks last among 31 nations for public EV charging infrastructure, with only 1,200 chargers as of April 2024—approximately one charger per 59 electric vehicles. The government promised 10,000 public chargers by 2030, requiring 130 chargers monthly, but only 21 were built monthly last year. The removal of EV subsidies has caused new EV sales to plummet from 27% to 8% of the market, discouraging private investment. However, New Zealand leads globally in fast-charger deployment at 75% of its charging network. The government announced $257 million in funding and is redesigning its co-funding model. Key challenges include attracting capital investment, securing high-capacity electricity lines near main roads, and addressing parking constraints for apartment dwellers. Experts emphasize that most EV charging occurs at home, and strategic placement of chargers at retail locations could ease adoption concerns.

44.document_title: Hundreds Told to Flee Out-of-Control Bushfires in Australia
44.document_summary: Severe bushfires erupted in Victoria, Australia on Saturday, prompting evacuation orders for hundreds of residents near Grampians National Park, approximately 241km west of Melbourne. The fires, ignited by lightning strikes on Tuesday, have consumed over 28,000 hectares. Approximately 400 firefighters are battling the blazes using 100+ tankers and 25 aircraft. Authorities have issued the highest danger rating alert for rural areas including Halls Gap. The fire has stabilized following wind reduction. This incident follows warnings of a high-risk bushfire season, with comparisons to the devastating 2019-2020 "Black Summer" fires that destroyed an area the size of Turkey and killed 33 people.

Using real time climate attribution methods, they were also able to say how many days were made more likely by climate change. It found human caused climate change added 26 more days of extreme heat, on average, across all places in the world, to what there would have been without a warmed planet. In some places, nearly half the year was spent under unusually hot conditions, including parts of South and Central America, and south east Asia. In Ecuador, for example, the average person experienced 180 days of extreme heat above their local level during the past year, according to the analysis. Without the influence of climate change, it found that number would have been 10. Climate Central vice president for science Andrew Pershing said the figures illustrated the "huge burden" the burning of fossil fuels imposed on people around the world. "Different countries are each having their own story, and that's one of the things we tried to highlight in the report," Dr Pershing said. "Australia didn't have a particularly interesting summer this year, but in Africa it's just day after day after day of climate change just beating down on that continent." An extreme heat day is one that is warmer than 90 percent of all observed temperatures at the site from 1991 2020. Dr Pershing said this was considered the point at which heat became particularly dangerous, with increases in temperature related hospitalisations. He said having the past 30 years as the baseline also meant the extreme heat was out of the ordinary even within the context of the climate people were used to. While the report only looked at days of extreme heat, Dr Pershing said they had also seen the impact of global warming play out in intense rainfall and drought events. In April, the desert city of Dubai recorded more than a year's worth of rainfall within 24 hours, flooding airport runways and motorways. And Mexico is currently in the grip of a severe heatwave. How long will the record heat continue? A look at the global air temperature over the past year shows just how easily records have been set, even when compared to our modern day climate. During the latest month, May, the average near surface air temperature was 0.65 Celsius above the 1991 2020 baseline average, according to Copernicus's data, easily overtaking the previous record set in 2020. When compared to pre industrial levels (1850 1900), the month was 1.53C above average, breaching the Paris Agreement target of 1.5C for the 11th consecutive month. Temperatures were well above 45C in several cities in India at the end of last month. And it is not just air temperatures that remain off the charts. May 2024 also saw a continuation of record warm global sea surface temperatures, extending the run of unprecedented oceanic heat to 14 months in a row although sea ice around Antarctica has made a moderate recovery this year after record low ice extent in 2023. The hot May means the past 12 months are now also a record at 1.63C above pre industrial levels, and ensures that, on its current trajectory, 2024 is now likely to surpass 2023 as the warmest year on record unless an unexpected rapid cooling occurs during the coming months. While the recent global figures appear to indicate more than just a brief spike above the Paris mark, it is not likely to be permanent. The recent tumbling of climate records is partly due to an injection of warmth from the recent El Niño, a pattern US National Ocean and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) senior scientist Michael McPhaden is tracking. "It takes time for the heat that is released from the ocean in the tropical Pacific to be distributed around the globe and show up as elevated global mean surface temperature," Dr McPhaden said. "So there may be no relief in terms of global mean surface temperatures this calendar year. "We may see it next year, as La Niña has had a chance to develop and take hold." What's driving global heat? Several factors have played into the Earth's record heat over the past year, some of which scientists are still trying to fully understand. The onset of El Niño, in particular, has been flagged as one of the major year to year climate drivers that has helped boost global temperatures into record territory. But climate scientists say by far the most significant contributor is rising greenhouse gas emissions, caused primarily by the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation, which have been responsible for approximately 1.1C of warming from 1850 1900 to 2021. "The escalator and climate change go in only one direction and it's up, so don't be surprised when more records are set," Dr McPhaden said. It has meant years of record heat have now become a frequent occurrence for the globe, while years of record cold are a rarity. Each of the top 10 hottest years on record occurred in the past decade, while the coldest 10 on record all occurred more than 100 years ago something Dr Perkins Kirkpatrick points out should not happen. "In a stable climate, record hot years and record cold years should statistically be occurring with the same probability, but that's not what's happening," she said. "So the fact that these heat events just keep on being broken they light up like Christmas trees every year is just showing the underlying stress the global climate is in." Adapting to a new climate reality The latest line of heat records has been met with a response that climate scientists have made many times before. They say to stop records from tumbling the world needs to stop burning coal, oil, and natural gas. "It's a, 'No shit Sherlock,' moment," Dr Perkins Kirkpatrick said. "These records will continue to be broken for some time, particularly if we don't reduce our emissions quickly." But Dr Perkins Kirkpatrick said it had now reached a point where adaption to heat extremes was also necessary. "We need to be really realistic and pragmatic of what we can achieve and in the time frame that we can achieve it," she said. "So we must also be looking at adaptation more seriously than we ever have before. "And the longer we leave that, the worse that becomes." To this end, Dr Pershing said while record hot months and years would not stop in a stable climate, their danger would become more manageable. "Once we get to zero emissions, many parts of the climate system will stabilise within a few years, and temperature is one of them," he said. "That's the thing to me that's really interesting, is that it's something we can then get used to. "Then we can say, 'This is the main temperature of our city, this is the infrastructure we need,' rather than, 'This is our temperature,' and then, 'Oh heck, it's even warmer, and we have to change even more.' "A more stable environment gives ourselves the opportunity to adapt and adjust." This story was first published by the ABC Related

45.document_summary: A comprehensive analysis of the past 12 months of record-breaking global heat reveals that 6.3 billion people experienced at least 31 days of extreme heat. International climate scientists found that human-induced climate change added an average of 26 extra days of extreme heat globally compared to a non-warmed planet. Countries in South and Central America and Southeast Asia were most severely affected, with Ecuador experiencing 180 days of extreme heat (versus 10 without climate change). May 2024 marked the hottest May on record, with temperatures 0.65°C above the 1991-2020 baseline and 1.53°C above pre-industrial levels, breaching the Paris Agreement target for the 11th consecutive month. The record heat is driven primarily by rising greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels and deforestation, with El Niño contributing as a secondary factor. Scientists emphasize that while emissions reduction is critical, adaptation strategies are now equally necessary given the trajectory of climate change.

47.document_title: New Zealand at 'Significant Risk' of Missing 2050 Climate Target, Government Making It Worse
47.document_summary: New Zealand faces significant risk of missing its 2050 climate target, according to the Climate Change Commission's 2025 emissions reduction monitoring report. While the country is likely to meet its first emissions budget (2022-2025) due to accounting changes, risks have increased for targets from 2026 onwards. Real emissions fell steadily from 2019 to 2023, reaching the lowest level since 1999, with positive trends in renewable energy, electrification, and process heat conversions. However, current government policies are insufficient for long-term goals. Key risks include unreliable carbon capture and storage in the gas sector, increased electricity generation emissions, and over-reliance on forest carbon removals. The commission recommends strengthening the Emissions Trading Scheme, accelerating renewable energy adoption, reforming transport and farming policies, and reconsidering subsidies for large emitters. Government actions like road user charges on electric vehicles and reopening offshore oil exploration have worsened the situation, while positive steps include ETS updates and renewable energy consenting streamlining.

48.document_title: Scientists May Have Found a Big, Mysterious Carbon Sink in the South Island
48.document_summary: NIWA scientists have discovered a significant carbon sink in New Zealand's South Island, particularly over Fiordland and southwest regions dominated by mature native forests. The study found approximately 171 million tonnes of CO2 are absorbed annually by New Zealand's natural environment—50-140 million tonnes more than previous estimates. However, researchers caution that further investigation is needed to determine whether this carbon uptake is due to native forests capturing more carbon than previously thought, or other processes like erosion and landslides transporting carbon away. If native forests are indeed the source, New Zealand could leverage pest control and conservation efforts to boost forest health and meet climate targets, potentially reducing reliance on international carbon credits.

49.document_title: New Zealand Government Consults on Carbon Capture and Storage Regime
49.document_summary: New Zealand's government is consulting on a carbon capture and storage (CCS) regime that would allow companies to earn carbon credits by capturing CO2 from the air or factories and pumping it into underground reservoirs. The captured carbon could also be sold for commercial uses like dry ice and welding. MBIE estimates CCS could remove nearly 5 million tonnes of CO2 over ten years from 2026. However, government experts acknowledge they cannot yet quantify the risks of CO2 leaks or cleanup costs. Climate activists worry CCS will become a "smokescreen" allowing fossil fuel companies to avoid reducing emissions, citing global examples where oil-backed projects absorb only tiny portions of emissions despite billions in investment. The government proposes incentivizing CCS through the Emissions Trading Scheme, similar to forestry credits. Climate Change Minister Simon Watts assures that CCS won't replace emission reduction targets, while the IPCC emphasizes CCS must accompany swift reductions in fossil fuel consumption to meet climate goals.

[Page 1] Will the Earth warm by 2°C or 5.5°C? Either way it’s bad 2024 10 09 12:01:53+13:00 [repub:theconversation] Jonny Williams and Georgia Rose Grant* [the_conversation_tracker] https://counter.theconversation.com/content/ 229497/count.gif?distributor=republish lightbox advanced Opinion Climate change is usually discussed in terms of rising temperatures. But scientists often use a different measure, known as "equilibrium climate sensitivity". This is defined as the global mean warming caused by a doubling of pre industrial carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels in the atmosphere. We use this measure to describe the range of potential temperature increases on longer timescales, and to compare how well climate models reproduce observed warming. But the predicted range of rising temperature has remained stubbornly wide, somewhere between 2C and 5.5C of warming, as assessed in several generations of reports issued by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. This is despite concerted efforts to narrow it down. Measuring long term climate sensitivity is central to future predictions, but we are already seeing the effects of warming across the world with extremes in weather, even at the low end of the range. We argue efforts to boil down Earth's response to climate change to one number may be unhelpful. The continued uncertainty could be seen as a failure of climate models to converge on the correct value. Using equilibrium climate sensitivity as a metric for "precisely" predicting the amount of warming expected from a given amount of greenhouse gases is, at best, ambiguous. History of climate sensitivity About a century before the first computational estimates of Earth's climate sensitivity were published in 1967, the Swedish physicist and 1903 Nobel laureate Svante August Arrhenius was the first to estimate values at 4 6°C. Since the early efforts to model Earth systems, computer simulations have steadily increased complexity. The first models only simulated the atmosphere, but they have evolved to include vegetation, processes in the ocean and sea ice. While undoubtedly beneficial to the understanding of fundamental science, each of these added processes has introduced uncertainties in the models' warming response. Indeed, given the level of complexity in (which differs between models) and resolution of some current models, it is not surprising the estimates of climate sensitivity differ so much. Self enforcing feedbacks Climate feedbacks are central to our argument that equilibrium climate sensitivity is poorly defined. An example of this is the relationship between ice volume and reflectivity. As highly reflective ice melts on land or sea, the underlying surface is exposed and less sunlight reflected back into space. This increases the amount of warming for a given amount of greenhouse gases. It's what scientists refer to as a positive feedback loop. Greenland's Ilulissat Icefjord glacier, the largest outside of Antarctica, has retreated 40km since 1850, attributed to the effect of climate change. Another such self enforcing feedback concerns potentially large climate impacts from the release of methane from tropical wetlands and permafrost melt. Atmosphere models can't account for this alone, and when they are coupled with an ice sheet or sea ice model, the estimate of climate sensitivity changes. Overheated arguments It quickly became apparent when studying some recent climate model results that some simulations are producing equilibrium climate sensitivity ranges noticeably higher than before. In some models, this has been linked to larger self enhancing cloud feedbacks and how aerosols are represented. There has been some hesitancy to trust the results produced by these models. They are considered "too hot". But we feel these high equilibrium simulations still have value. While we are not arguing they are correct, they force us to consider the what if situation of very high climate sensitivity, where a doubling of CO₂ would result in warming of 5°C or higher. We know the impact on our environment would be devastating. Some view high equilibrium climate sensitivity as more consistent with warmer climates in the past, but others have questioned this. There are several reasons why past climate sensitivity may differ from modern conditions. We may be in a different phase of Earth's orbital cycles or the balance between volcanism and weathering. Of course, we should treat all scientific results with caution, but the potential insights gained for uncertain futures are of particular importance when climate change is already being felt across the globe. Where to from here? We are continually improving our understanding of the climate how it has changed in the past and how we think it may change in the future. Equilibrium climate sensitivity has consequently become the single solution we are seeking from climate models, even though the precise value will arguably never be known. Equilibrium climate sensitivity is undoubtedly a convenient

50.document_title: Will the Earth warm by 2°C or 5.5°C? Either way it's bad
50.document_summary: This article examines the persistent uncertainty in climate sensitivity predictions, which range between 2°C and 5.5°C of warming from doubled pre-industrial CO₂ levels. The authors argue that relying on a single equilibrium climate sensitivity metric is problematic because it oversimplifies Earth's complex climate response. They discuss how climate models have evolved to include multiple processes (atmosphere, vegetation, ocean, sea ice), each introducing uncertainties. Key factors include self-enforcing feedback loops like ice-albedo effects and methane release from permafrost. Recent models producing higher sensitivity estimates are dismissed as "too hot," yet the authors contend these scenarios warrant consideration given their potentially devastating impacts. The article concludes that focusing narrowly on achieving model consensus on one number may hinder rather than advance climate understanding, and that communicating uncertainty in climate projections remains a significant challenge.

1.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth analysis of New Zealand's climate, defined as long-term weather patterns characterized by a temperate maritime climate. It details mean annual temperatures ranging from 10°C in the south to 16°C in the north, with at least 1,800 sunshine hours annually. Westerly winds and mountain ranges create distinct regional climate variations: the West Coast of the South Island is the wettest area receiving over 6,000mm of rainfall annually, while eastern regions are significantly drier, receiving as little as 400mm. Most areas receive 600-1,600mm of rainfall annually, with snow primarily in mountain areas. Temperature trends show a rise of approximately 0.7°C between 1920 and 2000, with 1998 being the warmest year recorded. Global climate patterns affecting New Zealand include the Antarctic Oscillation, El Niño–Southern Oscillation (with 3-7 year cycles), and the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation, which influence wind direction, temperature, and precipitation patterns. The document examines how New Zealand's climate significantly impacts three major areas of life: recreation (outdoor activities, gardening, sailing), health (extreme weather challenges, hospital admissions during cold periods), and the economy (agriculture production variations, renewable energy generation, and tourism activities).

chunkHighlights.text: In line with measurements worldwide, New Zealand temperatures rose substantially during the 20th century, increasing by about 0.7°C between 1920 and 2000. The warmest year (up to 2003) was 1998, closely followed by 1999. Climate change has produced other effects: fewer frosts, retreating glaciers and snowlines in the South Island, reduced alpine snow mass, and a rise in sea level of 14–17 centimetres.

4.filePath: pdf/Scientists struggle to explain record surge in global heat.pdf
4.fileDescription: Global temperatures have surged to unprecedented levels between June 2023 and September 2024, making 2023 and 2024 the hottest years on record. While scientists unanimously agree that fossil fuel burning drives long-term warming, they are still debating the causes of this exceptional heat spike. Potential factors include changes in cloud patterns, reduced sulphur emissions from cleaner shipping fuels, and weakened carbon sinks. The heat surge exceeded climate model predictions, with temperatures remaining elevated even after El Niño peaked. Scientists warn that without understanding these anomalies, they may be missing profound shifts in climate resilience, particularly concerning ocean warming and Arctic tundra emissions.

chunkHighlights.text: Scientists struggle to explain record surge in global heat

By Nick Perry for AFP The world has been getting hotter for decades
but a sudden and extraordinary surge in heat has sent the climate deeper into uncharted territory -- and scientists are still trying to figure out why. Over the past two years, temperature records have been repeatedly shattered by a streak so persistent and puzzling it has tested the best-available scientific predictions about how the climate functions. Scientists are unanimous that burning fossil fuels has largely driven long-term global warming, and that natural climate variability can also influence temperatures one year to the next. But they are still debating what might have contributed to this particularly exceptional heat surge. Experts think changes in cloud patterns, airborne pollution, and Earth's ability to store carbon could be factors, but it would take another year or two for a clearer picture to emerge. "Warming in 2023 was head-and-shoulders above any other year, and 2024 will be as well," said Gavin Schmidt, director of the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies, in November. "I wish I knew why, but I don't," he added. "We're still in the process of assessing what happened and if we are seeing a shift in how the climate system operates." 'Uncharted territory' When burned, fossil fuels emit greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide that trap heat near the Earth's surface. As fossil fuel emissions have risen to record highs in 2023, average sea surface and air temperatures have curved upwards in a consistent, decades-long warming trend. But in an unprecedented streak between June 2023 and September 2024, global temperatures were unlike anything seen before, said the World Meteorological Organization -- and sometimes by a considerable margin. The heat was so extreme it was enough to make 2023 -- and then 2024 -- the hottest years in history. "The record global warmth of the past two years has sent the planet well into uncharted territory," Richard Allan, a climate scientist from the UK's University of Reading, told AFP. What occurred was "at the limit of what we would expect based on existing climate models", Sonia Seneviratne, a climatologist from ETH Zurich in
Switzerland, told AFP. "But the overall long-term warming tendency is
not unexpected" given the amount of fossil fuels being burned, she

added. 'Difficult to explain' Scientists said that climate variability could
go some way to explaining what happened. 2023 was preceded by a rare, three-year La Niña phenomenon that had a strong cooling effect on the planet by pushing excess heat into the deep oceans. This energy was released back to the surface when an opposite, warming El Niño event took over in mid-2023, boosting global temperatures. But the heat has lingered even after El Niño peaked in January. Temperatures have not fallen as fast as they rose, and November was still the second-warmest on record. "It is difficult to explain this at the moment," said Robert Vautard, a member of the UN's climate expert panel IPCC. "We lack a bit of perspective. "If temperatures do not drop more sharply in 2025, we will really have to ask ourselves questions about the cause," he told AFP. Jury out Scientists are looking for clues elsewhere. One theory is that a global shift to cleaner shipping fuels in 2020 accelerated warming by reducing sulphur emissions that make clouds more mirror-like and reflective of sunlight. In December, another peer-reviewed paper looked at whether a reduction in low-lying clouds had let more heat reach Earth's surface. At the American Geophysical Union conference this month, Schmidt convened scientists to explore these theories and others, including whether solar cycles or volcanic activity offered any hints. There are concerns that without a more complete picture, scientists could be missing even more profound and transformational shifts in the climate. "We cannot exclude that some other factors also further amplified the temperatures... the verdict is still out," said Seneviratne. Scientists this year warned that Earth's carbon sinks -- such as the forests and oceans that suck CO2 from the atmosphere -- had suffered an "unprecedented weakening" in 2023. This month, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said the Arctic tundra, after locking away C02 for millennia, was becoming a net source of emissions. Oceans, which have acted as a massive carbon sink and climate regulator, were warming at a rate scientists "cannot fully explain", said Johan Rockstrom of the Potsdam Institute for Climate
Impact Research. "Could this be a first sign of a planet starting to show a
loss of resilience? We cannot exclude it," he said last month. - AFP

5.fileDescription: A comprehensive analysis of the past 12 months of record-breaking global heat reveals that 6.3 billion people experienced at least 31 days of extreme heat. International climate scientists found that human-induced climate change added an average of 26 extra days of extreme heat globally compared to a non-warmed planet. Countries in South and Central America and Southeast Asia were most severely affected, with Ecuador experiencing 180 days of extreme heat (versus 10 without climate change). May 2024 marked the hottest May on record, with temperatures 0.65°C above the 1991-2020 baseline and 1.53°C above pre-industrial levels, breaching the Paris Agreement target for the 11th consecutive month. The record heat is driven primarily by rising greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels and deforestation, with El Niño contributing as a secondary factor. Scientists emphasize that while emissions reduction is critical, adaptation strategies are now equally necessary given the trajectory of climate change.

A MetService temperature map of New Zealand as the heat reaches "alert levels" on 12 December 2023. Using real-time climate attribution methods, they were also able to say how many days were made more likely by climate change. It found human-caused climate change added 26 more days of extreme heat, on average, across all places in the world, to what there would have been without a warmed planet. In some places, nearly half the year was spent under unusually hot conditions, including parts of South and Central America, and south-east Asia. In Ecuador, for example, the average person experienced 180 days of extreme heat above their local level during the past year, according to the analysis. Without the influence of climate change, it found that number would have been 10. Climate Central vice-president for science Andrew Pershing said the figures illustrated the "huge burden" the burning of fossil fuels imposed on people around the world. "Different countries are each having their own story, and that's one of the things we tried to highlight in the report," Dr Pershing said. "Australia didn't have a particularly interesting summer this year, but in Africa it's just day after day after day of climate change just beating down on that continent." An extreme heat day is one that is warmer than 90 percent of all observed temperatures at the site from 1991-2020. Dr Pershing said this was considered the point at which heat became particularly dangerous, with increases in temperature-related hospitalisations. He said having the past 30 years as the baseline also meant the extreme heat was out of the ordinary even within the context of the climate people were used to. While the report only looked at days of extreme heat, Dr Pershing said they had also seen the impact of global warming play out in intense rainfall and drought events. In April, the desert city of Dubai recorded more than a year's worth of rainfall within 24 hours, flooding airport runways and motorways. And Mexico is currently in the grip of a severe heatwave. How long will the record heat
continue? A look at the global air temperature over the past year shows
just how easily records have been set, even when compared to our
modern-day climate. During the latest month, May, the average
near-surface air temperature was 0.65 Celsius above the 1991-2020
baseline average, according to Copernicus's data, easily overtaking the
previous record set in 2020. When compared to pre-industrial levels

(1850-1900), the month was 1.53C above average, breaching the Paris
Agreement target of 1.5C for the 11th consecutive month. Temperatures were well above 45C in several cities in India at the end of last month. And it is not just air temperatures that remain off the charts. May 2024 also saw a continuation of record-warm global sea surface temperatures, extending the run of unprecedented oceanic heat to 14 months in a row - although sea ice around Antarctica has made a moderate recovery this year after record-low ice extent in 2023. The hot May means the past 12 months are now also a record at 1.63C above pre-industrial levels, and ensures that, on its current trajectory, 2024 is now likely to surpass 2023 as the warmest year on record unless an unexpected rapid cooling occurs during the coming months. While the recent global figures appear to indicate more than just a brief spike above the Paris mark, it is not likely to be permanent. The recent tumbling of climate records is partly due to an injection of warmth from the recent El Niño, a pattern US National Ocean and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) senior scientist Michael McPhaden is tracking. "It takes time for the heat that is released from the ocean in the tropical Pacific to be distributed around the globe and show up as elevated global mean surface temperature," Dr McPhaden said. "So there may be no relief in terms of global mean surface temperatures this calendar year. "We may see it next year, as La Niña has had a chance to develop and take hold." What's driving global heat? Several factors have played into the Earth's record heat over the past year, some of which scientists are still trying to fully understand. The onset of El Niño, in particular, has been flagged as one of the major year-to-year climate drivers that has helped boost global temperatures into record territory. But climate scientists say by far the most significant contributor is rising greenhouse gas emissions, caused primarily by the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation, which have been responsible for approximately 1.1C of warming from 1850-1900 to 2021. "The escalator and climate change go in only one direction and it's up, so don't be surprised when more records are set," Dr McPhaden said.
It has meant years of record heat have now become a frequent
occurrence for the globe, while years of record cold are a rarity. Each of
the top 10 hottest years on record occurred in the past decade, while
the coldest 10 on record all occurred more than 100 years ago -
something Dr Perkins-Kirkpatrick points out should not happen. "In a
stable climate, record-hot years and record-cold years should

statistically be occurring with the same probability, but that's not what's
happening," she said. "So the fact that these heat events just keep on being broken - they light up like Christmas trees every year - is just showing the underlying stress the global climate is in." Adapting to a new climate reality The latest line of heat records has been met with a response that climate scientists have made many times before. They say to stop records from tumbling the world needs to stop burning coal, oil, and natural gas. "It's a, 'No shit Sherlock,' moment," Dr Perkins Kirkpatrick said. "These records will continue to be broken for some time, particularly if we don't reduce our emissions quickly." But Dr Perkins-Kirkpatrick said it had now reached a point where adaption to heat extremes was also necessary. "We need to be really realistic and pragmatic of what we can achieve and in the time frame that we can achieve it," she said. "So we must also be looking at adaptation more seriously than we ever have before. "And the longer we leave that, the worse that becomes." To this end, Dr Pershing said while record hot months and years would not stop in a stable climate, their danger would become more manageable. "Once we get to zero emissions, many parts of the climate system will stabilise within a few years, and temperature is one of them," he said. "That's the thing to me that's really interesting, is that it's something we can then get used to. "Then we can say, 'This is the main temperature of our city, this is the infrastructure we need,' rather than, 'This is our temperature,' and then, 'Oh heck, it's even warmer, and we have to change even more.' "A more stable environment gives ourselves the opportunity to adapt and adjust." -

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an integrated analysis of climate change, covering global climate systems, New Zealand-specific impacts, and future projections. It explains fundamental climate science, including the definition of climate as average weather over long periods and the role of solar radiation balance. The document details past climate variations, from glacial and interglacial periods to recent warming trends, emphasizing greenhouse gases as primary drivers of climate change. Atmospheric CO2 has risen from 280 ppm to 410 ppm since pre-industrial times, with the IPCC confirming that global warming is unequivocal and primarily caused by human activities since 1950. Assessment methods for understanding past climate include glacial ice cores, tree rings, sediment cores, and fossil pollens. New Zealand's climate history shows temperature increases of 1.1°C since 1909, with distinct rainfall pattern changes since 1930. The country's greenhouse gas emissions come mainly from agriculture (48%), energy sector (41%), and industrial processes (11%). Based on 2018 projections, New Zealand faces a temperature increase of 1.4°C by 2090, sea level rise of 46-105 cm by 2100, altered rainfall patterns, glacier reduction, and increased westerly winds. Agricultural impacts include potential crop relocation, increased droughts in eastern regions, northward spread of subtropical grasses, increased pests and diseases, and potential restrictions on kiwifruit production after 2050. The Paris Agreement aims to limit global temperature increase to under 2°C, with New Zealand committing to reduce emissions by 30% below 2005 levels by 2030.

chunkHighlights.text: New Zealand’s climate varies from year to year thanks to natural processes. Some parts of the country, for example, have dry summers and autumns when an El Niño weather pattern is present. Natural fluctuations need to be considered alongside human-created climate change when developing plans and policies. Beyond the next few decades, however, global warming, caused mostly by human activity, will begin to dominate. To understand the range of possibilities for future climate in New Zealand, it is helpful to first look at projections of global change.

8.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines the relationship between Earth's past temperatures and their impact on human civilizations. The first section details scientific methods for reconstructing historical temperatures using proxy data techniques such as oxygen isotope ratios in ice cores, fossil pollen, tree rings, and lake sediments spanning hundreds of thousands of years. The IPCC reports a 0.6°C rise in global average temperature over the past century, with current warming showing no precedent in the past 1000 years. Atmospheric CO2 levels have risen from 280 ppm pre-1750 to 360 ppm currently, with levels not seen in 20 million years. Temperature projections indicate increases of 1.4-5.8°C by century's end with sea level rises of 9-88 cm. The second section explores the historical correlation between climate change and civilizational collapse, demonstrating how environmental disruptions—particularly droughts and temperature fluctuations—coincided with settlement abandonment around 1100 A.D., evidenced by a 10-meter drop in Lake Titicaca's water level. Historical examples include the Akkadian empire drought and Maya civilization decline. While acknowledging that climate change may not be the sole cause of societal disruption, the document argues that the increasing correlation between climate events and civilizational collapse suggests climate has played a significant historical role with crucial implications for predicting climate's future impact on society.

chunkHighlights.text: By juggling these and other feedback systems and using complex computer models of the atmosphere, the IPCC estimates that the global average temperature will rise by between 1.4 and 5.8°C by the end of the century. These increases are projected to cause a rise in sea level of between 9 and 88 cm, resulting mainly from the thermal expansion of seawater, with a smaller contribution from partial melting of glaciers and ice caps. The wide range in this estimate is a measure of uncertainties in the predictive models as well as in the projections of future carbon dioxide and methane emissions.

9.fileDescription: This article examines the persistent uncertainty in climate sensitivity predictions, which range between 2°C and 5.5°C of warming from doubled pre-industrial CO₂ levels. The authors argue that relying on a single equilibrium climate sensitivity metric is problematic because it oversimplifies Earth's complex climate response. They discuss how climate models have evolved to include multiple processes (atmosphere, vegetation, ocean, sea ice), each introducing uncertainties. Key factors include self-enforcing feedback loops like ice-albedo effects and methane release from permafrost. Recent models producing higher sensitivity estimates are dismissed as "too hot," yet the authors contend these scenarios warrant consideration given their potentially devastating impacts. The article concludes that focusing narrowly on achieving model consensus on one number may hinder rather than advance climate understanding, and that communicating uncertainty in climate projections remains a significant challenge.

But scientists often use a different measure, known as "equilibrium climate sensitivity". This is defined as the global mean warming caused by a doubling of pre-industrial carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels in the atmosphere. We use this measure to describe the range of potential temperature increases on longer timescales, and to compare how well climate models reproduce observed warming. But the predicted range of rising temperature has remained stubbornly wide, somewhere between 2C and 5.5C of warming, as assessed in several generations of reports issued by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. This is despite concerted efforts to narrow it down. Measuring long-term climate sensitivity is central to future predictions, but we are already seeing the effects of warming across the world with extremes in weather, even at the low end of the range. We argue efforts to boil down Earth's response to climate change to one number may be unhelpful. The continued uncertainty could be seen as a failure of climate models to converge on the correct value. Using equilibrium climate sensitivity as a metric for "precisely" predicting the amount of warming expected from a given amount of greenhouse gases is, at best, ambiguous. History of climate sensitivity About a century before the first computational estimates of Earth's climate sensitivity were published in 1967, the Swedish physicist and 1903 Nobel laureate Svante August Arrhenius was the first to estimate values at 4-6°C. Since the early efforts to model Earth systems, computer simulations have steadily increased complexity. The first models only simulated the atmosphere, but they have evolved to include vegetation, processes in the ocean and sea ice. While undoubtedly beneficial to the understanding of fundamental science, each of these added processes has introduced uncertainties in the models' warming response. Indeed, given the level of complexity - in
(which differs between models) and resolution of some current models,

it is not surprising the estimates of climate sensitivity differ so much.
Self-enforcing feedbacks Climate feedbacks are central to our argument that equilibrium climate sensitivity is poorly defined. An example of this is the relationship between ice volume and reflectivity. As highly reflective ice melts on land or sea, the underlying surface is exposed and less sunlight reflected back into space. This increases the amount of warming for a given amount of greenhouse gases. It's what scientists refer to as a positive feedback loop. Greenland's Ilulissat Icefjord glacier, the largest outside of Antarctica, has retreated 40km since 1850, attributed to the effect of climate change. Another such self-enforcing feedback concerns potentially large climate impacts from the release of methane from tropical wetlands and permafrost melt. Atmosphere models can't account for this alone, and when they are coupled with an ice-sheet or sea-ice model, the estimate of climate sensitivity changes. In some models, this has been linked to larger self-enhancing cloud feedbacks and how aerosols are represented. There has been some hesitancy to trust the results produced by these models. They are considered "too hot". But we feel these high equilibrium simulations still have value. While we are not arguing they are correct, they force us to consider the what-if situation of very high climate sensitivity, where a doubling of CO₂ would result in warming of 5°C or higher. We know the impact on our environment would be devastating. Some view high equilibrium climate sensitivity as more consistent with warmer climates in the past, but others have questioned this. There are several reasons why past climate sensitivity may differ from modern conditions. We may be in a different phase of Earth's orbital cycles or the balance between volcanism and weathering.
