2.fileDescription: This comprehensive document provides an overview of Māori protest movements in New Zealand from the 19th century through the 2010s. It chronicles historic land rights protests including Hōne Heke Pōkai's flagpole cutting (1844-45), Parihaka land protests (1880s), the 1975 hīkoi led by Whina Cooper, the 506-day Bastion Point occupation (1977-78), Raglan golf course protests, and the Ihumātao occupation (2016-2020). The document details cultural rights campaigns including the 1972 Māori language petition leading to Māori Language Day, the He Taua confrontation against mock hakas (1979), and the establishment of the tino rangatiratanga flag. It covers Waitangi Day protests beginning with Ngā Tamatoa's 1971 activism and the significant 1984 hīkoi. The document addresses Māori opposition to apartheid South Africa, particularly the 1981 Springbok tour protests. Key government policies protested include the 1961 Hunn Report, the 1995 fiscal envelope, and the 2004 Foreshore and Seabed Act. Major outcomes include the establishment of the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), land returns through treaty settlements, the formation of the Māori Party, and the repeal of the Foreshore and Seabed Act through the Marine and Coastal Area Act 2011.

chunkHighlights.text: Ihumātao

In 2016 Ihumātao, originally known as Te Ihu-o-Mataoho, on the Manukau Harbour, which neighbours an ancient archaeological site known as the Ōtuataua Stonefields Historic Reserve, was sold to a developer to become the site of a large housing development. Along with much of South Auckland and Waikato, this land had been confiscated by the Crown from its original owners in the 1860s, following the New Zealand Wars .

A protest group named SOUL (Save Our Unique Landscape) and supporters from across the country occupied the site for the next three years. SOUL argued the land should be saved from development and returned to Māori ownership, although some mana whenua wanted the housing development to go ahead. In 2019 the protests came to a head, with clashes with police, protests in other cities, and a visit from the Māori king, Te Arikinui Tūheitia Paki, who offered to facilitate talks between the parties. In 2020 the government purchased the land from Fletcher Building, and a Memorandum of Understanding between the Crown, Kīngitanga and Auckland Council set out how they would work together in future.

3.fileDescription: The Otuataua stonefields near Mangere in South Auckland represent a significant archaeological reserve preserving 1000 years of Maori and Pakeha agricultural history. Originally established by Maori as horticultural settlements around volcanic cones, the 89-hectare site is among New Zealand's best remaining stonefields, with less than 200 hectares surviving from Auckland's original 8000 hectares. The Wai O Hua people settled the stonefields up to 1000 years ago, cultivating kumara, taro, and yams using sophisticated rotational farming systems. By the 18th century, approximately 400 people worked the gardens, creating stone walls, terraces, and enclosures still visible today. After European arrival in the 19th century, Pakeha settlers established dairy farms on the stonefields. In 1999, the site was jointly purchased as a reserve by Manukau City Council, the Lottery Grants Board, Auckland Regional Council, and the Department of Conservation, preserving this unique record of human settlement spanning from early Maori agricultural development to European pastoral farming.

chunkHighlights.text: Auckland once had more than 8000 ha of such stonefields, established by Maori as horticultural settlements around the isthmus’s numerous volcanic cones, among rocks formed from lava flows. Now less than 200 ha of stonefields remain. The rest have been destroyed by 150 years of quarrying and urban development.

4.fileDescription: The coalition government met with the Ihumātao steering committee for the first time to discuss the future of disputed land in Auckland. Minister Tama Potaka confirmed the May 10 meeting focused on determining the land's future. The steering committee, established by the Kīngitanga with five years to develop a plan, comprises Crown and iwi representatives. The 32-hectare site was purchased by Labour in 2020 for $29.9 million from Fletcher Building. The land has a complex history: confiscated by the Crown in 1863, it remained in private ownership for 150 years before being designated a Special Housing Area in 2014. This sparked protests, including a 2019 occupation by Save Our Unique Landscape (SOUL). The committee has not yet released substantive updates on their discussions regarding the land's development.

over the disputed land. The coalition government has met with the Ihumātao steering committee for the first time as discussions on the future of the disputed land in Auckland continue. Minister for Māori Development Tama Potaka confirmed to Stuff that he met with te rōpu whakahaere (the steering committee) on 10 May. In a statement, Potaka said he met with the steering group at their invitation and had a "good robust kōrero with a focus on determining the future". He added he "agreed to meet with the members again to progress our discussions". It was the first time Potaka had been updated on the latest from the steering committee, which has been in ongoing discussions around what to do with the disputed land, purchased by the Labour Government from Fletcher Building in 2020 for $29.9 million. The money to buy the land came from the government's land for housing programme which works with iwi and developers to develop social housing. Te rōpu whakahaere was set up by the Kīngitanga to decide an outcome on the future of the land and come up with a development plan. It has five years to do this. The committee was made up of two Crown representatives, a representative from the Kīngitanga, and three representing ahi kā groups, one each for Te Ahiwaru, Te Kawerau ā Maki and Te Ākitai Waiohua. When asked about what has been discussed so far, a spokesperson said there was "nothing to update" and the preference was not to talk to the media until there was something of "substance" to talk about. A hīkoi for Ihumātao in 2019. While in opposition, Potaka was vocal in his desire to see things move quickly and for there to be more action from the committee in terms of deciding on the land's future. At one point he described the committee and then government as "all hui, no action". This led to a war of words with the then Māori development minister Willie Jackson who attempted to distance the government from the steering committee discussions saying it made its own decisions. "Part of mana motuhake by Māori, for Māori is leaving Māori to work
things out and Tama needs to learn that," Jackson said at the time. The

meeting between Potaka and the committee comes during a year of
significant anniversaries for Ihumātao and the quest by local iwi to save the land from a housing development. 2024 was the tenth anniversary of the land being rezoned as a Special Housing Area in 2014, a move which eventually kicked off years of protest action. It was also the fifth year since significant public protest and occupation took place in 2019. This saw police issue eviction notices to some occupiers, while five people were arrested after some intense standoffs with police. The land at Ihumātao has a troubled history after it was first confiscated by the Crown in 1863 during the invasion of Waikato. The land had been occupied by Waikato-Tainui, Ngāti Whātua and groups connected to Waikato-Tainui, including Ngāti Tamaoho, Te Ahiwaru, Ngāti Tai Tāmaki, Ngāti Te Ata, Te Ākitai Waiohua, and Te Kawerau ā Maki. Police at Ihumātao in 2019. Local iwi were forced off the land and It subsequently went into private ownership for around 150 years before 32 hectares were designated as an SHA by Auckland Council. It was during this time that the land was sold to Fletcher Building, which wanted to build more than 400 houses, despite the land being an archaeological site of historic importance to Māori. This kicked off protest action against the development and eventually the formation of the group, Save Our Unique Landscape, who began occupying the site in 2016. SOUL even appealed to the United Nations in 2017 about the status of the land, with the UN recommending that the designation of Ihumātao as an SHA be reviewed by the Government to "evaluate its conformity with the Treaty of Waitangi". After months of protest and heightened political attention in 2019, both the Labour Government and Kīngitanga intervened and a deal was reached with Fletcher Building to buy back the land with the proposal that some of it be used for housing purposes. The government
has since left it up to the steering committee to decide the land's future.

5.fileDescription: Four years after the Crown purchased the disputed Ihumātao land in south Auckland for $30 million in December 2020, little progress has been made on its future use. The land, which had been occupied by protesters opposing a 480-unit housing development, is now managed by a steering committee (Rōpu Whakahaere) comprising mana whenua representatives and Crown officials. Despite costing $500,000 to date, the committee took 18 months to first meet due to disagreements over representation and differing views among mana whenua groups. Housing Minister Chris Bishop and Māori Development Minister Tama Potaka have expressed frustration with the lack of progress, with Potaka questioning whether the committee is delivering value. However, Labour leaders argue the five-year timeframe for decision-making hasn't expired and the process should be given space to reach a constructive solution.

Housing Minister Chris Bishop and Māori Development Minister Tama Potaka have expressed frustration with the lack of progress, with Potaka questioning whether the committee is delivering value. However, Labour leaders argue the five-year timeframe for decision-making hasn't expired and the process should be given space to reach a constructive solution.

chunkHighlights.text: The government is reviewing the management of the highly-disputed land at Ihumātao almost four years after the Crown purchased it. In December 2020, the then-Labour government announced it had struck a deal with Fletcher Building to buy the land for just shy of $30 million. By that point, those opposed to a 480-odd housing development at the site had been blocking any construction and occupying the area in south Auckland's Māngere for years. Housing Minister Chris Bishop told RNZ on Tuesday coalition parties opposed the deal at the time, and little progress has been made by the committee tasked with deciding how to use the land. "All I'll say is, it obviously is frustrating that you've got land there that could be being used for housing and that's not happening at the moment," he said. "Clearly we've inherited a fudge of a situation ... I don't think anyone was happy with what happened under the previous government and we were critical of it at the time." Ihumātao, pictured in 2019. Bishop said he had not yet met with his associate minister, Tama

Potaka, about the matter and did not want to get too far ahead of any
decision-making. Potaka, who is also Māori Development Minister, said on Tuesday that he was working on finding a constructive and enduring solution and supported the group set-up to manage the land to do that. Those comments contrasted previous remarks where he raised the prospect of dissolving the group if it was not working. "There are different groups involved, and there are different views, and that includes the Kiingitanga," he told reporters on Tuesday. The steering committee - Rōpu Whakahaere - is made-up of three Ahi Kā representatives supported by the Kiingitanga, one Kiingitanga representative, and two Crown representatives. It took 18 months from the Crown purchasing the land before the group first met due to the various mana whenua involved and differing views on who should be represented and trepediation about the process. As it stands, the Ahi Kā representatives are made up of mana whenua from Te Aakitai Waiohaua, Te Kawerau aa Maki and Te Ahiwaru. But Potaka said the lack of consensus amongst those groups was making progress difficult. "We have to be very careful when we throw a korowai of mana whenua over a question without being deliberately clear who we're talking about," he said. "What I'm focused on is ensuring we get a constructive and enduring solution, what we can't do is presume all the mana whenua groups have the same view, we cannot do that." Potaka said there had been a number of discussions over the years about the role of the Rōpu Whakahaere and "whether or not they're doing the job". "Certainly when the land was bought several years ago for $30m by the previous Labour government, we thought it was an outrageous step into a space that was quite challenging." He said nothing of substance happened in the next two years despite it having cost the Crown $500,000 so far. Potaka bristled at a question line on Tuesday morning about how mana whenua responded to the idea of dissolving the Rōpu Whakahaere. "I think it's a pretty rich question when you don't know who you're talking about ... who are you talking about, which mana whenua?" Prime Minister
Christopher Luxon said Cabinet has not had discussions yet about
scrapping the deal that was struck in 2020, which included leaving it to
the steering committee to decide how to use the land. "I think Tama
Potaka's right to ask the question, saying we've spent $500,000, we've
had four years and nothing much has happened, are we getting good
value for money or not?" Labour's Willie Jackson, who was Māori

Development Minister when the steering committee formed, said Potaka's comments about its future were unacceptable. "The reality is they should be given space and time, there's a long history there, and yes it's taking time but we have an agreement and he should just step out." Labour leader Chris Hipkins told RNZ the government had set aside five years for the various representatives to determine how to use the land, "and that five years isn't up". "If that process does reach an agreement and gets something constructive coming out the other side of it then that will be money well spent," he said. "Ultimately that site is sitting there empty at the moment and we do need to figure out what is happening with it." retrieved_chunks.text: Ihumātao In 2016 Ihumātao, originally known as Te Ihu-o-Mataoho, on the Manukau Harbour, which neighbours an ancient archaeological site known as the Ōtuataua Stonefields Historic Reserve, was sold to a developer to become the site of a large housing development. SOUL argued the land should be saved from development and returned to Māori ownership, although some mana whenua wanted the housing development to go ahead. retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] By Jock Phillips Māori views Land was very important to Māori. In Māori tradition, the North Island was Te Ika a Māui, a fish caught by Māui. New Zealand was called Aotearoa the land of the long white cloud. Māori told stories about how the land was shaped, and the places their ancestors had lived. The first Europeans The first Europeans in New Zealand looked at the landscape to see how it could be used. British explorer James Cook and his crew saw good soil for growing plants, rivers for fishing, and trees th at could be cut down for timber. But they thought the mountains of the South Island were ‘nothing but barren rocks’. British settlement In the 19th century, British people were encouraged to move to New Zealand. When they arrived, they wanted to make money from the land by farming, gold mining or timber milling. New Zealand was much wilder and more isolated than the English countryside. Many settlers found it desolate and lonely. They planted English trees to help them feel at home, and cut down native forests to clear land for farming. Missionaries and artists Some missionaries admired New Zealand’s rugged landscapes as the work of God. Artists also valued the land’s beauty, and painted the mountains, lakes and waterfalls. Tourism and scenery From the late 19th century, overseas tourists visited New Zealand to see the geothermal area near Rotorua, the lakes of the South Island, and the Southern Alps. Guidebooks were written, with photos of beautiful scenery. New Zealanders became proud of their scenic landscapes. The Scenery Preservation Act, passed in 1903, protected areas of important natural scenery. Mid 20th century writers and artists From the 1930s, writers and artists worked to make a New Zealand culture that did not borrow from British culture. The country’s wild landscapes helped them define their identity. Saving the bush After the 1960s, more people came to think that the bush was important. There were campaigns to save forests and other…

[Page 9] The importance of land to Māori was summed up in the proverb: ‘Te toto o te tangata he kai. Te oranga o te tangata he whenua .’ (The lifeblood of a person is derived from food; the livelihood of a people depends on land.) The loss of land meant the loss of a key economic resource for Māori. Land purchases were first entered into with the idea that Māori would benefit from Pākehā settling nearby. Māori were eager to have access to markets, and new goods and technologies that Europeans would bring. Much of the success that Māori had in supplying early settlers and the towns they set up was based on Māori control of significant areas of land, which was communally managed to produce food. But land transfer usually gave settlers the best arable lands closest to towns and cities. The 19th century became a period of massive transfer of land from Māori ownership to government and Pākehā ownership. This had a severe impact on Māori tribal structures, and on tribal economies.

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 1] Landscape The Auckland region lies between two coastlines, and beaches are within easy reach. To the west, the Tasman Sea pounds rugged beaches such as Piha. To the east is the Pacific Ocean coastline, with sheltered, sandy bays. Here too is the Hauraki Gulf, dotted with islands including Waiheke and Rangitoto. Auckland city is on a narrow strip between two harbours: the Waitematā and the wide, shallow Manukau. Further north is the Kaipara Harbour, a habitat for wading birds. Volcanic cones mark the skyline, and the Waitākere Ranges rise steeply in the west. The major river is the Waikato in the south. Early history Among the Māori names for the Auckland isthmus Tāmaki makau rau (Tāmaki of a hundred lovers). Ngāti Whātua, Ngāti Pāoa and other tribes settled there, growing kūmara (sweet potatoes) in the fertile soil. European traders and missionaries arrived in the 1820s. In 1840 Lieutenant Governor William Hobson set up the town of Auckland at Tāmaki. It was the country’s capital until 1865. Pākehā hunger for Māori land led to war in the 1860s, and tribal claims for compensation for loss of land continue today. From the 1870s the region began to grow, exporting gold, kauri timber and kauri gum. Rapid growth During the 20th century Auckland city grew faster than other centres, and became New Zealand’s main city. New motorways encouraged urban sprawl and a reliance on private cars. [Page 12] Bejewelled with volcanic monticules and set between two harbours, the site for Auckland has long been admired for its natural beauty. Best remembered of the city’s earliest settlers, Sir John Logan Campbell wrote excitedly that the view from the summit of Mount Hobson (Remuera) surpassed that even from the Acropolis in the ornate Greek city of Corinth. For hundreds of years before Campbell’s time, Maori tribes fought for occupation of the district, rich as it is with fertile volcanic soils for gardening, coastal waters for fishing and hills for pa sites. The city is still known by the Maori name for the isthmus, Tamaki makau rau, “Tamaki of the hundred lovers” a popular place indeed. In Maori mythology, Auckland’s isthmus sustained its volcanic wounds in a battle between the mystical forest dwelling Turehu people of the Waitakere and Hunua Ranges. During the conflict, which came to be known as Pakurangarahihi, a tohunga from the Hunua side caused the sun to rise prematurely, blinding the Waitakere combatants. Many were brutally dispatched in the resulting confusion. When night fell once again, the Hunua warriors pressed on towards the Waitakere Ranges, but didn’t get far. A Waitakere tohunga invoked the volcano deity Mataoho to intervene, and he promptly threw the whole isthmus into convulsions of volcanic activity. The Hunua warriors were quickly put to rout by great explosions, tides of lava and billowing ash. However, fires started by the volcanoes swept towards the forests of the Waitakeres, so a tohunga had to call upon rain to quench them. To this day, Auckland’s swarm of volcanic features, together with high rainfall in the Waitakere Ranges, remind us of these events. Not surprising, then, that the Maori who occupied the land much later were keen to keep Mataoho happy. Offerings to placate him were made in the crater of Mount Eden, which has the shape of an enormous food bowl.

## Ko e Palemia ʻo Nu Sila

ʻOku ʻuhinga ʻa e fehuʻi ko ʻeni ki he Prime Minister ʻo New Zealand. ʻO fakatatau ki he ngaahi polokalama fekumi, ko **Christopher Luxon** ʻa e Prime Minister ʻo New Zealand. 1.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's political leadership from 1856 to 2023. It explains how the prime minister's role evolved from "colonial secretary" to "premier" and finally "prime minister" (formally adopted in 1906). Early leadership was unstable with 24 ministries between 1856-1891, but the Liberal Federation's 1891-1912 tenure marked the rise of organized political parties. The document examines how technological advances—from train travel and aviation to radio (1920s), television (1960), and the internet—reshaped the prime minister's role as government spokesperson. It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

2.text:
[Page 1] Premiers and prime ministers The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government. His or her main responsibilities are: appointing ministers and leading meetings of cabinet acting as the spokesperson for the government, within and outside of Parliament providing advice to the sovereign (the head of state) or the sovereign’s representative in New Zealand (the governor general). Leaders in the 19th century New Zealand was granted internal self government by Britain in 1856. Initially the leader of the country was known as the colonial secretary or premier, but in the early 20th century the term ‘prime minister’ was formally adopted. New Zealand’s leadership changed frequently in the first 40 years of self government. Different leaders each had their own ideas about what were the most important issues for a new nation. Members of Parliament in New Zealand did not belong to political parties at this time. The rise of the party The first political party to govern in New Zealand was the Liberal Federation, which held power from 1891 to 1912. The prime minister became the leader and public face of the governing party, and his public image became increasingly important. Modern leadership Changing technologies in the 20th century also influenced the prime minister’s role as a spokesperson for the government. Radio broadcasting, followed by television and later the internet connected prime ministers to the voting public. They had to become experts at communicating in the media. From 1996 prime ministers usually led coalition or minority governments under the mixed member proportional (MMP) electoral system. This meant prime ministers had to lead governments made up of several political parties with differing values. Lasting legacies? In the early 2000s there were four statues of former premiers and prime ministers in Wellington. Geographical features such as glaciers, mountains and rivers, and small towns, have also been named after leaders. The role of prime minister The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government.
{}

[Page 3] Until 1 January 1951 New Zealand had an upper house, the Legislative Council. Premiers and prime ministers were usually from the House of Representatives (the lower house), but they governed from the council on five occasions: Frederick Whitaker (1863 64 and 1882 83), George Waterhouse (1872 73), Daniel Pollen (1875 76) and Sir Francis Henry Dillon Bell (1925). As legislative councillors were political appointees on life or seven year terms, these were the only unelected politicians to lead the country.

5.text:
[Page 5] From 1840 New Zealand’s governors ruled autocratically (with absolute authority), advised by the Executive Council and Legislative Council and answerable to the authorities in London. In 1854, though the new Parliament was still only there to provide advice to the governor, politicians had already asked for self governance in domestic matters, rather than having to defer to Britain. That year, while awaiting the reply from London, the acting governor, Colonel Robert Wynyard, appointed politician James FitzGerald to his Executive Council. Thomas Forsaith succeeded FitzGerald in the role. However, neither the ‘FitzGerald ministry’ nor the ‘Forsaith ministry’ lasted long. Their leaders were not true premiers. New Zealand’s earliest genuine ministries, formed after Parliament became responsible (fully self governing for most internal policy) in 1856, were short lived. The first premier, Henry Sewell, was sworn in on 18 April 1856, but was gone by 20 May. His successor, William Fox, was replaced by Edward Stafford on 2 June. In all there were 24 ministries between 1856 and 1891. To many it is a blur of beards, names and dates, but power was transferred peacefully each time, showing that the fledgling democracy worked.
{}

[Page 7] The 1890 election introduced government by party for the first time, when new premier John Ballance established the Liberal Federation. Ballance died in 1893 and was succeeded by Richard Seddon (sometimes known as ‘King Dick’), who effortlessly dominated New Zealand politics for the next 13 years. There was little real parliamentary opposition until 1909, when William Massey welded together the Reform Party. Thereafter political power centred on parties and their leaders. Personality became increasingly important for political success. The charismatic Gordon Coates ensured victory for Reform in 1925, and Labour’s Michael Joseph Savage, with his genial, fatherly image, enjoyed mass adulation in the 1930s.

7.document_title: Colonial and Provincial Government in New Zealand: Evolution from 1840 to Modern Regional Administration
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's governmental structure from 1840 through the modern era. It begins with New Zealand's transition from New South Wales to a separate British crown colony in 1840 under appointed governors. The document details the initial provincial divisions and the pivotal 1852 Constitution Act, which established six provinces with elected superintendents and councils exercising significant autonomy over land sales revenue and customs duties. It covers the New Provinces Act 1858, the impact of the Waikato War (1863) on provincial finances, and centralization efforts including the capital relocation to Wellington in 1865. A critical turning point came in 1876 with the abolition of provincial governments, driven by financial pressures and Colonial Treasurer Julius Vogel's national public works program. The provinces were replaced with counties and road boards, marking a shift toward centralized administration. The document concludes by examining the 20th-century evolution from provinces to regions and the significant restructuring of health administration from hospital boards (1935) through area health boards (1983), crown health enterprises (1992), district health boards (2002), and finally to Te Whatu Ora Health New Zealand and Te Aka Whai Ora Māori Health Authority in 2022.

8.text:
[Page 7] Religion was politically divisive in the early 1900s when Sir Joseph Ward (a Catholic) and William Massey (Protestant) led the major parties, Liberal and Reform. Generally, though, it seldom raised political ripples in New Zealand. Because the Anglican Church is not an established (that is, official state) church in New Zealand, Frederick Weld, a Catholic, could become premier in 1864. Julius Vogel, who was Jewish, became premier in 1873. By contrast, in 2017 Britain had still not had a Catholic or Jewish prime minister. Non belief was also not a bar to office in New Zealand; colonial premiers Alfred Domett, Robert Stout and John Ballance were freethinkers.

[Page 8] Greater independence For a while New Zealand’s prime ministers opposed greater independence from Britain. New Zealand and Australia resisted the structural reforms towards independence pushed by other dominions at the 1926 and 1930 imperial conferences. The 1931 Statute of Westminster confirmed that dominions had exclusive power to make their laws. However, New Zealand did not adopt this statute until 1947, and then only as part of a political manoeuvre to make it constitutionally possible to abolish the Legislative Council. Increasingly, however, New Zealand began to act independently in foreign affairs. During the 1940s the prime minister’s profile rose as the country signed a number of international treaties. Prime Minister Peter Fraser established a New Zealand embassy in the United States and played an important role in setting up the United Nations.

21.document_title: David Russell Lange: Life, Political Career, and Leadership as New Zealand Prime Minister
21.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical document traces David Russell Lange's life from his birth in Ōtāhuhu, Auckland in 1942 through his tenure as New Zealand's youngest 20th-century Prime Minister (1984-1989). Born to a medical practitioner father and Methodist mother, Lange studied law at the University of Auckland and practiced as a criminal defence counsel before joining the Labour Party in 1963. He won a by-election in Māngere in 1977 and became Labour leader in 1983. Following Labour's landslide victory in June 1984, he became Prime Minister at age 41. His government implemented radical economic reforms known as "Rogernomics" under Finance Minister Roger Douglas, including currency devaluation, GST introduction, and privatization of state assets. As Foreign Minister and PM, Lange became the public face of New Zealand's nuclear-free policy, controversially refusing USS Buchanan entry in 1985 and navigating the Rainbow Warrior bombing incident with France. His 1987 re-election increased Labour's majority, and he pursued education reforms emphasizing efficiency and equity. However, internal cabinet conflicts with Roger Douglas over economic reforms, particularly the proposed flat tax in 1988, weakened his position. Despite exceptional oratorical skills and inspirational rhetoric, Lange lacked interest in policy detail and struggled to build factional strength within cabinet. He resigned as party leader in August 1989, ceding power to former allies who had become adversaries. He died in 2005 at age 63 from heart failure.

22.document_title: Edward William Stafford: Colonial Premier of New Zealand - Political Career and Legacy
22.document_summary: Edward William Stafford (1819-1901) was a prominent Anglo-Irish politician who served as New Zealand's colonial premier for approximately nine years across two terms (1856-1861 and 1865-1872). Born in Edinburgh, he emigrated to New Zealand in 1843 and became the first superintendent of Nelson in 1853. Stafford championed responsible government, universal suffrage, and progressive policies including free secular education and public works programs. As premier, he navigated complex constitutional issues, provincial rivalries, and Māori affairs with pragmatic effectiveness. He managed expensive Māori wars (1865-1868), including the Pai Mārire uprising and campaigns by Tītokowaru and Te Kooti, while reducing war expenditure from £886,259 to £327,180 and increasing revenue to £1,058,029 through taxation increases. Stafford established four Māori electorates in 1867, advocated for railway construction, and opposed forced land confiscation. His final ministry (1872) was defeated over public works administration and Māori land return policies. Though personally unpopular due to retrenchment policies, he was recognized as an able administrator who strengthened ministerial representation during New Zealand's formative parliamentary era.

23.document_title: Bill Rowling: Life, Political Career, and Prime Ministerial Legacy in New Zealand
23.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical document traces Wallace Edward "Bill" Rowling's life and political career in New Zealand. Born in Motueka, Nelson in 1927, Rowling came from a politically active Labour family and became a teacher with economics degrees from Canterbury University. He entered Parliament in 1962 representing the Buller electorate and served on agricultural committees. As Labour Party president (1970-1972), he modernized the party organization, contributing to Labour's 1972 election victory. Appointed Finance Minister by Norman Kirk in 1972, Rowling advocated for overseas borrowing and economic stimulus during the oil crisis. Following Kirk's death in August 1974, Rowling became Prime Minister at age 46, the youngest since 1887. As PM, he maintained focus on domestic affairs, supported nuclear-free policies, and defended heavy borrowing to protect employment. After his 1975 election loss to Robert Muldoon, Rowling served six years as opposition leader despite defeats in 1978 and 1981 elections, facing leadership challenges from David Lange and Roger Douglas before stepping down in 1983. He later served as ambassador to the United States (1985-1988) during the ANZUS rift and opposed Lange's neo-liberal reforms. His legacy reflects quiet nationalism and commitment to New Zealand independence, culminating in his role developing Te Papa Tongarewa national museum. He received a knighthood in 1983 and died in 1995.

24.document_title: Francis Henry Dillon Bell: New Zealand Statesman and Lawyer
24.document_summary: Francis Henry Dillon Bell (1851-1936) was a prominent New Zealand lawyer, politician, and statesman. Born in Nelson, he was educated in England at Cambridge and called to the English Bar before returning to Wellington in 1875. Bell became a leading advocate in the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal, serving as Crown solicitor and helping establish law reporting in New Zealand. He was elected mayor of Wellington (1891, 1892, 1896) and served in Parliament from 1893-1896. After retiring from politics, he became recognized as leader of the New Zealand Bar and was appointed King's Counsel in 1907. Under Prime Minister William Massey, Bell held multiple ministerial portfolios and briefly served as Prime Minister in 1925, becoming New Zealand's first native-born PM. He was instrumental in drafting wartime legislation, managing Western Samoa's mandate, and reforming New Zealand's conveyancing system. Bell was appointed KCMG (1915), GCMG (1923), and Privy Counsellor (1926). Regarded as an outstanding lawyer and statesman, he exemplified a "tory radical" approach, balancing conservative principles with progressive social policies.

25.document_title: George Robert Laking: New Zealand's Twentieth-Century Public Servant, Diplomat, and Law Reform Pioneer
25.document_summary: George Robert Laking (1912-2008) was a prominent New Zealand public servant and diplomat with a 40+ year career spanning government service, diplomacy, and law reform. Born in Auckland, he joined the Customs Department in 1929 and studied law at Victoria University College. During WWII, he worked in the Prime Minister's Department and was instrumental in establishing the Department of External Affairs. His diplomatic career included postings as counsellor in Washington (1949), deputy high commissioner in London (1958), ambassador to the EEC (1960), and ambassador to Washington (1961-1967). As secretary of Foreign Affairs and head of the Prime Minister's Department (1967-1972), he advised Prime Ministers on Cold War foreign policy, Vietnam withdrawal, and China recognition. After his diplomatic career, Laking established a second influential career in government accountability and law reform. As the first privacy commissioner for the Wanganui Computer Centre (1977-78) and later as chief ombudsman (1977-1984), he championed citizens' rights against state intrusion, particularly regarding police accountability and official information access. He significantly expanded the ombudsman's jurisdiction. Laking contributed substantially to law reform through the Public and Administrative Law Reform Committee (1980-85) and the Legislation Advisory Committee (1986-91), notably chairing a working party that modernized New Zealand's alcohol legislation in 1987. He also led the New Zealand Institute of International Affairs (1979-84) and served on the Human Rights Commission (1978-1984). Described as a courteous yet formidable personality with sardonic humor, Laking exemplified impartial public service, exercising significant behind-the-scenes influence on domestic and international policies. He received honors including appointment as a Companion of the Order of St Michael and St George (1969) and promotion to Knight (1985), passing away in Wellington on January 10, 2008, at age 95.

27.document_title: Sidney George Holland: New Zealand Prime Minister - Life, Leadership, and Political Legacy (1893-1961)
27.document_summary: Sidney George Holland (1893-1961) was a prominent New Zealand politician who served as Prime Minister from 1949 to 1957. Born in Canterbury to English parents, Holland worked in business before entering Parliament in 1935 as MP for Christchurch North. He became leader of the National Party in 1940 and led it to victory in 1949, ending 14 years of Labour rule. As Prime Minister, Holland abolished the Legislative Council and took a hard line against militant unions during the 1951 waterfront dispute. His government deregulated the economy by ending rationing and removing price controls while maintaining full employment and social security. New Zealand signed the ANZUS treaty in 1951 under his leadership. Holland introduced the PAYE taxation system and established the Tourist Hotel Corporation. By 1956, his health deteriorated significantly, and he announced his retirement on August 12, 1957, succeeded by Holyoake on September 20. He was knighted and made a minister without portfolio, retiring from Parliament in November 1957. Holland died in Wellington Hospital on August 5, 1961. His major contribution was establishing the National Party as a dominant force in New Zealand politics throughout the latter twentieth century.

28.document_title: Norman Eric Kirk: New Zealand's Labour Prime Minister - Political Biography and Legacy
28.document_summary: This biographical account traces Norman Eric Kirk's remarkable political journey from his working-class origins to becoming New Zealand's fourth Labour Prime Minister. Born in 1923 in Waimate, South Canterbury, Kirk rose from humble beginnings as a roof painter, railway worker, and boiler engineer to become a transformative political figure. After joining the Labour Party in 1943, he served as mayor of Kaiapoi from 1953, implementing progressive infrastructure reforms. Elected to Parliament in 1957 representing Lyttelton, Kirk distinguished himself as an excellent debater and advocate for constituents and the disadvantaged. He ascended through Labour ranks, becoming party vice president in 1963 and president in 1964, before defeating Arnold Nordmeyer on December 9, 1965, to become leader of the parliamentary Labour Party at age 42. His 1969 campaign slogan "Make things happen" emphasized planned economic development, though he narrowly lost to Keith Holyoake. Labour's 1972 electoral victory brought Kirk to the Prime Minister's office, where his government pursued activist policies including establishing diplomatic relations with China, opposing racial discrimination, and resisting nuclear testing. However, global economic slowdown, oil price increases, and rising inflation undermined his ambitious agenda. Kirk's health deteriorated following a grueling international tour and leg surgery in April 1974. Despite declining health, he continued working through mounting industrial unrest until his death from congestive cardiac failure on August 31, 1974, at age 51. Kirk left a lasting legacy as Labour's last passionate advocate for big government.

29.document_title: Robert Stout: Life, Political Career, Legal Legacy, and Educational Reform in New Zealand (1844-1930)
29.document_summary: Robert Stout (1844-1930) was born in Lerwick, Shetland, Scotland, and emigrated to Otago, New Zealand in 1863, becoming a prominent figure in Dunedin society. He served as attorney general and minister for lands and immigration (1878-1879) under Sir George Grey, championing land reform and state intervention. As premier (1884-1887) in alliance with Julius Vogel, Stout advocated for civil service reform, secondary education, and technical education. His most enduring legacy emerged through his appointment as Chief Justice (1899-1926), where he decided over 1,400 cases with liberal statutory interpretation. Throughout his career, Stout championed women's rights, including the Electoral Bill (1878) and the Married Women's Property Act (1884). He profoundly influenced New Zealand's university system, founding Victoria College and serving as Chancellor of the University of New Zealand (1903-1923). Appointed KCMG in 1886 and privy counsellor in 1921, Stout exemplified the rare intellectual politician who emphasized educating public opinion and moral development, making him a key architect of democratic New Zealand.

30.document_title: John Ross Marshall: New Zealand Politician, Legal Professional, and Prime Minister
30.document_summary: This biographical account chronicles the life and political career of John Ross Marshall (1912-1988), a prominent New Zealand politician and legal professional. Born in Wellington to Scottish parents, Marshall studied law at Victoria University College, earning his LLB in 1934 and LLM in 1935. He served in World War II as a major in the New Zealand Division, participating in campaigns across Fiji, Norfolk Island, New Caledonia, and Italy. Marshall entered Parliament in 1946, representing Mount Victoria (later Karori) for the National Party, serving until 1975. He held ministerial positions for 20 years, including 12 years as Deputy Prime Minister and nearly one year as Prime Minister (February 1972-December 1972). As Minister of Labour from 1968, Marshall navigated complex industrial disputes, deregistered the Seamen's Union during a 1971 strike, and introduced the Stabilisation of Remuneration Bill. His most significant achievement was establishing the Accident Compensation scheme, providing income-related compensation to injured workers regardless of fault. Marshall's key contributions included housing policy expansion, health and justice reforms, and the New Zealand-Australia Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). He was instrumental in negotiating favorable transition arrangements for New Zealand's butter, cheese, and lamb exports during Britain's applications to join the EEC. Known as 'Gentleman Jack' for his courteous demeanor and Christian principles, Marshall was knighted in 1974 and retired from Parliament in 1975, becoming a consultant, university fellow, and patron of charitable organizations.

36.document_summary: Former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern's upcoming memoir "A Different Kind of Power" will be published in early June 2025 by Penguin Random House New Zealand. The deeply personal memoir will explore Ardern's leadership style and her philosophy on kindness as a powerful force in politics. Ardern, who became the world's youngest female head of government at 37 in October 2017, will share insights into pivotal moments from her tenure, including the Christchurch mosque terror attacks (2019), the Whakaari White Island eruption (2019), and the Covid-19 pandemic (2020). She will also detail her decision to step down as Prime Minister. The memoir emphasizes Ardern's belief that kindness possesses strength and power, capable of giving people hope, changing minds, and transforming lives—challenging perceptions that kindness is merely sentimental or naive.

38.document_title: How the Sound and Voices of Politics Have Changed from 1912 to 1990
38.document_summary: This article explores the evolution of political communication in New Zealand through audio recordings of fourteen Prime Ministers and a Speaker spanning from 1912 to 1990. The piece highlights how political speech, accents, tones, and presentation styles have transformed over nearly eight decades. Early leaders like William Massey and George Forbes employed formal, gentler speech patterns, while later politicians such as Rob Muldoon and David Lange adopted more modern, recognizably "Kiwi" accents and contemporary communication styles. The article notes that many early politicians were immigrants with strong accents, and that political communication has shifted from formal Empire-praising rhetoric to more direct, populist approaches. The audio compilation, curated with assistance from RNZ's audio historians, provides comparative insights into how New Zealand's political voices have evolved, reflecting broader changes in political culture and public communication.

39.document_title: 'The prime minister is dying': 50 years since Norman Kirk's last public appearance
39.document_summary: This article commemorates the 50th anniversary of Norman Kirk's final public appearance on August 18, 1974, at St Peter's College in Palmerston North, New Zealand. Despite severe illness—including an enlarged heart, blood clot in his lungs, and liver problems—Kirk insisted on attending the school opening ceremony for his friend Joe Walding. His wife Ruth confided to the school's board chair that "the prime minister is dying." Kirk died 13 days later on August 31, 1974, aged 51, making him the first New Zealand prime minister to die in office since 1940. During his two-year tenure, Kirk's government recognized China, protested French nuclear testing, refused entry to a racially selected Springbok rugby team, and introduced a retirement savings scheme. The article features insights from his private secretary Margaret Hayward and reflects on how Kirk's death prompted massive public grief followed by rapid public amnesia as successor Bill Rowling took office.

fileAuthor: Gavin McLean, Manatū Taonga (Ministry for Culture and Heritage)
4.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's political leadership from 1856 to 2023. It explains how the prime minister's role evolved from "colonial secretary" to "premier" and finally "prime minister" (formally adopted in 1906). Early leadership was unstable with 24 ministries between 1856-1891, but the Liberal Federation's 1891-1912 tenure marked the rise of organized political parties. The document examines how technological advances—from train travel and aviation to radio (1920s), television (1960), and the internet—reshaped the prime minister's role as government spokesperson. It covers the shift from personality-driven, policy-focused governments to party-based systems, the abolition of provincial governments in 1876, and the introduction of the MMP electoral system in 1996 requiring coalition management. Key figures include Richard Seddon, Norman Kirk, Jacinda Ardern, and Chris Hipkins. By 2023, 41 prime ministers had served, with only 3 women. The document also documents institutional developments including the establishment of the Prime Minister's Department in 1926 and Premier House as an official residence, along with information about prime ministerial memoirs, rankings, and memorials.

chunkHighlights.text: Premiers and prime ministers

The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among
those forming the government. His or her main responsibilities are: appointing ministers and leading meetings of cabinet acting as the spokesperson for the government, within and outside of Parliament providing advice to the sovereign (the head of state) or the sovereign’s representative in New Zealand (the governor-general). Leaders in the 19th century New Zealand was granted internal self-government by Britain in 1856. Initially the leader of the country was known as the colonial secretary or premier, but in the early 20th century the term ‘prime minister’ was formally adopted. New Zealand’s leadership changed frequently in the first 40 years of self-government. Different leaders each had their own ideas about what were the most important issues for a new nation. Members of Parliament in New Zealand did not belong to political parties at this time. The rise of the party The first political party to govern in New Zealand was the Liberal Federation, which held power from 1891 to 1912. The prime minister became the leader and public face of the governing party, and his public image became increasingly important. Modern leadership Changing technologies in the 20th century also influenced the prime minister’s role as a spokesperson for the government. Radio broadcasting, followed by television and later the internet connected prime ministers to the voting public. They had to become experts at communicating in the media. From 1996 prime ministers usually led coalition or minority governments under the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system. This meant prime ministers had to lead governments made up of several political parties with differing values. Lasting legacies? In the early 2000s there were four statues of former premiers and prime ministers in Wellington. Geographical features such as glaciers,
mountains and rivers, and small towns, have also been named after
leaders.
The role of prime minister
The prime minister is the leader of the largest political party among those forming the government.

response.response_text:
What a special experience awaits you — a pōwhiri is a profound and meaningful welcome ceremony with roots going back hundreds of years. Here's what you should know as a first-time visitor (manuhiri).

## Understanding the pōwhiri

The pōwhiri developed historically as a way of establishing whether visitors were friends or enemies, and its rituals remain much the same as they have been for centuries [[1]](cite://1/1). As a manuhiri, you are considered *waewae tapu* (sacred feet) if you've never visited that particular marae before [[2]](cite://2/1).

The ceremony may include a *karanga* (call), a *wero* (ritual challenge), *whaikōrero* (speeches), *waiata* (songs), and the hongi — and can range from quite formal and dramatic to low-key and informal, depending on the occasion [[3]](cite://3/1)[[4]](cite://4/1). Don't be alarmed if it feels confrontational at first — that's part of the tradition [[3]](cite://3/2).

## During the welcome

- Do not eat or drink during the welcome [[5]](cite://5/1)
- Do not walk in front of a speaker on the *marae ātea* (the courtyard) [[5]](cite://5/2)
- Males typically sit at the front on most marae, though this varies — some marae allow both women and men to sit on the front seat [[5]](cite://5/3)
- If a *haka pōwhiri* (ritual action chant) is performed as you're welcomed on, receive it respectfully [[6]](cite://6/1)
- At the conclusion of the welcome, you'll be invited to *harirū* (shake hands) and *hongi* (press noses) with your hosts [[5]](cite://5/4). On some marae a cheek kiss is also considered appropriate; on others, a hongi and harirū are preferred [[5]](cite://5/5)
- Bring a *koha* — a donation, usually money in an envelope — to give to the hosts [[1]](cite://1/2)[[4]](cite://4/2)

## After the pōwhiri

- Wash your hands — water will be provided [[5]](cite://5/6)
- In the *wharekai* (dining room), wait to be called in and let *kaumātua* (elders) go first [[5]](cite://5/7)
- Wait until a *karakia* (grace) has been said before eating [[5]](cite://5/8)
- Do not pass food over a person's head, and don't sit on tables [[5]](cite://5/9)

## In the wharenui (meeting house)

- Remove your shoes before entering [[5]](cite://5/10)[[7]](cite://7/1)
- Do not eat or drink inside the wharenui [[5]](cite://5/11)
- Do not step over people, and do not sit on pillows [[5]](cite://5/12)
- Be aware that certain areas may be reserved for particular guests or tangata whenua (hosts) — check before sitting or putting anything down [[5]](cite://5/13)

## A word on variation

It's important to know that every marae has its own *kawa* (protocols) and *tikanga* (rules), and these can differ significantly between iwi and regions [[8]](cite://8/1)[[9]](cite://9/1)[[10]](cite://10/1). For example, some marae have all tangata whenua speakers go first, while others alternate between hosts and guests [[1]](cite://1/3). The single best piece of advice is to ask the local people what their expectations are before you arrive [[10]](cite://10/2).

The pōwhiri ends with an invitation to mingle, eat and drink together — you'll move from being a stranger to a welcomed guest [[3]](cite://3/3). Enjoy it; it's a genuinely moving experience.

Would you like to know more about the hongi specifically, or what to expect during the mihimihi (introductions) inside the wharenui?

2.text:
[Page 3] Large and important welcomes (known as pōwhiri ) may include extra elements such as laments to the dead, traditional songs and chants, and wero ceremonies that are deliberately confrontational and even alarming to outsiders. However, not all such ceremonies are so dramatic. Many are low key and informal. Whether large or small, the pōwhiri ends with an invitation to the manuhiri (visitors) to mingle with their hosts, the tangata whenua , and to eat and drink with them. They are no longer potentially threatening strangers, but guests to be cared for as long as they remain in the hosts’ territory. Providing plentiful food to guests is central to Māori custom.

2.document_title: Māori Manners, Social Behaviour, and Cultural Customs: From Traditional Practices to Modern Adaptation
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Māori social customs and cultural practices that have endured through centuries of change. It covers welcome rituals including karanga (call), wero (challenge), whaikōrero (speeches), and hongi (nose pressing), which served practical peacekeeping functions. The text explains kinship, whakapapa (genealogy), and the marae as cultural centers. It details customs surrounding death through tangi (funeral ceremonies) where whānau gather to support the wairua (spirit), as well as birth traditions like placenta burial. The document emphasizes marae-based practices, cemetery customs, and the honored status of elders. It demonstrates how traditional customs have adapted to modern urban settings and are increasingly adopted by non-Māori New Zealanders, reflecting a thriving national culture.

3.text:
[Page 1] Kawa of the marae The kawa of the marae is the protocols or rules that operate on the marae . Different marae have different ways of doing things, but there some things are common to all. It is an honour to have an official role during the pōwhiri (welcome onto the marae ). Kaikaranga (women who call at the beginning of the welcome) and kaikōrero (the people who make speeches, usually men) are usually the eldest and most respected in their families. On some marae all the speakers from the tangata whenua (hosts) speak first, followed by the manuhiri (guests). At other marae the speeches alternate, with each speaker from the hosts followed by one from the guests. Pōwhiri process When the manuhiri have gathered outside the marae , the tangata whenua begin to call them onto the marae . If an especially important person is visiting, there will be a ritual challenge first, where warriors lay down batons and the guest picks them up. When the guests are on the marae , usually on the courtyard in front of the wharenui (meeting house), whaikōrero (speeches) are given, followed by waiata (songs). A koha of money (usually in an envelope) is given to the hosts, and then the guests and hosts hongi (press noses) and harirū (shake hands) in greeting. The next stage of the welcome is a hākari (feast). In the evening, inside the meeting house, there is a mihimihi, where people introduce themselves by sharing their ancestral ties. When the visitors are ready to leave, they begin the poroporoaki (formal farewells). Mythology and pōwhiri Important gods are symbolised by parts of the marae . The courtyard outside the meeting house is the domain of Tūmatauenga (or Tū), the god of war, and speeches in that area are allowed to be forceful. The meeting house is the domain of Rongo, the god of peace, and speeches inside are expected to be peaceful. History of pōwhiri The pōwhiri process developed as a way of checking whether people were friends or enemies. In the past members of one tribe might use a meeting to attack another tribe. Historical accounts of pōwhiri suggest that the process has remained much the same for hundreds of years.
{}

4.text:
[Page 1] Welcome and hospitality Māori rituals for greeting visitors date from before Europeans arrived in New Zealand, and had a practical function. The women of a settlement would call out to approaching strangers, asking them to identify themselves and their intentions. Warriors would then challenge them in the wero ceremony. After this, once it was known that the visitors came in peace, they could enter and were welcomed and fed. Today the rituals include the karanga (call), wero , whaikōrero (speeches) and hongi (pressing of noses). The manuhiri (visitors) are then invited to eat and drink with their hosts. They can respond by giving a koha in the past, a gift of food or precious objects, but today usually money. Kinship, families and marae Kin relationships are very important and underpin many customs. Speeches often begin with the speaker’s whakapapa (genealogy), which may relate to the group addressed or the issue discussed. Most Māori, even if they live in the city, retain links with their tribal area and return there for events. Hapū (sub tribes) have rights over particular marae , and are known as tangata whenua (people of the land) of those marae . They can host gatherings, weddings and funerals, and must maintain the marae and its reputation. Kaumātua and kuia (male and female elders) have an honoured place in Māori communities. Tangi and birth In Māori tradition, when someone dies, their spirit leaves their body and travels to a sacred place at the northern tip of New Zealand. Their whānau (family) gathers at a tangihanga to be supported by the wider whānau and community. Tangi are usually held on the marae most closely associated with the deceased. Mourners stay with the family and the tūpāpaku (corpse) for several days. Urupā (cemeteries) are extremely tapu (sacred). When a baby is born, Māori traditionally bury the whenua (placenta) on land associated with one or both of the parents. Some Pākehā also now follow this custom. Māori social customs today Some customs have been adapted to non traditional situations. For instance, many marae in cities or outside New Zealand are multi tribal, so tribal traditions have to be adapted. Māori ceremonies are also used in non Māori settings, such as the opening of the Te Māori exhibition in New York in 1984. Welcome and hospitality Greeting visitors

[Page 9] Kārangaranga putiputi (flower ceremony) In Northland, a tradition has developed which acknowledges the attendance of different iwi and hapū at a marriage. At the cutting of the wedding cake the master of ceremonies calls out the name of a hapū , or sometimes an iwi , if visitors are attending from a distance. ‘E karanga ana kia Ngāti ____, kia haere mai, ki tā koutou putiputi.’ (I call on Ngāti ____ to come and collect your flower). A representative will come forward to take the cake and is then expected to perform a haka or waiata . Marae dining halls A late 20th century description of a hākari at a marae reflects a common pattern for hākari inside the wharenui or dining hall. When the dining hall is prepared for a feast, it is a tremendous sight. Streamers hang from the roof, the tables are laden with trifles, sweets and jellies; mounds of apples and oranges stand between plates of seafood and great round home baked loaves; and by each setting stands a bright coloured bottle of ‘fizz’. The local ladies put great effort into arranging the tables so that they look hospitable and plentiful. All sorts of rare delicacies are collected, and there are special signs of thought, like apples bristling with cigarettes on toothpicks, or piles of toffees for the children. Waitresses walk to and fro from the serveries with steaming plates of vegetables and meat, and schoolchildren serve cups of tea from large enamel teapots. 1

11.document_title: New Zealand Manners and Social Etiquette: Historical Evolution and Modern Practice
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of manners and social etiquette in New Zealand from the 1800s through the 2000s. It examines how settlers brought formal English manners tied to class systems, which gradually transformed into New Zealand's distinctive informal, egalitarian approach to social behavior. Key historical developments include the relaxation of Victorian formality in the colonial context, the rise of working-class respect and equality, and the shift in the meaning of "gentleman" from wealth and status to courtesy regardless of class. The document addresses cross-cultural awareness, particularly regarding Māori protocols and the Māori renaissance from the 1970s onward, which increased understanding of marae etiquette among Pākehā New Zealanders. It discusses cultural misunderstandings in communication, such as eye contact differences between Pākehā and Māori/Samoan cultures. The text examines how manners changed from the 1970s onward, influenced by youth activism, feminism, and international exposure, leading to more casual dress codes. Rather than declining, manners have evolved to address modern contexts, including new etiquette for digital communication, social media, and cell phone use. The document concludes with practical guidance on contemporary New Zealand social conduct, including face-to-face interactions, public behavior, dining customs, greetings (including the hongi in formal Māori situations), and courteous conduct in various social and professional settings.

It covers welcome rituals including karanga (call), wero (challenge), whaikōrero (speeches), and hongi (nose pressing), which served practical peacekeeping functions. 15.text:
[Page 1] The marae The marae is where a community bound by ancestral ties comes together to celebrate, grieve and discuss issues no matter how far away from each other they normally live. Each marae is on communally held land. It generally has a wharenui (meeting house), a wharekai (dining room with attached kitchen) and an ablution block. It may have a constitution or charter containing details of its management and running. The marae trustees Every marae has trustees, elected by the people who belong to that marae . The trustees must be formally approved by the Māori Land Court, and their roles are governed by regulations. The trustees have the ultimate responsibility for all marae matters. However, the wider community keeps the marae going, and there may be a separate marae committee responsible for its everyday running. Preparing for tangihanga and other events A person who dies is brought back to their ancestral marae . At what may be very short notice the hau kāinga (the people who live nearby and keep the marae going) must prepare for the arrival of the whānau pani (the bereaved). Their tasks include cleaning, organising bed linen and buying groceries. The kitchen team prepares food for the whānau pani for the duration of the tangihanga . The marae community Marae upkeep is expensive. There are bills for insurance, electricity, phone, maintenance and repairs, as well as accountancy fees, catering expenses and more. The trustees occasionally call for working bees to get through essential maintenance tasks. To help meet expenses, a marae generally charges a per day fee for hui and meetings. Most marae do not charge for tangihanga , but the whānau gives a koha (donation). Nonetheless, there is often still a shortfall. Extra fundraising activities may include raffles, galas, dinners and classes. Because of the costs involved some marae have fallen into disrepair. However, many thrive thanks to the hard work of community volunteers.

17.document_title: River Language
17.document_summary: This essay explores the philosophical and legal recognition of rivers as living entities with personhood. It examines the 2014 Whanganui River settlement in New Zealand, which declares the ancestral river a "legal person" with rights and duties. The author contrasts this with Western thinking that separates humans from nature, arguing for an ethics of respect and reciprocity. Drawing parallels with Aboriginal Australian practices of constant conversation with the land, the essay advocates for recognizing human-nature interdependence. Through personal reflection on the Waitaha River, the author demonstrates how acknowledging rivers as sacred beings challenges human exceptionalism and offers a new way of dwelling in the world.

18.text:
[Page 2] The 47 year old, whom I last saw shelling oysters, is wearing a neatly ironed shirt with koru symbols over his corpulent puku and waiting for us by the wharenui, or meeting house. The students stand quietly by the gate onto the marae. All the young women are wearing long black skirts. A few locals are standing in the door of the wharenui. They start the powhiri, the formal welcome. Nichola leads the mihi, or greeting, with another student. She seems very nervous, almost scared. It is a powerful ritual with an ancient tradition. A muscular man in a flax skirt and brandishing a taiaha (spear) performs the wero (challenge). André, the only male Maori student in the class, picks up the piece of greenery he offers and looks into the warrior’s eyes. Nichola answers the call of the women at the door with words that her grandmother has taught her. Her ringing karanga acknowledges the dead, the living and the business of the day. Her hands are trembling—not from fear now but in the movement typical of women when they karanga. Her words are clear and strong in the autumn air. The Auckland girl who loves netball hardly speaks any te reo. It’s years since she was on a marae. The visitors remove their shoes. One by one we enter the wharenui in our socks and walk to the far end of the big room. I look at the many portraits on the walls. Old men, children, young mothers—all passed on. Every framed picture shows not only a face but a life. I have never seen such a gallery of ancestors before. It’s eerie and comforting at the same time—as if some of those lives hang around us in this quiet, spacious room with its new carpeting. Each of us is greeted with a hongi. I find it a sincere and friendly gesture, spiritual and intimate at the same time. The brown faces right in front of me are no longer those of strangers. A bond has been formed by this “breath of life”. The speeches that follow—in Maori—are another thing I am not accustomed to. The students sit on the floor and listen to words few of them understand. “Trees have a korero,” says Howard Reti as he leads the blindfolded Tutavake Petero to greet a tree. After returning to the group, the blindfold is removed and Tutavake must find his tree among the maze of similar pines.

18.document_title: Maori Cultural Exchange and Education: Cross-Cultural Learning in New Zealand
18.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection documents transformative cross-cultural educational experiences in New Zealand, focusing on Maori-Pakeha cultural exchange and immersion. The primary narrative follows 29 physical education students from Auckland College of Education, led by instructor Maureen Legge and facilitated by Howard Reti, a Maori educator, as they travel to Northland for intensive cultural learning at a marae. Students participate in traditional Maori rituals including the powhiri, hongi, karanga, and haka, while learning about core cultural concepts such as wairua (spirit), tinana (body), and hine-ngaro (mind). The program encompasses guided forest experiences, flax weaving, stick-fighting instruction, and reflective discussions about cultural identity and historical injustices. A pivotal breakthrough occurs when Nichola, a half-Pakeha woman, performs the traditional karanga role—an unprecedented event. Throughout the experience, students engage in frank discussions about racism, stereotypes, colonialism, and the Treaty of Waitangi, gradually moving from defensive positions to genuine cultural understanding. The course emphasizes oral tradition, sensory connection to nature, understanding Maori genealogy and protocols, and cultural preservation. The experience culminates in students hosting village elders, preparing feasts, performing waiata, and exchanging handmade gifts, demonstrating how immersion in cultural practices and honest dialogue can foster bicultural unity.

19.text:
[Page 10] It isn’t just the oral stories, but other aspects of Maori culture, too, that have an impact on visitors. Napier says people view the whare runanga (meeting house) in the Waitangi Treaty Grounds, with its tukutuku (decorative panels) and carved poupou (pillars representing human ancestors), as a kind of temple. New Zealanders, observes Napier, usually stand with their heads bowed. “Culturally, that’s very significant to me. They feel the ambience of spirituality in this building and they humble themselves.” Most international visitors “are in awe. They can’t believe it.” Maori stories connect. They’re passed down from generation to gen eration, just as they’re told to visitors staying with tangata whenua on marae, in wharenui, in the mountains, in the bush, on the rivers and on the sea. No one can tell these stories like tangata whenua, for only tangata whenua have a direct link with the land. The closest visitors can get to the land is to hear stories from someone like Mihaka, who “talks like a proud Maori because I am one” [Chapter Break]

20.document_title: Honouring the gift of Puhiwai Rangi
20.document_summary: This article documents the traditional Māori harvest of a 55-tonne sperm whale named Puhiwai Rangi, which stranded in the Coromandel and was towed to Wharekaho in October. Led by 25-year-old Te Kaurinui Parata, a team of over 40 cutters, medics, and support crew from multiple iwi conducted a three-day hauhake (harvest) guided by mātauranga Māori and local tikanga. The process involved careful deconstruction of the whale, with spiritual and practical significance: the eye was returned to Tangaroa, the jaw was removed intact for its prized teeth, and hundreds of litres of spermaceti were collected for medicinal and protective purposes. The bones and teeth were buried to decompose naturally, while excess flesh was placed to sustain the food chain. The harvest exemplified Māori mana motuhake and tino rangatiratanga, connecting whales as descendants of Tāne-mahuta and demonstrating the integration of traditional knowledge with modern methods.

[Page 14] It is of little surprise, therefore, that a recommendation, in 2001, by the Maori Tourism Advisory Group (MTAG, a party to the government’s 2010 strategic plan for tourism) that a quality system be established imme diately to determine whether Maori tourism businesses are culturally ko sher has still to be acted on. Ask industry people how to protect Maori culture in tourism and they talk about honesty, authenticity, integrity and tikanga, but in the end Damien O’Connor, minister of tourism, is probably right when he says: “The genuineness of the people and the authenticity of the product will ultimately determine its ongoing success. If you start to water it down with highly commercial objectives, you run the risk of destroying it over time.” There are less tangible cultural concerns, too: Maori request people not to stand on mountain summits, as it shows disregard for their tupuna; some non Maori operators take visitors to tapu sites or share iwi stories without permission to do so, something Maori themselves must acquire. Hickton suggests cultural protection is best achieved by understanding the culture, for understanding leads to respect. Most would agree, but the question still remains: how is understanding to be encouraged?

[Page 18] Hickton agrees. “Much of [it] is the result of what’s been on offer in the past, the concert/hangi thing, and a lot of people will probably say, ‘I’ve seen one of those, I don’t need to do it again.’”Te Puia CEO Andrew Te Whaiti says Maori need to fit their tourism businesses with what New Zealanders want. Most New Zealanders loathe being thought of as tourists in their own country (or in any country), yet whenever someone leaves their usual residential area, for a day trip or overnight, they become a tourist. What is more, they frequently experience Maori tourism without realising it, often without paying a cent. When they visit the Maori section in a museum, or a Maori historical site; when they go to a Maori sports fixture, look at Maori public art or visit a Maori art gallery; even when they visit Auckland’s Otara market in all such instances they experience Maori tourism. Then there are the increasingly high profile Matariki (Maori New Year) celebrations. Tak itimu has taken the lead in celebrating the Maori New Year planting season, attracting thousands from throughout its rohe in Hawke’s Bay/Wairarapa, but an increasing number of events are being held all over the country.Perhaps we need to redefine Maori tourism before we can say how many Kiwis really participate in it.

[Page 12] Tūhoe want manuhiri, the lake’s visitors, to be part of that relationship. It starts when they come to what they think is the visitor centre—an impressive new Tūhoe tribal building near the lakeshore at Aniwaniwa—but find instead they are in a whare wānanga, a place to meet and talk to the tangata whenua, to orient themselves to Te Urewera, the living person, and to Papatūānuku, the mother of all. This can cause some awkwardness and uncertainty, says Tina Wagner, team leader at the centre. “People say, ‘This isn’t like a DOC visitor centre,’ and of course they’re right!” Having to take their shoes off at the door is a good indication of that. So, too, is a log burner, comfortable couches and long tables with board games walkers can play while waiting for their shuttle or water taxi. Wagner is often the person walkers speak to about their plans for either the Great Walk around the lake or the many shorter walks on offer. She doesn’t worry if visitors feel awkward at the start. “Awkwardness can be good if it helps to reset your thinking,” she says.

25.document_title: Deep History: Lake Waikaremōana's Geological, Cultural, and Ecological Legacy
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores Lake Waikaremōana in Te Urewera, New Zealand, through interconnected geological, cultural, and ecological narratives. Geologically, the lake formed 2,200 years ago when massive landslides blocked the Waikaretaheke River, creating the North Island's deepest lake at 256 metres, with ancient trees preserved underwater. Culturally, Ngāi Tūhoe, Ngāti Ruapani, and Ngāti Kahungunu peoples tell of the lake's origin through the taniwha legend of Haumapuhia. The document details colonial dispossession: despite a 1918 Native Land Court ruling recognizing Māori ownership of the lake bed, the government refused to acknowledge this for 52 years while operating tourism and hydroelectric schemes that lowered the lake by five metres (1929-1948). Ecologically, the sunken forest provides crucial habitat for fish, crayfish, and encrusting organisms, while facing biosecurity challenges from invasive species like lagarosiphon and hornwort. The 2014 Te Urewera Act recognized Te Urewera as a legal person with its own mana and mauri, restoring indigenous stewardship. The lake's name, Waikaremōana whanaunga kore (beholden to no one), reflects its personhood and autonomy, with the visitor centre at Aniwaniwa functioning as a whare wānanga.

26.text:
[Page 7] A Maori working in the tourism in dustry, therefore, doesn’t necessarily offer Maori tourism. That, says Edmonds, is the province of people such as Mihaka and Teki. Or, to be precise, the one offers Nga Puhi tourism, the other Ngati Pamoana tourism. “That is, they share aspects of themselves, their culture, their tupuna [ancestors]. They share personally. They don’t talk third person.” George Hickton, CEO of Tourism New Zealand (TNZ)—the organisation, with an annual government provided budget of $55 million, responsible for marketing New Zealand internationally—says: “Historically, people have pigeon holed Maori tourism as a kapa haka group behind the swimming pool at the Sheraton kind of thing. I think we’ve made the break from the historical performance, almost like a culture that’s captured in time, to one far more contemporary.” He encourages all tourism operators, not just Maori, to incorporate some Maori culture in what they do; for instance, greeting visitors with “Kia ora”. “Why is it that people are only in Hawaii for five minutes and they’re ‘Aloha this’ and ‘Aloha that’ but they won’t say ‘Kia ora’ here? This is our own unique greeting that says something about our country, and every tourism operator should use it. It’s a simple thing.”

27.text: Axes, hacksaws, and boning knives are used to butcher meat for the traditional boil-up—a soup featuring meat bones, pūhā, and potatoes, which is a staple of marae meals. Many urban returnees find a comfortable role working in the back of the marae, while their cousins with a better grasp of language and protocol take a more visible stance at the front.
